en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Vinayapiṭaka*: An Exposition of the Offenses Entailing Confession and the Rest.
Having briefly explained the Greatly Compassionate Lord,
we shall now provide the analysis of the meaning for the commentary on the *pācittiya* offenses and the rest.
5. The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa) 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning False Speech (Musāvādasikkhāpada):
"Of the minor ones" (khuddakānaṃ) means of those that are small because they reveal slight offenses, or of those that are many because of their great number.
The connection is with the words “of whose training rules. The word “yesaṃ” (of whom) takes the genitive case in the sense of identity with the word “saṅgaho” (the compendium).

It is that which is compiled (*saṅgahīyate*) that is the “compendium” (*saṅgaho*). The phrase “by nine sections” (*navahi vaggehi*) functions as the instrumental case in relation to the two words “saṅgaho” and “suppaṭṭhito” (well-established).
The particle “dāni” is an indeclinable expressing time ending in the locative; it is a synonym for “idāni” (now), meaning “in this time.”

"Tesam" means "of those minor [offenses]"; this is the connection for the commentary. Regarding the word "bhavati" (it occurs), here the particle *ti* expresses certainty (*ekaṃsa-atthe*) and refers to the future tense, as in such passages as "Surely I shall go to hell; of this there is no doubt for me.
For although the word *nūna* exists here as an expression of certainty, it is not so in the word "bhavati"; rather, it is so by way of its meaning (*atthato*).

However, the meaning should be understood as: "surely this commentary will come to be. Alternatively, it expresses a future time in the sense of something that is certain to happen, as in such phrases as "we shall certainly become Buddhas.
Granted, although there is the word *dhuvam* here which denotes a sense of certainty, the word *bhavati* does not; yet, in terms of its meaning, it implies: "surely this commentary will come to be."
The meaning should be understood as follows:
"Therein" (*tattha*) is a collective term of specification for the phrase "of the Chapter on False Speech" (*musāvādavaggassa*); the meaning is "among those nine chapters.
Alternatively, it means "the first training rule" (*paṭhamasikkhāpada*), that is, "among those minor training rules" (*khuddakesu sikkhāpadesu*). "Son of the Sakyans" (*Sakyānaṃ putto*).
They are called *Sakyas* because they were able to maintain the boundaries of the world by living together with their sisters, or because they protected [their lineage] from the confusion of birth.
Alternatively, they are called *Sakyas* because they built a city in the Sakya grove; these were former kings.

Because they arose in their lineage, even the kings of the present day are called *Sakyas*. The meaning is: "the son of them. The word "at the time of the Buddha" (*buddhakāle*) [is connected] with "they went forth" (*pabbajiṃsu*).
The word *pade* means "support. The connection is with the phrase "having gone forth from the Sakyan clan.
By the words "cast by debate" (*vādakkhitto*), etc., it shows the meaning as "cast by debate" or "in debate. The phrase "wherever" (*yatra yatra*) is connected with "in whichever view he proceeds.
"Having despised" (*avajānitvā*) means having effected a separation through a denial; for the prefix *ava-* expresses the sense of separation. It is also [read] as "having rejected" (*apajānitvā*).
"Reading" (*pāṭha*) means having removed what was admitted (*paṭiññātaṃ*). "Faults" (*dosa*) refers to the fault of illogicality; it is to be construed with the phrase "being observant.
In the expression "while speaking, while speaking" (*kathento kathento*), the word *anta* functions like the word *māna*. For the meaning is "while being spoken, while being spoken.
"Having acknowledged" (*paṭijānitvā*) means having made it an admission (*paṭiññātaṃ*). "Advantage" (*ānisaṃsa*) refers to a faultless quality (*guṇa*). The root *car-* preceded by *pati-*...
“‘For the purpose of concealment’ means he said: ‘He wanders about; he conceals. When asked, ‘But is form permanent or impermanent?
he says, ‘It is impermanent. When asked, ‘Why? he says, ‘Because it is to be known.
If that is so, then even Nibbāna would be called impermanent because it is to be known. Having thus spoken, and seeing the flaw in his own reason, he says: ‘Because it is to be known...’”
“I do not state a cause; rather, I say ‘because it is subject to birth. But you, because of having heard [it] wrongly, speak thus,” having said this, he evades the point with something else.
The word “in the Kurundi” is the locus for the word “stated. “Of this” refers to the statement:
“Form is impermanent because it must be known as such. “Therein” means in the Kurundi. “Of that” refers to the act of acknowledging and then denying.

The word “for the purpose of concealing” (*paṭicchādanatthaṃ*) is the recipient (*sampadāna*) for the word “speaks” (*bhāsati*). The word “in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā” (*mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ*) is the locus (*ādhāra*) for the word “is said” (*vuttaṃ*).

The word “in daytime dwellings and so forth” (*divāṭṭhānādīsu*) is to be supplied. This [phrase] is a collective expression of specification (*niddhāraṇasamudāya*) for the phrase “in such-and-such a place” (*asukasmiṃ nāmapadese*).
3. It is called *saṃvādana* because one speaks correctly by means of it; it is a mind of an upright nature. *Visaṃvādana* is not speaking correctly;
showing that it is a mind proceeding with the intention to deceive, he says "the mind of deception" (*visaṃvādanacitta*).
By the words "speech" (*vācā*) and so forth, he shows the meaning as "that by which one speaks is speech. The particle *hi* indicates emphasis; thus, by this [mind], it is truth.
The meaning is as follows: the word "vācāya" (by speech) has the same sense as the word "byappatho" (mode of expression), and it is the object (*kamma*) for the verb "vuccati" (is spoken).

Because of the following word "patha," the substitution of the vowel *i* for the final syllable of "vācā" has been made. The connection is that "pure volition (*suddhacetanā*)" is what is being described. The construction is:
"accompanied by the sound produced by that [volition]" means that the volition is described as occurring together with the sound arisen from that volition.
The word *eva* is an illustration (*nidassana*) or an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the word *dassetvā*.
The word *dassetvā* is the prior-time action (*pubbakālakiriyā*) for the two-word phrase *dassento āha*. The word *ante* means at the end of the five words beginning with *vācā*.
In the word *āha*, the letter *a* of the present third-person plural ending is [replaced] by the word *idāni*, which expresses the present time.

“Because it is applied. The word “therein” (*tattha*) is the locus for the phrase “the meaning is to be understood. “In this context” (*ettha*) refers to such passages as “What was not seen has been seen by me,” and so forth.
The word “in the Pāḷi” is the locus for the phrase “the teaching was given.

He said, “only by means of the gross [organ],” because it is stated that “it is seen with the eye” by way of the translucent matter (*pasāda*) which is the support, rather than by way of the consciousness dependent upon it.
4. *Tassa* refers to the statement beginning with "in three ways. *Attho* (the meaning) is the object of the verb *veditabbo* (should be known).
*Hi* is a particle indicating a distinction; the sense is: "I shall explain the distinction. *Tattha* means in the fourth Pārājika. *Idha* means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
9. *Ādīnam pi*: the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion.
11. Since *manda* denotes one who is dull-witted, he said, “because of dullness and because of dull-wittedness. The connection is with the phrase, “but he says something else.
The word “by the novice” (*sāmaṇerena*) is the agent for the word “spoken” (*vutto*). The particle *api* expresses a question and should be construed with the word “did you see?
(*passittha*); thus the meaning is, “Did you even see [it]? From such statements as “I have seen what was not seen,” another [meaning follows].
Showing that there is indeed such a thing as a "filling discourse" (*pūraṇakathā*), he said: "There is another so-called 'filling discourse'.
A filling discourse is a talk that proceeds by way of filling out a meaning that is incomplete due to deficiency. To the question, "What is this so-called filling discourse?
he said: "One [person]," and so forth. For this person, upon seeing or obtaining even a small amount of oil or a piece of cake in a village...
Alternatively, because it is spoken by way of filling out what has been made much, it is called "filling discourse" (*pūraṇakathā*).
One can also say that there is "deficient discourse" (*ūnakathā*) because even when one sees or receives many oils or cakes, it is spoken by way of deficiency by making them few.
However, since this is not mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it should be accepted after investigation. [This refers to] the meaning of filling out what is much...
The analysis should be made thus: "a talk that proceeds by way of deficiency is 'ūnakathā'. First [section]. 2.
The Training Rule on Slandering (omasavāda).

Regarding the second [term], showing that *masa* occurs in the sense of piercing—as in such examples as "omaṭṭha" (pierced) and "ummaṭṭha" (pierced)—he said: "omasantīti ovijjhantī" (they pierce means they stab).
13. The word “this subject” (*idaṃ vatthu*) is the object of the verb “brought forth” (*āhari*). One who is to be gladdened is *nanda*;
that which he possesses, such as beauty, strength, and so forth, is *nandi*. One who possesses large or broad horns is *visāla*.
Thus, the analysis of the compound *nandivisāla*—as one who is both *nandi* and *visāla*—is shown by the phrase “named Nandivisāla,” and so on. He...
Nandivisāla is the agent (kattā) for the word "āha" (said). "In that very place" means in the very place where it was applied.

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of those with rootless rebirth-linking," the particle *pi* expresses inclusion; the meaning is: "how much more so in the case of those with two-rooted or three-rooted rebirth-linking.
Because the conjunction *ca* in the phrase "and by that" has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated, it includes the meaning "and by one's own kamma."
He said, "And by his own kamma. "His own" refers to Nandivisāla.
"In this" means in this word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*); in the word "said," it is the locus (*ādhāra*).

The word "because" is the reason (*hetu*) for the desire to analyze [the following] word. Since [the phrase] "even by an inferior one" was stated in the introduction (*aṭṭhuppatti*) but was not mentioned in the word-commentary, this [explanation] is now stated.
It should be seen. "Of the bamboo-worker class" means of the basket-maker class.

"Of the hunter class": here, the fisherman class is also included. *Pū* is said to mean dung; one who scrapes (*kusati*) that away is a *pukkusa*. *Puppha* is said to mean dung or a flower; one who discards that is a *pupphachaḍḍaka*.

One who cuts (*kuṭati*) is a *koṭṭha*, and that itself is a *koṭṭhaka*. Having combined the letters *ya* and *bha* together as "yabha," the abusive term that exists [therein] is the application: "this is called a base insult."

16. *Sabbapadesūti*: in all instances, namely in the cases of names (*nāma*) and so forth. *Etthāti*: in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). *Alikanti asaccam*, *micchāvācanti sambandho*: "False" means untruth; it is to be construed with "wrong speech.

*Yopi vadatīti yojanā*: "Whoever speaks"—this is the construction. 26. *Pariharitvāti*: having set aside speaking directly to the face. *Davakāmo*: one who desires sport or jesting; the state of being such is *davakamyam*;
that very thing is *davakamyatā*. *Anupasampannanti*: here, taking the letter *a* in the sense of similarity [to the negative particle].
It must be understood in another sense; thus he said, "excepting a bhikkhu," and so forth.

For if it had the same meaning [as "one not fully ordained"], then a *sāmaṇera* would also be called "one not fully ordained" because of the similarity in physical form and gender; therefore, it should be seen that it must be understood in another sense.
Regarding the term "all beings" (*sabbasatta*), here the word "all" (*sabba*) has the sense of "without exception" with respect to humans.
Because all beings—whether their nature is to understand or not to understand the meaning of words based on [the Buddha's] teachings—are included.
35. The connection is: "It should be understood as 'that which has the purpose (attha) as its priority'.

With reference to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is stated as "action" (*kiriya*) and so forth in the neuter gender; with reference to the offense (*āpatti*), it is stated as "act" (*kiriyā*) and so forth in the feminine gender. These are words for blameworthy deeds.
Whether they look toward the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) or not, because their gender is fixed as neuter, they are indeed neuter;
therefore, it should be understood that those two are not mentioned among the bases for offenses (*āpattiṭṭhāna*). Second.
3. The Training Rule on Slander (*pesuñña-sikkhāpada*).

36. Regarding the third [section], although it should have been stated as “of those who have given rise to quarrels” (*jātabhaṇḍanānaṃ*), it is expressed as “of those who have arisen into quarrel” (*bhaṇḍanajātānaṃ*) by way of placing the qualifier after the qualified, as in the case of *agyāhito* and so forth;

thus he says, “of those in whom quarrels have arisen. Having stated “the preliminary stage,” he shows its specific nature with the words “by this and that,” and so on. It is called *vivāda* because one speaks in opposition by means of it; it is contentious speech.

"Those who have fallen into that" means those who have fallen into dispute; [it refers to] theirs. One who grinds or crushes is "slanderous" (*pisuṇa*); a person. That which belongs to him is "slander" (*pesuñña*).
Showing the meaning as "speech," he said: "Slander (*pesuñña*) means slanderous speech. 37.
"In slander among monks" (*bhikkhupesunne*) is a genitive compound meaning "in slanderous speech brought forward in the presence of monks."
38. “Having seen” (*disvā*) is a prior action relative to the word “speaking” (*bhaṇantassa*); the meaning is “having become one who sees. This is the third [section]. 4.
The Training Rule on Reciting Together with the Text (*padasodhamma-sikkhāpada*). 44.
In the fourth [section], he says “without deference” (*appatissavā*) to show that those who listen attentively face-to-face are *paṭissā*, whereas those who do not are *appaṭissā*.
45. Regarding the term “padaso,” since the suffix *-so* here expresses repetition (*vicchatti*), he says “padaṃ padaṃ” (verse by verse).
“Therein” means among those four kinds [of verses]. Here, what is called a *pada* is neither that which illuminates the meaning nor a word ending in a case-suffix;
rather, it is intended as the fourth part of a verse as defined by worldly convention—namely, a single *gāthāpāda* (verse-quarter). Thus he says: “‘Pada’ means one quarter of a verse.”
Because it is spoken after [the first], the second line is called *anupada* (the subsequent line).

By the phrase "anubyañjana" and so forth, the meaning of "anubyañjana" (the subsequent expression) is shown as being "a syllable (*byañjana*) that is similar (*anu*) [to the preceding]. The word *byañjana* is a synonym for *pada* (line/word).
Not just any word is called an *anubyañjana*; rather, only a subsequent word that is similar to the preceding word is called an *anubyañjana*.

The construction is: "Having become one who recites, he brings it to completion. In the phrase "each single word," the word *pada* is the object of the action (*kāritakamma*) in the word *niṭṭhāpeti*.
The word *therena* is the agent (*kattā*) in the word *vutte*, and *ekato* expresses the sense of "together with" (*sahattha*).
The connection is: "the novice recites without having reached [the end]. In the phrase *mattameva*, the word *eva* indicates the restrictive sense of the word *matta*.

By this, he rejects that [accusation]. Regarding the two words "anicca" and "aniccā," although there is a distinction in gender, because they are merely variations in phonetic form (*anubyañjana*), there is no release from the offense;
thus he says, "there are *pācittiya* offenses according to the count of the phonetic forms.
In the phrase "the *Brahmajāla* and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the long discourses such as the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta*.
By the word "etc. (*casaddena*), the Saṃyutta suttas such as the *Oghataraṇa-sutta* and others, as well as the Aṅguttara suttas such as the *Cittapariyādāna-sutta* and others, are included.
The construction is: "He" should be understood as spoken by a deity;
this connects with the phrase "even though he says. Here, moreover, the word "even though" (*kiñcāpi*) expresses censure, while the word "but" (*pana*) expresses favor.
Regarding the phrase *Meṇḍakamilindapañhesu*: it refers to both the *Meṇḍakapañha* and the *Milindapañha*. The connection is that "this discourse (*sutta*) has been spoken.
Because it is stated by way of a series (*peyyāla*), the terms *ārammaṇakathā*, *buddhikakathā*, *daṇḍakakathā*, and *ñāṇavatthukathā* should be applied accordingly.
They say these are indeed "treatises" (*pakaraṇa*). It was compiled after being recorded in the *Mahāpaccarī* and other such works.
The connection [of the words] is as follows: they go to the Sutta. 48.
*Tatra* (therein) refers to the statement, "while having them recite from one side. *Uddisāpenti* (they cause to recite) means they cause the teacher to teach;

it is expressed in the plural because it depends upon many agents. *Tehi* (by them) refers to those who are both ordained and unordained. *Dvepi* (even two) refers to both the ordained and the unordained.
"Vicinity" (*upacāra*) means a space of twelve cubits. "Of whom" refers to the monks. "A book for fleeing" refers to a treatise that one proceeds to avoid; the construction is: "the novice takes it.
"He causes to fall" means he causes to drop; the sense is "he causes to slip away. "Even in the *Sutta*" means even in the *Veyyākaraṇa-sutta*.
"That" refers to a text that is for the most part well-mastered. "Suspecting" means being filled with dread. The connection is: "but whatever word was spoken."
"Kiriyasamuṭṭhānattā" means "because this training rule originates from an action. This is the fourth [section]. 5.
The Training Rule on Sleeping Together (Sahaseyyasikkhāpada) 49.

In the fifth [section]: "Those whose mindfulness is lost" are *muṭṭhassatī*. "Those who lack clear comprehension" are *asampajānā*. "At the time of crossing over the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgotiṇṇakāle*) means at the time of falling asleep.
50. The word “pakatiyā” (naturally) is an adjective qualifying the word “dentī” (giving). The connection is: “those bhikkhus give.
Both the words “gāravenā” (out of respect) and “sikkhākāmatāyā” (out of a desire for training) are the reasons for the word “dentī.
“Ussīsa” means a pillow for the head; that which is made for it is “ussīsakaraṇaṃ”; its very meaning or purpose is “ussīsakaraṇattho,” for the sake of that.
In that context, *tatra* (therein) refers back to the preceding statement; the meaning is: "by way of the desire to train. The word *nidassanaṃ* (illustration) is the remainder [of the sentence].
Alternatively, *sikkhākāmatāya* is a locative used in the sense of the subject itself (*paccatte bhummavacanaṃ*), as in such passages as "this too is his virtue" (*idampi assa sīlasmiṃ*).
The construction is: "This too is by way of the desire to train"—that is, this desire to train, the state of desiring to train, exists. This is the same.
This method [of interpretation] applies also in such passages as, "In this regard, concerning the state of being 'completely admirable' (*samantapāsādikā*) in the *Samantapāsādikā*," and so forth.
The construction is: "The monks throw. "That" refers to the Venerable Rāhula. "Then" means after the throwing. "This" refers to the matter.

This was said with reference to the sweeping and the discarding of refuse. The construction is: "Was it indeed thrown down by that Venerable Rāhula? Furthermore, "that Venerable one goes... [is the continuation].
Connection. "Not to be used by others" means they are not to be enjoyed by others.
51. *Hi* means truly, or because. A bed (*seyyā*) is the act of reclining; it is called a bed because one lies down upon it, such as a couch, a stool, and so forth.
Taking both of these together—either by the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*) or by a general designation—they are collectively termed "sleeping together" (*sahaseyya*).
Showing that it has been stated, he said, "A bed," and so forth. "Therein" means in the two types of beds.
"Therefore" means because two types of beds have been shown; thus, the construction is: "The definition is stated by [the words] 'entirely covered' and so forth.
"Common parlance" means speech well-known in the world. "In a cloth-covered hut" means in a hut roofed with cloth. As it was stated in the commentaries...
To the question, "What fault is there if only the fivefold enclosure is taken? he says: "In the case of the fivefold enclosure itself," and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase, "the lodging which is enclosed. "By a wall" means by brick, stone, or wood; "or by another" means by palm-leaf mats and the like.
The word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even by a cloth" indicates that it is even more so in the case of bricks and the rest. "Of which" refers to the lodging.

"Of the bed. The construction is either "above" or "all around. It is said to be "having a single precinct" (*ekūpacāra*) with reference to the fact that one may enter through a single door and utilize the entire palace.
Or, the connection is that a four-sided hall (*catussāla*) with a hundred rooms has a single precinct.
"That" refers to the bed, which is designated as a lodging (*senāsana*).
“In that place” means on this bed, which is designated as a lodging (*senāsana*). The construction is: “if there are several novices (*sāmaṇera*), [and] if there is one monk.

The term “novices” is stated by way of proximity, or rather as an illustration, because the offense of sleeping together with others can also occur with [other types of persons]. “Them” refers to the novices. “Of all” refers to the monks.
"Of him" means of the novice (sāmaṇera). "In this very way" means this is the method, not another method; such is the meaning.
Alternatively, "in this very way" means this is like that method; the meaning is that this method should be understood as being similar to that one.
"Furthermore" (api ca) means emphatically. "In this" refers to this training rule (sikkhāpada). "The fourfold" refers to: [one dwelling in the same residence and one who is not fully ordained].

There is a fourfold group consisting of: one who is in the same residence and not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*), one who is in a different residence and not fully ordained, and one who is in a different residence and not fully ordained; or it refers to a measure of four. "He" (*yo*) means a bhikkhu. The word "hi" (*hisaddo*) is an indicator of expansion;
the meaning is that "I shall expand upon that statement," or "the expansion is being stated by me. "Daily" (*devasikaṃ*) means day after day. For the suffix *-ṇika* expresses the sense of repetition.

The phrase "there is also an offense for him who lies down with her" should be connected [to the previous rule]. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*), it refers to the statement "even with an animal.
[The examples are: "For those without feet, the snake and the fish; for those with two feet, the hen;
for those with four feet, the cat—these are the bases for the *pārājika* offense."

It was said, “in the very manner already stated,” with reference to this verse. Therefore: because it is to be understood, therefore. A *godha* is a monitor lizard. A *biḷāra* is a cat. A *maṅgusa* is a mongoose.
The construction is: “of a palace built without supporting walls. Regarding the word *tulā*:
here, a *tulā* is a specific type of timber placed above the pillars according to their width from south to north; it is so called because it floats or rests upon the pillars.
As for those [buildings], by the lower limit there are three, but by the upper limit there are five, seven, nine, and so forth.
"In a palace with various surrounding areas" is the connection.
"In tiger-skin patchwork robes, etc. means in patchwork robes and the like made by displaying the form of a tiger; by the word "etc.," it includes woolen cloth (*tula*).

And here, "saṅghāṭa" refers to a specific type of timber placed above the rafters according to their front and back alignment, so called because the rafters and other structural elements join properly therein.
There are three of these. "Within the interior of the nibbakosa" means within the edge of the roof-covering.
The connection is: "the dwelling (senāsana) is either circular or square."

"In that place" means in that lodging (*senāsana*). "Those whose interior space (*gabbha*) and precincts (*upacāra*) are not delimited" refers to all those [lodgings] whose interior spaces and precincts are undelimited;
the meaning is that they enter them. The construction is: "of the monks who have reclined.
"In that place" means in that front hall (*pamukha*). Because the front hall is entirely covered and entirely enclosed, one incurs an offense—this is the construction.

Is it not the case that in front there is only what is concealed (*channa*), but not what is enclosed (*paricchanna*)? To this he says: “the enclosure of a womb,” and so forth. “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly.
The connection is with the phrase, “but that which was stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. *Jagatī* is a name for both the earth and the ground of a house’s porch;
however, here the specific types of ground designated as the site of a house’s porch are intended. “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.
He said, "Even ten cubits high," and so forth, to explain why this does not accord with the Canon (pāḷi). The word *hi* means "because.
*Tattha* means "in the Andhaka-ṭīkā. The construction is: "even those which are great palaces (*mahāpāsāda*).

*Tesupi* means "even in those great palaces. Regarding the phrase "of the plastered pavilion," here the term "plaster" (*sudhā*) is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), [meaning] by whatever [material].

Because the *chadana-maṇḍapa* (canopy-pavilion) is also intended here. "Maṇḍa" refers to the rays of the sun; it protects (*pāti*) those [rays], or people know [it] from that, hence it is called a *maṇḍapa*.
To the objection, "Is it not the case that there is a single common area because of the gaps in the wall?", he says "No," and so forth.
"Hi" means "truly" or "because. The particle "eva" (only) should be construed with "vaḷañjanatthāya eva" (only for the purpose of use). Therefore he said: "Not for the purpose of cutting off use."
Alternatively, because it has been stated that "a word expresses its meaning by excluding other meanings," it was said, "not for the purpose of cutting off the flow [of sound].
Regarding the term *kavāṭa*, here it is the door itself that is intended, since it is expressed by way of a synonym;
furthermore, in the absence of a door, there can be no door-panel (*kavāṭa*). It is called *kavāṭa* because it makes the sound *kavati* at the time of being closed or opened.
In this context, "therein" refers to the statement "because of being a single enclosure. "Of whom" refers to the opponent. The construction is: "there might be an inquiry.
"Here" means in this training rule regarding sleeping together; it connects with the word "stated. "Therein" means in a room with its door closed.

"He" refers to the opponent. The construction is: "because of being entirely covered, there is an offense," as it has been stated. This same method applies to the phrase "because of being entirely enclosed."
Regarding the phrase "it does not exist," here too [the same applies]. "He will return" means he will come back; the sense is that he will return again.
"By the mere phrasing alone" means by the mere letters and words such as "all-covered" and so forth, and not by way of the meaning.
By the phrase "this being so," he demonstrates the fault of non-pervasiveness (*abyāpitadosa*). "From that" refers to from the non-offense; it is to be connected with the word "he would fall away."

Therefore, because it was stated regarding the indefinite cases, [it is said] "therefore. "Therein" means among the indefinite cases. "In this case as well" means even in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"Whatever" refers to the lodging (*senāsana*). "In all places" means in all lodgings; the connection is that there is an offense of lying down together (*sahaseyyāpatti*). 53.
Between the two explanations in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the explanation of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* alone is appropriate; therefore, it was stated last.

"By this too" means even by the Senambamaṇḍapa. "This" refers to the fact that the earth is unenclosed. "Yathā" has the sense of the relative pronoun *yaṃ* in the instrumental case; the meaning is "by which [means] the Senambamaṇḍapa.
This is the fifth [section]. 6. The Second Training Rule on Sleeping Together:
In the sixth [section], it is called an *āvasatha* because guests dwell there (*āgantukā vasanti ettha*). It is an *āvasatha* and it is a house (*agāra*), thus it is an *āvasathāgāra*.
Pointing this out, he said, "a lodging for guests. The phrase "having heard the words from people" should be construed as an ellipsis (*vacanaseso*).

"A garment" (*sāṭaka*) refers to an upper garment (*uttarasāṭaka*); some also say it refers to the cloth worn as a lower robe (*nivatthavattha*). To show the connection of the word ending in the suffix *-tvā*—namely, "having approached" (*accāgammā*)—he said, "proceeded.
Just as in the training rule concerning abusive speech (*omasavāda-sikkhāpada*), [one speaks] with the desire to revile a khattiya...

When one says, "He is a caṇḍāla," even though one is speaking falsely, there is no offense under the training rule on false speech (musāvāda-sikkhāpada), but there is an offense under the training rule on abusive speech (omasavāda-sikkhāpada).

Likewise here, for one who lies down with a woman, there is no offense under the first training rule on sharing a bed (paṭhamasahaseyya-sikkhāpada), but it should be understood that there is an offense under this very [present] rule. The sixth [section].
7. The Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma (Dhammadesanā-sikkhāpada) 60.
Regarding the seventh [rule], "at the great door": it refers to the great door standing outside.

Because one comes from there or enters from there to reach the dwelling place, the room is called an *āvasatha* (dwelling); thus he says, "at the door of the room. "Having gone out well" means having properly emerged outside.
Regarding the word *gatena* [in the phrase] *saddena*: by stating "to understand" (*ājānitum*), he rejects the meaning of the word *aññātum* as "not to know" (*na ñātum*).
By this, he shows that it is not a particle (*nipāta*) consisting of the phonetic change of the letter *na*, but rather that *ā* is a prefix (*upasagga*).
By saying "by a person in human form" (*purisaviggahena*) instead of merely saying "by a wise man" (*viññunā purisena*), he indicates one who stands having assumed the physical form of a human being.
This shows that it is not permissible to teach a woman who is standing together with a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or an animal.
The construction is: "Not with a *yakkha*" means it is not permissible to teach a woman who is standing together with a *yakkha*.
This same method applies to the phrases "not with a *peta*" and "not with an animal" as well.
66. Regarding the phrase *chappañcavācāhi*: here, “five” (*pañca*) is stated by way of the elegance of speech, as there is no specific purpose [for limiting it to five].

In that context—that is, in the word *chappañcavācāhi*—one who says that a single line of verse (*gāthāpāda*) is one utterance (*vācā*) shows, according to the *Cuṇṇī*, that a single inflected word is what is called an utterance;
neither a word that merely indicates the meaning nor a syntactical sentence should be taken [as an utterance].
By the statement, “One word from the Pāḷi, five from the Aṭṭhakathā,” the same method should be understood for such cases as “Two words from the Pāḷi, four from the Aṭṭhakathā,” and so forth.

For the measure is simply the non-exceeding of six words. In the phrase *tasmim*, when there is a change of case-ending (*vibhattivipallāsa*), there is also a change of gender, because it was expressed in the masculine as *tasmin*. And when there is a change of case-ending...
“Tassā” (of her) refers to that which occurs in the feminine gender. “Mātugāmassa” (of a woman):

since a reference to a fixed masculine gender is impossible here, it is stated in the feminine gender as “ekissā” (of one) by way of its meaning. By this, he shows that there is also a relationship between the qualifier and the qualified based on distinct genders.
“Tumhākaṃ” (for you) is a collective expression used for selection. Instead of saying “suṇātha” (listen), it is also appropriate to say “ābhoga” (attention).
He said, "The first," and so forth. "The first" means precisely the first. Therefore it was said, "not afterwards. The construction is:
"having been asked, the bhikkhu speaks. This is the seventh [section]. 8.
The Training Rule on Announcing What Has Occurred (Bhūtārocanasikkhāpada).
67. In the eighth [case], "therein" refers to the fourth *pārājika* training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Here" refers to the training rule concerning the announcement of what has actually occurred.

"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "Speech associated with requisites" (*payuttavācā*) means speech joined with the [four] requisites. "Thus" (*tathā*) means for the sake of announcing those qualities;
the construction is: "the Noble Ones consented" (*ariyā sādiyiṃsu*).
Because words beginning with *yata* (from which) have a constant connection [with a relative pronoun], it is said "those who" (*ye*) and so forth.

"All" means both ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and noble ones (*ariya*). "Existent" (*bhūta*) means existing. Why did they all admit it? One might ask: "Should it not be admitted, since the noble ones do not proclaim their own virtues?
To this he says: "Of the noble ones as well," and so forth. *Hi* means "truly" or "because. Within the ranks of the noble ones as well...
The construction is as follows: "Because the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) was real, therefore all [the noble ones] professed, 'The Blessed One spoke what is real'.
The construction "because it was as if spoken" is likewise to be understood. The connection is: "the Noble Ones professed.

"Those who do not see danger" means those whose nature is to fail to see faults. The connection with "by them" refers to the Noble Ones, and with "spoken" it is connected. "That alms-food which they produced... [is the further connection].
The construction [is as follows]: "Others" refers to worldlings (*puthujjana*). "By way of including all" means by way of encompassing all worldlings and noble ones (*ariya*).
"Also in the analysis of the training rule" means also in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*) on the training rule. "Therein" refers to the fourth *pārājika*.
"Here" refers to this present training rule.

77. This was said with reference specifically to superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), not to qualities such as learning and so forth; this is the meaning. "In the interval" means at a time other than the moment of final Nibbāna.
"By one being dragged along" means by one being excessively pressured. Regarding the phrase "of one who is insane," here the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*);
by it, [the cases of] "one whose mind is deranged" and so on are included. "Of those possessed of right view" (*diṭṭhisampannānaṃ*).
"Of those endowed with the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the fruit. Regarding "there is no offense": it should not be said that there is no offense for a *pācittiya* offense;
rather, it is indeed an offense. Therefore, the intended meaning is that one should not say, "There is no offense for one who is insane.
This is the eighth [section]. 9. The Training Rule on Announcing What is Grave.
78. "In that ninth [chapter]" refers to the Pāḷi text beginning with "Those called *duṭṭhulla*," etc., or to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) on those Pāḷi passages.
"Investigation" means examination. "In the word *upasampanna*" means in the state of being the meaning of the word *upasampanna*.

For here, when the word is mentioned, the meaning is also expressed by virtue of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between word and meaning; thus, even without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-paccaya*), the sense of the abstract state is conveyed.
Because it is something to be known, the state [of being] must also be grasped; therefore, it is said: "in the sense of the state of the word *upasampanna*.
This same method applies here as well in the phrase "in the word *duṭṭhulla*. That which has this as its measure is "this," namely, the statement "the thirteen *saṅghādisesas*.
The meaning is that only this should be stated, and not "the four *pārājikas*. Therein...

In the Pāli: the construction is, "there might be doubt for someone; what [doubt] might there be? When one confesses an offense, because [the offender] is equal to one who reviles, it is said, "this being so," and so forth.
The word *ca* (and) in the phrase "only a pācittiya" has a sense of exclusion (*byatirekattha*), meaning that one does not incur a dukkaṭa.
The particle *hi* means "truly. "This" refers to the fact of incurring a pācittiya, as in: "[He] is impure... [etc. ...for one who speaks in disparagement."

The connection is: "or the word, it is said. "In this" means in the Pāḷi. Regarding the phrase "but the teachers of the Commentary," here the particle *eva* (only) is used in the sense of restriction;
it should be connected with the word "authority" (*pamāṇa*), meaning "it is the authority alone. Therefore it is said: "there is no other deliberation.
Alternatively, *aññā* is a nominative plural used in the sense of equality, meaning "of others"; thus, "the deliberation of others is not the authority."
The meaning is as follows. For if this were so, the particle *eva* would indeed be used in its proper place. "Even previously" means even at the time of beginning the composition.

"This" refers to the authoritative status of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). The construction is: "It was permitted solely for the sake of restraint, and solely for the sake of non-transgression.
Therefore he said, "Not for him," and so forth. "Therefore" means because there is no such thing as the state of being a monk (*bhikkhubhāva*).
"Therefore, it is well-said" is the connection. 80.
"That" refers to the formal authorization (*sammuti*) of the monks; "it is to be performed by the Saṅgha" is the construction.

"In some place" means in a certain location. "Here" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The word "because it has been stated" is the reason for the word "to be performed. "This one" refers to that monk.
*Hitesitāya*: by the seeking of welfare; the meaning is "by the desiring of benefit. 82. *Sesāni*: the remaining ones;

that is, the five training rules following the first five training rules. *Assa*: of one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). *Ghaṭetvā*: having connected; that is, having established the relationship [between the words].
The ninth [training rule]. 10. The Training Rule on Digging the Earth.
86. The construction is: "The Blessed One shows [this] in the tenth [chapter]. "Therein" means on the earth. "In those" refers to those stones and so forth.
"From the measure of a fist" means from the measure of a handful. "She" refers to the unburnt earth. "In the Elephant-Belly" refers to the place named after that.
The connection is: "earth filling a single basket. "Of those very [beings]" refers to those whose tracks contain little dust and little soil.
"Evam. "Hi" means "truth" or "because. "Etam" refers to the pentad of stones and so forth, which constitutes the majority [of the material]. "Tam" refers to the lazy person. Regarding "āṇāpetvā":
since the root *āṇ* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha as "in the sense of sending," it is the root *āṇ* itself that expresses the causal sense known as "sending," and not the suffix *-āpe*.
That suffix, moreover, functions within the meaning of the root itself; for it has no separate denotation of its own.

There is [no other meaning], because there is no referent other than the sense of the root (*dhātu*). “Tāva” means first, regarding the analysis outside the canonical text (*pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya*), or from that point onward.

“Pokkharaṇī” means that which leads to a lotus (*pokkhara-paduma*). The word “sodhente-hi” has the sense of the agent (*kattā*) with respect to the words “to empty out” (*ussiñcitum*) and “to remove” (*apanetum*).
The word “yo” is to be connected with the phrase “tanukaddamo”; for the meaning is “that which has little mud.”
“With jars” means with pots. “To pour out” means to lift up or draw out and then pour. “Therein” refers to the dry mud;
in the word “which” (*yo*), it is the substratum for the whole.
“Which” refers to the dry mud. “The bank” means the shore. “In the vicinity of the water” means near the water. “Less than four months” means less than four months.
"Ovaṭṭhaṃ" means it has been rained upon by the deity; this is the construction. "Patati" means it falls down the slope.
"Udakeyeva" means in the natural water itself. "Udakassa" means of the rainwater. "Tattha" means on the surface of the rock.
"Paṭhamameva" means even before the digging of the well. "Udake pariyādiṇṇe" means when the water has dried up. "Pacchā" means after the water was full.
*Pacchā* means afterwards. *Tattha* means in the *soṇḍi* (the hollow). *Udake yeva* means in the water at the very root. *Udakaṃ* means incoming water. *Allīyati* means it clings to the back stone.
*Taṃ pi* means even that fine dust. *Akata-pabbhāre* means in a natural cleft not made by human labor.
It is called a *vammika* because it is vomited up by termites, or because it vomits forth creatures such as house-lizards and the like.
Because the hoof of a cow is like a thorn, it is called a *gokaṇṭaka* (cow-thorn); mud cut by that is also called a *gokaṇṭaka*. The construction is:
"It is an old lodging, either with its roof-covering intact or with its roof-covering ruined. "From that" means from the old lodging;
the connection is that it is permissible to take [it]. "The remainder" refers to what remains after the ruined roof-covering. "The remainder."
It should be construed as: "with the perception, 'I am taking a brick. "By that" means by the brick and so forth. "Which clay" refers to the clay.
"Not wet" means not moist; the meaning is not soaked.
"In that" means in the heap of clay. "The whole" means the entire heap of clay. "Of it" means of the heap of clay. "By those who prepare what is allowable" (kappiyakārakehi).
In the phrase "having moved the foot," the word [pada] functions as the object of the action. Why is it permissible? He says: "by water," and so forth.
"Hi" means "truly" or "because. "Therein" refers to the earthen wall. "Another too" means something other than the pillar of the pavilion.

"By that pretext" means by that excuse of rolling stones and such. "Of the stream of urine" means of the urinary passage. "With a walking-stick" means with a staff. For here, one walks (kattarayati) with it.
Because he has become slack due to the looseness of his limbs and members, an elderly person is called *kattara*;

since it must be grasped by such a person exclusively, the staff is "grasped by a *kattara*," or alternatively, because it belongs to a *kattara*, it is called a *kattarayaṭṭhi* (an old man's staff), that is, a *kattaradaṇḍa*.
It should be recited with the first syllable of *danta* [as *da*]. [The compound] means "for the purpose of exerting energy."
The meaning is: for the purpose of thoroughly exerting energy (*vīriya*), for the purpose of uplifting energy. "Some monks" is the construction. 87.

"There too" means even in the case of bricks, potsherds, and so forth. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "Because of their non-appropriation" means because those bricks and other things lack fuel for the fire.
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "Those" refers to the bricks and so forth. "Because of being outside the scope" means because of [being outside] the offense.
"Because there was no opportunity. "A grass torch" (*tiṇukka*) means a torch made of grass. "Right there" refers specifically to the *Mahāpaccarī*. "Araṇī" is that in which [the fire] is produced;
it is rubbed (*arīyati*) for the purpose of generating fire, and thus it is the lower wood to be churned. "Sahita" means that which moves or functions together with the bow (*dhanu*);
it is the upper wood used for churning. "Araṇīsahita" is the araṇī and the sahita; the construction is: "having generated fire by means of that."
The connection is: "Act in such a way that it does not burn while being made.
(88) "Knows the pit" means he knows how to make a pit, or rather, he knows how to dig one.

Regarding the phrases "know thus the great clay" and "know the husk-clay," here too the construction is achieved by supplying a word expressing the recipient (*sampadāna*) as appropriate to the context.
It should be done. That is the earth. By that means, by rolling [the seed] and so forth. The tenth.
The first chapter on False Speech is finished.
2. The Chapter on Living Beings and Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Plants (Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada) 89.
In the first [rule] of the second section, "of her" refers to the deity. "Lifted up an axe" means an axe raised upwards.
"To restrain" means to cause it to stop or to turn back. "Beyond the range of the eye" refers to the physical eye (pasāda-cakkhu).
"Beyond his range. "In the presence of the Great King" means in the presence of the Great King Vessavaṇa. "Right at the base of the tree" means right near the tree.
"In the Himalayas" means in the forest where snow falls, or that which is possessed of snow. "Therein" means in the Himalayas, or at the gathering of deities.
"The nature of a tree" means the inherent characteristic of a tree. And what is called the nature of a tree refers to [the state of] trees regarding cutting, breaking, and so forth.
Because anger is insentient, its non-arising occurs; a deity established in that "dharma of the tree" is said to be "established in the dharma of the tree. The intention is this:
when cutting, breaking, and so forth are performed, the non-anger of the deity residing in the tree—just as with the tree itself—is what is meant by being "established in the dharma of the tree.
"Therein" (tattha) refers to those deities assembled there. "Thus" (iti) refers to this failure to obtain [the desired object].

The connection is: "in this non-attainment, there are dangers. The word *ca* ("and") in the phrase "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato ca*) should be joined with the term "former conduct" (*pubbacarita*).
Alternatively, the construction should be made by way of combining the sentences: "He saw this danger and recollected the former conduct of the Blessed One.
*Tenā* means "by that reason," namely, by the reason of seeing and recollecting. *Assa* refers to the deity. His father exists.
*Assa* means "his," referring to the son together with his wife. (*Tāva* means "exceedingly"; it is to be construed with *paṭisañcikkhantiyā*, "while she was reflecting.
Having said, "He will establish a boundary," he spoke [the next phrase] to show its meaning: "He will lay down a training rule. Thus, the construction is:
"While she was reflecting in this way, this thought occurred to that deity."
"Whoever" means any person whatsoever. "Veti" means certainly. "Uppatitam" means fallen upon oneself by way of arising.
"Bhantam" means wandering or running about; "vāraye" means one should restrain or subdue it—this is the meaning.
"Tam" refers to that person. Here, however, is the construction: just as a charioteer restrains a wandering chariot, so too [one should restrain] whoever [restrains] anger that has arisen.

I call him a charioteer who restrains that [horse]. Any other person who, distinct from the one who restrains anger, serves as a driver for kings, vassals, and so forth, is called a "reins-grasper" or a "rope-grasper.
In the second verse, the physician [treats] the "spread-out" or extensive poison of a snake—the venom, the *gala*, of a venomous serpent (*āsīvisa*).
"Just as one might dispel [a disease] with herbs, medicine, and mantras, so too, monks, the monk who dispels arisen anger with loving-kindness (*mettā*)—
just as a serpent, a slithering snake, casts off its old skin from its former existence, worn out because it is ancient— he likewise casts off this near shore,
which is reckoned as the 'not-far' shore, namely the five lower fetters (*pañca-oraṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*). Thus the construction should be made.
"In those two verses" refers to *tatra*. "But the basis is recorded in the Vinaya" is the construction. "Then" (*atha*) means afterwards.
"Of which son of the gods" (*yassa devaputtassa*) means by which son of the gods. "Appropriated" (*pariggaho*) means taken after having delimited it.

"He" (*so*) refers to that son of the gods. "From there" (*tato*) means from the approach. The construction is: "when it happens, then. "Among deities of great influence" (*mahesakkhadevatāsu*) means among those with large retinues.

"Among the deities" means among those of great majesty. "They retreat" means they depart. The construction is: "even the question that the deities ask. "Right there" means right at his own dwelling place.
"Upaṭṭhānaṃ" is for the purpose of attendance; here the accusative case is used in the sense of the dative.
Alternatively, it is called *upaṭṭhāna* because one stands near (*upagantvā tiṭṭhati*) there; it refers to standing in the presence of the Blessed One.
"Having come to that" is the meaning. "Taṃ" means "that," or this is simply another reading for the word.
By the word "bhavanti" (becoming), he indicates young trees, shrubs, and the like, which, having grown from roots and attained a dark-green state, are still increasing.
By the phrase "ahuvatthuṃ" (they have become), however, he indicates large trees, shrubs, and the like, which have grown and now stand established.
In the expression “ahuvatthu,” there is a substitution of *uv* for the vowel *ū* of the root *hū* following the *tthuṃ* suffix, which denotes the past day (the immediate past).
However, the reading “ahuvatī” found in certain manuscripts should be regarded as incorrect.
By the word “jāyanti,” he shows that the root *bhū* has the sense of arising; by the word “vaḍḍhanti,” he shows that it has the sense of increasing.
This much is what is called “the group of beings” (*bhūtagāma*). It is called *pātabya* because it is drunk—that is, enjoyed according to one’s desire—or because it is to be drunk or enjoyed;
the prefix *pā-* has the sense of enjoying according to one’s wish. Therefore he said: “The meaning is that it is to be enjoyed as one pleases by means of cutting, breaking, and so forth.”

91. The word “now” (*idāni*) is a locative of time (*kālasattamī*) with respect to the word “said” (*āha*). “In which” refers to the seed. “That” refers to the seed. Regarding the phrase “five kinds of seeds,” this was stated thus in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) with reference to the sense of “becoming that” (*tabbhāvattha*) for the word “born” (*jāta*).

The Compiler (*saṅgahakāra*), however, stated “they do not agree” with reference to the fact that [the commentary’s definition] does not accord with the canonical text (*pāḷi*) “they grow from the root” (*mūle jāyanti*), because it refers to the sense of “becoming that.”

According to the opinion of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), if the word *jāta* were taken in the sense of "becoming that" (*tabbhāvattha*), then in expressions such as “growing at the root” (*mūle jāyanti*), there would be the fault of [implying] that roots grow at the roots. Bearing this in mind, he said “no indeed” (*na hi*), and so forth.

“Indeed” (*hi*) means truly; or, because. “Those” (*tāni*) refers to trees and the like. “Of that” (*tassa*) refers to the phrase: “A ‘community of beings’ (*bhūtagāma*) consists of the five kinds of seeds.”
This is the name “born from seeds. When it is said that they are “born from seeds” (*bījesu jātāni*), it accords with [the definition] “born from roots” and so forth.
By this—namely, by the phrase “from the seed” and so on—there is a connection in the sense of inclusion.

The word “by which” (*yehi*) is the ablative case relative to the word “because of being born” (*jātattā*), or it is the instrumental case relative to the word “stated” (*vuttāni*), or it is the agent.
"Of those" means of the seeds. It is called a "seed" (*bīja*) because it produces—that is, generates—the growth of trees and so forth.
By the phrase "from the seed" (*bījato*), etc., the cause is shown through a metaphorical designation of the effect; thus, he illustrates the figurative application of the cause.

As for the other things—whether they be shrubs, creepers, trees, or whatever else exists and is found—the construction is: "those shrubs, creepers, trees, and so forth are born, they are produced. "Those" refers to...

"Creeper-vines, trees, and so forth. And that root, as well as the turmeric and other items mentioned in the Pāḷi, all this is what is called "root-seed"—this is the connection. "In this regard" means among seeds or among stem-seeds.
(92) "By way of designation" means by way of the designation "seed. The word "therein" (*tattha*) serves as the locative support for the word "to be understood" (*veditabbo*).

By the phrase beginning with “yathā,” he demonstrates the metaphorical application of the fruit (*phalūpacāra*), because the effect is spoken of through the metaphorical application of its cause (*kāraṇopacāra*).
The construction is: “That seed which was mentioned is the basis for the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭavatthu*). This should be connected with the word “ādipada. “Tenā” means by that initial term.
It is called *ruta* because it is sounded or spoken by the Blessed One; it is the Pāḷi. “Yathāruta” means corresponding to that [Pāḷi]; the meaning is “not transgressing the Pāḷi.”
*Ettha* means in the phrase beginning with “perceiving it as a seed in what is a seed,” or in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). That which stands or exists in water is *udakaṭṭha*;
likewise for *thalaṭṭha*. *Tattha* means among those things that stand or exist in water and on land. *Sāsapamattika*: that moss whose measure or size is that of a mustard seed.
*Tilabījaka*: that moss whose seed-measure is that of a sesame seed.
Regarding the meaning of "measure" (*pamāṇatthe*): by the word "etc. (*ādi*), *saṅkha*, *paṇaka*, and so forth are included among the types of algae (*sevāla*).
Among these, that which is the size of a sesame seed, remains submerged in water, and possesses colors such as blue, is called a "sesame-seed [algae]" (*tilabīja*).

A specific type of algae that has leaves, a small stalk, possesses roots, and is the size of a mortar-lid or similar object, is called a "conch" (*saṅkha*). A specific type of algae that is shaped like a bee and is blue in color is a "moss" (*paṇaka*).
[The word] *nāma*. It frequents water, thus it is *sevāla* (moss). "Therein" means among the mosses. "It" refers to the moss. The connection is: "the moss is established.
"Anywhere at all" means on a root, or a reed, or a leaf. "Having pulled out" means having uprooted.
The word "with hands" is the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) for the word "having cleared away. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Of that" means of the moss. "To this extent" means...
"By the mere act of shifting here and there. The construction is: "The moss that emerges is 'moss' (*sevāla*). "Through the strainer's interstices" means through the holes of the strainer.

"Uppalinī" is so called because blue lotuses (*uppala*) go forth (*gacchati*) in this; "paduminī" is so called because red lotuses (*paduma*) go forth in this—the suffix *-ino* is used here to indicate the feminine gender.
"Right there" means in the water itself. "Those" refers to the creepers and grasses. "Hi" (for) signifies truth or reason, meaning "because."
Or: "Anantako" refers to a mustard-seed-sized fragment of moss (*sevāla*). It is called "anantaka" because there is no end (*anta*) to its wretchedness;
that is, having made it so by way of its being a miserable moss. The intention is that it is subtle by its very nature, and there is no moss more subtle than that.
"Therein" means in the state of being the basis for an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "That too" refers to the statement: "It is not a complete living organism. The word "too" (*pi*)...
This refers to the words of the masters of the *Mahāpaccarī* and other commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). *Hi* means "truly" or "because. The construction is:
"Since it has not come [in the texts], therefore it does not agree. *Atha* means "when that has not come. *Etaṃ* refers to the "endless moss" (*anantaka-sevāla*) and so forth.
The connection is: "one might say 'it will go. *Tampi* means "even that statement, namely 'it will go. The particle *pi* refers back to the words of the masters of the aforementioned commentaries.
"Because it has its root in a non-living grove, such as a grove of seeds": here, the "grove of seeds" is threefold.
First, that which, having itself been a living grove, produces another living grove, such as the mango-stump and so forth.
Second, that which, having itself been a living grove, does not produce another living grove, such as the stumps of palmyra or coconut trees. Third, that which is itself [not] a living grove...
Without itself being a seed-plant, it does not produce another seed-plant. "Moss outside water-jars and the like" refers to this.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of seed-plants (*bhūtagāma*): that which, being itself a seed-plant, produces another seed-plant, such as the mango tree and so forth at present;
and that which, without itself having been a seed-plant, produces another seed-plant, such as the mango tree and so forth at the beginning of the eon (*ādikappa*).
However, that which itself is a seed-plant but does not produce another seed-plant is the blue-colored flowering plantain tree and so forth.
That which neither itself is a seed-plant nor produces another seed-plant is the *anantaka* moss and so forth mentioned here.
In this context, it is said with reference to the fourth class of living beings: "because such a seed has its root in what is not a [living] plant."
Now, this is the distinction between the third "seed-group" (bījagāma) and the fourth "being-group" (bhūtagāma):
in the third seed-group, roots and leaves are not found; in the fourth being-group, they are found. Because roots and leaves are not found, it is called a "seed-group";
because they are found, it is called a "being-group. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction. [End of] self...

It is grave because it constitutes a *pācittiya* offense according to the *Vāda*; it is light because it constitutes a mere *dukkaṭa* offense according to the *Mahāpaccarī* and other [commentaries]. "This" refers to the situation.
Having thus shown what pertains to water (*udakaṭṭha*), he said "on land" (*thalaṭṭhe*) and so forth to show what pertains to land (*thalaṭṭha*).

The construction is: "The determination regarding what pertains to land should be understood in this way. "Therein" means in the case of green sprouts and stumps. "It grows upward" means by the emergence of new branches.
It grows from above the cut-off portion; that is the stump (*khāṇu*). The construction is: "The stump of a fruit-bearing plantain tree is included within the category of 'seed-germ' (*bījagāma*).
It is called *phalitā* because fruit has arisen upon it. The word *tathā* draws forward the phrases "included by the very category of living beings" (*bhūtagāmena eva saṅgahitā*).
*Yadā* means at which time. *Ratanappamāṇāpi* means even those measuring a cubit (*hattha*). *Atha* has the sense of an ablative (*apādāna*).
The meaning is: "other than by making them into a heap. The connection is with the phrase "burying in the ground.

Regarding the words "both in the roots and in the leaves," the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) alone, not the sense of option (*vikappa*); thus he says, "but in those consisting merely of roots," and so forth.
"Seeds" refers to seeds such as roots and the like. The connection is with the word "are placed. By the word "above," [the implication is] that the roots are below.
He makes known the meaning by way of this method (*naya*). It is not merely when the sprout has just emerged;

rather, it is only when the green color of the leaves has appeared that the inclusion within the "grove of beings" (*bhūtagāma*) should be applied—thus he says "in the green," and so forth. The connection is with "the root of the palm trunks.
"Like an ivory needle" means like a needle made of elephant tusks. Just as the third portion [of the offense] does not constitute an incomplete grove of beings...
It has arrived; thus, it is not the case that the community of beings (bhūtagāma) is rootless. However, since it has indeed arrived, he said, "in the rootless community of beings.
The meaning is that it is included within the rootless community of beings just like a rootless creeper (amūlikalata).
"Vandākā" refers to a tree-climbing plant (rukkhādanī); for although it grows supported by a tree itself, [it serves] its supporting trees...
Because it is eaten and consumed, it is praised and extolled; thus it is called "vandākā. "Or another" means other than the *vandākā*. "That" refers to the *vandākā* and so forth.
"From that" means from the tree. "Creeper" (*vana*) is a small shrub. "Cluster" (*pagumba*) is a large shrub.

"Staff" (*daṇḍaka*) is a tree, so called because of its resemblance to a staff. "Of this too" refers even to the rootless creeper (*amūlikā-latā*). "This very same analysis" applies to the *vandākā* and the others.
The construction is: "This [case] is to be understood as being like that [previous] decision.

Because it is stated, "two or three bowls," the meaning is that even a single bowl, when it arises, is included under the category of "seed at the tip" (*aggabīja*). The word "by one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannena*) is the agent for the word "of one who has smeared" (*littassa*).
"In the heat of summer" (*nidāghasamaye*) means during the hot season. "Not subject to dispute" (*abbhohāriko*) means a factor of an offense (*āpatti*).
It is not to be spoken of; the meaning is that it does not deserve to be spoken of. "This" refers either to the state of being beyond conventional expression (*abbhohārikatā*) or to the statement:
"If... [omission] ...it should be neglected. It covers a snake (*ahi*), thus it is *ahicchatta*; that very thing is *ahicchattaka*.

For etymological derivation may occur in any manner whatsoever, while the determination of the meaning follows common usage (*ruḷhi*). "Therefore" means because of disturbing that [state]. "Therein" means in the *ahicchattaka*. Below, it is called "a water-bubble" (*udakapappaṭaka*).
Having stated this, since it is said here, “even on a tree-creeper,” it should be understood that the word *pappaṭaka* is of two genders. “That” refers to the creeper (*pappaṭika*).
The connection is with the word “exudation” (*niyyāsa*) when it is present. The same applies to the word “adhering” (*lagga*). “With hand-fidgeting” means with a restless hand.
The phrase “even while cutting” provides the reason for the statement.

“By one desiring a dwelling” (*vāsatthikena*) means by one wishing for a residence. In the phrase “should have [the trees] stripped,” the agent is implied. “By those who are tearing up” means by those who are uprooting. “Of them” refers to the novices (*sāmaṇera*). This is to be connected with “a branch was taken. The construction is: “of the ginger (*siṅgīvera*) that had been set aside.
“Capable of being cut” (*chijjanaka*) means fit to be cut; the meaning is “worthy of being severed.

By the words “I will show the place for walking,” he shows that walking meditation (*caṅkamana*) is permitted under the heading of this duty. By the words “it breaks,” even a knot (*gaṇṭhi*) [is indicated] when it is not being broken.
"It should be made" is what is being shown. "A wooden monkey": the hand of a monkey is called "monkey" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*);

it is a "little monkey" (*makkaṭaka*) because it is like a monkey—the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of similarity. A "wooden monkey" is a monkey consisting of wood. "They strike it"—this is the grammatical connection.
"Because of its unspecified nature": because this word is unspecified. This is a great general term (*mahāsāmañña*), and it is also a specific general term (*visesasāmañña*).
"It is permissible," he says, [expressing this] with the words "even by taking the name" and so forth.
"All" means every word. In the phrase "in cases such as 'he knows this,'" the term "in cases such as 'he knows this'" serves as the locus for the phrase "the meaning should be understood thus.

"He knows this root medicine" refers to the knowledge; "he knows how to compound this root medicine" refers to the compounding. "By this much alone" means by the mere statement "he knows this," and so forth.
“Permissible” (*kappiya*) means that which is appropriate or suitable for the terminology of a recluse (*samaṇa*), or for the discourse [of such a person].

“In this regard” refers to the statement, “it must be made permissible. “Only seed extracted” means only the seed itself, having been extracted from the fruit and set aside separately. “Therein” refers to the Sutta. The construction is:
“by the monk who is performing it, it must be made. By the phrase “or having said ‘it is permissible,’” it is shown that [the seed] must first be prepared.
This shows that once one has pulled out the fire, the weapon, and the nails, it is not permissible to speak [of them] afterwards.
"Of an iron weapon" means of a weapon made of iron such as bronze and so forth. "By those" refers to the nails of humans and others. "By those" refers to the hooves of horses and others.
"By those" refers to the nails of elephants. "By which" refers to the nails. "Even by those produced therein" means even by those produced in that very weapon.
The connection is with the word "nakhehi" (with nails).
"Therein" (*tattha*) refers back to the preceding statement; it refers to the statement beginning with "by one making [it] allowable" (*kappiyaṃ karontena*).
If one thinks, "I will make sugarcane allowable," one pierces only the sugarcane, let alone [other things]. If one thinks, "I will make wood allowable," [one pierces] the sugarcane...
He pierces it; or he pierces wood itself, thinking, "I will make the wood allowable. They say this is permissible because they are joined together as one.
"That" refers to the rope or the creeper. "All broken pieces" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Therein" means among the pepper preparations.
"Kaṭāha" is the name for a particular type of vessel; however, here it is used because of its similarity to that [vessel] by virtue of being a container for seeds.
The fruit and the wood are called the "cauldron" (*kaṭāha*). "Bound together" means bound together with the cauldron. "Those" refers to the grasses.
"By that" refers to the rolling of the tree and so forth. "Therein" means in that place of setting down or throwing down.
The phrase "In the commentary on the offense of a human being" is a common noun construction for the word "stated. The connection is: "the monk is overwhelmed. "Opāta" means...
In a pit. For that is called an "abyss" (*opāta*) because it is a place for falling down. "A tree" means a tree that overhangs.
"The ground" means the firm ground of the abyss. "For the sake of life": this is the nominative case used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is "for the purpose of life.

The word "by a monk" (*bhikkhunā*) functions as the agent of the verb "should cause to be removed" (*nikkhāmetuṃ*), whether as the natural agent or the causal agent. "The monk who is overhanging" (*ajjhotthaṭabhikkhu*).

Or rather, the phrase “a monk who has fallen into misfortune” (*opātabhikkhu*) should be supplied to complete the legal act (*kamma*). “Therein” (*tattha*) means in the state of non-offense, or regarding the state of non-offense.
“Of this” (*etassa*) refers to the sutta. The connection is: “but another performs it out of compassion. “This too” (*etampi*) refers to the compassion as well.
“For” (*hi*) means truly, or because. First [section].
2. The Training Rule on Speaking Otherwise (Aññavādaka-sikkhāpada) 94.
Regarding the second [term], *anācāra* means that which is not to be practiced: the transgression of the doors of body and speech.

Because the word *sabba* has an indefinite sense, he says here that it refers to "speech" (*vacana*), namely, "one thing by another speech. *So* refers to the bhikkhu; the connection is with the verb *vadati* ("speaks").
*Ko*: Which person? *Kinti*: What [offense]? *Kismim*: In what matter? *Kinti*: What [formal] act? *Kaṃ*: Whom? *Kinti*:

What statement? *Ettha*: In this context, namely in the Pāli passage beginning with "Who has fallen into [an offense]? The word "by the monks" (*bhikkhūhi*) is the agent for the word "spoken" (*vutto*). *Asāruppaṃ*: Unbecoming.
It is unbecoming for monks. "This" (eso) means this matter; "non-existence" (vibhavo) is the meaning.

"That" (etaṃ) refers to the object. The connection is: "being one who speaks, he evades with one thing after another. "Therein" (ettha) means in a concealed seat. "The ear" (sotaṃ) is the ear-door. "The eye" (cakkhu) is the eye-door.

98. *Aññaṃ* means another matter not asked about, distinct from the matter that was asked. Since this is a designation of the agent (*kattuniddesa*) where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant, he says:

"This is the name for evading one thing with another. *Tuṇhībhāvassa* means of silence, of not speaking. He says "let him bring forward" (*āropetu*), because the prefix *ā-* has been elided in the grammatical indication.
The same applies to the word "not brought forward" (*anāropite*). Therefore he says: "when it has not been brought forward."
101. This refers to the act of speaking otherwise, harassing, or causing injury. *Assa* means "might be" or "is. 102.

*Kiṃ* means "what kind of speech. *Yena* means "by which disease"; the construction is that such a disease exists in the mouth, such that one is unable to speak. *Tappaccayā* means "on account of that," i.e., because of the reason already mentioned.
This is the second [section]. 3. The Training Rule on Causing Resentment (*ujjhāpanaka-sikkhāpada*).

103. Regarding the phrase "they cause the monks to grumble": here, because the monks are the agents of the action (*kāritakamma*), the word "monks" (*bhikkhū*) is used in the accusative case to express the agent;

thus he says, "by those monks. Furthermore, showing that the vowel *u* is a modification of the vowel *o*, and that the sound *jhe* has the meaning of "knowledge," he says, "they cause [them] to despise.
The phrase "that venerable one" (*taṃ āyasmantaṃ*) is the object (*dhātukamma*) for the verb "they cause to despise."
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *jha* carries both the sense of looking and the sense of thinking; therefore, he says, “causing them to look,” and so forth.
“Therein” refers to the phrase “they cause the bhikkhus to grumble. “For the sake of desire” means for the purpose of [arousing] desire.
The meaning is that it serves as an object of affection toward himself in those for whom he arranges lodgings and assigns meals. However, in the Commentary...
“*Chandāyāti chandenā*” is what was stated. By this, the method of changing the grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsanaya*) is expressed.
The meaning is: “out of affection for oneself toward others. “By partiality” means by causing [others] to fall into one’s own faction. 105.

It is called *ujjhāpanaka* because one causes [others] to complain by means of it; it is called *khiyyanaka* because one causes [others] to revile by means of it—showing this, he said: “by whatever speech,” and so forth.
106. To show the connection [of the phrase] “desiring to make disparagement (*maṅku*) of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and approved by the Saṅgha,” he says:
“one who is fully ordained and approved by the Saṅgha,” and so forth. *Sambajjhana* means connection; it should be construed as “it is to be made.
By changing the case endings, the connection is: “desiring to make disparagement of one who is fully ordained and approved by the Saṅgha,” that is, desiring to make infamy.
Showing this, he said: “A change of case-ending must be made. The word “vasena” (by way of) is an adjective qualifying the phrase “a change of case-ending must be made.
Since there is no distinction [between the two], the construction is: “therefore it is called ‘katam’” (it is done). “Tat” refers to the word “khiyyanaka” (one who reviles).
“So ca bhikkhu” means that both the one who censures and the one who reviles are that same bhikkhu. “Atha” means therefore, because of being both a censurer and a reviler.
"Assā" means "of a bhikkhu. "Assā" means "he would be.

In the phrase "he reviles," the word "one who is fully ordained" (*upasampanna*) is the direct object (*dhātukamma*); the word "one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*) is the indirect object (*kāritakamma*).
The word "one who is not fully ordained" functions as the indirect object in relation to the causal action of "reviling. "He censures" (*khīyyati*)...
He says "or of him" and so forth because there is a reversal of case endings due to the expectation of a pure action (*suddhakiriyā*).
"Of him" is connected with "in the presence of one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampanna*). "Him" refers to one who is fully ordained and authorized by the Saṅgha.

Regarding the phrase "not authorized by the Saṅgha," it does not mean not authorized by a motion (*apalokanakamma*), but rather not authorized by the formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*); thus he says "by the ritual proclamation" and so forth.
Showing that it is "not authorized" because it is impossible to authorize two or three [monks] by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*), he said, "In which," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase, "one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) but authorized by the Saṅgha," he said this to show that, since it is impossible to grant authorization to one who is not fully ordained,
the term "authorized" is used here according to previous usage.

“*Kiñcāpi*,” etc. *Taṃ* refers to that which remains in the state of not being fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). *Byattassa* means of one who is competent (*viyatta*). The construction is: “or performed by the Saṅgha.
This is the third [section]. 4.
The First Training Rule on Lodgings (*Senāsana*).
108. In the fourth [verse], "himanta" means simply "winter"; that which is connected with winter is "hemantika. He says "in the winter season" (*hemantakāle*) because it refers to a time.
The connection is "they departed while warming themselves. Since the word *kāla* (time) is a relative term, it requires a correlative;
thus he says "of anyone whatsoever. "By the snowy rain" (*himavassena*) means by both snow and rain.
110. “*Vassiko* (of the rains)” means not having a fixed time; thus it refers to those for whom the time is unfixed (*avassika-saṅketa*).

Although “eight months” is stated in general terms, because it is specified as “for those with an unfixed time,” it should be understood as referring specifically to the winter and summer months; hence he says, “four winter months,” and so forth.
“*Yattha*” means in which tree. The connection is “they do not urinate. In the phrase “or crows,” the word *vā* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).
Therefore he said, "or other birds. "Tasmā" means because he permits it; "tasmā" [is used] for that reason.

"Yattha" means in which tree; the construction is: "having rested there, they go. "Yasmiṃ" means in which tree; the construction is: "having made [their home] there, they dwell. He said "only for eight months" with reference to what is possible;
"in those countries," etc., refers to those regions. "Tesupi" means even in those countries. [This concludes the section on] the avassika-saṅketa.

Thus, speaking from the perspective of possibility, he says “where,” and so forth. “Where” means in those districts. By the phrase “the sky is clear and free from clouds,” he indicates that if the sky is not free from clouds or is not clear, it is not permissible to set [the bowl] down.
The phrase “at such a time” serves as the locative support for the phrase “it is permissible to set [the bowl] down.”
“Even by one who is an open-air dweller” means even by one endowed with the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of living in the open air. The word *api* (even/also) refers back to the tree-root dweller.
Expanding upon the duties, he said, “For him,” and so forth. “For him” means for the open-air dweller. The word *hi* indicates the reason for the expansion.
“Right there” means right on his own private couch (*mañcaka*). The connection is with the phrase “a couch belonging to the Saṅgha. “A woven couch” means a couch made of woven material.

In that case, since even an old bedstead (*purāṇamañcaka*) that has lost its frame is considered priceless, it is said: "An old bedstead may be taken. "Covered with leather" means it is upholstered (*onaddha*);
that very thing is called an "upholstered one" (*onaddhaka*). And the construction is: having taken it and prepared it, it is not permitted to lie down upon it.
"At the wrong time" means at a time other than the rainy season. "Even with four folds" means even with four layers.
"Vaṭṭa" means that clouds revolve during this time; thus it is "vaṭṭula. That very thing is "vaṭṭalika.
A "seven-day vaṭṭalika" (sattāhavaṭṭalika) refers to a seven-day period that is circular; those things of which that is the beginning are "sattāhavaṭṭalikādīni.
By the word "ādi" (etcetera), periods shorter or longer than seven days are to be understood. "Kāyānugatikattā" means because of following after the body.
The meaning is "resembling the body.
"In leaf-huts" means in huts covered with leaves. "Of fellow-monks" refers to monks who are like oneself;
this connects with the word "in the presence of. The construction is "in a place sheltered from rain. "Having hung up" means having suspended; or rather, this [term] itself [means that].
