The recitation: In the phrase “having taken the broom,” the word “broom” is the object not explicitly stated for the verb “having taken”; in the phrase “it should be placed,” it is the object explicitly stated.
“Having washed” means having made the broom clean. “In the Uposatha hall, etc.”—by the word “etc.,” the surrounding cells and so forth are to be included.
The construction is: “by whichever monk should wish to go. “Therein” means in the hall. “Anywhere at all” means...
"In whatever place" means in any location whatsoever. "In its natural place" means in the place where it was originally situated.

"Right there" means in those very same places, such as the courtyard of the cetiya and so forth. "Eating hall" (*asanāsālā*): it is called an *asanā* because they sit (*āsanti*) and eat (*bhakkhanti*) in that hall;
thus, it is an eating hall (*asanāsālā*), meaning a dining hall. "Therein" means while he was sweeping it, in that [hall].
Or, in the reading "the procedure (vatta) must be known": "from the middle" means from the center; "from the pure place" is the meaning.
"Facing the place where one stands" means facing the spot where the one sweeping stands. "The sand must be removed" means that both the dust and the sand are to be cleared away;
the intention is that they should be pushed out with the dust-heap broom (sammuñcanī-salākā). "Outside" means outside of the surface to be swept.
111. Regarding the term *masārakoti*: here the word *iti* is a synonym for a name; thus the meaning is "that which is called *masāraka*. This applies similarly to terms such as *bundikābaddho*.
It is called *masāraka* because the axle-pins (*aṭani*) are inserted there after the foot has been rubbed and pierced. *Bundika* is simply *bunda*, meaning the foot;
that which has its axle-pins (*aṭani*) bound or fastened to that [foot] is *bundikābaddha*. Its foot is like the foot of a crab.
"Of which": this refers to the crab-legged bed. Just as a crab has crooked feet, so too it is said to have "crooked feet.
An *āhaccapādaka* is one whose foot is inserted there after striking and piercing the frame.

An *āṇi* is a front peg. It is called a *mañca* because it supports (*mañcati*) and bears a person. It is called a *pīṭha* because it crushes (*pīṭhati*) and destroys uneven suffering. A *paṇava* is...
"A particular kind of musical instrument" means having made its shape; for that [shape] nowadays is the cross-legged (pallaṅka) form of a Buddha image.
"That" refers to the stool (koccha). "They indeed make it" is the connection [of the sentence]. "In this regard" means in the use of lodgings. "Indeed" (hi) means truly. "That" refers to the stool;
because it is of great value, it is also called a "costly seat" (bhaddapīṭha). "By whom" means by whichever monk.
By the phrase “of one of middle stature,” it excludes one of middling size.
“Therein” refers to the expression “or should go without asking permission. The construction is: “the Elder commands.

Regarding “commands,” since the verbal root *āṇ* itself denotes the sense of sending—which is the causal meaning—the word *āṇāpeti* is synonymous with *sāveti*. “He” refers to the junior monk. “In that manner” [refers to the aforementioned way].
The meaning is: "having done it exactly as stated by the Elder. *Tattha* means "in that place," namely in the daytime resting place or on a bed and chair.

*Tato* means "from the time of placing [the bedding]. Regarding *palibodho*: one lies down (*seti*) bound (*pari-buḍh-eti*), thus it is an impediment (*palibodho*). The prefix *pari-* is an intensifier; through a change in form, it has become otherwise.
That impediment elsewhere refers to a residence and so forth, but here it refers to the bed and such items that have been spread out. *Sāyanti*...
In the evening—this accusative case ending refers to the ground. "The elder speaks" is the connection [of the sentence]. Regarding the word "therein," it means on the bed and chair.
Having said, "He is a fool," he spoke "one who has not mastered the duties" in order to show its meaning:
one by whom the duties have not been mastered is "one who has not mastered the duties," namely the elder. "He threatens" means he terrifies. "In him" refers to the youth. "His" refers to the elder.
"At the very moment of the command" means at the very moment of the elder’s dispatching [the message]. The construction is: "The young man speaks.
The word "the elder" is the agent (*kattā*) for the two phrases "having spoken" and "goes," and it is the object (*kamma*) for the phrase "should be made to do.
"It" refers to the bed and chair, stated thus in relation to the phrase "having prepared. "It" refers to the young man. This is stated in relation to the word "having spoken."
Thus it was said. "Right there" means right on the bed and chair. "His" refers to the Elder. "There" means in the daytime resting place.
"Going elsewhere from the dining hall" means having departed from the dining hall, going to a place other than the spot where the bed and chair were arranged;
this is to be construed with "the Elder. "Right there" means in the daytime resting place itself. "Wherever he wishes" refers to whichever place—

The meaning is "he wishes to go. Regarding "in the interval between the assemblies," the construction is: "when there is an assembly in the interval, without having assembled for the entire day and night.
"There" means in that place. The connection is "the newcomers receive [it]. "From there" means from the time of receiving. "Of them" refers to the newcomers.
"By whom" means by whichever monks, whether they be residents (*āvāsika*) or newcomers (*āgantuka*). "Those" refers to the monks who are seated. Above...
One who causes the recitation of the Pāli text to proceed is an *ussāraka* (a prompter). One who is skilled in a discourse on the Dhamma is a *dhammakathika*.
"In that" refers to either the prompter or the preacher of the Dhamma. "Day and night" (*ahorattaṃ*) means both day and night;
it is a term expressing continuous connection. "In another" is to be construed as: in a monk other than the one who was seated first. "Only within the vicinity" (*antoupacāraṭṭhe yeva*).
"Only when standing within the vicinity defined as the range of a thrown clod"—this locative case is used here in the sense of disregard.
"In all instances" refers to both the section on offenses and the section on non-offenses. 112.

Regarding the phrase "or a mat of *cimilika* grass," etc., the construction should be understood as follows: "the analysis [of the offense] is to be known thus. "That" refers to the mat of *cimilika* grass.
“Uttari attharitabbaṃ” (to be spread out over) is said in order to show that it is an *uttarāsaṅga* (upper covering); thus he says, “What is called an *uttarāsaṅga*,” and so forth.
“On the ground” means on natural ground that has not been prepared with lime or other such materials. “A piece of hide”:
here, because the leather itself is broken off at the edges and cut, it is called a “piece of hide. [Objection: But surely lion skins and the like are not permitted?
He said, "In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)... and so forth. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because it is not seen; therefore.
"Only in carrying away" (*pariharaṇeyeva*) means only in carrying that [object] to various places, having delimited it as "belonging to oneself" or having grasped it as "personal property.
It is called a "foot-wiping cloth" (*pādapuñchanī*) because by means of it the foot is wiped and cleaned; thus, rags made of rope are called "foot-wiping cloths."
Regarding the word "is called," he says, "it is called a 'foot-wiping cloth' (*pādapuñchanī*)," and so forth.
Since the term *phalakapīṭha* is stated by eliding the sound *maya*, he says, "a 'wooden bench' (*phalakapīṭha*) is a bench made of wood.
Or, to show that it means both a plank and a bench, he says, "or else. By this—namely, by the phrase "wooden bench"—it is "included."
In the word *pade*, it is either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the agent (*kattā*). *Bījanipattakaṃ* means a four-sided fan;

it is called a "fan-leaf" because it resembles a bird’s wing, the suffix *-ka* being used in the sense of similarity. The word *ajjhokāse* (in the open air) is the locus (*ādhāra*) for the word *pacitvā* (having cooked).
*Aggisālāyaṃ* means in a hall for cooking with fire. *Pabbhāre* means on a mountain slope resembling a cave. *Yattha* means in which place.
"In which person": by the phrase "it is as if it were one's own private property," he shows that there is no offense. 113.
"Whatever monk is conscientious" or "toward such a monk"—this is the construction.
Having stated "is conscientious," he says "he regards it as his own impediment" in order to show its meaning. "Whoever" refers to the monk who requests permission.
Expanding upon the meaning stated briefly as “Is it troubled by anything? he said, “Even if,” and so forth.
The word *hi* indicates an elaboration. The connection is: “An elder monk takes [it]. “That place” refers to the location where the lodging has been established.
“In calamities” means in misfortunes. This is the fourth [section].
5. The Second Training Rule on Bedding (Senāsana-sikkhāpada) 116.
Regarding the fifth [term], *mañcakabhisī*: a cushion (*bhisī*) to be spread upon a bed (*mañca*) is called a *mañcakabhisī*. The same applies to a cushion for a chair (*pīṭhakabhisī*).
As for *pāvāra* and *kojava*, since these two are stated to be types of coverlets (*paccattharaṇa*), he says "pāvāra," and so forth.
“Stated” means stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). “In the case of the second transgression” means in the case of crossing over the second foot.
“From the lodging” means: if there is one lodging, then from that; if there are many lodgings, then from the very last lodging.
One stone’s throw constitutes the precinct of a lodging, while another [stone’s throw] constitutes the enclosure; thus he said, “two stone’s throws.”
If there are three—a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, and an ārāmika—the sāmaṇera or the ārāmika must not be asked for permission without first asking the bhikkhu.

Then, showing that if there are only two—a sāmaṇera and an ārāmika—the ārāmika alone must not be asked for permission without asking the sāmaṇera, he said: "When the bhikkhu is present," and so forth. When none of the three are present...

In order to show the procedure for taking leave, it is said: “If even he is not present,” and so forth. “By whom” refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*), acting as the agent (*kartṛ*) in the word “caused to be done.
“His” refers to the owner of the monastery. The construction is: “If even he is not present, one should go.
“On stones” means on stone slabs. “If he is able” means if he is capable. “The monk who is able must set [the boundary]” means...

The construction [is as follows]: *te pi* (they too) refers to the lay followers (*upāsakas*), and it is connected with the phrase *na sampaṭicchanti* (they do not accept). *Tattha* (therein) refers to wooden vessels and so forth.

It is called a *pariveṇa* because it is seen (*veṇīyati*) as being surrounded (*pari*) by a boundary. The word *atha kho* (then indeed) indicates a lack of approval toward the word *veditabbaṃ* (should be known).
By the word *āsanne* (near), the sense of the prefix *upa-* in the word *upacāra* is shown to mean "standing near" or "planting nearby."
"He turns back. The construction is: "because it becomes nothing more than a heap of anthills. "Upacikā" means ants;
the meaning is that [the dwelling] crumbles and perishes because of them as its cause. "Senāsana" means a vihāra. "Khāyituṃ" means to eat;
or rather, this is the reading itself. "Taṃ" refers to the bed and chair. Having not assigned the bed and chair within the vihāra, [one should place them] in the vicinity of the vihāra.

In order to show the specific result of the act of laying out [the bedding], he said: “But in the vicinity of the vihāra,” and so forth. The connection is: “It was laid out in the vicinity of the vihāra.
Regarding the phrase “by one who is going,” it is the agent for the phrase “should go.

“In the same way” means just as the previous monk does. The construction is: “The bedding should be put away by the monk staying there. “Night-station” (rattiṭṭhāna) means the place where one dwells during the night.
The construction is: "In whatever long hall or leaf-hut is a place where termites arise. *Tasmiṃ* means "in that," referring to the long hall and so forth.
*Hi* means "truly" or "because"; it connects with the word *santiṭṭhanti* ("they settle"). *Siluccayo* means a mountain;
a cave in such a mountain is a *siluccayaleṇa*, meaning a mountain cavern. *Upacikāsaṅkā* means a place where termites arise.
“Suspicion. “From there” means from a dwelling place prepared on a stone slab or on stone pillars.
“The visiting monk who lives in accordance [with the rules]”—this is the connection. “He” refers to that visiting monk. Again, “he” refers to the visiting monk himself.
“From there” means from living there with authority after having taken possession. “Both” refers to both the resident and the visitor.
"Bhikkhus. "In those" means in two or three. "Of the last" means of the very last one. "By the mere act of attention" (ābhogena) means there is no release by mere attention;
the intention is that he must indeed ask for permission. "Elsewhere" (aññato) means from another residence. "Elsewhere" (aññatra) means in another residence.
"Right there" (tattheva) means in the very residence from which [the robe] was brought. "By him" refers to the senior; he is the agent of the word "having accepted" (sampaṭicchite).
"Accepted": they say that even if it has been accepted by the senior [monk], it is permissible for the other to go because he has asked permission.
"Or lost": the construction is that when the lodging has been lost, there is no liability for compensation (*gīvā*).
"Of another": of a person who is not trustworthy. "Lost": when the beds and benches have been lost.
An elder bhikkhu, a powerful spirit (*yakkha*), a lion, a wild beast, and a black snake; [the compound] *vuḍḍha-pe-kaṇhasappā* means those for whom the elder, etc., and the black snake are the first;
[it refers to] among them. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), spirits (*petā*) and so forth are included.
*Yattha* means in which place. *Assa* means of the bhikkhu. The meaning of the word *palibuddho* is...
It is said "afflicted" (*upadduta*) in order to show this. The fifth [section]. 6.
The Training Rule on Intrusion (*Anupakhajja-sikkhāpada*). 119.

In the sixth [rule], "having crowded in" (*rumbhitvā*) means having obstructed, that is to say, having made a barrier. "By seniority" (*vassaggena*) means by the calculation of the years since ordination.

Regarding the term *anupakhajja*: since it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—specifically in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* under root number 15, the *dakārantadhātu*—that the root *khada* signifies "to harm," the word *khada* has the sense of harming.
Showing that approaching closely (*anusamīpaṃ upagantvā*) and harming (*khadanaṃ hiṃsanaṃ*) is indeed entering into close proximity, he says: "having entered into" (*anupavisitvā*).
120. Regarding the word "knowing" (*jāna*), it is stated here—"this is not to be carried out"—in order to show the mode of knowing.

"By that very reason" means by the reason of knowing itself. "Of this" refers to the word "knowing. "For" (*hi*) indicates a detailed explanation. "But the Saṅgha gives" is the syntactical connection.
"To whomsoever" refers to anyone among those who are senior, ill, and so forth. "In this case" refers to among those who are senior, ill, and so on. [This applies] even to one who is ill.
The construction is: "he gives. The word "sick" (*gilāno*) is the object of the two phrases "should not be troubled" and "should be shown compassion.
Because the word "indeed" (*kāmañca*) indicates the sense of favoring, the particle *pana* indicates the sense of censure.

121. The connection is: "the vicinity of beds and chairs. "From wherever" means from any place whatsoever. The construction is: "as far as the bed and chair exist, that is called the vicinity. The connection is: "of the monk standing within that vicinity, [this is] the vicinity."

Regarding the phrase “he sits down or lies down,” the words “or” (*vā*) are used here to indicate the sense of an indefinite alternative; thus it is said, “by merely sitting down,” and so forth. “From this” (*ito*) means from this section.

“Here” (*idha*) refers to this particular section on *pācittiya* offenses. “Just as stated” (*yathāvutto*) connects with the phrase “in this very manner. “In all cases” (*sabbattheva*) means in every instance, including all monasteries and courtyards.
“His” (*assa*) refers to a person of a different gender or class (*visabhāga-puggala*). “Even here” (*idhāpi*) means even in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
“Therein” means: in a trustworthy person.

Regarding the word “in times of distress” (*āpadāsu*) in the text, it should be connected with the supplied word “enters” (*pavisati*); thus he said, “‘In times of distress,’ etc. This is the sixth [section]. 7.
The Training Rule on Expelling.
126. Regarding the seventh [section], the construction is: "those palaces (pāsāda) or those four-halled buildings (catussālā). Those which have four floors are "four-storied" (catubhūmaka).
Likewise for "five-storied" (pañcabhūmaka). "Koṭṭhakāni" means gate-towers (dvārakoṭṭhaka).

The word "ye" is stated in reference to the word "palaces," while when the word "four-halled buildings" is referred to, there is a change of gender in the word "yāni. [This applies] to the lodgings (senāsana).
The connection is: "By a single application, he causes a monk to pass through many doors. The construction is:

"For one who causes a monk to pass through various doors by means of various applications. By the phrase "by the counting of doors," it is made known that the meaning is also "by the counting of applications," since this is evident from the sense.
"Without touching" means without having contacted.
"Ettakāni" means "of this measure. "Tassa" refers to the bhikkhu who is being expelled.

"Gāḷhaṃ" means firmly. 127. "Idhāpi" means in this training rule as well. The word "pi" (also/even) refers back to the previous training rules. "Sabbattha" means in all training rules. "Yatra" means in whichever training rule. 128.
"So" refers to the bhikkhu who creates discord and quarrels. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Pakkhaṃ" means one's own side.
[Regarding] the section on the person being expelled: it should be connected as "if one expels or causes to be expelled a person who is insane [from the side of those being expelled].
Regarding the section on the person who expels: it should be connected as "there is no offense for one who is insane. This is the seventh [section]. 8.
The Training Rule on the Upper Story (Vehāsakuṭi).
129. Regarding the eighth [case], because its floor is not covered, it is "above" (*upari*) and "in the air" (*vehāsa*); thus, it is *uparivehāsā*.
Since that is a hut (*kuṭī*), he says "of the hut situated above in the air" (*uparivehāsakuṭī*) to show this.
To demonstrate the actual form of that hut, he says "of a two-storied hut," and so forth. The word "bed" (*mañca*) should be connected with the prefix "towards" (*abhi*).
He says, "having overcome. Or rather, it should be construed with the verb "sits down" (*nisīdati*); thus he says, "or in the sense of a locative," and so forth.

Here, the word "this" (*etaṃ*) refers to the expression "the bed" (*mañcaṃ*), which is in the accusative case. Alternatively, "this" refers to the word "bed" (*mañcaṃ*) itself, which possesses the accusative ending.
And here, in the latter connection, the prefix *abhi-* is merely an ornament of the word, a mere embellishment of the term.

He said: "‘Abhi’ means ‘this indeed,’ and so forth. Regarding "for the sake of beautifying the word," the intended meaning is for the purpose of the word’s ornamentation or embellishment—that is, for the purpose of making the word blossom.
Regarding "having descended" (*nipatitvā*), he says "having fallen" (*patitvā*) because here the prefix *ni-* follows the sense of the verbal root.
Alternatively, since it expresses the sense of "going out," he says "or having gone out" (*nikkhamitvā*). By this [explanation], the prefix *ni-*...
It illuminates the specific meaning of the verbal root; the sense is "having gone out and fallen. *Hi* means "because. *Āṇī* means "the upper pin. 131. The construction is:
"That hut which does not touch the head is called 'not touching the head' (*asīsaghaṭṭā*).
By the phrase "of one of medium stature," it excludes one of medium strength. "By all those below" means by those situated beneath all the building materials.
“Tulāhī” means by means of specific pieces of wood placed upon the house pillars for the sake of expansion.
By this statement from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), the actual form of the *tulā* is made clear. However, some describe the actual form of the *tulā* differently.
The connection is that it is shown by the phrase “not striking the head of a man of medium height. “Hi” means truly. Any hut whatsoever—
The construction is: "it is said. "Above" means on a floor above the ground within a two-storied hut;
"with an uncovered ceiling" means with a roofless ceiling, which is to say, without a canopy. "But here," however, refers to this training rule (sikkhāpada).
133. "For" (hi) means truly, or because. "Which" (yāyaṃ) refers to this hut. "Therein" (tattha) means in that hut which strikes the head.
The construction is: "by a monk who has not bent down. "Of which" refers to the hut. "Not to be used" means it should not be utilized;
the sense is that it is not fit for use. "Patāṇī" means a pin or wedge for preventing falling, a front stake.
For it is called a "pin" (āṇī) because it leads to binding and causes movement. "Where" means on which bed or chair. "Do not fall out" means they have come forth.
Having offered [the oblation], they do not fall. *Āhaccapādaka* means having struck and pierced a structural member, and then inserting a foot (pillar-base) therein.

Regarding *nāgadantakādisu*: it is like the tusk (*danta*) of an elephant (*nāga*), hence *nāgadantaka*; the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of similarity. Those of which this is the first are *nāgadantakādayo*;
[the phrase refers to] among those. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), things such as wall-peg supports (*bhittikhīla*) are included. This is the eighth [section].
9. The Training Rule on Large Dwellings (Mahallakavihārasikkhāpada) 135.
Regarding the ninth [rule], "of the door-frame" (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa): this refers to the door-post.
For it is called a *piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa* because it possesses a joining (*saṅghāṭa*)—meaning a connection or meeting—of two door-panels upon its back (*piṭṭhe*). It is stated thus in the *Kurundi*.
The connection is as follows: the construction is "it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. "That" refers to the statement spoken in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
The same applies here in the phrase "that very [thing]. "For" (*hi*) means "truly" or "because. "By the Blessed One too" (*bhagavatāpi*) is to be construed as:
"it was not only stated by the teachers of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, but it was also performed by the Blessed One. This is because the bolt is invariably concomitant with the closing of the door.
Even when "for the purpose of setting up the bolt" (*aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya*) is stated, the meaning must be understood as "for the purpose of setting up the door-fastening together with the bolt";
thus he said, "for the purpose of setting up the door-fastening with its panels. *Aggaḷo* means a door-panel.

"With reference to this very matter" (*imamevatthaṃ*) connects to "with reference to this very matter spoken by me. "In this" (*ettha*) refers to the expression "for the purpose of setting up the bolt."
“Intention” (*adhippāyo*) means the Blessed One’s underlying purpose. The word “for” (*hi*) indicates an elaboration. “Shakes” (*kampati*) means it shakes violently.
“Trembles” (*calati*) means it trembles slightly. “By that” (*tena*) means by that cause of falling due to looseness.

Since there is no connection for the phrase “for the purpose of fixing the bolt” (*aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya*) in either the matrix (*mātikā*) or the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*), the words beginning with “therein” (*tattha*) are stated in order to show its connection.
The connection is: "In this and that [place]" is not stated in the phrase "for the purpose of fixing the bolt. *Atthuppatti* means the arising (*uppatti*) of a matter (*attha*), which is the cause;
it is called *aṭṭhuppatti* by changing the letter *tth* to *ṭṭh*. It should be understood from the context—that is the construction.
As for the phrase "the statement which was spoken," that is the connection. "Of which" refers to the Mahāvihāra. "Above" means above the door.
“In three directions” means on both sides; “above” means in the third direction. “There too” means even in a small dwelling.
“Even if the precincts are not complete” means even if the precincts are not complete on all sides by the measure of a door-width. “By the highest limit” means by the maximum measure.
The intention is that it should not be plastered beyond the reach of the hand. Only in three directions.
"It need not be plastered" means that if there is a space for plastering, it should be plastered even on the lower part; thus he said, "But if [there is] of it," and so forth.

"Of it" refers to the monastery (*vihāra*). Regarding the term "light-openings" (*ālokasandhi*), which means they connect with or close off the light, he said, "The window-panels are what are called [this]," showing that by "light-openings" only the window-shutters are meant.
It is called a "window" (*vātapāna*) because it drinks the wind; it is a door. In that—
The door-panels and the window-panels are fixed. The connection is: "those [window-panels] strike. "Therein" means in the light-opening.
"In all directions" means on both sides, below, and above—thus in the four directions.

The word "therefore" (*tasmā*) is the reason for the two phrases "it should be plastered" or "it should be caused to be plastered. "Therein" refers to the phrase "for the preparation of the light-opening."
"By this" means by this white color and so forth. "All this" refers to all this beginning with the white color.

"Which" refers to the task (*kicca*). The connection is: "the task that is to be done. Although the word *dvatti* is separated by other words, it forms a compound with the word *pariyāya* through the use of a distributive term;
thus he says, "the two or three ways of covering. This means two or three ways combined together.
In the compound *dvatti-pariyāya*, it is a *digu* (numeral) compound; when the word *ti* follows, the letter *a* replaces the *i* of *dvi*. *Parikkhepo* means a gradual encircling.
Because the prefix *apa-* expresses negation, the phrase “not on greenery” (*aharite*) is stated. “In this” refers to the word “not on greenery” (*apaharite*).
The connection is that [the term] “greenery” (*harita*) is intended here. It occurred prior to cultivated food during the period of the primordial eon (*ādikappa*).
*Annaṃ* is the first crop; *aparaṇṇaṃ* is the food that occurs after the first crop.
The two instances of the letter *na* have been changed to the letter *ṇa*.

It is precisely because it is intended in this sense [of "planted"] that it is said to be "sown" (*vuttaṃ*), just as in the passage, "The Blessed One became Sumedha," where even though he had not yet attained enlightenment, he was still called a "Bodhisatta."

The Blessed One is called "Sumedha" because he will certainly become so; likewise, even a field that has not yet been sown is called "sown" because it will certainly become so—this is the meaning shown by the passage beginning with "In whatever field... and so forth.

The phrase "only in one that is unsown" (ahariteyeva) is to be construed as "in a field devoid of being sown. "There too" (tatrāpi) means even in a field that is unsown. The word "of the backbone" (piṭṭhivaṃsassa) [is used].
In the phrase “*passe*,” the genitive case has the sense of identity (*sāmi-attha*), by which he indicates the natural house.

In the phrase “*kūṭāgārakaṇṇikāyā*,” the genitive case has the sense of identity, [meaning] “above, on the pinnacle”; by this he indicates a multi-storied building or similar structure possessing a single peak.
The connection is “the standing bhikkhunī. The construction is: “any person whatsoever who is sitting. “*Tassa*” refers to that place where she was standing.
"Anto" means inside; for this space is the place where [the roof] falls—this is the construction.
136. Regarding the term "chāditaṃ": here the word *chādita* has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvattha*); therefore he says "covering" (*chādana*).
"Ujukameva" means straight up from the point where the covering was placed. "Taṃ" refers to the covering. "Apanetvāpi" means even after having removed it, that is, destroyed it. "Tasmā" (therefore).
Because it is obtained, therefore one should depart; this is the connection. "By means of a fence" (*parikkhepena*) is to be construed with "covering by means of a surrounding [enclosure].

"In this case as well" (*idhāpi*) is to be construed with "having made a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*) even regarding covering by way of a stratagem. "Having become silent" (*tuṇhībhūtena*) means having become silent.
"Above the covering" (*chadanupari*) means on top of the covering. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. Regarding the phrase "if beyond that" (*tato ce uttariṃ*), here "from that" (*tato*)...
Showing that it is "above" by way of two or three sequences, he says: “or of three paths,” and so forth. 137.

Since it is to be reaped, cut, gathered, or taken with the hand (*kara*), it is called *karāḷo*; thus, according to the *Atthapakaraṇa* and other sources, it refers to a handful of grass. Therefore, he says: “of a handful of grass. Ninth. 10.
The Training Rule on Living Beings (*Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada*).

140. Regarding the tenth [offense], since it refers to a group such as those going along, he says “knowing. That which contains living beings (*pāṇa*) therein is “with living beings” (*sapāṇaka*). “This” refers to the water.
Whether one knows it oneself or causes another to know it, it is indeed called “knowing”;
thus he says “in whatever way. In the phrase “water with living beings,” this accusative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; therefore he says “by that.”
“With water. “Formerly” refers to the training rule concerning digging the earth and others.
“Therein” refers to the phrase “should sprinkle or cause to be sprinkled. “Stream” means a flow. “Facing the channel” means facing toward the channel.
“In this and that place” means in various locations. “He leads it from one place to another place” means he carries it from one spot to another.
The construction (*yojanā*). Regarding the statement “water containing living beings,” although it is a general term, it is restricted to a specific instance;

and since a specific [term] need not be explicitly employed when its meaning is already implied by the context, he says “this, however,” etc., in order to show that what is intended here is water as a specific kind.
The connection is: “this, however, was not stated. As for the word “water” (*yaṃ*) in the phrase “it goes”:
The doer. "Where" means in which water. The tenth [chapter].
The second section, the Chapter on Living Beings.
3. The Chapter on Exhortation.
1. Commentary on the Meaning of the Instructional Training Rule (Ovāda-sikkhāpada) 144.
Regarding the first [rule] in the Chapter on Nuns (Bhikkhunīvagga): "Of them" refers to the elders (theras). The construction is: "having gone forth after leaving great families. The connection is:
"the daughters of noble families speak of their existing virtues. The phrase "of the kinsmen and people" (ñātimanussānam) [is to be understood].
In the word *kathayanti*, the case is the dative. "From whom? means "from which elder (*thera*)? This is the sense. "Of them" is connected with "the qualities of the elders.

Regarding the phrase "existing qualities," although one might have said "qualities that exist" in view of the word "to tell" (*kathetuṃ*), it was instead stated as "possessing existing qualities" (*vijjamānaguṇā*) in view of the word "are found" (*vaṭṭanti*). "Hi" means "truly" or "because. "Tato" [means]...
The connection is: "They brought [the robes] for the sake of speaking. "By that" means by the cause of bringing them.
"Of them" refers to the group of six (chabbaggiyā). "In them" refers to among the bhikkhunīs. The word "bhikkhunīs" is the object of the verb "having approached.
The group of six's approaching the bhikkhunīs was due to craving for gain; [as for] the bhikkhunīs...
The visiting of the group-of-six monks occurs due to their fickle minds; this is the distinction between those who visit one another.
By saying “animal-talk,” he shows that *tiracchānakathā* means talk concerning animals—that is, useless talk.
The word “even” (*pi*) in the phrase “even in going on the path to heaven” indicates what kind of talk there might be when going toward liberation. Talk concerning kings is *rājakathā*.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), stories concerning thieves and so forth are included. 147.
"Those monks" refers to the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*); this is how the connection is to be understood. "Those by whom the truth has not been seen" are *adiṭṭhasacca*;
the state of being such is *adiṭṭhasaccatta*. Therefore, the construction is: "having bound them because of their state of not having seen the truth" (*adiṭṭhasaccattā*).

"Regarding the Chabbaggiyas": the connection is that he intends to act by means other than [the usual], namely by a cause designated as "having obtained formal authorization" (*sammuti*) which was not previously obtained. "From another" (*parato*) means in another [place], subsequently, or above;
the construction is that he said this while acting as one who is performing [the rite] outside [the boundary]. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because; for they have never existed before.
The meaning is: "thus, he acts as one who excludes him from that.
*Tattha* means "in the statement beginning with 'I authorize' (*anujānāmi*). Regarding the word *sīlavā*: here, the suffix *-vantu* expresses praise, excellence, and constant connection.
*Tassa* refers to the one who has received the formal authorization (*sammuti*). *Taṃ* refers to the virtue (*sīla*). [This concerns] the words *pātimokkha* and *saṃvara*.
In order to show that [the compound] has the nature of a *kammadhāraya*, and that the word *saṃvuta* [in the phrase] *tehi saṃvuto* has the nature of a *tappurisa*, it is said:
“*pātimokkhovā*,” and so forth. In this context, it should be understood that the word *eva* indicates the nature of a *kammadhāraya*, while the word *ena* indicates the nature of a *tappurisa*.

It “proceeds” (*vattati*) means it causes the personal existence (*attabhāva*) to continue. For the *kārita*-suffix has here become invisible. By this, the maintenance of the postures (*iriyāpathavihāra*) is shown.

Among the four dwellings—the divine dwelling (*dibbavihāra*), the sublime dwelling (*brahmavihāra*), the noble dwelling (*ariyavihāra*), and the dwelling in postures (*iriyāpathavihāra*)—this demonstrates the dwelling in postures as the manifestation of one’s personal existence.
"Hi" means truly. "Etaṃ" refers to the statement: "He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Vibhaṅge" means in the Jhāna-vibhaṅga.
The eight terms beginning with "sīla" share a common grammatical basis (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). This, however, is the connection here: virtue is of the wholesome...
It is the foundation for the attainment of states (*dhamma*), the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the control, the liberation, and the complete release.
"For the attainment" means for the purpose of attaining. The seven terms beginning with "endowed" (*upeto*) are synonyms for one another.

In this context, "endowed" (*upapanno*) means joined or devoted. "Possessed" (*samannāgato*) means having come from all sides, repeatedly; thus he is "possessed," that is, he has become fully equipped.
The meaning is as follows. Here, the prefix *sam-* expresses the sense of "all around," and the prefix *anu-* expresses the sense of "not cut off.

"By that" means by that reason. "He protects" (*pāleti*) means he guards the personal existence (*attabhāva*) from harm. "He sustains" (*yapeti*) means the personal existence continues. "He maintains" (*yāpeti*) means he causes the personal existence to continue.
For in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), the root *yapa* signifies "maintaining," and "maintaining" is defined as "continuation."
It is stated [in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* under the root beginning with *p*, No. 18]: "In the word *viharati*, the particle *iti*, which expresses the sense of 'thus', is indicated as being elided;
or rather, the construction is *iti vuccati* (it is said thus) or *iti vuttaṃ* (it is spoken thus).
Demonstrating that the words *ācāra* and *gocara* form a *dvanda* compound, and that the word *sampanna* forms a *tappurisa* compound with them:

He said: “Endowed with proper conduct and resort,” and so forth. Therein, by the word *ca* (and), he indicates a copulative compound (*dvanda*), and by the word *ena*, he indicates a tatpuruṣa compound.

The word *aṇu* means "small," and the word *matta* means "measure"; thus he said, "in even small matters. By the phrase "one whose nature is seeing" (*dassanasīlo*), he shows that in the word *dassāvī*, the suffix *-āvī* has the sense of "one who is habitually so" (*tassīlattha*).
Regarding the term *samādāya*, [it refers to] the root *ā* preceded by the prefixes *saṃ* and *ā*.
Because the word *dāsa* (slave) requires an object of action, it is said "that and that training rule" (*taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ*) in order to show that object.
By this, he shows that in the phrase "in the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Alternatively, "in the training rules" is a locative used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); he shows that the object, namely "that and that training rule," must be supplied.
Regarding the phrase “having taken up” (*samādāya*): in order to show the meaning of the prefix *saṃ*, the root *dā* preceded by *ā*, and the letter *y*, it is said “having grasped thoroughly.
“In this” refers to this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). The construction is: “But the detailed exposition (*vitthāra*) should be grasped.
“He” refers to the son of good family (*kulaputta*).
"Assa" means "of one who has received permission. The construction is: that which is called "much heard" (bahu-suta) is not merely the hearing itself.
"In a casket" (mañjūsāyaṃ) means in a box; for it is called a "casket" because it is thought to contain the wealth of its owner.
The construction is: just as jewels are accumulated in a casket, so too is what has been heard accumulated in this person.
By this [phrase], namely the word “accumulated,” it is shown—this is the connection. “He” refers to the monk who has received formal authorization.
“Just like one who has accumulated jewels” means as if for one who has accumulated jewels. “That” refers to the statement beginning with “those things which.
“In this” means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “For him” means for the monk who has received formal authorization. “Therein” [refers to] “by speech...”
In the passage beginning with "well-cultivated" (*paricitā*), the construction should be understood as follows: "the meaning is to be known thus. "Skilled" (*paguṇā*) means straight.

For that which is straight is called "skilled" in the sense that it is an outstanding (*pakaṭṭha*) and supreme (*uttama*) quality because it is not crooked. "Contemplated" (*anupekkhitā*) means having approached again and again, it has been looked upon;
the meaning is "seen" or "observed. "From the meaning" (*atthato*) means from the expressed meaning; the meaning is "from the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathāto*).
“By way of cause” means by way of the Dhamma; that is the meaning of the word *pāḷito*. Because the word *diṭṭhi* is a synonym for *paññā*, it is stated as “by wisdom.
“Well-made manifest” means well-proclaimed, having been made directly before the sense faculties.
In the phrase “one of great learning,” in order to show the threefold nature of one who is greatly learned, he says “this, moreover,” and so forth. By way of support.
One who releases from dependence is a *nissayamuccanaka*. One who attends upon an assembly is a *parisupaṭṭhāka*. One who exhorts the bhikkhunīs is a *bhikkhunovādaka*.
"Therein" refers to among the three kinds of those who are learned (*bahussuta*). The connection is: "By one who releases from dependence, this much should be mastered.
"Of the full ordination" means having conferred full ordination. "One who has five years [of seniority]" means one for whom there are five years; by him...
The construction is: "should be mastered. "By the very last" means by that which occurs at the end of all limits, being the most inferior.
"Familiar" (*paguṇā*) means not crooked, but straight. "Reached the lips" (*vācuggatā*) is a synonym for that same term.
For when the recitation of the text is familiar to someone during the time of rehearsing, it has reached their lips; or conversely, when it has reached their lips, it is familiar. Therefore...
Those words are synonyms for mutual causality. "On the fortnight days" means on the days included within the bright and dark fortnights.
"For the purpose of proclaiming the Dhamma" means for the purpose of making the assembled assemblies hear the Dhamma;
this is the intended meaning. Regarding the term "sāvanatthāya," it should be understood that because the suffix *yu* follows, there is the elision of the *kārita* suffix.

Therefore, the etymological meaning of *sāvana* should be understood as "that which is caused to be heard" (*suṇāpīyate*) or "that which is made to hear" (*sāvīyate*). The connection is: "The sections for recitation (*bhāṇavāra*) are to be mastered.
"Of those who have arrived" means of those who have come into one's presence. "For the purpose of private conversation" means for the purpose of speaking with a private circle or an embrace;
the meaning is for the purpose of speaking with speech characterized by low sound. This is because it is stated as "the path of discourse" (*kathāmagga*).
Only the discourse on the subject (*vatthukathā*) is intended here, not the recited text of the Canon (*pāḷipāṭha*) known as a *sutta*.

It is called *anumodanā* because by means of it, the donors rejoice (*modanti*) afterwards (*anu*) or repeatedly (*punappunaṃ*). "Ascetic duty" (*samaṇadhamma*) refers to either *jhāna*, the Path (*magga*), or the Fruit (*phala*).
The construction is: "it should be learned for the purpose of performing that. The word "hi" means "truly" or "because. He is unobstructed in the four directions.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied in the sense of "unobstructed" (*apaṭihata-tthe*).

The construction is: "it must be performed by one who establishes the assembly. In the *Abhivinaya*, that is, within the Vinaya Piṭaka which is mutually distinguished [from the Sutta Piṭaka], there are two *vibhaṅgas*:
the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga* and the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*. By the one who establishes the assembly, being unable [to perform it alone]...

The connection is with the word "bhikkhunī" (nun). Having thus shown what should be learned for one's own sake, he now says "But for the sake of the assembly," etc., showing what should be learned for the sake of the assembly.

"In the Abhidhamma" refers specifically to the Sutta Piṭaka as distinguished from the other [Abhidhamma], not to the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. "Three sections" refers to the Sagāthāvagga, the Nidānavagga, and the Khandhavagga.
There are three sections. The word *vā* has the sense of an indefinite alternative. *Ekaṃ* means one particle. *Tato tato* means from each respective collection (*nikāya*).
*Samuccayaṃ katvā* means having made a heap. *Na vuttaṃ* means not mentioned in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
The construction is: "But he for whom it does not exist does not obtain [the benefit]. *Suttante ca* means, moreover, in the Sutta Piṭaka. *Uggahito* means by way of a literal description.
"Seized" means uttered. "Foremost in all directions" means the leader among those such as monks who reside in all directions.
"Going wherever he wishes" means going according to his desire.
"In the four Nikāyas" means in the Dīgha Nikāya and others, excluding the Khuddaka Nikāya. "Of one" means of a certain individual.
"By a single method" means by the method obtained within a single *nikāya*. "Hi" means "truly" or "because.
"Therein" refers to the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on the four treatises (*catuppakaraṇa*). "Various purposes" means various objectives. "That" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"To this extent" means by such a measure of proficiency. "It is" (*hoti*): the word "iti" here signifies completion. The construction is: "Thus the completion should be understood."
"But both of these indeed for him," etc., is the connection [to what] was stated. "In another" means in that which is other than the Vinaya Piṭaka.
"Therein" refers to the statement beginning with "But both of these indeed for him. The construction is: "to show the manner in which they have come down, in whatever way [they were transmitted].
"Free from the faults of repetition and confusion of words" means [free] from those things consisting of the repetition and confusion of words.
[They are] devoid of [proper] syllables. And here, "reversion of words" (*padapaccābhaṭṭha*) means the turning back, the shining-forth, or the slipping away of words;
the meaning is "falling away. "Confusion of words" (*padasaṅkara*) means the failure or destruction of words.
Although it was stated generally as "sutta by sutta," it should be understood specifically as the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra* suttas; thus he said, "from the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra*."
Regarding the phrase *anubyañjanaso*: here, the word *byañjana* denotes both a syllable (*akkhara*) and a word (*pada*). Thus he says, “and for the completion of syllables and words.
The word *hi* means “truly” or “because.
The phrase “of the soft and hard [consonants], etc. is the object of the word “by speech”; the word “by speech” is the object of the word “has arrived at perfection.”

The terms *hetu*, “*vissaṭṭhāya anelagaḷāya atthassa viññāpaniyā*,” are qualifiers for the term “*vācāyā*. By the word “*ādi*” in the phrase “*sithiladhanitādīnan*,” it includes the eight types of phonetic intelligence (*byañjanabuddhi*) known as:
the nasalized (*niggahita*), the released (*vimutta*), the connected (*sambandha*), the determined (*vavatthita*), the long (*dīgha*), the short (*rassa*), the heavy (*garu*), and the light (*lahu*).
By the expression “according to the prescribed method,” [it refers to] those of the grammarians (*akkharacintaka*).
Just as by the expression "speech that burns. It is "made," "spoken," or "uttered" by speech alone; having changed the letter *ca* to *ka*, it becomes *vāk-karaṇaṃ*.
The word *hi* is used for that very reason. Since women delight in the excellence of speech (*sarasampatti*), the construction is:
"therefore she despises" (*hīḷeti*). The phrase "devoid of the excellence of speech" is made a qualification of the word "speech."
In the word *hīḷeti*, it should be understood as a qualifying term included within the cause (*hetu*), because it arises by way of being a cause.

*Sabbāsaṃ* means "of all [the bhikkhunīs]. By the phrase "through the perfection of virtue and conduct" (*sīlācārasampattiyā*), the meaning of birth, clan, physical form, wealth, and so forth is excluded.
*Kāraṇañca* means "and the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathā*). *Tajjetvā* means "having terrified. *Tāsaṃ* means "of the bhikkhunīs. *Gihikāle* means "at the time of being a householder."
The connection is: "He has never previously committed [an offense] while being a householder during his time as an exhorter of bhikkhunīs. For that alone is appropriate.

The word "mātugāmo" (a woman) is the simple agent (*suddhakattā*) with respect to the verb "na karoti" (does not do), and it is the causal agent (*hetukattā*) with respect to the verb "uppādeti" (arouses).

The construction is: "even for the preaching of the Dhamma by a standing bhikkhu. The particle *api* has the sense of censure (*garahattho*). "By those who are unsuitable" (*visabhāgehi*) means by those who are discordant.
By means of robes and objects. In an improper place means in a location unsuitable for those who have gone forth. Lust and passion means powerful craving. By that means by that cause.
In the passage beginning with “And herein,” this is the summary:
“Virtuous and learned, well-versed and eloquent;”
“Dear, capable, and not yet consumed—these are the twenty.

(148) Regarding the phrase *vatthusmiṃ*: it refers to the origin story (*aṭṭhuppatti*). Because the letter *ka* has been elided, they are called *garudhammā*; thus he said, “by means of heavy matters (*garukehi dhammehī*)”.
*Te* refers to those heavy matters. *Hi* means because. As for the word *ekato*, which was stated in a general sense, [it is now specified] by way of distinction...
It is stated, "in the presence of the bhikkhunīs," in order to show that [the offense] must be confessed.

"In accordance with the basis" (*yathāvatthuka*) means precisely a *pācittiya* offense. For it is called "in accordance with the basis" because it occurs in conformity with the basis, which is the cause for the offense.
149. "Early morning" (*pāto*) means before [noon], that is, first; the connection is with "that which ought to be swept but has not been swept. Regarding the failure to sweep...
Making the fault evident, he said, “*Asammaṭṭhaṃ hi*,” and so forth. *Hi* indicates the making of that [fault] evident. *Taṃ* refers to the pariveṇa.
The connection is with the words “having seen, they might be. *Tenā* means by that very reason for being, as if they were unwilling to listen.

Having shown the benefit of sweeping the pariveṇa, he spoke [the following] while demonstrating that same [benefit] regarding the provision of drinking water and water for washing: “From within the village...”
“Panā” and so forth. “Tasmiṃ” means in that drinking water or water for rinsing.
“Sākhābhaṅgampi” means even a branch to be broken off. “Dutiyoti” means with a wise person as a companion.
To show the place where one should sit, he says “nisīditabbaṃ” and so forth. Having stated it generally as “in the middle of the monastery,” he speaks to show the specific location.
It is said: "At the gate. It is called an *osaraṇa* because they descend (*osaranti*) or enter (*avasaranti*) there;
that which is both this and a place is an *osaraṇaṭṭhāna*, and [the word refers to] that. Regarding the term *samaggatthā*: here, the verbal root *gam* is preceded by the prefixes *sam-* and *ā-*.

From that, either the suffix *ttha* belonging to the past tense (*hiyyattanī*) occurs, or the form *ttha* occurs as the suffix *ttha* belonging to the ablative case (*pañcamī*), because it follows a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*).
The prefix *ā* becomes short; thus, in order to show this meaning, he said, "having come together" (*sammā-āgatattā*).
Therein, by the word "together" (*sammā*), he shows the meaning of the prefix *sam*; by the word "onward" (*ā*), the prefix *ā*; by the word "gone" (*gata*), the verbal root *gam*;
and by the word "at" (*ttha*), either the suffix *ttha* known as the past tense (*hiyyattanī*), or the suffix *tha* known as the ablative case (*pañcamī*).
Or it shows the abstract state (*tthatta*). However, this is the meaning here: "You have come together" (*samaṃ tumhe āgatattha*).
When the suffix *ttha*—which is reckoned as the fifth case ending—is applied to the verbal root *thā*, it means "you have come together; may you be" (*samaṃ tumhe āgā attha bhavatha*).

By the word "coming" (*āgacchantī*), he shows the meaning of the verbal root *vat* in the word "occurring" (*vattantī*); by the words "skilled" and "mastered," he shows the intended meaning (*adhippāya*).
"Pāḷī" refers to the Pāḷi of the Garudhammas.
"Tattha" means in that Pāḷi, or in those four [acts] beginning with salutation. "Maggasampadānaṃ" is the giving of space to a bhikkhu by clearing a path for him.
"Bījanaṃ" is fanning with a fan. "Pānīyāpucchaṇaṃ" is asking [if he would like] drinking water.
The request for drinking water. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the request for water for use (*paribhojanīya*) and so forth are included.
"And here" refers to these four acts beginning with salutation (*abhivādana*). The six phrases beginning with "inside the village" serve as the locus for the phrase "must certainly be done.
"For the purpose of clearing the way for the King" means for the purpose of clearing the way for people by the King's authority. A great community of monks (*mahābhikkhusaṅgha*) assembles.
"Herein" means in the Great Assembly; the construction is: "when [the Teacher] was seated in that place, the Great Assembly.
"Rising up" (*paccuṭṭhāna*) means rising beforehand. "That" refers to the act of respectful service.
"Having honored" means having shown esteem; the meaning is, "having shown reverence. Therefore he said, "as it was done," and so forth. Of the three...
"Of duties" refers to the three duties consisting of "having honored, having revered, and having respected.
Since the suffix *-anīya* has the sense of an object (*kamma*), he said, "it must not be transgressed.
A residence where no monk is present is an "abhikkhuka" (monkless) residence; as for how far such a place extends, it is that extent of a residence which is devoid of monks.
He said “if,” etc., because it is indeed so. The word “from the residence” (*upassayato*) is the ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the word “inside” (*abbhantare*).
“Therein” (*ettha*) means in a monastery that is devoid of monks. “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly. “From there” (*tato*) means from a residence situated within half a *yojana*.
“In another” (*paraṃ*) refers to another monastery; this accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. “After the meal” (*pacchābhattaṃ*) means after the meal.
*Therein*: in a residence (*āvāsa*) that is devoid of monks. The word "nuns" (*bhikkhuniyo*) is the object (*kamma*) for the word "saying" (*vadanti*).

*Of the stated measure*: within the stated measure reckoned as half a *yojana*. *Even in a bower of branches* (*sākhāmaṇḍape*): even in a bower covered by branches. By the word "even" (*pi*), it is shown:
"What indeed is the case regarding a residence? *Stated*: inhabited. *To this extent*: for one night.
“By the mere fact of having dwelt. “Therein” means in a residence where monks are present. The construction is: “The nuns who are approaching must request.
“Of the fortnight” refers to the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī. It should be connected with the word “on the thirteenth” by way of the relationship between the whole and its part.
“We” means ourselves. “From which” is to be construed with “by which direct path. Therefore he said, “by that path.”
"By another path" means by a crooked path other than the straight path. "This" refers to this monastery (*āvāsa*). "From there" means from the monastery of the monks or from the nuns' quarters;
the latter is more appropriate, for he will say, "at a distance of a *gāvuta* from our quarters.
"In a secure place" means in a place free from fear. For it is called "secure" (*khema*) because they are freed (*khīyanti*) from fear therein.

Because it is both secure and a place, it is called a "secure place" (*khemaṭṭhāna*) by taking these two qualities together. "By those bhikkhunīs" means by those living at a distance of half a *yojana*.

"Those bhikkhunīs" refers to those living at a distance of one *gāvuta*. "In between" (*antara*) means in the interval or middle between your dwelling place and our dwelling place, or from the dwelling place; it is used here in the sense of a locative case.

This is an ablative expression (*nissakkavacana*). The connection is with the word "standing on the path" (*ṭhite magge*). The word "from the presence of" (*santikā*) is the ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the word "come" (*āgata*).

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the dwelling place (*upassaya*) of other bhikkhunīs. The construction is: "thus she should be requested. "From there" (*tato*) means from the bhikkhus being requested; it connects with the word "further" (*paraṃ*).
"On the fourteenth" means on the day that completes the fourteen days of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī.

"Here" means in this monastery. The word "instruction" (*ovāda*) is the object of the word "following" (*anu*). "Those who live following" means those who, having followed [the instruction], carry out their livelihood and conduct.
This is to be connected with the phrase "spoken to the bhikkhus. "On the second day" means on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī. Now...
“Immediately after departing. “Therein” means in the absence [of the monks] due to their having departed.

By the phrase “having formed the intention,” it is indicated that it is not permissible to stay without forming the intention. The intended meaning is that one must indeed go to a residence where monks are present.
“That” refers to the offense of interrupting the rains-retreat. “For” (hi) means truly, or because. “By some cause” means by such things as the failure to obtain almsfood.

“By some reason. The word *hi* means “truly. To address the question of whether one who is staying in a residence where no monks are present—due to reasons such as the monks having departed—should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony in that very monkless residence, he says: “But for her who is performing the *pavāraṇā,*” and so forth.
Regarding the term *anvaddhamāsaṃ*, here the prefix *anu-* expresses frequency (*vicchā*) and is a verbal noun; because it denotes the application [of the action], [it is used in this sense].
The locative case is used in the sense of "on" or "at," as he said: "every half-month.
Regarding the word *paccāsīsitabbā*, since the verbal root *sidh* preceded by *pati* and *ā* has the meaning of "to desire," he said: "they are to be desired. There is a doubling of the root *sidh*.

It is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) that the prefix *ā* [with *sidh*] means "one who desires. The word *tattha* refers to the expression "the inquiry regarding the Uposatha. [The word] *pakkhassa*...
"Of whichever fortnight. The connection is: "But it is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*.

"Requesting instruction" (*ovādassa yācanaṃ*) is [called] "instruction" (*ovāda*) by the elision of the latter member of the compound; that very thing is the purpose or motive, hence "for the sake of instruction" (*ovādatthāya*).
"From the first day of the lunar fortnight" (*pāṭipadadivasato*) means from the second day. For it is there that the moon moves toward both increase and decrease, or by which [it does so].
"Paṭipadā" is what is said. "Iti" means in the manner thus stated. The construction is: "The Blessed One proclaims.
"Of another" means other than the act of listening to the Dhamma. "Uninterruptedly" means constantly; in the word "paññapeti," it is used as a neuter noun.
"Hi" indicates the detailed explanation. "And this being so" means when there is such great benefit. "Yaṃ" refers to that Dhamma. "Sātthikaṃ" means possessing the goal.

"With purpose" means with a specific aim. "According to the instruction" means in accordance with the instruction given. "All the bhikkhunīs as well"—this is the construction. "Hi" means indeed, truly.
"She goes for the exhortation" means she goes to the monastery of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to request the exhortation.

"The exhortation is not to be gone for" means the monastery of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is not to be gone to in order to request the exhortation. And in the phrase "the exhortation," the accusative case is used in the sense of the dative (or locative).

It must be understood in this way; otherwise, the application of the words would be contradictory. "To go for instruction" means to go to the monastery of the Saṅgha of Bhikkhus for the purpose of requesting instruction.
In the phrase "two or three bhikkhunīs," it is the second case (accusative) in relation to the word "having requested. In the word "should be sent," it is the first case (nominative).
"Approaching for instruction" (*ovādūpasaṅkamana*) means approaching for the purpose of receiving instruction. "The monastery" (*ārāma*) refers to the monastery of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
"From there" (*tato*) is connected with "after going" (*gamanato paraṃ*). "By that bhikkhu" (*tena bhikkhunā*) refers to the bhikkhu who has received the instruction.
"Him" (*taṃ*) refers to the bhikkhu who has been authorized.
“Is able” (*ussahati*) means he is capable. “By the pleasing” (*pāsādikena*) means by bodily, verbal, and mental action that brings about confidence, that generates confidence—this is the meaning.
“Let him accomplish” (*sampādetu*) means let him accomplish the threefold training. “By this much” (*ettāvatā*) means by the mere statement, “let him accomplish by the pleasing.
“For” (*hi*) indicates the result. “This” (*etaṃ*) refers to the expression “therefore” (*tāhi*).
And here, for the bhikkhus, there are three modes of expression according to the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual;
when these three modes of expression are multiplied by the three modes of expression for the bhikkhunīs—according to the Saṅgha, the group, and the individual—there are nine modes of expression.
Showing that arrangement, he said: "In this regard, this is the sequence of the expressions. Therein:
It refers back to the preceding statement. The manner of the statement is indeed clear.

A single bhikkhunī—or one speaking on behalf of many bhikkhunīs sent from various bhikkhunī residences for the purpose of receiving exhortation—says, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs and the noble ladies," etc., demonstrating the manner of the statement. By that too:
the word "exhortation" (*ovāda*) is the object of the word "by the receiver" (*paṭiggāhakena*). Again...

The phrase “exhortation” functions as the object for the phrase “not to accept. One is a fool (*bāla*) because one lives merely by means of inhalation and exhalation, and not by the life of wisdom (*paññājīvita*).
One is sick (*gilāna*) because one suffers and is afflicted. One is a traveler (*gamika*) because one is capable of going;

that is, a monk who is capable of going, who will go, and who will undertake the journey. This, then, is the construction here: [the monk] who is capable of going, who will go, and who will set out on the journey.

Therefore, that bhikkhu is called "one who is going. Alternatively, because a bhikkhu is capable of going and will go—that is, he will undertake the journey—for that reason he is called "one who is going.
The term "capable" (*bhabbo*) is a qualifying attribute included within the cause. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to among the three types of persons beginning with the fool.
"On the second day of the fortnight" (*dutiyapakkhadivase*) means on the second day of the lunar half-month following the first day of the month (*pāṭipada*).
“Uposathagge” means in the uposatha hall. For it is called “uposathagga” because they observe the uposatha there, or because the uposatha is observed within it.

Having shown the indicative [passage] for the statement “should not announce,” he says “another [passage] is also stated,” etc., showing that very same [indicative passage] for the statement “should not bring back.”
*Tattha* means "among those monks who have accepted the exhortation. *No cassa* means "if it should not be so. *Sabhaṃ vā* means "or an assembly hall" (*samajja*).
For it is called a "hall" (*sabhā*) because people speak together there, or because it shines (*bhāti*) with the virtuous;
thus the construction is: "I shall approach that hall. *Tatra* refers to that hall and so forth; the same applies to the word *tattha*.

"Cātuddasa" means one who completes fourteen; the connection is "having performed the *pavāraṇā* on that [day]. "In the community of monks" (*bhikkhusaṅghe*) means in the presence of the community of monks;
here, this locative form expresses the sense of proximity. Regarding "on this very day" (*ajjatana*):

here, "today" (*ajja*) is derived from the word "this" (*ima*) with the suffix *-jj-*, meaning "on this day," and the vowel *a* is substituted for the word "this"; thus, "this very day" is *ajjatana*, for the suffix *-tan-* has the sense of "self" (*sva*).
On another day, from the word *aparañ-ja*, the suffix *-jjapaccaya* is applied in the sense of "a day" (*ahani*), resulting in a locative form.
"Therein" (*ettha*) means in the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), or in the statement beginning with "I authorize" (*anujānāmi*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly.
"Commotion" (*kolāhala*) means a great clamor. "First a bhikkhunī should be requested" means that first a bhikkhunī should be requested by the Saṅgha.

The construction is: "It should be said by that bhikkhunī. "Seeing, he will make amends" means: having become one who sees what is a fault (*vajja*) and what is not a fault (*avajja*), he will make amends.
"Of both" refers to the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī. "In their respective places" means: whatever place is its own proper place, in that very place.
"By some means" means: by some cause or reason. The word *vara*, preceded by the prefix *ava*, has the sense of being closed off or concealed.
He said, "It is closed. "Speech alone" means precisely the speech of exhortation. "Path" (patha): it is called a path because it is the cause for standing in the position of the eldest.
"But the fault" (dosaṃ pana) refers to the disadvantage in advancing and so forth. "They smear" (añjenti) means they defile. The construction is:
"but it is proper for bhikkhus to exhort and instruct."
"Another" means other than the instruction. "This" refers to the *garudhamma*.

Regarding the phrase "in an illegal procedure" (*adhammakamme*), he asks, "What is called a 'procedure'? and replies, "In the case of 'illegal procedure,' etc. Therein refers to among illegal and legal procedures. 152.

When giving the recitation, he says, "there is no offense"—this is the construction. "He reinstates" means he speaks. "In the fourfold assembly" means within the fourfold assembly. "There too" means by that reason of the nuns listening. First [section].
2. The Training Rule on the Cessation of the Mind (Atthaṅgata-sikkhāpada) 153.
Regarding the second [instance], he says "by turn" (*vārena*), because the word *pariyāya* has the sense of a turn (*vāra*).

And since a "turn" is simply a sequence, he says "the meaning is 'in succession'. To show that one whose mind is superior is "one possessing higher mind" (*adhicetta*), he says "of one possessing higher mind," and so forth.
“Higher mind” (*adhicitta*) here refers specifically to the mind of the fruit of Arahatship, not the eightfold meditative attainments that serve as the basis for insight (*vipassanā*);

thus he says, “by the mind of the fruit of Arahatship. For in such passages as “the training in higher mind,” it is the eightfold meditative attainment that serves as the basis for insight which is called “higher mind.
“Not being negligent” means for one who does not neglect. “By constant practice” means by performing [the task] continually.
He is called a *muni* because he reflects upon (*munati*) and knows both worlds; and *mona* is said to be knowledge in the sense of reflecting (*munana*) and knowing (*jānana*).
Showing that one who possesses this is a *muni*, the author says, "He reflects," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "he who reflects...
[and] by means of reflection," he demonstrates the first meaning; by the phrase "*Mona* is said to be... [and] is so called," he demonstrates the second meaning.

Since it is stated in the *Dhātupāṭha* (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, under the root beginning with *pa*) that "muna means to go," one should understand that in the phrase "he who knows (*yo munatī*)" it is the root *muna* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class that is intended,

not the root *mud* belonging to the *kryādi* class. Alternatively, since it is stated in the *Dhātupāṭha* (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, under the *kryādi* class) that "muna means knowledge (*ñāṇa*")...
“*Monātī*” belongs to the *kīyādi* class [of roots]. It should be understood that there is a dropping of the letter *n* at the end of the root.

Furthermore, regarding the statement “*mona* is said to be knowledge (*ñāṇa*)”, here “knowledge” refers specifically to the knowledge of Arahantship. When it is said “the path of *mona* is the *monapatha*,” it is the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) alone that are intended;
thus he says, “in the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment. Alternatively, the trainings in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) and so forth are intended.

He said: "Or in the three trainings. "The preliminary practice" (*pubbhāga-paṭipadā*) refers to the practice consisting of virtue, serenity, and insight, which occurs prior to the knowledge of arahantship.
"In the preliminary stage" (*pubbhāge*) means in the stage preceding the knowledge of arahantship.
"In this context" (*ettha*) refers to the statement: "Of one whose mind is exalted... training. The word "of such a one" (*tādino*) should be construed with the word "of the sage" (*munino*).

He said: "Of such a one, a sage whose taints are destroyed. Regarding the phrase "for such a one there are no sorrows," it is stated "of lust and the rest" in order to show that he is "calmed" because he has pacified lust and so forth.
Because the word *manta* means "possessing mindfulness" (*satimant*), and thus signifies a constant connection with mindfulness, he said: "of one who is not devoid of mindfulness."
It is called *ākāsa* because it is neither ploughed (*kasīyati*) nor scratched (*vilekhīyati*); that very thing is space (*ākāsa*).

It is called *antalikkha* because it must be looked at through an opening in between. For space is fourfold: unclouded space (*ajaṭākāsa*), space revealed by the removal of a kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa*), delimited space (*paricchinnākāsa*), and space as the delimitation of form (*rūpaparicchedākāsa*).

Among these, it is unclouded space alone that is intended here, because of the specific qualification "in the sky" (*antalikkhe*). Therefore he said: "not in the space revealed by the removal of a kasiṇa."
"But not in the delimitation of form. The space that is delimited is also included within the space of the delimitation of form.

The word "me" is the object (kamma) for the word "despising. "Only this much" means only this extent—the very words designated as "of one with over-refined mind" (*adhicetasa*) and so forth—and no other word of the Buddha;
such is the meaning. "This one" refers to the Elder Cūḷapanthaka. "Handa" is used in the sense of "now" or "well then."
This is a particle. The intention is: "I shall show you my power; look, seize it!

"Having emerged" means having emerged from that fourth jhāna. Regarding the phrase "even while disappearing," he says "disappearing even" (*antaradhāyatipi*) to show that the word *pi* (even/also) has the sense of "at the same time.
This same principle applies to the phrase "even while lying down. "The elder" refers to Cūḷapanthaka.
The Elder. This word should be connected to the appropriate places throughout the text and linked with the phrase "he recites that very [verse].
"Of the elder brother" means of the elder Mahāpanthaka, who was his eldest brother.
Regarding the verse beginning with *padma*, three quarters are *indravajrā* and the fourth quarter is *upendravajrā*. Therefore, it is called *padma*.
In this case, when the letter *m* follows, the *u* of *duka* is elided and the following consonant is nasalized; thus, it should be written as "padma" with a doubling of the vowel.
In the word *avītagandha*, the long pronunciation of *vīti* alone is appropriate. It is called *paduma* because it moves or grows in the mud (*paṅke davati*).
It is called *kokanuda* because it pushes away or removes the taking up of foul odors (*kokaṃ duggandhassa ādānaṃ nudati*). It is [called *sugandha*] because it possesses beautiful fragrance.

"Sugandhaṃ. Herein, this is the construction: just as there might be a lotus known as a *kokanuda*—fragrant, blossomed and fully opened by the early morning sun, shining forth with its scent undiminished—so too [is he] like the *Aṅgīrasa*, who shines having become radiant with the essence streaming forth from his limbs, like the sun scorching in the sky.
"He sees the Perfectly Enlightened One shining as it were within the threefold world.
"Paguṇa" means that which has become familiar through recitation. "Tato" means from that which is impossible [to do]. "Naṃ" refers to Cūḷapanthaka. "Thero" refers to the Elder Mahāpanthaka;
the connection is that he had him expelled. "So" refers to Cūḷapanthaka. "Atha" means at that time. "The Blessed One said."

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "With the Buddha-eye" means with the eye of the omniscient Buddhas, which is comprised of the knowledge of the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the degrees of the faculties of others (*āsayānusaya-indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*).
"Him" refers to Cūḷapanthaka. "His" refers to Cūḷapanthaka. "Then" (*atha*) means at that time of reporting. "To him" (*assa*) refers to Cūḷapanthaka;
it is to be connected with "having given" (*datvā*). It is called *rajoharaṇa* because it removes—that is, takes away—dust and dirt (*raja-mala*).
*A pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ* means a piece of rag. *So* refers to Cūḷapanthaka. *Tassa* (of it) refers to the piece of rag;
in the word *antaṃ*, there is a relationship of part to whole (*avayavi-sambandha*). *Parisuddham pi*: the word *pi* (even/also) shows that what need is there to speak of an impure piece of rag?
*Saṃvegaṃ* means agitation, terror, or fear. *Atha* means at that time of undertaking [the task]. *Assa* refers to Cūḷapanthaka. The word *taṃ*...
The construction should be made by connecting it with the phrase “the state of being mine. This is the second [section].
3. The Training Rule on the Nuns’ Quarters (Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada). 162.
Regarding the third [rule], although it is stated in general terms as “she instructs, there is an offense of expiation” (ovadati pācittiyassa), the specific meaning must be understood.
He said: "There is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who exhorts [a nun] by means of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma).

"From this" means from this training rule (sikkhāpada). "In whichever [rule]" means in whichever training rule. "In all those cases" means the application [of the penalty]. This is the third [section]. Miscellaneous Discussion.
"In this" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The connection is: "this incidental matter has been stated.
"Three *pācittiya* offenses" means there is one *pācittiya* because the monk is not authorized, one because the sun has set, and one because he has approached the nuns' quarters;
thus, there are three *pācittiya* offenses. The construction is: "How? meaning by what cause does it come to be? "Therein" means...
To the nuns' quarters. "Of that very one" means of the monk who has been formally appointed. "By another rule" means by a rule other than the heavy rules (garudhamma).
"But during the day" means from the rising of the sun until it has not yet set.
4. The Training Rule on Material Goods (āmisasikkhāpada).

164. Regarding the fourth [verse], "bahukatā" means those by whom much pride (*māna*) has been practiced. To show the meaning that, having become so full of pride, they do not offer instruction, he said, "not being full of pride," and so forth.
"Dhamme" refers to the qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). The construction is:

"the intention" refers either to the phrase "not being full of pride" or to the intention of the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*). The phrase "desiring to act," etc., has a grammatical connection (*vācaka-sambandha*) with the word "the meaning."

The construction is as follows: "one who is not appointed" (*asammata*) should be understood as one who has been set aside. "Appointment" (*sammuti*) refers to the appointment as a teacher of the bhikkhunīs. "Subsequently standing on the level of a novice" (*sāmaṇera*) is the construction.
This is the fourth [section]. 5. The Training Rule on Giving Robes (Cīvaradāna-sikkhāpada) 169.
In the fifth [section], "on the carriage road" (*rathikā*) means on a street. For it is called a "carriage road" because it is suitable for a carriage (*ratha*). "Seen face-to-face" (*saṃdiṭṭha*)...
It is called *sandivṭṭhā* because it was shown by way of bringing [the past and present] together. It is called *mittā* because they are friends merely by being seen.
"The rest" refers to the remaining words following the stated expression. "Therein" means in the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes. "For" (*hi*) indicates a distinction.
"Here" (*idha*) means in this training rule concerning the giving of robes. This is the fifth.
6. The Training Rule on Sewing Robes (Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpada) 175.
Regarding the sixth [rule], "Udāyī": there are three Udāyīs—Mahā-Udāyī, Kāḷa-Udāyī, and Lāḷa-Udāyī. Among them, the third is intended here; thus he says, "Lāḷa-Udāyī.
Since it stands or proceeds by means of its own splendor (*pabhāva*), it is called *paṭṭha*; when this is established, one who is indeed capable (*paṭibala*) [is meant].

It is possible. Therefore he said, “capable. “Skilled” means proficient. By the phrase “a mind fashioned by ingenuity,” he shows that there is an elision of a middle word in the compound “ingenuity-mind” (*paṭibhānacitta*).
“He” refers to Lāḷudāyī; the connection is “he did it. “Of that” refers to the robe.
Regarding the term “just as it was stitched together,” he says “just as it was stitched together indeed,” indicating that the particle *eva* should be supplied here.
176. The construction is: that robe which is capable of being worn as an undergarment or put on as an upper garment is called a "robe" (*cīvara*).
"In this way" (*evaṃ hi*) means "just so. By the word "offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*), he indicates an intermediate offense in the context of the rule:
"If she sews it herself, there is an offense of expiation" (*pācittiya*). *Ārā* means a needle; for it moves and enters by way of its lack of attachment (*nissaṅgavasena*).
“Ārā” is said [to mean a plough]; its path or course is “ārāpatha. In that [context], because it concludes with the act of taking away (nīharaṇa), it is called “nīharaṇe.
“Satakkhattumpi” means many times. “Āṇatto” means one who is commanded; [it is derived from] “āṇāpīyati,” meaning he is being commanded.
Where “āṇāpito” should have been used, the syllable “ṇāpa” is elided and the letter *i* is changed to *a*, and then [the verb] “ādatte” is used as the verbal form.
This was stated by treating the suffix *ta* and the word *te-vibhattiyā* as having a dual nature. Therefore he said: "It is said that one sews a robe once.
Now, however (*atha pana*) means otherwise than that. "Of one who is commanded" (*āṇattassa*) means of one who has been ordered.
