The connection is: "there are also several *pācittiya* offenses."
The construction is: "Those who are dependent sew. The connection is: "while the teachers and preceptors are sewing. "Of them" refers to the teachers and preceptors.
"Of them too" refers to the dependents as well. "The robe of the kinswomen bhikkhunīs" is the connection.
The word "by the pupils" (*antevāsikehi*) is the instrumental object of agency (*kāritakamma*) for the word "have [them] sewn" (*sibbāpentī*). "There too" refers to by the teachers and preceptors.
Regarding "having cause to sew": the word "antevāsike" (pupils) is the simple action (*suddhakamma*) in relation to the word "having deceived";
it is the causative action (*kāritakamma*) in relation to the word "having cause to sew. "The others" refers to the teachers and preceptors. This is the sixth [offense]. 7.
The Training Rule on Arrangements (*Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada*).

181. Regarding the seventh [case], he said, "the bowl and robe of those going behind," because the words "going behind" (*pacchā gacchantīnaṃ*) must be construed with the elliptical remainder of the text, "bowl and robe" (*pattacīvara*). He said, "those bhikkhunīs...
the thieves," having applied a shift in grammatical case (*vibhattivipallāsa*) so that "those bhikkhunīs going behind" is to be construed with the phrase "they violated."

"they defiled. Alternatively, by applying a shift in case endings, one should understand that the word "alms-bowl and robe" (*pattacīvara*) is to be supplied after the word "cut off" (*acchindimsu*), and the reading "virtue" (*sīla*) is to be supplied after the word "defiled" (*dūsesuṃ*).
182–3. Since the verbal root *dhā* preceded by the prefixes *sam-* and *vi-* takes the suffix *-tvā*, it says "having made an agreement" (*saṃvidahitvā*). "Cock" (*kukkuṭo*)...

*Tambacūḷo*. For he seizes (*ādāti*) insects and the like for the sake of food by means of his beak (*kuka*), thus he is a *kukkuṭo* (cock). *Ayanti gāmo*: [the suffix] *ṇa* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*).

Thus it says, "they assemble (*sampadanti*) here. And "here" means in this village. Because the latter member of the compound has the sense of a locus, there is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) with the former member;
hence he says, "of the cocks," and so forth. In this way, the word *ṇa* has the sense of a locus.

Having shown the genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) by means of the preceding phrase, he now says "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) in order to show the meaning of the suffix *ṇa* as "state" (*bhāvattha*) and the external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) by means of the preceding phrase.
"Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the latter reading. "Having flown up" (*uppatitvā*) means having risen and leaped upward into the sky.
"Herein" (*ettha*) refers to the latter reading. "In two ways" (*dvidhā*) means in a twofold manner, namely by way of going on foot and by way of flying through the air.
By the phrase “no conventional designation is obtained,” it is shown that there is no interval between villages; rather, it is but a single village, and therefore the offense is also but one.
“At dawn” means at daybreak. For it is called *paccūsa* because it drives away (*useti*), that is, destroys, the opposing darkness (*timira*).
“While raining” means while thundering. The word “because of the statement” [is connected] with the word “it is indeed an offense.”
The indicative reason (*ñāpakahetu*). "Separated by at least a jewel" means separated by an interval the size of a hen's egg.
"Therein" refers to the expression "from village to village. "For" indicates the detailed explanation.
"Both" refers to the connection that both monks and nuns make an appointment. "They do not say" means the teachers of the commentaries do not state this. Of the four paths...
A *catukka* is a place where four roads meet; a *siṅghāṭaka* is a place where two, three, or more than four roads are interconnected.
"There too" means even when entering the vicinity. "From the village" means from one's own village. "As long as they have not yet entered" is the construction.
"With reference to" means starting from. "Then" refers to that time of departure. "Even both" means both the bhikkhu and the bhikkhunī.
The connection is "they go. "That" refers to the statement. "Indeed" (*hi*) indicates a distinction.

In the first method, "from village to village" means there is no offense (*anāpatti*) for crossing [the boundary], but there is an offense (*āpatti*) for entering [the village]; this is the distinction. 184. "In a place previously visited" (*gatapubbattha*):

the meaning is that it is a place where one has gone before. The construction is: "He says, 'Come, let us go,' or 'You should come. "For the purpose of worshipping a cetiya" means for the sake of worshipping a stupa (*thūpa*).
185. Regarding the phrase "by a breach of appointment" (*visaṅketena*): here, there are three kinds of breach of appointment—a breach of time, a breach of door, and a breach of path.
Among these, he said, "If they go by a breach of appointment, there is no offense," with reference specifically to a breach of time as the basis for non-offense.
There is no release from an offense through a breach of door or a breach of path. Demonstrating this point, he said:
“Before the meal,” and so forth. “Mounted on a wheel” means properly mounted upon either the wheel of postures (*iriyāpatha-cakka*) or a cart-wheel (*sakaṭa-cakka*).
“Districts” (*janapada*) refers to divisions of people. “They go around” (*pariyāyanti*) means they go and come again and again. The seventh [section]. 8.
The Training Rule on Boarding a Boat.
188. In the eighth [verse], *aññamaññaṃ thavanaṃ* (mutual praising) is *abhitthavanaṃ*; it is what is meant by "association" (*santhavo*), which is to say "meeting" (*saṅgamo*).

Association by way of friendship is "friend-association" (*mittasanthavo*). That which is to be enjoyed by the world and is also that friend-association is "world-enjoyment-friend-association" (*lokassādamittasanthavo*).
One who has mastery over that, or one who is dependent upon it, is "one who has mastery over world-enjoyment-friend-association" (*lokassādamittasanthavavaso*).
By that [term]. To show that it "goes upward" (uddhaṃgāminī), he said "upward" (uddhaṃ) and so forth. And here, "upward" means against the current (paṭisota).

Therefore he said, "against the current of a river. Connecting the summary phrase (mātikāpada) "going upward" with its word-commentary (padabhājaniya) "upstream-bound" (ujjavanikāya), he said "because," and so forth.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu. "From upstream-velocity" means from going against the current.
"By that" means by that cause. "Assa" refers to the word "going upwards. Since "downstream" here means "downwards," he said "downstream.
"Assapi"—the particle *pi* (also/even) refers back to what precedes. "Therein" refers to the statement "whether going upwards or going downwards.
"Yam" connects with "they carry the boat. "For the purpose of steering properly" means facing correctly toward the opposite direction.
The meaning is "for the purpose of making [them] straight" or "for the purpose of inducing uprightness. "Therein" means "in the boat.

He said, "having set aside," considering the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*), that it is an ablative used in the sense of the accusative. When the heading term (*mātikāpada*) "elsewhere" is considered, the ablative is indeed appropriate in the sense of the ablative.
189. “One bank is a forest without a village” is the construction [of the sentence]. “There are *pācittiya* offenses by the calculation of half-yojanas” is the connection.

The word “also” (*pi*) in the phrase “even when traveling by way of the middle” indicates that one might ask: what indeed would be said regarding traveling along the side of a bank in a forest without a village?
The construction “not only by a river” means that there is no non-offense (*anāpatti*) not only in the case of a river, but also in other cases such as the ocean and so forth.
The intended meaning is "there is no offense. The connection is "even that monk who goes.
*Hi* means "truly" or "because. 191. There are three kinds of appointment: appointment regarding time, appointment regarding a landing place, and appointment regarding a boat.

Among these, with reference to the absence of an offense due to an appointment regarding time, it is said: "If they board by appointment. If they do so by any other appointment, there is indeed an offense.
Showing this meaning, he said, “In this case also,” and so forth. This is the eighth [section]. 9.
The Training Rule on Those Who Have Reached Maturity (Paripācita-sikkhāpada).
192. Regarding the ninth [rule], “while the Great Nāgas are present”: while the Great Arahants are standing there, being present; [and] among the novices who are like servants or messengers.
The intention is that he invites the bhikkhus. "Otherwise" means in another manner, either by a change of case-ending (*vibhattivipallāsa*) or by supplying an ellipsis (*pāṭhasesa*).
Showing that "intermediate talk" (*antarakathā*) refers to talk that has reached the middle or the interval, he says "the conclusion," and so forth.
It is called "prepared" (*pakatā*) because it was scattered; when it is said "not prepared" (*na pakatā*), meaning "unfinished," he says "being performed" (*kariyamānā*).
“...occurs. *Addhacchikena* means with half an eye. *Tehī* refers to those elders (*theras*). 194.

*Laddhabbaṃ* means what is worthy of being obtained. Regarding the phrase *assā* (“of it”), he says “it is called ‘well-commenced’” (*samāraddhaṃ vuccati*) in order to show that *samārambho* means “that which is to be properly commenced. *Paṭiyāditassa* means of that which has been prepared (*paripācitassa*).
“Of the meal. “The undertaking of householders” means *gihisamārambho*; this is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative (a partitive genitive).
“From that” means from that meal. “Except for” means without. Explaining that meaning, he said: “setting aside that alms-food.
This connects with the phrase “stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). The term “by those invited by kinsmen” relates to the term “not undertaken.”
“Maker”: from the sense of being prepared by a nun. “Therefore”: because it is indeed commenced from the standpoint of its purpose (attha), therefore.
195. “Provided” means prepared. Showing that what is naturally prepared is “naturally provided,” he says “naturally,” and so forth.
The connection is with the statement found in the *Mahāpaccarī*. “Of him”: of that very same monk.
"Of another" means of a monk other than that [first one].
Regarding the phrase "even if prepared by a nun," the word "even" (api) indicates the question: "What indeed would be the case if it were not prepared by a nun? The ninth [section].
10. The Training Rule on Sitting in Seclusion.

198. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the text (pāḷiattha) in the tenth": here, the word *pāḷi* should be joined with the word *vinicchaya*, thus forming "the determination of the text" (*pāḷivinicchayo*).

The particle *hi* means "truly" or "because. Because the term "this training rule" (*idaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ*) has the same meaning as the term "a single section" (*ekaparicchedaṃ*), it functions as the object (*kamma*) for the term "laid down" (*paññattaṃ*). "In the subsequent [section]" refers to the Acelaka-vagga. This is the tenth.
The third chapter: On Exhortation.
4. The Chapter on Food.
1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Alms from a Lodging House.
203. In the first section on food (*bhojanavagga*), the phrase "in a lodging" (*āvasathe*) is used to show that alms-food prepared in a lodging is called "lodging-alms" (*āvasathapiṇḍa*);
thus he said "surrounded by," and so forth. "Enclosed" (*parikkhitta*) is connected with "lodging" (*āvasatha*), meaning it is surrounded.

"Travelers" (*addhikā*) are those going along a journey. "The sick" (*gilānā*) are those who are ill or suffering from disease. "Pregnant women" (*gabbhiniyo*) are those who have a fetus (*gabbha*)—a being residing in the womb—within them.
"Those who have gone forth by shaving off their hair are *pabbajitā*; the connection [of the phrase] is 'in accordance with those.

It is called *paññattamañcapīṭha* because beds and chairs are arranged there; that [place]. The construction is: 'having made a dwelling (*āvasatha*) consisting of many room-divisions and many entrance-halls.
*Tattha* means in that dwelling. *Tesaṃ tesaṃ* refers to travelers (*addhika*) and others. [This is said] regarding the word *hiyyo*, which signifies the day immediately preceding."

And because it expresses that which is "not yet arrived" and "immediately following," he says here "one who expresses what is not yet arrived and immediately following" by means of the words "even tomorrow.
The construction is: "it was asked, 'Where have they gone? To show the verbal root (*nāmadhātu*) of the word "kukkuccāyanto," he says "performing remorse" (*kukkuccaṃ karonto*).
By the phrase "half a league or a league," he shows the object (*kamma*) of the word "to set out" (*pakkamituṃ*); by the word "to go" (*gantuṃ*), [he shows the object of the same verb].
This shows the meaning of the various derivations (*padavikkhepa*) of the word *kama*. To show that the word "anodissa" has the suffix *-tvā*, it is stated as "anuddisitvā.
One who casts a snare (*pāsaṃ ḍeti*) is a heretic (*pāsaṇḍo*); the meaning is that he casts the snare of views into the minds of beings.

Alternatively, one who casts (*ḍeti*), that is, scatters (*uḍḍeti*), the snare of craving and the snare of views is a heretic (*pāsaṇḍo*); [the text refers to] that heresy (*taṃ pāsaṇḍaṃ*). This is the sense of the word "yāvatattha."
“Is prescribed” (*paññatto hoti*) means that it is prescribed to the extent that there is need; this is how the construction should be understood.

There is also a reading “yāvadattho,” which has the same meaning. The letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). “To be eaten once” (*sakiṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ*) means it is to be eaten once on a single day. Therefore he said, “it is to be eaten on one day.”
"Herein" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The connection is "prescribed by a single family.
The intention is that it is not permissible to eat [food] because it was prescribed for [members of] one [family]. "Alms-food prescribed by various families" is the construction.
It is permissible to eat because it was prescribed separately, with various families not being together as one; this is the intention. "Even that alms-food which is divided" [is also permissible].
The connection [is as follows]. "Having cut off" means having cut off due to an unfaithful or otherwise evil state of mind.
"Having dwelt repeatedly" means having stayed again and again. Since he was traveling on the road, it is indeed appropriate to say "he eats while going";
however, how can it be said that he eats "in the place already gone," since he has already departed? Even that which is proximate to the present is considered past.
It is appropriate because it is included therein, as in such passages as, “From where, monk, have you come?

For that vicinity is also of the same nature. Because [gifts] belonging to various families in various places are by nature non-offenses, the statement “there is no offense” is said with reference specifically to what belongs to a single family in various places. Because of the interruption of what had been undertaken, “again...”
“It is said that one may eat on a single day. Although it was stated generally as “for those designated,” it should be understood as referring specifically to monks;
thus he says, “only for monks. First. 2.
The Training Rule on Eating in a Group.
209. In the second [verse], showing the reason why gain and honor were abandoned, he said, “So kira,” and so forth. “So” refers to Devadatta.

The words “ahosi” (was) and “pākaṭo jāto” (became well-known) should be construed together. “Ajātasattu” means Ajātasattu because his father, King [Bimbisāra], was an enemy (*sattu*) to one who was not yet born (*ajāta*).
In the word “mārāpetvā” (having caused to be killed), it is the indirect object (*kāritakamma*). “Rājānaṃ” refers to King Bimbisāra.
In the word *mārāpetvā*, there is a causal construction (*dhātukamma*). *Abhimāreti* means having approached and hidden himself, he sent an archer for the purpose of killing the Blessed One.
*Gūḷhapaṭicchanno* means being concealed and hidden. *Parikathāya* means by means of a discourse of concealment.
In the word *rājānampi*, there is a causal construction with the word *mārāpesi*. *Pavijjhi* means he discharged [the arrow]. *Tato*...
The connection is: "Then, after what was said, they rose up. "City-dwellers" (*nāgarā*) means those living in the city. "The king" refers to King Ajātasattu.
"Thorn of the Dispensation" (*sāsanakaṇṭaka*) means one who is like a thorn to the Dispensation because of his hostility toward it. "From there" means from the place where he was being expelled.
"Even attendance" (*upaṭṭhānam-pi*) means even the act of attending, or for the purpose of attending. "Others too" means others besides the king. "His" refers to Devadatta.

The phrase "something to be given" (*dātabba*) should be connected with "some food or soft food" (*kiñci khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ*). Alternatively, "something to be done" (*kātabba*) is linked with "salutation and so forth" (*abhivādanādi*).
Showing the reason for eating after having requested it from families, he said, "May [it not be... and so forth.
The connection is: "he eats while acting as a supporter."
211. To the question, "Why does a limited robe arise for those who do not accept alms-food? he says: "For those not taking alms-food," and so forth. 212.
To the question, "Why do they invite the robe-making monks with alms-food? he says: "In the village," and so forth. 215. Regarding the term *nānāverajjake*:
here, "kingdom" (*rajja*) means belonging to a king; a dissimilar kingdom is a "foreign kingdom" (*virajja*); it is of various kinds.
*Virajjaṃ* means various kingdoms. Those who have come from various kingdoms are *nānāverajjakā*. He said, "There is growth in the middle," meaning "those who have come from various other kingdoms.
"From other kingdoms" means from kingdoms other than Rājagaha.

Regarding the word *rañjitabba*, when it is stated as *rañjanti*, it is said with reference to the absence of the nasalization (*niggahita*) [in the derivation], and thus there is also the reading *nānāverañjake*.
218. Regarding *gaṇabhojana*: eating by a group is *gaṇabhojana*; the eating of a *gaṇabhojana* is *gaṇabhojana*.

The meaning is that in such a *gaṇabhojana*, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). One should understand that, as in the case of the phrase "one who has abstained from food for the night" (*rattūparato*), there is an elision of one instance of the word "eating. [An objection is raised:
"Is it not the case that on the Uposatha day, two or three people constitute what is called a 'group'? To this he replies: "In this context, a 'group' means four," and so forth.
This shows that two or three do not constitute a *gaṇa* (group), but starting from four and upwards they are called a *gaṇa*.
Regarding the phrase "that, moreover" (*taṃ panetaṃ*), here the word "that" (*eta*) is a rhetorical ornament; among the two types of pronouns, the former is generally predominant.
"It procreates" (*pasavati*) means it increases; the sense is that it is born. Or by way of a synonym: "I invite [you] with food."
"Or by way of turn, [saying] 'I invite you with food. "In another language" means in a language other than the original tongue (*mūlabhāsā*).
"The monks invited together" is the grammatical connection. "Hi" means "truly" or "because. "Measure" (*pamāṇa*) means the cause or reason.
Having applied a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) to the word "four," it should be construed with the word "in the monastery" (*vihāre*). "While they were standing" is the phrase.
This is a collective compound of selection (*niddhāraṇa-samudāya*). The connection is: "one [of them] was invited.

The connection is: "he should request four monks. *Pāṭekkaṃ* means the state of being separate; the sense is "individually" (*visuṃ*). The connection is: "he should request either together or separately.
It is called "a great hide" (*mahācamma*) because the inner skin is thick compared to the outer skin, which is what is designated as "flesh" (*chavi*).

"Phālita" means that a "phāla" (a furrow or split) has arisen in these feet; the connection is with the word "uppādentī" (they cause to arise). The construction is: "when [the ground] has merely been struck.
That which is fit by way of a "leso" (a mark or sign) is "lesakappiya" (fit by a mark), referring to the mind that has come into play.
"And a thread" refers to the thread for inserting the needle-eye. Is it not the case that there is also a specific time for making robes, just as there is a specific time for giving robes?
[The question is: "It exists; why then was it said 'whenever'? To this he says, "For separately," and so forth. "Hi" means truly, or because.
Since there is no such thing as a "robe-making season" distinct from the "robe-giving season," the intention is that I said "whenever.
Therefore, the construction is: "Whatever monk makes [the robe], by him it must be worn. "A needle-wrapper" means...
For the purpose of sewing, two pieces of cloth are joined together and pierced with a needle.
"He arranges" means he prepares them by dividing them into five parts, seven parts, and so forth. "He cuts" means he cuts with a knife or with his hand.

"A false thread" (*moghasutta*): *mogha* means delusion; it refers to a mind that is deluded regarding the points that ought to be grasped and understood according to their meaning. The "thread" is the cutting of that [delusion].
The *Moghasutta*: the "incoming border" (*āgantukapaṭṭa*) refers to the border placed upon the primary border of a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭacīvara*).
"Returning" (*paccāgata*) is used in reference to borders on robes and the like. "He ties" means he ties the incoming border with the primary border. "Anuvāta":
that which is woven or bound after the robe has been turned over is called *anuvāta*; he cuts that. "He strikes" (*ghaṭṭeti*): two...
"Anuvātante" means they are joined to one another. "Āropeti" means he places it upon the robe. "Tattha" means on the robe.
"Suttaṃ karoti" means he winds the thread that is to be inserted into the needle-eye. "Valeti" means having wound it, he twists it around the rod for wrapping the thread.
"Pipphalikā" means a knife; for it indeed cuts even what is dear (*piya*), thus it is *pipphali*, and that itself is called *pipphalikā*.

Having made it into a grindstone, it is called "pipphalika"; the meaning is that one sits upon it or grinds [the pepper] upon it. As for the one who speaks, the construction is: "excluding this person.
Because the highway is two *gāvutas* long, it is said: "within half a *yojana*, that is, within a *gāvuta*. By one who has mounted...
“Should be eaten” is the connection [of the sentence]. “Where” means at which time. “Assembling” is stated by way of many agents.
One who avoids what is unwholesome is a wanderer (*paribbājaka*); or, having taken up the guise of one who has gone forth, he wanders, goes, and proceeds—thus he is a wanderer.
Since the state of being a wanderer is to be understood even without the abstract suffix (*bhāva-paccaya*), it denotes the state of a wanderer.
One who has entered into the state of a wanderer is a "wanderer-entered" (paribbājakasamāpanna). Alternatively, one who has entered into or is included among the wanderers is a "wanderer-entered.
The word "of these" (*etesaṃ*) forms a collective ablative construction with the phrase "by anyone whatsoever" (*yena kenaci*).
220. The connection is: "those monks who are eating. "Therein" refers to the statement "two or three together. "Without being invited" (*animantito*).
"Of which quartet there is a fourth who has not been invited" means: one who is a fourth without having been invited is "one with an uninvited fourth.
This same method applies to other cases of being a fourth as well. "Here" means in this teaching. "Invites" means invites with an improper invitation.
"Among them" refers to among those four bhikkhus. "He" refers to the lay follower. "Another" means another than the bhikkhu who has not yet arrived.
"Or from a monk who has been invited. "At that very moment" (*taṅkhaṇappattaṃ*) means obtained at the moment of asking or speaking.

"Hi" indicates the detailed explanation. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that place or in the house. "By them" (*tehi*) refers to the monks acting as the agents. "He" (*so*) refers to the alms-collector (*piṇḍapātiko*).
"Even though he does not come himself" (*anāgacchantampīti*) means even though he does not go there personally. "You will receive" (*lacchathā*) means you will obtain.
"Sopī" means even that novice; "not only the alms-food eater" is the meaning.
"Therein" refers to the fourth [category] consisting of the sick, or among those four. The construction is: "The sick person, however, serves as the completer of the group for the others.
"Because of being a completer of the group" means because of being a completer of the group obtained by agreement. "Tetrads" refers to the tetrad for giving robes and the tetrad for making robes.

The fourfold group consisting of traveling on a journey, the fourfold group consisting of embarking on a boat, the fourfold group consisting of a large assembly, and the fourfold group consisting of a meal for ascetics—these are the six sets of four.
When combined with the preceding ones, eleven sets of four should be understood.
"A single wise bhikkhu was seated" is the connection [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase "among those three," the construction is: "when they have gone, he goes. Having eaten...

Even when they have arrived and are standing there, it is likewise non-offensive. Why is there non-offense for all? [The questioner asks: "Is it not the case that four monks are taking [the meal] together?
To this he replies, "Of five," and so forth. "Hi" means "truly" or "because.
"Of foods only" means not of rice-gruel, dry food, fruits, or other such items. "And those" refers to those foods with which there is no disagreement. "By them" means by the four monks.
“Those” refers to the rice gruel and so forth. “Thus” is to be construed as “therefore there is no offense.
“Someone sent by an unwise person says” is the construction. “Sent by one desiring to act” is the connection.
Regarding the phrase “or ‘Take the meal’,” the word “or” (*vā*) includes: “Take the boiled rice, take the food, take the alms-food, take the *kura* [grain].”
It also includes such statements as “Take [it]! “Inviting” means accepting an invitation; thus, she is one who accepts invitations (*nemantanikā*).
“Alms-fooders” (*piṇḍapātikā*) means those engaged in the ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) of alms-gathering. The construction is: “On the following day, O Bhante, it was said.
“Having removed” means having taken away. “From there” connects with “beyond that speaking. “Distraction” means various kinds of scattering. “Those” refers to such-and-such [persons].
"And the village-dweller, O Venerable Sir"—this is how it should be construed. "He too" means even the unwise person, not only the village-dweller; such is the meaning.
"Why do I not receive [alms], O Venerable Sir?"—this is how it should be construed. The same applies here to the phrase, "How did they invite you, Venerable Sir?
"Therefore" means for that reason. "This" refers to this village. "That" is used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative (bhūmatthe).
The meaning is: "Go about in that village. "What is the use of this? means: what is the purpose of this question?
"In this" refers to the questioning. "He says, 'Do not neglect it,'" is the grammatical connection. "On the second day" means on the day following the day of the invitation.
"In the principal village" (dhuragāme) means in the main village, or in a nearby village. As for the state (bhāva), because it consists of an action, it is indeed one and the same; therefore...
The plural number should not be used here with reference to the agent, the object, or the relationship; therefore it is said, "one should not be among those who are difficult to speak to.
The word *tesu* (among them) is connected with *gāmikesu bhojentesu* (among the village headmen while they were feeding). *Asanasālāyaṃ* means in the dining hall.
For it is called *asanā* because one eats there (*bhuñjati ettha*), and it is called *sālā* because they enter (*salanti*) or go into it (*pavisanti*).
Because it is both a seat (*āsana*) and a hall (*sālā*), it is called “the Assembly Hall” (*āsanasālā*) in the sense of being a hall for sitting.

Now, however (*atha pana*) means otherwise than that; for the word *atha* here has the sense of an ablative (indicating a contrast). In those various places (*tattha tattha*) means in those respective locations, such as the intermediate streets and so forth.
Having first done so (*paṭikacca eva*) means having first performed [the action]. From the village among the monks...
"Even before they have departed" means that it has already been said. "It is not permissible" means it is not permissible because [the messenger] was sent with the instruction, "Take the meal.
The connection is: "those people who are feeding [the monks]. Regarding the phrase "when it is said, 'Turn back,'" this refers to the verbal expression "turn back.
"It belongs to anyone whatsoever" is to be construed as: "it is for the sake of anyone whatsoever. To turn back...
"It is allowable" means that since he was not told, "Take food," it is allowable for him to turn back.

"Having made a connection" means having made [the connection] without interruption by the word "bhante," as in "Turn back, bhante. When it is said with interruption by the word "bhante," as in "Sit down, bhante;
take food," it is allowable to sit down at the word "sit down. Then, [if it is] interrupted by the word "bhante"...
If one says, "Sit down and take your meal," without establishing a connection [by saying "I will give you food"], it is permissible to sit down.
By the phrase "the same method applies," this principle is extended. This is the second [case].
3. The Training Rule on Eating in Succession (Paramparabhojana).
221. Regarding the third [section], in order to show the connection of the meaning for the reading “...not indeed... they do not perform,” he said, “By whatever method,” and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase “by whatever method,” he shows that the word *yathā* (as) in the expression “just as these humans” has the sense of the word *yaṃ* (which).
“By that” means by that method. By this, he shows that the word *yathā* indicates the method.

By the word “is known” (*ñāyati*), he indicates the remainder of the verbal construction. By the phrases “instruction” (*sāsana*) or “gift” (*dāna*), he shows the meaning of the pronoun “this” (*idaṃ*).
In the expression “to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha,” these locative forms are used in the sense of the dative;
thus, the meaning is “a gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. By the word “paritta,” he shows the meaning of the word “inferior” (*oraka*). By the word “lāmaka,”...
It excludes the sense of "surrounding" from the word *paritta*. By saying “*Kirapatiko* means one who is intent upon the appearance (*patibhāva*)”;
he shows the meaning as follows: “In the phrase ‘*kirapatiko*’,” etc. “*So*” refers to the *kirapatiko*. The connection is: “he causes the work to be done.
“By way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra-vasena*)” means by way of common usage (*vohāra*), by way of a defining characteristic (*upalakkhaṇa*), or by way of prominence (*padhāna*).
The intention is that it was not only jujube fruits, but many other kinds of solid and soft foods as well that were prepared.
"Mixed with jujube" (*badaramissa*) means mixed with jujube; thus he said, "with jujube salad" (*badarasāḷavena*).
That which is mixed with jujube powder, honey, sugar, and so forth, is called "jujube salad."
222. When it is said that "the sun has risen high" (*ussūro*) in the sense of "it is time," he says "it is past noon" (*atidivā*), meaning the day is too late.

226. The construction is: "This [act] is called the assignment of food (*bhattavikappanā*), and it is permissible. Regarding the phrase "among the five fellow-practitioners" (*pañcasu sahadhammikesu*), this is a collective ablative;
it is connected with the term "of such-and-such a person" (*itthannāmassa*). However, if it is also permissible to assign it in their presence, then together with oneself...
To the question, "Why is it not permissible [to assign] this to the Blessed One while he is standing?", he says: "And this," and so forth.

The connection is that "this assignment (vikappanā) is included" [in the Sangha]. To the question, "Why is it not fitting to assign it to the Blessed One?", he says: "For in the Blessed One," and so forth. "Hi" means "truly" or "because. The connection is that "it was performed by the Sangha."
229. Regarding the words “two or three invitations,” he says “two or three invitations” because they are instances of a shift in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
The connection is: “he eats meals which are invitations, because one is invited by means of these. The construction is: “scattering two or three families [of food].
“Soup and condiment” (*sūpabyañjana*) means both soup and condiment. There is no offense if [the food comes] from a single [source].
The intended meaning is "because it is mixed. "The primary invitation" refers to the first invitation for food.
"Below" means underneath. "Even a single mouthful" means even a single morsel. "In whatever way" means by whatever manner or form.
"Therein" means in that food. "Or a flavor" means a flavor other than milk. By which flavor of milk it is overwhelmed—
The food becomes of one flavor; the construction is: "she pours that milk or that sauce [into it].

For the word *yaṃ* (which), standing in the subsequent sentence, implies the word *taṃ* (that) in the preceding sentence. Food mixed with milk is "milk-food" (*khīrabhatta*); likewise for "sauce-food" (*rasabhatta*).
"Others as well" means others besides those who give milk-food or sauce-food. There is no offense regarding the food.
The intended meaning is "because it was not missed. The word *bhuñjantena* (by one eating) functions as the agent of the verbal noun in the word *bhuñjituṃ* (to eat).
*Sappipāyāsepi* means even in the case of food prepared with both ghee and milk-rice.
*Tassa* refers to the great lay follower (*mahā-upāsaka*). Regarding the two commentarial positions—that there is an offense and that it is permissible—one should consider which is more logical.

It is said, beginning with “the Mahāpaccariya,” in order to show [the teaching] by means of the *Mahāpaccarivāda*. For although there are two distinct traditions of commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) in their verbal expression, they differ only in their specific phrasing;
in meaning, however, they are one. The connection is: “stated in the Mahāpaccari. “Alone” (*eko*) means alone in the pot.
“Successive eating” (*paramparabhojana*) means the eating of one person after another. “I was invited” (*nimantito’mhi*) means: I have been invited.
"Indeed," is the meaning. "Even after having asked permission" means even after having asked permission from the great lay follower (*mahā-upāsaka*).
"He" refers to the monk who offers the expression of thanks (*anumodaka*). "Him" refers to that monk. "Another" means a certain other person. "Why? means for what reason.

"Because of being invited" means because of the state of having been invited. Even if one is invited by an entire village, it is permissible [to eat] only if invited together as one group, not if invited separately and individually.
He said, "Having become one. "In a group" means even in a multitude who, having been encouraged, are performing meritorious deeds.
Showing the manner of the invitation for the phrase "being invited," he said, "Take food. "By which portion" means by whichever part; the meaning is "by which division.
Between the two explanations of the Elder, the explanation of the Elder Mahāsiva alone is appropriate; therefore, it was stated later. Third.
4. The Training Rule on Kāṇamātā (230).

Regarding the fourth [training rule], in phrases such as “Nakulamātā,” two meanings are possible: “Nakulamātā” may mean either “the mother of the Blessed One Nakula” (*nakulassa bhagavato mātā*) or “she who is both Nakula and his mother” (*nakulañca bhagavato taṃ mātā ca*). Similarly, in phrases such as “Uttaramātā,” [the same analysis applies] to Uttara.
The meaning "mother" or "stepmother" is indeed possible for both [terms].
Among them, just as the meaning "the mother of a one-eyed woman" (*kāṇamātā*) is possible for the word *uttaramātā*, he said "the mother of a one-eyed woman" (*kāṇāya mātā*).
To show that this daughter was renowned by the name "One-Eyed," he said "It is said that she... and so forth. That girl became well-known.
The connection [is as follows]. "Assā" means "of the Great Laywoman. "Ye ye" refers to those men. By the phrase "they become one-eyed through passion," it shows the meaning:
"men are called 'one-eyed' (kāṇā) because they close their eyes (kaṇanti/nimilanti) due to passion for her. "Tassā" means "of that one-eyed woman.

Regarding "āgataṃ," he says "arrival" (āgamanaṃ), taking the suffix -ta in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva). "Intention" (adhippāyo) refers to the phrase "as if in what? or to the mother of the one-eyed woman.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Empty" (*rittā*) means hollow; the sense is "void" (*suññā*). By the phrase "in this journey," he shows that it is a compound with an external object (*bāhiratthasamāsa*).
By the phrase "noble female disciple" (*ariyasāvikā*), etc., he shows that the noble ones' wealth is not partitioned among the monks.
It did not go to ruin merely for something specific, but rather for everything; thus he says, "it went to total ruin."
“Kāṇāpi”: the word “also” (api) indicates that it was not only the mother who shared in the attainment of the path and its fruit, but that Kāṇā herself also became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).
“That man too”: this refers to the husband of Kāṇā. “In her very own place”: in the position of the senior wife.

“In this case,” however, means in this case of the cake-offering. “This” refers to the provision for the journey (pātheyya). “From the state of being a noble disciple” (ariyasāvakatta): from the condition of being a disciple of one who has become noble (ariya), or from the condition of being a disciple of the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha).
233. Because the words *paheṇaka* and *paṇṇākāra* are synonyms for one another, it is said: “For the sake of a gift (*paheṇaka*) means for the sake of a present (*paṇṇākāra*).
Herein, in the phrase “or with cakes,” or in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “Mixed dough” (*baddhasattu*) refers to dough mixed with honey, sugar, and so forth.
“Piled up” (*thūpīkataṃ*) means having made it into a heap.
In order to show that the phrase "dvattipattapūre" functions as an adjective, it is said: "pūre patte. Two or three bowls are "dvattipattā";

this is a numeral-dual-external-object compound (saṅkhyobhayabāhiratthasamāsa) used in the sense of the particle *vā* ("or"). Because the word *ti* follows, the vowel *a* is substituted for the *i* of *dvi*.
Then, "dvattipattā" and "pūrā" form the compound "dvattipattapūrā," meaning "full of two or three bowls"; these are "dvattipattapūre."
“Having taken” is the construction. Showing the manner of explaining for the statement “it should be explained,” he said, “In this regard, by me,” and so forth.

“By him also” means by the second [monk] as well. Indicating the first monk’s taking of one [robe] and announcing it to the second monk, and the second monk’s taking of one and announcing it to the third monk, he said, “By whom,” and so forth.

In this context, "by whom" refers to the first monk. Since "recess" (*paṭikkamana*) is said to be where they go back after having eaten, it should be understood as the dining hall; thus he says "dining hall. "Where" means in which dining hall.
He says "his own," etc., because looking at the face [of others] is not permitted. "Elsewhere" means other than the recess. "His" refers to the monk.

To show the manner of sharing referred to by the statement "it should be shared," it is said: "If there are three," and so forth. "Yathāmittaṃ" means according to whichever friend [is present]. "Akāmā" means not out of desire; this is an ablative used in the sense of a causal condition (*kāraṇatthe*).
235. "Antarāmagge" means the interior of a path, i.e., "antarāmaggo"; the long vowel is used for ease of pronunciation. The construction is:
"even for one who accepts much from these relatives who have invited him, even though they are giving much. [This is stated] in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāsu*).
"But it was said" is the connection. "The statement of the commentaries does not agree with the Pāḷi. This is the fourth [point]. 5.
The First Pavāraṇā Training Rule (Sikkhāpada): 236.

Regarding the fifth [rule], "having invited" (*pavārita*): here there is the invitation at the end of the rains-residence (*vassaṃvutthapavāraṇā*), the invitation regarding requisites (*paccayapavāraṇā*), and the invitation consisting of a refusal (*paṭikkhepapavāraṇā*).

Regarding the phrase "and the invitation for as much as one desires" (*yāvadatthapavāraṇā*), he says "by the brahmin," etc., in order to show that among the four types of invitations, two invitations are intended here: the invitation for as much as one desires and the invitation with a restriction. The connection is "invited by the brahmin.
The word *sayam* is an instrumental case ending, connected with the word "invited" (*pavāritā*). The word "and" (*ca*) [indicates] another point.
It should be applied to both the invitation for as much as needed (*yāvadattha-pavāraṇā*) and the refusal of the invitation (*paṭikkhepa-pavāraṇā*).

Regarding the term *paṭivissaka*—meaning those who enter or go into one's own house facing it—it refers to those living in nearby houses; thus he said "those living in neighboring houses" (*sāmantaghara-vāsike*).

237. An upward-moving sound is *orava*; that very sound is the "sound of *orava*" (*oravasadda*). Showing that this is the "cawing sound of crows" (*kakora-vasadda*), he said "of crows," and so forth.
239. To show that the suffix *-tavant* has the sense of the past, it is said: “And therein,” and so forth. “Therein” means in the word *bhuttavā*. The construction is:
because that bhikkhu by whom [the food] has been swallowed, therefore he receives the designation “one who has eaten” (*bhuttāvī*).
*Saṅkhāditvā* means having made it into powder with the teeth. *Tenā* means for that reason. *Assa* means...

Regarding the word *bhuttāvī*: in order to show that a monk is one who has been invited (*pavārito*) when he invites others and then refuses them, [the author] says "one who has performed the invitation" (*katapavāraṇo*).
The connection is: "And that too" means "that refusal also occurs. Regarding the word "of him" (*assa*), it refers to the word "one who has been invited" (*pavārito*).
Regarding the phrase "where food is seen," etc., because one is also reckoned as "one who has eaten," therefore [the author] says, "we do not see [it]."

The *yojanā* (explanatory synthesis) is as follows: In the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*), the statement “a meal is seen” is said in order to show that it does not correspond to the heading-word (*mātikāpada*) “one who has finished eating.

This is expressed by the passage beginning with “by this [phrase], ‘a meal is seen’,” and so forth. “And whatever” (*yañca*) refers to the food. In the phrase “two nights, etc. (*dirattādī*), the word “etc.
(*ādi*) includes the mention of five nights and so on. “This” (*etaṃ*) refers to the word “one who has finished eating” (*bhuttāvī*).
The connection [of the commentary] is as follows: "In such passages as ‘A seat is discerned’ (āsanaṃ paññāyati), the analysis should be understood thus.
Regarding the word “is discerned” (paññāyati), it is stated “is seen” (dissati) in order to show that the root *ñā* has the sense of appearing.
Regarding the phrase “within arm’s reach” (hatthapāse), he says “measuring two and a half cubits,” because a handspan of twelve cubits is not intended here. Nor is verbal offering intended.
Therefore he said, "by the body. "Brings toward" means he brings it forward. "That" refers to the food. "This" refers to the state of having five factors, or the statement:
"It is manifested by five... [etc.]... by wisdom.
"Therein" refers to the statement beginning with "eating is manifested. "Eats" is because it belongs to the *kī* group of roots, and because that root consists of a single syllable.
The combination of *sakāra* and *nakāra* should be observed. *Taṃ* refers to food. It moistens (*undati*) and produces vitality for those who eat it; thus it is called *odana*.
Because barley and other grains are made into a paste (*pūti*), they are smeared with or touched by what is vile; thus it is called *kummāsa*. It comes into being through a mixture (*samavāya*);
thus it is called *sattu*. It must be killed for the sake of its sauce; thus it is called *maccha*. It is measured out (*mānīyati*).
"By those who eat" refers to meat. "Therein" means among the five kinds of food, such as boiled rice and so forth. It is *sāli* because it is the essence (*sāra*) among other grains.
It is *vīhi* because it carries (*vahati*) the life of those who eat it. It is *yava* because even when unmixed, it becomes as if mixed [with others].
It is *godhuma* because it conceals (*gudhati*) or surrounds (*pariveṭhati*) the food of the barbarians (*milakkha*). It is [called] *śobhana-śīrṣa* because of its beautiful head.

It is called *kaṅgu* because it attains a desirable state (*kamanīyabhāva*). It is called *varaka* because, due to its large heads and sweet stalks, it is chosen (*varīyati*) or sought after (*patthīyati*) by people.
It is called *kudrūsaka* because it corrupts (*dūsati*) the blood (*kora*) of those who eat it. "The rice that has been produced" is the connection [of the sentence].
"Therein" means among the seven grains. Regarding the word "sālī," the particle *iti* here is a synonym for "namely. *Sālī*.
The meaning is "name. This same method applies to the expressions "rice" (*vīhī*) and so forth as well.
"In this" means among the various types of grass-grains. *Nīvāra* is a derivative of *sāli* (paddy), and *varakacora* is a derivative of *varaka*.
"In sour milk-rice and so forth"—here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as milk-rice are included. "Odhī" means a limit or a boundary.
The meaning is as follows: for that which is carried away (*avahīyati*) and cast off (*cajīyati*) is called a "heap" (*odhi*). The construction is:
even a rice gruel (*pāyāsa*) or sour gruel (*ambilayāgu*) that does not show a heap does not produce an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).

It is called *pāyāsa* because it is made with water (*payas*) and milk (*khīra*). [The term *odhi* arises] from two etymological bases: that which is to be drunk (*pātabba*) and that which is to be eaten (*asitabba*).

Or it is called "rice porridge" because it arises [from it]. "From the hearth" means from the cooking fire; for it is called a "hearth" (*uddhana*) because pots and other vessels are placed and set upon it.
"Having turned one's attention" means having directed the mind. "The state of solidity" means the state of hardness.
In this sentence as well, the words "that which is" (*yo so*) should be supplied. "Formerly" means at the time when it was still warm. "In the invitation" means in the place of the invitation.
The connection is: "They give by pouring [the gruel] over the meal. It is called *yāgu* because one goes (*yāti*) by means of it for the sake of sustaining oneself.
Even though it is thin, the construction is: "nevertheless... By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in water, etc.," substances such as *kiñjika* (rice gruel) and milk are included.
Why does it fall under the category of *yāgu*? The intention is: "because the water and so forth have been boiled. "In that" refers to the meal together with the boiled water and other ingredients.
"Or in another" means in water or the like other than boiling water and so forth.
The construction is: "In whatever water or the like they throw it, that produces the invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"Pure broth" (*suddharasaka*) means pure broth of fish and so forth, unmixed with pieces of fish, meat, or sinews. "Broth-gruel" (*rasakayāgu*)...
*Rasakabhūtā* means having the nature of a liquid; *yāgu* is gruel. *Ghanayāgu* means thick gruel. *Ettha* means in the thick gruel. *Pupphiatthāya*:
that which has a flower (*puppha*)—meaning it is blooming (*phulla*)—is called *pupphī*; the purpose or utility of that flower is *pupphiattha*.
"Made for that purpose" is the grammatical connection. *Te taṇḍule* refers to those steamed rice grains. Because they are ground into powder, they do not count as whole grains (*sattu*).
Because they are uncooked, they do not count as food. "By them" means by those steamed rice grains. The connection is: "they cook those rice grains; they prepare them.
By the plural form "by barley," the seven types of grain are also included. This same method applies here to the phrase "by rice, paddy, and barley."
"Thus" means "it is indeed excellent. "Having made [them] leave" means having caused them to retreat. "That" refers to the powder; the connection is that it goes [to them].
"Of those roasted by a harsh fire": "harsh roasting" is *kharapāka*; "roasted by a harsh fire" is *kharapākabhajjitā*; [the phrase refers to] those.
"They do not offer" means they do not offer out of a desire to include non-enemies; this is the intended meaning. "Even the scrapings" means even the husks. He offers.
The intention is "for the sake of gathering [the] enemy. "By them" means by the parched grains (*lāja*).

"Pure snacks" refers to pure fruits and other edible foods unmixed with flour. The construction is: "giving to one who is drinking rice-gruel (*yāgu*). "Those two" refers to the two pieces of fish and meat.
The intention is that he did not offer [them] because the two pieces of fish and meat had not been eaten. "From that" means from the two pieces of fish and meat.
“Having removed one” is the connection, or [the connection] is with those [two]. “He” refers to the monk who is eating.

“Another” refers to food other than the two pieces of fish and meat, sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*). “Because of the lack of basis” means because the invitation lacks a foundation. Elaborating on that, he said: “For that which... The word “for” (*hi*)...
[This is] an explanation in detail. "Yanti" means meat. "Idaṃ pana" means this meat, however.
Prohibited meat does not lose its status as meat even though it is prohibited, because it stands in a place where it is not to be prohibited due to its being allowable (kappiya). [Objection:
But surely, meat that has been eaten loses its status as meat even while being eaten, because it stands in a place where it is to be prohibited due to its being unallowable (akappiya)?

He said, "But as for that which... and so forth. "Those beginning with family-corrupting acts, medical practice, claiming superhuman states, and accepting money" refers to those things—namely, family-corrupting acts, medical practice, claiming superhuman states, and accepting money—which are the first among the deceits and so on; thus they are called "those beginning with family... and money.
"In all instances" means in all sections.
"Thus," and so forth, is an indication of the conclusion. "That" refers to the food. "In whatever manner" means by whichever mode. The construction is:
"He rejects and invites [the guest] in the manner in which it has been swallowed. "In some place" means in a certain bowl or similar vessel.
"If in that interval" means if at that very moment. "Elsewhere" means in another location. [This applies when one] does not wish to swallow the food already present in the bowl.
The construction is: "it is thus, as it is. *Hi* means "truly. *Sabbattha* means "in all places. *Tattha* refers to the *Kurundi* commentary. Regarding *ānisadassa*:
it is called *ānisada* because one sits (*nisīdati*) by means of it; the connection is "from its rear part. Regarding *paṇhiantato*:
it is called *paṇhī* because it touches the ground when standing or when walking; [the meaning is] "from the end of that. The word "of the donor" (*dāyakassa*)— [End of excerpt]
There is a connection with the whole (*avayavin*) by means of the words “*pasāritahatthan*” (with outstretched hand) and “*aṅgan*” (limb).
“*Hatthapāso*” means the reach or vicinity of the hand; or, it is called *hatthapāsa* because the hand reaches (*pasati*) or touches (*phusati*) at that place.
It refers to a space of two and a half cubits (*aḍḍhateyyahattha*). “*Tasmin*” means in that reach of the hand.

"Brings near" (*upanāmeti*) means he brings close. "Even though seated immediately next to him" (*anantaranisinnopi*) is to be construed as: even a monk who is seated in the very next place, not having left the reach of the hand, speaks.
"A basket of food" (*bhattapacchi*) is a basket into which food has been placed. "Slightly" (*īsakam*) is a neuter adverbial form.
It should be connected with either "having lifted up" or "having moved aside. "At a distance" (*dūre*) means at a new seat.
"Iti" means "from the bowl. "Gato dūto" is the connection [of the phrase].
"Parivesanāya" means for the purpose of serving food, or in the dining hall. "Tattha" means in this serving of food. "Taṃ" refers to the food-bowl.
"Phuṭṭhamattāva" means merely touched. The construction is: "But when food has been lifted with a ladle, there is an invitation to stop (pavāraṇā)."
*Hi* means "truth" or "because. *Tassa* refers to the distributor. *Abhihaṭe paṭikkhittattā* means because of the state of having rejected food that has been brought forward.
The meaning stated in brief—"there is an invitation for one who rejects [food] by body or by speech"—is now explained in detail:
Showing this, he said “therein,” and so forth. “Therein” means among those restraints of body and speech.
“Macchikabījanī” means a fan for scaring away flies. For the letter *kha* is changed to *cha*, as in the word “macchikā” (fly), just as in “sacchikatvā” (having realized) and similar terms.
For in that case, where one should say “sakkhikatvā,” the letter *kha* becomes *cha*.
The connection is with the words "one says. "Having removed" means having removed from the bowl. "In this" refers to the statement. The construction is: "How?

meaning "in what manner does it come to be? Regarding the phrase "of one who says indeed," the word *nāma* here has the sense of reproach (*garaha*) and should be construed with the word "there is" (*atthi*).
Thus, the meaning is "there indeed is. "Even from this" means even from the bowl. "There too" means even in that statement.
“Together with meat” (*samaṃsaka*) means occurring together with meat. “Juice” (*rasa*) means liquid. “That” refers to the statement. It occurs for one who rejects [the compound]. Why?
Because the meaning is possible as either “fish and juice” or “juice mixed with fish. “This” refers to the substance.
“Having separated the meat” means that by the expression “the juice of the meat” (*maṃsassa rasaṃ maṃsarasaṃ*), the referent of the word “meat” is given prominence.
The meaning is: "without making [the meat] so, but making the flavor-substance itself the primary thing.
"Asking permission" means asking permission by saying, "Take some meat broth. "That" refers to the meat. "Karambaka" is a designation for a mixture;
for whatever they prepare by mixing various things together is called "karambaka. This, however, is the etymological derivation (*vacanattha*) here: [it is so called because it is] mixed (*kīrati*).
— It makes a whole (*samūha*) out of parts (*avayava*), thus it is a "maker" (*kara*); or, it is made by a whole as its parts, thus it is a "made thing" (*kara*), meaning a part.

That which speaks of or takes up that [part] is a "cluster" (*karambaka*), meaning a whole. There is also the reading "kadambaka," which is likewise appropriate because it has been approved by the wise.
This is also the case in the *Abhidhāna*. However, the meaning should be considered differently. Or else, in this sense:
The letter *ra* should be changed to the letter *da*. A *karambaka* (gruel) mixed with meat, or marked by meat, is a "meat-karambaka.
"Does not invite" means that because it is mixed with anything whatsoever, one does not invite [others to eat]. "Invites" means that because it is mixed with meat, one invites [others to eat].
However, the construction is: "But he who refuses, he is indeed one who has already invited [himself]. "In an invitation" means at the place of invitation. "Hi" (indeed).
It is true. *Tattha* means in the *Kurundi*. *Yena* means by which meal. *Ettha* refers to such statements as "Take rice gruel.
*Adhippāyo* means the intention of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). *Ettha* refers to such statements as "Take the mixed [food].
*Duddasaṃ* means difficult to perceive. *Idañca* refers to the statement "Take the mixed [food]. *Na samānetabbaṃ* means it should not be brought together.
It should not be brought to equality, nor should it be made equal. “Hi” means truly, or because. “This, however” (idaṃ pana) refers to the mixed. “In this” (ettha) refers to the mixed.
“Having separated” (visuṃ katvā) means having made the juice, milk, and ghee distinct. “That” (taṃ) refers to the juice and so forth. It is called *kaddama* because it is kneaded and crushed.
It is called *udaka* because it moistens, produces, or increases; or alternatively, because it moistens—that is, causes wetting.
It is called *udaka* because it carries (*karoti*) [beings]. It is called a *gumba* because it protects (*gupati*) beings who have settled there, or because it conceals (*guhati*) or restrains them.
"Moving along" means moving by turning around in succession. "That" refers to either the boat or the bridge. "At midday": the middle of the day is *majjhanha*;
this is a substitution of *nh* for the word *aha* (day), and thus *majjhanha* itself becomes *majjhanhika*. In the manuscripts...
However, there is a reading "majjhantika," but that is not the correct reading. The construction is: "He who invites while standing must eat while remaining standing.
"Ānisada" refers to the flesh of the buttocks touching the seat. "Acāletvā" means without moving; or rather, this is the very reading itself.
It means without releasing [the body] from the upper parts and the sides. This is like the displacement from one's place in the case of taking what is not given (adinnādāna).
It should not be understood [in that way]. "To transmigrate" means to wander through saṃsāra. "He" refers to the bhikkhu.
"Atiritta" means that which remains over or exceeds; explaining the meaning as "that which is not *atiritta*," he says "not *atiritta*.
By the word "adhika" (excessive), he excludes the sense of "exceeding" (*atisuñña*) from the term *atiritta*.
It is called *adhika* (extra) because it comes about by being set aside (*adhi-hutvā*) and then proceeds [to be used]. The connection is: "But that, however, is not left over (*anatiritta*).

Regarding the phrase "in that case" (*tattha*), it refers to the statement beginning with "that which has been made unallowable" (*akappiyakata*). The construction is: "The detailed explanation should be understood in this way.

Regarding "in that case" (*tattha*), it refers to the matters among those things that must be made left over. The construction is: "Whatever fruit or whatever bulbous root, etc., is unmade" (*akata*). [This refers to] unallowable food.
The connection is: "Does there exist food that is not allowable, produced by such acts as defiling a family? "He" refers to a monk who is an expert in the Vinaya.

The construction is: "done by him. From the statement, "It is done by one who has finished eating, who has refused further food, and who has risen from his seat," it is established that this must be performed by one who has finished eating, who has not refused further food, and who has risen from his seat. Therefore, [this applies] in the morning on a journey...

When two people are traveling, even if one has already finished his meal (pavārita), the other may indeed do so as well—having gone for alms and received food, he may declare, "This is enough for all," even if he himself has not eaten it.
"Yaṃ" refers to solid and soft food. By the phrase "both of these," the meaning is shown:
that which is both "leftover" (atiritta) and "not leftover" (anatiritta) is simply "leftover" (atiritta). It is not the case that what is not leftover is called "leftover."

*Tasseva* means *of that very same [food]*, namely, of that which is not leftover (*anatiritta*). *Ettha* means *in this*, i.e., regarding that which is not leftover, or within the seven modes of formal monastic acts (*vinayakamma*) beginning with "made allowable" (*kappiyakata*).
*Anantare* means on a seat immediately adjacent to the one who holds the Vinaya. *Nīharitvā pattato* is the connection [to the verb].
*Tattheva* means right there, at the very place where he is eating. *Tassa* refers to the one who is seated. *Tenā* means by the monk bringing the food; it should be eaten [by him].
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "By a monk who is seated"—here, the formal act (*kamma*) that has been performed must be brought forward.

Asking why it was said, "having washed his hands," he says, "Why? The word *hi* indicates the reason. The intention is: because it would be improper (*akappiya*), therefore I have said, "having washed his hands.
"Of him" refers to the one bringing the food. "By whom" refers to the one who upholds the Vinaya.
"Puna yenā" means in this very same way. "Yaṃ ca" refers to both hard food and soft food. It means that it must be done by that same Vinaya-holder who first did not do it;
it is stated that whatever hard food or soft food was first left undone, that very thing must now be performed.
"Tattha" means in the first vessel. "Hi" means truly. Having washed the first vessel clean...
Even that which has been made [into *atiritta*] is entirely free from fault. "By that bhikkhu" means by the bhikkhu who has offered the invitation (*pavārita*).
"In a pan" (*kuṇḍe*) means even in a cooking pot (*ukkhali*); for it is called a "pan" (*kuṇḍa*) because it "boils" (*kuṇḍati*), that is, it cooks rice and so forth.
"That" refers to the solid and soft food that has been made into *atiritta*. "But by whom" (*yena pana*) means by the one who maintains the Vinaya. "Causing the bhikkhu to sit down" means...
The connection: "An invitation for auspiciousness" means at a place where an invitation is made for the sake of auspiciousness. "Therein" means in that invitation for auspiciousness.
"By one who performs [it]" means by the Vinaya-holder who performs it.
Not only is what remains after a sick person has eaten called *gilānātiritta* (leftover from a sick person), but also that which is intended specifically for a sick person.
Showing that what has been brought is indeed called "the leavings of one who is ill," he said, "not only," and so forth.

"Any kind of illness" means any illness whatsoever, whether of one who is fully ordained or one who is not. The connection is to be made thus: "The offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) that was mentioned was stated by way of [food] that is not mixed [with medicine].
"For the purpose of non-food" means for the purpose of quenching thirst or for the purpose of alleviating disease.

241. Regarding the phrase "when there is a condition" (*sati paccaye*), in order to show the actual form of that condition, it is said: "when there is thirst" (*pipāsāya sati*) and "when there is illness" (*ābādhe sati*).
"By this or that" refers to [medicines] used for a period of seven days and those used for as long as life lasts.

"Of that" refers to the illness. This word is connected to the word "for the purpose of allaying" (*upasamanattham*); here, the connection is with the verbal root *samudhātu*, and [the suffix] is by means of the *yup*-suffix.
"In the context of the connection, 'action' (kamma) should be understood"—thus ends the fifth [section].
6. The Second Training Rule on Invitation (Pavāraṇā). 242.

Regarding the sixth [rule], when it is said "it should not be practiced," that which is called "improper conduct" (anācāra) refers to a transgression of the formal rule (paṇṇatti); thus he says, "a transgression of the formal rule."
By the word *karoti*, he shows that the term *carasadda* has the meaning of the root *kara*, as in such expressions as “he practices himself” (*attānamācarati*).
Regarding *upanandhi*, he says “enmity” (*upanāhaṃ*) and so forth, demonstrating that here the prefix *upa* has the sense of enmity (*upanāha*), while the verbal root *nah* has the sense of binding.

That by which enmity is produced is “one who has produced enmity” (*janitaupanāho*). By this, he explains the word *upanandho* [as derived from] “he binds against” (*upanahati*), thus “one who binds against” (*upanandho*).
It shows where the meaning lies.

Regarding the word *abhihaṭṭhuṃ*, since the suffix *-tuṃ* here has the sense of the suffix *-tvā*, he says "having brought. The connection is with the phrase "stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
The construction is: "the meaning is indeed common [to both]. The word *assa* means "of the bhikkhu. By "in three ways" means...
It is [established] by three causes: by knowing it oneself, by informing others, and by that person’s informing [others].
To show that "āsādana" means that which is approached (āsādīyate) or made despondent (maṅkuṃ karīyate), he said "āsādana" and so forth, [meaning] one who has regard for that approach (āsādanāpekkho).
The connection is: "for whose sake they are brought. "Of the other" refers to someone other than the one who brought it, namely, one who has eaten. This is the sixth [section].
7. The Training Rule on Eating at the Wrong Time (Vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada) 247.
Regarding the seventh [rule]: "On a mountain" (*girismiṃ*) means on a hill.

For it is called a "mountain" (*giri*) because it swallows (*girati*) or emits (*niggirati*) water by way of being a snowy range and so forth, as well as substances such as medicinal herbs that constitute its essence. "The foremost assembly" (*aggasamajjo*) means the most excellent assembly.

By these words, *agga-samajja* means a festival (*samajja*) that is foremost (*agga*); thus, it shows the meaning of a "festival on a mountain peak" (*giragga-samajja*), as it occurs on a mountain (*girismiṃ*).
And *samajja* is a gathering (*sabhā*). For it is called a *samajja* because people (*jana*) go (*ajanti*) there, coming together (*samāgamaṃ*).
By the phrase "or of the mountain," and so forth, the peak (*agga*) or summit (*koṭi*) of the mountain is the "mountain peak" (*giragga*); [the festival] occurring therein—
The meaning shown is that *samajja* refers to a mountain-top festival (*giraggasamajja*). "That" (*so*) refers to the mountain-top festival. The construction is: "It will surely take place.
"In a location on the ground" (*bhūmibhāge*) is the container for the whole; it connects with the verb "gathers together" (*sannipatati*). "Actors and drama" (*naṭañca nāṭakañca*) is *naṭanāṭakāni*.
This triad—dancing, singing, and instrumental music—is called "drama" (*nāṭaka*). "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the actors and the drama.
"For the purpose of seeing" means for both seeing and hearing; for hearing is indeed included within seeing itself.
"When the training rule had not yet been laid down" refers to the fact that the training rule concerning those under twenty years of age had not yet been promulgated.

"They" refers to the group of seventeen. "Therein" refers to the Giraggasamajja festival. "Then" refers to at that time. "Of them" refers to the group of seventeen; "they gave" means they presented [the gifts].
*Saṃbandho*: "Having smeared" means having applied various kinds of ointments in diverse ways.
Although it is stated generally as "at the wrong time," one must understand it as referring specifically to the [forbidden] time; thus he says, "the time," and so forth.
"And that" refers to the time for eating. The construction is: "it is midday. "By that very fact" means precisely because the time for eating is intended.
“Assā” means of the word “vikāle. By the word-analysis (*padabhājana*)—“What is called ‘unseasonable time’...
[omission] ...until the rising of the sun”—it is shown by way of meaning that the period from the rising of the sun until midday is what is called “time. “Tato” means from the established midday.
Because the sun moves very swiftly, it would pass the established midday with speed; therefore he says: “But by one who is anxious...”
"It should not be done. "A time-pillar" (*kālatthambha*) means a pillar for the purpose of knowing the time. "Within the time" (*kālantare*) means inside the time.
Regarding the phrase "the remainder is called *khādanīya* (food to be chewed)," the construction should be understood as follows:
"Whatever *khādanīya* there is"—this is the connection. Whatever *khādanīya* there is, classified as roots of trees and so forth, that too falls under the category of *āmiṣa* (material food).
The construction is: "it occurs. *Seyyathidaṃ* is a collection of particles used to introduce a question.
The meaning is: "What indeed is this solid food (*khādanīya*)? *Idampi* means "this twelvefold [food] as well. By the word *pi* (also/as well), he shows that it is not only cakes and such.

*Tattha* refers to among the twelve kinds of solid food; it is the locative case used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāre bhummam*). It is so called because one establishes oneself (*patiṭṭhāti*) therein, or by means of it.
"Or the root. "To be chewed" means *khādanīya* (chewable food). "Root-chewable-food" (*mūlakhādanīya*) is that which is a root and is also chewable;

the analysis of this term should be understood in this way—this is the construction. The "root of the radish" (*mūlakamūla*) and so forth should be understood according to worldly convention based on location alone.
Since those who do not know each of these names would be utterly confused, we shall explain the meaning of the words along with their synonyms.

"Soup" (sūpa) means that which is beneficial for soup; "soup-leaves" (sūpeyyapaṇṇa) refers to those whose leaves are used as soup; "roots of soup-leaves" (sūpeyyapaṇṇamūla) refers to the roots of those.

That which is brought inside, that which is introduced within, is called "bait" (āmisa); the letter *ā* has the sense of "internalizing. "Those whose destination is like the destination of bait" (āmisagatikāni) refers to those [roots] whose course is similar to that of bait.
"Therein" (ettha) means among the roots. "Half-rotten" (jaraḍḍhaṃ) means half that has become decayed. "And another" (aññampi) means other than the roots of the *vajaka* and *kali* plants.

The construction is: "But those roots which have been mentioned, they are [to be used] for as long as life lasts. The connection is with the phrase "mentioned in the Pāḷi. Regarding the term *khādanīyatthaṃ*:
it means the purpose of solid food (*khādanīya*), or that which exists within solid food, or the task to be performed by means of solid food, or its utility; thus, it is "for the sake of solid food.
By this term ["in solid food"], [the meaning is clarified] in such passages as "the Abhidhamma meanings mentioned therein," and so forth.
This demonstrates that, as in the case of the compound *khādanīyattha*, the meaning of the latter member is predominant.
In this context, the "function" (*kicca*) existing in, or to be performed by means of, edible food (*khādanīya*) is precisely the removal of hunger.
For when one eats edible food such as cakes and the like, and hunger is thereby removed, that is what is called its "function."

This has been stated. They neither pervade nor accomplish that task or purpose. This same method applies here as well in the phrase, "they do not pervade the purpose of food in what is fit for eating.
The connection is with "of those," meaning either within the roots or their characteristic. In one particular region, regarding the purposes of hard food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*)...
The distributive expression “in those various countries” is stated for the purpose of showing that [the qualities] indeed pervade other countries as well while they are pervading [this one].
For although edible and consumable food may be abundant in many countries due to the excellence of the essence of earth and the essence of water,
it may nonetheless be deficient in a single country due to the deficiency of the essence of earth and the essence of water.
It would not be sufficient; however, because it functions there by way of transformation (*vikāra*), that country should not be taken as the measure—it must indeed be accepted.

"By way of natural food" (*pakati-āhāra-vasena*) means by way of performing the function of food according to its own nature, unmixed with other types such as *yāvakālika* or *sattāhakālika*. By the word "of humans," [the inclusion of] others, such as animals and so forth, is excluded.
This shows that even when it extends to the purpose of solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*), it is not [exceeding] the proper measure. "That" refers to the root.
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "In the case of names and designations" (*nāmasaññāsu*) means among those designations known as names.
The construction is: just as the characteristic was shown for the root, so too the characteristic which is shown for the bulbous roots (*kanda*) and so forth should be understood.
Not only is the root of turmeric and the other items mentioned in the Pāḷi permitted for life-long use, but their bark and so forth are as well;
thus he said, “And that which...,” etc. The connection is: “that which is this eightfold [root].
Having thus shown the determination regarding edible roots, he now says, “Regarding edible tubers,” etc., in order to demonstrate that determination concerning edible tubers.
In this context, regarding the term *kandakhādanīya*: that which gives pleasure (*kaṃ*) is a *kanda* (root), such as the root of a lotus and so forth;

however, those roots that do not give pleasure are called "roots" (*kanda*) by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*). A "root-eatable" (*kandakhādanīya*) is simply an edible root (*kando eva khādanīyaṃ*).

The construction [of the sentence] should be understood as: "In that regard, the analysis is to be known thus. This same method applies to what follows as well. The word *yaṃ* refers to the root (*kanda*). By this, it does not depend on the pronoun *taṃ*.
The word *yaṃ* (which) also indicates that [the term] exists. "Therein" means among the bulbous roots (*kanda-khādanīya*).

The qualifying terms "tender" (*taruṇa*) and "easily edible" (*sukha-khādanīya*) should be applied accordingly to what follows as well. The connection is: "such bulbous roots as these are 'to-be-eaten-at-the-proper-time' (*yāvakālika*).
"Unwashed" (*adhota*) means that the pungent sap has been rinsed away with water. "They" refers to the bulbous roots; the connection is that they are included [in the category].
It is called *muḷāla* because it grows or spreads at its root (*mūle alati pavattati*); or, because it closes or shuts up as soon as it is pulled out from the water, it is *muḷāla*.

Such and other types of spreading *muḷāla* are to be understood as "permissible for the time being" (*yāvakālika*). The connection is: "all that" means all that *muḷāla* is included [in the category].

It is called the *matthaka* (head) because one dies (*masati*) or pierces (*vijjhati*) there. Such things as these—the head and so forth—are to be understood as "permissible for the time being" (*yāvakālika*). The term *jaraḍḍhabunda* refers to a foot that has become worn out or half-worn away.

It is called a *khandha* (trunk/branch) because it is carved out (*khanīyati*) or split open (*avadārīyati*), or else it is called a *khandha* because it is eaten (*khāyati*). The phrase "gone into the inner earth" is to be construed only with the phrase "the trunk of a noble *sāla* tree," and not with others.

Such things as these—the trunk and so forth—are to be understood as "permissible for the time being. The term "the rest" (*avasesā*) refers to those remaining after the three [categories], such as the staff and so on.
It is called *taco* (skin) because it stretches (*tacati*), restrains (*saṃvarati*), and covers (*paṭicchādeti*). The word "only" (*sarasoti*) should be construed here with the particle *eva*;
thus the meaning is "only sap. Their "conjunction" (*saṅgaho*) means their connection. "Indeed" (*hi*) signifies truth.

"This" (*etam*) refers either to the medicinal decoction (*kasāvabhesajja*) or to the statement: "I authorize... for the purpose of food. "In this" (*ettha*) refers to the medicinal decoction. "Of these too" (*etesampi*) refers even to the skin of the head and the trunk.

"It falls" means *pattaṃ* (a leaf). "Of these" refers to the radish and so forth. The construction is: "leaves of such a kind are exclusively *yāvakālika* (to be used within the same day). The construction is:
"the leaf of that salt-creeper which climbs up is *yāvajīvika* (to be used for as long as one lives). "Dwellers of the island" means dwellers of Tambapaṇṇi Island or dwellers of Jambudīpa.
Or, the connection is: "those which are called 'spreading'. "Of these" refers to the neem trees and so forth. This...
The word *pada* (foot/step) is dependent on what precedes and follows it; therefore, it should be understood as being stated between two others. The connection is: "there is no end to leaves.
It blooms and expands, thus it is called *puppha* (flower). The construction is: "flowers such as these are *yāvakālika* (to be used within the same day).

*Tassa* means "of that flower. *Assa* means "in this very way. It bears fruit, thus it is called *phala* (fruit). *Yāni* means "which fruits. The connection is: "they spread (*pharanti*). *Nesaṃ* means "of those fruits," and [the phrase refers to] their limit (*pariyanta*).
The connection [is as follows]: the construction is that those which have been mentioned are for life (*yāvajīvika*).

"Of these too" means the connection is with the fruits (*phala*) as having a limit. *Aṭṭhi* means it is thrown, cast, or discarded. The construction is that such filling bones (*aṭṭhi*) are for a single meal-time (*yāvakālika*).

"Of these" refers to the bones. *Piṭṭha* means it is ground or made into powder. The construction is that such filling flours (*piṭṭha*) are for a single meal-time. *Adhotaka* means not washed with water. "Of these" refers to the flours.
*Niyyāsa* means that which is extracted when [the substance] is squeezed continuously. *Sesā* means the remainder from sugarcane juice (*ucchuniyyāsa*).
