The connection is with "the juices mentioned in the text. *Tattha* refers to among the edible juices. The construction is: "the limit of the juices included therein.
*Evaṃ* and so forth is the conclusion.
"Vuttameva" (already stated) means that it was already stated below in the first *pavāraṇā* training rule. This is the seventh [section].
8. The Training Rule on Storing (Sannidhikāraka-sikkhāpada) 252.
In the eighth [rule], "internal" (*abbhantara*) means born within. "Great Elder" (*mahāthera*) means one endowed with great qualities of steadfastness.
By this, he shows that the name of the designation, "Belaṭṭha," refers to the designatum.
"In the house of striving" means in a single residence designated as a place for striving (*padhāna*) in serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Regarding "dried rice" (*sukkhakura*):
it is not called "dried rice" because it is dried there, but rather because it is devoid of curry and sauce; thus he says, "rice without curry or sauce. Even [the term] "dried rice" (*sosanakura*)...
This is indeed appropriate. For he will say: “Having moistened that alms-food with water. By the word “rice” (*odana*), he shows that the word *kura* is a synonym for rice.
For it is called *kura* because it produces vitality, complexion, and so forth. “He” refers to Belaṭṭhasīsa.
“And that” connects to the phrase “he brought that dry *kura*. “Because of greed for requisites” means:
“Because of greed regarding the requisite of almsfood”—this is the connection with the phrase “the elder eats.

It is called “seven days” because the single meal of human beings lasts for only seven days. “Than that”—the connection is “than eating. In the phrase “even four,” the word “even” (pi) indicates that more than seven days should also be understood.
253. *Iti* means "this. In the compound *sannidhikāro assa*, it should be understood as a genitive-tatpuruṣa (visesanaparanipāta) [meaning "one who has storage"].
By the phrase "the meaning is 'the act of storing' (*sannidhikiriyā*)," he shows that the sense of the object (*kamma*) is expressed by the word *kāro*, derived from the root *karoti* ("to do").
*Ekarattaṃ* is stated by way of the ultimate limit; however, more than that is also intended. *Assa* refers to the word *sannidhikārako*.

Because it serves as the condition for an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) regarding a seven-day medicine kept in store, [the text] says "or a night-time medicine" (*yāmakālika*), meaning that even though a night-time medicine is not the same as food or soft food kept in store, it nevertheless becomes a condition for a simple offense of expiation (*suddha-pācittiya*) due to the desire to swallow it.
"In the receiving" (*paṭiggahaṇe*) means both in the act of formally accepting and in the act of taking hold of it. "With the desire to swallow" (*ajjhoharitukāmatāya*).

For it is said: "both in the receiving and after having received and holding. The construction is: "that bowl which, when rubbed with a finger, shows a streak, is poorly washed, provided that [it is] so" (*sace*);
for, seeing the word *yaṃ* in the subsequent sentence, the word *taṃ* is to be understood in the preceding sentence.
"Of a knotted bowl" means of a bowl with a binding. "That" refers to the moisture.
The connection is: "it drips" and "is visible. "Such as that" means in a case where it is difficult to wash, or where there is a knot.
"Therein" connects with "having poured [the water] into the washed bowl. "Hi" (indeed) means truly. "Abbohārikā" means not to be spoken of;
the meaning is that it is not fit to be designated. "Yaṃ" (that which) connects with "they relinquish the solid and soft food. "Hi" (indeed) means truly, or because.
The connection [of the phrase] is: "having taken out from that which has not yet been relinquished as food or soft food.
"Among unallowable meats" is a collective term used for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇa*). "When there is a requisite" means when there is a requisite consisting of thirst.
"Not made into leftover" (*anatirittakata*) is to be construed as: "food or soft food that is not made into a remainder (*atiritta*) by one who stores it away (*sannidhikāraka*)."
The connection is: "only one *pācittiya* offense. Regarding the "two alternatives": in the two alternatives known as "with food" (*sāmisa*) and "without food" (*nirāmisa*).

Regarding "all alternatives": in all alternatives known as "out-of-season" (*vikāla*), "stored" (*sannidhi*), "unfit meat" (*akappiyamaṃsa*), "improper time" (*yāmakālika*), and "conditioned" (*paccaya*).
255. "Mixed with food" (*āmisasaṃsaṭṭha*): that which is mixed with food, namely the seven-day medicine (*sattāhakālika*) and the lifetime medicine (*yāvajīvika*).
256. Showing both the form and the etymological meaning of what pertains to the four periods of time, he says: “In the training rule on eating at the wrong time,” and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase “the solid and soft food that has been pointed out,” he shows the form of what pertains to the proper time (*yāvakālika*).

By the phrase “as long as... [omitted] ...pertaining to the proper time,” he shows the etymological meaning. By the phrase “together with... [omitted] ...drinks,” he shows the form of what pertains to the watch of the night (*yāmakālika*).

This shows the meaning of the term. By the phrase “as long as... pe ... for a limited time,” it shows the meaning of the expression. By the phrase “the five kinds of medicine beginning with ghee,” it shows the actual nature of the seven-day medicine.
By the phrase “for seven days... pe ... for a limited time,” it shows the meaning of the expression. By the phrase “excepting... pe ...
even all of it,” it shows the actual nature of the lifetime medicine. By the phrase “as long as... pe ... for a lifetime,” it [shows the meaning].
He shows the meaning of the words. The meaning of all the terms is merely light; however, the grave meaning should be understood as follows:
"As long as" refers to the time up until midday, which is the *yāvakāla*; that which is fit for that time, or that which is to be consumed during that time, is *yāvakālika*.
"A watch of the night" is *yāmakāla*; that which is fit for that time, or that which is to be consumed during that time, is *yāmakālika*.
A period of seven days is "seven-day time" (*sattāhakāla*); that is its duration. Having stored it for that duration, it may be consumed; thus it is "seven-day timed" (*sattāhakālika*).
As long as life lasts is "as-long-as-life" (*yāvajīva*); that is its duration. Having kept it for as long as one lives, it may be consumed;
thus it is "for-life" (*yāvajīvika*).

“In that regard” means among the four kinds of [food] taken at the proper time (*kālika*). “A hundred times” means many times. The construction is: “for one who eats as long as the time has not elapsed. The connection is: “for one who eats day and night. This is the eighth [section]. 9.
The Training Rule on Exquisite Food (Paṇītabhojana-sikkhāpada) 257.

Regarding the ninth [rule], since it is said that what has been brought to a state of excellence is “exquisite” (*paṇīta*), the word *paṇīta* signifies the sense of “supreme”; thus he says, “exquisite foods.”
"Sampanna" does not mean the quality of sweetness itself, but rather food that possesses the quality of sweetness; thus he says "endowed with excellence.
The genitive case here is used in the sense of the instrumental; its meaning is "by what.
By the word "surasa," he shows the etymological form of the term "sādu," which means "that which is tasted" or "that which is relished."
259. Regarding the phrase, “But whoever... should eat,” the analysis (vinicchaya) here should be understood as follows:

this is the construction. “Pure” (suddhāni) means unmixed with boiled rice (odana). “Boiled rice mixed with *sabbi* and so forth” is the connection [to be made]. “In this” (*ettha*) refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly.
By the term “mixed with delicacies” (*paṇītasaṃsaṭṭhāni*), it refers to foods mixed with delicious *sabbi* and so forth.
This shows the meaning of "exquisite foods. By the phrase "produced from the seven grains," he shows the specific nature of those foods.
Among the five alternatives beginning with "rice with all [condiments]," the word "rice" (*bhatta*) should be construed with three of them.
Having thus formed the sentence and shown the offense in the case of making it understood, he now shows the offense in the case of making it understood by forming a compound.
Showing this, he said, “Give me food with all its accompaniments,” and so forth.

“Iti” (thus) is connected with “gāvito laddhena” (obtained from a cowherd). “Visaṅketaṃ” means that which is devoid of or separated from what is made known by convention (saṅketa). “Hi” means truly. By this, he shows the virtue and fault of being free from convention. The construction is:
“Give me food with allowable accompaniments,” meaning food mixed with allowable accompaniments. This same method applies [to the following].

"Also [the words] *sesesu pi* (and so on). *Yena yena* means by whichever [substance], such as curd (*sabbi*) and so forth. *Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ*—here too, the meaning should be understood according to the distributive sense (*vicchā*).
In the Canon, 'curd' (*sabbi*) refers to cow's curd, goat's curd, buffalo curd, and the curd of those animals whose meat is permitted.
'Butter' (*navanīta*) is exactly the same. 'Oil' (*tela*) refers to sesame oil, mustard oil," and so on.
Madhuka oil, castor oil, and fat oil. Honey means honey from bees.
Treacle means that which is produced from sugarcane. Fish means a water-dweller; there is no such thing as "fish" not included in the Canon.
Meat means the meat of those animals whose meat is permitted. Milk and curd are exactly like [the previous categories]. As it has been said: "curd-rice... [and so on].
In such cases as "Give me [something]," the construction is that there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for requesting rice-soup or boiled rice.
"Hi" means "truly. "So ca" means "that very same meaning. "Tattha" means "in that sense. "What is the purpose?"—the intention is that there is no purpose at all.
"Food already obtained"—this is the connection. "Of one flavor" means having a single function. "From that"—the connection is "having taken out from those nine kinds of refined food."
"Sabbañi" (all) is said with reference to the nine *pācittiya* rules.
261. "Of both" means of both monks and nuns. Here, "sabbi" refers to that which, for the purpose of increasing strength and vitality in one who consumes it, goes everywhere and flows;
thus, it is clarified butter (*ghata*). By the third syllable alone...

It should be recited and written down. Why? Because in the *Dhātupāṭha*, the root *gati* (to go) with the meaning of "going" is listed as *sabbagatiyaṃ* specifically in the third syllable-position. Ninth.
10. The Training Rule on Tooth-sticks (*dantapona-sikkhāpada*).
263. “Dantakaṭṭha” means a tooth-cleanser. For it is called “dantakaṭṭha” because by means of it the teeth are scraped and polished.
With the words “all,” etc., he shows the meaning as follows: “all rags” is *sabbapaṃsukūla*; one who has that is a “sabbapaṃsukūlika.
The connection is: “that bhikkhu, it is said, uses [it]. “In a charnel ground” means in a cremation site; for that—

By way of etymology (*niruttinaya*), it is called "charnel ground" (*susāna*) because it is a place for laying the dead. "Therein" means in the charnel ground. Again, "therein" means in that very same way.
To show both the form of a noble person (*ayya*) and the form of one who has been cast away (*vosāṭitaka*), it is said:

"In this context, 'noble and cast-away'. Therein, by the phrase "Nobles... [down to] grandfathers," he shows the form of a noble person. By the phrase "Cast-away... [down to] foods fit for eating," he shows the form of one who has been cast away.

"Discarded food" (*vosāṭitaka*) means: the analysis (*viggaha*) should be made thus: "edible and consumable foods that have been discarded or cast away for the sake of, or dedicated to, one's ancestors known as 'noble ones' (*ayya*).
"People reportedly set it aside" is the connection. "Which" refers to the edible and consumable food. "Of them" refers to the relatives. "Bite by bite" (*piṇḍaṃ piṇḍaṃ*).
"Having made" means having folded it together, layer by layer (*saṅghāṭaṃ saṅghāṭaṃ*). "Other" means other than the aforementioned soft foods (*khādanīya*) and hard foods (*bhojanīya*).

"Even at the threshold" (*ummārepi*) means even at the threshold-post (*indakhīla*) of the cemetery; for that is called "the threshold" (*ummāra*) because the Māra of the defilements (*kilesamāra*) has been removed from there.
For when the Bodhisatta was about to go forth, thinking "I shall kiss my son," he stood at the threshold-post of his chamber and looked out upon his mother.
Seeing his wife sleeping with her hand placed upon her son’s forehead, he thought, "If I were to take my son, his mother would wake;

if she wakes, there would be an obstacle. Out of fear of an obstacle to his Great Renunciation, he abandoned his son and wife, turned back from the threshold of the gate, and set forth on the Great Departure. Therefore, regarding the Bodhisatta—

Because it is the place where Māra—consisting of attachment to wife and children—is uprooted once one has stood there, that threshold-stone (indakhīla) is called a "step" (ummāra) in its primary sense;
others, however, [use the term] by way of conventional usage. *Thira* means firm (*thaddha*). *Ghanabaddha* means bound by density;
the meaning is that it is bound by tough flesh. It is called *vaṭha* because it becomes thick (*vaṭhati*); this is a word with *muddha* as its second member.
He says, "‘Vaṭharo’ means ‘thūlo’ (stout)," showing that *assatthī* means *vaṭharo*.

By the word "sallakkhemā," he shows that in the phrase "maññe," the verbal root *man* has the sense of observing (*sallakkhaṇa*), and that the letter *m* [in *maññe*] is actually the vowel *e*. "Hi" means "truly. "Tesam" refers to those humans.
"Sammā" means "unerringly. "Asallakkhetvā" [refers to] the fact that the word *āhāra* is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in the sense of things to be chewed, eaten, and so forth.
The connection is: "But the Blessed One set it aside. "In whatever manner it arose" means in whichever mode it had arisen. The construction is:
"Just as a father instructs his child, who is reckoned as a son, so the Blessed One instructed those bhikkhus.
265. "This very thing" refers to that which was indeed not given, by way of any one of the three modes; this is the connection. "For" (hi) is used as a particle.
True. There is no place in the *mātikā* where the word "given" (*dinna*) is mentioned; therefore, he asks, "Why is it mentioned only in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*)?
and says, "‘Given’—this [is what is meant]," and so forth. The connection is: "‘Given’—this is what is extracted.
And in the *niddesa*, the construction is: "extracted as ‘giving with the body... and so on. "In this way" means by these three modes.
The connection is with the word "giving" (*dadamāna*). "In this way" means by these two modes. The connection is with the word "being received" (*ādīyamāna*).

"Even the dust raised by a chariot" (*rathareṇumpi*) refers even to the dust that has arisen on a carriage road. "In the past" (*pubbe*) refers to the training rule concerning the first invitation (*paṭhamapavāraṇasikkhāpada*).
The construction is: "Food accepted in this manner is called 'given'. Regarding the phrase "only this," since such a thing is possible, it refers to its result.
The words beginning with “not this” are stated in order to demonstrate [this point]. The construction is: “it is not called ‘given away’. Therein means:
in the statement beginning with “with the body,” etc. “Hi” means truly. It is called *natthukaraṇī* because one performs the act of blowing the nose (*natthu*) by means of it;
[the meaning is] “by that [instrument]. The connection is: “he receives it with the nostril. “Akallako” means one who is ill. “Hi” means truly. With the body...
“Connected” means connected to the body, such as a spoon and so forth; thus he says, “in spoons and so forth,” etc. “Hi” means truly.
“Being poured” means being caused to be poured. “Therein” means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). Showing the expansion of the phrase “by five factors,” he says, “of one of medium strength,” etc.

“That” refers to the object to be given. “Therein” refers to the statement, “the range of the hand is discerned. One who is walking is also included by [the category of] one who is standing. “Of one standing on the ground” means...
“Standing on the ground. “Standing in the air” means standing in the sky. A connection with the parts [of the body] should be made by means of the words “hand” and “limb.
“In the same manner as stated” means in the very manner stated [previously] by the passage beginning with “and with the head of one standing on the ground,” etc. “A bird” means a winged creature;

for it is called a “bird” (pakkhī) because it is possessed of wings (pakkha). “An elephant” means a kuñjara; for it is [called an elephant] because it is possessed of a trunk (hattha) known as a *soṇḍa*.
It is called an "elephant. Because it has seven and a half *ratana*s in length, it is "seven-and-a-half-*ratana*"; [this refers to] the elephant. "By that" means by the elephant.
"One donor says" is the connection [of the phrase]. "Bows down" means it inclines downward. "To this extent" means merely by accepting a portion.
"From that" means from the acceptance. "Having uncovered" means having opened. "With a carrying-pole" means with a *byābhaṅgi*; for that indeed carries (*kacati*).
That which binds various burdens is called *kāca*; when the letter *ca* is changed to *ja*, it is also correctly formed as *kāja*.
That which measures thirty cubits (*hattha*) in *ratana*s is "thirty-cubit" (*tiṃsahattha*), referring to a bamboo pole. A "lump-pot" (*guḷakumbha*) is a jar filled with molasses (*phāṇita*).
It is said that "it has already been accepted" because, even though the jars stand outside the reach of one's hand, they remain within the reach of the hand of the person offering them.
"It has already been accepted" is what is meant. "From the sugar-cane press vat" means from the pit of the sugar-cane pressing machine.
"Many bowls were placed there" is the grammatical connection. "Where" means in which place. The construction is: "within arm's reach of the standing bhikkhu.
Having stood and touched [the bowl], it should be connected with the elliptical phrase "of the sitting bhikkhu. By one who is standing...
The connection is: "it is given by a donor who is standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.

The connection is: "they are standing upon the earth. "Whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) refers to whichever bowl (*patta*). "In any place whatsoever" (*yattha katthaci*) is connected as "in any [of those] whatever" (*yesu kesuci*).

"That" (*taṃ*) refers to that statement. "Produced there" (*tatthajāto*) means produced in that place; this is a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*), and it is precisely that which is "produced there" (*tatthajātako*); [the word] "in that" (*tasmiṃ*) refers to that.
*Hi* means "truth" or "because. The construction is: "Just as it does not grow in that which is born there, so too it simply does not grow.
*Saṃhāriyaṃ* means "that which is to be well-carried by a man of medium strength"; making the letter *ya* into the letter *ma*, that very word becomes *saṃhārimaṃ*.
*Asaṃhārimaṃ* means "not to be carried"; [it refers] to that. *Tepi* means "even those," referring to those things that are not to be carried. *Hi* means "truth."
"Or because": *tatthajātakasaṅkhepūpagā* means they have come to a state of being cast away or discarded after being gathered together in the *Tatthajātaka*.
*Hi* means "truly" or "because. It should be understood that this is stated repeatedly because it constitutes a separate sentence.
*Tāni* refers to leaves such as those of the *tintiṇika* tree. *Sandhāretuṃ* means to hold [them] properly. The connection is with the words "the donor stands."
Because it is a place for storing whatever item has been obtained, or because it is a place where items are placed, it is called a *thavikā* (a bag), as it is praised or commended;

therefore [the word is used]. Regarding the phrase "having wiped and received," the particle *vā* (or) should be supplied to express an alternative or non-exclusive option, such that it means "either having wiped or having received.
It is called a *rañjanī* because it dyes or adheres to various items.
"Dust" (rajo) refers to that. "Offense of wrong-doing prescribed in the Vinaya" means a *dukkaṭa* offense as laid down in the Vinaya. "But that" (*taṃ pana*) refers to the alms-food (*bhikkhaṃ*).
"Having received it, give [it] to me" implies: "Having had me receive it, give it to me.

"From here and there" (*tato tato*) is connected with "having made him rise from each respective place. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the alms-food. "Of him" (*tassa*) refers to the one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

"He should be addressed" means that the monk who is being given [the cloth] should be addressed by the donor-monk; this is the construction. "This" refers to the cotton cloth. "By him" means by the monk who is giving it.
"It should be done in such a way" means it should be done exactly as stated by the donor-monk;
this is the meaning. "Uplavati" means it goes upward; for in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), specifically in the *Saddanītidhātumālā*, the root *plu* is defined as "going."
16. (The verbal root ending in *ḷ*). This has been stated. Here, the word "upari" is used for the purpose of showing the meaning of the prefix *uti*;
the conjunction of the letters *pa* and *ka* (*pakāra-lakāra*) is to be understood. However, in some manuscripts they write "uppilavati," but that is not the correct reading.
"Kañjika" means fermented gruel (*bilaṅga*). For it is called "kañjiya" because it is "anointed" (*añjiya*)—that is, made manifest—by some liquid (*jala*).
Having changed that very *kañjika* (sour gruel) from the letter *ya* to the letter *ka*. "Having removed it" means having expelled it or taken it away.
"Where" means in which place. "Dry rice" (*sukkhabhatta*) means rice that is to be eaten or consumed in a dry state;
in that [rice]. "In front" means in front of the bhikkhu, or previously. "Drops" means droplets. For these [drops] occur even in narrow places.
They are called *phusitāni* because they touch (*phusanti*).
An *uḷuṅka* is a particular kind of vessel with a long handle, named after the *kosiya* bird; [it is] by means of that.
*Thevā* refers to droplets. For these are called *thevā* because they are praised (*thavīyanti*) for being touched (*phusitattā*) even in narrow places.

*Carukaṃ*: It is called *caru* because it is moved about (*carīyati*) or consumed (*bhakkhīyati*); it is a cooked oblation (*habbapāka*). That by which one prepares this is a *caruka*, a small vessel such as a pan;
the connection is "being sprinkled with that. *Masi*: It is called *masi* because it is measured out (*mānīyati*) by those desiring black color.

*Chāra*: It is called *chāra* because it consumes (*khādati*). By changing the letter *kha* to *cha* and the letter *da* to *ra*, it becomes "alkaline taste" (*khārarasa*); she who has that [taste] is [the word *chāriṇī*].
*Chārikā*: ash. *Uppatitvā*: having flown up, having gone upwards.

*Hi*: indeed, or because. *Phāletvā*: having split, having cut. The connection is with "of those giving who are not ordained. *Pāyāsassa*: by means of the milk-rice. *Tathāpi*: even in that manner, even by that way of grasping with the rim of the mouth. *Ābhogaṃ katvā*:
having made an application of mind, having formed the mental attention, "I shall receive it. *So*: that monk who had fallen asleep.

"It is indeed permissible" means that because an intention (*ābhoga*) has been formed, it is indeed permissible. "Disrespectfully" (*anādaraṃ*): this is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental;
or it should be construed as "having become disrespectful. "Some": namely, the residents of Abhayagiri. "Connected with the body" (*kāyapaṭibaddha*): that which is connected to the body;

"connected with what is connected to that" (*kāyapaṭibaddhapaṭibaddha*): that which is connected to what is connected to the body; [it is permissible] by means of that. "Merely the words" (*vacanamattam eva*).
Regarding the phrase “connected-to-what-is-connected” (*paṭibaddhapaṭibaddha*): there is only a difference in terminology, with one term being redundant;

however, in terms of meaning, the intention is that it refers solely to what is connected to the body. “Whatever” (*yampi*) refers to the object. “Therein” (*tatra*) means in that turning. “That” (*taṃ*) refers to the permission.

“Of interpretable meaning” (*neyyatthaṃ*): the meaning is to be known by leading it to its underlying intention (*adhippāya*); thus, it is called “of interpretable meaning” because its sense is to be understood by leading it [to that intention]. “In this” (*ettha*) refers to the Sutta, or to the meaning of the Sutta.
The connection is: "the object goes and falls. *Parigaḷitvā* means having dissolved. *Suddhāya* means free from dust. *Sāmaṃ* means by oneself.
In the phrases beginning with *puñchitvā vā*, there are three uses of the particle *vā* (or), which signify non-restriction or optionality.

For the intention is that once one of the tasks, such as wiping, has been performed, there is no need to perform the other tasks. *Tenā* means by that bhikkhu. In the phrase *āharāpetumpi*: [End of provided text]
“An action performed” (*kāritakamma*). The question is: “Why is it not appropriate? *Hi* indicates the detailed explanation. The connection is with the phrase “by the Blessed One speaking.
“In this context” refers to the words of the Suttas. The construction is: “by the statement, ‘That, O monks, has been relinquished by the donors.
“The intended meaning” (*adhippāya*) means the explicit meaning; what is meant is that the intended meaning is the meaning established as such, not in a figurative sense, but as a known fact.
Having thus shown the intention regarding the explicit meaning (*nītattha*), he says "And because... and so forth, in order to show the intention regarding the implicit meaning (*neyyattha*).
The connection is: "that [act of] consuming was permitted. The word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "on the second day also" has the sense of inclusion;

the meaning is "on another day as well. "Intention" (*adhippāya*) refers to the implicit meaning; it is said that the intention is the meaning to be led to, the meaning to be inferred, or the meaning to be known.
The connection is with the phrase "of the monks who are eating. The word *hi* indicates an elaboration. *Dantā* means teeth;
they are called "teeth" (*danta*) because things are bitten (*daṃsīyanti*) or eaten by them. *Satthakaṃ* is simply *satthaṃ* (a knife) in the sense of being small;
[the phrase refers to] that knife which has been received. *Etaṃ* refers to the impurity. *Taṃ* refers to the mere smell of iron. *Pariharanti* means having received it.
"They take away. *Hi* means "truth" or "because. Since they do not carry that curd around for the purpose of consumption, the meaning is that this same principle applies.
What is meant is that there is no fault regarding the condition of having been received or the condition of being stored.
*Tattha* means "in those [cases of] buttermilk and milk. *Nīlikā* refers to blue-colored oils. *Āmakatakka-ādīsū* means "in raw buttermilk and so forth," that is, in uncooked buttermilk and milk.
*Kiliṭṭhaudakaṃ* means dirty water. *Tassa* refers to the novice (*sāmaṇera*). The connection is with "the rice that has gone into his bowl.
*Assa* also refers to the novice. *Uggahitako* means one who has taken [it] improperly. Just as in the case of words such as *uññāto*, the vowel *u* is a corruption of the vowel *o*;
because it was taken without having been formally offered, it is said to be "taken wrongly" (*duggahitako*).
"By this" means by the boiled rice (*odana*). The intention is that it has already been received because it has not been released from the hand.
"When there is a need to receive again" is the intended meaning. "From this" means from this bowl (*patta*). "The novice throws [it] in" is the syntactical connection.
"From that" means from the bowl. "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. "That" refers to the phrase "to be received again."
The connection is that the words of certain teachers should be understood.
"Yam" refers to the morning meal and so forth. "Attano vā" means "or for the novice (sāmaṇera) himself. "Sāmaṇera" is a form of address. "Tassa" means "of the novice.
"Bhājane" means in the vessel used for cooking rice-gruel. "Yāgukuṭaṃ" means a jar filled with rice-gruel. "Taṃ" refers to that jar of rice-gruel. "By a bhikkhu... [the sentence continues].
The phrase "having had it accepted" means that the performed action should be brought forward. The connection is: "having placed the neck [of the bowl], he directs his attention.
"Directs his attention" means he dedicates it.
"A load suitable for acceptance" refers to a portable load that can be carried by a man of medium strength. "By a strong novice" [is the further specification].
*Saṃbandho*: "A jar of oil" means a jar into which oil has been poured. "Laggenti" means they hang down; or rather, this is the reading itself.
"Nāgadantako": like the tusk (*danta*) of a nāga; the suffix *ko* is used here in the sense of similarity. "Aṅkusako":
that by which one is marked or characterized is a hook (*aṅkusa*), a thorny goad for piercing the head of an elephant. "Like a hook" means *aṅkusako*; or, they are hung upon that hook.
The connection is with the word "are. "Of one taking" means of one who is taking. "Under the bed" means beneath the bed; [it refers to] that. "That" refers to the oil-vessel.
A ladder is so called because it is constantly used by those ascending and descending; its middle is the "middle of the ladder," [it refers to] that.
"Ear-wax" is that which has arisen in the ear; it is called *kaṇṇika* because it is like *kaṇṇika* (ear-wax), for just as ear-wax...
"Arising from the ear, it proceeds by itself"—this means that having arisen from oil and so forth, it proceeds by itself.
"Solid powder" (*ghanacuṇṇa*) means hard powder. "It is indeed of that same origin" means that its origin is precisely from that oil and so forth;
this is the meaning. "This" refers to the *kaṇṇikā* (the wick-base) and so on. This term is dependent upon what precedes and follows.
"By means of a rope" (*yottenāti*) means by means of a cord. "Another gives" is the connection [with the previous phrase].
"Fence" (*vati*): that which encloses or obstructs as one enters and exits; that is what it is. "Sugar-cane" (*ucchūti*) means *rasāla*.
For it is called sugar-cane because it burns away poison (*usati visaṃ*); that is what it is. "Timbarusaka" means *tinduka*. For it moistens (*temeti*).
"Timbu" means one who eats a person by means of flavor (rasa); "rusaka" means one who devours—that is, destroys—what has been chewed;

thus, being both *timbu* and *rusaka*, it is called "timbarusaka," which [refers to that]. "In the fence-stakes" (*vatidaṇḍakesu*) means in the stakes driven into the ground for the purpose of a fence.
"But we" (*mayaṃ pana*) refers to us, namely the teacher Buddhaghosa, who is the author of this compendium (*saṅgaha*). "Himself" (*attanā*)...
This was stated by way of the plural number with intentional ambiguity (*sandhāya*). "The wall is not wide" was said with reference to exceeding two and a half cubits of stone.
"Even a hundred cubits" means even a hundred *ratana*s. "He" refers to the novice (*sāmaṇera*).
The construction is: "he gives to the monk. "Another" refers to the novice.
"Phalinī" means "one who has fruit," derived from the suffix *in* with the feminine indicator *ī*. The construction is: "a branch (*sākha*) of that [tree].

There is also a reading as a compound: "phalinisākhā. Regarding "for the purpose of warding off flies": they are called *makkhikā* because they settle (*nilīyanti*) on places smeared with honey, molasses, and so forth;
these very ones are *macchikā*, formed by changing the letter *kha* to *cha*; [the phrase means] for their prevention.
"Only the original receiving" means the very act of receiving at the root; it is said to be "only the first receiving.
"The bhikkhu goes" is the connection [of the sentence]. "With the oar" means with the *kenipāta*. For that by which a boat (*nāvā*) moves along is called an oar (*aritta*);
[it is used] with that. "That" refers to the goods worthy of being received. "By one who is not fully ordained" refers to the work performed. "In that case too" [refers to the same].
Also in Cāṭikuṇḍaka. "Him" refers to one who is not fully ordained.
"Traveling rice" means rice suitable for a journey. "Of them" refers to the novices. "By the others" means by the monks with the rice they had taken.
The connection is: "all the monks ate. "Therein" refers to [the rice] taken by the monks.
The connection is: "In the case of a novice (sāmaṇera), [the fault] is not seen when rice-gruel is cooked with rice.
"The reason" refers to the reason for both that which was eaten after being turned over and that which was eaten without being turned over.

The construction is: "The novice, desiring to cook the meal... The connection is: "It should be placed [on the fire] by a monk; the fire itself must not be made. The intention is: "There is no further requirement for formal acceptance (paṭiggahaṇa), because it was already accepted at the source."
"Assa" means of the novice. "Tato" means from the blazing of the fire.
"Tatte udake" means in heated water. "Tato" means from the throwing in of the rice.

"Pidhānaṃ" means the lid for the cooking pot (*ukkhalipidhāna*). "Tasseva" means of that very monk who was anxious about his hands. "Dabbiṃ vā" means a ladle or a spoon; for it is called a *dabbī* because by means of it one stirs (*darīyati*) or mixes (*viloḷīyati*).
*Tatra* means in that placing. *Tasseva* means of that very greedy bhikkhu. *Tato* means from the bowl. Again, *tato* means from the branches, etc. *Tattha* means in the fruit trees.
*Vitakkaṃ sodhetuṃ* means to clear away the thought, "He will give to me as well. *Tato* means from the mango fruits, etc.

Again, *tato* means from the oil taken for the sake of mother and father, etc. *Te* refers to the mother and father. *Tatoyeva* is connected with the phrase "having prepared it with those very same grains of rice."

"Herein" means in the heated water. The construction is: "with the very hand that did not let go. They go to destruction (*aṅga*), thus they are called "embers" (*aṅgāra*). They are split and shattered, thus they are "wood" (*dāru*).

"The novice was mentioned"—this is the construction. It makes a sound like "guḷa" when being consumed by cows; or, it protects life from poison (*visa*) by "gul-ing," thus it is "molasses" (*guḷa*). The connection is: "the monk distributing that [molasses]. "Of him" refers to the greedy novice.

It is called a "smoke-wick" (*dhūmavaṭṭi*) because it is rolled up for the purpose of smoke and made into a roll; that [is what is meant]. It is called a "mouth" (*mukha*) because it is opened or turned away. "Kaṃ" refers to the head; that which stands there [supporting] it is the "throat" (*kaṇṭha*).
"Food-vomit" (*bhattuggāra*): it is called "vomit" (*uggāra*) because one vomits or ejects upward; food itself is the vomit, hence "food-vomit," meaning "vomited food.
"Between the teeth" means in the gaps between the teeth. "At the approaching time" means at the time near midday. "Having gathered together" (*kakkhāretvā*); in order to show its meaning:
It is said: "having spat out two or three mouthfuls of saliva. That which has a horn (siṅga) known as a phalusa—that is, a prong—is *siṅgī*;
and because one must abstain from it due to its pungency and danger, it is called *siṅgīvera*. A tree is marked (*aṅkīyati*) as having newly emerged;
they are called *aṅkurā* because things are characterized (*lakkhīyati*) by them. In this [term], salt is equal to water, or water is equal to salt.
The ocean: its water, by way of the relationship between whole and part (*avayavī-avayava-bhāvena*), is "ocean-water" (*samuddodaka*);
the connection [in the compound] is with the phrase "not accepted by that. It hardens—that is, it attains a solid state from molasses—is "molasses" (*phāṇita*).
"Karakas" are things to be held in the hand; the meaning is "raindrops," as they are worthy of being grasped by the hand. "Kataka-stones" refers to those called *kataka*.
"With the bone of a certain specific tree. *Taṃ* refers to the water. *Kapittha* is the name of a specific tree with sour fruit. *Bahalaṃ* means turbid. *Sanditvā* means having overflowed.
*Kakudhasobbhādayo* refers to pools and such located near the *kakudha* tree. *Rukkhatō* means from the *kakudha* tree. *Parittaṃ* means small. The connection is:
"they were placed in the water-jars. *Taṃ* refers to the mere amount of water. *Tattheva* means in that very same [jar] containing the water scented with flowers.
The connection is: "a tooth-stick has been placed. The construction is: "of a monk who does not know.
This genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. "Hi" means "truly," or "because. The construction is:
"Which great element is permissible, and which is not permissible? "Yaṃ pana" means "but as for that great element. "Aṅgalaggaṃ" means...
The connection is: "the great element clinging to the limbs. "Therein" means in the sweat. "Well-burnt" means well-burnt by having been made like charcoal.

"Four" refers to the four: earth, ash, feces, and urine. "Great purificatory medicines" (*mahāvikaṭāni*) refers to the potent medicinal herbs to be administered at the time of transformation known as being bitten by a snake.
"Therein" refers to the statement: "when there is no one to make it allowable" (*kappiyakāraka*). *Kālodissa*.

"By name" means among the seven types of directions—namely, direction by name, direction by person, direction by time, direction by occasion, direction by place, direction by power, and direction by medicine—it refers to "direction by time. Tenth.
The fourth chapter on food is concluded.
5. The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga) 1. The Exegesis of the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 269.

Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics, he says “the place of distribution” (*parivesanaṭṭhāna*) in order to show that it is called a “distribution hall” (*parivesanā*) because people distribute food there.
Since the words *paribbājaka* (wanderer) and *pabbajjā* (renunciation) are synonymous, he said: “One who has attained the state of a wanderer is one who has entered upon renunciation.
That which fills to the level of the ford is *samatitthīka*; this refers to water in rivers and the like. Like that which is at the level of the ford, it is *samatitthika*;
this refers to rice porridge and solid food in bowls and vessels. “Of them” is connected with “of those giving to his mother and father. “Causes to give” means...
Since the recipient of the *dā* root here is easily understood, he does not show it and instead, pointing out only the "caused action" (*kāritakamma*), says:
"by one who is not fully ordained.
By the word "in the presence of" (*santike*), he shows that the prefix *upa-* in the phrase "having set down near" (*upanikkhipitvā*) carries the sense of proximity. Of those...
Of the sectarians. "Therein" means in the vessel. "From this" means from the bowl. "Here" means in my vessel. "That" refers to the hard and soft food.
"His" means of the sectarian. First [section]. 2.
The Training Rule on Sending Away.
274. In the second [case], because the sounds of the returning and the sitting hall are synonymous, it is said: “even in the sitting hall.
Since *bhattavissaggo* means the relinquishing of the meal, it is called the “meal-duty” (*bhattakicca*); thus he says: “the meal-duty.
Because the root *bhū* preceded by *pa-* has the sense of the root *āp*, it is said: “he did not reach.”
276. *Vuttāvasesaṃ* means the remainder [of the factors] other than those already mentioned, such as the desire to laugh together with women and so forth.
*Tasmiṃ* refers to the monk who has been sent away. *Atthato* means by way of the sense of the inseparable connection between the monk who is leaving and the monk who has left.
*Itarena* means by the monk who sent him away. *Tattha* refers to the statement: "either within the range of sight or within the range of hearing."
“*Ettha* (here)” is a collective term for selection; the meaning is “within the range of sight and the range of hearing.

By the word “*tathā* (thus),” he refers by extension to the measurement of twelve cubits. “*Tehi* (by those)” means by the walls and so forth. “*Tassa* (of that)” refers to the transgression of the range of sight.

By the phrase “the aforementioned improper conduct,” he demonstrates the ablative case of the word “*añña* (other)” in the expression “there is no other cause whatsoever”; and by the word “*kāraṇa* (cause)... [he demonstrates the instrumental case].

This is for the sake of the meaning of the word *paccaya*. 277. Regarding the two meanings of the word *kali*—namely, evil and defeat—it is said, “*Kali* is anger,” because anger is what is reckoned as evil.
By the word “*āṇā*,” he shows the meaning of the word *sāsana*. For it has been stated: “*Āṇā* and *sāsana* are to be known [as synonyms].”
"He speaks out of anger" is the connection. "He speaks having shown [something]" is the construction.
"See, sirs, his standing, sitting, looking forward, and looking aside" is the construction. "By this too" means "even by the speech of unpleasant words. This is the second [section]. 3.
The Training Rule on Eating Together.

279. Regarding the third [verse], it should have been said "in the bedchamber" (*sayaniyaghare*); however, by eliding the letter *ya*, it is stated as "in the sleeping chamber" (*sayanighare*), which is why he says "in the sleeping chamber.

As for the word *yata*, the particle *to* is seen here in the sense of the first [case] and others. In expressions such as "from whatever source" (*yatonidānaṃ*), it occurs in the sense of the first case.

In expressions such as "completely in the obstacle" (*antarāye asesato*), it occurs in the sense of the second case. In expressions such as "as impermanent" (*aniccato*), it occurs in the sense of the third case.

In expressions such as “from the mother’s side, from the father’s side,” it occurs in the sense of the ablative case. In expressions such as “that which [comes] from another by way of the condition of giving,” it occurs in the sense of the genitive case.
In expressions such as “in front, behind,” it occurs in the sense of the locative case. In expressions such as “from the footstep,” it is seen in the sense of cause.
Here too, it is in the sense of cause; thus he says, “because. Because alms were given to the noble one for that reason, therefore go.
“Bhante tumhe” means “Venerable sirs, you. “Yaṃ” refers to alms-food. “Vo” means “by you. “Adhippāyo” is a person’s underlying intention.
Although it is stated in general terms as “obsessed,” because of the context and so forth, what is intended is one obsessed by lust;
thus he says, “obsessed by lust,” meaning arisen having been overwhelmed by lust.

280. Regarding the term *sabhojana*: here, the letter *sa* functions as the word *saha*; because the letters *a* and *u* are dissimilar (*asarūpa*), there is the elision of the letter *a* after the letter *u*;

and in the three locations, there is a compound based on a common meaning for the latter two words, as well as an external compound based on a distinct meaning together with the preceding word. Thus, showing this meaning, he said:
“Together with both kinds of people. Alternatively, *bhojanaṃ* means that which is to be eaten; showing that food exists in this family, he says “alternatively,” and so forth.
*Hi* means truly. *Teneva* means precisely because of that mutual state of being fit to eat.
*Assa* refers to the word “in a family where there is food to eat” (*sabhojane*). In the word *ghare*, the preceding syllable *sa-ya-ni-* is elided.

He said, "In the bedchamber. By this, he indicates a compound with elision of the first member (pubbapadalopa), as in the case of "Datta" and other such examples. Regarding the phrase "of the door-panel joint" (piṭṭhasaṅghāṭassa):
here, "door-panel joint" does not refer to any other kind whatsoever, but rather specifically to that of the bedchamber room itself;
thus he says, "of that bedchamber room. "In whatever way or otherway" means by whichever manner or by whichever [other] manner.
"Made" means made either by mounting it upon a back-peg or without mounting it. This is the third [case]. 284.

Regarding the fourth and fifth [cases], the application is that just as the training rule on "with food" (*sabhojana*) originates from the first *pārājika*, so too do those two. These are the fourth and fifth.
6. The training rule on "going about" (*cāritta*).
294. Regarding the sixth [verse], why did they say, "Give us food, friends"? Is it not improper for monks to speak thus? To this he says, "In this matter, it is said... and so forth.
"Tasmā" means because it had been brought [to them]. 295. The connection is that he spoke these words. "Pasādaññathattaṃ" means the state of the confidence being otherwise.
"Taṃ" refers to the solid food (*khādanīya*). By the phrase "having taken it, they returned," the *u* sound in the word "ussāriyitthā" [is explained].
It shows the sense of grasping (*uggaha*) in *uggahattha*, the sense of going (*gati*) in *saradhatu*, and the sense of the suffix *-ttha* in the locative case ending *-attham*.
The meaning is: "Having grasped, they went forth; they departed.
(298) *Yattha* means "in which place. The construction is: "The mind of the standing bhikkhu arose. *Tato* means "from the arising of the mind."
“They go to the bhikkhu. By “natural speech” (*pakativacana*) is meant a statement uttered with a raised voice, a word used in its own inherent sense.
Thinking that [the phrase] “inside the monastery” (*antovihāre*) was too restrictive for the purpose of the statement, he said: “Furthermore, within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*).

(302) “A monastery stands between villages” means it is a monastery situated in the midst of villages; showing that one goes to such a place, he said “inside the village,” and so forth. The sixth [section].
7. The Training Rule of Mahānāma (Mahānāmasikkhāpada) 303.
In the seventh [training rule], the word “of the Blessed One” (*bhagavato*) is connected with the word “the son of the younger father” (*cūḷapituputto*);
it is the ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the word “older” (*mahallakataro*). “The son of the younger father” refers to Suddhodana, Sakkaudana, Sukkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana.
There were five brothers and two sisters—Amitā and Pālitā. Among them, the Blessed One and Nanda were the sons of Suddhodana, who was the eldest brother;
Ānanda was the son of Amitodana, who was the youngest brother;
and Mahānāma and Anuruddha were the sons of the third brother, Sukkodana. The sons of Sakkodana and Dhautodana were not well known. As for the Elder Tissa:
He is the son of the sister named Amitāyā; he was not disclosed as a son or daughter to Pālitā.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "the son of the younger father," namely Sukkodana. Regarding "in two fruits": in the two lower fruits.
The word *ussanna* is a synonym for "much"; thus he said "many. *Vajato* means from the herd (*goṭṭha*). For that [herd] is [driven] from the grazing place...
Having stepped back, they go or proceed for the purpose of dwelling; thus it is called a *vaja*.
"At that time" means at that time of the *pavāraṇā*. Regarding the phrase "by so many," since two kinds of meaning are intended—either by way of name or by way of measure—it is stated:
"by way of name and by way of measure. Among these, "name" [is explained as follows]:
Regarding the phrase "these medicines," the meaning of the expression "there are so many" should be understood as referring to their names;
regarding the phrase "the measure of these," the meaning of the expression "there are so many" should be understood as referring to their quantity.

As for the term "other medicine" (*aññaṃ bhesajjaṃ*), one might wonder whether the word "other" (*añña*) refers to a source (*apādāna*), a name, or a measure; therefore, he says, "he has been invited by all," and so forth.
310. "Yet the donors have invited [him]"—this is the connection. The seventh [section]. 8.
The Training Rule on Troops on March (Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpada). 311.
In the eighth [section], by the word "abhimukhaṃ," he shows the meaning of the prefix *abhi*. Regarding the term "uyyāto," having arisen...

Showing that he had departed, he said, "He has gone out from the city. By the phrase "having applied himself" (*katauyyoga*), he shows that one who rises up and exerts himself (*yuñjati*) and proceeds is called "exerted" (*uyyutta*).
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is also stated as "departed from the village.

314. "Twelve men for this elephant" means *dvādasapurisa*; "those with weapons in their hands" means *āvudhahatthā*. "Low ground" (*ninna*) refers to a low-lying place; the connection is "as the bhikkhu looked on. Eighth.
9. The Training Rule on Military Encampments (Senāvāsasikkhāpada) 319.
In the ninth [rule], by the words "or stands," etc., it shows the manner of staying.
The word "vā" (or) includes the sense of "or walks. "Any posture" means any one of the four postures. Just as when [the army] is encamped...
The movement is cut off; thus, she becomes obstructed and restrained—this is the construction.
By the word "ruddho" (obstructed), he shows the intended meaning of the verbal root *budh* preceded by the prefix *pari* in the phrase "palibuddho. [End of] the ninth [section]. 10.
The Training Rule on Military Displays (*Uyyodhika-sikkhāpada*).

322. "They fight" means they strike one another. By the phrase "the foremost of strength (*balassa aggaṃ*)," he shows a compound with a different grammatical case (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) and an external referent (*bāhirattha*).
The word "knowing" (*jānantī*) has been inserted for the sake of completing the sense.

"Foremost" (*agga*) means a portion. The etymological meaning is also appropriate: it is called "the foremost of strength" because strength is counted therein. Therefore, he said, "the place for counting strength. For this—
This statement is spoken according to the method of the *Ambasekanaka* (the sprinkler of water). How so?

By the commentator (*Aṭṭhakathācariya*) saying "the place for counting the forces," both the condensed meaning (*piṇḍattha*) of the word-analysis—"it is called *balagga* because they know the excellence (*agga*) of the force (*bala*) here"—and the analytical meaning—"it is called *balagga* because the force is counted (*gaṇīyati*) here"—are made known. It is thus displayed.
The word *byūha* means "arrayed formation. The phrase "the array of an army" (*senābyūha*) shows the meaning through the expression "the arraying of an army," and so forth.

It "rushes" (*aṇati*) by making a terrifying sound, thus it is an "army unit" (*aṇīka*); one who acts as a leader (*muddhajaṇakāra*). An elephant itself is an "army unit," hence "elephant-army-unit" (*hatthāṇīka*).
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. That which was previously called an "elephant" is to be construed here with the word "elephant-army-unit. The tenth [chapter].
The Fifth Chapter: On the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga).
6. The Chapter on Drinking Liquor (Surāpānavagga). 1. The Explanation of the Training Rule on Drinking Liquor (Surāpānasikkhāpada-atthayojanā).

326. Regarding the first [sutta] of the Surāpāna-vagga: he says "he" and so forth, demonstrating the meaning as follows: *bhaddā vati ettha* means "there is a fence (vati) that is auspicious (bhaddā) here," thus *bhaddavatikā*; alternatively, *bhaddā vati* is *bhaddavati*, and because she exists there, it is *bhaddavatikā*.

The connection is: "He [the village] obtained it. Regarding *pathāvinī*, which is derived from *pathaṃ gacchanti* ("going on the road"), he says "travelers (*addhikā*)" to indicate that they are indeed wayfarers.
“Addhikā” means those who go on a journey (addhaṃ gacchanti). There is also the reading “pathikā,” which has the same meaning.
The phrases “tejasā tejaṃ” are dependent upon a connection; because the words are identical, one might think that the connection is also identical.
Therefore, it is said “by his own power” in order to show both their connection and its dissimilarity.
"Of the Nāga's power. By the word "by the majesty" (ānubhāvena), he shows the meaning of the term *teja* (power).
"A dove-foot" (*kapota-pāda*) is a *kapota* by way of metaphorical designation; that which belongs to it is "dove-colored" (*kāpota*). Showing that its color is like that of a dove, he says:
"having a red luster with a color equal to a dove's foot. Regarding the word *pasanna*, there are [meanings such as] clarity, faith, and so forth.

It is said that this is a designation for the scum of liquor (*surāmaṇḍa*) in order to turn [the listener] back [from such things]. The construction is: "of one who possesses the five superknowledges" (*pañcābhiññassa*) means "of one who is equal to or like [the Buddha] Sāgata. 328.
By the phrase "made with the juice of *madhuka* flowers and so forth," it is shown that a fermented liquor (*āsava*) made from the juice of flowers is a "flower-fermented liquor" (*pupphāsava*).
This shows the meaning of the word. This same method applies to the terms "fermentation of fruit" (*phalāsava*) and so forth.
To show the distinction between *surā* and *meraya*, it is said: "What is called *surā*," and so on.

The connection is that *vāruṇī* is that which is prepared by being mixed with flour (*piṭṭha*) and *kiṇṇa*. And *kiṇṇa* is the seed of *surā*; for various ingredients are scattered (*kiranti*) and mixed together therein.
"Ettha" (here) means "kiṇṇa" (brewed). It should be construed as "of that very [brew]. "Surā" refers to what was made by a certain forest-dweller named Sura.
"Merayaṃ" is so called because it produces intoxication (*mada*).
"Loṇasovīrakaṃ" is a drink with that specific name. "Suttaṃ" is likewise. "Tasmiṃ" refers to the prepared soup.
"But cooking oil" (*telaṃ pana*) is the connection [to the previous clause]. "Without sharp liquor" (*atikhiṇamajjaṃ*) means that there is no sharp liquor in it;

the meaning is "in that very oil which is without sharp liquor. "But that which" (*yaṃ pana*) refers to the oil. "Sharp liquor for this oil" (*tikhiṇamajjaṃ*) means that there is sharp liquor belonging to this oil.
"In which" (*yattha*) means in the oil. "Ariṭṭha" is a medicinal preparation of that name. "With reference to that" (*taṃ sandhāyā*) refers to the word *ariṭṭha*.
“Avuttakammaṃ. Regarding this: the statement “it is not fermented liquor, it is aritta” means that in the word “vutta,” there is the act of speaking (*vuttakamma*). First. 2.
The Training Rule on Prodding with Fingers (Aṅgulipatodaka-sikkhāpada). 330.
In the second [rule], "prodding with fingers" (*aṅgulipatoda*) is the act of prodding with the fingers; showing that this very thing is "finger-prodding" (*aṅgulipatodaka*), he said:
“With the fingers,” and so forth. *Uttanta* means *avatapan* (sighing). Since *avatapan* in meaning is simply *kilamanto* (tiring), he said “tiring.
The construction is “having become tired. By the mention of inhalation (*assāsa*), exhalation (*passāsa*) is also to be understood;
thus he said “the movement of inhalation and exhalation. “Her too” means “the nun too. Second [section].
3. The Training Rule on Joking (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada). 335.

Regarding the third [rule], he says "that which was by the Blessed One," etc., showing that what is "made" (*pakata*) is that which is "laid down" (*paññatta*) by way of being established. "That which" (*yaṃ*) refers to the training rule. 336.

When it is said that "joking-nature" (*hasadhamma*) is a nature (*dhamma*) or inherent character (*sabhāva*) consisting of laughter, it means in actual fact just play; thus he says, "play is what is meant."

337. *Gopphakānaṃ* means of the ankles (*caraṇagaṇṭhikānaṃ*). For they are called *gopphā* because when one foot is placed upon the other, they protect (*gopīyanti*) each other; thus they are called *gopphaka*.
Indeed, when placing one foot upon the other, one foot must not be placed directly on top of the other. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Having crossed one foot over the other."
"Born from the lip" is the second [term]. The connection is "for a monk who is descending.
(338) "By means of a stone, a clod, etc."—by the word "etc.," ornaments and so forth are included. "Some say"—this is the connection.
"In the sections on falling and rising"—that is, in the section on falling and the sections on rising. "Therein"—that is, upon that thrown stone or clod.
*Hi* means "truth" or "because. The connection is with the phrase "for one playing, having set [the board] aside.

The intention is that it is permissible to write because the intent for play is absent. They say that even for one who writes a syllable indicating a meaning with the intent for play, there is indeed an offense.
*Ettha* means "in this training rule. The third [section].
4. The Training Rule on Disrespect (Anādariyasikkhāpada) 342.
Regarding the fourth [rule], he says "the tradition" (*tanti*) because "Dhamma" means precisely that. "The lineage" (*paveṇī*) is a synonym for that very same thing.
In the phrase "or not wishing to train in that," the words "by which it was prescribed" (*yena paññattena*) are stated in order to clarify the meaning of the pronoun "that" (*taṃ*).
With reference to what was not laid down in the Vinaya, he said, "by what is not laid down," and then specified, "as found in the Sutta or in the Abhidhamma.
"In the tradition" (paveṇiyā) means by the lineage of teachers beginning with Upāli, which is known as the *tanti*.
"Stated in the Kurundi" is the connection; "stated in the Mahāpaccarī" is the connection. "All that" refers to what is designated as the doctrine of the Kurundi and the doctrine of the Mahāpaccarī.

All that is the word. "Come down through the lineage" means in the doctrine of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), which is reckoned as having come down through the lineage. This is the fourth [section]. 345.
In the fifth, regarding "the human form" (manussaviggaha), it refers to the offense of defeat (pārājika) involving the human form. This is the fifth. 6.
The Training Rule on Fire (Joti-sikkhāpada).
350. In the sixth [case], because it is the name of a country, it is stated in the Pāḷi as “Bhaggesu” by way of the plural number.
It is called Susumāragiri because there is a mountain (giri) here, reckoned as a hill, shaped like a crocodile (susumāra);
or, disregarding the literal meaning that “at the time of its construction, a crocodile (susumāra) emitted (girati) or let out a sound (sadda) here,” it is stated as “the name of the city. That...
*Pana* means *vana* (forest). By the phrase “of the deer,” etc., it shows the meaning as *migadāyo*, which signifies a place where safety (*abhaya*) is granted to the deer.
352. To show that the word *jotike* refers to the making of light—that is, fire—it is stated as “in the making of light. 354.

The phrase “through the desire to kindle” is the reason for the phrase “from the preparation of the fire-drill wood. *Jālā* means a crest or flame; for it is called *jālā* because it burns and shines.

Regarding the phrase "he picks up a fallen firebrand" (*patilātaṃ ukkhipati*): here, although one should say "fallen firebrand" (*patitālātaṃ*), the letter *t* has been elided and it is expressed as *patilātaṃ* by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
Thus he says, "he picks up a firebrand that has fallen. "Firebrand" (*alāta*) means a brand.
For that, having been set on fire, is called a "firebrand" because it cannot be grasped or taken hold of due to its extreme heat. "Unextinguished" (*avijjhātaṃ*) refers to [a fire] that is burning.

The connection is: "a firebrand (*alāta*) that has not departed from burning. Burning is *ḍayhana*; it has been burnt (*jhāta*), and this firebrand has had what was burnt depart—thus it is "extinguished" (*vijjhāta*).

356. "Lamps and so forth" refers to lamps, torches, and the like. "Therein" means when those calamities consisting of wild beasts, humans, and so forth have become the occasion (*nimitta*); for here the locative case is used in the sense of an occasion.
The sixth [section]. 7. The Training Rule on Bathing (*Nahāna-sikkhāpada*).
366. In the seventh [verse], showing that it is not only permissible to bathe in a river containing water, but also permissible in a dried-up river, he said, "In a dried-up one," and so forth.
"Having strewn" means having scattered. "In the pits" refers to small depressions in the sense of being shallow; in those. The seventh [chapter].
8. The Training Rule on Making Ugly (Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpada) 368.
Regarding the eighth [rule], the phrase "alabhi" means "labha. By adding the suffix *a* (apaccaya), it is stated as "lābho" to show that the suffix *ṇa* has the same meaning as the base word;
thus, "labho eva lābho" (what is obtained is indeed a gain). Without adding the suffix *a*, the suffix *ṇa* is also perfectly appropriate when applied to the base form.

It should be seen. He says, "In the case of 'by the acquisition of new robes' (*navacīvaralābhena*), although it ought to be stated [as such], it is a compound because there is no difference in meaning from the other words" (*saddantaropi atthantarābhāvā samāso hoti*).

"The elision of the nasal" (*anunāsikalopa*) refers to the disappearance of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) in the word "new" (*nava*). For the *niggahīta* is called "nasal" (*anunāsika*) because it follows after the nose;
its non-appearance [is meant by "elision"], the sense being "having made [it] so. [This occurs] in the two words situated in the middle.
Between the two words “new” (*nava*) and “by means of the acquisition of robes” (*cīvaralābhena*), there are the two words “while standing” (*ṭhite pana*) and “by a monk” (*bhikkhunā*).
This locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). The word “nipāta” refers merely to a particle (*nipātamatta*).

He says “by a monk,” etc., in order to show the expressed meaning (*abhidheyyattha*) of the verbal root “to obtain” (*labhati*) as it occurs in the word “acquisition” (*lābha*). Thus he says: “by a monk,” and so forth.
The connection is: "But it is said in the *Padabhājana*. "Yam" means that robe (*cīvara*). To show the actual nature of the robe here, he says:
"That which is to be worn as an undergarment," and so forth. "Leather-dyer's blue" (*cammakāranīla*) is the blue color of iron dross placed in the three fruits used by leather-workers.
The connection is: "It is stated in the *Mahāpaccarī*. "Discoloring agent" (*dubbaṇṇakaraṇa*) is that by which one makes [the robe] discolored.
He said, "referring to the *kappabindu*," meaning "with reference to the *kappabindu*. The connection is that it should be taken by a monk who is beginning [the practice].
"In the corners" means at the edges. The word *vā* (or) has the sense of an indefinite option. "Or the size of the eye-socket" connects as: "the *kappabindu* is the measure of the eye-socket.
"On a cloth" means on a cloth for wiping the nose (*anuvātapaṭṭa*). "Or on a knotted cloth" means on a cloth with a knotted border (*gaṇṭhikapaṭṭa*).
*Pāḷikappa* (a line of dots): a mark made by forming a row of two, three, or more than that many dots. *Kaṇṇikakappa* (a cluster of dots):
a mark made by forming a cluster of dots like a *kaṇṇika* (a small circular ornament). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), marks such as the *agghiyakappa* (the trident-like mark) are included.
Regarding the phrase "in all cases": this refers to all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). He says, "a single round dot," because even a single dot must indeed be round.
371. Regarding "the bolt and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the windward side and the surrounding area are included. This concludes the eighth [section]. 9.
The Training Rule on Allocation (Vikappana-sikkhāpada). 374.
Regarding the ninth [rule], in the phrase "of that" (*tassa*), the referent of the pronoun *ta* is exclusively the owner of the robe; thus he says, "of the owner of the robe."
Since the scope of the second instance of the word *tassa* (of him) is the Vinaya-dhara alone, he said "by whom," and so forth.
To show that the phrase "not having confidence" functions as an adverbial modifier of the action, it was stated "without confidence. "By him" means by the Vinaya-dhara. The ninth [section].
10. The Training Rule on the Non-Seeking of Robes.
377. In the tenth [chapter], by the word “having removed,” he shows the meaning of the prefix *apa-*.
“They hide away” means they place [it] having concealed it. “With the intention of laughing” means an intention for laughter, or an intention for the purpose of laughing.
To show the actual form of the requisite, it is said: “alms-bowl bags and so forth. Because the bowl is mentioned in the Canon (Pāḷi), it is “the bag for the bowl.”
Only the bowl itself should be taken, not both the bowl and its bag. In the phrase “by one who is a recluse,” the word “recluse” is the agent of the verb “to be.
Tenth. The sixth chapter on drinking intoxicants is concluded.
7. The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇakavagga) 1. The Exegesis of the Training Rule on Intentionally Killing a Living Being (Sañciccapāṇasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 382.
Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on Living Beings: "That by which one shoots an arrow when it is not present is called 'issāsa'; thus, it refers specifically to the bow.

Primarily, one is called an *issāsa* (archer); however, the master archer is so called by way of metaphorical extension (*upacāra*). Since an *issāsa* is defined as one who "shoots" (*asati*) or "hurls" (*khipati*) an arrow, the term could refer to the master archer;
yet here, it should be understood either in its metaphorical sense or in its literal sense as the agent, which is why he says, "he was a master archer.
Because being an archer is inappropriate for one at the time of having gone forth into homelessness, he specifies, "during his time as a householder."
Regarding the term *voropitā*: here, it is stated as “separated” (*viyojitā*) in order to show the intended meaning of the verbal root *ruha* preceded by the prefix *vi*.
This is because it connects with the word “goes” (*gacchati*). As for the phrase “deprived of life” (*jīvitā voropitā*), why is it merely a conventional expression?
Is it not the case that when something is separated from anything else, the two entities remain distinct, like two separate things?
When one is separated from life by means of the breath, it is said that "the breath and the life" [are distinct]; thus he says, "Not here," and so forth. "Hi" means truly.
"Ettha" (here) is connected as showing it in the statement, "deprived of life. The construction is: "What indeed is called life?
However, the connection of the meaning here is this: when an ornament for the head is separated from the head, the head remains distinct from the ornament.
Just as, in this way, when life is separated from the living being, life does not remain apart from the living being; thus [it is said]. "Aññadatthu" means "absolutely.

Although "living being" (*pāṇa*) is mentioned in a general sense, because it is taken in the context of a *pārājika* offense regarding a human being, here—by the method of elimination—it must be understood as a "beast" (*tiracchāna-pāṇa*). Therefore he says: "only a beast. "That" refers to...
"Life" (*pāṇaṃ*). However, the connection is "great life" (*mahante pāṇe*).
385. The construction is: "while purifying, he removes. "Maṅgula" is a particular kind of insect that subsists on human blood;
for it is called "maṅgula" because it moves (*maṅgati*) here and there, from this place to that, for the purpose of drinking blood. For [it is derived from] the syllables of the word...
It should be understood that in some places the word-meaning is stated for the sake of avoiding error and so that listeners may obtain the opportunity for recitation and instruction.
"In that" means in that very seed which, by virtue of its smallness, is a "maṅgula-seed. "Tat" refers to the maṅgula-seed.
"Being one who breaks it" is how the construction should be joined. First.
2. The Training Rule on Water with Living Beings (Sappāṇakasikkhāpada) 387.
Regarding the second [rule], the phrase "together with living beings" indicates that it is water containing living beings; thus he says, "those living beings," and so forth.

The word "hi" means "indeed" (truly). The connection is: "even water filling a bowl. "By such [water]" means by water containing living beings. Even if one washes [with it], it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "A water-tub" (*udakasoṇḍi*) means a water-tub made of stone. "A lotus-pool" (*pokkharaṇī*) means a lotus-pool made of stone. The connection is:
"there is a *pācittiya* offense even for one who causes it to be raised. "From that" (*tato*) means from the tubs and lotus-pools. "Of water" (*udakassa*) means by means of water;

the connection is: "having poured [it] into a jar that was full. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the water. "In the water" (*udake*) refers to the place where the water is situated, namely, the water that has been poured [into the jar].
"Patissatī" means she takes up water from the trunks or the lotus-pools. This is the second [section]. 3.
The Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada). 392.

Regarding the third [rule], by the word "uccālentī," it is meant that she is reopening; here, the prefix *upa* is used for the purpose of expressing the meaning of opening (*ukkoca*) for the verbal root *kuṭ*.
[The word *yathā*] indicates the various meanings of the root (*dhātu*), because it has many meanings. "The state of being established according to how it is established" is *yathāpaṭṭhitabhāva*;
[the phrase refers to] by means of that. 393.

"Whatever phenomenon" (*yo dhammo*) means whatever phenomenon of serenity (*samatha*). Regarding the word "by the phenomenon" (*dhammena*), here the suffix *-ena* [is used] as in the expression "in accordance with the phenomenon" (*yathādhammam*).
The word *aṃitikāriyassa* shows that [the Teacher] demonstrated the performance of what was to be done.

By this, he shows that the word "according to the Dhamma" (*yathādhamma*) is to be connected with the word "settled" (*nihata*) in the phrase "the legal issue settled" (*nihatādhikaraṇa*). The word "by the Teacher" (*satthārā*) is the agent for the word "stated" (*vuttaṃ*).

When it is said "settled" (*nihata*)—meaning that which has no killing (*hana*) or act of killing (*hanana*)—it is, in its actual sense, simply the state of being calmed; thus he says "calmed" (*vūpasamitaṃ*).

395. Showing that whatever action it may be, if it is not a *dhammakamma* (a legitimate legal act), but rather only an action for the settlement of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇavūpasamakamma*) that is called a *dhammakamma*, he said: “By whatever action,” and so forth. “This one too” means this monk as well.
“The remaining phrases too” refers to the remaining phrases such as “being in doubt regarding a *dhammakamma*. “In this” means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). [The] detailed exposition.

"But it is said" is the connection [to the previous]. "In that very place" means in the Parivāra itself. "Here" means in this training rule (sikkhāpada) or in the Vibhaṅga. This is the third [section]. 4.
The Training Rule on Grave Matters (Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada). 399.

The intention is that they are similar because they are shown by way of the summary of contents (atthuddhāra) in the fourth [section] as having the nature of the meaning of the term "grave matter" (duṭṭhulla).
Regarding the word "dhura" here, because it possesses a defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇavantattā*), the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative; thus he says "dhure.
The construction is: "when merely having placed the burden (*dhura*) upon [oneself].
"Having thus laid down the burden" means having laid down the burden with the thought, "I will not tell anyone else. "To another" means...

"Object" (*vatthu*) refers to another person distinct from the individual [who committed the offense]. "He too" (*sopi*) refers to the second person. "Of another" (*aññassa*) refers to the third person. The construction is:
"As long as the limit is not severed, so long does he indeed incur [the offense]. "Of that very person" (*tasseva*) refers to the individual who has incurred the offense.

"The object-person himself" (*vatthupuggaloyeva*) means the very individual who has incurred the offense. "This one" (*ayaṃ*) refers to the first monk. "Of another" (*aññassa*) refers to the second. "He" (*so*) refers to the second.
"He reports" is the connection [of the sentence]. "By whom" means by the first bhikkhu. "Of him" means of the second [bhikkhu].
"Of that very same person" means of the first bhikkhu himself. With reference to the individual who is the subject matter, it is said: "by the third person, of the second. 400.

"The five classes of offenses" refers to the five classes of offenses beginning with the *thullaccaya*. "Misconduct" (*ajjhācāra*) is so called because it is to be practiced after having overcome [restraint] and transgressed [the rule]. The fourth [section].
5. The Training Rule on Those Under Twenty Years of Age (Ūnavīsativassasikkhāpada) 402.
In the fifth [rule], "fingers" (*aṅguliyo*) refers to the digits of the hand. For they are called "fingers" because they emerge from the hand after it has divided into five parts.
The connection is with "of Upāli as he was scratching. "By that" means by reason of the many things to be considered.
*Assa* means Upāli’s. *Uro* means the heart. For it is called *uro* because the heat of the mind consumes (*usati*) and burns (*dahati*) there.
*Rūpasuttaṃ* refers to the string of coins of money-changers, just as elephant trainers have an "elephant-string" (*hatthisutta*).
*Akkhīni* means the eyes. For they "endure" (*akkhanti*) in the sense that they pervade their objects, or else they are called "eyes" because one sees form (*rūpa*) by means of them.

[They] are so called. Since mosquitoes (*makasa*) have already been included by [the mention of] needle-mouthed insects (*sūcimukha*), one might think that gadflies (*daṃsa*) must refer only to brown flies (*piṅgalamakkhikā*);
thus he says, "Gadflies means brown flies. For brown flies are called "gadflies" in the sense of stinging and in the sense of biting.
Showing that these [insects] are difficult to endure, he says, "of those that are painful" (*dukkhamānaṃ*). [This refers to] "of the feelings" (*vedanānaṃ*).
The connection [is as follows]. To show the cause of what is unpleasant (*asāta*), it is said:
"of those that are not sweet. By this, it shows the meaning: "because they are not sweet, they are not to be relished; thus, they are unpleasant.

To show that the words *pāṇa* and *jīvita* are synonyms, it is said: "of those that take away life. They take away or remove life, thus they are "life-takers" (*pāṇahara*); the connection is "of those feelings" (*tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ*).
404. From the time of giving birth onwards, one who has reached twenty full years must not be accepted;
however, showing that it is from the time of conception, he said, "from the moment of taking rebirth.
A person who has completed his twentieth year, including the time spent lying in the womb, is a "person of twenty from conception" (*gabbhavīsa*). The word *hi* means "truly. As it has been said:
The construction is: "In whatever manner it is reckoned, in that same manner the Blessed One said. Alternatively, the construction is: "In what way did the Blessed One speak?
[The phrase] "having been twenty years from conception, he was ordained" is the connection. *Amhi* means *asmi*. The particle *nu* is a nipāta used in the sense of reflection.
The connection is: "They go according to the kind of first consciousness. By this, he shows the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
"First consciousness" is a synonym for that very same thing. "That" refers to the first consciousness, the first cognition. "Of him" means of the sentient being.
"That itself is the birth" means that very same rebirth-linking is what is called the "womb" (*gabbha*); such is the connection.
The construction is as follows: "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the text; "the exposition (*vinicchaya*) should be understood thus. "He" (*yo*) refers to the person.

"On the Great Invitation Day" (*mahāpavāraṇāya*) means on the full moon day of the month of Assayuja. For that [day] is called the "Great Invitation" (*mahāpavāraṇā*) because it is the honored invitation. "From then" (*tato*) means from the time the Invitation was performed. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the Great Invitation.
Regarding the phrase "and on the first day" (*pāṭipade ca*), here the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of an indefinite alternative.
The meaning is that he should be ordained on one of the days between the Pavāraṇā day and the first day of the lunar month (pāṭipada).
"Subtraction and addition" (hāyanavaḍḍhana) should be understood as subtracting when there are extra months spent in the womb, and adding when they are deficient.
"The ancient elders ordain," is the connection [of the sentence]. "Nineteen years" refers to what was stated immediately preceding.
"Twenty-nine years. "The day of departure" refers to the month of Sāvaṇa;

for it is called "the day of departure" because on that day the sun moves from the inner path to the outer path. "On the first day of the fortnight" means on the day of entering the rains-retreat during the later period.
"That ordination"—why? This is the question. The construction is: "Standing here, the resolution is stated by me. "In twenty..."
“In twenty years” means in the twenty years of a person who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*).

Because thirty nights and days constitute one month, it is said that “four months are lost. “They draw out” means they extend the rainy season retreat (*vassa*) further in order to eliminate one extra month.
“From there” is connected with the phrase “having removed [it] from six months. “In this case” refers to the statement beginning with “nineteen-year-old” and so forth.
The word *pana* has the sense of *hi*; the meaning is "indeed. *Yo* refers to the person.

*Tasmā* means because they confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) even after including those who have been in the womb for months in the calculation; therefore, the connection is "having dwelt for six months.
It is stated in the Suttantas and their commentaries that even one born after dwelling for eight months may not survive.
