"406. 'After the lapse of ten years' means after the passing of ten years from the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*).

'He grants full ordination' means he grants it either as the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or as the ritual master (*kammavācācariya*). 'Him' refers to that person who has not yet been fully ordained and who stands in the position of being the preceptor or the teacher.
When one grants full ordination while acting as the ritual master, if there is another ritual master present, [he should grant it] having released him."
He is fully ordained. If he himself pronounces the formal act (*kammavācā*), he is not fully ordained.

However, it should be understood that for those who, having known [the truth], do not ordain him again, there will certainly be an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the path. The fifth [section]. 6.
The Training Rule on the Caravan of Thieves.
407. Regarding the sixth [case], “facing the light” (*paṭiyāloka*): here, by the word “light,” the sun is expressed through figurative usage (*upacāra*).

For the sun, having risen from the eastern direction, goes toward the western direction; therefore, when it is said that one faces the light—which is designated as the sun—one must understand this as facing the western direction. Thus he says: “The meaning is ‘the western direction.’”
*Kammikā* means those engaged in or appointed to a task.
409. Regarding the term *rājānaṃ*: here, by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), that which belongs to the king is called "the king";
alternatively, taking that which belongs to the king as being "of the king," it is called "the king. Regarding *theyyaṃ*, having stolen; and regarding *sakkaccaṃ* and so forth...
The elision of the *niggahīta* occurs as if it were present. The meaning is: "having stolen a king or what belongs to a king, they go away.
Thus, showing this meaning, he said: "or having stolen from a king," and so forth. 411.
Regarding the four types of non-agreement (*visaṅketa*), there is no offense (*anāpatti*) in two cases, and there is indeed an offense (*āpatti*) in the other two. This is the sixth [section].
7. The Training Rule on Arrangements (Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada) 412.

Regarding the seventh [rule], concerning the phrase "smoking" (*padhūpento*): here, the verbal root *dhūpa*, preceded by the prefix *pa-*, functions in the sense of reviling; thus he says, "reviling" (*paribhāsanto*).
"Even you, though a renunciant, go together with a woman; this fault belongs to you alone, not to him."

“Of the man”: the meaning is that he was reproaching himself. By the word “expelled” (*nikkhāmesi*), it is shown that here the root *pat* preceded by the prefix *ni* has the sense of going (*gatyattha*). [This concludes] the seventh [case]. 8.
The Training Rule on Ariṭṭha.
417. In the eighth [verse], "gandhenti" means they are greedy. For they are called "gandhā" because they greedily desire (abhikaṅkhanti) a corpse;
thus they are "greedy. There is also the reading "gaddhenti," which is likewise appropriate, just as "yuganandho" and "yuganaddho," or "paṭibandho" and "paṭibaddho" are used interchangeably.
"Bādhayiṃsu" means they struck. "Assa" refers to Ariṭṭha.

In order to show the meaning expressed by the secondary derivative (taddhita), he says “te,” and so forth. “Te” means those things that are obstructive. “Tattha” means among the five kinds of obstructions.
By the word “tathā,” he refers back to the phrase “that which is called an obstruction to the task. “Taṃ pana” means, moreover, the act of violating a nun.
“Mokkhass’eva” means of liberation alone—that is, of the Path and Nibbāna—since it is the Path that is liberated from the defilements.
"Deliverance" (mokkha) means release. Herein, the jhānas are included because they are liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
Nibbāna is called "deliverance" in the sense that it is liberated. The fruit (phala) is also included here because it is the state of being liberated.
"States of fixed wrong view" refers to those states known as wrong views that have reached a state of fixity, or those that proceed by way of fixity. And these...

It is threefold by way of nihilism (*natthika*), causelessness (*ahetuka*), and non-action (*akiriya*). Because the mention of eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and so forth is merely illustrative, by the phrase “states of rebirth-linking” (*paṭisandhidhammā*), those states of rebirth-linking that are rootless (*ahetuka*) or have two roots (*duhetuka*) are to be understood, since all of them constitute an obstacle to fruition (*vipāka*).
These too create an obstacle only to liberation (*mokkha*), not to heaven (*sagga*). But as for those [who speak thus], namely, those who revile the Noble Ones (*ariyūpavādā*); only for that long...
The construction is: "those called obstructive censures. "Those" refers even to offenses committed intentionally.
The statement "or he claims the status of a bhikkhu" is said with reference to a *pārājika* offense. The statement "or he does not emerge from it" is said with reference to a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
The statement "or he does not confess it" is said with reference to a light offense.
"In that regard" means among the five kinds of obstacles. "This monk" refers to the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a leader of the Gandhabba spirits.
"The remaining obstacles" refers to the fourfold obstacles other than those that constitute an obstacle through transgression of a formal command.
"These householders" refers to these people who are habituated to living in a house. The connection is: "the monks see them, touch them, and enjoy their things."

Why are they not permissible? The intention is that they are indeed permissible. "Having blended flavor with flavor" means having brought together the flavor of what is clung-to (*upādiṇṇaka*) with the flavor of what is not clung-to (*anupādiṇṇaka*), or the flavor of what is not clung-to with the flavor of what is clung-to.

Because of the absence of systematic reflection (*yoniso paccavekkhaṇa*), sensual desire (*chandarāga*) exists therein; thus it is "with sensual desire" (*sacchandarāga*). That very enjoyment is "enjoyment with sensual desire" (*sacchandarāgaparibhoga*).
"Making that one" means making it uniform. The construction is: "having produced an evil speculative view as if he were trying to join [it together].
The word *kiṃ* has the sense of censure; the meaning is: "Why was the first *pārājika* rule laid down by the Blessed One? It should not have been laid down.
Just as one who attempts to dam the great ocean does what ought not to be done, so too is he who lays down the first *pārājika*.
The intention is that the Blessed One establishes what has not been established. "In this" refers to the first *pārājika*. "Those who sit" means those capable [of sitting].
"In the wheel of command" means in the wheel known as command (*āṇā*).

"Bone" (*aṭṭhikaṃ*) is simply "bone" (*aṭṭhi*); the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of contempt, for the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of contempt. "Dust" (*khalo*) is simply "bone" (*aṭṭhikaṃ*), in the sense of being lowly.

“By way of being loathsome”: having applied the grammatical augment (*niggahītāgama*) to *aṭṭhikaṅkhalo*. Because the simile is similar to that, it is called the “simile of the skeleton” (*aṭṭhikaṅkhalūpamā*).
The teachers explain this by taking the two words “bones” (*aṭṭhī*) and “skeleton” (*kaṅkhala*). “Similes of a pit of embers” means resembling a heap of embers, or like a pit filled with embers.
“Similes of a sword and a butcher’s block”: here, “sword” (*asi*) refers to a blade; for it cuts (*asati*).

That by which one throws is called "a sword" (*asi*). "Slaughter" (*sūnā*) means cutting or striking. For it is called "slaughter" because beings are slaughtered—that is, they go to a state of being crushed—therein.
"Sword-slaughter" (*asisūnā*) is slaughter by means of a sword; that which is similar to this is the "simile of sword-slaughter.
"Similar to spear and stake" means similar to a spear and a stake. "Therein" refers to this commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); [it is also found] in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*.

It should be understood from the *Alagaddūpama-sutta*. The phrase "evam viya kho" was stated to show that the word *viya* functions as a substitute for the words *evaṃ* and *kho*. This is the eighth [section]. 9.
The Training Rule on Associating with One Who Has Been Suspended (*Ukkhittasambhoga-sikkhāpada*).

424. To show the actual nature of *anudhamma* (conformity to the Dhamma) in the ninth [case], it is said: “The reinstatement was performed after seeing that the conduct was in accordance with the rule.

By this, it is shown that the act termed “reinstatement” (*osāraṇā*), performed after seeing that the conduct was in accordance with the rule (*anulomavatta*), is *anudhamma*. “Reinstatement” (*osāraṇā*) means causing to enter [the community].
“By that very fact” means precisely because the one who had been suspended had not yet performed the *anudhamma*. “Of this” refers to the phrase “by one who has not performed the *anudhamma*.”
"In giving or in taking": the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an indefinite alternative.
[This concludes] the ninth [section]. 10. The Kaṇṭaka Training Rule (Sikkhāpada). 428.
In the tenth [section], the construction is: "Just as it arose for Ariṭṭha, so too has it arisen for this person. Regarding "of one who is emerging":
For one who attends to it. The destruction of co-residence is "destruction of co-residence" (*saṃvāsanāsanā*). The destruction of the signs [of a monk] is "destruction of signs" (*liṅganāsanā*).

Destruction by means of a formal act of punishment is "destruction by formal act of punishment" (*daṇḍakammanāsanā*). "Therein" refers to these three kinds of destruction. Regarding the phrase "the corrupter...

should be destroyed," the construction here is that this destruction is called "destruction of signs. "This" refers to destruction by formal act of punishment. "In this" refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Or [it occurs] in the phrase “nāsetū. Therein, “tattha” (therein) refers back to the preceding statement; the meaning is: in the statement beginning with “And furthermore, monks, thus...
“Pare” is a term of address having the same meaning as the word *para*; thus he says “parā.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as “one who has not become internal to us” or “one who is opposed to us. By the word “amāmaka,” [the meaning of] the word “pare” is...
It shows the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*). The sense is: "one who deceives us," or "one by whom we are to be deceived. There is also a reading joined with the letter *ha*:
"amhāmaka"; the sense is "one raw (or immature) toward us. "Yattha" means "in which place. "Tesaṃ" is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative;
the sense is "them. The connection is: "or in the word *tava-rūpa*. "Na passāma" means "we do not see, we do not hear."
429. “By him” means by a novice (*sāmaṇera*). Regarding the word “should have [it] made,” it refers to a commissioned act (*kāritakamma*). The tenth [chapter].
The seventh section, on Water with Living Beings.
8. The Section on Fellow-Practitioners (*Sahadhammika-vagga*).
1. Commentary on the Meaning of the Training Rule Concerning Fellow Monastics (Sahadhammika-sikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 434.
Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on Fellow Monastics (Sahadhammika-vagga): "Yam" means that which has been prescribed.

In the phrase "by one training" (sikkhamānena), the expression "desiring to train" (sikkhitukāmena) is stated to show that the suffix "-māna" here carries a future sense. The word "sikkhamānena" [is explained] in relation to the word "bhikkhunā" (by a monk).
Thus, it is not only a qualification of the agent; rather, showing that it is also a qualification of the action in phrases such as "to be known," he said, "having been.
"From the word and from the meaning" means both from the words and from the meaning, or from the meaning of the words. First.
2. The Training Rule on Scratching.
438. Showing that a discourse connected with the second *vinaya* is called a *vinayakathā*, he said: “What is called a *vinayakathā*,” and so forth.
“That” refers to the *vinayakathā*. The construction is: “the commentary by means of the word-analysis (*padabhājana*) is called the ‘explanation of the *vinaya*’ (*vaṇṇa*) of the *vinaya*.
“That” refers to the explanation of the *vinaya*. Mastery is *pariyatti*; mastery of the *vinaya* is *vinayapariyatti*, which is designated as the mastery of the *vinaya*.
"Of this beauty, the root is the mastery of the Vinaya"—this means it has its root in the mastery of the Vinaya. "The bearer of the Vinaya obtains [it]"—this is the connection.
"Hi" (for) signifies elaboration. "The Blessed One speaks all of those"—this is the connection.

"Hi" (for) signifies truth. "Assa" (of him) refers to the bearer of the Vinaya. "Idha" (here) means in this teaching. In the phrase "alajjitā" and so forth, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
“Alajjitāya” means “without shame. Therefore it was said: “How [does one act] without shame? and so forth. “Ca” means “truly.

The word “sañcicca” (intentionally) should be applied to all three sentences. The meaning is: he intentionally commits an offense, he intentionally conceals an offense, and he intentionally goes on a wrong course.
“Manda” means a fool. “Momūha” means utterly deluded. “Virādheti” means...
He causes [the offense] to cease. "When remorse has arisen" means when remorse regarding the Vinaya has arisen, thinking, "Is this allowable or not?
The phrase "but this one," however, connects with "this person indeed transgresses.

Because the flesh of the hyena is similar in color and shape to the flesh of the pig, and because the flesh of the leopard is similar to the flesh of the deer, it is said: "the flesh of the hyena is the flesh of the pig," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "and an offense through forgetfulness," here the word *ca* (and) has the sense of including a statement not explicitly mentioned; the meaning is that one does not perform what ought to be done. The words "Thus" (*evaṃ*) and so forth constitute the conclusion.

Having thus shown the fault of one who does not master the Vinaya, he says "But the one who masters the Vinaya" (*vinayadharaṃ pana*) and so forth in order to show the virtue of one who masters the Vinaya.

"He" (*so*) refers to the one who masters the Vinaya. "Hi" (*hi*) indicates a detailed explanation. "Censure of others" (*parūpavādaṃ*) means the reproach of others. "In the pure end" (*suddhante*)...
"In the portions of the pure. "From that" means from the point of establishment; this is the connection. "His" refers to the one who upholds the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*).
"Thus," etc., is the conclusion. "His" refers to the one who upholds the Vinaya. "Of those overcome by remorse" means of those overwhelmed by remorse.
"He" refers to the one who upholds the Vinaya. "By them" means by those overcome by remorse. "Of the one who speaks in the midst of the Saṅgha who does not uphold the Vinaya."
The construction [is as follows]: *taṃ* refers to fear and timidity.
Those who seek (*atthayanti*) what is opposed (*paṭipakkhaṃ*) or contradictory (*paṭiviruddhaṃ*) are "enemies" (*paccatthīkā*);
the suffix *-ṇya* frequently denotes the agent. Thus, "one's own enemies" is *attapaccatthikā*. *Tattha* means "among those two kinds of enemies."
"These are Mettiya, Bhummaja, Vaḍḍha, and Licchavi; and also whatever other bhikkhus"—this is the connection.
"The bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, the novice Kaṇṭaka, and the Vajjiputtakas of Vesālī; Ariṭṭha... [etc. ...the Vajjiputtakas"—they are known as the enemies of the Dispensation (*sāsana-paccatthika*).
"Deception by others, ignorance, and being led astray by doubt; deception by others... [etc. ...being led astray. This is the connection.
"Those and others" refers to the doctrines such as *paru*... *vitaraṇa* and so forth. "Those are their doctrines" means they possess those [doctrines] such as *paru*... *vitaraṇa*;

thus, the connection is that "they are called enemies of the Dispensation (*sāsanapaccatthika*). The construction is: "The Mahāsaṅghikas and others who have embraced what is not the Buddha’s Dispensation as being the Buddha’s Dispensation are indeed called enemies of the Dispensation. Regarding the phrase "doubt, causing others to cross over, and so forth": [here...]

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the debates recorded in the *Kathāvatthu-pakaraṇa* are included. Regarding the phrase "the Mahāsāṅghikas, etc.," by the word "etc. here, the schools mentioned in the *Dīpavaṃsa* are included.
At the beginning, the term "those with perverted views" (*viparītadassanā*) is to be construed with all the subsequent terms.
To show the meaning of the term "in accordance with the Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*), it is said: "together with the reason" (*saha kāraṇena*). "In what manner" (*yathā*) means "by whatever mode."
The connection is with the word *niggayhamāne*.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means among the three kinds of true qualities (*saddhamma*). The construction is: "the great paths exist; this is all. And the phrase "the four fruits" (*cattāri phalāni ca*) should be construed by changing the grammatical gender.
Here, by the particle *ca*, the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) are included, for they too—

Because of the nature of the teaching as realization (*adhigama*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means among the three kinds of true Dhamma (*saddhamma*). "Certain elders" (*keci therā*) refers to certain elders who are preachers of the Dhamma.
"Yo kho" should be read with the second consonant (*d*) produced from the throat; however, in the manuscripts there is a reading with the letter *v*, namely "yo vo."

That is incorrect. Why? Because of what will be said later, namely, "So vo" (that for you), and because it is improper for two words with identical phonetic forms (*samānasuti*) to appear twice within a single sentence.
Regarding "some elders," the connection is that some elders who were refuse-rag wearers (*paṃsukūlika*) spoke.
As for "the other elders," these are elders distinct from both the Dhamma-preaching elders and the refuse-rag wearing elders. "They" refers to the five monks.
"They will perform" is the connection [with the previous sentence]. "In the borderlands of Jambudīpa" means he stays in a border region;
in such a place. "In the center of Jambudīpa" means he stays in the middle; or else, the dwelling place of the pure ones, such as the Buddhas and others, is the "middle," and in such a place.
"A group of twenty" means that which has twenty sub-groups (vaggas); that very collection is the "group of twenty."
"Taṃ. "Evaṃ" and so forth is the conclusion. "Tassādheyyo" means dependent on that;

what is meant is "belonging to that. The construction is: "The invitation (pavāraṇā) is dependent [on it], the formal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) is dependent, the going-forth (pabbajjā) is dependent, and the full ordination (upasampadā) is dependent.

"These which are the nine Uposatha days" is the connection. And "these which are the nine invitations" is the construction. "Tassa" refers to the one who holds the Vinaya (vinayadhara). "Tāsaṃ" refers to the nine invitations.
It should be connected thus: "And these four sanghakammas. And here, the ellipsis "those [acts] depend solely on those who are experts in the Vinaya" must be supplied.
Furthermore, the construction is: "and this going-forth and full ordination are to be performed. "Hi" means "truly. "Another" means one other than an expert in the Vinaya.
"He himself" means the expert in the Vinaya himself. "Upajjha" is a passive action (dhātukamma), while "by a sāmaṇera" is a causative action (kāritakamma).
It should be brought forward. And here, "and in the Uposatha and so forth" means that one may also say:
"Having distinguished between the granting of dependence (*nissaya*) and the attendance upon a novice (*sāmaṇera*), one obtains twelve benefits.
"Having made them separate" means having divided them into distinct sections, such as "five," and so on, up to "eleven"—seven [sections].

The intention is that he speaks after having divided [the text] into sections. "He praises" means he praises in the presence [of the person]. "He commends" means he commends in the absence [of the person].
To show the meaning of the word "to be mastered" (*uggahetabba*), it is said "to be thoroughly learned" (*pariyāpuṇitabba*).
"Enduring for a long journey" (*addhaniya*) means good for a long journey; the sense is "enduring a journey" or "suitable for a journey. The suffix *-niya* is used in the sense of "good" (*sādhu*).
(Moggallāne 4.33.73). The construction is:
"Many bhikkhus—both elders, novices, and those of middle standing—are mastering it.
Regarding the phrase "while being pointed out" (*uddissamāne*), it was stated as "while being indicated" (*uddisiyamāne*) to show that it is a verbal noun (*kammarūpa*). Furthermore, that...
"But the Pātimokkha": the construction is "because it is indeed being recited. "Or while it is being recited" means *uddisante* or *uddisiyamāne*.
"Or while it is being caused to be recited" means *uddisāpente* or *uddisāpiyamāne*; for the word *anta* functions here as the word *māna*. "He" refers to the bhikkhu. "It" refers to that Pātimokkha.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates two alternative phrases for the expression "minor and very minor rules," [the first] in the preceding clause...
The elision of the letter *ka* is to be understood. "Of these" means of the minor and secondary rules. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "These" refers to the minor and secondary rules.

"Yet" (*ye*) refers to the monks. The construction is: "As long as [the heavy rules] arise, so long do [these] conduce [to the welfare of the Saṅgha]"—this must be joined with the remaining portions of the text according to this method. Perceiving their gravity while demonstrating their lightness:
He said, "Or rather," and so forth. *Ativiya* means *ati* + *eva*. The vowel *i* has disappeared due to euphonic combination (*sandhi*).

The word *viya* expresses the sense of the particle *eva*; just as the word *iva* is used in the phrase "it is better for us [to have] much," it should be understood here as meaning "having become *ati*, it is indeed (*eva*).
In the expression "of one who is ordained" (*upasampannassa*), the genitive case is used in the sense of proximity (according to *Rūpasiddhi* sutta 316).
He said: "In the presence of one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*). "Of him" means of the one who is fully ordained. "In that" refers to the Vinaya.
"Disparages" (*vivaṇṇeti*) means not merely disparaging him, but rather censuring him; thus he said "censures" (*nindati*). "Reproaches" (*garahati*) is a synonym for that.
Alternatively, "censures" means he censures him in the presence of the one who is fully ordained. "Reproaches" means...
"She censures in his absence. This is the second [section]. 3.
The Training Rule on Deception (Mohana-sikkhāpada). 444.
Regarding the third [rule], he says that the prefix *anu-* includes the sense of "succession" (*paṭipāṭi*) and expresses the meaning of "in order," thus: "in successive order" (*anupaṭipāṭiyā*).
“Every half-month, every half-month. *Sa* refers to the Pātimokkha. “It should be recited at each Uposatha” means it is *anuposathika*.
For here too, the prefix *anu-* expresses frequency. *Sa* refers to the Pātimokkha; the construction is: “it is called ‘being recited.
By the phrase “in that misconduct,” he shows the meaning of the word “therein. By the phrase “whatever offense,”...
It shows the scope of the word *yaṃ*. Regarding the phrase *yathādhammo*, it is said that by the word *dhamma* here, both *dhamma* (the Teaching) and *vinaya* (the Discipline) are intended;
thus he says, "the *dhamma* and the *vinaya*. *Yathā* means "in whatever manner. The word *sādhu* has the sense of "beautiful," while the word *ka* is for the purpose of completing the meter;
thus he says, "well" (*suṭṭhu*). Both the words *aṭṭhiṃ* and *katvā* should be understood [as forming a single compound].
Alternatively, *aṭṭhikatvā* is a single word. Regarding that, according to the first method of interpretation: *aṭṭhi* means "that which has a purpose" (*yassatthī*);
having changed the letter *t* to *ṭ*, it becomes *aṭṭhi*. *Katvā* does not form a compound with the following word due to the suffix *tvā*.
In the phrase *aṭṭhikabhāvaṃ*, the word *ika* indicates the suffix *ī* in the term *aṭṭhī*; the word *bhāvaṃ* indicates the abstract suffix *bhāva*.

This shows that the meaning of the word *aṭṭhi* (bone) must be made known [by derivation]. The meaning, however, should be understood as follows: "having made it into the state of a bone" (*aṭṭhibhāvaṃ katvā*).
In the latter method, the meaning is "that which has a purpose" (*yassatthīti aṭṭhiko*); according to the former method, the letter *tth* is changed to *ṭṭh*.
Alternatively, *aṭṭhiko* means "that which is to be sought after" or "desired" (*atthayitabbo icchitabbo*); thus, the suffix *tvā* should be applied to the nominal stem *aṭṭhika*.

“Aṭṭhikatvā” (having made it a bone) is an adverbial modifier of an action. It is stated that when an adverbial modifier of an action is present, either the verbal root *kṛ* or the verbal root *bhū* should be employed;
thus they have said “katvā” (having done) and “hutvā” (having become). Showing all of this, he said:
“‘Aṭṭhikatvā’ means having made it the state of being a bone, having become a bone. This is the third [section].

4. The Training Rule on Striking (Pahārasikkhāpada) 449. Regarding the fourth [offense], why do the group of six (Chabbaggiya) give blows to the group of seventeen (Sattarasavaggiya)? Is it not because they give blows without cause? To this he says, “Friend,” and so forth. By this, he shows that they give blows because they have not acted in accordance with what they say. 451. As for the phrase “even if”:

here, by the word *pi* (“even”), he shows that if [the victim] does not die, what need is there to mention [the offense]? It is simply a *pācittiya*. “By a blow” means by reason of a blow. “In such a way” means in whatever manner. “This one” refers to the bhikkhu. “Does not shine” means it does not look well.

452. Regarding the phrase “of one who is not fully ordained” (*anupasampannassa*), it is stated “or of a householder,” etc., in order to show that the vowel *a* here has the sense of “other than. “Or of one who has gone forth” (*pabbajitassa vā*) means either a wandering ascetic (*paribbājaka*) or a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*).
453. To show the meaning of the word “by anyone” (*kenaci*), it is stated “by a human being,” etc.

“From that” (*tato*) means from the harassment; by this, he shows the ablative case regarding liberation (*mokkha*). By the word “of oneself” (*attano*), he shows the connection. “Aspiring” (*patthayamāno*)—
By this, he shows the meaning of the word "intention" (*adhippāya*). "Or with a mallet" means with a staff that is half the length of a four-cubit staff.
"He" refers to a thief or the like. This is the fourth [section].
5. The Training Rule on the Hand-Blade (*tala-sattika-sikkhāpada*).
454. *Pañcame*: "Tala" refers to the palm of the hand. It is called "tala" because anything held that is placed upon it settles there (*talati*).
"Satti" means a spear; for it is so called because it is capable of piercing (*sakati*). Since the palm resembles a spear, it is a "palm-spear" (*talasattika*);
the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of similarity. Taking that "palm-spear" metaphorically, [the text continues...]

“‘Even the body’ (kāyam-pi) is what was said. Because one picks it up by grasping with the body—referred to here as the *tala-satti* (palm-club)—even something other than the [target] body, it is said: “‘Even that which is connected to the body’ (kāya-paṭibaddham-pi).
Regarding the term “accumulated by blows” (*pahāra-samuccitā*), the prefix *sam-* and the prefix *upa-* in the word *ci* refer to that which is practiced or familiarized;
thus he says: “‘Accustomed to blows’ (*pahāra-paricitā*). By means of the blow, *sam-* [indicates] again and again...
"Accitā" and "paricitā" mean "accumulated. It was said with reference to this very meaning: "Even previously... [etc. ...the meaning.
To show another method of recitation, it was said: "Trembling from fear" (*pahārassa ubbiggā*). "Of that" (*tassa*) refers to that reading.

"From fear" (*pahārassa*) means "from fear" (*pahārato*); here the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. By the word "afraid" (*bhītā*), the prefix *upa-* in "trembling" (*ubbiggā*) is indicated.
It shows the weapon of the Vijjādhātu. 457–8.

*Viraddho* means having become a *paṇṇaka*. *Pubbe* means in the previous training rule (*sikkhāpada*). *Vuttesu vatthūsu* means in the matters stated as "a thief or an enemy," and so forth. This is the fifth. 6.
The Training Rule on Groundless Accusations (*Amūlaka-sikkhāpada*).

459. "Six" refers to the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*). "They reproach" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Because of their manifold faults" means because of the disorderly nature of their defects.

"In this way" means while being reproached. "Protecting themselves" should be construed as: they reproach while providing protection—that is, guarding—themselves and their own circle on all sides. This is the sixth [case].
7. The Training Rule on Intentional Action (Sañcicca-sikkhāpada).

464. Regarding the seventh [rule], because the verbal root *upa-pubba-daha* is transitive, it is stated "causing to arise" (*uppādentī*) in order to show that it is included within the sense of causing another to act.
Regarding the phrase "of one not fully ordained" (*anupasampannassā*), it is stated "of a novice" (*sāmaṇerassā*) in order to show the synonymous meaning of the vowel *a*.
For a novice (sāmaṇera) is similar to one who is fully ordained (upasampanna) in both physical form and male gender. The connection is: "He causes remorse in the novice.
The construction is: "I think he is sitting," "I think he is lying down," "I think he has eaten," "I think he has drunk," "I think he has done [it].
"Sitting" means having sat; "lying down" means having lain down. This is the seventh [section].
8. The Training Rule on Eavesdropping (Upassuti-sikkhāpada) 471.

Regarding the eighth [training rule], in the phrase "of legal issues that have arisen" (*adhikaraṇajātānaṃ*), he says "of legal issues consisting of disputes that have arisen" (*uppannavivādādhikaraṇānaṃ*) in order to show that, by way of its context, *adhikaraṇa* has the nature of a legal issue consisting of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), and that it functions as a qualifying term for the subsequent word. In that regard, by the word "arisen" (*uppanna*):
It shows the meaning of the word *jāta*. By the word *vivāda*, it shows the specific nature (*sarūpa*) of the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
"Suti" means speech; in order to show the meaning "a place near to hearing (*suti*)," it is said "near to hearing" (*sutisamīpa*).
By the word "near" (*samīpa*), it shows the meaning of the prefix *upa*. By the phrase beginning with "where," [it explains] the prefix *upa* in the term "eavesdropping" (*upassuti*).
He shows its true form because of its being a gerund (*padhāna*). "Yattha" means in which place.
Regarding "mantentaṃ," since the accusative case here is intended in the sense of the locative, it is stated as "mantayamāne.
473. Regarding "vūpasamissāmi," in order to show that the root *idh* has the meaning of "going," it is stated as "vūpasamaṃ gamissāmi."
"State of being non-agents" means a state free from fault. The construction is: "It might be an action by way of going out of a desire to hear.
From the subsequent [text] as well, this is the same method.
The eighth [section]. 9. The Training Rule on Obstructing Work.

474. "We are called the group of six" means we, those named the *Chabbaggiyas*. "Because of having done" means because of having performed actions (*kamma*). "Dhamma" means the actual intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "In these" means in these four formal acts of the Saṅgha. This is the ninth [section]. 10.
The Training Rule on Not Coming Without Having Given Consent. 481.
In the tenth [section], one who accuses is one who charges another with a fault; by that accuser, the fault is to be accused of.
“Should be charged” means one who has been accused; he is the very same as the accuser, and by him [the charge is made]. “An investigator” means one who is an expert in the Vinaya.
For he is called an investigator because, having inferred the opinions of both the accuser and the accused, he investigates—that is, he knows. “Even by this much” means even by this measure.
The tenth [section].
11. The Rule on the Weak (Dubbalasikkhāpada) 484.
In cases such as “alajjitā,” there is an elision of the letter *y* in the grammatical analysis; thus he says, “by way of intimacy (*yathāmittatāya*).

By the phrase “whosoever (*yo yo*”), he shows the distributive sense of the word *yathā*. This is similar to [the usage] in “according to seniority (*yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*)” and so forth, where it means “whosoever.”

The meaning of the word *mitto* (friend) should be understood as “according to the friend. Regarding the phrase “in all instances,” this refers to all the instances such as “according to what has been seen,” and so forth.
This is the eleventh [section].
12. The Training Rule on Diversion.

489. In the twelfth [section], there is the statement known as the "Analysis of the Meaning of Words. *Tattha* means in the section of thirty [rules]. *Idha* means in the section of ninety-two, or in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). *Puggalassa* means of another person. This is the twelfth.
The eighth chapter, the Chapter on Those Who Share the Dhamma (*Sahadhammika-vagga*), is concluded. 9. The Jewel Chapter (*Ratana-vagga*).
1. Commentary on the Antepura Training Rule (Antepurasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 494.
In the first section of the Rājavagga, "parittaka" means small by virtue of its quality.
To show that the word "pāsādavara" (excellent palace) must be connected with the word "upari" (above), it is said: "gone above the excellent palace. By this, [the meaning of] the excellent palace...
"Having gone to the excellent upper palace" (*uparipāsādavaragata*) indicates the meaning of the phrase as "having gone to, having approached, that excellent upper palace.

"Of the noble ones" (*ayyānaṃ*) refers to the monks. By the word "for the sake of" (*kāraṇā*), he shows the meaning of the word "by means of" (*vāhasā*). "By them" (*tehi*) refers to those noble ones. 497.
"In the interval" (*antaraṃ*) means a moment, an opportunity, or a gap. "To be killed" (*ghātetuṃ*) means to be slain. "He desires" (*icchatīti*)—by this [he shows the intention].

This shows the meaning of "requesting" regarding the relic. The construction should be understood as follows: "The meaning of the words in [passages] such as ‘the king’s inner apartments, crowded with elephants’ (rājantepuraṃ hatthisammadda) is to be known thus.
"Crowded with elephants" (hatthisammadda) means a place congested with elephants. "Crowded with horses" (assasammadda) is so called because there is a crowding of horses there.
"Crowded with chariots" (rathasammadda) is so called because there is a crowding of chariots there; thus he indicates the etymological meaning by extension.
He said: "The same method applies. Regarding the phrase "sammattaṃ," because the reading with the initial syllable *sam* is cramped and does not convey the meaning, it was stated:
"That should not be accepted. The word "therein" (*tattha*) refers to the reading [of the commentary].

By the phrase "the crushing of elephants" (*hatthīnaṃ sammaddaṃ*), he shows that the meaning of the latter member of the compound is "crushing" (*sammaddanaṃ*), and by the former member, he indicates a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*). In the previous reading...
However, this shows that the latter member has the sense of a locative and forms a *tatiyā-samāsa* (instrumental compound) with the former member;

it is also called an "external compound" (*bāhiratthasamāsa*). In the latter reading, the statement "there is an elephant-trampling" (*hatthisammaddo atthī*) is said in order to show the change of gender in the phrase "elephant-trampling" (*hatthisammadda*) and its connection with the elliptical word "is" (*atthi*). "Those things to be dyed" (*rajitabbāni*)...
*Rajanīyāni* means "fit to be colored" (or "desirable"). By this, in the first reading, one must apply a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) to read *rañño antepure*.
However, in the second reading, it is appropriate in its primary sense. Therefore it was said: "in that inner apartment. 498. *Avasittassa*:
of one who has been consecrated with the kṣatriya anointment. *Ita*: from the bed-chamber. By this, a genitive-bahubbīhi compound is formed.

[The text] shows this. A queen is called a *ratana* (jewel) in the sense that she generates delight for the king. And a "great queen" (*mahesī*) is a consort who has received consecration (*abhisecanā*).
To show that the verbal root *gam*, preceded by the prefix *ni*, is synonymous with the verbal root *kam*, preceded by the prefix *ni*, it is said:
"gone out" (*niggata*) means "departed" (*nikkhanta*). First.
2. The Jewel Training Rule (Ratanasikkhāpada) 502.
In the second [verse], "having forgotten" means having forgotten through the lapse of mindfulness. "A full bowl" (puṇṇapatta) refers to the gift of contentment.
For it is called a "full bowl" because it is a portion to be obtained by one whose wishes are fulfilled. To show its actual nature:
It was stated, “five kahāpaṇas constantly. However, here, because there are five hundred kahāpaṇas, twenty-five kahāpaṇas are intended.
To show that the word *ābharaṇa* is a synonym for the word *alaṅkāra*, it is stated, “an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
By the phrase “called Mahālata,” he shows that this is not just any ornament, but rather a specific kind of ornament.
Because there are great works of garland-making and creeper-work here, it is called a "great creeper" (*mahālatā*). For by the mention of "creeper," the "garland" is also included.
It is "worth nine crores" (*navakoṭi-agghanaka*) because its value is nine crores; or alternatively, it is "worth nine crores" because it deserves a value reckoned as nine crores.
(504) Because he dwells near at hand (*ante*), being of virtuous conduct (*sīla*), the attendant is called an "antevāsī"; thus he says "attendant" (*paricāriko*).
506. "Two throws of a clod" means two throws of a clod by a man of medium strength. "The Saṅgha... [etc.]... The construction is:
for one who acquires or causes to be acquired [gold or silver] for the purpose of new building works, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
"The remainder" means that which remains apart from gold and silver. "Even a palm-leaf worn on a mother’s ear" means even a palm-leaf ornament worn on a mother’s ear.
“Of one who is taking back” is the connection [with the preceding].
By the phrase “it becomes allowable property,” it is shown that unallowable property is not permitted.
“This” refers to the property. “A hindrance” means a personal hindrance for oneself. “Even by consent” means even by reason of the consent of carpenters and others.
"Even out of fear" means even for the sake of fear caused by those favored by the king. "By force" (*balakkārena*): *kāra* is the act of doing;
the act by force is *balakkāra*; by that. The meaning is: having become one who acts by force, having cast [it] down.
"Therein" means in the great monastery. "Wherever" means in whatever place; the connection is "where suspicion arises. "In places frequented by the great multitude" means...
In places frequented by many people. To show the reason why it should not be taken up, it is said:
"there is no impediment. The intended meaning is that because there is no impediment, therefore it should not be taken up.
"One" refers to the connection with "one monk sees. "Having entered" means having gone into.
The word *rūpa* is a synonym for "goods" (*bhaṇḍa*), hence he says "goods. The construction is: "Goods are what is called *rūpa*. A "bundle" (*bhaṇḍika*) is a small bag associated with goods.
"Having counted" means having performed a calculation. Regarding the phrase "the sign (*nimitta*)":

here the word "iti" is a synonym for "name. The construction is: "A mark such as a brand and so forth is what is called a 'sign'. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "brand and so forth," blue rags and the like are included. "With lac" means with resin (*jatū*).

"Suitable" (patirūpā) here means those who possess a sense of shame and scrupulousness; thus it says, "those who are modest and conscientious. "Stationary" (thāvaram) refers to that which is stationary as opposed to moving.

"For a long time" (addhuno) means for the duration of time. "Having encouraged others" (samādapetvā) means having urged others [to give]. The meaning is: "having requested according to the manner stated in the passage, 'The Noble Ones stand for the sake of [others]; this is the solicitation of the Noble Ones.'"
507. "Considred as jewels" means [things] for the enjoyment and use of human beings. This is the second [section]. 3.
The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time. 508.

In the third [section], by the phrase "animal-like talk," he shows that the term *tiracchānakathā* is a *tulyanissita-samāsa* (a compound based on similarity). "Connected with kings" means connected with kings.

512. “A number of bhikkhus” is the connection. “In that village” means in that first village entered. “That business” means that desired business. “Between” (*antarā*) refers to the space between the village and the monastery;

this is an ablative used in the sense of a locative. “Or at a family house” means at a house of relatives or a house of supporters. “For oil alms” means for the purpose of begging for oil. “On his side” means near his own side; this is what is meant.
“By that” means by way of the middle of the village. “Without descending” (*anokkamma*).
"Without descending, without departing"—this is the meaning. The third [section].
4. The Training Rule on the Needle Case (Sūcighara-sikkhāpada).
In the fourth [section], it is stated, "The very act of breaking is 'breaking' (bhedanaka)," in order to show that the letter *ka* serves to complete the meter.

The suffix *apacca* is used in the sense of "possessing" (*assatthiya*); thus he said, "that which belongs to him" (*taṃ assa atthi*). "To him" (*assa*) refers to the one who has committed the *pācittiya* offense.
The meaning is that after first breaking the needle-case, one must subsequently confess the *pācittiya*. "Araṇidhanuka" means a bow for the fire-sticks (*araṇi*).
"Vedhaka" means a fastener for the waist-band (*kāyabandhana-vedhaka*). This is the fourth [section].
5. The Training Rule on Beds (Mañcasikkhāpada) 522.
Regarding the fifth [rule]: *chedanaka* means simply "cutting" (*chedana*); it is stated as "in the same manner as previously described" with reference to the meaning that one possesses such cutting.

"Having buried" means having buried it beyond the prescribed measure. "Or having turned it face up" means having turned it over from bottom to top. "Having placed" means having placed it so that it hangs down. The fifth [rule].
6. The Training Rule on Cotton-Filling (Tūlonaddha-sikkhāpada). 526.
Regarding the sixth [rule], "here" refers to the bed and chair. "To be covered" means to be spread over; thus, the meaning "covered with cotton" (*tūlonaddha*) is also appropriate.
"Having inserted cotton" means having spread a mattress (*cimilikā*) upon the bed and chair, and then having placed cotton on top of it.
"Having inserted"—this is the meaning. The sixth [section]. 7.
The Training Rule on Sitting Mats (7).
531. Regarding the seventh: "Where? means in which chapter (khandhaka) or in which subject matter (vatthu)? "For" (hi) means truly. "Therein" (tattha)...
In the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*, or in the section concerning the matter of superior food:
by the phrase "just as if" (*yathā nāma*), he shows the meaning of the expression "even as"; and by the phrase "an old leather-worker," he shows the meaning of the expression "an old leather-cutter.
For a leather-worker is called a "leather-cutter" (*asikoṭṭha*) because he cuts—that is, slices—leather with a knife (*asi*). This is said with reference to the time when the matter arose.
It was said, "ancient. Making that very simile clear, he said, "Just as...

The word *hi* serves to clarify that; for the meaning is, "I shall indeed make it clear. The connection is: "the leather-worker drags [it]. *Vitthataṃ* means wide or extensive. *Sopi* refers to Udāyī as well.
The construction is: "he drags that sitting mat. *Tenā* means by reason of that dragging. *Taṃ* refers to Udāyī.
"Similar to a rug" (*santhatasadisa*) means similar to a rug. "In one end" (*ekasmiṃ ante*) means in one part;
it is to be construed with "having torn" (*phāletvā*). This is the seventh [section]. 8. The Training Rule on the Itch-Covering Cloth (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādi-sikkhāpada*).
537. In the eighth [verse], the words beginning with “kattha” are exactly as explained by the method already stated. 539. To show the scope of the word “yassā,” it is said “of the bhikkhu.
By the phrase “below the navel,” it shows the etymological meaning of *adho-nābhi* as that which is beneath the navel; by the phrase “above the kneecaps,” it shows...
“*Ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ*”: above the kneecaps. The word *ubbha* is a synonym for “above” (*upari*) and is used here as a locative case ending.
Because it is a synonym for the words *kaṇḍu* and *khajju*, it is said: “*Kaṇḍū* means *khajjū*. It is called *kaṇḍu* because it scrapes (*kaṇḍati*) or causes breaking;
it is called *khajju* because it gnaws (*khajjati*) or causes piercing. In some manuscripts there is the reading “*kacchū*,” but that is incorrect.
“Lohitatuṇḍikā” means one whose beak (tuṇḍa) is red (lohitā). It is called a “piḷakā” because it presses or afflicts.

An “assāva” is so called because it causes impurity to flow out or trickle excessively; showing this derivation, he says, “the trickling of impurity. These are hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and diabetes.
By the word “etcetera,” conditions such as dunnāmaka (dysentery) and others are included. Therein, like an enemy (ari)...

It is called *arisa* because it "rules over" (*īsati*) or "overcomes" (*abhibhavati*). *Bhaga* refers to the urinary passage; that which "tears" (*darati*) or "lacerates" (*phāleti*) it is *bhagandara*, a specific type of ulcer arising near the anus.
*Madhumeha* is so called because it "sprinkles" (*mihati*) urine and other fluids like honey (*madhu*);
this affliction is of many kinds, such as *muttamēha*, *sukkamēha*, and *rattamēha*. Since the word *thulla* is a synonym for "great," he said "mahā" (great). This is the eighth [chapter].
9. The Training Rule on the Rain-Cloak (Vassikasāṭika). 542.

It is called "rain-cloak" (*vassikā*) because it is to be determined [for use] during the rainy season in the ninth year; and since it is both a rain-cloak and a cloak (*sāṭikā*), it is termed a "rain-cloak" (*vassikasāṭikā*).
This is the ninth. 10. The Training Rule on the Elder Nanda.
In the tenth [section], by the phrase "by four finger-breadths" (*catūhi aṅgulehi*), he shows that *caturaṅgulā* is a non-collective compound (*asamāhāra-dvigu*).
"Of inferior measure" (*ūnakappamāṇo*) means having a measure inferior to that of the Blessed One. It should be understood that by this, the meaning of the word *omaka* as "inferior" is demonstrated.
The tenth [section].
The ninth chapter, the Ratana-vagga,
is finished. Thus ends the application of the commentary on the Minor Section (Khuddaka-vaṇṇanā) within the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.
6. The Section on Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa) 1.
Exegesis of the First Rule on Confession (Paṭhamapāṭidesanīyasikkhāpada-atthayojanā):

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: immediately after the minor rules (Khuddaka), those rules known as the “Confessions” (Pāṭidesanīya) were established by the compilers of the Council; now, this commentary on those rules follows.
552. First, regarding the first *pāṭidesanīya*, the construction should be understood as follows: "The meaning is to be known thus. Regarding the phrase "at the time of returning":

this refers to the time of departing from the place where one went for alms, or the time of returning after having turned back. Regarding the word "sabbe" (all): here, the euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) occurs by means of the elision of the nasalization (*niggahīta*);
thus he says "sabbameva" (all indeed). By the word "kampamānā" (trembling), the meaning of trembling is indicated for the verbal root preceded by the prefix *pa-*.
It shows [this]. Regarding *apehi*, since the root preceded by *apa-* here has the sense of "going," he says, "depart" (*apagaccha*).
553. That by which the manner in which one should confess is shown is "the demonstration of the manner of confession.

To show that the two words are synonyms, it is said: "a carriage road (*rathikā*) means a street (*racchā*). It is a "carriage road" because it is beneficial for a carriage (*ratha*); [it is formed] with the suffix *ṇya*.
In the *Moggallāna* treatise (4.72), it is stated that the word “racchā” means a street. A street that has not been pierced through by another street is called a “byūha”;
thus he said, “without piercing through,” and so forth. It is called a “byūha” because it crowds or gathers people together by preventing them from going elsewhere.
A “siṅghāṭaka” is a junction of roads; thus he said, “a place where paths converge. One “siṅghati” (sniffs/gathers) at the convergence of paths.

It is called a *siṅghāṭaka* because one gathers (*karoti*) [there]. "In these" refers to the carriage-roads and so forth. "In this very same manner" extends the rule by analogy to the *dukkaṭa* and *pāṭidesanīya* offenses.
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. The word "from the statement" (*vacanato*) is the indicative cause for the word "is to be understood" (*veditabbo*).
The construction is: "by way of the nun who is giving. "In this" refers to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Therefore" means because it is not a fixed measure, therefore.
The connection is that the words “this was said” [apply here]. The construction is: “in the three time-periods, when [the robe] has been mixed and made of a single substance.

Regarding the phrase “causes to be given,” it is stated—“by someone other than a non-relative”—in order to show the agent and the object of the action performed by means of a causal function (hetuttha-kiriya).
“By someone else” means by another person than oneself. [This refers to] either “by that very bhikkhunī herself” or “by someone else.”
The words [in the phrase] "having caused to be accepted" are the object of the action performed (kāritakamma). First. 2.
The second Pāṭidesanīya training rule: 558.
Regarding the second [rule], the intention is that by means of the preceding training rule, there is an offense [if one eats] within a house. By this training rule...

The intention is that there would be an offense for one who becomes complacent. However, for the giver, there is no offense by virtue of this [rule] nor the previous one, because it is the meal of another; such is the intention. This is the second.
3. The third training rule on offenses entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*).
562. Regarding the third [phrase], "from both" (*ubhato*), he says "by two" (*dvīhi*) to indicate the instrumental case.

Both the analysis (*byāsa*) and the compound (*samāsa*) of "one who has confidence from both sides" (*ubhatopasanna*) are appropriate; however, in the compound, there is the elision of the suffix *-to*. To show the actual form of the word "from both," it is said:
"by a male lay follower (*upāsaka*) and also by a female lay follower (*upāsikā*). As to why it is "confident from both sides," he says: "It is said that in that [case]... and so forth.
Because it is said that in that family... [and so on] ...they were indeed stream-enterers, therefore it is called "faithful on both sides.
In the phrase "even if," the word *pi* (even/also) includes even more than eighty million in wealth. He shows the reason for the decline with the words beginning "because."
569. Regarding the phrase “having brought out from the house,” the words “the sitting hall or the monastery” are stated to show the object of the word “having brought out.
By the word “having brought” (ānetvā), he shows the meaning of the verbal root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *ni*. “At the door” means at the door of his own house.
The third [section].
4. The Fourth Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule 570. Regarding the fourth [rule], the word *avaruddha* is a synonym for the word *pariruddha*;
thus he said, “they are *pariruddhā*. The meaning is that they are obstructed or enclosed on all sides by the forest dwelling (*āraññaka-senāsana*).

573. In the phrase “of five,” the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), and it must be connected with the selected object (*niddhāriya*) expressed by the term “whatever.”

It is said, “among the five types of fellow practitioners, whatever [is available],” in order to show this. By the phrase, “having sent [someone], we will bring hard food and soft food,” the manner of being informed is demonstrated.

Although it is stated generally as “the monastery,” since the monastery intended here is specifically that of a forest dwelling, he says, “and the monastery of the forest dwelling. “Of that” means of the monastery of the forest dwelling.
To reconcile the question “Why? with the answer “For the sake of liberation,” the word must be treated as an ablative used in the sense of the dative.
For the meaning is: “For what purpose? And “for the sake of liberation” (*paṭimocanatthaṃ*) is the accusative used in the sense of that [purpose].
For the meaning is: “For the purpose known as liberation. Furthermore, the word *attha* denotes a motive or purpose; for the meaning is: “For the motive. Alternatively,
“‘For the purpose of liberation’ (paṭimocanatthaṃ)”: this refers to the answer. To correspond with the question “Why?”, the word must be put in the nominative case in the sense of the ablative.
For the meaning is: “The purpose (attha) is that which is called liberation. Furthermore, the word *attha* denotes a cause;

for the meaning is “because of the cause. For in this way, the method of investigation (*vicayahāra*), which consists of the sequence and correspondence between the question and the answer, becomes complete.
It should be understood as follows: "Of us" means of us who are warding off solid food and soft food.
"Us" refers to us who are designated as thieves. To show the meaning of the word "tassā," it is said: "of this rice-gruel.

"Other families too" means other families besides those from whom one has already informed. "By that" means by that family from whom one has informed. According to the Kurundi commentary, having made the notification regarding the rice-gruel...
The intention is that it is permissible to bring cakes and such items without taking rice gruel.

575. "Of one" means of a single bhikkhu. "For him" refers to the bhikkhu who has made the formal announcement; the construction is "for the sake of four or five bhikkhus. "Also for others" means for those other than the four or five bhikkhus. "Only more" means...
"Only what remains after it has been consumed. Regarding "but whatever," the construction is: "but whatever solid or soft food she brings from the forest and gives.
To show the referent of the word *tatra* (there) in the phrase "grown there," it is stated:
"in the monastery. The connection is with "given by another. "That" refers to the root-vegetables and so forth. "Formally acknowledged" (*paṭisaṃvidita*).
The meaning is: "having first made it well known beforehand. This is the fourth [section].
Thus ends the commentary on the *Pāṭidesanīya* rules within the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Exposition is completed.
7. The Section on the Training Rules (Sekhiyakaṇḍa) 1. The Exposition of the Meaning of the Chapter on Being Well-Circled (Parimaṇḍalavagga).

The construction is as follows: "Now, this is also the method of commentary for those training rules which were spoken by the Blessed One as 'the Sekhiyas'— by the Blessed One who has trained in the three trainings, who has trained in the trainings by means of the four paths, who is 'such-like' (tādi) in the sense of being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions,
or who is 'such-like' in the sense of remaining unchanged amidst the desirable and the undesirable."
576. *Tattha* means "in the rules of training (*sekhiya-sikkhāpada*)," and the construction is that "the meaning should be understood thus.
By the word "on all sides" (*samantato*), he shows the sense of the prefix *pari-*.

Regarding the phrase "from the navel-circle to the knee-circle," he says "above," etc., because the words "upward" (*uddham*) and "downward" (*adho*) must be supplied here. *Aṭṭhaṅgulamattam* is a neuter noun used as an adjective.
"Should be worn" is the connection [of the sentence]. "From that" means from the measure of eight finger-breadths. The construction is: "for one who wears it so that it is concealed.
"In this regard, this is the measure" means this is the measure for that lower robe (*nivāsana*).
"Of such a kind" refers to a lower robe that is five fist-lengths in length and two and a half cubits across. It is for the purpose of concealing the kneecaps.
"It is allowable" is the construction. "Therein" means among the robes. "It does not remain" means it does not remain because of its sparseness. "It remains" means it remains because of its density.
Regarding the phrase "for one who is wearing [it]," the word *ca* (and) here has the sense of restriction; the meaning is "only for one who is wearing [it]. The construction is:
"For one who wears it only in this manner, there is no *dukkaṭa*; however, even for one who wears it in that [other] way, there is indeed a *dukkaṭa*."
"But those which are faults of the lower garment" is the connection. "Other" means other than those worn by hanging them in front and behind.
"All those" refers to all those faults of the lower garment. "In this" means in this Vibhaṅga. "Right there" means in the Khandhaka itself. The connection is:
"there is no offense for one who wears it unintentionally. This same method applies here as well in the case of "through lack of mindfulness. "Not knowing" means...
In this context, ignorance is twofold: ignorance regarding the procedure for wearing the lower robe (*nivāsanavatta*), and ignorance regarding whether [the robe] has been properly put on or not.
Here, referring to ignorance regarding whether it has been properly put on or not, he says "to one who does not know" in order to show this; thus he says, "Regarding 'to one who does not know'...
and so forth. The word *hi* means "indeed" (as a truth). *Tassa* refers to the procedure for wearing the lower robe. *Assa* refers to the bhikkhu.
"But that" refers to the failure to be released from the offense. "Therefore" means because it is appropriate; therefore. "He" refers to the bhikkhu.
The connection is with what was stated in the *Kurundi*: "One whose shanks are dry is a 'dry-shanked' one.
"One who has large calf-muscle flesh is a 'large-calf-muscle' one. "Of him" refers to the bhikkhu.

*Vaṇo* means a wound. For it is called a *vaṇo* because it wounds—that is, it causes the mangled disintegration of the body. In the phrase "wild beasts or thieves," the word *vā* (or) has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned;
by this, other misfortunes such as water, mud, and so forth, are also included. *Idha* means in this analysis (*vibhaṅga*) or in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
*Ubho kaṇṇe* means the two ears that protrude both in front and behind. *Avisesena* means generally, without making a distinction between "within a house" and "in a monastery."
"In the monastery" is said with reference to times such as when the Saṅgha is assembled, when attending upon the Buddha, or when attending upon the elders.
(578) Since the word "body" (kāya) applies to a single part of the body, he says, "the knee or the chest.
By the phrase "not with the head covered," he rejects the fault of over-extension regarding the term "well-covered" (suppaṭicchanna). "A knot" (gaṇṭhika) means a loop; for that indeed...
It is called a *ganthi* because it ties (*ganthati*) or binds (*bandhati*), or because one ties or binds things therein; thus it is termed a "knot" (*ganthika*).
Alternatively, when the letter *nth* is changed to *ṇth*, it becomes *gaṇṭhika*; having fastened that *gaṇṭhika*. "Both corners" refers to the two corners of the robe.
Regarding the term *galavāṭaka*: here, *gala* means the throat. For it is there that the fourfold food—consisting of what is chewed, swallowed, licked, and drunk—is [received].
Food, having become liquid, falls into the belly; thus it is called *gala*. A small pit is a *galavāṭaka*;
the suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of smallness. A pit situated in the throat is a *galavāṭaka*.

For there is the elision of the letter *a* from *ā*, as in the case of "papa" and so forth. Here, the word division is *pa-āpanti*, with the elision of both the letter *a* and the letter *ā*. It has increased (*pavaddhaṃ*).
“Āpaṃ papaṃ” means “a great amount of water”; this is the connection with the phrase “having uncovered his head.

(579) Rejecting the interpretations that it means “one who has entered for the sake of dwelling” or “one who has approached by means of dwelling,” he said: “of one who has approached for the purpose of dwelling.
(580) Showing that one who does not dally with hands and feet is indeed “well-restrained,” he said: “not playing with the hand or the foot.”
582. Regarding "Okkhittacakkhu": here the prefix *os-* is a synonym for "below," thus it says "one with eyes cast downward.
By the word "having been" (*hutvā*), it shows the state of being an adverbial modifier of the action. "Yugayuttaka" means one who is yoked to a yoke. "Damiyittha" means tamed.
"Ājāneyyo" means one who thoroughly knows what is the right cause and what is not. "Ettakaṃ" refers to the measure of four cubits. He who goes [thus]...

The construction is: "for that bhikkhu there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Both readings—"the state of being a danger" (*parissayabhāva*) and "the absence of danger" (*parissayābhāva*)—are indeed appropriate. Regarding the term *itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*:
this manner of hanging up the robe is "thus" (*itthaṃ*); [the suffix -tā indicates] that which exists or proceeds in such a way.
“Bhūto” means “become,” O Bhikkhu. That by which something is characterized is a “lakkhaṇaṃ,” namely, a robe (cīvaraṃ). “Ittham bhūto” means “having become thus”;
its characteristic mark is an “itthambhūtalakkhaṇaṃ,” and [the word] refers to that. The construction should be understood as: “the instrumental case is to be seen.
He said, “The nature of an adverbial qualifier is called ‘itthambhūtalakkhaṇaṃ’,” explaining: “the meaning is ‘having become on one side... and so forth.”
"Within the village boundary" means within the village boundary of the *indakhīla*. This is the first chapter. 2. Commentary on the *Ujjagghikā-vagga* (Chapter on Loud Laughter) 586.

Laughing loudly—that is, laughing with a loud sound—is *ujjaggha*; that itself is *ujjagghikā*, [meaning] by that. Thus, showing this meaning, he said: "laughing with a great laugh. "In this" refers to the word "by loud laughter" (*ujjagghikāya*).
588. *Kittāvatā* means "by what measure. The connection is: "while the elders were sitting thus.
This locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). *Vavatthapeti* means he defines or explains, saying "this and that. *Ettāvatā* means "by this much measure. 590.

He says "having made motionless" and so forth because the straightening of the body by making it motionless is called "bodily exertion" (*kāyapaggaha*). The same method applies to "arm-exertion" (*bāhupaggaha*) and "head-exertion" (*sīsapaggaha*). The second chapter.
3. Khambhakatavagga-atthayojanā 596.
One who has made a support is called *khambhakata*. A "support" (*khambha*) is that which is tied or fixed.
To the question "Tied to what?", he says: "having placed his hand on his hip. One who covers or wraps around the head is called *oguṇṭhita*.
He said, "I am covered up to my head.
To show that one knee is raised for the purpose of this walking, he said, "It is called *ukkuṭikā*," and so forth. Regarding the word "here" (*ettha*), it refers to the term "*ukkuṭikāya*. 601.

Between the two types of *dussapallatthikā*—namely, the *hatthapallatthikā* and the *dussapallatthikā*—the *āyogapallatthikā* is also included within the category of *dussapallatthikā*; thus he said, "The *āyogapallatthikā* is indeed the same as the *dussapallatthikā*."
602. Regarding "the establishment of mindfulness with care," he said, "having established mindfulness.

603. "Even while giving almsfood" means even while putting the almsfood into the bowl. "Bowl-perception" (*pattasaññā*) is the perception regarding the bowl; one who possesses that is "one possessing bowl-perception" (*pattasaññī*). By the word "having done" (*katvā*), he shows that it functions as an adverbial modifier of the action.
604. Regarding "almsfood with equal curry": here, there might be a suspicion that the curry and the almsfood are in equal proportions.
He said: “‘Equal curry,’ and so forth. *Yattha* means in the alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*). The construction is as follows:
where the curry is equal in measure to one-fourth of the meal, that alms-food is called “equal curry.
*Oloṇī*, potherbs, curry ingredients, fish broth, and meat broth form a *dvanda* compound. Therein, *oloṇī* is a particular kind of sauce. *Sākasūpeyya* refers to the curry of potherbs.
“Hita-sūpeyyaṃ” means soup; “sāka-sūpeyyaṃ” means vegetable soup. By this, all varieties of vegetable soups and condiments are included.
Regarding the phrase “maccha-rasa-maṃsa-rasādīni,” the word “ādi” (etc. includes all remaining varieties of condiments.
All of that, being the essence of flavors, is called “rasaraso” (the essence of flavors).
605. *Samapuṇṇaṃ* and *samabharitaṃ* are synonyms. He said, “It is called ‘made into a stupa’ (*thūpīkato*)”, and so forth, in order to show the meaning of “the stupa was made” (*thūpaṃ kato*).
In that context means in the statement beginning with “made into a stupa. “Of them” refers to the Elder Abhaya and the Elder Cūḷanāga, who was versed in the Three Piṭakas.
The construction is: “Thus they asked, and they reported the dispute of those elders. “The elder” refers to the Elder Cūḷasumana.
“Of this” refers to the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga. “Seven times” means seven occasions. “From whom? means from which teacher.

“Therefore” means because it is delimited by what is to be used at the proper time (yāvakālika); therefore [the construction is] as follows: “whether it be food consisting of boiled rice and gruel, or various fruits.
“And that too” refers to that which has crossed the water’s edge. “But by the other,” however, means by that which does not come within the scope of formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
"But by means of the bowl": the construction is that whatever—such as cakes, sugarcane pieces, or various fruits—descends below, that is "the cakes, sugarcane pieces, and fruits.

Regarding the term *pūvavaṭaṃsaka*: here, *vaṭaṃsaka* means an ear-ornament (*uttaṃsa*). For it is called *vaṭaṃsa* because it is worn (*tasīyate*) above and used for adornment; having changed the vowel *u* to *va* and the consonant *t* to *ṭ*, that very thing is *vaṭaṃsaka*.
A particular kind of ornament worn on the head. Because it resembles a cake (*pūva*), it is called a "cake-ear-ornament" (*pūvavaṭaṃsaka*); that [is one].
A "flower-ear-ornament" (*pupphavaṭaṃsaka*) and an "ear-ornament made of *takkolaka*, *kaṭuka*-fruit, and so forth"—this is a *dvanda* compound;

those [are the two]. "Here" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). But surely, since accepting anything that has been completely covered is unallowable, the consumption [of it] would also be [unallowable]?

"It is not permissible," he said, and so forth, beginning with "But in all cases. Therein, "in all cases" means in all instances where [the objects] have been made into stūpas. This is the third chapter. 4.
Commentary on the Chapter on Thoroughness (Sakkaccavagga). 608.
Therein, "there and there" means in each respective place. "Limit" (odhi) means a boundary or demarcation.
610. *Thūpakato*: "Thūpaka" is simply "thūpa" with the suffix *-ka*; thus, showing that it means "from the thūpaka," he said "from the summit (*matthakato*). 611. *Māghātasamayādīsu*:

"Māghāta" is so called because kings cause the drum to be beaten there with the proclamation, "Do not kill living beings. That very time is the "māghāta-time. By the word "etc. (*ādi*)," other concealed reasons for slaughter should be understood.
615. *Tesam*: [This refers to] "the peacock eggs and the chicken eggs. The Fourth Chapter.
5. *Kabaḷavagga-atthayojanā* 617.

Regarding the phrase “the mouth-door,” it is stated as “the mouth-door when not brought [to the lips]” in order to show the connection between the action of “not bringing” and the action of “I shall open.
618. “The entire hand” is said with reference to the five fingers.
619. Regarding the phrase *sakabaḷena*: here, by the word *kabaḷa* (mouthful), all causes for the incompleteness of speech are to be understood. 620.

In the expressions *piṇḍukkhepakaṃ* and so forth, the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of repetition (*vicchatti*). Thus he says: "having thrown up morsels, having thrown up morsels. By the word *tvā*, he shows that it functions as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kiriyāvisesanabhāvaṃ*). 624.
By the word *avakiritvā* ("having scattered"), he shows that in the expression *sitthāvakārakaṃ*, it is the root *kir* preceded by the prefix *ava* that is intended, and not the root *kar*.
626. "Capucapū" means making such a sound; "capucapū" means an imitative noise. This is the fifth chapter. 627.
"Surusurū" means making such a sound; "surusurū" means an imitative noise. "Davanaṃ" means playing.
In this sense of the word, he said, "A jest is called *dava*," explaining: "*Dava* is a term for a jest. "That" refers to that *dava*;
here there is a reversal of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). The connection is: "it should not be done, it should not be done.
"*Silakabuddho*" means a Buddha made of stone, or a Buddha associated with stone; "*apaṭibuddho*" means an unawakened Buddha—this is a term used in jest.
*Godhammo* means the nature of cows. *Ajadhammo* means the nature of goats. *Migasaṅgho* means a herd of deer.
*Pasusaṅgho* means a herd of cattle. 628.
The word *bhuñjantena* (by one eating) functions as the agent of the state expressed by the word *nillehitun* (to lick up).
“Evaṃnāmako” means that the palace has such a name as “Kokanuda”; thus it is called by that name, and [the phrase refers to] that palace.
By the expression “padumasaṇṭhāno” (lotus-shaped), he shows how the palace received the name “Kokanuda” through its resemblance to a lotus.
“Tenā” means because of its lotus-shape. “Assā” means of the palace. “Puggalikampi” means even that which belongs to another person should be taken.
“Even his own property”: because it is taken separately as belonging to the individual himself. “Even a water-jar (*saṅkha*)”: even a water-jar for drinking. “Even a bowl (*sarāva*)”:
even a bowl for drinking water. “Even a dish (*thālaka*)”: even a dish for drinking water. 632.

Regarding the statement “having lifted up,” which is expressed in general terms, it is said “the grains from the water” in order to show the objects and the source of the action. “Having broken”: having reduced them to powder and fragments. “Outside”: outside of the inner house.
634. Regarding the phrase *setacchattaṃ*: here, the word *seta* is a synonym for *paṇḍara* (white), which is why he says "white umbrella" (*paṇḍaracchattaṃ*).
"Enveloped with cloth" (*vatthapaliguṇṭhitaṃ*) means wrapped all around with cloths. A white umbrella is a *setacchatta*. An umbrella made of *kiḷañja* grass is a *kiḷañjacchatta*.
An umbrella made of leaves is a *paṇṇacchatta*. That which is bound in a circle is *maṇḍalabaddha*.
"Bound by tally-sticks" (*salākabaddha*) means bound with tally-sticks. "Those" refers to the three umbrellas. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. The construction is:
"even that which is a single-leaf umbrella. "Among these" refers to the three umbrellas. "Of him" refers to anyone at all, whether a householder or one who has gone forth.
"He" refers to whoever it may be, a householder or one who has gone forth. "Or from the umbrella-stand" (*chattapādukāya*) means from the place where the umbrella-handle is set down.
"Or with a sandal. "In this" means in this training rule (sikkhāpada).
"Of medium size" means of medium measurement. By the phrase "measuring four cubits," he shows that a staff shorter or longer than four cubits is not called a "staff.
He says, "in the same manner as already stated," pointing out the etymological meaning: "that which has a staff in the hand is [a staff-bearer]."
636. Regarding the phrase “one with a weapon in hand,” since it is specifically the sword that is intended here, he says “a sword.

*Asi* means a blade. 637. Showing that the statement in the Pāḷi, “A weapon (*āvudha*) is called a bow (*cāpa*) or a *kodaṇḍa*,” is merely illustrative, he says “regarding ‘one with a weapon in hand,’ etc.
The construction is: all varieties of bows should be understood as weapons.
Just as one who stands having girded his sword does not come to be designated as "sword-in-hand," so too, one with a bow slung around the neck is not called "weapon-in-hand";
therefore, he says "but if... and so forth. By this, he shows that only when a weapon is actually grasped by the hand is one called "weapon-in-hand. The sixth chapter.
7. Pādukavagga-atthayojanā 638.
"A finger's breadth" (*aṅgulantara*) means the space between the toes. "Shoes" (*pādukā*) refers to a specific kind of footwear.

For it is called "shoes" (*pādukā*) because one goes by means of them (*pajjate*); they may consist of many layers or be made of leather or wood. "Having put on" (*paṭimuñcitvā*) means having fastened the shoes.
640. "Taken by two people" is the connection. "By means of a bamboo" means by means of a reed; "seated in a vehicle" is the connection.
"Having dismantled" means having brought about ruin. "Both" refers to both persons, namely the preacher of the Dhamma and the receiver of the Dhamma.
"It is appropriate" means it is appropriate to preach.
641. *Sayanagatassa* means "one who has gone to a bed"; the meaning is "one who is lying down on a bed. The connection is that it is not permissible to teach the Dhamma to one who is lying down. 642.
Showing that it is not permissible to teach the Dhamma to one sitting in any of the three types of cross-legged postures (*pallatthikā*), he said, "In a cross-legged posture," and so forth.
643. The construction is: "to one whose head is wrapped" such that, when it is wrapped, the hairline is not visible.
Because *chapaka* and *caṇḍāla* are synonyms, it is said, “of a *caṇḍāla*.
For one who cooks a dog (*saṃ-sunakhaṃ pacati*) is called a *chapaka*, with the letter *s* changed to *ch*. This woman belonging to a *chapaka* is a *chapakī*, that is, the wife of a *caṇḍāla*.
Regarding the word “wherein” (*yattha*), he says “who indeed,” because the suffix *-tra* is used here in the sense of identity (*paccatte*).
The statement, "A king who, having sat upon a high throne, shall master the mantras," implies that such a king is exceedingly unrighteous (*adhammika*).
Regarding the phrase "all this" (*sabbaṃ idaṃ*), he says "all this" (*sabbo ayaṃ*) because the word *idaṃ* undergoes a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
By the word "world" (*loka*), he shows the scope of the term "here" (*idha*). The word "last" (*carima*) is a synonym for "final" (*antima*). "Final" (*antima*)...
And it is called *lāmaka*. Here, *lāmaka* means misfortune (*vipatti*); thus he says "confusion" (*saṅkara*). "Confusion" refers to misfortune.
By the word "without distinction" (*nimmariyāda*), he shows the intended meaning of the phrase "fallen into confusion. "Gone to the end" (*carimagata*) means having reached the finality;
the meaning is that this entire world has gone to its end. And here, as well as in certain manuscripts of the Jātaka, [it is so read].
The reading “camarikata” exists, but it is indeed incorrect. “Tattheva” means right there at the foot of the mango tree.
“Tesam” refers to the king and the brahmin. “Tattha” means in this verse. “Pāḷiyā” means by the text (pāḷi) reckoned as the book that elucidates one’s own conduct.
Regarding “na passare,” the word *re* here is a suffix (*antissa kāriyo*), thus he says “na passantī. “Yo cāyam” means “and whoever this [person] is.”
The word *ayaṃ* is used merely as an ornament for the verse; its meaning is "this. *Ajjhāyati* means "he studies," which is to say, "he trains.
*Tato* connects with "after" (*paraṃ*) from the verse spoken by the Bodhisatta. *Tassa* refers to the verse. *Bho* is an address to the Bodhisatta.
To reveal that the word *bhutto* functions as the object of the verb, it is stated: "*mayā*" (by me). *Assa* refers to the rice (*odana*).
By this [phrase], he shows the external compound *sucimaṃsūpasecana* as meaning "that which has pure, thoroughly purified meat as its sauce (*upasevana*).
Regarding *dhamme*, it means in the sense of proper conduct (*ācāra-dhamma*). *Baddho hutvā* means having become stiff;
or rather, this very reading (*baddho*) is the correct one. To exclude other meanings such as shape for the word *vaṇṇa*, it is stated as "praised" (*pasattha*).
*Thomito* is a synonym for that very same thing. *Atha* means "thereupon" (in the sequence).
*Taṃ* refers to the brahmin. *Tassa* refers to the two verses. *Brāhmaṇa* is used as a vocative addressing the chaplain.
*Sampati* means "in the present" (*sandīṭṭhike*). Regarding the connection between the words: "That livelihood which [comes] from falling into ruin, or from practicing unrighteousness."
It is said “he lies down” in order to show this.
Regarding the term “Mahābrahmā,” since the word *brahmā* here denotes a brahmin, he says “great brahmins. Regarding “others as well,” this means others besides the royal brahmins.
When it is said “they cook,” because of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the meaning “they eat” must also be understood; thus he says “they cook.”
"And they eat. By the words "not only" (*na kevalam*) and so forth, he shows that the particle *pi* (also/even) here has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍanattha*).
The connection is: "you will practice. Again, *tvam* is the accusative case used in the sense of the dative;
it is to be connected with the word "do not split" (*mā bhidā*). By the word "stone" (*pāsāṇo*), he shows that the term *asma* is a synonym for stone (*pāsāṇapariyāyo*).
"Tenā" means by way of the cause of schism.
(648) "It should not be told" is said with reference to asking about one's own points of doubt.
(649) "With an equal yoke" (samadhurena) means with an equal yoke; the meaning is "with an equal mouth."
