652. The construction is: "whether it goes by way of the root or by way of the branch. "In the trunk" means in the trunk of the tree.
"It issues forth" means that feces and urine issue forth. "A grass mat" (tiṇaṇḍupaka) means a mat made of grass or consisting of grass.
"In this" refers to the context of feces, urine, and saliva.
653. To show what water is intended, it is said: "only water for use. This concludes the seventh chapter.
"Therein" means among the training rules (*sekhiya*). Regarding "concealing the curry and condiments": one conceals the curry and condiments with rice. The training rules are completed. 8.
The application of the meaning of the seven methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).
"655. *Saṅkhyāparicchedo* means 'delimitation by number. *Tesam* refers to the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
*Tassa* refers to those [texts] consisting of the Khandhakas and Parivāra. *Tattheva* means in those very Khandhakas and Parivāras.
*Sabbattha* means in all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)."
Thus ends the *Yojanā* (Exegesis) on the Commentary on the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga* within the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya,
recited by me under the name Jādilañchita for the sake of many.
Excellent! The method of exposition for the Mahāvibhaṅga is complete.
This concludes the Exposition of the Meaning of the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, Chapter 1: The Section on the Pārājika Offenses.
Having thus established the method of exposition for the *Bhikkhu-vibhaṅga*, I shall now establish the method of exposition for the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*.
*Yo*: This is the analysis (*vibhaṅga*). *Vibhaṅgassa*: Of that which has an analysis. *Assa*: It is. *Tassa*: Of that, namely, of the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*.
"Yato" means "because. Here, however, the construction is as follows:

since the turn has arrived for the commentary on that *vibhaṅga* of the nuns which would have been compiled immediately after the *vibhaṅga* of the monks, therefore, first of all, in order to provide a word-by-word explanation of the previously unexplained terms of that *vibhaṅga* of the nuns, [the author begins] with the *pārājika* offenses.
“This is the commentary. *Apubbapadavaṇṇanā* means the commentary on words not previously [explained]; that [is what follows].
Regarding the first *pārājika* training rule: “By him... [etc.

...Sāḷha,” here the word “herein” (*ettha*) is to be supplied as a textual remainder (*pāṭhaseso*) and connected [to the following]. Among those things designated as substance, quality, action, genus, and name—
In order to show that among the five types of sounds, the sound of a name (*nāmasadda*) is the sound of "Sāḷha," it was said:
"Sāḷha is his name. "Of Migāramātā" means of Visākhā; for she is called Migāramātā because she was placed by the merchant Migāra in the position of a mother.
To show that she oversees new construction work (*navakamma*), he said: "The overseer of new construction. [Regarding the phrase] "by wisdom..."
By the phrase "endowed with," it is shown that *paṇḍā* refers to wisdom (*paññā*); thus, the meaning of the word "wise" (*paṇḍita*) is demonstrated as one in whom that [wisdom] has arisen.
Regarding "by proficiency" (*veyyattikena*): one who is distinguished (*viyatta*) is so called because he specifically (*visesena*) is known (*añjati*) or becomes manifest;

such a person is a *viyatta*, and his state is *veyyattika*, which is knowledge. By this [knowledge], the distinction between the wisdom referred to as "*paṇḍā*" and the wisdom referred to as "*medhā*" is indicated.

To show this, it is said: “In the grasping of the Pāḷi,” and so forth. For the wisdom (paññā) called “medhā” has a distinction from the wisdom called “paṇṭā” because it is accompanied by mindfulness (sati).
The compound “tatrupāyāya” is an aluttasamāsa (a compound without elision), as in “tatramajjhattatā” and other such cases.
By the word “kammesu,” he shows the scope of the pronoun *tad*. [The phrase] “by the investigation of duties to be performed” refers to those duties that ought to be done.
For the purpose of investigation. By the word *ca*, he indicates that the phrase "done and not done" (*katākata*) is a compound (*dvandava*).

Regarding "in the place of distribution" (*parivesanaṭṭhāne*): it is called a "place of distribution" (*parivesana*) because people enter (*pavisanti*) or go into it (*visanti*) there in order to eat;

that very place is the "place of distribution," and [it refers to] therein. Regarding "in the corner" (*nikūṭe*): showing that it is a space devoid of a peak (*kūṭa*)—that is, a summit—he says, "resembling a corner."
"Having been shown as profound. He says "the word *vippakāra*" because the prefix *vi-* denotes transformation (*vikāra*) and the word *sara* denotes sound (*sadda*).
"A foot" (*caraṇa*) is that by which one moves; she who has arisen [with a disease] in that [foot] is "one with a foot-disease," which he shows by saying "possessed of a disease of the feet."
657. By the word “tintā,” it is shown that here the term *avassuta* refers specifically to the sense of being “soiled” (*kilinna*), and not in any other sense.

“*Assā*” refers to the phrase “*avassutā*. The connection is with the words “stated in the word-commentary” (*padabhājane vuttaṃ*). “Therein” (*tattha*) means in the word-commentary. The construction is:
“just as cloth is dyed by various colors, so too she is thoroughly dyed by the passion for physical contact.”
“Endowed with longing (*apekkhā*)”: by this, he shows the meaning as “possessing longing,” in the sense that she has longing for him.
Showing that her mind is bound to him, he says, “as if having placed her mind in bondage. “Also in the analysis of the second term”:
even in the commentary on the second term, “one who is lustful (*avassuta*). [This refers to] the word *puggala* (person).

Because the word *puruṣa* expresses a commonality with the [other] seven, he qualifies it with the word *puruṣa*. The phrase "below the collarbones" (*adhobbhakkhakānam*) is stated in order to show that the particles (*nipāta*) are to be compounded with the genitive case.
One might ask: "Is it not the case that just as 'below the collarbones' is stated here, so too should it be stated in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*)?
Why is it not stated there? To this he says: "In the word-analysis," and so forth. "According to the sequence of the words" (*padapaṭipāṭiyā*).
“Below” (*adho*) and “the collarbone” (*akkhaka*) refer to these terms in their respective order. “Therein” (*ettha*) means: in the regions below the collarbone and above the kneecaps.

“By the common *pārājika* offenses” (*sādhāraṇapārājikehi*) means: by those *pārājika* offenses common to both monks and nuns. “A mere name” (*nāmamattaṃ*) means: nothing more than the name itself. 659.

“Thus” (*evaṃ*) is connected with the phrase “having analyzed according to this canonical text” (*imāya pāḷiyā vibhajitvā*). “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the statement beginning with “when both are emitting semen” (*ubhato-avassute*).
The reading “*ubhato-avassute*” is indeed the original text itself; it was stated as “*ubhato-avassuteti ubhato avassute*” by making a distinction to show that there is no other [reading].

Here, in the word “*ubhato*,” it was stated—“*of both the nun and the man*”—to demonstrate both the form of the word *ubha* and the occurrence of the particle *to* in the sense of the genitive case. In that context, by the words “nun” and “man,”...
It shows that both have the same form. By the two words “yā” (which) and “sa” (she), the sense of the genitive case is expressed by the suffix *to*;

the meaning is: "when both are in a state of lust. He says "in a state of lust" (*avassutabhāve*) because it should be understood that the abstract sense (*bhāvattha*) is conveyed even without an abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*).
"In whatever way they are delimited" means: "below the collarbone, above the kneecaps," and so forth, according to each respective [limit].
"By one who is delimited. "Of herself" means of the bhikkhunī. "Or of him" means of the man. "Even here" means even when there is touching of the body with what is connected to the body.
"Therein" means among those monks and bhikkhunīs. The intention is that she is not to be charged [with an offense], because it has not been stated, "She should consent to bodily contact.
"Even without moving" means even without shaking; the word *pi* (even) has the sense of inclusion, by which [it is implied] that she is also [charged] if she moves.
"Pagevā" indicates "at that very moment. "But when this is so" means: but when she is enduring it by means of the mind alone.
"The state of being originated by action" refers to the fact that this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is originated by action.

"By way of predominance" means by way of its frequent origination in that particular action, as in the cases of "a forest-ranger" or "one who dwells on the battlefield," and so forth. "It" refers to that state of being originated by action.
660. *Ettha* means "in the regions above the collarbone and below the knees. 662.
Regarding the phrase *“ekato avassute”* (when one is lustful), here too the suffix *-to* expresses the sense of the genitive case.

Because even a general term can be restricted to a specific instance, and because a specific [term] need not be explicitly employed when its meaning is already implied by the context, he says: “of the nun herself.”

Therein, "tatra" refers to the statement beginning with "ekato avassute. By the phrase "tathaiva," it extends by implication the meaning that one is "avassuta" (lustful) through lust for bodily contact.
"Catūsu" means in the four [offenses] reckoned as: lust for sexual intercourse, lust for bodily contact, affection arising from laughter, and pure-minded affection. "Yattha" means in which place.
663. "Or for one who does not know whether this is a man or a woman" means "or for one who is uncertain.
This is the first [case]. 2. The Second Pārājika Training Rule. 664.

Regarding the second [rule], in the phrase "kacci no sā," the word *no* has the sense of the particle *nu*; thus he says, "kacci nu sā. "Failure of the retinue" (*parivāra-vipatti*)... [text continues]

The destruction of one’s retinue. Regarding the term “disrepute” (*akitti*), it is stated “or blame behind one’s back” (*parammukhagarahā*) in order to show that while “blame” (*ayasa*) refers to censure received in one’s presence, this refers to censure received in one’s absence.
By the phrase “she who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense,” [the commentary] shows the referent of the pronoun “she” (*sā*) in the expression “or she. Of the four...
This genitive case ending is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); the meaning is "among the four. "After" means after all the *pārājika* rules.
"In this place" means in the position situated between the first and third *pārājikas*. "Laid down" means placed by the compilers of the Council. "Here" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"There" refers to the training rule concerning grave offenses (*duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada*). This is the second [section].
3. The Third Pārājika Training Rule. 669.
Regarding the third [rule], the phrase "in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya" refers to the words *dhammena vinayena*. The connection is that the word-commentary has been stated.
To show that both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvana*) constitute the Teacher’s instruction, he said: "The motion... [etc.]..."

"And by means of accomplishment" (*sampadāya*): "by the Teacher’s instruction" (*satthusāsanena*) means by the Teacher’s command (*āṇā*). "Formal act" (*kamma*) refers to an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "does not accept the word," as in such expressions, "does not accept the Saṅgha" means he does not comply;

thus he says "does not comply" (*nānuvattati*), for here "not accepting" is simply non-compliance. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among the Saṅgha and so forth. This, first of all, is "living together" (*saṃvāsa*). Together with...
“Living together” (*saṃvāsa*) means that monks dwell there; in this sense, it refers to living together through such acts as performing formal legal acts (*ekakamma*).

By the phrase “by way of moving together,” he shows the etymological meaning of *sahāya* (companion): they move or proceed together, thus they are companions. “By them” means by those monks. “And with whom” means with those monks.
“Of him” means of the one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*). “By him” means by the one who has been suspended. “Of himself” means of the one who has been suspended. This is the third [section].
4. The Fourth Pārājika Training Rule. 675.
In the fourth [rule], those who are "lecherous" (*avassuta*) through lust for sexual intercourse are not intended; rather, those who are lecherous through lust for physical contact are intended.
Thus it says, "lecherous through lust for physical contact. The phrase "of a male person" (*purisapuggalassa*) is not to be construed with the word "hand" (*hattha*).
Showing that it must be connected with the word "seizing" (gahaṇa) itself, he said: "That which by a man," and so forth.
Regarding "that," he said "also other [acts]" and so forth, because the statement "taking by the hand" is merely an illustration.
Therein, "also other" means other than taking by the hand. "In a case not constituting an offense of defeat" (apārājikakkhette) means above the navel and below the knees.
“Assā” means of the phrase “taking by the hand. “Ettha” means in the phrase “for the purpose of engaging in unrighteous conduct.
“Kāyasaṃsaggo” means bodily contact itself; therefore it is said, “not sexual intercourse. “Hi” means truly, or because.
“Ettha” refers to the mention of bodily contact. “Sādhakaṃ” means an indicator.
“Tissitthīyo” (three women) is an accusative case used in the sense of a locative. For the meaning is “in three women,” or it should be construed as “having approached three women.
The same method applies to the following cases as well. The construction is: “whatever sexual intercourse exists, that he does not practice.
Regarding “na seveyya,” it means “he does not practice”; for the letter *t* becomes *e*. “Tayo purise” means “in three men.”

"Having approached them": this is to be construed as "having approached those three who are reckoned as ignoble—namely, the *ubhatobyañjanaka* (those with both sexual organs) and the *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs)—and having approached them. "And he does not practice sexual intercourse with his own organ":
he does not practice sexual intercourse with his own [sexual] mark. This was said with reference to the *anuloma-pārājika* (the retrogressive offense of defeat). "Chejjaṃ" (cutting off).
"By reason of sexual intercourse" means that because of the act of sexual intercourse there might be a cutting off; the meaning is that it would become a *pārājika* offense.
"By those skilled" means by those clever in answering questions, or by those desiring cleverness. This question was stated with reference to the eight bases (*aṭṭhavatthuka*).
It is called a "sweat-inducing verse" because it causes perspiration in those who reflect upon it for the purpose of answering the question. "It is contradicted" means...
By the statement “not sexual intercourse,” the statement “there may be cutting off on account of sexual intercourse” is contradicted;
the meaning is that it does not accord. If one should say this, [the reply is: it is not contradicted. Why?

Because it is the preliminary stage to sexual intercourse—this is the construction. By this, it is shown that bodily contact, being the preliminary stage to sexual intercourse, is figuratively designated there by the term “sexual intercourse.”
This indicates that it was not spoken regarding the "pairing of two by two. The particle *hi* serves to indicate expansion (*vitthāra*). The connection is: "They were spoken only in the *Parivāra*.
"Praise and blame" refers to sexual intercourse (*sukkavisaṭṭhi*). "Causing the acquisition of wealth" refers to acting as a go-between (*sañcaritta*).
"By this method" means by this pretext or by way of proximity. "By this means" refers to the phrase "he should consent to the grasping of the hand."
By the method already stated. "In all instances" means in all such passages as "he should consent to the grasping of the corner of the outer robe," and so forth.

"Api ca" (but also) means "certainly"; the intention is: "I shall state a specific distinction. By the phrase "a place of such a name," he clarifies the meaning of the expression "this place has such a name for this [person]."

676. In the phrase "it blows every other day" (*ekantarikāya vāti*), the word "or" (*vā*) includes "every second day" (*dvantarikā*) and so forth. "By this or that" (*yena tena*) means "by whichever [means] or by that [means].
The two, three, four, five, or six bases should be understood either through the use of the elipsis (*peyyāla*) or by the word "or.

Furthermore, the phrase "api ca" (moreover) implies: "In addition to this, I shall state further particulars. Regarding the word "here" (*ettha*): it refers to the expression "having confessed the offenses" (*āpattiyo desetvā*).
Regarding the word *vacane*: *hi* means "truly. *Vuttaṃ* means "stated in the Parivāra. *Tattha* refers back to the preceding statement. The construction is:
"the offense taught there is subject to counting. The construction is: "a bhikkhunī who has fallen into one matter.
"Having made a renunciation of the burden" means having made a renunciation of the burden [of the offense] by thinking, "I shall not fall into this matter, nor into any other matter."
"But she who teaches while still having the intention [to continue]"—this is the construction. The fourth [section].
"Common" means common with the bhikkhunīs. "In this" refers to the statement beginning with "The rules have been recited, noble ladies.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The application of the commentary on the section on the Pārājika offenses in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is completed.
2. The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses:
1. Application of the Meaning of the First Saṅghādisesa Training Rule.
"Pārājikānantarassa" means "of that which is placed immediately after the Pārājikas," or "of the Saṅghādisesa section"; this is the connection [to be made].

The construction is as follows: "This commentary on the meaning of words not [previously] explained (anuttāna) will now take place at this time. This is a commentary on the meaning of those words whose meanings have not been explained.

678. Regarding the first [term], he says, “*Udosita* means a storehouse,” showing that it is called *udosita* in the sense of being “covered with water,” because water was stored there and it was constructed as a covering.
For here, the word *uda-* is a synonym for water; thus, the connection [of the prefix *ut-*, which implies emergence,] is indeed not appropriate.
“Storehouse” (*bhaṇḍasālā*) refers to a hall for storing goods such as vehicles and the like. “Speak falsely” (*accāvadatha*).
Here, the prefix *ati* has the sense of "transcending," while the prefix *ā* conforms to the meaning of the verbal root; thus he says, "speak having transcended.
(679) Speaking by way of arrogance is "arrogant speech" (*ussayavāda*); showing that this very thing is "one who speaks arrogantly" (*ussayavādikā*), he says, "arrogant speakers," and so forth.
By the phrase "by way of arrogance of pride and by way of arrogance of anger," he shows the divisions of arrogance. "She" refers to the one who speaks arrogantly.
*Atthato* means according to its own form (*sarūpato*). *Ettha* refers to the word-commentary (*padabhājane*).

Taking *aḍḍa* as "the act of challenging" (*abhiyuñjana*), the challenge between two people becomes a matter for adjudication by judges; therefore it is said: "The term *aḍḍa* refers to the adjudication of judges.
[In this case] only the third syllable, *ja*, is the head-letter (*muddhaja*). *Yaṃ* refers to the challenge (*aḍḍa*). *Yattha* means in whatever place whatsoever.
"Legal experts" (*vohārikā*) means those who know the legal proceedings of two litigants; they are the judges. "Between two people" means between two people who are litigants.
"Whoever" means either the litigant or anyone else. "In this case" refers to the statement beginning with "he informs one [of them].
"Wherever" is connected to the phrase "even when he has come to any place whatsoever. "Then" means afterwards. "She" refers to the bhikkhunī. "He" refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*).

The word "by the kappiyakāraka" (the one who makes things allowable) is the causative construction (*kāritakamma*) for the word "causes to be told. "Therein" refers to among the kappiyakārakas and others.

It is connected with the phrase "done by judges. "Gone to its destination" means that which has been reached after a long time. "Previously heard" means heard before. "Then" means precisely because it was previously heard.
"They" refers to the judges; it is connected with the verb "giving."
"First" means prior to the formal admonition (*samanubhāsanā*). "Offense" (*āpatti*) means the act of falling into it.

"Of this" refers to the *saṅghādisesa*. "This indeed" means this very one; the sense is "this which is about to be explained. "In this" refers to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). "Together with the transgression of the matter" (*saha vatthujjhācārā*):

[this is] with the transgression of the matter; it is a syntactical compound, not a grammatical compound. "Transgression of the matter" (*vatthujjhācārā*) is an ablative expression used in the sense of the instrumental case.
It must be seen. Therefore it was said: "together with the transgression of the matter. "A bhikkhunī" means a bhikkhunī who has fallen into an offense.
"From the Saṅgha" means from the community of bhikkhunīs. Since the word *anīya* expresses the agent of the cause, he said:

"it is to be sent away (*nissāraṇīyo*), thus it is an offense entailing sending away. It is called "entailing sending away" because one is sent away from the community of bhikkhunīs by means of it, or because one is caused to be sent away.

The sense of the instrumental case is also appropriate here. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). "It" (*yaṃ*) refers to the *saṅghādisesa* offense. "He" (*so*) refers to the *saṅghādisesa*.

The meaning of the word-commentary should be understood through the metaphorical application of the cause (*kāraṇopacāra*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "By anyone" (*kenaci*) refers to a person; it is connected with "is not expelled" (*na nissārīyati*).
"By that factor" (*tena dhammena*) means by that which has become the instrument (*karaṇabhūta*) or the cause (*hetubhūta*). "It" (*so*) refers to that factor.

The construction is: "being spoken to by the men who were building the house. "They lie down" means of their own accord. "From that" refers to the departure; it connects with "further. Or, the construction is: "let him report what was done by the nun.

"Dhammika" means endowed with the Dhamma, that is, with its essential nature. "Yathā" means in whatever manner. "Taṃ" refers to that manner. "Tattha" refers to the statement: "he points it out indiscriminately.
"Deceivers and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," thieves and others are included. "Sā" refers to the pointing out. "Taṃ" refers to the pointing out. "Tesam" refers to...
"Of village boys and so forth. "A fine" means a monetary fine. "There is a debt" means there is an obligation. "Even when there is an intention" is the construction [of the sentence].
"Of him" means of one who practices improper conduct.
"Merely" means exclusively. "That" refers to protection. "In the case of the perpetrator" means in the case of the one who commits the misconduct. "Of them" means of the perpetrators.
“Tesam” means “of those who take away. By the phrase “through a desire for their harm,” he shows that there is no fault when it is spoken out of fear and so forth.
“Hi” indicates that a fault has been incurred. Regarding the statement, “It is proper to speak to one who carries out one’s own instructions...”:
since it is said that one will accept one’s word, even if the person does not accept the word and takes up a staff, there is no fault, because taking up a staff is prohibited.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "slaves, slave-girls, ponds, etc.," fields and so forth are included.
"In the same manner as stated" means precisely by the method stated when explaining with reference to the past.
By the phrase "for the sake of non-doing in the future," he shows the specific explanation with reference to the future. Regarding the question, "By whom was this done?"—with reference to the past—
He asks about what was previously done. In the phrase "sāpi," the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*).
In the word *hi*, *hi* means "truth" or "because. The connection is: "the judges punish. "Punish" means they issue an order by way of either corporal punishment or a fine.
And in the phrase "yo cāyaṃ," *yo ca ayaṃ* means "and this which. Whatever method has been stated for the nuns, that same method applies to the monks as well.

The exposition (*yojanā*). In order to expand upon the statement, "This is the same method," he said, "A bhikkhunī also," and so forth. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he refers by extension to the term "specifically designated" (*odissa*).
"And those" (*te ca*) means those judges. "For" (*hi*) means truly, or because. First. 2.
The second *saṅghādisesa* training rule.
682. In the second [verse], *vara* means that which is to be chosen or desired; showing that this very thing is called *varabhaṇḍa*, he says "valuable goods" (*mahagghabhaṇḍa*).

By the words "pearls" (*muttā*) and so forth, he shows its specific nature. 683. The word *loka* preceded by *ā-* has the sense of looking toward (*abhimukhaṃ lokana*); preceded by *upa-*, it has the sense of looking upward (*uddhaṃ lokana*); preceded by *opa-*, it has the sense of looking downward (*adho lokana*);
preceded by *vi-*, it has the sense of looking here and there or surveying (*vītiharaṇa-lokana*); and preceded by *apa-*, it has the sense of taking leave (*āpucchanattha*).
But here, because it has not been mentioned previously, it is for the purpose of seeking permission; thus he says, "without having asked permission.
Regarding the phrases "the Malla-gaṇa," "the Bhaṭiputta-gaṇa," and so forth: the Malla-gaṇa is a group devoted to Nārāyaṇa. The Bhaṭiputta-gaṇa is a group devoted to Kumāra.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), other groups capable of governing villages and towns are also included. Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows:]
“Mallagaṇa” means the group of Mallarāja kings; for they, having formed a confederacy, ruled the kingdom in Kusinārā, and it is with reference to them that the term “Mallagaṇa” is used.

“Bhaṭiputtagaṇa” is another synonym for the Licchavi confederacy. For the former kings of the Licchavis were the sons of a matted-hair ascetic named Bhaṭi, and the lineage continued through their descendants.

Even now, the Licchavi kings are called "sons of Bhaṭi. However, because the ascetic Jaṭila rescued the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī as they were being carried away by the river current, brought them to his own hermitage, and acted as their protector and nourisher, he was called "Bhaṭi.
Since they were his sons, the Licchavi clan is called "the sons of Bhaṭi. Having formed themselves into that clan, they [resided] in Vesālī.
They rule the kingdom; it is with reference to this that it is said, "the guild of hired laborers.
A "guild of the Dhamma" (dhammagana) is a group devoted to the Dhamma of the Dispensation. A "guild of perfumers" (gandhikasenī) is a group of artisans of the same caste who work with fragrances.
A "guild of clothiers" (dussikasenī) is a group of weavers of the same caste who work with cloth. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the guilds of carpenters, dyers, and so forth are included.
“Wherever wherever” means in whichever place. “Indeed” (hi) means truly. “Those very ones” refers to the groups and so forth. “Again, those” refers to the groups and so forth.
“This” refers to the statement beginning with “or a group. “In this regard” refers to among kings and others. Because asking the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha alone is the primary reason, he said:
“The Bhikkhunī-saṅgha must be asked for permission. “Kappagatika” means that which goes toward what is allowable (kappa); thus it is *kappagata*.
That [boundary] itself remains valid for an eon (*kappagatikā*).

The construction is as follows: "without having gone to the *khaṇḍasīma* (partial boundary) for some business, and while the nuns have departed for some business. "Of a group dependent on [her]" means of a group of students (*antevāsika*). "Ordaining" means conferring full admission (*upasampadā*).
The second [offense]. 3. The third Saṅghādisesa training rule.
In the third [offense], the connection is with "the mere act of crossing over with the second foot.

The place eligible for enclosure is defined as the first throw of a clod from the vicinity of the house. Showing the meaning stated in brief in detail, he says: "Moreover, in this case," and so forth.
"In this" refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Or in the vicinity" refers to the place eligible for enclosure in the case of an unenclosed village.
"From there" means from another village; the connection is that she enters either by way of a broken wall or through a gap in the enclosure.
"Those whose enclosure is connected" (*sambaddhavatikā*) refers to two villages. "The monastery" (*vihāra*) refers to the nunnery. "But from that village" means from the other village;
the connection is that the nun must stand [waiting] once she has departed from there.
“Or a proclamation” means a proclamation by people.
“People” refers to village headmen. “A certain village” means any village one might desire. “From there” means from that village.
By the question “Why? the reason for the statement “it is permissible to go to a certain village while staying [in retreat]” is provided.
He asks. He answers that question with the reply: “Because the monastery is shared by four villages.

“In which” means in whichever river. The construction is: “That river is so called because even if one crossing it has one’s inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) moistened by as much as one or two finger-breadths, it is [considered] a river.
“Dressed” means dressed in such a way that, when being worn, it covers the three circles (*timandala*).
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "For a nun who is crossing, it is an *antaravāsaka* (inner robe)"—this is the connection. "In any place whatsoever" means in whatever location.
By the phrase "If she goes by way of a bridge, there is no offense," it is shown that the offense applies only to one who is crossing on foot.
"At the time of crossing" means at the time of crossing over a river. "Traveling through the air" means traveling by means of psychic power (*iddhi*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...
It includes the back of an elephant and so forth. "Akkamantiyā" means "crossing over. "Ettha" refers to when there are two or three bhikkhunīs. "Orimatīram eva" means "only this side of the bank.
"Tameva tīraṃ" means "that very bank," namely, only this side of the bank. "Paccuttarati" means "returns and crosses over. The construction is:
"the bhikkhunī who is making [the crossing] does so. "Assā" is to be connected with "even though the bhikkhunī herself is unaware."
In this context, the word *sāmī* (master) is used in a sense of disregard. Furthermore, the particle *atha* here is a synonym for *yadi* (if);
it should be construed with the verb. Thus, the meaning is: "If he stays," or "If he does not descend. *Acchati* means "he dwells. *Hi* signifies "truly" or "indeed.
*Idha* refers to the phrase: "or should she spend one night apart [from him]."
“Having the characteristics thus stated” means having the very characteristics stated by way of the Abhidhamma method.

“But that” refers to that forest. “By that very reason” means by the cause already mentioned. “In the Commentary” means in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. “When they enter among the bhikkhunīs” is the connection;
and this locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). “Therein” means within the range of sight and the range of hearing.
The construction is as follows: "In whatever place the companion sees [the monk], that place is called the 'range of sight' (dassanūpacāra).

"Even between a cloth screen" means even when separated by a cloth screen. The construction is as follows: "In whatever place she stands... hears the sound, that place is called the 'range of hearing' (savanūpacāra).
"By the sound of those lost on the road" means by the sound of those who have become lost on the road. "By the sound of announcing the listening to the Dhamma."

The construction is as follows: "he hears the sound of her crying out 'Noble lady!'"—just as one hears the sound of someone crying out due to the noise of announcements for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, and just as one hears the sound of someone crying out due to the noise of announcing the hearing of the Dhamma.
"Saddāyantiyā" means "making a sound"; this is a nominal verb root (*nāmadhātu*). "Evarūpā" (of such a kind) [is the object].
“Like by the sound of one who has lost the way,” and so forth—such [expressions] are what is meant.
“Or having gone over to the abodes of the sectarians (titthāyatana)” means having gone to the dwelling places of the heretics (titthiya).

By this, since the word *pakkha* in the phrase “having gone over to the faction” (*pakkhasaṅkantā*) denotes an opposing side, it should be understood that only the heretics, who are the adversaries of the Teaching, are intended here.
[The Blessed One] shows this. For the sectarians are adversaries of the Teaching.
This is the third [section]. 4. The Fourth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 694.
In the fourth [rule], a stool for placing the foot is a *pādapīṭha*. A stand for placing the foot is a *pādakathalika*.
Showing [the meaning], he said, “What is called a footstool,” and so forth. Regarding the word *anaññāya*, the letter *y* here is a grammatical modification (*kāriya*) of the suffix *-tvā*;
thus he said, “without having known. Regarding *netthāravatte*: it refers to the conduct (*vatta*) that is the cause for emerging from a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*).
By the word “occurring” (*vattamāna*), he indicates by way of inference the suffix *-anta* in the word “they occur” (*vattanti*). This is the fourth [section].
5. The Fifth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 701.

Regarding the fifth [rule], in the phrase "if one is lustful on one side" (*ekato avassute*), although the word "on one side" (*ekato*) is stated generally according to the method explained below, it must be understood as referring specifically to the nun;
furthermore, the suffix *-to* functions in the sense of the genitive case within the word *avassuta*.
And in order to show the meaning of the term *bhāva*, it is said: "The lustful state of the nun is to be understood. *Etaṃ* refers to the statement "the lustful state of the nun.
*Taṃ* refers to the non-statement. *Pāḷiyā* means "by this rule of training (sikkhāpada-pāḷi).
This is the fifth [section]. 6. The sixth Saṅghādisesa training rule.
705. Regarding the sixth [offense], the suffix *-to* is used here in the sense of cause; thus he says, "because" (*yasmā*). To the question "To whom do they belong?", the construction is:
"To which nun do the instigator (*uyyojikā*) and the one instigated (*uyyojitā*) belong?
"Does not give" means the instigator does not give to the one instigated. "Does not accept" means the one instigated does not accept from the hand of the instigator. Acceptance (*paṭiggaho*).
"Therefore it does not exist": for that very reason, there is no offense for the one who receives from the hand of the one who incited [the gift].
"She incurs a grave offense, not a light one": even though this is so, the one who incited incurs only a grave offense, namely a *saṅghādisesa*, and not a light one.
"And that": and that very incurring [of the offense]. "On account of her enjoyment": on account of what is reckoned as the enjoyment of the one who incited.
This is the meaning of the verse regarding the "reasons.
But as for the other, namely the nun who has been dismissed: "the first training rule" refers to the fifth training rule.
For since the fifth training rule is similar to this one by virtue of being its counterpart, it is called "the first" with reference to this [present] rule. This is the sixth [section].
7. The Seventh Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 709.
Regarding the seventh [rule], the meaning of the term *yāvatatiyaka* (up to the third time) should be understood as the meaning of the word uttered as "yāvatatiyaka"; this is the connection.
The seventh [rule]. 8. The Eighth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule

715. Regarding the phrase "in some legal issue whatsoever" in the eighth [section], he says "of the four" because that which is being singled out (the *niddhāraṇīya*) is inseparable from the group from which it is singled out (*niddhāraṇa-samudāya*).
But why is it stated in the form of a group from which something is singled out?

Is it not the case that all four types of legal issues are mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)? To this he replies with the words "But in the word-commentary... and so forth. This concludes the eighth.
9. The Ninth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule 723.
Regarding the ninth [rule], he says “mixed” (*missībhūtā*) because the word *saṃsaṭṭha* is a synonym for being mixed.

By the phrase “in an improper manner” (*ananulomena*), he shows that in the expression “in an unsuitable manner” (*ananulomikena*), the suffix *-ika* has the sense of “that which is. [The actions include] pounding, cooking, and grinding with fragrant substances.
And stringing garlands. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), other inappropriate physical acts are included.
And conveying messages and returning messages, and acting as a go-between. By the word "and so forth," other inappropriate verbal acts are included.
These are [the offenses] of the bhikkhunīs. "Fame" means renown. The ninth [chapter].
10. The Tenth Saṅghādisesa Training Rule. 727.
Regarding the phrase *evācārā* in the tenth [rule], he says “*evaṃācārā*” because the sandhi occurs through the elision of the *niggahīta* [anusvāra].
By the words “*yādiso*,” etc., [he refers to] the eleven meanings of the word *evaṃ*, such as illustration (*nidassana*), and so forth, as found in the Abhidhānappadīpikā (verse 1186).

This shows the intended meaning. “In all places” means in all instances such as “those who speak thus, those whose world is thus. Regarding the word *uññāya*, he says “by contempt (*avaññāya*”), because here the vowel *u* is a reversal of the vowel *o*.
By the phrase “knowing by making [it] low,” he shows that the prefix *ava-* has the sense of lowness, while the verbal root *ñā* has the sense of understanding.
Although one should have said “by knowing through contempt (*paribhavaññāya*”), it is expressed [as *uññāya*] by the elision of the latter member of the compound.
Regarding the statement “by contempt,” he said, “by knowing [them] with contempt. Regarding “impatience,” here it is specifically *sahana-khanti* (endurance) that is intended;
showing that it is neither *anuloma-khanti* (conformity-patience) nor *diṭṭhi-nijjhāna-khanti* (patience through contemplation of views), he said, “by way of non-endurance.
Regarding “boastfulness,” here “boastfulness” (*vibhāsa*) means that which speaks out or shines forth in a special way, i.e., power (*ānubhāva*); thus, it means this Saṅgha possesses such power.
The word *vibhassa* possesses the sense of both multiplicity (*bahuttha*) and excellence (*atisayattha*).
Why? Because it has the suffix *-mantu*, as in the case of words such as *lomaso*; thus, it means that the Saṅgha is of great power (*bahuānubhāva*) or of preeminent power (*atisayaānubhāva*).

Due to the subsequent position of the conjunct consonant (*saṃyogapara*), the vowel *ā* is shortened. The state of being *vibhassa* is *vebhassiya*; it is precisely the state of having great power or preeminent power.
Thus, demonstrating this meaning, he said: "By way of being loud speech.
Therein, by the word *balavā*, he shows the sense of the suffix *-mantu*—which occurs in the sense of possession—as having both the sense of multiplicity and the sense of intensity;

by the word *bhāva*, he shows the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāva*) of the suffix *-ṇiya*; and by the word *ena*, he shows the state of the ablative case occurring in the sense of the instrumental. Revealing that very same meaning:
He said: "By manifesting one's own power. Therein, "one's own" (*attan*) refers to the Saṅgha, which is designated as "self.
"By manifesting power" means by manifesting great majesty, or by manifesting pre-eminent majesty. Since manifesting power in its actual sense is simply the terrifying of others, he said:

"The meaning is 'by terrifying'. Regarding the phrase "by [manifesting] weakness," the word *bhāva* here— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

It should be understood that by means of the word *ena* (in *enai*), the ablative case is shown to have the sense of the instrumental case, while the suffix *-ya* (*ṇya*) has the sense of "being" (*bhāva*).

The phrase "in all instances" (*sabbattha*) refers to all locations such as "out of contempt" (*uññāya*) and so forth. He says, "The word *ca* is indicated as elided," meaning it should be understood as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
In the word *viviccatha*, the prefix *vi-* has the sense of the word *vinā* ("without"), and the verbal root *vic-* has the sense of "existence" (*satta*).
He said, "Except for *hothā*. This is the tenth [section]. The connection is:
"having inserted immediately after. The construction is: "these three training rules have been brought from the Mahāvibhaṅga. The connection is:
"nine should be understood as offenses at the first instance (*paṭhamāpattika*). The construction is: "all these phenomena (*dhamma*). Regarding the word "here" (*ettha*):
In the passage beginning with “*Uddiṭṭhā kho*,” the phrase “*Taṃ panā*” means “as for that *pakkhamānatta* (probation for a fortnight).
Thus [ends the section] in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* of the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The exposition of the commentary on the Seventeen [Khandhakas] is completed.
3. The Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa). 1. Exposition of the Meaning of the First Offense of Expiation involving Forfeiture (Paṭhamanissaggiyapācittiya-sikkhāpada-atthayojanā).
The construction is as follows: "Of those thirty *nissaggiya* rules which have been proclaimed by the Blessed One for the bhikkhunīs, this is now the sequence of the commentary at this time.
Regarding the first rule, "a shop for vessels" (*āmattikāpaṇa*): here, the word *āmatta* is a synonym for a vessel; thus he says "vessels" (*bhājanāni*).
For vessels are called "vessels" (*amattāni*) because they "measure" (*amanti*), that is, they come to be used. They are "measured" (*amattāni*).
To show the meaning of the word *āmattika* (“selling”), he says “those,” and so forth. “Of them” means of the *āmattikas*. “That” means the *āmattika* shop.

(734) By the word “store” (*sannidhi*), he shows that the root *ci*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, has the sense of “accumulating. The particle *hi* indicates a specific distinction. “Therein” refers to the Mahāvibhaṅga; “here” refers to the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.
*Idampi*: this refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The word *pi* (also) refers back to the training rule in the Mahāvibhaṅga. First [section]. 2.
The second Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule. 738.

Regarding the second [rule], even in the case of unwashed cloth (*ahata-cola*), when it is soiled with sweat, dirt, and the like, it is described as "worn-out cloth" (*jiṇṇa-cola*) because of its unsightly state. By the phrase "even, noble lady" (*api ayyāhi*), he precludes the alternative word-analysis "away, noble lady" (*apa ayyāhi*).
740. “All this is robe-cloth” is the construction. “Thus obtained” means obtained after having thus relinquished it.

“In the very same manner as it was given” means it should be applied to that very gift; the meaning is that it should be included among the non-seasonal robes (*akālacīvara*). This is the second [section].
3. The Third Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule. 743.

Regarding the third [rule], he says, “*Handā* means ‘take it’,” because the word *handā* is a particle used in the sense of an exhortation (*vavassagga*). The connection is with the phrase “many items subject to relinquishment” (*bahūni nissaggiyāni*). “Having gathered together” (*saṃharitvā*) means having collected them individually.
This is the third. 4. The Fourth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule.
748. Regarding the fourth [case], he says "by means of the price" (*mūlena*) because "price" (*kaya*) has the verbal sense of "that by which one buys.

"She" refers to Thullanandā; the connection is with the phrase "it is said. Since the root *ñā* has the sense of "understanding," he says "or having requested" (*yācitvā vā*) to show that the root *ñā* can also have the sense of "requesting."
752. “All the oil, etc. means that very same oil, etc. “In pairs” means having made the oil and the rest into a pair.
“By the physician” means by the healer (*bhisakka*). For he is called a physician (*vejjā*) because he knows the science (*vijjā*) reckoned as the measure of life;
and he is also called a physician because he finds (*vidati*)—that is, knows—the disease, its cause, and the medicine. “From him” means from the physician.
The reason for stating it [thus] is as follows: "Of a kahāpaṇa" means "by means of a kahāpaṇa"; the connection is that it was "brought. This is the fourth [section]. 5.

The Fifth Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule 753. In the fifth [rule], *sāti* refers to a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*). *Ayaṃ* refers to this trainee nun. *Addhā* means "certainly" or "absolutely. Regarding the word "having caused to be bought" (*cetāpetvā*), since the word *citi* here has the sense of "knowing," he says "having caused to be made known. This is the fifth.
6. The Sixth Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule 758.
Regarding the sixth [rule], in order to show the meaning of the term *chandaka* as "that which is taken after having generated a desire," he said:

"a *chandaka*," and so forth. *Dhammakicca* means a meritorious deed (*puññakaraṇīya*). Here, the word *dhamma* is a synonym for merit. *Yaṃ* refers to the object (*vatthu*). *Paresaṃ* means... [of others].
"By oneself for others. "This" means this name, "Chandaka. By the phrase "given for the sake of another," it shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*):
"the purpose of another is *aññadattha*"; the letter *da* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). That which is given for that purpose is *aññadatthika*.
By the phrase "given having designated another," it shows that what is given having designated another is *aññuddisika*.

It shows the meaning of the word. By the phrase “given up to the Saṅgha,” it shows the meaning of the word *saṅghika* (belonging to the Saṅgha) as that which has been relinquished to the Saṅgha. 762. *Yadatthāya*:
for the sake of those robes and so forth. Because of its status as a compound with the word *ya*, there is the elision of the *niggahita* (anusvāra) before it.
It exists. "That" refers to the robe and so forth. "By you" is said with reference to the donors. "In calamities" means in misfortunes such as famine and the like.
"Whatever it may be" means either a robe or other requisites such as almsfood; thus, "whatever it may be. This is the sixth [offense]. 7.
The seventh Nissaggiya-Pācittiya training rule.

764. Regarding the phrase "by means of what has been asked for" (*saññācikenā*) in the seventh [offense], it is stated "by means of what was personally requested" (*sayaṃ yācitakena*) in order to show that the prefix *sam-* functions here in the sense of "self.
"This very [term]" refers to the word "by means of what has been asked for" (*saññācikenā*). "In this" refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
This is the seventh. 8. The eighth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.

769. Regarding the eighth [offense], "of a group" means of a group of bhikkhunīs. By this, it is indicated that in the phrase "by a large number of people," it is specifically a group of bhikkhunīs that is intended by the term "large number.
This concludes the eighth [offense]. 9. The ninth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule: 774.
Regarding the ninth, "from this" means from this eighth training rule. "More" means exceeding [the limit]. This concludes the ninth [offense].
10. The Tenth Nissaggiya Pācittiya Training Rule. 778.
Regarding the tenth [rule], by the word "is destroyed" (*vinassati*), the meaning of "perishing" is shown here for the verbal root *ud*, because roots have multiple meanings.
"Falls away" (*paripatati*) means it falls after having dissolved. By this, the manner of perishing is demonstrated.
“Only this much” means that the measure is only two spans. [The Tenth. 11.
The Eleventh Nissaggiya-Pācittiya Training Rule. 784.
Regarding the eleventh, “heavy cloak” (*garupāvuraṇa*) refers to a cloak used during the cold season; thus, he said: “during the cold season.”
“Cloak. For during the cold season, people wear thick cloaks.
Regarding the phrase “not exceeding four *kaṃsa*,” the word *kaṃsa* is seen in three senses: as a food bowl, as a specific metal such as gold, and as four *kahāpaṇa* coins.
Showing that here it refers to four *kahāpaṇa* coins, he said: “A *kaṃsa* means one consisting of four *kahāpaṇas*.”
"...occurs. "Catukkaṃsaparamaṃ" means that for this [person], the maximum is reckoned as four kaṃsas;
thus it means a cloak worth sixteen kahāpaṇas. This is the eleventh.
12. The twelfth Nissaggiya Pācittiya training rule.

789. Regarding the twelfth [offense], he said, "a cloak in the hot season," showing that it is a garment for covering oneself during the heat. For in the hot season, people wear fine cloaks. This is the twelfth.
To show that there are thirty rules of expiation (nissaggiya), he said, "in the Mahāvibhaṅga," and so forth. The connection is with the phrase "having removed from the Cīvara-vagga.
"Aññadatthikāni" refers to the training rules (sikkhāpada) expressed by the term "for another purpose. "Iti" means "thus."
“Designated on one side” means designated for one [of the two]; “designated on both sides” means designated for both.
“In this context” refers to the statement beginning with “What has been recited.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The application of the commentary on the Thirty [Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules] in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga is completed. 4.
The Section on Pācittiya Offenses.
1. The Garlic Chapter (Lasuṇavagga) 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada-atthayojanā):

Immediately after the Thirty [Training Rules], at the time following the Thirties, there are one hundred and sixty-six [rules] comprised within six groups of sixty, plus an additional one hundred and sixty-six.

The construction is as follows: "Now, at this time, there is also this commentary on those teachings (dhammas) which are comprised by the training rules (sikkhāpada) and recited by the compilers of the Council.
793. "Therein" means among those one hundred and sixty-six training rules; it is connected with the phrase "the first training rule."
Regarding the phrase “two or three,” the word *vā* (or) is indicated here as being elided; thus he says, “two or three.
*Phoṭalaka* refers to a bulbous root (*kanda*) or a pith (*miñja*). The word *etaṃ* (“this”) refers to the name “*gaṇḍikā*.

By the term “measure” (*pamāṇa*), he shows that the word *matta* has the sense of measure (*pamāṇa*) alone, not the sense of little (*appa*), nor the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). *Lasuna* is the white-colored root with a large bulb.

For *mahākanda* (the great bulb) is called *lasuna* (garlic) because it "gladdens" (*lasati*)—that is, it is desired (*kantīyati*)—due to its overcoming the "raw stench" (*āmagandha*) in soups, condiments, and so forth.

"The womb of the golden swan" (*suvaṇṇahaṃsayoni*) means a womb of a swan equipped with a golden-feathered wing. "One who remembers his births" (*jātissara*) means one who remembers (*sarati*) and knows (*jānāti*) his birth (*jāti*) or existence;
thus he is "one who remembers his births. "Then" (*atha*) refers to the fact that the one who remembers his births has been accomplished; for the word *atha* signifies accomplishment.
"By former affection" means by the affection cultivated previously during his human existence. "Of them" refers to Pajāpatī and her three daughters.
"But that" refers to the bowl. 795.
"In Magadha" means in the districts situated within the kingdom of Magadha. "For" (hi) means truly, or because. "Here" (idha) means...
Regarding the phrase “one should eat garlic”: *tampi* means even that which is from Māgadha. *Gaṇḍikalasuṇameva*:
it has a *gaṇḍa*—that is, a bulb—therefore it is *gaṇḍika*. For the word *gaṇḍa* is a synonym for a bulb; the suffix *-ika* is used in the sense of abundance.
Thus, what is meant is “garlic with many bulbs. For the word *gaṇḍa* applies to two meanings: a bulb and a cheek; however, in this context...
It should be understood that [the word] "phoṭe" occurs [there]. However, in the manuscripts there is a reading with the fourth consonant produced by the lips (*oṭṭhaja*);

that should be adopted after careful consideration. For in many ancient manuscripts, two letters—the third consonant produced by the throat (*kaṇṭhaja*) and the fourth consonant produced by the lips (*oṭṭhaja*)—are found existing with their positions interchanged. [The phrase] "not even one, two, three, or four seeds" means:
"One with one core (*ekamiñja*) is not an onion (*palāṇḍuka*); one with two cores (*dvimiñja*) is not a *bhañjanaka*; one with three cores (*timiñja*) is not a *haritaka*—this is the meaning.
However, it is stated in the *Kurundi*—this is the connection [to the preceding]. "Having chewed" means having made it into a powder with the teeth. 797.
"Onion" (*palāṇḍuka*) is a single type of garlic known as *sukandaka*. The terms *bhañjanaka* and so forth are to be understood according to worldly convention and instruction.
"Hī" means "truth. "Tassa" refers to the *cāpala-suṇa* (the restless dog). "Sabhāveneva" means by its own nature alone, without [the addition of] soup, condiments, and so forth.
"Taṃ" refers to the Māgadhaka; it is to be connected with "to be added. "Hī" means "truth. "Yattha katthaci" means "in whichever [places].
This is the first. 2. The second training rule.
799. In the second [case], it obstructs, hinders, and constricts in this place;
thus, showing that by the meaning of the word, a concealed spot is called a "constriction" (*sambādha*), he says: "in a concealed spot. "Both armpits" refers to the two roots of the arms.
For they are called "armpits" (*upakacchaka*) because whatever garment is placed upon them is tucked or bound there.
[These things] are so called. "The urinary organ" (*muttakaraṇa*) is the path for urine; for it is called the "urinary organ" because one urinates by means of it.

That by which hair is cut or shaved is a "scissors" (*kattarī*); or else, that which bites the hair very firmly is a "tweezer" (*saṇḍāsa*), and that itself is a "tweezer" (*saṇḍāsaka*), or by that; that which shaves, i.e., cuts the hair, is a "razor" (*khura*), and by that.
"Or causes it to be removed"—this is the connection. "Causes it to be removed" means she causes it to be taken away. This is the second [offense]. 3.
The Third Training Rule (Sikkhāpada): 803.

Regarding "striking the surface of the urinary organ" in the third [rule]: "Striking the surface of the urinary organ" (*muttakaraṇatalaghātana*) refers to the act of striking or hitting the surface of the urinary organ (*muttakaraṇa*).
In that striking of the palm of the hand against the urinary organ, which serves as the sign. "So great" means exceedingly large.
"Even by the filament" means even by the pollen; for it is called *kesara* because it moves (*sarati*) in the water (*ke*).
805. "A boil" means a pustule; "or a wound" means an ulcer. The third [section].
4. The Fourth Training Rule. 806.
Regarding the fourth [rule], in order to show the meaning of the terms *rājorodhā* (royal women of the harem) and *purāṇarājorodhā* (former royal women of the harem), he says "purāṇe" and so forth.
By the word "gihibhāve" (in the state of being a householder), the actual form of the suffix *-ṇa-* in the term "purāṇe" is indicated.
It shows [this]. *Cirāciraṃ* is a particle-like expression (*nipātapaṭirūpaka*). Therefore it is said: "after a long time, after a long time.
By the word "are you able" (*sakkotha*), it shows the meaning: "Are you able to sustain yourselves by warding off the mind of lust?
*Anārocitepi* means even when not reported as it actually happened.
807. *Jatunā* means with lac. *Paṭṭhadaṇḍaka*: that which stands firm or proceeds by way of its sharpness (*paṭubhāva*) is called *paṭṭha*;

that very thing is the shaft (*daṇḍa*), hence *paṭṭhadaṇḍa*. The insertion of that is *paṭṭhadaṇḍaka*, [occurring] when that serves as the instrumental cause. *Etam* refers to this expression, namely, "*jatumaṭṭhake*.
This is the fourth [section].
5. The Fifth Training Rule (Pañcamasikkhāpada) 810.
Regarding the fifth rule, the term “very deep” (*atigambhīra*) is an adverbial modifier of the action; thus it says, “having inserted [the finger] to the very end.
By the phrase “performing a washing with water,” it shows that the meaning of the term “water-purification” (*udakasuddhika*) is the performance of purification by means of water.
812. *Dvaṅgulapabbaparamaṃ*: here, "two fingers and two finger-joints" is *dvaṅgulapabbaṃ*; this is a compound where the first member of the latter term has been elided.
That for which two finger-joints are the maximum measure is *dvaṅgulapabbaparamaṃ*, referring to this purification by water.
It is stated that it is at most two fingers in width and at most two finger-joints in depth.
[It] exists. Therefore he said, “In detail,” and so forth. The connection is with the phrase “inserting a finger. “Hi” means “truly.
The expression “or of four” is stated by way of the maximum; the meaning is that even three joints are not permitted, let alone four.
This is the fifth [section]. 6. The sixth training rule.
815. Regarding the sixth [term], when "the relinquishing of food" (*bhattavissagga*) is stated, he says "the duty of eating" (*bhattakicca*) to show that it means the act of eating.
By the word *pānīya* (water), the water-vessel is to be understood; by the word *vidhūpana* (fanning), the fan is to be understood;
and since the prefix *upa-* signifies proximity, he says "with one hand," etc., to demonstrate all of this. As for the phrase "accāvadati":
Having passed over the manner of speaking, he shows [the meaning] by means of the words beginning with "Even before" (pubbepi).
With the words beginning with "Let it be pure water," he shows that the expression "with water" (pānīyena) is an illustration (upalakkhaṇaṃ).
"Curd-scum" (dadhimatthu) means the cream of curd, the essence of curd; it is said to be the clear liquid [that settles] in curd. "Flavor" (raso)...
“Fish broth, meat broth. By the phrase “even as much as the hem of a robe,” he shows that the mention of the “fly-whisk” is merely an illustration.
819. “Gives” means gives himself; “causes to be given” means causes another to give. “Both” refers to both the drinking water and the fly-whisk.
This is the sixth [offense]. 7. The seventh training rule.

822. Regarding the seventh [point], by the phrase "the preliminary offense of wrong-doing (*pubbapayoga-dukkata*)," he indicates the preliminary offense of wrong-doing among the eight offenses of wrong-doing mentioned below.
To show that there is not only this much preliminary offense of wrong-doing, but rather many others as well, he says "therefore," and so forth.
"Even in the case of collisions" means even in the case of stirring up. "Chews with the teeth" means with the teeth.
He crushes it into powder. "In this" means in this training rule; the connection is with the phrase "having had it prepared by another bhikkhunī.
The word "by another" (*aññāya*) is the object of the causative verb in the word "having requested" (*viññāpetvā*).

Regarding the phrase "even her mother," the word "even" (*pi*) indicates that this applies all the more so to one who eats after having requested it from someone else. "Or by her" means by the bhikkhunī who made the request.
“*Taṃ*” refers to raw grain. “*Taṃ*” refers to the statement spoken in the *Mahāpaccarī*. “Contradictory in its earlier and later parts” means contradictory from beginning to end.
In the earlier statement, “If she knows... [etc.]... it is merely a *dukkaṭa* offense,” only a *dukkaṭa* is mentioned; yet again, in the later statement, “If she knows... [etc.]...
a *dukkaṭa*,” both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa* are mentioned. Therefore, it is said to be “contradictory in its earlier and later parts.”
It has been said. *Hi* means "truly" or "because. 823.

The connection is with "raw grain that is available. "Or anything else whatsoever" means either mung beans, peas, and so forth; or gourds, cucumbers, and so forth; or any other [grain] such as sesame, and so on.
This is the seventh. 8. The eighth training rule.

824. Regarding the phrase *aṭṭhame nibbiṭṭharājabhaṭo*: here, demonstrating both a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) for the latter member and an external-meaning compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) with the former member, he says “*nibbiṭṭho*,” and so forth.
Therein, by the expression “the king’s servant” (*rañño bhatī*), he shows the genitive compound as “the king’s servant” (*rājabhaṭo*).
By the expression “by this,” he shows the external-meaning compound. “*Nibbiṭṭho*” means... [text continues]
"Established" means firmly set up. "Keṇī" is a designation for the revenue to be given to the king.

"By this" refers to the brahmin. "From there" means from that position. Because it was made into a path for the hire known as *keṇī*, he said, "that very position," calling it the "hire-path" (*bhaṭapatha*).
826. "The four bases" refers to excrement and so forth. "Individually" means separately, one by one. Regarding the phrases "or excrement," etc., he says "tooth-sticks... [and so on]...
an offense of expiation (pācittiya) indeed" because the word "or" includes tooth-sticks and other such things as well. "In all cases" means in all instances involving excrement and so forth.
This is the eighth [offense].
9. The Ninth Training Rule (Navama-sikkhāpada) 830.

Regarding "in a place where plants have been planted and in a place where there is greenery" (*ropima-haritaṭṭhāne*): it refers to both a place where things have been planted (*ropima-ṭṭhāna*) and a place where there is greenery (*harita-ṭṭhāna*).
It is called *ropima* because things are planted therein (*ropiyati asmin*); the *ya*-sound is changed to the *ma*-sound. "These" (*etāni*) refers to excrement and so forth. "Of all" (*sabbesaṃ*)...
[This applies] to monks and nuns. "But where" means in whatever field.
The ninth [section]. 10. The Tenth Training Rule. 835.
In the tenth [rule], "a snout" means a snout for liquor (*surā*). "Peacock" means a peacock (*mayūra*). "Parrot" means a parrot (*suka*). "Monkey" means a monkey (*vānara*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), snakes and so forth are included; the connection is that even monkeys and others should dance.

Or, regarding the phrase "of unrestrained monks" (*asaṃyata-bhikkhūnaṃ*): it refers to monks who are unrestrained in their verbal actions; the construction is that there should be the singing of a Dhamma-reciter.

"Bound by a string" (*tantibaddhā*) means bound by a string (*tantiguṇena*). A drum (*bheri*) is so called because it has a mass (*rāsa*) known as "bhi. A drum made with a wooden frame is a *kuṭabheri*.
*Kuṭabheri*: a broken drum; *kuṭabherivādita* means that which is played on such a broken drum, or that [sound] itself. *Udakabherī* means a drum placed in water;
the connection is that it refers to what is played upon by that [drum].
836. *Tesaṃ yeva*: of those very people whose dancing one sees. However, if the dancing, singing, and instrumental music are separate—
He says "But if... and so forth, showing that one sees and hears separately, meaning that the offenses are distinct.

"From elsewhere" (*aññato*) means from another location; it is connected with the word "sees" (*passati*). When the word "having looked" (*oloketvā*) is expected, the suffix *-to* occurs in the sense of the accusative.
For the meaning is "having looked at something else. The construction is: "he sees [someone] speaking from elsewhere. "The nun does not obtain [it]"...

The connection [is as follows]. "Others may also speak" is the connection. "Offering" means worship. "Attendance" means service. "In all cases" means in all instances of dancing and so forth by oneself.

837. "Or within the monastery" means either inside the monastery. "Or outside the monastery" means either outside the monastery. "Or by another" means by something other than tickets for meals and so forth. "By such [a thing]" means by whatever kind of calamity there might be, such as from thieves and the like. The tenth [chapter].
The First Chapter on Garlic.
2. The Chapter on Darkness. 1.
Commentary on the First Training Rule.

839. In the first [sutta] of the *Andhakāravagga*, because it is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) as "he does not light a lamp," [the commentator], showing that other lights should also be understood, says: "In a lamp, moon, sun, or fire," and so forth. "Of this" (*assa*) refers to the word "without a lamp" (*appadīpe*). 841. The construction is:
"having regard for the enjoyment of human life" and "being engaged in something other than the enjoyment of food.
By this, he shows that the phrases "stands still" or "converses" function as adverbs (*kiriyāvisesana*) of the action. Or, by means of giving, which serves as the causal sign (*nimitta*).
The construction is: “He counsels for the sake of worship, which has become the cause. This is the first. 2.
The Second Training Rule (Sikkhāpada):
In the second [rule], the connection is: “This very word is different. This is the second.
3. The Third Training Rule (Tatiyasikkhāpada) 846.
In the third [rule], the phrase "this very" (idameva) is to be repeated. "Just like that" (tādisameva) means exactly like the first; such is the meaning. This is the third. 4.
The Fourth Training Rule (Catutthasikkhāpada)

850. In the fourth [case], *nikaṇṇaṃ* means "near the ear. When that very same term is called *nikaṇṇikā*, he says it means "the root of the ear," as in the phrase "it is called the root of the ear" (*kaṇṇamūlaṃ vuccati*).
By the word "at the root of the ear" (*kaṇṇamūle*), he shows that in this instance of "*nikaṇṇikā*," the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.
"For the purpose of bringing" (*āharaṇatthāya*) means "for the purpose of causing to bring" (*āharāpanatthāya*). This is the fourth.
5. The Fifth Training Rule. 854.

"Of those" (tesaṃ) means of the owners of the house. "The house too" (gharaṃ pi): the meaning is that one should clean not only the seat, but the house as well. "From there" (tato) means from the deliberation;
it is connected with "another" (paraṃ). 858. "Or thieves have arisen"—this is the construction. The fifth [training rule].
6. The Sixth Training Rule. 860.

Regarding the phrase "should sit down" (*abhinisīdeyya*) in the sixth [rule]: showing that here the prefix *abhi-* is merely an intensifier (*upasagga-matta*), he says "should sit down" (*nisīdeyya*). This same method applies to the phrase "should lie down" (*abhinipajjeyya*) as well. The connection is "two offenses.
The sixth [rule] is concluded. 7. The Seventh Training Rule.
864. In the seventh [section], "all" means the entire speech that is to be spoken. This is the seventh. 8.
The eighth training rule: 869.
In the eighth, there is no statement that is not already explained. This is the eighth.
9. The Ninth Training Rule (Navama-sikkhāpada) 875.
Regarding the ninth rule, concerning the phrase "should swear" (*abhisapeyya*):

here, having included the root *sap-* in the sense of reviling, he says "should make an oath" (*sapathaṃ kareyya*) to demonstrate the meaning of the root *kar-*. "I am reborn in hell" (*niraye nibbattāmhi*) means: "I am reborn in hell."
The construction is: "We [are]. "May she be reborn in hell" means: "May this bhikkhunī be reborn in hell"—this is the construction.
"May she be like this" means: "May she be like me. "One-eyed" means: one who is blind in one eye or blind in both eyes. "Lame" means: one who has crooked hands, feet, and so forth.
878. "Of such a kind" means: of a deformed appearance and so forth. "Desist" means: stop. "Addhā" means: certainly. The ninth [chapter].
10. The Tenth Training Rule. 879.
In the tenth [rule], there is no obscure point. The tenth [is concluded].
The second chapter, the Chapter on Darkness, is finished.
3. The Chapter on the Naked (Naggavagga) 1. Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 883.
Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on the Naked: "By the holy life practiced"—what indeed by the holy life practiced?
The meaning is "he indeed. By the phrase "by the practicing of the holy life" (*brahmacariyassa caraṇena*), he shows the etymological meaning of the word *ciṇṇa* as "practiced" (*caraṇaṃ ciṇṇaṃ*).
By the phrase "no other robe," he shows this very meaning, namely, the exclusion of anything else. First.
2. The Second Training Rule.
887. In the second [case], there is no point that has not already been clarified.
This is the second. 3. The Third Training Rule. 893.

Regarding the third [rule], the term *anantarāyikinī*: here, because there is no obstacle (*antarāya*) for her, she is *anantarāyā*; explaining the meaning of the word as being precisely that, he says "without obstacle" (*anantarāyā*). This is the third.
4. The Fourth Training Rule. 898.

Regarding the fourth [rule], "five days" (*pañcāha*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvigu*); the suffix *-ika* has the sense of "belonging to. As for the phrase "the movement of the *saṅghāṭī*," he asks:

"In what sense is it called a *saṅghāṭī*, and what is the meaning of the word 'movement' (*cāra*)? To this he says: "Either by way of use," and so forth. Therein, "by way of being sewn together" (*saṅghaṭita-ṭṭhena*) means:
"In the sense of being gathered together. By this, he answers the question: "In what sense is it called *saṅghāṭi*? By the word "turning over" (*parivattana*), he resolves the objection:
"What is the meaning of the word *cāra*? "In five" means in the five [robes]: the triple robe (*ticīvara*), the water-bath cloth (*udakasāṭikā*), and the inner bodice (*saṃkaccikā*).
This is the fourth [section].
5. The Fifth Training Rule. 903.
Regarding the fifth rule, in the phrase “a robe that is to be transferred” (*cīvarasaṅkamanīya*), it is called *saṅkamanīya* because it is to be transferred or returned.

This is derived from the verbal root *kam*, meaning “to give back,” and the suffix *-anīya*, which has the sense of the object. Thus, [the compound] means “that which is a robe and is to be transferred.”

Regarding the term *cīvarasaṅkamanīya*, he says "a robe that is to be transferred" (*saṅkametabbaṃ cīvaraṃ*) in order to show both its status as a qualifying subsequent word and its objective case function.
Therein, by the phrase "a robe that is to be transferred," he demonstrates both the objective sense and the status of the qualifying subsequent word.
By the phrase "a robe to be returned" (*paṭidātabbacīvaraṃ*), he demonstrates the meaning of the verbal root *dā* (to give) according to its intended purpose. This is the fifth [section].
6. The Sixth Training Rule. 909.
Regarding the sixth rule, in the phrase "another requisite," he says "whatever" and so forth to show the nature of that requisite.
The connection is with the words "any one of these. As for "of what value": by what measure of price is it worth?
*Cīvaraṃ*. "Dātukāmattha" means "you should desire to give"; this is the meaning.

"Katipāhena" means "after a few days"—*katipāhaṃ* is [formed] with the elision of the letter *ya*. The word *katipaya* is a conventional term (*rūḷhisadda*) signifying "two or three," hence "by katipāhena.
"Samaggha" means "of little value. For the prefix *saṃ-* expresses the sense of "little" (*appa*). The sixth [section].
7. The Seventh Training Rule. 911.

Regarding the phrase "they departed" (*vipakkamiṃsu*) in the seventh [rule], he says "they went here and there" (*tattha tattha agamaṃsu*) to show that they departed for various places. The connection is: "there will also be coming for us. 915.
"It will arise within a few days" means that the robe (*cīvara*) will arise within a few days. "From that" (*tato*) means at the time when that robe arises. The seventh [training rule].
8. The Eighth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 916.
Regarding the eighth [rule]: the construction is that those who perform a play (*nāṭaka*) are called "actors" (*naṭa*).

By this, he shows the etymological meaning of the word *naṭa* as "those who perform a play. The construction is that those who dance are called "dancers" (*nāṭaka*). By this, he shows [the meaning] as "those who themselves dance."
The word *nāṭaka* illustrates the meaning of the term. Regarding the phrase "bamboo, leather straps, and so forth": here, *vaṃsa* means bamboo; *varattā* means leather straps;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), ropes and other such items are included. The construction is: "those who perform the act of leaping are called *laṅghakas*. Regarding the term *māyākāra*:
here, *māyā* is so called because it was created by the asura named Maya in order to deceive the gods (*sura*).
“Māyā” means that which belongs to *māyā* (illusion); one who performs that is a *māyākāra*. This refers specifically to the asura named Māya.
However, others are called “*māyākārā*” by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*). *Sokajjhāya* is the brooding or burning caused by sorrow (*soka*);
one who causes the brooding of sorrow among the gods is a *sokajjhāyika*. This refers specifically to the asura named Māya. However, others are called “*sokajjhāyikā*” by way of conventional usage.
Thus, in order to show this meaning, it is said: “‘Sokajjhāyikā’ means illusionists. Regarding the term *kumbhathuṇikā*:
here, because it is sounded (*thavīyati*) when released, *thuṇo* is a sound. A *kumbha-thuṇo* is a pot-sound.
Those who play with that are *kumbhathuṇikā*; this meaning is shown by the phrase “those who play with a jar.”
"Bimbisaka" refers to the striking of square-shaped drums; those who play them are "bimbisaka-players. This is the eighth [offense].
9. The Ninth Training Rule: 921.
Regarding the ninth, "of them" refers to those who say, "Venerable lady, we are not able. "Will give" means she will present [it]. This is the ninth.
10. The Tenth Training Rule (Dasama-sikkhāpada) 927.

Regarding the tenth [rule]: "Of whom" refers to the *kaṭhina*. "Rooted in suspension" means having its basis in the suspension (*ubbhāra*). "For the sake of protecting their faith" means for the sake of protecting the faith of one who requests the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. The tenth.
The third chapter, the Section on the Naked (*Naggavagga*).
4. The Chapter on Reclining (Tuvaṭṭavagga). 1.
Explanation of the First Training Rule (Sikkhāpada). 933.

Regarding the first [rule] of the Chapter on Reclining, because the term “*tuvaṭṭa nipajjāya*” is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*; specifically as the root ending in *ṭ* in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, no. 18), it is said that “*tuvaṭṭeyyun*” means “they should lie down. This is the first.
2. The Second Training Rule (Dutiyasikkhāpada) 937.

Regarding the second [rule], the phrase beginning with "one" (*eka*) is stated in order to show that the latter members [of the compound] form a *dvanda* (copulative compound), while the first member forms a *bahubbīhi* (exocentric) compound.
Furthermore, by means of the word "and" (*ca*), the status of a *dvanda* is indicated therein.
By the word “of these,” he indicates that this is an external compound (bāhiratthasamāsa). “This” refers to the name “sharing one bed and one upper garment.
This is the second [section]. 3. The Third Training Rule 941. Regarding the third [rule]:

“Noble families” (uḷārakula) means families of the highest birth, or families extensive in terms of power, wealth, and so forth. “By virtues” means by virtues such as moral discipline (sīla) and the like. By the phrase “noble means esteemed,” he demonstrates that this is an *itilopa-tulyādhikaraṇa* compound.

By the word “abhibhūtā” (overcome), he shows that although the verbal root *kar* in the phrase “apakatā” (harmed) expresses the meaning of all verbal roots, here—due to being preceded by the prefix *apa*—it specifically functions in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhavana*). “Etāsanti” means “of these bhikkhunīs.
By the word “saññāpayamānā” (persuading), he shows the etymological meaning of the term as “persuasion” (*saññatti*). In the phrase “hetūdāharaṇādīhi,” the word “ādi” (etcetera) [includes...]
It includes similes and so forth. By the phrase “making known through various methods,” it shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as “informing through various ways is *viññatti*. 943.

Regarding the statement that one should not be dealt with according to an offense by counting the steps on a walking path, he says: “by counting the turns. This means by counting the steps, sub-steps, and so forth. The third [section].
4. The Fourth Training Rule: 949.
There is no obscure point in the fourth [rule]. This is the fourth. 5.
The Fifth Training Rule.

952. In the fifth [training rule], the construction is: "a nun who has been commanded. And this is stated by way of proximity, meaning that she is capable of commanding anything whatsoever. The fifth [is concluded]. 6–9.
Regarding the sixth and subsequent training rules: 955.
In the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth, there is no statement requiring further explanation. These are the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth.
10. The Tenth Training Rule (Dasama-sikkhāpada) 973.
Regarding the term *ahundarikā*: at that time, or in that place, this was the name for a narrow space; thus it is said, “*Ahundarikā* means a narrow space (*sambādha*).
975. Just as in the expression “with more than five or six words,” the word “five” has no specific meaning here, being used merely for the sake of euphony (*siliṭṭhattha*) in the phrase.
This was stated according to worldly convention; it is not so here. However, there is a specific meaning here: even for one who has traveled five *yojanas*, there is indeed no offense.
Thus he said: “Having invited [the Sangha]... [etc. ...there is no offense. “Returns” means she turns back and comes.
The tenth [case]. The fourth chapter, the *Tuvatta-vagga*.
5. Cittāgāravagga 1.
