Commentary on the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 978.
Regarding the first [rule] of the Cittāgāravagga, the meaning of the term *rājāgāra* is "the house (*agāra*) for the king’s pleasure (*kīḷana*)"; thus is the etymological explanation.
Explaining this, he said: "The king’s pleasure house. *Cittāgāraṃ* means a house of the mind.

Regarding *ārāma*, he said it is a "grove" (*upavana*) because it is a park not too far from the city. *Uyyānaṃ*: it is called a park (*uyyānaṃ*) because people go (*yanti*) there, looking upward at it, due to its abundance of flowers and fruits.
*Pokkharaṇī*: it is called a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*) because it leads (*neti*) to the lotus (*pokkhara*).

"Five" refers to the five [types of dwellings], such as royal palaces and so forth. "In all cases" means in all instances: both when going for the purpose of seeing them and when having gone and looking at them.

(981) By the phrase "in the vicinity of a monastery" (*ajjhārāme*), etc., it is shown that there is no offense even for one standing within a monastery who sees a royal palace or similar structure built outside the monastery grounds. "Those" refers to the royal palaces and so forth.
This is the first [sub-section]. 2. The second training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
982. In the second [case], there is no point that has not already been explained. This is the second [section].
3. The Third Training Rule. 988. Regarding the third [rule]:
"as much as" (*yattakaṃ*) is connected with "the thread" (*suttaṃ*). "Drawn out" (*añchitaṃ*) means pulled. In that [context]...
The connection is with the word *tattake* (in that much). Regarding the phrase *takkamhi*: here, *takka* refers to a specific iron tool for spinning thread.
For it is called *takka* because thread (*sutta*) is spun (*takīyati*) or bound (*bandhīyati*) therein, or because it is by means of it; [the locative case] is *tasmiṃ*. Regarding *kantanatō*:
*kantana* is that which is spun (*kantīyate*), that is, that by which cotton and so forth are cut (*chindīyate*); [the ablative case] is *tato*.
989. Regarding the phrase "a thread from the fringe (*dasikasuttādi*)," here *dasa* refers to a part of the cloth. For it is called *dasa* because it is given (*diyati*) or cut off (*avakhaṇḍīyati*).
That which occurs upon such a fringe is *dasika*; that very *dasika* is a "fringe-thread" (*dasikasutta*). By the word "etc.
(*ādi*), one includes the threads from the border-edges (*dukkantita*) and so forth, which will be explained later. This is the third [case].

4. The Fourth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 992. "Beginning with the fourth" means beginning with washing and so forth. "Regarding hard foods and the like" refers to cakes and other such hard foods. "By way of counting the forms" means by way of counting the shapes of the cakes and so forth.

993. "In the drinking of rice-gruel" refers to drinks designated as rice-gruel. "Of them" refers to human beings. "Having set aside those who perform services for oneself" means having set aside one's mother and father, who occupy the position of performing services for oneself. This is the fourth [rule].
5. The Fifth Training Rule (Sikkhāpada). 996.
Regarding the fifth [rule], the construction is: "the nun who settles" means "the nun who settles a legal issue (adhikaraṇa). This is the fifth. 6.
The Sixth Training Rule.
999. In the sixth [offense], there is no statement that has not already been explained.
7. The Seventh Training Rule. 1007.

Regarding the seventh, in the phrase "again by way of turn" (*puna pariyāye*), the word *pariyāya* is a synonym for "turn" (*vāra*); thus he says, "again by turn. "A costly robe" (*mahagghacīvara*) means a costly robe for a guest-house (*āvasatha*). The seventh.
8. The Eighth Training Rule 1008. Regarding the phrase "without having relinquished" (*anissajjitvā*) in the eighth [rule]:
here, it is not a failure to relinquish by means of a permanent gift to Brahmā (*brahmadeyya*); rather, it is shown that it is merely for a limited time (*tāvakālika*).

Thus he said, "for the sake of protection," and so forth. 1012. *Paṭijaggika*: one who protects. *Vacībhedam*: the verbal expression, namely the utterance, "Look after [it]. *Raṭṭhe*: in the kingdom, that is, in the realm (*vijita*). For it is called a "kingdom" (*raṭṭha*) because villages, towns, and so forth dwell (*tiṭṭhanti*) therein. The eighth [rule].
9. The Ninth Training Rule (Navama-sikkhāpada) 1015.

In the ninth [rule], the word *sippa* (craft/skill) should be applied individually [to each term]: “the craft of elephants, the craft of horses, the craft of chariots, the craft of archery, and the craft of swordsmanship.
Therein, “the craft of swordsmanship” (*tharusippa*) means the craft of sword-play. The word *manta* (incantation/lore) also...
Each term should be applied individually: "the *āthabbaṇa* spell, the *khīlana* spell, the *vasīkaraṇa* spell, and the *sosāpana* spell.
Therein, the *āthabbaṇa* spell is a spell prescribed by the *āthabbaṇa-veda* that causes harm to others.
The *khīlana* spell is a spell for securing [a site] by chanting over a stake made of heartwood and burying it in the earth. The *vasīkaraṇa* spell is...
A *manta* (incantation) that, when recited, causes another person to fall into a state of madness.
A *sosāpana-manta* is an incantation for causing the drying up of another’s flesh, blood, and so forth. An *agada-payoga* is the application of potent antidotes.
By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), other arts (*sippa*) that cause harm to others are also included. A *yakkha-paritta* is protection from all sides against *yakkhas*. A *nāga-maṇḍala*...
The *maṇḍalabandha* spell is for the purpose of preventing the entry of snakes. By the word "etcetera," spells for counteracting poison and so forth are included.
This concludes the ninth [section]. 10.
The Tenth Training Rule.
1018. In the tenth [case], there is no "unveiled statement" (anuttānavacana). The tenth [section].
The fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Painted Hall (Cittāgāravagga).
6. The Chapter on the Monastery (Ārāmavagga).
1. Explanation of the Meaning of the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 1025.
Regarding the first [rule] in the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga): "The vicinity" (*upacāra*) refers to the area surrounding an unenclosed monastery that is suitable for enclosing it.

1027. Although it is stated generally as "looking toward the head," he specifies "of the bhikkhunīs" because it is the heads of the bhikkhunīs alone that are meant. "Wherever" means in whatever place. This is the first [rule].
2. The Second Training Rule (Dutiyasikkhāpada) 1028.
Regarding the second [term], "inside" (*abbhantara*) means included within or born within.

By the word "she diverted" (*saṅkāmesi*), the sense of "shifting" is shown here for the verbal root *har* in the term *saṅkamana*. "Barbers" (*nhāpitā*) refers to hair-cutters; for they wash and shave.
They are called barbers. "That" refers to the wearing of the saffron robe. Second. 3–4.
Regarding the third and fourth training rules:
there is nothing obscure in the third and fourth. Third and Fourth.
5. The Fifth Training Rule (Pañcama-sikkhāpada) 1043.
Regarding the fifth [rule], the word-meaning (*vacanattha*) of “miserliness toward a family” (*kule maccharo*) should be understood as “miserliness” (*maccharana*).
The construction is: “She speaks dispraise of that family, saying, ‘That family is faithless and lacks confidence. [The text continues: “The nuns...”
The construction is: "he speaks dispraise of the bhikkhunīs, saying they are immoral and of evil character.
Regarding the phrase "even though there is indeed a danger," it is stated "of the family or of the bhikkhunīs" in order to show the connection with what follows;
by this, the connection is not with only one of the two, but rather with both.
"He shows": this is the fifth [section].
6. The Sixth Training Rule: 1048.

Regarding the sixth rule, "for the purpose of exhortation" (*ovādāya*): here, it is not just any kind of exhortation that is meant, but rather specifically the exhortation concerning the heavy rules (*garudhamma*).
He said: "For the sake of the *garudhammas*. Since one dwells together here, or by means of this, it is called "co-residence" (*saṃvāsa*) according to the meaning of the word;

thus he said, "for the sake of requesting the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā," [meaning] "Uposatha and Pavāraṇā are what is called co-residence. By the phrase "for the sake of requesting," he shows that in the expression "for co-residence" (*saṃvāsāya*), there is an elision of the latter member of the compound.
"Here" means in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga, or in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), or in the Canon (*pāḷi*). The sixth [section].
7–9. The Seventh, Eighth, and Ninth Training Rules (Sikkhāpada). 1053.

Regarding the seventh, eighth, and ninth [rules], there is no unique statement; rather, the phrase "of this too" is the distinction, meaning "of this Pāḷi as well. These are the seventh, eighth, and ninth.
10. The Tenth Training Rule.
1062. In the tenth [section], there are two bodies: the upper body and the lower body. Therein, from the waist upwards is the upper body; below that is the lower body.
Regarding this, "the groin" (*pasākha*) is a name for the lower body; thus he says "in the lower part of the body" (*adhokāye*). The word *hi* means "truly.
From "there" (*tato*) means from the lower part of the body. By this, he demonstrates a genitive-bahubbīhi compound. Of the tree...
The construction is: "as if the branches had split and gone away," and "as if both thighs had split and gone away.
Regarding the word *phālehi* (split), the particle *iti* here has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*). By this, it includes the four terms beginning with *dhova*.

"Offenses of wrong-doing due to commands" refers specifically to the Vinaya-offense among the eight wrong-doings mentioned previously. "In the remaining cases" refers to [the offenses] other than the act of splitting.
"In the sense-fields, such as the fissures," etc. The tenth [chapter].
The sixth section, the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga).
7. The Chapter on Pregnant Women (Gabbhinīvagga).
1. Explanation of the Meaning of the First Training Rule (Paṭhamasikkhāpada-atthayojanā) 1069.
Regarding the first [rule] of the section on pregnant women (*gabbhinīvagga*): "One who has a being entered into her womb" is *kucchipaviṭṭhasattā*.
The reading *kucchiṃ* is also found. By this, it is shown that in the word *gabbhinī*, the term *gabbha* denotes a being residing within the womb (*kucchi*).
For the word *gabbha* (in verse 944 of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*) applies to a being residing in the womb, to the womb itself, and to a room. First [section].
2. The Second Training Rule.

1073. Regarding the second [offense]: "One who drinks breast-milk" means one who is nursing; a child. To show that she has such a child, he said, "one who is nursing breast-milk. This is the second. 3.
The Third Training Rule 1077. Regarding the third:
"She will cross over" means she will cross over from the suffering of saṃsāra.
1079. Regarding the phrase “abstention from taking life”: here, it is called *veramaṇī* in the sense that one abstains (*viramati*) from taking life by means of this;
thus, the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is named *veramaṇī*. Therefore, he says: “the training rule of abstention from taking life. The connection is with the words “that which is the training rule.
“In all cases” refers to all such statements as “abstention from taking what is not given,” and so forth. For one who has gone forth...
The connection is with the term "novice nun" (sāmaṇeriyā). "In these" refers to the six training rules (sikkhā). This is the third [section].
4. The Fourth Training Rule: 1084.

In the fourth [rule], the word "consent for ordination" (vuṭṭhānasammuti) is the agent (kattā) for the verb "there is" (hoti), and it is the object (kamma) for the phrase "must indeed be given" (dātabbāyeva). This is the fourth [section].
5–9. The Fifth and Subsequent Training Rules: 1095.
Regarding the training rules beginning with the fifth and ending with the ninth, there is no point that requires further explanation. These are the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth.
10. The Tenth Training Rule.
1116. Regarding the phrase "in the tenth [case], she should depart": here, showing that the root *kās* has the sense of "going," he says "she should go. Tenth.
The Seventh Chapter on Pregnant Women.
8. The Chapter on Maidens.
1–2–3. Explanation of the Meaning of the First, Second, and Third Training Rules (Sikkhāpada). 1119.
Regarding the first, second, and third rules of the Chapter on Maidens (Kumāribhūtavagga), the connection is: "But those who are great trainees (mahāsikkhamānā).
The phrase "the first two great trainees" refers to those mentioned at the very beginning of all trainees in the Chapter on Pregnant Women (Gabbhinīvagga).

There are two types of *mahāsikkhamānā*. Regarding the phrase "but those," it means: as for the *mahāsikkhamānā*, they should be referred to simply as "probationers" (*sikkhamānā*) in formal acts of authorization (*sammutikamma*), because that is the general term to be used.

They should not be called "married women" (*gihigatā*) or "maidens" (*kumāribhūtā*); the intention is that if one were to call them such, the formal act would be invalidated. In this context, "married woman" refers to one who has gone over to another man. She...
For because one has gone with a person reckoned as a householder—that is, by way of misconduct—or because one has gone to a householder, therefore it is called "gone to a householder.
This is to be connected with the term "this trainee" (*sikkhamānā*). One who is "a maiden" (*kumāribhūtā*) is called a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*);
for she, because she has not gone to a householder, having been a maiden, has become [so], or having attained the state of a maiden, has gone [to it].
Therefore, she is called a "maiden" (*kumāribhūtā*). "The three as well" means: the one who has gone forth from the household life, the maiden, and the great trainee (*mahāsikkhamānā*)—these three.
A "trainee" (*sikkhamānā*) is so called because she honors the training (*sikkhaṃ māneti*). [This concludes] the first, second, and third [rules].
4. The fourth training rule.
1136. In the fourth [section], there is no statement that is not fully explained.
This is the fourth. 5. The Fifth Training Rule.
Regarding the fifth training rule, the connection is as follows: "of that statement which was spoken here in this training rule, namely, 'it must be delimited by the Saṅgha. This is the fifth.
6–8. The Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Training Rules.
Regarding the sixth, seventh, and eighth, there is no point that requires further explanation. These are the sixth, seventh, and eighth. 9.
The Ninth Training Rule.
1158. *Anto* in the ninth [compound] means "within. By this, he shows the meaning of the prefix *ā-*.

Because it "causes to dwell within" or "causes to enter," it is called *āvāsa*. By the words "sorrow" (*soka*) and so forth, he shows the etymological meaning as "that which causes sorrow to dwell within" is *sokāvāsa*.
Just as householders enter a house, so too does this [person] enter into sorrow; such is the construction. *Iti* means "thus. *Yaṃ*... [refers to the person].
"Sokaṃ. "Svāssā" means "she would be that. "So" refers to sorrow (*soka*). "Assā" refers to the trainee (*sikkhamānā*).
"Āvāsa" means the dwelling place. By the phrase "of such a kind as this," he demonstrates the manner of not knowing in the context of "not knowing.
The ninth [section]. 10. The tenth training rule (*sikkhāpada*).

1162. Regarding the phrase "without having asked permission" (*anāpuccha*) in the tenth [offense], it is said "having not asked" (*anāpucchitvā*), because here the suffix *tvā* is elided. "Twice" (*dvikkhattum*) means two times. "Once" (*sakim*) means one time. 1163.
"That which has a previously unarisen origin as its head" (*apubbasamuṭṭhānasīsa*) means that this [offense] has a previously unarisen origin as its primary point.

"In both places" (*dvīsu pi ṭhānesu*) refers to both places: namely, from speech and from both body and speech. "Without having caused to be authorized" (*ananujānāpetvā*) means by neither the mother and father nor by the husband.
"Having obtained permission": this is the tenth [section]. 11.
The Eleventh Training Rule (Sikkhāpada) 1167.
Regarding the eleventh: "therein" refers to the statement, "by the giving of consent for one who is undergoing probation. "Elsewhere" means another place.
“Entreat one” means they appoint a single bhikkhu for the purpose of delivering a Dhamma talk. “But another” means one other than the one observing the Uposatha.
“Therein” means among those bhikkhus. “He recites the auspicious and inauspicious constellations” refers to an astrologer (*nakkhattapāṭhaka*).
“Dreadful” means harsh. “Them” refers to the bhikkhus. “His” refers to the bhikkhu who is the astrologer. “While he is waiting for the constellation...”
“Profit has passed by the fool”—thus says the Jātaka commentary. Herein, this is the construction:
profit, that is, welfare, has passed by—that is, having gone beyond and approached—the fool who is waiting for the [proper] constellation. The eleventh [section].
12. The twelfth training rule.
1170. Regarding the twelfth [offense]: "It is not sufficient" means she is unable to have the bhikkhunīs clothed.
This is the twelfth. 13. The Thirteenth Training Rule 1175.

Regarding the thirteenth: "One year" (*ekaṃ vassaṃ*); here the word *vassa* is a synonym for "year," and the accusative case functions in the sense of the locative. Therefore, he says, "in one year. This is the thirteenth.
The eighth chapter: The Chapter on Maidens.
9. The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
1. The Exegesis of the First Training Rule.
1181. In the first section of the *Chattavagga*, "mud and so forth" (*kaddamādīni*) refers to muddy places and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), water and other such things are included.

"Bushes and so forth" (*gacchādīni*) refers to small shrubs and the like. By the word "and so forth," other congested places where it is impossible to hold an umbrella are also included. This is the first [section].
2. The Second Training Rule (Dutiyasikkhāpada) 1184.
Regarding the second [rule], "by vehicle" (*yānena*): it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because by means of it one goes easily to the desired place. This is the second [rule]. 3.
The Third Training Rule (Tatiyasikkhāpada).

1191. Regarding the third [offense], because the verb "they were scattered" (*vippakiriyiṃsu*) is inseparable from its agent, it is stated "gems" (*maṇayo*) in order to show that agent. "Gems" (*maṇayo*) means jewels (*ratanāni*). This is the third. 4. The Fourth Training Rule. 1194.

Regarding the fourth, in the phrase "on head-ornaments, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes neck-ornaments and so forth. "Whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) refers to an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). This is the fourth.
5. The Fifth Training Rule (Pañcamasikkhāpada) 1199.
Regarding the fifth [rule]: "With perfume" (*gandhena ca*): it is called *gandha* because it scents—that is, it indicates and makes manifest its own base (*vatthu*).
"And with cosmetic" (*vaṇṇakena ca*): this refers to ointment (*vilepana*). For that which colors—that is, makes manifest the beauty of the skin—is called *vaṇṇaka*. By the word "and" (*ca*),...
It illuminates the compound sentence of the collective dvanda. This is the fifth [section].
6. The Sixth Training Rule: 1202.
In the sixth, there is no word that requires further explanation. This is the sixth.
7. The Seventh Training Rule (Sattama-sikkhāpada) 1208.
Regarding "rubbing" (*ummaddana*) in the seventh [rule]: it means rubbing by pressing firmly. Regarding "massaging" (*saṃbāhana*): it means massaging repeatedly. This is the seventh. 8–10.
The Eighth and Subsequent Training Rules.
1210. Regarding the three [rules] beginning with the eighth, there is no unique terminology. These are the eighth, ninth, and tenth.
11. The Eleventh Training Rule. 1214.
In the eleventh, "abhimukham eva" means "precisely facing. For the etymological meaning of *abhimukha* is "facing toward the face" (*mukhassa hi abhi abhimukhan*).
It should be done; the letter *a* [is used] in the locative case. By this, he shows that in the phrase "in front of" (*purato*), the suffix *-to* is used in the sense of the locative.
"Vicinity" (*upacāra*) means a vicinity of twelve cubits. The eleventh [section]. 12.
The twelfth training rule.

1219. Regarding the twelfth [section], it is stated "one who has not made an opportunity" (*akata-okāsa*) in order to show that the term *anokāsakata* is neither an improper compound nor a compound where the qualifying word stands outside the compound. It means: "a monk by whom no opportunity has been made" (*okāso na kato yena*).
By the word "without specifying" (*aniyametvā*), it shows that the term "without distinction" (*anodissa*) ends in the suffix *-tvā*. This is the twelfth.
13. The Thirteenth Training Rule. 1226.

Regarding the phrase "even in the vicinity" (*upacārepi*) in the thirteenth [rule]: this refers even to the vicinity (*upacāra*), which is defined as the area suitable for a boundary around an unenclosed village.
1227. Although the term "one whose robe has been stolen" (*acchinnacīvarikā*) is stated in general terms, it is intended here specifically; thus he says, "only the *saṅkaccika* robe."
It is called *saṅkacci* because people look at it from all sides and desire to cut it there; it is the area below the neck and above the navel.
It is called *saṃkaccika* because it should be worn covering that area (*saṅkacce nivasitabbaṃ*). That itself is the robe, thus it is the "saṃkaccika robe. This is the thirteenth [offense].
The ninth chapter, the Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear, is finished.
"All training rules" is the connection [of the phrase]. "From that" means from those one hundred and eighty-eight training rules; "having removed" is the connection.
"Therein" means among those minor rules. "In this" refers to the ten training rules.
This concludes the commentary on the minor rules in the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga.
The Exposition is complete.
5. The Exposition of the Meaning of the Pāṭidesanīya Training Rules:
Immediately following the Minor Rules (Khuddaka), there are eight rules known as the Pāṭidesanīyas, which have been included in this compendium in brief.
The construction is as follows: "By the compilers [of the Canon], this commentary on those eight rules known as *pāṭidesanīya* was set forth in brief.

(1228) "Whatever oils and so forth" is the connection. "Hi" indicates the detailed exposition. "Therein" refers to among the eight *pāṭidesanīya* rules. "Excluded from the *pāḷi*" means those excluded from the canonical text. "In all" means in all [instances] such as oils and so forth without exception.
The commentary on the *pāṭidesanīya* section of the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* is completed.

*Panā* indicates an alternative position. The connection is: "those phenomena which have been recited. *Tesaṃ* refers to the *pāṭidesanīya* (offenses requiring confession). Again, *tesaṃ* refers to the *sekhiya*, *adhikaraṇa-samatha*, and other categories of phenomena.
*Taṃ* refers to the exposition of the meaning; the connection is: "the wise say [this]. The letter *ya* serves as a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*). The construction here, however, is as follows:
immediately after those *pāṭidesanīya* offenses, there are the seventy-five *sekhiya* rules and those other phenomena.
The word *ca* is indicated as being elided; and regarding those seven rules for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*)—

which are called "legal issues" and were taught by the Blessed One— the wise declare that the same exposition of their meaning (*atthavinicchaya*) which I have stated in the *Vibhaṅga* for the training rules (*sekhiya*) and the rules for settling legal issues applies to the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* as well.
Therefore, the commentary on the meaning of those *sekhiya* and *adhikaraṇasamatha* rules has not been stated by me separately in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.
These commentaries on the meaning have not been stated by me here either, nor even in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*;
the particle *pi* is used here as an elided expression (*luttaniddiṭṭha*). The negative particle *na* should be construed with both actions.
“May all beings, having generated within their own mental continuums this path that destroys all taints through this meritorious deed, behold Nibbāna.
This verse does not exist in the manuscripts today, but it is found in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*); therefore, the construction here should be understood in this way.
"By this meritorious deed consisting of the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, and by this meritorious deed as well as other meritorious deeds"—
for the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. "All beings," meaning all sentient beings,
having generated and produced within their own personal continuum— the path that destroys all taints, the path to Arhatship which brings an end to all defilements— [may they realize it].
"May they behold Nibbāna, the final extinguishing of the aggregates, through the illumination of knowledge.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga within the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The exposition is complete.
By me, under the name Jādilañchita, the method of exposition for the analysis of the nuns' rules has been fully recited for many. Thus ends the exposition.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Explanation of the Mahāvagga: 1.
The Mahākhandhaka (The Great Section)
1. The Discourse on Awakening:
Having completed the method of exposition for the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*, I shall now provide the method of exposition for the *Mahāvagga* and the *Khandhaka*.
"Of both" means of both [the monks and nuns]. "Of the Pātimokkhas" means of the Pātimokkha-vibhaṅgas.
For here, by the mention of "Pātimokkha," their Vibhaṅgas are also included, either because they are not distinct or by the elision of the latter member of the compound.
"Khandhaka" refers to a collection of formal rules (paññatti). Here, the word *khandha* denotes the formal rules themselves; for the formal rules of the Vinaya are called "khandha. Of these...
“Khandhaka” means a collection (*samūha*). Alternatively, “khandha” means a heap (*rāsi*); for the word *khandha* expresses the sense of a heap.

The heap of the formulated rules of discipline (*vinaya-paññatti*) is called “khandha. The letter *ka* denotes one who makes manifest (*pakāsaka*). Thus, “Khandhaka” means that which makes manifest the heaps of the formulated rules of discipline;
that is the Khandhaka. Here, however, the construction is as follows: immediately after the recitation (*saṅgīti*) of both Pātimokkhas—
The great elders, who were experts in the *Khandhakas* and skilled in the *Khandhakas*, have recited this *Khandhaka*.
Now that the turn has come for a commentary upon that *Khandhaka*, this is the explanation of its obscure meanings (*anuttānattha-vaṇṇanā*). The connection is with the word "ye" (which ones).
The particle "hi" is an ornament of the sentence. "Yesaṃ" refers to the words; "te" refers to those meanings. "Bhave" (in the sense of...).
"Bhaveyya" means "it would be," or "it would be possible to be. "Tesaṃ" refers to the meanings. "Kiṃ" means "what purpose?

"Teti atthe, ñātūti" is the connection [meaning: "those meanings should be known"]. Alternatively, "teti atthā, avaṇṇitā" is the connection [meaning: "those meanings have been explained"]. "Tesaṃyeva" means "of those very meanings.
This, however, is the construction here: regarding those words for which the Blessed One has revealed the meanings in the word-analysis (padabhājanīya), of those...
"Of the words" (*padānam*) is a remainder of the text (*pāṭhaseso*). If we were to state their meaning again, when would there be an end, a completion of the commentary?
The intention is that it would never come to pass. Furthermore, what is the purpose of commenting on those meanings which are already plain?

The intention is that there is no purpose. [The phrase "by the intention, the connection, and the phrasing"] refers to the intention (*adhippāya*), the connection (*anusandhi*), and the phrasing (*byañjana*).

Furthermore, as for those meanings that have not been made explicit, since it is impossible to know those meanings or the meanings that have not been commented upon, this method of commentary applies specifically to those very meanings.
The word *iti* signifies completion. In passages such as "By him...
[he went] to Verañjā," there appears to be a specific causal reason expressed in the instrumental case; however, in the passage "By him... [he was] first fully enlightened," [there is none].
The construction here is: "Even though there is nothing [else]. This is an incomparable simile (*asadisopamā*). The word *kiñcāpi* indicates censure, while the word *pana* indicates esteem.
In the phrase "only by means of the instrumental case," the particle *eva* excludes both the accusative and the locative cases.
"Expression" (*abhilāpa*) means that which expresses the meaning directly; it is a sound (*sadda*). "From the beginning" means from the Verañjā Chapter (*verañjakaṇḍa*).
This refers to the statement beginning with, “At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was at Uruvelā.
Having said, “In others as well,” he stated, “In those following this,” in order to demonstrate that very point.
Anticipating the objection, “If there is no distinguishing reason, what then is the purpose of this statement? he says, “What then is the purpose of this? and so forth.
“Of this” refers to the statement beginning with, “At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was at Uruvelā.
The construction is: “The purpose is called the showing of the setting (nidāna). To clarify that very meaning, he said, “For which,” and so forth. The construction is:
“That which is both the going-forth and the full admission authorized by the Blessed One. And the connection is with the words “those which were authorized. “Those” [refers to them].

"Going forth," and so forth. "Perfect enlightenment" (*abhisambodhi*) refers both to the knowledge of the path of arahantship which has omniscience as its proximate cause, and to omniscience itself which has the knowledge of the path of arahantship as its proximate cause.

"At the great seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimahāmaṇḍe*) means at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the place where the great knowledge of the path and omniscience became manifest. "Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion.
*Therein*: with reference to that which was stated as “At that time, at Uruvelā,” and so forth. Regarding *at Uruvelā*, he says “at Mahāvelā” because the word *uru* here is a synonym for “great.
By the phrase “on a heap of sand,” he shows that the word *velā* has the sense of a “heap,” thereby excluding meanings such as “time” or “boundary.
However, if *uru* were the name of the sand itself, then *velā*— [The sentence is incomplete in the source text.]
Since this is the case, does it not follow that the meaning should be understood as "the broad limit"? To this he says:

"Because of the transgression of the limit, the broad [place] was brought [there], thus it is Uruvelā. By this he shows that the transgression of the limit (*velā*) results in *velā* through the elision of the final member of the compound, while "Uruvelā" is derived from "the broad [place] brought by the limit" through the transposition of the word order. "Therein" refers to the word "Uruvelāya. This very same point...
While explaining, he said: "In the past, it is said... and so forth. The connection is: "having gone forth when no Buddha had appeared.

"The ascetic’s going forth" means the going forth of a seer (*isi*), not the going forth of a recluse (*samaṇa*). "Agreed-upon observance" (*katikavatta*): "done" (*kata*) is the act; that which proceeds by what has been done is "agreed upon" (*katika*);
that very observance is "agreed-upon observance. The connection is: "they indeed made [it]," and so forth. "Whoever" (*yo*) means anyone at all. "Another" (*añño*) means other than himself.
"Another. The connection is with the word "let him scatter. "With a leaf-bag" means with a bag made of leaves. "From that" means from the making of the agreement and the observance of the rule.
"There" means in that place. "From that" means from the creating of the great heap of sand; it connects with the word "another. "It" refers to that place.
"That" refers to the great heap of sand.

Regarding the phrase “At the foot of the Bodhi tree,” he says, “Bodhi is called the knowledge in the four paths,” and so forth, in order to show that the name “Bodhi” was obtained by way of the vicinity of the Assattha tree.

By this, he demonstrates—according to the etymological meaning of “one who awakens to the four truths” (bujjhati) as *bodhi*—that the knowledge in the four paths is what is called “Bodhi. “Therein” (*ettha*) means at the Bodhi [tree], or in the Bodhi.
Or: this locative case is used in the sense of proximity (*samīpattha*). By the word "also" (*pi*) in "even a tree," he shows that it is not only path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*).

"At the root" means nearby. Regarding "firstly enlightened" (*paṭhamābhisambuddho*), he says "firstly enlightened" (*paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho*) to indicate a euphonic combination (*sandhi*) by way of the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsikalopa*).
By the word "having been" (*hutvā*), he shows the neuter past participle form of the word "first" (*paṭhama*). [It means] "right at the very beginning."

The connection is: "having become fully enlightened before all people. By saying "with a single cross-legged posture" (*ekena eva pallaṅkena*), he shows that it is an emphatic compound (*avadhāraṇa-samāsa*) meaning "one and only one cross-legged posture.
With the phrase "once... having folded [the legs]," he demonstrates the result of that emphasis.
Furthermore, "cross-legged posture" (*pallaṅka*) refers to the sitting position with the thighs bound together. "Experiencing the bliss of liberation" (*vimutti-sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī*).

Among the five kinds of liberation here—beginning with that by way of factor (tadaṅga)—it is specifically the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), which is termed "tranquillization" (paṭippassaddhi), that is intended;
thus he says, "the bliss of the attainment of fruition. The "attainment of fruition" refers to the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.
For it is called "liberation" (vimutti) in the sense of being freed from opposing defilements; the bliss associated with that is "bliss of liberation" (vimuttisukha).

It is the bliss of the attainment of the fruit of arahantship belonging to the fourth jhāna. Alternatively, the bliss born from that [attainment] is the bliss of liberation, the bliss of the subsiding of all defilements and suffering.
By the word "experiencing" (*paṭisaṃvedayamāno*), he shows that in the term "one who experiences" (*paṭisaṃvedī*), the suffix *ṇī* has the sense of the agent.
One is called "one who experiences" because one repeatedly and thoroughly speaks of it—that is, one experiences it.
The connection is: "he sat having experienced.

"The mode of conditionality" (*paccayākāra*) means the manner of arising of conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*). To the question, "Why is the mode of conditionality called dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)?", he says:

"For the mode of conditionality," and so forth. The word "for" (*hi*) means "truly" or "because. By the word "mutually" (*aññamañña*), [the meaning of] the term "dependent" (*paṭicca*) is [indicated].
By the word "shows" (*dasseti*), he indicates the function (*kamma*). By the word "in combination" (*sahite*), he indicates the sense of the prefix *sam-*.

By the word "in the Dhamma" (*dhamme*), he indicates its essential nature (*sarūpa*). "In this" (*ettha*) means in this *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the phrase "in forward and reverse order," or to the forward and reverse orders themselves.

The construction is: "That very mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*) is what is being spoken of. By the phrase "because of performing the task to be done by oneself," [he explains] the word "forward" (*anuloma*).
It shows the meaning of the word *sabhāva*. "That very same" refers to the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) itself. "That function" is the function to be performed by oneself.
"Due to its non-performance" means due to the non-performance of the function to be performed by oneself. By this, it shows the meaning of the word *paṭiloma* (reverse).
"By the very same method as before" means by the same method as before, starting with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.
"Vāti" means "or. "In the occurrence" (pavattiyaṃ) means in the occurrence of saṃsāra. "Anuloma" means favorable or corresponding.
"Itara" refers to the mode of conditions stated as "it is precisely from ignorance," and so forth. "Of that" refers to the occurrence. "Paṭiloma" means contrary;
"herein" refers to the compound term "anulomapaṭiloma. "The meaning should be understood" implies that here the meaning alone is intended, as is possible.

Showing either its fruit, or the exclusion of other word-meanings—according to the statement, "A word expresses meaning by excluding the meanings of other words"—he says, "But from the beginning," and so forth.
The word *yāva* denotes a limit. The connection is: "having reached the end as far as [that limit].

"From these" means from these two meanings already stated. In the phrase "he attended to it with the mind" (*manasākāsī*), the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs through the elision of the vowel *i*.
He said, "He attended to it with the mind. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it refers to the expression "he attended to it with the mind.

"In what way" (*yathā*) means by whatever mode. "This" (*idaṃ*) refers to this very mode. The construction is: "therein," in the textual passage beginning with "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavattho*) should be understood in this manner.
He says "ignorance" because, in the middle of a compound, the gender and number of the preceding member must be taken.
"And it is both that [condition] and a condition. However, in a sentence, the gender and number of the pronoun *taṃ* (tasaddena) must be taken according to the word immediately preceding it.
Since the phrase "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*) is to be connected with the phrase "arise" (*sambhavantī*), he said:
"Therefore, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. "In all phrases" means in all phrases such as "with volitional formations as condition, consciousness," and so forth.
"But in what way" (*yathā pana*) means: "but by whatever manner. "This" (*idaṃ*) refers to this manner. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the statement beginning with "the cessation of ignorance... etc.
Regarding the phrase "only of ignorance" (*avijjāyatveva*), one should analyze the compound as "Bhaddiya indeed" (*bhaddiyo iti eva*), as in "Bhaddiyotveva" and similar cases;
it should not be analyzed as "of ignorance indeed" (*avijjāya iti eva*). Rather, it should be understood as "of ignorance, however" (*avijjāya tu eva*). Thus he said.

"But it is precisely regarding ignorance (*avijjā*). This should be understood as being expressed here by a set of particles (*nipāta*), just as it was expressed in such passages as "the supreme release" (*pa-atimokkha*) or "the supreme excellence" (*atipamokkha*) by a set of prefixes (*upasagga*). Therein, the word *eva* excludes [the notions of] a sentient being, a life-principle, and so forth.
The word *tu* indicates another alternative position (*pakkhantara*). From the position of the direct order (*anuloma*), there is another position known as the reverse order (*paṭiloma*).

The meaning is "he made it with the mind. The compound *asesavirāganirodha* is an improper compound (*ayuttasamāsa*), and because it is a compound with a third-case term as the latter member, he says:

"from the complete cessation by means of the path known as dispassion (*virāga*). In that context, failing to connect the word *asesa* (complete) with the word *virāga* (dispassion), but instead connecting it with the word *nirodha* (cessation), is what is called an improper compound. By the phrase "by means of the path,"...
This shows the meaning of the word *virāga*. For the path is called *virāga* in the sense of "fading away" (*virajjana*).
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of formations," because they are ceased by means of the path, there is a cessation consisting of non-arising;
thus he says, "there is the cessation of formations as non-arising. And "cessation as non-arising" means cessation by way of non-arising, because it is ceased by way of total eradication. Thus...
The meaning is: “Just as with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations;

so too [is it] thus. Regarding the word *tattha* (“therein”), it refers to the statement beginning with “Thus of this” (*evametassā*). He says “of the whole” (*sakalassa*) because the word *kevala* is a synonym for *sakala*; the meaning is “without remainder.

Alternatively, he says “or of the pure” (*suddhassa*) because its meaning is unmixed due to being unmixed with [notions of] a sentient being, a life-principle, and so forth; [the meaning is] “devoid of a sentient being” (*sattavirahitassa*).

By this, he shows the state of purity. Regarding the phrase "of the mass of suffering" (*dukkhakkhandhassa*), since the word *khandha* here signifies a "heap," he says "of the heap of suffering" (*dukkharāsissa*).
Regarding the phrase "having understood this meaning" (*etamatthaṃ viditvā*), in order to show the referent of the word "this" (*eta-*) there, it is said "that which... and so forth. Therein:
The construction is: "there is cessation... by way of ignorance, etc. This is the meaning that has been stated. The connection is: "and there is an origin.

"At the time of being known" means at the time when it is manifest, at the time when it is established. Regarding the phrase "this inspired utterance," here the word *imaṃ* (this) is dependent on what is being spoken.
The construction is: "when that meaning has been known. "By way of understanding" means by way of thorough comprehension (*pakārena*).

Of the state of knowing. "Arising from knowledge associated with joy" means arising through knowledge that is associated with joy by way of simultaneous origination and so forth; or the connection is: "the utterance (*udāna*) is the associated source known as knowledge.
In this context, in what sense is it an "utterance"? It means in the sense of exultation (*udāna*), in the sense of rejoicing (*modana*), and in the sense of sporting (*kīḷana*). What is this?
What is called *udāna*? It is an utterance prompted by a surge of joy.
For just as that which, being unable to be contained within a vessel such as oil, flows over and spills out, is called a "spillage" (*avaseka*);
and just as water that cannot be held back by a pond, but flows over it, is called a "flood" (*ogha*); even so, that which is prompted by a surge of joy—

The heart is unable to sustain the expansion of the thought; that [expansion], becoming excessive and not remaining within, issues forth through the door of speech as a specific utterance independent of a recipient—this is called an "udāna.
By the phrase "he uttered words of gladness," the meaning of the verbal root *ud-ā-hṛ* as "uttering" is demonstrated.
The construction is: "The meaning of this *udāna* should be understood in this way. Regarding the word *yadā*, in order to show the explanatory phrase for the sense of the suffix *-dā*, he says:
"at which time. The particle *hava* is used in the sense of "expert" (*byatta*); for its meaning is "clearly manifest" (*pākaṭa*).
As for the word *pātubhavanti*, since the meaning of the prefix *pātu-* is already expressed by the particle *hava*, [it is not repeated].
Showing the meaning of the word *bhū* (to become), he said, "they arise" (*uppajjanti*).

"Accomplishers of penetration into the modes of conditionality in direct and reverse order" means they are those who accomplish the penetration into the modes of conditionality both in forward and backward sequence.

"Factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) refers to the thirty-seven states that belong to the side of enlightenment—that is, to the knowledge of the path. Alternatively, by the rule of eliding the middle term (*pātunipāta*), it is [equivalent to] the phrase "they come into being" (*bhavanti*).
Showing the meaning, he says: “They illuminate. In this method, the word *have* expresses the sense of certainty;
for its meaning is “indeed” or “certainly. “By way of clear realization” means by way of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*).
For path-knowledge is called “clear realization” (*abhisamaya*) because it proceeds toward and fully understands the four truths directly.

By the phrase "in the sense of burning away the defilements" (kilesasantāpanaṭṭhena), he shows the etymological meaning [of *ātāpa*] as: "it burns the defilements thoroughly, thus it is *ātāpa*. It is not a mere synonym for energy (*vīriya*) in general;
rather, it is specifically the energy of right exertion (*sammappadhāna*). Therefore, he says "possessing the energy of right exertion" (*sammappadhānavīriyavato*).

By this, he shows that in the term "*ātāpī*," the suffix *-ī* has the sense of possession (*vantu-attha*). [It possesses] the characteristic of closely contemplating the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇena*).
And by means of jhāna reckoned as the eight attainments, which has the nature of close contemplation after approaching an object such as a kasiṇa;

and by means of jhāna reckoned as insight, path, and fruit, which has the nature of close contemplation after approaching the characteristics such as impermanence—this is what is meant by "by means of jhāna with the characteristic of close contemplation of characteristics.
By the phrase "of one who has warded off evil," it is shown that evil (pāpa) has been warded off (bāhita).
By the word *anena*, he shows the meaning of the term *brāhmaṇa*. For the sound *aṇa* is a synonym for evil (*pāpa*).
By the phrase “of one whose taints are destroyed,” he shows its essential nature. “Then of him” means then, at that time, of the brahmin;
this is the connection with the words “those doubts which were spoken. And by the method beginning with “Who indeed...? and so forth, as well as “Which...? [it is explained].

The construction is: "And [these] were spoken in the manner beginning with ‘Now indeed... and so forth, regarding the mode of conditions (paccayākāra). “An ill-timed question” means an improper question;
the sense is that this is a bad question. “Thus” means either in this way or otherwise. The connection is: “and the sixteen doubts that have come down.
“Doubts because of non-penetration” is the construction. Regarding the “sixteen doubts”: five concern the past object, and [five] concern the future object...
There are five [types of doubt] regarding the past and six regarding present objects; thus, there are sixteen kinds of doubt. *Vapayantī* means they depart (*vi-apayanti*);
this euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs through the elision of the letter *i*. The prefix *vi-* follows the meaning of the verbal root, while the word *apayanti* has the sense of "departing";

therefore, he says "they depart. By the word "cease" (*nirujjhanti*), he illustrates that very same sense of departing by way of a synonym. By the question "Why? (*kasmā*), [he indicates] "from what..."
The phrase “he understands phenomena with their causes” shows the causal relationship with the preceding statement. Regarding the term *sahetudhamma*:
here, it is “with cause” (*sahetu*) because it is accompanied by causes such as ignorance; it refers to phenomena that have arisen from conditions, such as volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
To show the etymological meaning—that it is a phenomenon (*dhamma*) which is “with its cause” (*sahetu*)—he says, “by means of [ignorance] and so forth,” and so on. “He penetrates” (*paṭivijjhati*).
In the phrase "understand by means of this" (*iminā pajānā tī*), it shows the meaning of the verbal root *ñā* as "awakening" (*avabodhana*) and excludes other meanings such as killing or praising.
"Iti" means "therefore"; the construction is "vapayantīti" (they cause to flow).

2. Regarding "of the destruction of conditions" (*paccayakkhayassa*), the construction is "of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) which is the state of the destruction of conditions. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the second Udāna.
"Khayaṃ" means that conditions perish (*khīyanti*) therein; thus he said, "Nibbāna is the so-called destruction of conditions.
By the word "aññāsī" (he knew), he shows here that the root *vid* has the sense of knowing (*ñāṇa*), and excludes meanings such as experiencing or obtaining.
Therefore, it is connected with "vapayantī" (they cause to vanish). "Vuttappakārā" means similar to what was stated in the first udāna.
"Dhammas" refers either to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) or to the dhammas of the Four Noble Truths.
The connection is: "He uttered this exclamation (*udāna*). The construction is: "by which path it was known. "Therein" refers to the third exclamation.
The connection is: "that brahmin stands. Or [it means] by those arisen factors conducive to enlightenment, or by whichever noble path...
The phenomena of the Four Truths have become manifest; by that Noble Path, they shake off [the defilements]—this is the interpretation.
"Of the kind described" means of the kind described in the *Sutta Nipāta*. "The army of Māra" refers to the tenfold army of Māra, beginning with sensual desire (*kāma*).
By the word "shaking off" (*vidhamanto*), the sense of "dispelling" is shown here through the verbal root *dhūpa*, excluding senses such as "smearing."
By the phrase “shaking off [dust]” (*vidhamento*), he shows here the sense of shaking off (*dhaṃsanattha*) for the element *dhamu*;

he excludes other meanings such as those of sound (*saddattha*). In showing the meaning of the phrase “shining like the sun” (*sūriyova obhāsayaṃ*) as “like the sun” (*sūriyo iva*), he says “just as” (*yathā*) and so forth. “The sun” (*sūriya*) means the sun (*ādicca*).
For it is called “the sun” because it produces heroism (*sūra*) for the beings of the first eon.
“Abbhuggata” means gone upward toward the sky, or risen up into the sky. For the word *abbha* is a synonym for space (*ākāsa*).
Space is called “*abbha*” because it shines and gleams intensely (*ābhuso bhāti*); therefore, it is so termed.
Herein, this is the application of the simile: just as the sun stands illuminating [the world], so does the Brahmin [stand] regarding the Truths.
While penetrating [the truth]. Just as the sun stands dispelling darkness, so too does the brahmin scatter the army of Māra.
"In this" means in these three utterances (*udāna*). The connection is that "the first utterance arose.
Connecting the *Udāna-pāḷi* with this *Khandhaka-pāḷi*, he said: "But in the *Udāna*," and so forth. The connection is that it was "stated in the *Udāna*. "That" [refers to...].
The word "spoken" (*vutta*) connects with the statement in the *Udāna*. "By transgression" (*accayena*) means by passing over; explaining that very meaning, he said, "For then," and so forth.
"Then" (*tadā*) refers to the time when the attention was generated during the night, thinking, "I shall rise from my seat tomorrow.
The connection is: "The Blessed One took it to heart. The construction is: "The first two verses of the *Udāna* serve as an illustration of his majestic power (*ānubhāva*)."
“Of him” means of one who has attained the understanding of the mode of conditions and the destruction of conditions.
“Each one only” means each one only among the forward and reverse sequences. “And during the first watch” is the accusative case used to denote continuous connection;
the meaning is “during the time of the first watch without interruption. “But here” means but in this Khandhaka. Expanding upon that same point, he said: “For the Blessed One,” and so forth.
In this context, the connection is: "Therein the Blessed One uttered an inspired utterance. "On the full moon day of Visākha" means on the full moon day joined with the constellation Visākha.
The connection is: "at the time when it should be said, 'The dawn is about to break. "Omniscience" (sabbaññutaṃ) means the state of being omniscient;
the meaning is unobstructed knowledge. "From that" means from the rising of the dawn. "That day" is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative; it means "on that day."
The meaning is "on that very day. Alternatively, with the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*), the meaning is "during that time on that day.
"Having brought it thus to mind" means having brought it to mind in the same way he did on that day—both in direct and reverse order; such is the meaning. "Iti" means "thus. The construction is:
"That seven-day period which was described as 'at the foot of the Bodhi tree... [and so on]... he sat'—[that was spent there]. "Right there" means right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
2. The Discourse on the Cowherd (Ajapālakathā) 4.
Regarding the phrase "na bhagavā" (the Blessed One did not): here, the negative particle *na* should be construed with the word "upasaṅkamī" (he approached).
Thus, the meaning is "he did not approach. "From that concentration" means from that concentration of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. Immediately thereafter, there was no approaching.
Revealing it by means of a simile, he said, “Just as,” and so forth. The construction is: “It is not stated in this way. “This” refers to this collection of meanings.
“In this” refers to the sentence “having eaten, he lies down. “Thus” indicates the object of comparison (*upameyya*).
“In this case too” refers to this Pāḷi passage beginning with “Then the Blessed One. The construction is: “This” meaning is what is being illustrated.
*Ettha* means in the passage beginning with “Then the Blessed One.
*Aparānipi* means other [periods] besides the seven days spent on the couch. *Tatra* refers to the statement beginning with “aparānipi. The construction is: “when the Blessed One was seated.
The particle *kira* indicates an elaboration. *Kiṃ nu kho* is a particle used in the sense of reflection.
"Of some" means of some who are of little power. "Of them" refers to the deities.
"The place of attainment through power" means the place attained by means of power and majesty. "With unblinking eyes" means with eyes that do not blink. "For seven days":

this is the accusative case used in the sense of the object (*kamma*), or it expresses continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*). For if it is so, then "time" should be understood as the object. "That place" refers to [the place] with unblinking eyes.
The place being gazed upon by his eyes. "Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the seven days of not blinking. "The jeweled walkway" (*ratanacaṅkama*) refers to a walkway made of jewels.

"That place" (*taṃ ṭhānaṃ*) refers to the location of the walkway. "From there" (*tato*) means from the seven days spent at the walkway. "The jeweled house" (*ratanaghara*) refers to a dwelling made of jewels.
"Therein" (*tattha*) connects with the phrase "searching through the Abhidhamma Piṭaka" within the jeweled house. "In this" (*ettha*) refers to the jeweled house.
Or, in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this locative case is used in the sense of selection. "That place" means the place for investigating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.
"Thus," and so forth, is an indication of the connection of the subsequent statement by way of a conclusion to the preceding statement.
"By that" means by reason of the goat-herders' sitting there. "Of him" refers to Nigrodha. By the words "it was called 'the Goat-herders' Banyan,'" [it is shown...]

This shows the acquisition of a name by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Regarding the etymologies also shown in other treatises: it is called *Ajapāla* because the brahmins (*ajapā*) take up their residence there;
or, because in the heat of the season he protects (*pāleti*) the goats (*aja*) that have entered within his own shadow, he is called *Ajapāla*;
and since he is both *Ajapāla* and a banyan tree (*nigrodha*), he is called *Ajapālanigrodha*. In that context as well...

“Also at the Ajapāla banyan tree. “From the Bodhi tree” means from the tree of enlightenment (*bodhirukkha*). “There” refers to the Ajapāla banyan tree. The construction is: “while the Blessed One was seated there.
“In that place” refers to the passage beginning with “Then a certain...”. “He” refers to the brahmin.

“Named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika” means, it is said, he was named Diṭṭhamaṅgalika among the three types of those who regard omens—namely, those regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed. “By way of being a youth... [and so forth].

By the phrase "it is said," the meaning of the word *huṃhuṅkajātika* is shown: one who makes the sound "huṃ-huṃ" is a *huṃhuṅka*; one whose birth-nature or inherent character (*jāti-sabhāva*) is that of a *huṃhuṅka* is a *huṃhuṅkajātika*.
"By him" refers to the brahmin. "Reached the crest" means reached the summit. "Of it" refers to the *udāna*. "Who" refers to the person; "claims" means...
The connection [is as follows]: By the phrase “not because of making a sight auspicious,” he shows the fruit of the restriction.

By the phrase “because of having expelled evil states” (*bāhitapāpadhammattā*), he shows the etymological meaning: one by whom evil states have been expelled is “one who has expelled evil states” (*bāhitapāpadhamma*). By the phrase “by the abandoning of the *huṃ-huṃ* sound,” he shows the etymological meaning:
one for whom there is no *huṃ-huṃ* sound is “one free from *huṃ-huṃ*” (*nihuṃhuṃka*). [This is] by virtue of the absence of the taints such as lust and so forth.
By the phrase "this one has no taints such as lust," it shows the etymological meaning (*vacan-attha*) of *nikkasāva* (taintless) as "one whose [mind] has no taints.

By the phrase "because his mind is devoted to the practice of development," it shows the etymological meaning of *yatatta* (self-controlled) as "one whose mind is controlled (*yata*) and devoted (*anuyutta*) to that.
For here, the word *yata* denotes energy (*vīriya*) and is derived from the verbal root *yat*; the word *atta* is a synonym for the mind (*citta*). Regarding the word *yata*:
In order to show that it is produced from the Yamudhātu element, it is said: "Or by restraint of virtue," and so forth.

By the phrase "by means of a restrained mind" (*saññatacittatāya*), it shows the etymological meaning of the word *yatatta*: one who restrains (*yamati*) and fully restrains (*saṃyamatīti*) is *yata*; one whose mind (*citta*) is *yata* is *yatatta*.
According to the etymological meaning, "those which know (*vidanti*) and understand (*jānanti*) the truths" are called *vedā*; thus, the knowledges of the Path (*maggañāṇāni*) are named *vedā*.

Pointing this out, he says: "By means of the knowledges comprised within the four paths. Having changed the case ending in the phrase "of those comprised within the four-path knowledges," it should be joined with the word "of the Vedas" (*vedānam*).
"End" (*anta*) refers to Nibbāna; for since it is born at the conclusion of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it is called the "end.
Again, "end" refers to the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*); for since it occurs at the completion of the path, it is called the "end."

It has proceeded; therefore, it is called "the end. By the phrase "because the holy life (brahmacariya) of the path has been lived," he shows the meaning of the expression *vusitabrahmacariyo* as one by whom the holy life, which is defined as the path, has been lived.
In order to show the meaning of the statement "one should speak the Brahma-declaration in accordance with the Dhamma," he said: "I am a Brahmin"—this is the declaration.

“He should speak according to the Dhamma. Regarding “according to the Dhamma,” this means by way of what is real and its true nature. Regarding “in the world,” since the world of sentient beings is intended here, he says:
“in the entire habitation of the world. 3.
The Discourse on Mucalinda.

5. Regarding the phrase "unseasonable cloud" (*akālamegho*): it is not "unseasonable" because the time for sowing and so forth is absent; rather, it is called "unseasonable" because the rainy season has not yet arrived.

Thus he says, "when the rainy season has not yet arrived. By the phrase "a cloud that has arisen," he demonstrates the literal meaning of "unseasonable cloud" (*akālamegho*) as a cloud that has arisen at an improper time.
"In the last month of the summer" refers to the months of Jeṭṭha and Mūla. "In that [cloud]" refers to that very cloud. "Cold winds and cloudy days" means...

Here, by saying "the day was spoiled by a cold wind for this little hut," he states the meaning of the expression *sītavātaduddinī* (a day of cold wind and rain), beginning with the words "And that [hut], etc. The connection is: "And that little hut for seven days was known as 'a day of cold wind and rain'.
By the phrase "born near the lotus pond," it is shown that he was born in the vicinity of Mucalinda.
He shows the meaning of the word *mucalinda*. *Mucalinda* is a *nicula* tree; it is also called *nīpa* and *piyaka*.
Although the serpent’s hood (*bhoga*) is only one, because it possesses seven coils, it is expressed in the plural as “with hoods” (*bhogehi*).
The construction is: “while that king of serpents was standing there. “His” refers to the king of serpents. “Because” means because [the tree] was the size of a storehouse chamber.
Because it was so; therefore. It is called "the exposition of the cause of the occasion" (*ṭhānakāraṇaparidīpana*) because by means of this [passage] the cause of the occasion is fully illustrated;
it refers to the words beginning with, "Do not let the cold distress the Blessed One. "He" refers to the Nāga king. "Indeed" (*hi*) signifies truth.
He said, "Do not let the cold distress the Blessed One," because the verb "distressed" (*bādhayittha*) must be supplied from the text. "Therein" refers to: "Do not let the Blessed One..."
In the passage beginning with “It is cold,” the connection is with the phrase “while there was a seven-day rain. “That too” refers to the heat as well.
“Him” refers to the Blessed One. “His” refers to the nāga king. “Ubbiddha” means an opening above; for the words *viddha* and *chidda* are synonyms.
When the sky is covered by a mass of clouds, it appears as if near; when the mass of clouds has vanished, it presents itself as if distant.

Therefore it was said: "become distant through the disappearance of clouds. Regarding the phrase "devoid of clouds" (*vigatavalāhaka*), the word *vigate* expresses the sense of "gone away," and the word *valāhaka* is a synonym for "cloud";
thus he said, "devoid of clouds. Because it shines like an indranīla gem, it is called *deva*;
according to this etymological meaning, space is called *deva*. Thus he said, "space is *deva*. "Its own form" means its own...
"Shaped like a nāga. By this, he shows that in the phrase "his own form," the word *saka* (own) denotes the self (*atta*), and the word *vaṇṇa* (form) is a synonym for shape (*saṇṭhāna*).

Regarding "seclusion is bliss," among the five kinds of seclusion—namely, those consisting of seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*), suppression (*vikkhambhana*), eradication (*samuccheda*), tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*)—it is the seclusion of escape, which is Nibbāna; and among those consisting of seclusion of body, mind, and acquisitions (*upadhi*)...

Regarding the three kinds of seclusion (*viveka*), it is said that the seclusion from the substrates (*upadhiviveka*), which is synonymous with Nibbāna, must be included; thus he says, "the seclusion from the substrates, which is synonymous with Nibbāna.
By the phrase "with satisfaction through the knowledge of the four paths," he excludes [other forms of] contentment such as contentment with alms-food (*piṇḍapātasantosa*).

Regarding the term "of the heard Dhamma" (*sutadhammassa*), he states "of the proclaimed Dhamma" because the word *suta* here is a synonym for *vissuta* (renowned); that is, of the clearly manifest True Dhamma (*pākaṭasaccadhamma*).

The meaning [is as follows]. Regarding the word "passato" (seeing): since there might be a misconception here that it refers to the function of the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), he says, "by the eye of knowledge" (*ñāṇacakkhunā*).

By the phrase "the state of being unshakeable" (*akuppanabhāvo*), both the fact that the word *vyāpāda* denotes "hatred" (*dosa*) and the fact that the suffix *-ṇya* has the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvattha*) are shown.
"By this" refers to the term "abyāpajja. "The preliminary stage of loving-kindness" (*mettāpubbabhāgo*) refers to [the preliminary stage] of non-affliction (*abyāpajja*).

The state of having arisen through loving-kindness (*mettā*) in its prior stage. Regarding the phrase "restraint toward living beings" (*pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo*), since the terms *pāṇa* and *bhūta* here function as synonyms for "beings" (*satta*), he says "and toward beings.
The "prior stage of compassion" (*karuṇāpubbabhāgo*) refers to the state of having arisen through compassion in the prior stage of restraint.
"That" (*yā*) refers to that state of dispassion (*virāgatā*). Because of the complete abandonment of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) by means of the non-returner path (*anāgāmimagga*).
It is said: "By this, the path of non-returning is explained. Because the conceit of "I am" has been ceased by the path of arahantship, it is said:
"'I am'... [etc. ...is explained. "From this" means from arahantship. 4.
The Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree.
6. "In the eastern corner" means in the eastern horse [quarter], that is to say, in the southeastern direction. "The Rājāyatana tree" refers to the *khīrikā* tree.
Regarding the phrase "At that time," having asked about the scope of the word *tad* (that), he says, "By what occasion?
The construction is: "of the Blessed One who was seated. As for the term "Devarāja" (King of Gods), there are others such as Pajāpati and so forth.
It is said that he is called "Sakka" because he can cause the kings of the gods to turn back. "That" refers to the myrobalan fruit (*harītaka*).

The connection is with the phrase "as soon as it had been consumed by the Blessed One. When the Blessed One was seated—by the words "at that time," it is indicated that at the very time the Blessed One sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree—by that...
"Then at that time" indicates the meaning [of the occasion]. "From the country of Ukkala" means from the country named Ukkala.
The construction is: "the region where the Blessed One was dwelling. "Therein" refers to the phrase "having set out on the high road toward that region.
"Of them" refers to the merchants. Since the words *ñāti* and *sālohita* are synonyms for one another, when *ñāti* is mentioned, the word *sālohita* [is also implied].
In order to show that the purpose was accomplished, it is said: “the deities who were formerly kinsmen. “She” refers to the deity. “Of them” means of the merchants.
“From that” means from the cause of the cessation [of the caravan]. “They” refers to the merchants. “This” refers to the cessation. “Force” means an offering. “Of them” refers to the merchants.
The phrase “having combined with honey, molasses, and so forth” looks back to what precedes and forward to what follows; therefore, it belongs in the middle.

It has been stated. Regarding the word *patimānetha*: since it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—specifically in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* under root number 18, the *nakārantadhātu*—that the root *māna* signifies "worship" (*pūjā*) and "affection" (*pemana*), [the commentator] said "attend upon" (*upaṭṭhahatha*) because, in meaning, worship and affection consist of attending upon.
Regarding the phrase *taṃ vo*: here the pronoun *taṃ* refers to the object of worship, while the particle *vo* is a substitute for the word *tumha* among the three instances of that particle.
The suffix *vos* has the sense of the fourth case; thus he says, "that [suffix] for you as the object. For the function (*kāriya*) of the word *tumha* is threefold:

the function of the personal pronoun, the function of the second-person plural ending, and the function of a verse-filler (*padapūraṇa*). Among these, the function of the word *tumha* as a personal pronoun is fivefold, by way of the nominative, accusative, instrumental, dative, and genitive cases. Therein, the function of the word *tumha* as a personal pronoun...

Here, the word *sampadāna* (recipient) is intended; therefore he says, "yours" (*tumhākan*). Since the scope of the word "which" (*yaṃ*) is the sense of receiving, he says, "that which is the receiving.
*Assa* means "it would be. The construction is: "that bowl which had been [there]. *Assa* refers to the Blessed One. *So* refers to the bowl.
The connection is: "as Sujātā was coming. This genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. By that... [end of fragment].
"By way of the cause of disappearance. "Of him" (assa) means of the Blessed One. "In the hands" (hatthesu)—this locative expression is used in the sense of the instrumental;
for the meaning is "by means of the hands" (hatthehi).

"In what? (kimhi) means by what. "From here" (ito) means from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī. "This much time" (ettakaṃ kālaṃ) refers to this measure of time, a period of forty-nine days.
*Jighacchā* means the desire to eat. *Pipāsā* means the desire to drink. *Assa* means of the Blessed One (*bhagavato*).
Because the words *cetasā* and *ceto* require a correlative, it is stated "of himself" (*attanoti*) and "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) to show their connection.
This shows that because these correlatives are dissimilar, the relationship itself is also dissimilar. "Of himself" refers to [the mind] of the four...

[He said] "to the Great King. He spoke thus, "from the four directions," showing that a compound primarily emphasizes the whole (the aggregate), whereas a sentence primarily emphasizes the parts. In the original text (*pāḷi*), the word "having come" (*āgantvā*) is to be supplied as a remainder.
By the word "made of stone" (*silāmaye*), he shows the meaning to be "made of rock" (*selāmayam*). "This" refers to the expression "in the bowl made of stone" (*selāmaye patte*). "Yet" (*ye*)...
"In bowls made of stone the color of green mung beans. "From that" means from the presentation of the bowls made of sapphire (*indanīlamaṇi*);
"to them" is the connection [with the following]. "Of those" refers to the four Great Kings. "All four also resolved" is the connection. "In such a way" means by whatever manner;
it should be construed as "while they were being resolved. "Identical" means absolutely identical. "When the bowls had been resolved" is the connection.
The locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; for the meaning is "he received with a bowl.
Regarding the word *paccaggheti*, since the vowel *e* is a grammatical modification (*kāriya*) of the locative suffix *smiṃ*, he says "in *paccagghasmin*" [to indicate the locative].

Having analyzed the compound into *paṭi* and *agghanti*, he shows that the prefix *paṭi* has a distributive sense, and that although it is stated generally as "worth" (*agghanti*), its specific meaning here is "of great value."
He said, "It is expensive when separate. By this, he shows that four [items] together are not expensive, but when separate they are expensive.
Alternatively, since the word *paccaggha* with its prefix (*pa*) is a synonym for "new," he said, "in what is new.
And "new" is a name for cloth that has not long been worn; because it has not long been worn, it is [called] "new."
It is as if it were fresh; therefore, it is said, "fresh. By the phrase "arisen at that very moment," he clarifies this same meaning.
Showing that the word *dvivācikā* is formed both by means of a compound (*samāsa*) and by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), he says, "two utterances," and so forth.
Regarding the word *pattā*, one particle (*iti*) is indicated as being elided. Thus, [the term is] *dvivācikā*.

"Meaning" (*attha*) is the connection [to be made]. "They" (*te*) refers to the merchants. "Then" (*atha*) means at that time. "Those" (*te*) refers to the hair. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the merchants. "Carry away" (*pariharatha*) means:
having accepted it as the place for one's own salutation and rising from one's seat, or having demarcated it, carry it away;
such is the meaning. "They" (*te*) refers to the merchants. "As if with the Deathless" (*amateneva*) means as if with the Deathless; the connection is "as if anointed."
5. The Discourse on the Request by Brahmā.
7. “The Blessed One approached” provides the connection. “In that” refers to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
“Practiced and well-practiced” means practiced and rightly practiced; it was not practiced by one Buddha alone, but rather practiced and well-practiced by all Buddhas.
*Atiāciṇṇo* means "constantly practiced. Expanding upon the meaning stated in brief, he says, "For they know," and so forth.
*Dhammadesanaṃ* refers either to the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, or to the Blessed One for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, or to the Blessed One as the teaching of the Dhamma.
*Tato* means "because of that request. *Hī* signifies "truly" or "since. The dwelling of the world holds the Brahmā in high esteem.
The construction is: "Because [of this], therefore they will cause [them] to arise. The phrase beginning with "iti" is the conclusion.

Regarding the word "tattha," it refers to the reading in the section on the modes of reflection (*parivitakkana*). By the phrase "they cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇesu allīyanti*), he shows the meaning of the term *ālaya*: "They cling" (*allīyanti*) means they adhere; they are called *ālayas* because one clings to them and becomes attached to them in the sense of something to be enjoyed.
Thus, "the five strands of sensual pleasure are *ālayas*" is the literal definition. "They cling" (*allīyanti*) means they adhere.
There is also a reading: “*pañca kāmaguṇe allīyantī*. This being the case, the etymological meaning should be understood as follows:

they are called *ālayā* (attachments) because they are clung to (*allīyanti*)—that is, resorted to—in the sense of being enjoyed; thus, the five strands of sensual pleasure are attachments. “*Allīyantī*” means they resort to [them]. “*Te*” refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Regarding the phrase “*yadidan*,” by dividing it into the words “*yaṃ*” and “*idan*,” both “*yaṃ*” and “*idan*” are pronouns.
Thinking that there might be doubt, he said: “*Yadidaṃ* is a particle.
By this, he shows that because it does not undergo destruction, modification, or change across the three genders and two numbers, it is called *abyaya* (indeclinable);

however, its meaning should be understood as being exclusively that of a pronoun (*sabbanāma*). The connection is: “of that,” namely, of the particle *yadidaṃ*; [the word] “meaning” (*attha*) is the link.
“*Ṭhānaṃ*” refers to the word “*ṭhānaṃ*. “*Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ*” refers to the word “*paṭiccasamuppādo*. It should be understood that the meaning is indeed appropriate.
“*Imesaṃ*” refers to the formations (*saṅkhārā*) and so forth, which have arisen through conditions. “*Paccayā*” means causes such as ignorance (*avijjā*).
By the phrase “*idappaccayā eva*,” he illustrates here the specific sense of the suffix *tā* in the term *idappaccayatā*, just as in words such as “*devatā*.”
Regarding the phrase "it would be weariness for me," he says, "that which is called teaching those who do not understand," showing the scope of the word *taṃ* (that).
By this, he shows that the scope of the word *taṃ* consists of two action-phrases—namely, "I would teach" and "they would not understand"—and not of a single action-phrase alone.
The word *so* (it) refers to the application of body and speech known as "teaching"; by this, [he indicates] the scope of the sentence.

This shows that the word *ta* takes on the gender and number of the following member (*uttarapada*) alone; however, when situated in the middle of a compound, the word *ta* takes on the gender and number of the preceding member (*pubbapada*).
Therefore it is said: “It is ignorance (*avijjā*) and it is a condition (*paccaya*),” and “It is the Abhidhamma and it is a Piṭaka,” and so forth.
*Kilamatha* means the cause of bodily fatigue. It is called *kilamatha* because one becomes fatigued by means of it.

*Kilamatho* means "fatigue. *Assā* means "there might be. *Sā* refers to the teaching, which consists of the application of body and speech. *Vihesā* means "affliction" (*vihimsā*), because it is the cause of bodily affliction.

It is called *vihesā* because one is afflicted by means of it. However, for the Buddhas, there is neither fatigue nor affliction of mind, because both have been utterly eradicated by the path of Arahantship.
Regarding the word *paṭibhaṃsu*: here, because of its connection with the accusative case (*kammappavacanīya*), [the word *bhagavantaṃ*] is used [as the object].
Here, because it is used in the sense of identity, he says "of the Blessed One. By the phrase "not non-wondrous," he excludes the analysis of the word as "not wondrous";

the meaning is that they were wondrous again and again. Regarding the word *paṭibhaṃsu*, here the prefix *pati-* has the sense of "manifestation" (*paṭibhāna*), and the verbal root *bhā* has the sense of "appearing" (*khāyana*);
thus he says, "they became the objects of knowledge known as manifestation."
By the phrase “they became the range,” he shows that what is called "manifestation" (khāyana) is, in meaning, existing as the state of being a range.
The connection is: "I proclaimed the Dhamma attained by me," or "by me.

When it is said that the stream of the Noble Path is "against the stream" (paṭisota), he says "Nibbāna itself is called 'against the stream,'" because it is Nibbāna that is meant. [The term] "leading to Nibbāna" means...
The Noble Path. For since the Noble Path leads to Nibbāna, it is therefore called "leading to Nibbāna" (*nibbānagāmī*).

Regarding the phrase "by the mass of darkness" (*tamokhandhena*), here the word *tama* is a synonym for ignorance (*avijjā*), and the word *khandha* has the sense of a heap or collection; thus he says, "by the heap of ignorance.
By the word "enveloped" (*ajjhotthaṭā*), he shows that in the word *āvuṭā*, the verbal root *vudh* has the sense of covering. "To a state of indifference" (*appossukkatāya*)...

Here, the prefix *apa-* has the sense of absence (*abhāva*), while the suffix *-tā* has the sense of being (*bhāva*); thus he says, "by way of the state of being free from anxiety" (*nirussukkabhāvena*).
