8. "In the world" (*loke*) means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "Great Brahmās" (*mahābrahmā*) refers to the Great Brahmās.

Regarding the term "of a nature with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*): here, those who have little dust (*raja*) in their eyes are "those with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhā*); those whose birth-nature (*jāti*), that is, their inherent character (*sabhāvo*), consists of such [persons] are "of a nature with little dust in their eyes" (*apparajakkhajātiko*).
Showing the meaning of the words, he said, “consisting of wisdom,” and so forth. By the term “consisting of wisdom,” he excludes the sense of “consisting of flesh.
“Of these” refers to sentient beings. In the word “dhammassa,” the genitive case is used in connection with the suffix *tu*.
Since the verbal root *ñā* preceded by the prefix *ā* has the sense of “penetrating,” he said, “those who have penetrated.”
“Those who possess impurity (mala) are ‘impure ones’ (samalā), namely the six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa;

it is by means of them [that the term is used]. By the phrase “by lust and so forth,” he shows the essential nature of that impurity. Regarding the word *avāpuretaṃ*, since the verbal root *pur* preceded by the prefixes *ava-* and *ā-* has the meaning of “opening,” he says, “open this.
By changing the letter *va* to *pa*, there is also a reading as *apāpuretaṃ*. [This refers to] the word *amata*.
It was stated "of Nibbāna" in order to exclude water and so forth. The connection is: "May these beings hear.
Regarding the word *vimalena*, he says "due to the absence [of stain]" because the prefix *vi-* here has the sense of non-existence.

By this, he shows the etymological meaning: "that which has no stain (*mala*) is *vimala*. With the phrase "by the Fully Enlightened One," he shows the nature of the external referent (*aññapadatthasarūpa*). In due order...
Regarding the phrase "to be awakened by the path," when it is said "awakened to" (anubuddha), it means that the Dhamma of the Four Truths is to be grasped;
thus he says, "the Dhamma of the Four Truths. By the word "selamaye" (made of stone), he shows the etymological meaning as "that which is produced from stone is 'selo'.

By the phrase "with omniscient knowledge" (sabbaññutaññāṇena), he shows the actual nature of the Universal Eye (samantacakkhu). The construction is: "You, O Blessed One, too [are like that]. The word "dhamma" is a synonym for wisdom (paññā).
He said: "Consisting of Dhamma, consisting of wisdom. One from whom sorrow has departed is "one whose sorrow has departed" (apetasoko), referring to the Blessed One.

Those who have plunged into sorrow are "those plunged in sorrow" (sokāvatiṇṇā), referring to the multitude of people. The word "and" (ca) should be construed with both "plunged in sorrow" and "overcome by birth and old age.
By this, he shows that the word "and" is indicated as being elided.
The word “Bhagavā” should be connected with “Vīro” and so forth. By the phrase “on account of possessing heroism,” he shows the etymological meaning: one who has heroism (*vīram*) is a hero (*vīro*).

In the context of grammatical analysis (*viggaha*) within the meanings of words used as modes of address, no analysis should be performed; however, this was stated here for the purpose of demonstrating their meaning.

It should be seen thus: by the phrase “the son of the gods... because he has conquered,” the etymological meaning is shown as “one who has conquered the battle” (*vijitasaṅgāma*), since the battle against Māra has been won by him.
And here, the Māra of the aggregates (*khandhamāra*) is included within the Māra of Death (*maccumāra*), because both Māras have been conquered together.
It is joined with the first syllable “*satta*” (seven) and the second syllable “*sattha*” (leader).
In this context, regarding the term *satthavāha*: when it is spoken figuratively as "caravan leader" (*satthavāha*), it is connected with the second syllable;
when it is spoken in its primary sense as "one who carries beings" (*sattavāha*), it is connected with the first syllable. Here, however, he says it is connected with the first syllable:
"He carries beings, thus he is a 'carrier of beings' (*sattavāha*). The Blessed One is *aṇaṇo* (debtless), meaning that he has no debt.
9. Regarding "the Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakkhu*): here, the eye is twofold, by way of the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*) and the wisdom eye (*ñāṇacakkhu*).

Therein, the fleshly eye is also twofold, by way of the sensitive eye (*pasādacakkhu*) and the structural eye (*sasambhāracakkhu*). Among these, the sensitive material form is called the sensitive eye;
the mass of flesh delimited by the eyebrows and the bones is called the structural eye. The wisdom eye, however, is fivefold.
By way of the divine eye, the wisdom of the Dhamma, and the Buddha’s universal eye. Therein, the knowledge of the supernormal power of the divine eye is called the "divine eye";
the three lower paths are called the "Dhamma-eye"; the knowledge of the path of Arahantship is called the "wisdom-eye";

and the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties as well as the knowledge of their underlying tendencies is called the "Buddha-eye"; [and] omniscient knowledge— [Note: The provided text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* or a similar work.]
It is called "the all-seeing eye" (*samantacakkhu*). However, since it is stated here as "by the Buddha-eye," he says, "and by the knowledge of the faculties...
etc.," because it refers specifically to the two aforementioned knowledges. "Hi" means truly. "Of whom" refers to sentient beings. "Faith and so forth":
by the word "etc.," he includes the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. "Sharp" means keen. "Gentle" means more subtle.
“Ākāra” means causes. These three pairs are stated by way of external compound (bāhiratthasamāsa).

To show the meaning of the words “easily made to understand” (*suviññāpayā*) and likewise “difficult to make to understand” (*duviññāpayā*), he said: “those for whom the reasons have been told,” and so forth.

“The other world and blame” (*paralokavajja*) refers to the other world and blame; those who see these as fearsome are “those who see fear in the other world and blame” (*paralokavajjabhayadassāvino*).
Showing the meaning of the words, he said “ye,” and so forth. These two pairs are spoken of by way of a gambler;
here, in the latter pair, the second phrase “not even some [who] see fear in the blame of the next world” is not stated, but in the Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi it is stated by way of a couplet.
According to the etymological meaning—“there are blue lotuses (*uppala*) here”—it refers to a grove (*gaccha*).
A creeper, a lotus pond, or a forest is called "uppalinī" (a place of blue lotuses); however, here he says "in the forest" (*uppala-vane*).
The connection is with the word "being submerged. "Nourishing" means they grow;
by this, he shows the etymological meaning of *antanimuggaposīnī* as "nourishing while remaining submerged within. By the phrase "equal to the water," [he indicates] by the water...
"Level and level with the water" shows the meaning of "standing level with the water.
By the word "having surpassed," it shows the meaning of the phrase "having risen above" as "having risen very high.
"Covered" means those that have been clothed; "uncovered" means those not clothed. In its actual sense, "uncovered" means an opening.
He said, "It is 'opened'"; this refers to the Noble Path. "Hi" means "truly. "In the last two lines" means in the final two lines of the verse.
"This very meaning" is to be construed as: "this meaning which is about to be explained should be understood in this way. "Hi" indicates elaboration.

Regarding the phrase "they do not speak," because he is a supreme person (*uttamapurisa*), it is stated as "I. Although one should say "among gods and men," the term "among men" is used by way of the grammatical principle of *ekasesa* (retaining only one of two similar terms).
He said, "Among gods and humans," because it was so stated.
6. The Discourse on the Group of Five. 10.
*Ṭhānuppattiyā* means by way of the arising through a cause. One whose birth-nature (*jāti-sabhāva*) is free from defilement is called "one of undefiled birth" (*nikkilesajātiko*).

Although it is stated without qualification as simply “knowledge” (*ñāṇa*), in its actual meaning it is specifically the knowledge of non-obstruction; thus he says, “the knowledge of omniscience” (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
“From this” means from the day of the reflection, “I shall teach the Dhamma”; the connection is with the word “below.
However, the deity knew only of Āḷāra’s passing away, not his rebirth in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*); but the Blessed One—
He knows everything; therefore it is said, “reborn in the sphere of nothingness.
By the phrase “because of being deprived,” he shows the meaning of the verbal root *hā* in the word *mahājāniyo*. “Of him” (*assa*) refers to Āḷāra.

Regarding “one who has great loss” (*mahājāniko*), when it should have been said “one who has great loss” (*mahājāniko*), the letter *k* was changed to *y*, and thus it is said “mahājāniyo. “Inopportune moment” (*akkhaṇe*) refers to [the lack of opportunity] for living the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"In the open space" means in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*). "Yesterday" means on the day immediately preceding. "He too" refers to Udaka Rāmaputta;
the word "too" (*pi*) refers back to Āḷāra. In that regard, since Āḷāra Kālāma was an attainer of the jhāna of the base of nothingness, he was reborn in the base of nothingness.
Udaka Rāmaputta was an attainer of the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
Therefore, it should be understood that he is reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).
To show that both readings—“bahukārā” and “bahūpakārā”—are appropriate, it is stated: “bahukārāti bahūpakārā.
The construction is: “to one whose self (*attabhāva*) has been sent forth. By this, he shows that in the word *pahitatta*, the term *atta* denotes the body.

11. Because it is connected with the particle *antarā*, the accusative case is used here in the sense of comparison in the phrases "Gaya" and "Bodhi"; thus he says, "of Gaya and of the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Among the four occurrences of the word *sabbam* in the verse, he states "all phenomena of the three planes," etc., showing that the second occurrence of *sabbam* has the sense of "without remainder" (*anavasesa*), while the others have the sense of "with remainder" (*sāvasesa*).
The meaning of the words is easy to understand. [This applies] even to the fruit of arahantship.
Because of the destruction of craving, it is said: "in the destruction of craving, in Nibbāna. The word *sayaṃ* is a synonym for *atta* (self), while the word *abhiññāya* contains the suffix *-tvā*;
thus he says, "having known by oneself. By the phrase "all phenomena of the four planes," he shows the object of the verbal root *ñā* (to know).
"This is my teacher" is an illustration of the manner of pointing out.
By the phrase “supramundane states,” the Teacher shows that there are indeed mundane states.

Regarding the term *paṭipuggala*, he says “a counterpart person” (*paṭibhāgapuggalo*), because here the prefix *pati-* has the sense of “counterpart. The meaning is that there is no person who is his equal.
“Become cooled” (*sītibhūto*) means having become cool, or having attained the state of coolness.
“Kāsī” is the name of the provinces (*janapada*), as it is stated in the plural form. Because a collection of provinces is called a kingdom (*raṭṭha*), it is said “in the kingdom of Kāsi.
By the word “city” (*nagara*), he shows that the term *pura* is a synonym for city. “For the sake of obtaining” means for the purpose of causing [it] to be obtained.
By the word “drum” (*bherī*), he shows that the word *dundubhi* is a designation for a drum. Drum.
Indeed, because it is filled with both [kinds of sound] by means of the sound "duṃ-duṃ," it is called *dundubhī*.
There is also a reading *dun-dubhī* formed by joining the letters *da* and *ra*, but that is simply not a valid reading.

In the phrase "I shall strike" (*paharissāmi*), the word *pahāra* indicates the meaning of the verbal root *ā-han* (to strike) with the prefix *ā-*; and by the word *ssāmi*, the suffix of the present tense (*ajjatanī*) is shown.
He shows that the state of occurring in the future time [is implied], and by the word *iti*, he shows the elision of the word *iti* which expresses the mode of going.

"Anantajina" (Victor of the Infinite) means one who has conquered all enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*) by means of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, which serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) designated as "the infinite";
by this metaphorical application of the fruit, he shows his status as the Victor of the Infinite. "Huveyya pāvuso" (May the venerable one call upon me).

Here, having analyzed the phrase as “huveyya api āvuso,” he says, “Friend, ‘it might indeed be so’ (evaṃ nāma bhaveyyā),” showing that the verbal root *hud* expresses the sense of existence (*satta*) and the particle *api* expresses the sense of such a name.
By changing the letter *va* to *pa*, the reading “hupeyyā” is likewise appropriate.

12. By the phrase “practicing for the sake of abundance,” he shows the meaning of the term *bāhullika* as one who practices for the sake of abundance. “From exertion” means from striving in difficult ascetic practices.

By the word “fallen” (*bhaṭṭho*), he shows that here, in the sense of “one who has departed” (*vibbhanto*), the meaning is “fallen” (*bhaṭṭho*) in the sense of the non-abiding of the verbal root *bhram* (to wander/deviate). Regarding the word “stream” (*sotaṃ*) here...
Because the term *sota-sadda* (ear-sound) denotes ear-consciousness (*sota-viññāṇa*) and so forth, it is called the "ear-faculty" (*sotindriya*). Regarding the word *iriyā*:
here, showing the etymological meaning as "moving about" (*iriyana*), "wandering" (*caraṇa*), or "conduct" (*iriyā*), he says, "of difficult conduct" (*dukkara-cariyā*).

Regarding the phrase *abhijānātha no*: here, the word *no* has the sense of the particle *nu*; thus he says, "do you recognize? (*abhijānātha nū*). The word *vākya* means that which expresses. Regarding the word *saññāpetuṃ*: [it means] to cause to perceive.
The phrase "I am the Buddha" was spoken in order to demonstrate the manner of making himself known. (13) "Iti" means from the beginning, starting with the words "the eye-maker.

"Padatthato" means both according to the words and according to the meaning, or else according to the meaning of the words. "Iti" means as previously stated. "Hi" means truly. "Suttantakathaṃ" refers to the statement spoken by way of the discourses. (18) "By tens of millions of deities" means by tens of millions of deities reckoned as Brahmas.
This is to be construed with the connection: "of that venerable one who was established. "That very [ordination] is the *ehibhikkhu* (come, monk) higher ordination"—this is the construction.
19. The connection is: "On the second day, the Dhammacakkhu arose. The phrase beginning with "on the second day" is stated in reference to the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipadadivasa*).
"Of the fortnight" means of the dark fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī. "All those bhikkhus" is the construction.
"By the *Anattasutta*" means by the *Anattalakkhaṇa-suttanta*.

"On the fifth day of the fortnight" means on the fifth day of the lunar half-month (*pakkha*). "In the world" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). By the phrase "human arahants," he shows that divine arahants are numerous.
7. Discourse on Going Forth (Pabbajjākathā) 31.
"Ancient and further ancient" means those things belonging to the past and the further past. "Sixty-one" means one and sixty, or sixty plus one; thus, it is sixty-one.
*Therein*: among those sixty-one human arahants. *Former application*: a means previously employed; the meaning is "former support. *By binding in groups*:
by forming them into a collective. *They*: those fifty-five people. *We shall burn*: we shall be consumed by fire.
*They carried out*: they carried them out from the village. *Among them*: among those fifty-five people. *Setting aside five people*.
The connection [is as follows]. "The rest" means those remaining from among the five people. "He" refers to the boy Yasa. "Those too" refers to all four people.

"Therein" means in the body. "All of them" refers to all those companions together with Yasa’s mother, father, and wife. "By that" means by the power of their former application. "Addressed" means he spoke.
32. Showing that the divine objects are "divine" because they exist among the divine [spheres] and are snares of greed (*lobhapāsa*), he said, “The so-called divine,” and so forth.
“Snares of greed” means bonds consisting of greed. Regarding the phrase “by not hearing,” the word is in the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental;

thus he said, “by not hearing. Regarding the phrase “they fall away,” he asked, “By what do they fall away? and replied, “From the attainment of distinction (*visesādhigama*). “From the attainment of distinction” means—
Because of the attainment of the distinction known as the path and its fruits (maggaphala). 33.
To show the etymological meaning of "antaka" as one who makes [beings] "anta"—that is, base—he says "base.
By the phrase "inferior beings," he shows the actual nature of the "antaka. This is a vocative address. "That" refers to the snare of lust. "Hi" means truly.

He is Māra the Evil One. Because he is a bond even for those who possess the five higher knowledges (*pañca-abhiññā*) as they move through the sky, the term *antalikkhacaro*—meaning "one who moves in the sky" according to its etymological sense—is used by Māra the Evil One to refer to the snare of lust (*rāga-pāsa*). 34.
"From various countries" means from various countries within even a single direction. [This is seen] in such passages as: "I allow... you should give the going-forth," and so forth.
The construction is: "The exposition (vinicchaya) is to be understood thus. The connection is: "He should be ordained by the monk who ordains.
The construction is: "Those persons who are prohibited. "From another" means in another [text]. The construction is:
"beginning with the canonical text (pāḷi): 'Monks, ... pe ... he should not be ordained. "They" refers to those prohibited persons. "And he too" means that person as well. It is indeed permitted.
"He should be ordained" is the connection [of the sentence]. "And of him" means of that person; or else, "and of those parents.
This is an inversion of the word order. "I shall explain the characteristic of permission" is the connection.
"In this way" refers to the method stated by this [word]. The word "and" (ca) serves to connect the sentences. "If he has unshorn hair," and so on.
“If there are other monks as well within the same boundary”—this is the meaning. “Others” means those besides himself.
“Bhaṇḍu” means shaven-headed; that very act is “bhaṇḍakamma. “Of that” refers to the act of shaving. “Opportunity” means the occasion for going forth.
Having said, “He does not obtain an opportunity,” the passage beginning with “If” is stated to show the reason for that.
Regarding the word *api* (also/even) in the phrase "even though he has not [yet been ordained]," the particle *pi* indicates the question: "What indeed is this so-called 'going forth' (*pabbajjā*)?

In the context of "one causes him to go forth with reference to a preceptor," there are four kinds of going forth: the going forth of an ascetic (*tāpasa-pabbajjā*), the going forth of a wanderer (*paribbājaka-pabbajjā*), the going forth of a novice (*sāmaṇera-pabbajjā*), and the going forth of full ordination (*upasampadā-pabbajjā*).
Among these, the removal of hair and beard is called the "going forth of an ascetic" because it must be undertaken first, prior even to the taking up of bark garments and other such requisites.

The "going forth as a seer" (*isipabbajjā*) is another name for that very same thing. The "wandering ascetic’s going forth" (*paribbājakapabbajjā*) consists simply in the removal of hair and beard, because these must be discarded immediately prior to taking up the saffron robes and so forth.

The "novice’s going forth" (*sāmaṇerapabbajjā*) consists in both the removal of hair and beard and the donning of the saffron robes, because these must be discarded immediately prior to taking the refuges.

The "going forth by full ordination" (*upasampadapabbajjā*) is threefold: the going forth by full ordination through the "Come, monk! formula (*ehibhikkhuupasampadā*), [the going forth by formal act of the Saṅgha, and the going forth by self-ordination].

There are two types of going forth by ordination: going forth by taking the three refuges as the ordination, and going forth by ordination through the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthavācikūpasampadapabbajjā*).

Among these, in the case of going forth by ordination through the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhūpasampadapabbajjā*), everything—including the removal of hair and beard—is accomplished all at once, because it is effected by the Blessed One’s words, "Come, monk.

Going forth by taking the three refuges as the ordination is exactly like the going forth of a novice (*sāmaṇera*). This includes both the removal of hair and beard and the donning of the saffron robes.

And the taking of the refuges, as well as the formal act of going forth (*pabbajjā*) through the procedure consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthavācikūpasampadā*), must be excluded right at the beginning because they involve the undertaking of the ritual formula (*kammavācā*).
In that context, with reference to the going forth of a novice (*sāmaṇera*), it is said: "He causes him to go forth by designating a preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
"By designating a preceptor" means having established the requirement for the preceptor to perform the duties of service. Regarding the formal act of going forth...
The meaning is: "without making it one's own authority. A young bhikkhu must indeed perform three duties: cutting the hair, donning the saffron robes, and granting the refuges.
Some, having introduced the reading here as "but the refuges must be granted by oneself," claim that the refuges should not be granted by a young bhikkhu; that should not be accepted.
Because he is a young bhikkhu, and because it is permissible for bhikkhus to grant the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).

If the preceptor (*upajjhāya*), without first performing the cutting of the hair and the donning of the saffron robes, simply grants the refuges for the purpose of the going-forth, the going-forth does not take effect, because that which ought to be done for the going-forth has not been performed.
If, however, having recited the formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*), he confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon those who have not yet received the robes, the full ordination takes effect.

Because full ordination (*upasampadā*) has been accomplished and because there is no failure of the ritual act (*kamma*). A "broken boundary" (*khaṇḍasīma*) is a formally established boundary (*baddhasīma*) that occupies the space of a functional boundary (*upacārasīma*).

The phrase "having given the going forth" (*pabbājetvā*) is said with reference to the cutting of the hair, because the wearing of the saffron robes is mentioned separately in the words "having clothed them in saffron robes.
Furthermore, because it is not appropriate for a novice (*sāmaṇera*) to give the refuges (*saraṇa*), it is said: "The refuges must be given by oneself."
It has been stated. The connection is "to ordain a man. "Hi" means "truly. "By command" means by the command of the bhikkhus.
"By anyone whatsoever" means by anyone among those who are householders or those who have gone forth.
Having said "one who is capable," it was stated "possessing the cause" in order to show its meaning. "Possessing the cause" refers to the paths and fruits.
It occurs together with the proximate causes (*upanissaya*). "Renowned" means endowed with both the renown of a retinue and the renown of fame.
"Even having made space" means precisely by making space. "Himself" means that no one else should be commanded. "From this very place" means from the very spot where he was seen.
"His" refers to one who is seeking the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). "Or itching" means scratching; there is also a reading, "or scabies," which refers to a skin eruption (*pāma*).
The meaning is "it blows. "Or pustules" means "or boils. "By this much" means by this measure—by merely rubbing and bathing.
"Of a nature not to turn back" means having a disposition not to return to the state of a householder. "Grateful" means having the habit of recognizing a favor done.
"Recognizing what has been done" means making known the awareness of the favor that was performed.
The "discourse on the non-leading" (*aniyyānikakathā*) refers to such talk as: "Sleep as much as you wish, eat as much as you wish, and dwell without longing, playing with your mind.
Having shown what should not be told, he says "Then indeed to him" (*athakhvassa*) to show what should be told.
"To him" (*assa*) means to one who is seeking the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). Showing the manner of explaining, he says "And by one explaining," and so forth. ... [the praise] ...
"By way of" (*vasena*) means by way of color, shape, odor, habitat, and location; this is to be connected with "should be explained.
"Hi" indicates the result; the meaning is: "I shall state the result of the explanation. "He" refers to one who seeks the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
"In the past" (*pubbe*) means in a previous existence, or prior to the act of going-forth. He is like a fully ripened boil awaiting being pierced by a thorn.
The construction is: "knowledge proceeds. *Assa* means "of one who is seeking the going-forth. *Indāsanī* is the thunderbolt weapon of Sakka;
for it is called *indāsanī* because it is hurled or thrown by Indra (*indena asīyati*). The construction is:
"just as [the thunderbolt] would pulverize all defilements, so too does it pulverize them, like a mountain being pulverized by the thunderbolt. *Khuraggeyeva* means "on the very edge of the razor."
The meaning is: "at the very conclusion of the formal act. "Hi" means "truly. "Tasmā" means "because [he] has attained [it], therefore.
"Assa" refers to one who is seeking the going-forth. "Gihigandhaṃ" means the scent of people dwelling in a household. "Athāpi" connects with the phrase "even if he covers [himself].

"Assa" again refers to one who is seeking the going-forth. "Ācariyo vā" means either the teacher who grants the refuge, or the teacher of the formal ritual (kammavācā), or the teacher of exhortation (ovāda).
"Or him" means either that very person or one who is seeking ordination. "By that monk" means by the monk who is the preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya).

"Without being instructed" means without being instructed by the preceptor or teacher. By this, it is shown that because of not being instructed by the preceptor or teacher, no one at all should perform tasks such as providing lower robes and so forth. "By the monk" means by the monk who is the preceptor or teacher.
“Of that very person” means of one who is seeking admission to the going-forth (*pabbajjā*). “Rooted in the preceptor” refers to the lower garment and upper robe rooted in the preceptor;

such is the analysis. “Therein” means in the place of going-forth and full ordination (*upasampadā*). “Of them” means of the monks. “Then” means after the making of salutations, or immediately following the salutation.
By way of indicating the method of the canonical text, [the phrase] “Speak thus” means: “That which I say, speak it.”
"Tell me that," thus he indicates the method according to the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary). "Then" (*atha*) means immediately after that. "To him" (*assa*) refers to the one seeking ordination;

it is connected with "should be given" (*dātabbāni*). "Even a single word" (*ekapadam-pi*) means even a single syntactical member among the three members of a sentence, or even a single inflected word among the nine.
"Even a single syllable" (*ekakkharam-pi*) means even a single syllable among the twenty-four consonants.
"Purification on one side" means by means of the purification of the officiating master (*kammavācācariya*) alone through the perfection of his vocal organs and articulation (*ṭhānakaraṇasampatti*).
"Purification on both sides" means precisely by means of the purification of both the master who grants the refuge and the novice (*sāmaṇera*).

"Perfection of vocal organs and articulation" refers to the perfection of the vocal organs, such as the chest and so forth, and the articulations, such as the *saṃvuta* [consonants] and so forth. "To speak" means to speak with the perfection of vocal organs and articulation.
The construction is: "one cannot say" means "one is not able to say.

The word *imāni* (these) refers to the refuges (*saraṇāni*). The particle *ca* is used as an introductory conjunction (*upanyāsa*), and the particle *pana* is a poetic ornament (*padālaṅkāra*). The phrase *ekasambandhāni* means "connected together.
Having made the final vowel nasalized, at the time of giving [the refuge], one says "Buddhaṃ," and for the words "refuge" (*saraṇaṃ*), one likewise says "refuge" (*saraṇaṃ*).
It is stated that the words "gacchāmi" and so forth should be given as a single connected unit, without making an interruption between them. Why?
Because there is no intervening syllable whatsoever between the three words. "Having interrupted" means having made a break.
This refers to the time of giving [the gift] after making it end in the letter *m*, without forming a single connection between the three words.
It is said that [the words] must be given after having been separated [by the particle *ca*]. Why?
Because there is the presence of the nasalized *m* (makāra) as an intervening separator between the three words. The connection is: "It is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.

The word *taṃ* is the agent (*kattā*) in the phrase "there is not" (*natthī*), and it is the object (*kamma*) in the phrase "it was not stated" (*na vuttaṃ*). "In that way" (*tathā*) refers to [the formula] beginning with "Venerable sir, I am Buddharakkhita," and so forth.

The meaning is this: for one who does not speak with the correct *ākāra* (vowel sound), the refuge (*saraṇa*) is not invalidated; rather, the refuge is invalidated only for one who fails to provide the proper phonetic realization (*ṭhānakaraṇasampada*) of consonants such as *bu* and *da*.
By the word "three times," it is indicated that once or twice is not sufficient. More than three times—
However, it is indeed permissible even a thousand times. "Therein" (tattha) means in those [acts of] going forth and full ordination.

"From another" (parato) means from another person. "That" (sā) refers to full ordination. The connection is that "going forth," however, was already permitted. In the phrase "even from another" (paratopi), the word "even" (pi) refers back to what precedes.

"That" (sā) refers to going forth. "By this much" (ettāvatā) means by this much: the cutting of hair, the donning of the saffron robe, and the granting of refuge. "Hi" is a particle indicating the result.
*Esa* means "this novice" (*sāmaṇera*). Having said "one who has gone," he spoke "wise by nature" to show its meaning.
*Atha* means "in this case. *Assa* refers to the novice. *Tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne* means "in that very place," namely, in the very position established as the stage of a novice.
The construction is: "Just as they were recited by the Blessed One, so should they be recited. *Etaṃ* refers to "I authorize... [gold and] silver... (*jātarūpa*).
The phrase is “abstention from accepting silver.
The word “that” refers to the statement as it is stated in the Andhaka-ṭīkā. The particle “eva” (just/exactly) has the sense of determination;
therefore, they must be recited exactly according to the text. It means that after answering according to the text, they must be recited in no other way.
It prevents dispute. Even if one recites otherwise than according to the text—saying, for example, "I undertake the training precept of abstaining from taking life"—one is indeed without fault.
*Hi* means "truly" or "because. *Tāni* refers to the training precepts (*sikkhāpadāni*). *Yāva* means "for as long as [a time]";
the connection is that "he does not know [it], he is not skilled. *Santikāvacaroyeva* means "only one who dwells in the presence of" the teacher and preceptor.
"Nearby" means in the vicinity. "Of him" means of the novice.

"The allowable and the unallowable" refers to that which is allowable—excluding the ten training rules—and that which is unallowable, such as improper contact (*parāmasa*) and so forth. "By him too" means by the novice as well. "Factors for the loss of the mark" refers to the factors for the loss of the religious emblem (*liṅga*).
"Should be trained thoroughly" means that for one who does not train thoroughly, there is the loss of the mark.
The intention is that there is both the formal act of punishment (*daṇḍakamma*) and the suspension (*nāsana*).
10. The Second Discourse on Māra. 35.
Demonstrating that the word *mayham* (of me) functions as the genitive case of the agent in relation to the phrases "attained" (*anuppattā*) and "realized" (*sacchikatā*), he said:

“*Mayā kho* means ‘by me. By the words “*atha vā*,” etc., he shows the state of grammatical connection between the word “*mayhaṃ*” (of mine) and the phrases “*yoniso manasikārā*” (through wise attention) and “*yoniso sammappadhānā*” (through wise right effort).

Regarding the phrase “*yoniso manasikārā, yoniso sammappadhānā*,” since it is an ablative case used in the sense of cause, he says “*tena hetunā*” (by that reason). By the words “*puna*,” etc., [he explains] the word “*mayhaṃ*.”

In the phrases “through wise attention (*yoniso manasikārā*)” and “through wise right effort (*yoniso sammappadhānā*),” having applied the sense of mastery (*sāmibhāva*) in the sense of identity (*sāmyattha*), it is shown that in the subsequent phrases “attained (*anuppattā*)” and “realized (*sacchikatā*),” a reversal of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*) should be made in the sense of agency (*kattuttha*) by means of the sense of mastery. 11.
The Discourse on the Bhaddavaggiyas.
36. "Bhaddaka" means those who possess both auspicious form and mind. "Vagga" refers to a group-binding; by the elision of the final member of the compound, it becomes "vagga.

Those who move in groups are "vaggiya. To show the meaning—that they are both auspicious and group-dwellers—he said, "the Bhaddavaggiyas," etc., [adding] the letter *ka* [to form the compound] by its elision.
By the phrase "the suffix *-o* is merely a particle," he [indicates that] the word *tumha*...
And it negates the status of being an effect for the word "and. "Hi" means "truly. "Te" refers to the members of the Bhaddavaggiya group.
"Idaṃ" refers to the observance of the five precepts. "Pubbakammaṃ" refers to wholesome karma accumulated in the past.
12. The Discourse on the Miracle at Uruvelā.
38. Regarding the phrase *pariyādiyeyya*: here, because the prefix *pari-* and the root *ādi* function as prefixes (*upasagga*) with the sense of overcoming, he says "he would overcome.
39. Regarding the phrase *pacchā pakkhittā*: the meaning is that they were placed [there] by those who recorded them in books after the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*).
44. By the phrase "bending down as if speaking thus," he shows that the term *āharahattho* is a derivative formation (*taddhita*).
Because their openings are wide, they are called *mandāmukhī* in the sense of being "slow" (*manda*) and "low" (*hīna*) due to having very large mouths;
thus he said, "they are called fire-vessels. 51.
Because the time for subduing a snake takes a long time to pass or proceed, it is therefore called "long-delayed" (*cirapati*).
Therefore, the construction is: "She has been well-disposed since long ago. Thus, showing this meaning, he said: "From long ago" (cirakālato paṭṭhāyā). 52.
"In all places" (sabbattha) means in all the phrases beginning with "His matted hair" (jaṭāmissa). Regarding "a carrying-basket" (khārikāja):
here, the requisites of an ascetic, such as a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and so forth, are called a *khārī*; a basket filled with a load reckoned as a *khārī* is a "carrying-basket" (khārikāja).
Showing the meaning by way of a single part, he said, “a load of khārīs.
13. The Discourse on the Meeting with Bimbisāra.
55. The word *laṭṭhi* denotes a young tree, as in “Ambalaṭṭhikā” and so forth; here too, it refers to a young palm tree.
Pointing out that "laṭṭhi" means a staff, he said, "in the palm grove. "Vaṭarukkha" refers to a banyan tree (*nigrodharukkha*).
Here, by the word "vaṭa," he shows that because the banyan tree has many roots, it is well-established; thus, it is called "suppatiṭṭha" (well-established).
By the word "rukkhe" (on the tree), he shows that the term *cetiya* applies to a sacred tree (*cetiya-rukkha*), as well as to a temple and a stupa.
He turns it back. "Tassa" means of that banyan tree. "Etaṃ" refers to this name, "Suppatiṭṭhe cetiye.
According to worldly convention, having extracted it from the specific number designated as ten thousand, it should be applied [to the word].
Thus, showing that by the meaning of the term "niyuta" it is ten thousand, he said: "One niyuta is ten thousand. It is also called "nahuta."
That reading is incorrect because it would involve an unwarranted connection with the specific number known as *nahuta* through a state of confusion.
"Of them" refers to those twelve *niyutas* of brahmins and householders.

By the phrase "because of their emaciated bodies," he shows the meaning of the word *kisakā*: "those whose self (*atta*) is emaciated (*kisa*) are *kisakā*. The letter *ka-* [is used here for the sake of euphony].
*Hettha* means "here" (referring to the word *ovādaka*). By the term *ovādako*, it is shown that in the word *ovadāno*, the suffix *-ya* (*yupaccaya*) has the sense of the agent (*kattuttha*).

Due to the constraints of the verse meter (*gāthābandha*), the short vowel *a* is lengthened. With the phrase "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth, he shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as *kisakovadāno*, meaning "one who, being emaciated (*kisaka*), instructs others.
*Idam* means "this," referring either to this collection of meanings (*atthajāta*) or to this specific meaning. The syntactical connection is: "You laughed at this."
The construction is: "Those [fetters], you. Thus it is said.

Regarding "women in relation to sensual pleasures" (*kāme itthiyo*), he says "sensual pleasures and women," explaining that the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs through the elision of the vowel *e*.

Regarding "in the acquisitions" (*upadhīsu*), he says "in the acquisition of the aggregates" (*khandhupadhīsu*), because among the four acquisitions—namely, those consisting of sensual pleasures, the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations—it is the acquisition of the aggregates that is intended here.
Regarding "Kocarahī": here, the word *kosa* has the sense of the particle *kva*, as in such expressions as "What strength do you have, O Great King?
Thus he says "kvacarahī. This is merely a grammatical particle (*nipāta*). To exclude meanings such as "foot" (from the root *cara*) or "step," he states "the state of Nibbāna" (*nibbānapada*).

By the phrase "because its intrinsic nature is peaceful" (*santasabhāvatāya*), etc., it is "peaceful" (*santa*) because this state possesses a peaceful intrinsic nature. It is "without acquisitions" (*anupadhika*) because there are no acquisitions (*upadhaya*) therein. There is no...

"Kiñcanam ettha" means "having nothing here," thus it is *akiñcana*. "It does not adhere to the three realms of existence (*bhava*)" means it is *asatta*. "It does not become otherwise" means it is *anaññathābhāvi*.
"It cannot be led astray by anything else" shows the meaning of the term *anaññaneyya*. "By that" refers to the phrase beginning with "peaceful" (*santa*).
"Mine" (*me*) is my; "mind" (*mano*) is the connection. Here, in this world of gods and humans, my mind finds delight.
Regarding "nāmāti kiṃ vakkhāmi": the construction is "he shows this meaning.
56. "Tañcāti" means "and that state of being a disciple. 57. Regarding "assāsakā":
here, the verbal root *sās* preceded by the prefix *ā* is similar to the verbal root *sis* preceded by the prefix *ā*, because of its connection with the genitive case in "me."

The suffix *ṇvu* has the sense of "state" (*bhāvattha*); thus he says, "the act of wishing" (*āsīsana*). By the word "aspiration" (*patthanā*), he shows the meaning of the verbal root preceded by the prefix *ā*.

"Of him" (*assa*) means of King Bimbisāra. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the Triple Gem. "Only the going with certainty" (*nicchayagamanameva*) means that he has gone (*gato*) by knowing through the certainty [expressed by] "taking refuge" (*saraṇa*).
"Surrendering oneself" (*attasanniyyātana*) means the surrendering of one's own self to the Triple Gem. By this—

Among the four ways of going for refuge—consisting of surrendering oneself, prostration, making that one's highest aim, and entering into the state of a disciple—it explains the going for refuge by surrendering oneself.
"Ayaṃ" refers to King Bimbisāra. "Taṃ" refers to the state of certain refuge.
Regarding the phrase "and the going by prostration," here "paṇi" means the hand; for just as the words *pāda* (foot) and *pada* (word/step) exist in both long and short forms...
They say "caraṇa" means the foot; likewise, from the words *pāṇi* and *paṇi*, they say "kara" (hand).

Therefore it is said: "The hand is called *paṇi*. Falling down is *pāta*; the falling down of living beings (*paṇina*) is *paṇipāta*. In terms of meaning, this is what is meant by "bowing with joined palms" (*añjalipaṇamana*).
Its going is "one who goes" (*gacchanto*); by this, he illustrates the going for refuge through prostration (*paṇipātasaraṇagamana*). The word "and" (*ca*) [indicates] "manifest" (*pākaṭa*).
This should also be applied here; for the meaning is "making it manifest.
Regarding the phrase "the color of refined gold" (*siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo*): here, "refined gold" (*siṅgīnikkha*) refers to gold that has been refined (*siṅgī*);
since its color is identical to that, it is called "the color of refined gold. Demonstrating this etymological meaning, he said: "having a color equal to refined gold (*siṅgīsuvaṇṇa-nikkha*)."
In that context, by the word "suvaṇṇa" (gold), he shows that the word *nikkha* has the meaning of "gold," and excludes other meanings such as "five gold pieces" (*pañcasuvaṇṇa*).
By the word "samāna" (same), he shows that in the expression "of the same color" (*savaṇṇo*), the letter *sa-* is a grammatical modification (*kāriya*) belonging specifically to the word *samāna*.
"In all" means in all the faculties (*indriya*), such as the eye and so forth. "Tamed" (*danto*) means disciplined; thus, what is meant is "restraint of the faculties" (*indriyasaṃvara*).
Making this very point clear, he said, “Of the Blessed One,” and so forth.
59. To show the meaning of the term *oṇītapattapāṇī*—“one by whom the hand has been withdrawn from the bowl”—he said, “And from the bowl,” and so forth.
By the phrase “with the hand removed,” it is shown that the word *oṇīta* has the sense of “removed” (*apanīta*), and it should be construed with the word *pāṇi*.

It shows [this]. By the word "having observed" (*sallakkhetvā*), it shows that the object "the Blessed One" (*bhagavantaṃ*) should be construed with the elided reading "having observed" (*sallakkhetvā*).
Regarding "to one side" (*ekamantaṃ*): here the word *anta* has the sense of a proximate location or the sense of a limit;
and the accusative case has the sense of the locative. Showing this, he says "in one place. In the usage of the term for one who desires something (*atthika-payoga*).
Because it is possible for such an action to be performed, he says: "either by going to pay homage to the Buddha or by going to listen to the Dhamma.
Regarding the term *appākiṇṇa*, the word *appa* here has the sense of negation; thus he says "uncluttered" (*anākiṇṇa*).
There is also a reading *abbokiṇṇa*. Regarding *appanigghosa*, since the word *sadda* (sound) was already included by the phrase "little sound" (*appasadda*), by this [term]...
By way of elimination, it is the sound of the clamor of the city alone that should be understood; thus he said, "by the sound of the clamor of the city, [it is] 'without the clamor of people'.
Among the three readings, by the first reading, *janavāto* means the wind of the people;

he shows the alternative interpretation as *vijanavāta*, meaning "devoid of that. By the second [reading], *janavādo* means the talk of the people; he shows the alternative interpretation as *vijanavāda*, meaning "devoid of that."
[The text] shows this. By the third [term], it shows the alternative analysis as *vijanapāta*, meaning "devoid of the movement of people in the morning" (*janapāta*);
for *janapāta* refers to the movement of people in the early morning. *Rāhasseyyaka* means that which is made secret (*rahasseyyati*) therein.
By the words beginning with "of people," it shows the etymological meaning of *manussarāhasseyyaka* as "the place of secrecy for people."
14. The Discourse on the Ordination of Sāriputta and Moggallāna 60.
“Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna... ‘They have arrived,’ is the construction. ‘There’ means at the festival on the mountain ridge.
‘Then’ means immediately after that reflection. ‘His’ refers to Sañjaya. ‘The further shore’ means the opposite bank. ‘In this’ means in your doctrine.”
"‘Idaṃ’ (this): the meaning is that this discourse is only this much. ‘Yo’ (whoever): anyone whatsoever. ‘Amhe’ (we two): you and I.

For when three words—namely *nāma*, *tumha*, and *amha*—are to be treated by the rule of single-remainder (*ekasesa*), the single-remainder must be made of the last one. ‘Tenā’ (by that): by reason of making the agreement.
Showing in detail what was stated in brief, he said ‘idaṃ hī’ (for this), etc. ‘Atthīkehi’: by those desiring the Deathless (*amata*).”
"Upaññātaṃ maggaṃ" means the path to the Deathless has been approached and known.
By showing that when a word is transformed along with its prefix—as in "known and approached"—the meaning of the prefix and the meaning of the verbal root remain distinct, it makes this known.
Alternatively, it shows: "Those who desire [nibbāna] should follow us, seeking the path to nibbāna which has been approached."
He said, “Or rather,” and so forth. Nibbāna is "approached" (upaññāta) because it is to be known by approaching it through the knowledges of reviewing the path and the fruit.
He said, “seeking,” showing that it is for the purpose of searching with the faculty of the path.
The connection is that Sāriputta also asked the question. "From the water-pot" means from the *kuṇḍika*. [He asks] regarding himself and others...
"Paṭisandhāra" means that by not speaking, one joins together a gap in between; that [is what it refers to]. "Therein" (ettha) means in the phrase "I am not able to tell you.
The construction is: "The underlying intention (adhippāya) should be understood thus. "So much" (ettakaṃ) means this much question. "Of him" (imassa) means of the wanderer (paribbājaka).
"State of being outside his domain" (avisayabhāvaṃ) means the state of being beyond his own range of competence.
“Arising in dependence on a cause” means that, according to the sense of the expression *hetuppabhavā* (“originating from causes”), the five aggregates are what are called “originating from causes.
Thus he said: “The five aggregates are what are called ‘originating from causes. By the phrase “those phenomena which originate from causes,” [he refers to them].
“Of him” means of the wanderer Sāriputta. By the statement “the cause of those is called the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*),” [he shows this].
By the meaning of the words "it leads to this" (*hinoti etasmā*) and "they bear fruit" (*phalanti*), it shows that the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*) is called the cause (*hetu*).
"And that" (*tañca*) refers to the truth of origination. Regarding the word "of those" (*tesaṃ*), it is stated "of both truths" in order to show the referent of the pronoun *tad*.
It is called cessation (*nirodha*) because it ceases here by way of non-occurrence. "And that" (*tañca*) refers to cessation. By that [phrase] "and of those... [the text continues].
By the phrase "cessation" (*nirodho*). "Assa" refers to the wanderer Sāriputta. "Therein" (*ettha*) means in this verse, or among the four truths.

"By way of method" (*nayatoti*) means by way of the method of immediate sequence, or by way of the method of inseparable connection, or by way of the methods of guidance, teaching, and bringing forth.
Making that very meaning clear, he said: "In cessation," and so forth. [This is stated] by way of the grammatical rule of "single-remainder" (*ekasesa*) based on partial similarity.
Showing that the truth of the path (maggasacca) should also be included, he says "or else" and so forth.

Both cessation and the means to cessation may be treated as "cessation" by applying the grammatical rule of *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (retaining one member of a group that shares a common part). Regarding the phrase "and of these," they say that the word "and" (*ca*), in the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned, implies that the truth of the path should also be taken;
however, this method is not stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). "That very same meaning": [end of excerpt].
He concludes by saying, "He brings that very matter, known as the Four Truths, to fulfillment.
With the words "Even if," he explains the meaning of the term "if" (yadi). With the words "only this much," he explains the meaning of the term "just so far" (tāvadeva).
With the words "there is nothing beyond this," he shows the result of the emphatic particle *eva*. "From this" means from the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
By the phrase “This... [to be] attained,” he shows the essential nature of the meaning of the expression “only this much.
By the phrase “This very Dhamma,” he explains the meaning of the expression “this same Dhamma.

He says “penetrated” (*paccabyatthā*) because the root *vid* preceded by the prefixes *pati* and *ava* has the sense of penetration; thus he says “penetrated. The words “by you” are said with reference to the Elder Assaji.
By this [word], he indicates the *hyastanī* (past tense), *parasmaipada*, middle person, plural number, and case ending (*atthavibhatti*) for the word "paccabyatthā.

"Kappanahutehi" means by hundreds of thousands of *nahutas* of *kappas*; the meaning is: by hundreds of *nahutas* consisting of hundreds of thousands of millions of millions (*koṭipakoṭisatasahassa*).
"Abbhatītaṃ" means gone beyond (*abhiatītaṃ*). The meaning is: having remained unseen by us, it has been passed over.
62. Because Nibbāna, as the object, is profound, the knowledge that takes it as its object is also intended to be profound;
thus he says, "and of profound knowledge. For just as a fine needle is intended for the purpose of sewing fine cloth.
Nibbāna is called the "destruction of acquisitions" (upadhisaṅkhaya) in the sense of the complete destruction of the acquisitions; thus he says, "in the destruction of acquisitions."

"In Nibbāna. "Having that as its object" means having that Nibbāna as its object. "By liberation" means by the liberation of the fruit (*phala-vimutti*). "In the knowledge of the disciples' perfection" means in the knowledge of the perfection of the chief disciples.
"Among them" refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The connection is: "Within half a month, he was established in Arahatship.
"In the past" means at the end of an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus one hundred thousand aeons. "Of him" [refers to] the state of being a chief disciple in the presence of that Buddha.

The construction is: "he desired" (*patthesi*). "In the hermitage" (*assame*) means in the dwelling place of sages. For it is called an "hermitage" (*assama*) because therein anger (*krodha*) is stilled (*samyanti*), or because passion and the other defilements are thoroughly (*bhūsaṃ*) stilled;
[it means] in that [place]. And the connection is: "having desired, he sent. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the bower of blue lotuses.
"Among them" (*tesu*) means among those best of ascetics.
63. *Yesanti kulānaṃ*. By the phrase “*vidhavabhāvāya*” (for the state of widowhood), he shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as “the state of a widow” (*vedhavya*).

A “widow” (*vidhavā*) is one who is empty of a husband. She is called “widow” because she has departed from her husband (*dhavena vigatā*), and she is also called “widow” because her husband has departed from her (*vigato dhavo imissā*).
“By both kinds” refers to the two types consisting of the son’s going forth and the wife’s following him in his going forth.
Regarding the term *sañcayānī*: here, because the designation of the supported is applied to the support by way of metaphorical usage (*nissayūpacāra*), he says, "the female pupils of Sañcaya.
Alternatively, since the suffix *-ṇa* occurs in the sense of "belonging to that," he says, "the female pupils of Sañcaya.
Because it is stated in the plural as "of the Magadhans," he says, "of the country of Magadha. [The word] *Giribbaja*.
In this context, *vaja* means a mountain (*giri*). Because there is a mountain resembling a *vaja* here, it is called *Giribbaja*, referring to the city from top to bottom.
By the phrase "possessing great heroism" (*mahāvīriyavanto*), he shows the meaning of the word *mahāvīra*: that these Tathāgatas are great heroes (*mahāvīra*).
Regarding the line "What envy could there be for those who lead by the Dhamma, O wise one?"—here, according to the method of Kaccāyana:
(Regarding Kaccāyana Sutta 277: One might suspect that there should be the dative case (*sampadāna*) when used with *usūya* (envy); therefore, he says:
"The genitive case is used in the sense of the locative, or in the sense of the accusative. *Vijānantānaṃ* means "among the Tathāgatas who know" or "to those who know.
15. Discussion on the Duties toward the Preceptor (*Upajjhāyavatta*).
64. Regarding the term *anupajjhāyaka*: here, one who meditates (*jhāyati*) after having approached (*upagamitvā*) what is blameworthy (*vajja*) and what is blameless (*avajja*) is an *upajjhāya*.
Those who have no such person are *anupajjhāyaka*; showing this meaning, he says, "what is blameworthy and what is blameless," and so forth.

By the phrase "the bowl for wandering for alms" (*piṇḍāya caraṇakapatta*), it is meant that one stands up and remains by means of it for the sake of alms; thus, it is an *uttiṭṭha*, and that very bowl is an *uttiṭṭhapatta*.
It shows the meaning. However, in such passages as “uttiṭṭhe na pamajjeyya,” the act of wandering for alms is called “uttiṭṭha.
Therefore, in that context, the etymological meaning of the word *uttiṭṭha* should be understood as “standing up for the sake of alms” or “having stood up.
This expression, “the bowl for wandering for alms,” refers to the phrase: “for people there perceive it as leftover food.”
Having leaped over [the previous section], it should be connected with the phrase, "Therefore it is said, 'uttiṭṭhapatta'.
Thus, it is meant that because it is a bowl for wandering for alms, it is called "uttiṭṭhapatta. To the question, "What is the perception people have regarding it?
he says, "For regarding that, people have the perception of it being leftover (ucchiṭṭha). For indeed, regarding that very *uttiṭṭhapatta*, by virtue of its being used by those who have gone forth...
The construction is as follows: because it may be seized by people, or because it may be discarded by them, people perceive it as "leftover" (*ucchiṭṭha*).
It is called "the bowl from which one has risen" (*uttiṭṭhapatta*) because it is the bowl used for wandering for alms by those who have gone forth;
however, the intention is that it is called "the leftover bowl" (*ucchiṭṭhapatta*) because it is a bowl that has been seized by people. [This concludes the word] *uttiṭṭhapatta*.
Showing that this is merely a syntactical construction and not a compound (*samāsa*), he says "or else" (*atha vā*), and so forth.
By the word "having risen" (*uṭṭhahitvā*), he shows that there is the elision of the suffix *-tvā* in the form *uttiṭṭhati*. By the word "to take" (*gahetuṃ*), he indicates an ellipsis in the text.

"By way of love based on the home" (*gehasitapemavasena*) means by way of love dependent upon the home; the meaning is "by way of love preceded by loving-kindness" (*mettā*). "Being respectful" (*sagāravā*) means being deferential (*sappatissā*).

He said "having established" in order to show the meaning of "dwelling having offered. By the phrase "a common livelihood," he shows that in the expression "common mode of conduct" (*sabhāgavutti*), the word *vutti* has the sense of "livelihood" alone, and not the sense of "explanation" or the like.
They are called "acceptances of the state of preceptor" because one accepts the state of being a preceptor by means of them;
these very terms are synonyms for the acceptance of the state of being a preceptor.
"Three times" is stated according to the highest standard; even once is indeed permissible. The connection is:
"he makes himself understood by means of a word. "Hi" (for) means truly. "Therein" refers to the occasion of taking the preceptor.
Whether it be the proclamation by speech, or the making known of the meaning by body—this very proclamation and making known of the meaning constitutes the taking of the preceptor.
The exposition (*yojanā*). "Accepting with 'Well' (*sādhūti sampaṭicchanam*)" means that when the preceptor has said anything among the five points, the co-resident's acceptance by saying "Well.
"That" refers to the statement of some. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "In this case" (*ettha*) refers to the mention of the preceptor.
By the phrase "acceptance is not a factor," it is implied that only the requesting and the giving [of robes] are [the factors].
This shows that they are indeed limbs. The connection is: "should also be known by the co-resident student. By this word means: by the word "well done" (sādhu).
Regarding the phrase "therein, this is the proper conduct," the statement "that which was said as 'one should conduct oneself properly'" is intended to show the scope of the pronoun *taṃ* (therein).
By this, he illuminates only its status as the object of an action (*kiriyā*), not its status as the object of a substance (*dabba*). This [refers to] "this."
"Being told": this refers to the student (*saddhivihārika*). "For the purpose of protecting the washed feet":
for the purpose of removing dust and other impurities from the washed feet. "They": the sandals. "At the very early hour": from the time of dawn;
here the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka-attha*). "From those": from those three tooth-sticks; this is the ablative case (*apādāna*) with its suffix elided.
Among those three types of tooth-sticks: *yaṃ* means whichever tooth-stick; *atha* means at that time of taking it;
*tato* means by means of cold and warm water, or in cold and warm water; *vaḷañjeti* means he uses; *udakaṃ* means mouth-washing water;
by the term "from the latrine," the urinal is also to be understood; *evaṃ* means while sweeping; *asuññaṃ* means [not empty] due to the sound of people.

"Not trifling" (*atucchaṃ*). "Seat" (*āsanaṃ*) refers to the elder’s seat. "In that seat" (*tasmiṃ āsane*). The connection is: "the duty (*vattaṃ*) must be performed for the elder who is seated there.
To show the meaning of "messy" (*uklāpa*)—namely, "there is a mess in this place"—he said, "strewn with some rubbish.
And here, by the etymological definition of the word, "rubbish" (*saṅkāra*), "remnant" (*ucchiṭṭha*), "heap" (*kalāpa*), and "collection" (*samūha*) constitute the sense of "messy" (*uklāpa*).

It is called *kaca*. That which is woven (*kacīyati*) and bound (*bandhīyati*) therein is called *kaca*; that by which one is covered (*varīyati*) or desired (*icchīyati*) is called *kacavara* according to its etymological meaning.
In the phrase "even with the hand," the word "even" (*pi*) includes "even with a cloth strip" (*pilotikena*) and so forth.

"Having made into one" means having made it into a single uniform layer. Why is it called a *saṅghāṭī*? He says: "Because it is all... and so forth. "Because of being stitched together" (*saṅghaṭitattā*).
"It is to be gathered together by this" shows the etymological meaning of *saṅghāṭī*. The construction is: "It reaches the preceptor who has turned back and is looking [at him].
Or, it connects with the phrase "by a single step. "Included among those things belonging to the bowl" means that the bowl itself is included among those things that keep [the contents] warm;
alternatively, *pattapariyāpanna* means that the rice gruel and so forth contained within the bowl are also "included among those things belonging to the bowl."
It is indeed appropriate. "In the course of alms-round" means at the place for wandering for alms. The connection is with "or having obtained rice-gruel. "His" refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
"That bowl" refers to that bowl which has fallen into [the category of] being hot and so forth. "Or elsewhere" means in the monastery (*ārāma*) or similar places. "His" refers to the preceptor.
The connection is with the phrase "when the instruction is not finished. From this point onward, [it applies to the rule]: "Not [taking] from the preceptor..."

"From the word *bhaṇamānassa* mentioned here [onward]": this indicates that there is no offense regarding the prohibitions such as "one should not go too far," which were stated previously, because of the negative particle (*na*) used therein.
"Anywhere" means in any of those [rules], such as "the robe must not be stored in the heat.
"This" refers to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "Near to an offense" (*āpattisāmanta*)...
In this context, showing that "āpatti-sāmanta" means "near to an offense," he says, "near to an offense.
By the word "āsanna" (near), he demonstrates both that the word *sāmanta* is a synonym for "near" and that the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayogatthe*).
The construction is: "Venerable sir, it is indeed fitting to speak such words."
“Earlier than from the village” means earlier than [the time] the preceptor [leaves] the village. “By that very person” means by the preceptor himself.
This is connected with the phrase “by the co-resident returning. Having said “moist,” in order to show that same meaning, it is stated “taken up by perspiration.
By this word “sinnam,” it shows the meaning as “that which sinks because of this perspiration. By the phrase “having made an excess,” [it explains the sense of] the word “having pushed forward.”
It shows the intended meaning; what is meant is "having repeatedly brought [the mind] back. In order to show that the preceding statement is the cause for the subsequent statement, it is asked:
"For what reason? Revealing the fault of breaking [the concentration] in the middle, he says: "Having made even," and so forth.
"From that" means from having made it even and withdrawn [the mind]; the connection is "it is constantly breaking. Or, [it means] "from breaking in the middle."
The connection is with the word "weak. "This" refers to the statement, "having turned up the ear by four finger-breadths.
"In which way" connects with "when being gathered together. To show the meaning of *obhoga* as the inner fold (*oro*) of the robe's usage, he said, "the waistband," and so forth.
The preceptor. Having said "only in the village," it was stated "or in the interior of a house, or on the way back" in order to demonstrate that same meaning.
"On the way back" means in the dining hall. "Of him" means of the preceptor. "One who has obtained almsfood" (*laddhabhikkho*) refers to one by whom almsfood has been obtained;
or [it refers to] his. The construction is: "there is almsfood. "Of him" means of the preceptor. Almsfood...
The connection is "it does not exist. In the phrase "even that which has been obtained by oneself," the word *pi* (even/also) includes the sense of "even that which has been obtained by a preceptor.
In the expression "let it be brought," the suffix *-tu* denotes a request; the meaning is "how might it be brought?
"Time" refers to the time for eating. "He ate" means he has eaten; the connection is "when that [time] exists. "Approached" means near to midday.
Regarding the phrase *anantarahitāya*: here, "vanished" (*antarahita*) means that which has disappeared, such as a wooden board or a piece of hide.

Since there is nothing vanished within the space between these bowls, it is called "unobstructed" (*anantarahita*); showing this meaning, he says "for the sake of non-obstruction. The construction is:
"It is either black-colored, or plaster-bound, or free from dust and clay. "That" refers to the bowl. Also, "even with washed sand."
"Even on pure sand. "Therein" means among dust, dirt, gravel, and so forth. "Again, therein" means upon the leaf-stands.
The connection is that this statement was spoken. "Facing toward" means facing oneself. "Gently" means slowly.
"But at the edge" means at the corner of the robe. The construction is: "for the student who is laying it down, [it is] the fold of the robe."
Regarding the phrase "the powder is to be mixed," he says, "it should be made into a lump," showing that the meaning here is that it is to be led [together] by means of the gathering of the powder.
By the words "in a smokeless place," he shows that the meaning of "to one side" is "in a place at one end.
"In a sauna" (jantāghare) means in a fire-hall; for it is called *janta* because the fire burns and shines there.
"Jantāghara" means that which produces (*janeti*) perspiration in the body; thus it is called "jantā," and that very thing is called a "jantāghara" (a sweat-house).

In that [sweat-house], because it is performed by way of complete honoring (*paripūjā*), it is called "preparation" (*parikamma*). Showing that, in this sense, the giving of charcoal and so forth is what is named "preparation," he said: "What is called preparation," and so on.
By the phrase beginning with “Not by any illness,” he shows the reason for the encouragement. “Hi” means truly. The construction is:
it must be done even by a sixty-year-old co-resident who is not ill. “By way of disrespect” means by way of neglecting the performance of duties.
“In those connected with the letter ‘na’” means in those cases connected with the prohibitive particle ‘na’. “In the sections” refers to [the passage]: “Not [to the preceptor]...”
In such phrases as "while speaking, an interruption should be introduced from time to time," the term *bhūmiyaṃ* (on the ground) is stated by way of illustration;
it also includes the wall, because [the door] must not strike against it. By the phrase "and a bench-frame" (*piṭhasaṅghāṭañca*), the door-latch (*kavāṭapīḷanī*) is meant here;
this is either through the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) or by way of referring to a part for the whole (*ekadesavohāra*).
He shows that it blows. By the word “without touching,” he shows the meaning of the verbal root *ghaṃs* (to rub) in the phrase “not rubbing.
Regarding “santānakam”: since one protects oneself and others well by means of this, it is a “protection” (*santāna*);
showing that, in the sense of being a protection, things such as insect nests and spiderwebs are called “santānaka,” he says “santānakam,” and so forth. From above...
*Vitānato*: For that which is gathered (*lucīyate*) and tied above is called *ulloka*; by changing the letter *c* to *k*, it is also called *ulloka*.
By the suffix *-to*, he shows that the vowel *ā* is subject to the grammatical operation of the locative case ending (*smā*).
"To be carried away" (*apaharitabba*) means to be removed. There is also a reading, "to be taken down" (*avaharitabba*), meaning to be brought down or cast below.
Regarding the phrase *ālokasandhibhāgā*, since the word *bhāga* follows a dvanda compound, it must be applied individually to each preceding member;
thus he says, “the light-vent openings (*ālokasandhibhāgā*) and the eaves (*kaṇṇabhāgā*)”. To show its meaning, he says, “inner and outer,” and so forth.
By the expression “the windows and shutters (*vātapānakavāṭakāni*),” he shows that the term *ālokasandhi* is a synonym for the windows and shutters.
By the word “koṇa,” he shows that it is a synonym for the word *kaṇṇa* (ear).
By the phrase “just as the first,” etc., he shows that only what was formulated in the first instance should be formulated, and not otherwise.
This was said with reference to a suitable formulation made in the first instance; however, in the case of an unsuitable formulation made in the first instance, it may be formulated otherwise.
"It should be displayed. "For this very purpose" means for the sake of that which was displayed according to its arrangement.
The construction is: "If it had been displayed, then being so... "This" refers to the act of displaying [the image] after removing it from the wall.

One who is intensely attached to mats and fans due to their excellence is called a "mats-and-fan enthusiast" (*kaṭasāraka*). "Having turned back" means having gathered them together. "Eastern" (*puratthima*): here, the *y*-sound has been elided.
"Explanation" means he said "from the east.
Regarding "should be removed," since the root *kas* here has the sense of "going," he said "should be led elsewhere.
The meaning is that having taken the preceptor, one should go to another place. "Elsewhere" means to another location. Regarding "should be separated": here...
Showing that the preceptor must be separated from his adherence to wrong views, he says, "he should be made to relinquish [them].
Having stated, "another should be told," he shows the manner of doing so with the words beginning "Venerable Sir. The connection is that "that particular bhikkhu should be requested.
"He should be caused to give by another" means that the probation (parivāsa) for the preceptor should be granted by another bhikkhu acting on his behalf.
“Kinti nu kho” means “By what means indeed should he give?”—this is the sense. For the word *iti* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇattha*).
The Commentary also shows this very method by means of the phrase “by what means indeed. “In all cases” refers to all the statements beginning with “How indeed should he set it aside?
Regarding the threefold *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) among the seven types of formal acts:
Because it is important, it is said: "without having performed the *ukkhepanīya* (act of suspension). Expounding upon that very point, he says "Therefore, then," and so forth.
The connection is: "it should be requested by that co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*). "If they are indeed performing [the act]" means if the monks are indeed performing the formal act (*kamma*).
Again, "if they are indeed performing" means if the monks are indeed performing the *ukkhepanīya* act.
*Atthāti*: when that action has been performed. *Itīti*: thus, by means of this request. *Nanti*: him, that preceptor (*upajjhāya*).
Regarding the term *samparivattaka*, as in the case of *piṇḍukkhepaka* and other such terms, the word *samparivattaka* is an adverbial modifier of the action;
furthermore, since the suffix *-ka* here has the sense of repetition, he says: "having turned it over again and again. *Yadīti*: until. The word *yadi* [indicates]...
For according to that method, it is said: "One should not depart yet. The construction is: as long as even a small amount of dye remains dripping, one should not depart.
"By means of a person of a different class" means by means of a person of a different class acting as the instrument.
Regarding the statement, "One should not enter a village without having asked permission of one’s preceptor," this does not refer to any other business whatsoever.
It should be entered. However, lest there be the suspicion that "one must enter for alms," he said "or for alms," and so forth.

By the word "without having asked permission" (*anāpucchitvā*), he shows that in the phrase "without asking" (*anāpuccha*), the vowel *ā* is the grammatical modification (*kāriya*) of the suffix *-tvā*.
"Alms-round" (*bhikkhācāra*) means the place for wandering for alms; the construction is that it is to be gone to by the preceptor. "Pariveṇa" refers to [the preceptor's]...
"Pariveṇaṃ. "He sees" means he sees the preceptor.
"Or for the purpose of seeing" means either for the purpose of seeing the foul (asubha). By this, it removes the apprehension that one should not go even for the purpose of staying.
"Kamma" refers to the act that is the cause for departing; this is said with reference to the failure to grant permission.
“Up to the third time”: *taṃ* refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). *Assa* refers to the student (*saddhivihārika*).
By the phrase “it does not succeed,” it is shown that if it does succeed, one should not depart. *Kevalaṃ* means without the success of recitation and so forth.
The construction is: “even while such a preceptor is preventing [the departure]. By the term “from illness,” the requirement for a limit is indicated for the word “departure” (*vuṭṭhāna*).
[The word] "shows" is used. "His" refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). "Another" means someone other than himself. "Of him" refers to another bhikkhu. 16.
Discussion on the Duties of a Co-resident (*saddhivihārika*): 67.

The application [of the rule] should be understood as follows: "The determination regarding proper conduct (*sammāvattanā*) is to be known thus. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by recitation and so forth," questioning (*paripucchā*) and other such activities are included.
He gathers them together. Since the word *saṅgaha* is also used in the senses of "abridgment" and "grasping," it is stated as "favor" (*anuggaha*).
Alternatively, gathering should be performed in their presence and favoring in their absence; or gathering by means of material gifts, or favoring by means of the Dhamma;
or gathering for the sake of welfare in this life, or favoring for the sake of welfare in future lives; or for the sake of worldly aims...
Or assistance should be rendered for the sake of the supramundane. Regarding the phrase "by means of recitation, questioning, exhortation, and instruction":

therein, "recitation" (*uddesa*) refers to the verbal sense of "reciting"; showing that this is called "recitation" in the sense of reading the *pāḷi*, he says, "Recitation is the reading of the *pāḷi*.
By the phrase "the commentary on the meaning of the *pāḷi*," [he shows] that it is done again and again...

"Paripucchā" (thorough questioning) indicates the meaning as the inquiry into the sense of the text from all sides. "In the matter" means in the matter of what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided.
"This" refers to what is to be practiced; again, "this" refers to what is to be avoided.
By the word "vacana" (speech), he shows the etymological meaning of "ovāda" (instruction) as "counseling. When a matter has arisen, [the instruction is given]: "Do this; do not do that."

The construction is: "speech" means "instruction. By the phrase "repeated speech," he shows that the prefix *anu-* in the word *anusāsanī* does not have the sense of "following after" (*anupacchinna*).
Although it was stated generally as "if the preceptor has a bowl," it does not mean an ordinary bowl;
rather, it is an extra bowl—thus he says "extra bowl. "In all cases" means...
In all those passages such as "If the preceptor has a robe," and so forth. "Another" means other than the bowl and robes.
"Requisites of a recluse" refers to the requisites of a recluse, such as the sunshade, sandals, and so on. "Here" refers to the duties of a student (*saddhivihārika*).
"By way of method" means by the proper way. "The search for a means that arises" refers to a means that is arising, or for the sake of what is arising.
Regarding "seeking": *itoti* means from the scriptural text, [namely], "How indeed might requisites arise for the student (*saddhivihārika*)?
Regarding "while dyeing the robe": here, the meaning should not be understood as "by the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) who is dyeing";
rather, showing that the meaning is "by the student," he said, "having heard the method from the preceptor, while dyeing. From the preceptor, the method...
The means obtained from the preceptor.
68. Discussion on Improper Conduct:

"The duty toward the preceptor" refers to the conduct that must be observed toward the preceptor. "He" refers to the student (saddhivihārika). [For failing to do so, there is] an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

"Āpajjati" means "he incurs"; thus the construction is: "he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Regarding "he should be sent away," the root *nam* preceded by the prefix *pa-* has here the sense of "removing" or "expelling" according to its contextual meaning;

hence it is said, "he should be expelled. "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means exceeding the proper measure. "Affection based on the household life" (*gehasita-pema*) refers to the oiliness of loving-kindness (*mettāsineha*).
"By way of the opposite of what was stated" refers to the opposite side of the factors mentioned in the dark category (*kaṇhapakkha*).
Regarding the phrase "alaṃ paṇāmetuṃ": here, among the two meanings [of the word *alaṃ*] excluding the sense of "worthiness" (*araha*), it is the sense of "worthiness" that is intended;
thus he says, "it is fitting to pay homage.

Regarding the phrase "he becomes one who has transgressed" (*sātisāro hoti*): here, "transgression" (*atisāra*) refers to the occurrence of going for refuge by overstepping the natural state; it is a fault.
He said, "he has fault" (sadoso hoti), showing that "it is with transgression" (sātisāro) means that which exists for him.
To show its meaning, it was stated, "he incurs an offense" (āpattiṃ āpajjati). "An offense" refers to an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa-āpatti). "That" refers to the duty (vatta).
"Of them" refers to the co-residents (saddhivihārikānaṃ). "The duty" refers to the duty of many co-residents. "Consenting" (sādiyanaṃ).
Regarding the phrase "he is a fool" (*bālo hoti*): here, in order to show the cause of his being a fool, it is said, "he does not know whether there is approval or disapproval.
What is meant is that he is a fool because of his lack of knowledge regarding approval or disapproval.
In order to show the cause of this lack of knowledge, it is said, "he is a fool. Because of his foolishness, [he does not know] approval or disapproval...
