Or rather, it is said that he does not know. "Among them" means among the many co-residents (saddhivihārika). "Of him" refers to the bhikkhu who is perfect in his duties.
"Of them" refers to the other co-residents.
This is the story concerning the Brahmin Rādha.
69. The construction is: "Even though the Venerable Sāriputta knew. By this, he dispels the suspicion: "Could it be that he asked because he did not know? The connection is:
"The Blessed One was desirous of granting permission. The word *pana* has the sense of censure; thus the meaning is: "even though he knew in such a way.
*Lahukaṃ* (lightly) is a qualification included within the reason. It is said: "because of its lightness, having rejected [the offense]."
It exists. "Of the Blessed One" (*assā*)—this is the connection with "the intention" (*ajjhāsayam*).

Demonstrating the logical justification for the statement "having understood the intention," he said, "For the Buddhas," and so forth. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "And this one" (*ayañca*) refers to the Elder Sāriputta.
"Foremost" (*aggo*) means the pinnacle of excellence. "Best" (*seṭṭho*) means preeminent and supreme.

Regarding the phrase “by a learned and competent monk,” it is stated “one who is called learned,” and so forth, in order to show the distinction between being learned (*byatta*) and being competent (*paṭibala*). Therein, the construction is as follows:

he whose mastery of the Vinaya Piṭaka, together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakatha*), proceeds from his lips is called “learned. “In him” refers to the monk from whose lips the Vinaya Piṭaka has been mastered. “Of whom” refers to that monk.
“Suggahitaṃ” means well-grasped together with the commentary (*sāṭṭhakathā*). “Ayampi” (this one too): the word *pi* refers back to the previously mentioned bhikkhu.
“Imasmiṃ atthe” means in this matter, in this instance, or in this domain.

Showing the capacity [of the person] by way of positive and negative concomitance (*byatirekānvaya*), he said “yo panā” and so forth. The connection is: “but he who is not able. To the question “Why?”, he said: “by means of coughing, consumption, phlegm, and so forth.”
“Or,” and so forth. Therein, cough, consumption, and phlegm—these are the primary [symptoms] of that illness, thus it is “cough-consumption-phlegm-and-the-rest.

By the word “and-the-rest” (ādi), dumbness and so on are included. Lip, tooth, and tongue—these are the primary [parts] of which the palate and so on are comprised, thus they are “lip-tooth-tongue-and-the-rest”;
[the phrase refers to] those. “By words and phonemes” means by the syllables of the words. Here, the word *byañjana* (phoneme) [is used].

"A speaker of syllables. "He causes to fail" means he causes it to fail because it has slipped away. "Or it should be spoken otherwise" means it should be spoken in another manner, such as with lax articulation and so forth.
"He speaks otherwise" means he speaks in another manner, such as with forceful articulation and so forth.
"The opposite of that" refers to the connection with the monk who is the reverse of that incompetent person. "From that" means from what is to be made known. "Which" refers to that which...

This is an act performed by a formal motion (*ākāra-kamma*); this is an act performed by the Saṅgha (*saṅgha-kārita-kamma*). Here, it is said that the act performed by the Saṅgha is what is intended. 71.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after being fully ordained" (*upasampanna-samanantara*):

here, in order to exclude the meaning of "immediately after one who has been fully ordained," he says, "having become fully ordained, immediately thereafter. By the word *eva*, he excludes a long period of time. "May he lift me up" (*ullumpatu*)...

Here, because verbal roots have multiple meanings—either by virtue of a prefix or by virtue of an intensification of the sense—he says "let it lift up" (*uddharatu*) to show that the root *dhar* preceded by *upa* functions here in the sense of that [lifting]. The meaning is: "having raised up" or "having lifted up, let it hold.
To demonstrate that very same meaning, he says "unwholesome," and so forth. In that context, "having caused them to emerge from the unwholesome" (*akusale vuṭṭhāpetvā*).

By means of this prefix *ut*, he shows the meaning of the prefix *upa*. By means of this support (*sahādhāra*), he shows the meaning of the verbal root *dhr* in the phrase "to establish in what is wholesome.
While demonstrating that the prefix *ut* has the sense of "lifting up," he says: "having lifted [them] out from the state of a novice.
Regarding the word *paṭicca*, one should not take the lexical meaning here as "having taken up in proximity" (*samīpe ādiyitvā*).
Because it is well-known in the sense of its conventional meaning (*saṅketattha*), he shows that conventional meaning; the sense is that he shows the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*).

73. Regarding the term *adhiṭṭhitā*, he says "occurring constantly" (*niccappavattinī*) while demonstrating the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*): that which stands (*ṭhāti*) or proceeds (*pavattati*) by way of being constant (*nicca*) is "constantly established" (*adhiṭṭhitā*).
As to why the four conditions are called "supports" (*nissaya*), he says "because," and so forth.

By the words beginning with “four,” he shows the unexpressed object of the gerund *nissāya* (depending upon), namely that the personal existence (*attabhāva*) lies—that is, proceeds—depending upon the four conditions.
18. Discussion on the Duties toward Teachers. 75.
Regarding the phrase *kintāyaṃ*, he says *kiṃ te ayaṃ* because the sandhi occurs through the elision of the vowel *e*. By the word *ovaditabbo* (“he should be exhorted”),...
*Ovadiyo*: here, it shows that the *ṇya*-suffix has the sense of the object (*kamma*).

By the phrase “for the sake of that” (*tadatthāya*), having seen the word *yaṃ* in the subsequent sentence “namely, that which binds one to a group,” it indicates the presence of the word *taṃ* in the preceding sentence; the meaning is “for the sake of that abundance.
76. *So*: the wanderer Pasūra. *Tenā*: by the Elder Udāyī. *Sahadhammikaṃ*: together with the Dhamma.
By reason of this. Let it be that one who is "learned" possesses the characteristics previously stated; however, how is one who is "competent" to be known?
To this he says, "But he who... and so forth. The connection is: "he who is able. "Cā" means truly. "Etam" refers to the state of being competent, or else to the statement:
"by five... [qualities]... to discipline."
77. "Among those who have gone over to the faction of the *titthiyas*" means among those who have gone over to the opposition of the Dispensation, which is designated as the *titthiya* faction.
"One who trains in conduct and observance" (*ācārasamācārasikkhāpaka*) means one who trains [them] in the morality of higher practice (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*), which must be practiced exceedingly.
By this, he shows the etymological meaning of the word "teacher" (*ācariya*): "one who trains in conduct" (*ācāraṃ sikkhāpeti*). "Merely a name" refers to the term "teacher."
Or, "resident pupil" (*antevāsika*) is merely a name. "Separation" (*nāna*) means separation from either the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*).
20. Discussion on Sending Away and Requesting Forgiveness. 80. The connection is:

"the characteristic that has been stated. The construction is: "it must be performed by the resident pupil who is under dependence. [This applies] to those who are resident pupils in the Dhamma regarding going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*).

[There are three types of pupils: the pupil for going forth (*pabbajjantevāsika*), the pupil for full ordination (*upasampadantevāsika*), and the pupil for the Dhamma (*dhammantevāsika*). "Of these" means of those who are pupils for going forth, full ordination, and the Dhamma.
"Among these" means among these three types of pupils. "Of the teacher" means: the pupil for going forth [is the pupil] of the teacher for going forth;

the pupil for full ordination [is the pupil] of the teacher for full ordination—this is the meaning. "In the presence of" refers to the teacher of dependence (*nissayācariya*) and the teacher of the Dhamma (*dhammācariya*).
And "nearby. Therefore, because a pupil must conduct himself properly toward his teacher, for that reason.

"By the teacher also" means by the one who provides dependence (*nissaya*), the one who grants going-forth (*pabbajjā*), and the one who confers full ordination (*upasampadā*); the teacher of the Dhamma is also included among them. The teacher of exhortation (*ovādācariya*) is included within those.
"Among them" refers to the four types of pupils.
22. Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence;
Determination of the Command. 83.

“In the case of ‘the cessation of dependence’ (nissayapaṭippassaddhi),” this is a collective locus (*samūhādhāra*). “‘The preceptor has departed,’ and so forth,” this is a distributive locus (*avayavādhāra*).
“Desiring to depart” (vippavasitukāmo) indicates a state of being without attachment. “Thus gone” (evaṃ gato) is to be construed as “when the preceptor has thus gone.
“At another time” (aññadāpi) means at any other time; that is, at the time when the preceptor has departed.

“Sharing in one enjoyment” (ekasambhogaparibhogo) refers to sharing in the same use of requisites or the same use of the Dhamma, whether with oneself or with the preceptor. “Even for a single day” (ekadivasampi).
The word *pi* has the sense of censure; the meaning is "how much more so" in the case of two or more [days].
"There is no avoidance" means there is no avoidance of the offense; the intention is that there is no warding off or removal of the offense.
"A conscientious and virtuous one" is to be connected as "a monk who, being conscientious, is of a pleasant character. "On that very day" means on the day the preceptor had departed.
"Thus" means: just as [the teacher] asks, "Will the preceptor come quickly?", so it is said, "I will come quickly"—this is the meaning.
"If he speaks" is to be construed as "if the teacher speaks. "His" refers to the bhikkhu. "A sense of shame" means a state of being modest and virtuous.
"Until his arrival" means until the preceptor's arrival. In the phrase "he causes him to dwell," the object of the causative action is expressed.
*Therein* means at the place where the preceptor has gone. *By him* means by the preceptor. *Occurrence* means the act of occurring.
The connection is "or being afflicted by a river flood. Because of the river flood, he awaits the rising of the water;
because of being afflicted by thieves and the like, he seeks out companions. *He* refers to the preceptor.

By the phrase “the sending away of dependence” (*nissayapaṇāmanā*), it is shown that, according to the meaning of the word *āṇatti* as “commanding,” the sending away of dependence is called a command.
“Sending away of dependence” means the sending away of the one who is dependent, namely the preceptor or teacher. Therefore, the connection is:
“he becomes one who has been sent away. Regarding the phrase “by ‘having asked for leave,’ etc.,” here the word “etc. includes [the following]: “Do not let me go to the cemetery...”

This includes [passages] such as “having asked for leave,” and so forth. “By him” means by the student (saddhivihārika). “Should be asked for forgiveness” means he should be made to endure [the offense].
“First” means first by the great elders (mahātheras), or else first among the great elders. “Elsewhere” means to another monastery than the preceptor’s (upajjhāya) monastery.
“Perhaps even” is to be construed as: “perhaps even he might forgive. “In that very same place” means in another [monastery] indeed. “Due to the fault of famine and so forth.”
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), faults such as separation from kinsmen are to be understood. "That very [place]" means that same location where one has resided oneself.
"Of another" is to be connected with "of a monk other than the preceptor" (upajjhāya).
By this, it is indicated that because one has been relinquished by this preceptor, there is no cessation of dependence (*nissaya*) upon the meeting with the preceptor.
The Determination of Synonyms:
“Having asked for permission” means having asked the resident pupil (*antevāsika*) for permission. “There too” refers even to the teacher and the resident pupil.
“When? means at what time? “In the evening or at night” means either this very evening or at night. “At that very moment” means at the very moment of receiving [the request].

"So" refers to the resident pupil (*antevāsika*). "From there" means from the village. "Well-gone" (*sugata*) means one who has gone well; the intention is that the formal dependence (*nissaya*) is extinguished.

"Furthermore" (*athāpi*) means moreover. Having shown the determination regarding departing after having asked for permission, he said, "Without asking the teacher," etc., in order to demonstrate that [consequence] when departing after having asked for permission.
"Transgressing the boundary of the precinct" (*upacārasīmātikkame*) refers to the boundary of the precinct.

The construction is: "when there is transgression, or because of transgression. And here, "boundary of the precinct" (*upacārasīmā*) refers to the very enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or for an unenclosed one, the area suitable for an enclosure.
"In the evening or during the night" means either this evening or during the night. "Tomorrow" (*sve*) means on the following day.
"Outside the boundary" means outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*). "From there" means from outside that boundary.

"Two throws of a clod" means two throws of a clod from the resident pupil (*antevāsika*). "Having passed beyond" means having passed beyond the precinct boundary, from the place where the resident pupil and his co-resident (*saddhivihārika*) dwell.
"Desiring to be released" means desiring to be released from his pupil. "Dismisses" means dismisses by means of body and speech.
"With attachment" means having regard for the teacher. Having said "without attachment," the phrase "no longer... and so forth is stated to show its meaning.
"Even thus" means even when the burden has been laid down. When the burden is laid down by both, or due to the laying down of the burden, it subsides.
The connection is: "one should proceed with that which has been sent away.

Expanding upon this very meaning, he said, "If indeed," and so forth. "The teacher" refers to the preceptor (*nissayācariya*). The connection is: "or [the disciple] while paying homage to a cetiya, [should wait for] the preceptor";
or the construction is: "[he should wait for] the preceptor who has set out on the road. "Because of being far away" means...
"By way of distance": "on top of the palace" means upon the palace. "Him" refers to the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). The connection is with the phrase "the seated preceptor.

The construction should be understood as follows: the detailed explanation regarding the combination [of factors] by way of hearing is to be known thus. The connection is with the phrase "the sound of the preceptor. 23.
Discussion on the Five Qualities for Ordination (*Upasampadā-pañcaka-kathā*)
84. Now, the connection is: "the characteristic which has been stated. "In brief" means concisely, without enumerating the individual factors (*aṅga*).
"Therein" refers to where it was said: "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors... and so forth.
"By means of factors devoid of virtue" means by means of factors lacking in good qualities. "He" refers to the bhikkhu. "He should not be ordained"—here...

One might suspect that [the rule] "one should not confer full ordination while acting as a *kammavācā*-teacher" implies that one should not confer full ordination while acting as a preceptor (*upajjhāya*);
therefore, he said, "one should not confer full ordination while acting as a preceptor. "In these" refers to these five sets of five.

Regarding the word "and so forth" (*ādīsu*), here the particle *iti* is elided for the purpose of illustration; thus, the meaning is "in these and so forth. "By way of what is improper" means by way of what is unsuitable. "Who" refers to the bhikkhu.
“Hī” means “truth,” or “because. The connection is with the phrase “and [he] encourages others. “Therein” refers to the aggregate of virtue and so forth.
“He maintains” means he carries away or removes the assembly from danger (*parissaya*). “His” refers to the bhikkhu.

The term “by virtue and so forth” is the ablative (*apādāna*) in relation to the phrase “he surely falls away,” and it is the instrumental (*karaṇa*) in relation to the phrase “he does not increase. “Therefore,” and so on, refers to the qualities already attained.
"By ten" means by a monk. To the question "Why is it not stated by way of the factors of an offense? he says, "For not," and so forth. "For" (hi) means because.

"Of that very one" means of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) alone. "He would not speak" means he would not speak because dissatisfaction has not arisen among those whose taints are destroyed.
If the status of preceptor and teacher is permitted only for one whose taints are destroyed, then why [is there mention of] the group of five whose taints are destroyed?
He said, "But because," and so forth, to explain what was stated. The connection is: "because it does not decline.
"Antaggāhikāya" means that which grasps or causes one to grasp an extreme—namely, the extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism—which are base; thus, by that [view].
"Diṭṭhiyā" means by wrong view. "Yattakaṃ sutaṃ" (as much as has been heard) is what is stated in the Bhikkhunovādaka-sikkhāpada.
"Whatever has been heard"—by that "heard" [text], such as the *Ṛgveda*. The construction is: "That which is an offense and so forth must be known by means of that.

Regarding the phrase "he does not know the offense," in order to show the meaning "he does not know that he has fallen into an offense," the author says: "This is called... and so forth. Therein, by the word "fallen into" (*āpanno*), it is shown that the term "offense" (*āpatti*) should be construed with the elliptical reading "fallen into" (*āpanno*).
Regarding the term "pertaining to higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārikāya*): herein, it is to be practiced rightly in a way that is superior to the virtue included within the two Vibhaṅgas.

"Regarding higher conduct" (*ābhisamācāraṃ*) refers to the virtue of performing duties (*vatta-paṭipatti-sīla*) included in the Khandhakas; the training rules included in the Khandhakas are "pertaining to higher conduct" (*ābhisamācārika*), being prescribed with reference to that.

Regarding the phrase "of the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyakāya*): here, the "beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariya*) is the boundary or limit of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) known as the Path;
those [rules] that operate within that are "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyaka*), namely, those included in the two Vibhaṅgas.

"Training" (*sikkhā*): it is training in the sense of that which is to be practiced. "The designation for trainees" (*sekkhapaṇṇatti*) means that it is training because it is to be practiced, and it is the "designation for trainees" because it was designated by the Blessed One.
Alternatively, training is the act of practicing; it is the "designation for trainees" because it is designated by the Blessed One for the purpose of that practice.
This refers specifically to the training included within the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*. Regarding the phrase "in the Abhidhamma": here, [it is distinguished] from the Sutta-piṭaka.

When it is said that "Abhidhamma" refers to a doctrine that is superior (*abhi*) or distinguished (*visiṭṭha*), one speaks of the "Abhidhamma Piṭaka" as that which delimits name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-paricchedaka*);
thus he says, "in the delimitation of name-and-form. Regarding "Abhivinaya": here, it is called "Abhivinaya" because it disciplines the body and speech by overcoming them;
or, when it is said that "Abhivinaya" is that by which one disciplines the body and speech after having overcome them, it refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
He said: "In the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. The construction is: "The meaning is to be seen everywhere," that is, in all locations or in all words.

In the phrase "by way of cause" (*kāraṇena*), the word *kāraṇa* excludes the meanings such as "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*) associated with the word *dhamma* in the phrase "by way of the Dhamma" (*dhammato*), and instead indicates the sense of "cause";
this is for the purpose of qualifying the suffix *-to* by means of the particle *ena*.
*Iti* means "thus," that is, in the manner already described; such is the sense. *Catutthe* refers to the fourth pentad.
Having taken three terms from the fourth pentad and two terms from the fifth pentad, and having formed a pentad [from them], it is stated as "four pentads.
This is the connection with the phrase "in the eight pentads."
Thus ends the application [of the commentary] to the analysis of the sixteen pentads.
24. Discourse on the Sixfold Set of Those to Be Ordained. 85.
“That” refers to the phrase “one who is less than ten years [of standing]. “In all cases” means in all six sets. “Therein” means within those six sets. “The Pātimokkhas...”
Because it was stated "in detail," they should be understood by way of their analysis (vibhaṅga); thus he said, "stated by way of both Vibhaṅgas.
They are "well-analyzed" (suvibhattāni) because they must be thoroughly analyzed by way of the Analysis of the Matrices (Mātikāvibhaṅga).

They are "well-proclaimed" (suppavattīni) because their excellent application has been mastered through oral recitation. They are "well-determined" (suvinicchitabbāni) because they must be properly defined according to the Suttas and the secondary characteristics (anubyañjana).
Showing the meaning, he said: "By way of the matrix and the analysis," and so forth. 25.

The Discourse on the Case of One Formerly a Member of Another Sect. 86. "But whoever" means whoever was formerly a member of another sect. "Another one as well" refers to someone other than Pasūrata. "In this" means in this [text].
In the Teaching. "In that" refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect. "Therein" refers to the statement beginning with, "Whosoever, monks, is another...
This refers to the probation (*parivāsa*). Having stated, "only for a naked ascetic," it was said, "or for an Ājīvaka or an Acelaka," in order to show the distinction between them.
Therein, an Ājīvaka wears a single garment by tucking it into his armpits.
"Below" means naked. However, an *acelaka* (a naked ascetic) is naked in every respect. "He too" refers even to a naked wandering mendicant (*paribbājaka*).
"Of hair-blankets and so forth": a blanket made of hair; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hair-blankets and the like are included.
"His" refers to the wandering mendicant. "Of another" refers to someone other than the naked wandering mendicant. "Of those with white garments and so forth."
One whose limbs—that is, his body—are white or clothed in white garments is called *paṇḍaraṅga*; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those such as *nīlaṅga* (blue-limbed) and others are included.
"In this way" refers to the shaving of hair and beard and so forth. The connection is with "by the monks who are ordaining [him]. "In him" refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect;
it is to be construed as "even while he is sitting. This locative case is used in the sense of disregard. "Of him" refers to the one who was formerly of another sect.
“‘These are not [monks], these are not monks’—this is the connection.
‘He’ refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect. 87. The construction is: ‘In this way... [he is] one who does not succeed’; this statement is the matrix (mātikā).
‘His’ refers to one who was formerly of another sect. ‘Of that very same’ refers to that very matrix. ‘Therein’ means in the Vibhaṅga. Regarding ‘too early’: having performed the meal-duty here...”
Showing that even at the very time of performing the formal duties (vatta) it is called "past time," he said, "at the very time of performing the formal duties.
By this, he also shows that the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. "Right there" means in the families' homes themselves. "Aññadatthu" means "certainly" or "absolutely";

by the word "performing," he indicates a syntactical ellipsis. Thus, the construction is: "even while performing [the duties] in this way, one who was formerly a member of another sect (aññatitthiyapubba)."
By the word “sampādako,” he shows here that the term *ārādha* has the sense of “accomplishing” (*sādhana*), thereby excluding meanings such as “pleasing.

A “prostitute” (*vesiyā*) is so called because those seeking illicit conduct (*ajjhācāra*) enter (*visanti*) or penetrate her; or else, she is a prostitute because she wears a “disguise” (*vesa*) consisting of an attractive appearance.
Hence it is said: “easily accessible for illicit conduct,” and so forth. “Dust” (*kiñjakkha*) refers to material gain (*āmisa*) itself, in the sense of being something trivial.

*Āmisakiñjakkha* is a compound with *visesana* (qualifier) as the first member and *parapada* (the subsequent word). Alternatively, *āmisa* and another thing called *kiñjakkha* together form *āmisakiñjakkha*;
the dative case of that is *āmisakiñjakkhasampadāna*. The word *kiñjakkha* primarily denotes a filament (*kesara*), but it is used by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*) for something very small.
Regarding the word *vidhavā*, here the term *dhava* denotes only a husband, not...
Showing the specific type of tree, he said, "or one whose husband has died," and so forth. By these words, he demonstrates the etymological meaning of *vidhavā*:
either those from whom the husband (*dhava*) has departed due to death or due to absence, or those who have departed from their husband; thus it is *vidhavā*.

Showing that they are "stout young women" (*thullakumārikā*), he explains that they are called so because they are either in the prime of youth or have passed beyond youth, and are therefore stout and large.

He said, "Having reached youth," and so forth. Regarding "eunuchs" (*paṇḍaka*): among the five types of eunuchs, such as the *āsitta-paṇḍaka* (the drenched eunuch) and others, it is the neuter eunuch (*napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*) that is intended here;
thus he said, "neuters. "Commonly ordained" means ordained together with the monks. "From there" means from a state of trust.
"Therein" means among courtesans and the like. "Of them" means of the courtesans. "He" refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect. "In all cases" means in all instances.
Regarding widows and so forth: showing that [the house] must be visited, he said, “But if...,” and so on. “Tathā” means just as it was stated that [the house] must be visited, so too [here].
Regarding “uccāvacāni”: here, that which accumulates (*cayati*) and increases upward is “high” (*ucca*);

that from which accumulation has departed—that is, separation—is “low” (*avaca*). Thus, by the literal meaning of “high and low” (*uccāvacāni*), it signifies “large and small”; hence he said, “large and small.”
By the word “kammāni,” he shows the formal identity with the term “karaṇīyāni.
And by showing that, the etymological meaning of the word *karaṇīyāni*—namely, “those things which ought to be done”—should be understood. “Tattha” means among the great and small tasks.

Regarding the phrase “he is not skillful therein,” it is stated “in various new works” (*tesu tesu navakammesu*) in order to show the scope of the pronoun *tatra*. “Endowed with initiative and energy” (*uṭṭhānavīriyasampanno*).
By this, he shows the etymological meaning of "analaso" (diligent), namely: "there is no laziness (*alasa*) or indolence (*kosajja*) in him.
Regarding the word "tatra" (therein), he says "tesu tesu" (in those various [instances]) to show that the suffix *-tra* is used here in the sense of the locative case to indicate distribution.

To demonstrate the meaning of the statement "by means of investigative wisdom arising on the spot" (*ṭhānuppattikāya vīmaṃsāya*), he says "this very," and so forth: "wisdom arisen at that very moment."
By this, he shows that in the phrase “arising from the occasion” (*ṭhānuppattikā*), the word *ṭhāna* has the sense of “that moment.

Regarding the phrase “to be sufficient to act” (*alaṃ kātuṃ*), he says “capable of acting” (*kātuṃ samattho*) because the word *alaṃ* here signifies the sense of sufficiency among its three meanings—namely, adornment, restraint, and sufficiency. “Intense desire” (*tibbacchando*) means sharp desire.

By the phrase “strong desire” (*balavacchando*), he shows the sense of intention (*adhippāya*). “Development of mundane concentration” (*lokīyasamādhibhāvanāya*) refers to the development of mundane concentration consisting of the eight attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*).
"Come hither" means come to this teaching. "Of the owner of the *titthāyatana*": a *tittha* (ford) is so called because beings cross over it, float upon it, and emerge and submerge within it;
that is, the sixty-two views. That very thing is the *āyatana* (sphere) for those who follow such views; thus it is a *titthāyatana*.
Alternatively, those for whom a *tittha* exists are *titthins*, and their *āyatana* is the *titthāyatana*.
“His master” means the master of the sectarian order (titthāyatana); [the phrase] “his” refers to that.

Regarding the expression “his view,” the word *diṭṭhi* here is a synonym for *laddhi* (tenet), which is why he says, “by his own tenet. Why is that tenet called “inclination” (*khanti*), “liking” (*ruci*), and “adherence” (*ādāya*)?
To this he says, “Now,” and so forth. That very same tenet is what is meant by “it is approved,” “it is liked,” and “it is grasped.”
The construction [is as follows]: *tassa titthakarassa* is a genitive used in the sense of the agent (*katvatthe*).
*Tassa* means "of the owner of that religious system" (*titthāyatanasāmikassa*). *Bhaññamānāya* means "while it was being recited.

Regarding *anabhiraddho*, he says, "one whose intention is incomplete, not one whose mind is uplifted," showing that the meaning here is "displeased" (*anabhirādhito*) or "one whose mind is unsatisfied" (*aparitositacitto*). *Yadidaṃ* means "that which is this."
The connection is either with “displeasure” (*anattamanatta*) or with “pleasure” (*attamanatta*). By this, he shows the non-restriction of the word “this.
“These” refers to the monks. The construction is: “and that which is displeasure. “Of that very person” connects with “the displeasure of one who was formerly a follower of another sect.
“This” refers to the fourfold [classification]: two types of pleasure and two types of displeasure.
This is the class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*). "To be compiled" (*saṅghāṭanīya*) means it should be brought together; the meaning is that it should be collected.

By the words "in one who does not please" (*anārādhake*) and so forth, he shows the etymological meaning here as "that which is not to be pleased": "it is 'not-to-be-pleased' (*anārādhanīya*) because one does not please [the teacher] through this action.
"This" refers to the fourfold [classification]. "Sign" (*liṅga*) means cause. "Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) means mark. "From this" means from the eight factors.
The connection is with the word "extracted" (*nīhaṭena*). "By the reversal of what was stated" means by the opposite of what was stated regarding the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*).
Showing the eight factors combined on the bright side (*sukkapakkha*), he said: "Not entering the village too early, not returning [from alms] too late," and so forth.
By this same method, the eight factors should also be combined for the dark side. "Satisfying" (*paritosaka*)—
By this, he shows the meaning of *ārādhaka* as "pleasing. However, since it was stated previously as "accomplisher" (*sampādaka*), it should be understood that this shows the meaning of "achieving.

"In the ordination hall" (*upasampadamāḷake*) means even in a particular type of dwelling with many corners, provided it has a single peak, which serves as the location for the full ordination (*upasampadā*). That...
Indeed, because it is made with a single peak (*ekakūṭa*) and is covered and adorned by many corners (*koṇa*), it is called a *māḷa*.
By saying, "He must dwell in probation for four months," he makes this clear through a unique simile, stating, "Just as, however... and so forth. The word *hi* means "truly.
*Assa* refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect (*aññatitthiyapubbo*). The connection is: "while dwelling in probation, [he is] one who was formerly of another sect."
"Within four months" means inside the period of four months. "Of a nature to be agitated" means of a nature to perish.
"Grasps" means grasps by way of delimitation. "Distinguishes name-and-form" means he distinguishes it thus: "This is name, this is form.

"Characteristic" refers to the characteristic of bending (namana) and being molested (ruppana), or the characteristic of impermanence and so forth. "The abandoning of views and doubt by the path of stream-entry."
It was said with intentional meaning: “The arrows... have been eradicated. *Abbuḷhaṃ* means it was drawn out;
the sense is that it was carried upward. For the prefix *ā-* has the sense of going upward. “On that very day” means on the very day of attaining the path of stream-entry.
This accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. “That very same day” means on the very day of becoming a stream-enterer.
“Of him” means of one who was formerly a member of another sect. Since the bowl is not mentioned in the text, it is said: “The bowl is also likewise.
The meaning is that just as the robe must be sought with the preceptor as its basis, so too must the bowl. “This” refers to the bowl and robe.
“Of this” refers to one who was formerly a member of another sect. “Others” means other than the preceptor. “By them also” means by others as well. “Contrary” means...
In reverse order. *Āyattaṃ* means dependent. *Āyattajīvikattā* means because his livelihood is dependent upon the preceptor (*upajjhāya*). *Tassa* refers to the preceptor.

*Vacanakaro* means one who does what is said. Even though the word *vacana* occurs both in a sentence and in a compound, because it depends solely on the word *tassa*, the compound *vacanakaro* is formed.
This same method applies to "by the preceptor... [and so forth].
[This applies] also here [in the phrase] "because their livelihood is dependent.

"By that" means by the reason of being compliant with what is said. "Fire-worshippers" (*aggiparicaraṇakā*) refers to those who venerate fire. By this, he shows the etymological meaning of the word *aggika*: they are called *aggika* because they attend upon fire.

"Ascetics" (*tāpasa*) refers to those who wear matted hair (*jaṭādhara*). For since they possess both matted hair (*jaṭā*) and austerity (*tapas*), they are therefore called "matted-hair ascetics" (*jaṭila*).
And they are called "ascetics" (tāpasa). These are the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila). Demonstrating the meaning of the statement, "They do not deny action," he said:
"There is action; there is the ripening of action. "This very renunciation" means this very renunciation of an ascetic.
"Of these" refers to the matted-hair ascetics. "In the Dispensation" means in the Dispensation of the Buddha. "Of them" refers to their kinsmen.
The connection is that they "avoid this. "They" refers to the relatives. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Of the best of kinsmen" (*ñātiseṭṭhassa*):
he is a kinsman who is also the best, or the best among kinsmen; thus, he is the "best of kinsmen," and the connection is "of that Buddha.
26. Discourse on the Five Bases of Disease.
88. Regarding "In Magadha": because it is expressed here with a plural form, he says, "in the country named Magadha," indicating that it is the name of a province.
"And of non-human beings" means of beings other than humans. Both the word *ussanna* and the word *ussada* are synonyms for having reached growth;
therefore, he says, "abundant, having reached growth. By the phrase "having attained excellence" (*phātippattā*), he expresses that very same meaning.
[The text] shows this. "By those" means by the five diseases beginning with leprosy (*kuṭṭha*).
"In that" means among the five diseases beginning with leprosy. It is called a disease (*ābādha*) because it thoroughly (*ābhūso*) afflicts and oppresses;

it is called leprosy (*kuṭṭha*) because it cuts and carves the limbs and members of the body. In phrases such as "red leprosy," the word "or" (*vā*) includes white leprosy and the other varieties as well.

"Kīṭibha, daddu, khajju, and so forth"—this means *kīṭibha*, *daddu*, and *khajju* are "the kīṭibha, daddu, and khajju. Those which have these as their primary [manifestations] are "those beginning with kīṭibha, daddu, and khajju" (*kīṭibhadaddukhajjuādayo*).
Their classification is "the classification beginning with kīṭibha, daddu, and khajju" (*kīṭibhadaddukhajjuādippabheda*), and that too [is included].
In this context, the word division for *kīṭibha* should be made as *kīṭa-ibha*. Therein, *kīṭa* means a worm (*kimī*). By this—
*Kīṭakulāvaka* should be understood as "kīṭa"; it is called *kīṭa* because it is like a worm (*kīṭa*), a specific type of leprosy.
*Ibho* means an elephant. By this, the elephant’s tusk (*sabala*) should be understood as *ibho*; it is called *ibho* because it is like a tusk (*ibha*), a specific type of leprosy.
*Kīṭibho* is a *kīṭa* that is also an *ibho*, a specific affliction of leprosy, which is designated in the world as "a specific affliction of leprosy. *Daddū* means itch (*kacchu*).
For it bites (*daṃsati*), stings (*vidaṃsati*), or harms (*hiṃsati*) the body; thus it is called *daddu*.
By changing one *d* sound to an *r* sound, there is also the reading *daddu*, which is what is commonly referred to in the world as "pve. *Khajjū* means itching.
For it is that which the body is bitten by, distressed by, or devoured by; or because it harms, it is called *khajjū*. This is what is known in the world as "khajja."
They say [this]. There is also a reading “kacchū,” but that is not a valid reading because it has already been included by the word *daddu*.
“That” refers to leprosy (*kuṭṭha*). “In a place naturally concealed” means in a place naturally covered;
the meaning is: in a place such as where one is clothed and draped. By this, he specifically excludes what is [already] concealed. “If it is situated on the side of non-increase” means...
The construction [is as follows]: *pakativaṇṇe* means "in the natural skin. The meaning is: "just as the skin becomes scarred, so too [it becomes].
This was not said with reference to the site of a wound (*vaṇavatthu*).
*Medagaṇḍo*: it is called *medo* because fat (*meda*) exists therein; it is called *gaṇḍo* because it becomes a swelling (*phoṭo*); thus, it is a swelling consisting of fat itself.
*Medagaṇḍo*: that which in the world is conventionally called "a lump of fat. *Kolaṭṭhi*: "kola" is said to be the jujube fruit (*badaraphala*);
its seed is the *kolaṭṭhi*. The construction is: "when [the body] remains in the state of not increasing.
*Sañchavin*: possessing existing skin, or having skin produced. *Uṇṇigaṇḍā*: those that bend upward are *uṇṇiyo*; these very things, being lumps, are *uṇṇigaṇḍā*. Those which...
In the world, they speak of them as "uṇṇigaṇḍā. Therein, therein means in each respective part of the body.

"Khīrapīḷakā" means that which has milk (*khīra*) in it is "milk-like" (*khīrā*); those very pustules are "milk-pustules" (*khīrapīḷakā*). These are what people in the world refer to as "khīrapīḷakā" and so forth.
"Tāsu" means in those pustules. The connection is: "there are swellings called milk-pustules. "Kharapīḷakā" means...
An abscess is of a harsh nature. Because of its harsh nature, beings meet even death through it, or experience suffering equal to death.
That which is commonly referred to in the world as a "milk-boil" (khīrapīḷakā) is what is meant. The connection is that there are swellings called "lotus-seed-calyxes" (padumakaṇṇikā).
A lotus-seed-calyx is like the calyx of a lotus. That which is commonly referred to in the world as a "lotus-seed-calyx" is what is meant. It is the size of a mustard seed.

The connection is with the term *gaṇḍa* (boils). Those whose size is equal to a mustard seed are "mustard-seed-sized" (*sāsapabījakā*); they are those which are commonly referred to in the world as "mustard-seed-sized.
"All those" means all those pustules or types of boils. "In them" means in the pustules or in the types of boils. "The color of a lotus or white lotus petal":
a lotus (*paduma*) is red, while a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) is white; [this refers to] the petals of those flowers.

"Having the color of a lotus petal" (*padumapuṇḍarīkapattavaṇṇa*) means its color is like that; it is "conch-white leprosy" (*saṅkhakuṭṭha*). That which people in the world refer to as "conch-white leprosy, having the color of a lotus petal.
"By which" means by that leprosy. The construction is: "Just as the body of cattle becomes spotted, so too does the body of humans become spotted.
"In that" refers to *kilāsa* (vitiligo). "The disease of emaciation" (*sosabyādhi*) is a wasting disease. For it is because...
It dries up the flesh, blood, and so forth; therefore it is called *sosa*. That which in the world is designated as "consumption" (*sāṃsa*) and "the disease of consumption" (*sosabyādhi*).

In that [disease], namely the disease of consumption. *Apasmāro* is epilepsy. For because it has departed from its essence (*sāra*), it is called "departed-essence" (*apamāra*), with the letter *sa* changed to *ma*.
That which in the world is known as "epilepsy" (*apamāra*) and "arū? [a corruption of *arūpa* or similar].
And they speak thus. "Therein" refers to the two types of madness; this locative case expresses the locus (*ādhāra*). The connection is: "he becomes one for whom it is difficult to do what is right.
27. The Discourse on the Matter of the King’s Servant. 90. Regarding the word *uccinatha*:
here, showing that the root *ci* has the sense of increasing, he says "increase. From the state of being a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
“Because King Bimbisāra had attained the state of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). ‘Kill him’ means deprive him of life. ‘Strike him’ means hit him. ‘From him’ means from the preceptor (upajjhāya).
‘The teacher is the best’—this is the connection. ‘From him’ means from the teacher (ācariya). ‘This’ refers to the speech; ‘has come’—this is the connection.
‘The judges and great ministers said it was a lie’—this is the construction. ‘Ministers’ refers to those [appointed] to all royal duties.”
He is called an *amacca* because he exists (*bhavati*) together with (*amā*) the king. The word *amā* is a particle used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahattha*).

According to Moggallāna’s grammar (Sutta 4.23), the suffix *-acca* is applied after the particle *amā* in the sense of existence (*bhavatthe*). A *mahāmatta* is so called because great (*mahā*) authority (*mattā*) belongs to him;
thus he is a "great official. Here, the word *mattā* denotes authority or power. A *sevaka* is one who serves (*sevati*) and attends upon (*bhajati*) the king; thus he is a "servant."
*Bhattavetanabhaṭo* means one hired for the sake of food and wages. *Tassa* refers to that royal hireling. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in the phrase "sons, grandsons, brothers, etc.," nephews and so forth are included. *Yo pana* means "but as for the royal hireling. *Niyyātetī* means he sends him away.
*Taṃ ṭhānaṃ* means that position of the royal hireling. *Yena vā* means by whichever laborer. *Yaṃkammakāraṇā* means for the sake of which work.
"Or a royal official" means a soldier of the king. "Go forth" means cause [him] to go forth. 28.
The Discourse on the Story of the Robber. 91.
"Seen before" means Aṅgulimāla was seen previously. "This one" refers to the robber. "He" refers to Aṅgulimāla. Of others...
The construction is: "they hear the words from his presence. "They" refers to the people. "Are terrified" means they are terrified in body;
"are agitated" means they are agitated in mind. [An objection: "Was Aṅgulimāla not ordained by the monks?
Was he not rather ordained by the Blessed One himself? Then why was it said, 'Monks, [you must not ordain him]'? To this he replies: "The Blessed One is himself the Master of the Dhamma."
*Dhammassāmī* means the lord of the Dhamma; or, by virtue of the Dhamma, he is the lord of gods and humans—the sense is that he is the sovereign. The construction is:
"the training rule for monks (*bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ*) for the purpose of [ensuring] non-doing by monks. *Tattha* refers to the statement beginning with "Monks, not... (*na bhikkhave*).
Regarding the phrase "having hoisted a banner" (*dhajaṃ bandhitvā*), the binding of a banner is *dhajabandha*; it is called *dhajabandha* because it is like the hoisting of a banner.
The phrase "having bound his banner, he wanders" shows the meaning of the term *dhajabandha*. "Therefore" means because he is one who has bound his banner; "he" refers to the thief.
"Or plundering on the road" means plundering upon the highway. Regarding the words "and he is seen," the particle *ca* here serves to connect the sentences.
For the meaning is not only that he wanders about, but also that he is seen. "This" refers to...
*Corakammaṃ*: "Robbery. *Rajjaṃ*: "Kingship. *So*: "He," referring to the prince. *Hi*: "Truly," or "because. *Tasmiṃ*: "In him," referring to the prince.
*Pubbe*: "Formerly," in a previous time. *Taṃ*: "Him," referring to the thief. *Evaṃ*: "In this manner. The construction is: "and they know [him] in this way. *Adissamānā*:

"Not being seen," meaning not making themselves known. This was said with reference to thieves such as those who break into houses (*sandhicchedādi*), and not to thieves such as those who steal mangoes (*ambalabujādi*).
"Even afterwards" means even after the act of stealing. "Those too" refers to the thieves.

(92) "Out of fear" means from fear. "But these" refers to the monks. "Because they had obtained security" (*laddhābhayattā*): those from whom security (*abhaya*) has been obtained by them from the king are "those who have obtained security";

the state of being such is "the fact of having obtained security," and it is because of that. Regarding the term "breaker of the dam" (*kārabhedaka*), here the word *kāra*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
The term *ruk khavisese* (a particular kind of tree) occurs in the sense of honor and in the sense of a prison;
however, here it is shown to mean a prison, hence he says: “*Kāra* is called a prison-house (*bandhanāgāra*).
For they build it, and because they harm the people who have been cast inside it, it is called a “*kāra*. “Here” refers to the phrase “breaker of prisons. *Dīpabandhanaṃ*.

The construction is: "or [he may be] a prisoner. By these words, he shows that not only a prison is called *kārā*, but also fetters such as ankle-chains (*andubandhana*) and so forth are likewise called *kārā*. "He" refers to the thief. "Among these" refers to the bonds.
"Or having released" means either having untied the bond of rope. By these words, it is shown that it is not only from breaking out of a prison...
He is called a "breaker of prisons" (kārabhedaka); however, this shows that he is indeed called a breaker of prisons even by means of cutting, releasing, and opening [the locks].
"To another island" (dīpantara) means to another island different from the island where one was imprisoned;

the fact that he went to another world-system (cakkavāḷantara) after breaking through the boundary of the world-system (cakkavāḷabandhana) is not mentioned in the Commentary. "He" refers to the thief. "Villages, market towns, ports, and so forth."
Here, "port" (*paṭṭana*) refers to a harbor for ships and a port for carts. "Toll" (*keṇi*) is the revenue to be paid to the king. "That" refers to the toll.
"Treasure" (*nidhāna*) is wealth placed there by being buried. "Having brought" means having brought it into the presence of the king and others.
"That" refers to one who makes a living by means of agriculture and so forth. "Right there" means in the very place where he was bound.

93. *Yattha* means "in which place. The connection is with "anyone at all" (*yo koci*). *Naṃ* refers to "any person whatsoever" (*yaṃ kiñci janaṃ*). The construction is: "he causes to be written" (*likhāpeti*).

*Paṇṇe vā* means "on a leaf" or "on *kusa* grass. *Assa* means "of that person. *Daṇḍaṃ* means "a monetary fine" (*dhanadaṇḍaṃ*). *Likhitako* means "one who is to be written" (*likhitabbo*), thus he is "the written one" (*likhito*), and that very one is "the written one" (*likhitako*).
94. However, the connection is with the phrase "he who is struck with whips. By this, he shows the etymological meaning of *kasāhata* as "one struck by other whips.
By the phrase "let this very thing be your punishment," he shows the etymological meaning of *katadaṇḍakamma* as "one for whom the act of punishment has been performed.
*Allavaṇa* means a fresh wound. *Ghātetvā* means having killed; the sense is "having struck."
“Gaṇḍigaṇḍiyā” means by striking together. “Sannisinnāsu” means when they are seated in their natural posture upon the gaṇḍīs. 95.

Let it be understood that the state of having performed the formal act of punishment (daṇḍakamma) is to be known in the same manner as previously described; however, how is the state of being struck with a mark (lakkhaṇāhata) to be understood?
To this he says, “Yassa panā” and so forth. In that context, “tattena” means by heat. “Lakkhaṇaṃ” means a sign or token.
"Sota" means a person. "Bhujissa" means one who has arms (*bhujā*); thus he is a *bhujissa*.
It is said that, being neither protected by others nor made to swallow [food] by others, he himself is endowed with the protection of his own self and the swallowing of food.
"Assa" refers to one who has been struck by a mark. "Vaṇā" means wounds. For they are called *vaṇā* because the limbs are crushed.
They cause [pain], therefore they are called "wounds" (*vaṇa*). They are "healed" (*rūḷha*) because they have grown over with fresh flesh.
The connection is: "of people who possess the three circles and whose bodies are marked. 33. The Discourse on the Subject of Debtors.
96. Regarding the term *iṇāyika*: here, *iṇa* means "debt" (*uddhāra*). For it is called *iṇa* because it "goes" (*eti*), that is, it increases;
therefore, one who takes or holds that [debt] is an *iṇāyika*. The connection is: "or having placed such a person under obligation.
And "having placed" (*āṭhapetvā*) means having placed them in the presence of the owner of the wealth for the purpose of being sent. The letter *ā-* [is used].

For *hi* expresses the sense of a reason. The word *pi* (also) refers back to the previous person. By the word *dhāreti*, it is shown that the *āyika* suffix occurs in the sense of "bearing" (*dhāraṇa*).
*Aññe* means others than mother and father. *Hi* means "truly" or "because. *Te* refers to other relatives;
since they are not masters over placing that [debt] upon him, the construction is: "therefore he is not a creditor (*iṇāyika*). *Itaraṃ* means other than a non-creditor.
*Anyam*: of another person. *Assa*: of that person. *Tam*: that person. *Tesu*: among those such as kinsmen and blood relations.
*Tathārūpassa*: of one who is of such a kind; the meaning is "of one's own kinsman or blood relation. Showing the manner in which it should be announced, he said:
"With cause," and so forth. Therein, *sahetuko* means capable. *So*: the attendant. *Paṭipajjati*: he gives back. *Etam*: this allowable article (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*). *Añānitvā*: not knowing.
"Without having recognized the status of a debtor. "By one seeing [him]" means by one seeing the debtor.
By the phrase "there is no liability for one who does not see," it is shown that there is liability for one who has seen but does not report it.
"Even when being questioned" means even when being asked, "Are you a debtor? "Him" refers to the debtor. "Therein" refers to...
In another place. *Taṃ* refers to the creditor. *So* refers to the creditor. *Ayaṃ* refers to the debtor. *Ayaṃ* is the word used.
*Tattha* means regarding the ordination of the debtor. *Sāmīcī* means accordance with the Dhamma.
*Naṃ* refers to the debtor. *So* refers to the creditor. *Assa* refers to the Elder. The connection is "there is no liability (*gīvā*) for him. *Acchatu* means "let it go."
"Let him sit, let him sit down"—this is the meaning. "He" refers to the debtor. "Such as this" means one who has a cause [for his conduct] and is endowed with proper observance;
that is, one who greatly pleases the Elder through his conduct and behavior.
34. The Discourse on the Ten Bases for Slavery.
97. *Dāsā* means servants (*ceṭaka*). For they are called *dāsā* because they are dragged (*asīyanti*) or hurled (*khipīyanti*) by their masters into suffering or into evil deeds.

"Therein" refers to among the four types of slaves. By the phrase "the son of a female slave in the house," it shows the meaning of the term *antojāta* (born-in-the-house), namely one born from the womb of a female slave within the household.
The meaning of the term *dhanakkīta* (bought-for-wealth) is: one who has been purchased after wealth was given.
Explaining this, he said, "One who is purchased for wealth," and so forth. The etymological definition (*vacanattha*) as "one purchased for wealth" (*dhanakkīta*) is indeed appropriate.
"The conduct of slaves" (*dāsacāritta*) refers to the behavior of slaves according to place and time. Regarding the phrase "brought from a death-march" (*karamarānīta*):
here, *karamara* means a prisoner (*vandi*). For he is one who must die by the hand (*karena*) of the enemy.
"Karamara" is what is called [death]. "Brought by way of death" means brought by the state of being death (*karamarabhāvena*). "Bringing from another country" is the connection [of the sentence].
"Or having enticed" means or having lured. "From there" means from some village. "Human beings" (*mānussakāni*) refers to humans themselves.
Because it is common to both women and men due to its general nature, it is expressed in the neuter gender. By the word "api" (also), it is not only... [the rest of the passage follows].
They bring only wealth, but they also collect human beings; "therein" means among the human beings.

The construction is: "A slave brought as a captive of war (karamarānīta) of such a kind should not be ordained. "By way of common property for all" means by way of what is common to all at the time of cleaning the prison.
*Ādāsabyaṃ*: the state of being a slave is *dāsabyaṃ*; that [is what is meant]. Therefore it is said, "the state of slavery" (*dāsabhāva*).
By the word "himself" (*sayameva*), he shows that the term *sāmaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of "by oneself. "Free women" (*bhujissitthiyo*) means the king’s free women.
"By courtesans" (*vaṇṇadāsīhi*) means by those who adorn the city. For they are called "courtesans" (*vaṇṇadāsī*) because of their state of being slaves who are endowed with beauty (*vaṇṇasampanna*).

“*Tāsanti*”: [this refers to] female slaves (*bhujissitthī*). “*Paṇṇanti*”: [this refers to] a slave who has been sold (*dāsipaṇṇa*). Regarding the phrase “groups of hired laborers’ sons, etc.,” the word “etc.
includes groups such as the *mallaputtaka* (wrestlers) and others. By this, he indicates a slave with many masters. “*Tehī*” means by those groups of hired laborers’ sons and so forth.

“*Adinnā na pabbājetabbā*” means that if she has not been given away by even one among the many masters, she must not be ordained. “*Tepī*” means even those monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) who are slaves.
In this context, showing the commentary’s (aṭṭhakathā) position regarding the ordination of monastery attendants and slaves, he said, “The Mahāpaccarī,” and so forth.
The word *takka* is the object (*kamma*) for the word *āsittaka*. The word *sīse* is the locus (*ādhāra*) for the word *āsittaka*.
In certain regions, by way of local custom, the pouring of buttermilk on the head of slaves is the means of making them free.
This is the intention. The statement, “We give an attendant (ārāmika),” means that the words for slaves are being used for those who are free (bhujissa); this is what is expressed.

“By whatever designation” means by whichever designation—whether “we give an attendant,” or “we give a slave-attendant,” or “we give a kappiyakāraka” (one who prepares what is allowable)—by whichever [designation].
Since the Kurundi-vāda is mentioned last among the two commentarial traditions, it is that very one [which is followed].
It should be understood as "the measure. "People who have gone to misery" means people who have gone to suffering.
"These" refers to those people who have gone to misery. "It is not permissible to ordain him" is said with reference to a son born at a time when his parents have entered into the state of slavery.
However, if it is the parents who have entered the state of slavery and not the son, it is permissible to ordain him.
The word *bhikkhussa* has a possessive connection (*sāmisa-sambandha*) with the words *ñātakā vā upaṭṭhākā vā*; the word *dentī* is the recipient case (*sampadāna*).
*Assa* means "of the bhikkhu. *Imaṃ* refers to this slave. *Abhiramissati* means he will take delight in the state of a bhikkhu.
*Vibbhamissati* means he will turn back and wander about in the state of a householder. Thus, the connection is: "giving [it] after having said this."
"A masterless slave" means a slave who is devoid of an owner who possesses him. For a masterless slave, the king is the master;
therefore, it is permissible for one to make oneself free by oneself when not possessed by the king. When possessed [by the king], it is permissible to have the king grant freedom.
"Not knowing" means not knowing one's own status as a slave.
The connection is: "having departed from Anurādhapura, that is, from the city of Anurādhā. "He" refers to the son. "Here" means in Rohaṇa. The connection is:
"having asked his mother. "Having come" means having arrived. "Aticchatha" means "you wish to pass by"; it is said:
"There is nothing here to be given as a gift; you wish to pass this place and stay elsewhere."
[The word] *hoti* [is used]. *Tetīti* means those householders. The construction is: "They caused him to dwell while attending to him with the four requisites.
35. The Discourse on the Blacksmith’s Tools, etc. (Kammārabhaṇḍavatthu-ādikathā). 98.
*Tulādhāramuṇḍako* means a shaven-headed man who carries measuring instruments. By this [phrase], in the expression *kammārabhaṇḍū*, the word *kammāra* [is explained].
This shows that *tulādhāra* is a synonym for *kammāra* (smith) and *bhaṇḍu* is a synonym for *muṇḍaka* (shaveling).

For a *tulādhāra* is called a *kammāra* because he knows the work (*kamma*) involved in making ornaments and various articles. A *muṇḍaka* is called a *bhaṇḍu* because he is "bhaṇḍīyati"—that is, he is reviled as a "shaveling.
By the phrase "the son of a goldsmith" (*suvaṇṇakāraputta*), his specific appearance is shown. "Having informed" (*apaloketun ti*)...
Here, the word *loka* preceded by the prefix *apa-* has the sense of "requesting permission," which is why he says "to request permission" (*āpucchituṃ*).

By the phrase "for the sake of the shaving rite" (*bhaṇḍukamm-atthāya*), he shows that in the expression "for the shaving rite" (*bhaṇḍukammāya*), the fourth case is used in the sense of purpose (*tadatthe catutthī*). Therein refers to the statement beginning with "to obtain the leave of the Saṅgha.
"Included within the boundary" means included either within the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*) or the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). "Therein" refers to the monks.
The place of assembly. Regarding the phrase "and here": it means that among the five formulas for requesting permission, it is indeed permissible to recite any one of them.
By the word "also" (*pi*), the formula "I request permission for this person’s shaving" is also included.

"Of them" refers to twenty or more monks. The phrase "junior monks or novices" is stated by way of proximity. It is also permissible to send a layperson and have him request permission. Why? Because it is stated: "or without one who is seeking the going-forth."
There is no offense for one who ordains; thus he said, "there is no offense even for one who ordains," meaning that [the candidate] has indeed gone forth well.
The construction is: "especially if [permission] has been asked. "Within a *khaṇḍasīmā*" means within a *vihārasīmā* or an *upacārasīmā* while standing inside such a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
"But whoever" refers to one seeking ordination. "Or one who has disrobed" refers to one who has recently disrobed.
Or: "Two-finger-breadth hair is permitted for those who have gone forth," thus he said, "or two-finger-breadth hair.
"One whose hair exceeds [the limit] by two finger-breadths" means one whose hair is more than two finger-breadths long. The construction is: "even one who wears only a single tuft [of hair]. 100.
"By the plague of Māra" means the affliction that kills; for it kills beings in the sense of being death, and [it brings about] manifold suffering.

In the sense of burning, it is called the "disease of Māra. By the phrase "by this snake-wind disease," he shows that a disease occurring due to a wind resembling snake venom is called a "snake-wind disease. Expounding upon that meaning, he said, "For where... and so forth.
Therein, "where" means in whichever family. That disease first [afflicts] the bipeds and quadrupeds in that family.
"He seizes [them], and afterwards he seizes the owner of the house"—this is stated in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*.
"In that way" means just as another person, having broken through a wall or a roof and fled, or having gone beyond the village boundary and so forth, is released;
in that same manner. And here, the meaning is that both father and son were released from the family.
Regarding the term *kākuḍḍepaka*: one who causes crows (*kāka*) to fly up (*uḍḍāpeti*) is a *kākuḍḍepaka*; or, one who is able to eat his meal after having caused crows to fly up is a *kākuḍḍepaka*.

Demonstrating this meaning of the word, he said, "He who with his left hand," and so forth. In that context, *uḍḍāpetvā* means having caused them to go upward into the sky. *Taṃ* refers to the *kākuḍḍepaka*.

102. The word *ittara* signifies "slight" or "trifling," as in the expression *anipphannapāṭipadika* (an unprepared first day of the lunar fortnight); thus he said, "a trifling [amount]. By the phrase "only for a few days," he demonstrates its meaning.
40. Discussion on Release from Dependence. 103.
Regarding the term *ogaṇena*, the prefix *otu-* here expresses the sense of "inferiority"; thus he said, "by one who has fallen away from the group. Of oneself...
"One should receive dependence (nissaya) from a more senior monk alone," he said, beginning with "If this one is more senior," and so forth.
In that context, "this one" refers to the incompetent monk. "Upasampadāya" means having conferred full ordination (upasampadā).

"Āyasmato" means [from] the Venerable One; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. Alternatively, the construction is "the instruction (ovāda) of the Venerable One. "Sabbattha" means in all cases.

"In asking for leave" means in asking for permission for the purpose of departing for a particular direction, and so forth. "In this" refers to this section on the rules concerning dependence (*nissaya*).
"That" refers to that much which has been heard. "Of that" refers to the hearing.
41. The Story of the Case of Rāhula.
105. Regarding "Kapilavatthu": here, *kapila* refers to a seer (*isi*) of a dark-brown complexion;

because he dwelt there, it is called *Kapilavatthu*, meaning the hermitage (*assama*). Because the city was built at that location, it too is called *Kapilavatthu*. "This" refers to the discourse to be explained below.
Regarding "the Great King Suddhodana": here, *Suddhodana* is the name of that king. Alternatively, *suddha-odana* means pure rice.
"Of this one" refers to Suddhodana; he himself is the Great King Suddhodana. "He dwells, it is said" is the grammatical connection.
"He" refers to the Great King Suddhodana. "Rājagaha" refers to the city of Rājagaha. "Sādhu" is a particle used in the sense of a request;
for its meaning is "I entreat. "Me" means "my," which connects with "son"; or the genitive case is used in a sense of disregard. "He" refers to the minister.
*Sādhu* is a particle used in the sense of acceptance; its meaning is "yes. *Atha* means "at that time," namely, at the time of sitting down.
*Assa* refers to the minister who was accompanied by a thousand men. *Tato* means "because of the request. *Naṃ* refers to the minister accompanied by a thousand men.
*Tattheva* means "right there," namely, in Rājagaha itself. *Te pi* refers to the eight messengers as well. *Te* refers to the nine messengers.
*Atthā* means after that. *Ekadivasajātakan* means a birth [of events] on a single day. *So* refers to the minister Kāḷudāyī.
By the word *api* in *pabbajitvāpi*, the sense of *apabbajitvāpi* (even without having gone forth) is included.
*Tatheva* means just as the nine messengers with their retinues attained arahantship, so too; such is the meaning. *So* refers to Kāḷudāyī. *Sambhatesu* means...
"Among those who have gathered and finished [the work]" is the meaning. "Among those whose tasks are abandoned" means those for whom the works (*kammantā*) have been abandoned;
among them. "In full bloom" means in which beautiful flowers have grown. "Fit for proceeding" means suitable and capable for the purpose of proceeding.
The connection is: "he praised the excellence of the journey. "By about sixty" means...
"By those measuring sixty [yojanas]. "This" refers to the reason for this praise; he asked, "What is it? The construction is: "It is time to set out on the wandering tour.
"Therefore" (*tena hi*) is a particle used in the sense of encouragement. "The Blessed One set out" is the connection.

"Surrounded" (*parivuta*) means having been surrounded, encompassed, or hemmed in on all sides; this is the connection. "A wandering tour without haste" (*aturitacārika*) means a journey without speed.
"In this way" means by this method. "And when the Blessed One had departed" is how the construction should be joined.
"From the day of his departure" means from the first day of the month following the full moon of Phagguṇa. "With the finest flavors of food" means with the most excellent taste of food.

"You should give" means you should offer. "By that very reason" means by the very cause for the arising of faith. "Him" refers to Kāḷudāyin. "The Blessed One established" is the connection [between the words].
*Etadaggaṃ*: this is the foremost. *Yadidaṃ*: "which is this. *Etadagge*: in the position of being foremost. The connection is:
"The Sākiyas also sent [messengers]. *Ñātiseṭṭhaṃ*: the best among kinsmen, or the kinsman who is best; the construction is with "the Blessed One.
*Nigrodhasakkassa*: of the Sakyan named Nigrodha. *Tattha*: there, at the residence of Nigrodha the Sakyan.
In the monastery. "Going forth to meet" means going by rising up toward [the visitor]. "From there" refers to the one who sent them; "to others" is the connection. The construction is:
"They sent both princes and princesses. "Of them" refers to the princes and princesses.
"There" refers to the Nigrodha Monastery. "Mānajātika" means those whose nature or inherent character is pride (*māna*); [it is] by means of pride, or pride is stubborn.
"These are those arrogant and stubborn ones. "Those" refers to the Sākiyas; "they said" is the connection.
"Among them" means among the Sākiyas. "He" refers to the kinsmen. "Having emerged" means having emerged from the fourth jhāna. "Of them" refers to the kinsmen.
"At the foot of the Kaṇḍama tree" means near a mango tree planted by a park-keeper named Kaṇḍa. "The King" [is speaking].
"Suddhodana the Great King. "Vā" means "to you," which connects with "pāde" (at the feet). "Ayam" refers to the salutation.
"In the shade of the rose-apple tree" means in the shade of the *jambu* tree.
"Thus he said" is the construction. "Reached the crest" means reached the top; the meaning is "reached the pinnacle. "From there" means from the seat; it connects with "paraṃ" (further).
"Like a rain of lotuses" means like rain that has fallen upon a lotus grove. "Copper-colored" means red-colored.
"That"—the connection is that the Blessed One spoke of its not falling.
"On the second day" means on the day following the day he arrived at Kapilavatthu. "At the threshold" means at the city gate-bar.

"How" (*kathaṃ*) is to be construed as "in what manner did they conduct themselves? (*kenākārena cariṃsu nu kho*). "They came" (*āgamuṃ*) is to be construed with "what did they practice? (*kiṃ cariṃsu*) and "how? (*kinti*).

"Alms-round by sequence" (*sapadānacāraṃ*) refers to the practice occurring without skipping houses in order. "From that" (*tato*) means from the act of adverting the mind; it is connected with "the other" (*paraṃ*).

"This very lineage" (*ayaṃ eva vaṃso*) means this is the very lineage of the previous Buddhas. "This tradition" (*ayaṃ paveṇī*) is a synonym for that same thing. "Training accordingly" (*anusikkhantā*)— [End of excerpt]
Training in accordance with [the instructions]. "From the house where he was settled" means from the house where he had gone for the purpose of residing.
"Ayya" means lord or master. "Prince Siddhattha": he is called Siddhattha because the goal (*attha*) accomplished by all the world exists in him;
he is that very prince, thus Prince Siddhattha. "Lion-window" refers to a window; for indeed, having displayed the form of a lion—
Because it has a lattice-work, it is called a "lion-lattice" (*sīhapañjara*). "Engaged in seeing" means engaged in the act of seeing, or engaged for the purpose of seeing.
"The queen, the mother of Rāhula, also announced" is the grammatical connection. "With a skull in hand" means that the Blessed One had a skull in his hands;
this connects with the word "having become. "Resplendent with various colors" means in various places...
"For the sake of dispassion, for the sake of the radiant one. The connection is with "the Blessed One who is shining forth.
"From the *uṇhīsa*" means from the head-covering. For that which is bound upon the upper part of the head, or that which is fastened there—being bound or caused to be bound—is called the *uṇhīsa*.
"By the verses named 'Narasīha'" means by those [verses] whose names are the "Narasīha-gāthās. For they are so called because they concern the man himself.
Among all beings, the lion is the best; or, among men, the lion is the best—thus he is the "Lion among Men" (*narasīha*).
The verses that proclaim him are therefore called the "Lion among Men Verses. "Of the king" refers to either the father-in-law’s king or the maternal uncle’s king.
"With a heart agitated" means with a trembling mind. "Steadying" means establishing [the mind] well. "Hurrying, hurrying" (*turitaturitaṃ*)...
*Turitato turitan* means "very quickly" (*atisīgham*); this is the meaning. *Kiṃ bhante* means "for what reason, venerable sir? (*kiṃ kāraṇā bhante*). Regarding *ahuvattha*:
in the *ttha* case-ending belonging to the past tense (*hiyyattani*) in the second person plural, there is a substitution of *uva* for the vowel *ū* of the root *hū*;
therefore, the construction is: "you [plural] were thus perceived" (*tumhe evaṃsaññino ahuvattha*). *Vaṃsacārittam etan* means "this wandering for alms."
"Conduct from lineage and tradition. In this context, "from" (*ca*) refers to the kṣatriya lineage of Mahāsammata; "this" (*ayaṃ*) refers to the kṣatriya lineage of Mahāsammata.
"In the middle of the street" (*antaravīthiyaṃ*) means in the center of the street. The connection is: "standing, he spoke.
"Uttiṭṭhe" means either with reference to, or having stood up for, standing for alms. "Dhammaṃ sucaritaṃ" means that which should be well-practiced.
The "Dhamma" refers to that which is designated as the practice of alms-gathering (*bhikkhācariya*). "Practices" (*careti*) means he should practice it.

A "practitioner of the Dhamma" (*dhammacārī*) is a recluse whose habit is to practice this Dhamma designated as the practice of alms-gathering. "He sleeps happily" is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*);

the remaining postures (*iriyāpatha*) should also be understood through the method of characteristic inclusion (*lakkhaṇahāra*), because they share the same function. The construction is: "in this world and in the world beyond."
One should not practice that misconduct; one should not engage in that state of affairs known as the sphere of prostitutes and the like, which is wrongly practiced.
In this context, by reciting the first verse while in the middle of the street, he established the king in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*);
by reciting the second verse at his father’s residence, he established Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry and the king in the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmi-phala*).
"It should be understood as 'he established [him in the fruit]' (*patiṭṭhāpesi*). Having heard the *Dhammapāla-jātaka* means: having heard the *Dhammapāla-jātaka* again on another day.
At the time of death (*maraṇasamaye*) means: at the moment approaching death, or in the vicinity of the time of death; here the locative case is used in the sense of proximity. The connection is:
"having realized the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), he served. 'The entire female retinue' (*itthāgāra*) means: the whole harem."
For it is because it is the house (*agāra*) of women that it is called a "women's quarters" (*itthāgāra*). By this etymological meaning, the word *agāra* itself is understood in its primary sense;
however, it should be understood that the royal women are referred to by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). "She," moreover, refers to Rāhula’s mother.

"By her retinue" means by her attendants. "Him" refers to the noble son. The word "the king" is the indirect object (*kāritakamma*) of the verb "having caused to take," while the word "bowl" is [the direct object].

The analysis of the elements (*dhātukamma*) is right there. "Of the king’s daughter" means of the daughter of King Suppabuddha. "She" refers to that king’s daughter. "In the ankles" means in the ankle-bones of the feet;
the construction is "having grasped the Blessed One. Alternatively, the construction is "having grasped the Blessed One’s ankles.
For if it is so, it should be understood that the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative.

The connection is that "the king said. *Anacchariyaṃ* means not wonderful; the meaning is that it is not worthy of striking one with the palms of the hands (*accharaṃ*). The construction is: "That which the princess protected herself [from], this is not wonderful.
*Taṃdivasameva* means on that very second day. *Kesavisajjanaṃ* means the letting go of the hair—specifically the topknot-tuft tied during childhood for the purpose of binding the royal crest-jewel;
the meaning is "releasing" or "untying. *Paṭṭabandho* means... [the investiture with the turban].
"Such-and-such a king" refers to the binding of a golden fillet upon the forehead. "House-consecration auspiciousness" (*gharamaṅgala*) is the auspicious ceremony for entering a newly built house.

"Marriage auspiciousness" (*āvāhamaṅgala*) is the auspicious ceremony occurring at a wedding. "Umbrella-auspiciousness" (*chattamaṅgala*) is the auspicious ceremony performed at the time of raising the royal parasol.
"Having spoken of auspiciousness" means having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected with auspiciousness. "The most beautiful woman of the land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*).
They were endowed with excellence within the realm. "Quickly indeed" means very swiftly. "He too" refers to Prince Nanda.
The phrase beginning with "Thus" and so forth is the conclusion. "On the second day" means on the day following the arrival at Kapilavatthu.
However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "On the third day, he ordained Nanda."
"On the seventh day" means on the very seventh day from the day he arrived at Kapilavatthu. The construction is: "Behold this ascetic.
"Possessing the color of Brahma’s form" means one whose color is like the color designated as the form of Brahmā;
that [is what is meant]. "He" refers to this ascetic. "Of him" means of that [ascetic]. "Those" refers to the treasures. "Of him" refers to the ascetic. "That" refers to...
*Samaṇaṃ*: [accusative singular]. *Yācā* means "beg"; this is a verbal root governing two objects (*dvikammikadhātu*). *Hi* means "truly" or "because. The construction is:
"A son is the master of what belongs to the father; therefore, give it to me. This connects with the phrase "appropriate speech.
*Bhagavantaṃ anubandhī* means he followed closely behind the Blessed One.
"Is not able" means it is not capable. The construction is: "Whatever wealth this prince desires from his father's estate, that [he shall have].
"Followed by the round" means followed by the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*). "Accompanied by affliction" means accompanied by the five hostilities which cause affliction.
"His" refers to the prince. "Him" refers to the prince. "This one" refers to the prince. "Inheritance" refers to what is designated as the inheritance of the mother and father.
One who takes wealth is an heir (*dāyāda*); a son. That which belongs to him is an inheritance (*dāyajja*), namely the wealth of his parents.

Why did he say, "Venerable sir, how shall I cause Prince Rāhula to go forth"? Was it not because the Venerable Sāriputta did not know that the going-forth permitted by the threefold taking of refuge had been authorized in Bārāṇasī? He said, "Now," and so forth, referring to that specific going-forth.
The construction is: "both the going-forth and the full ordination were authorized. "From that" means from the going-forth and the full ordination.
"Having rejected the full ordination" is the connection. "Doubt" (*vimati*) means various desires. "And this meaning, moreover" refers to this very meaning designated as doubt.
"The General of the Dhamma said" is the connection. "That intention of the Blessed One" is the construction.
Regarding the passage, “Then... [he] gave him the going-forth,” one might ask: did the Venerable Sāriputta alone perform all the duties for the prince, such as cutting his hair and so forth?

To answer this, it says, “the Elder Mahāmoggallāna,” and so on. An *ovādācariya* is a teacher who instructs one in the rules of training (*sekhiyavatta*) concerning undergarments, upper robes, and the like, as well as in the higher codes of conduct (*ābhisamācārika*). Now, why is it said, “the Venerable Sāriputta”?
Regarding the statement, “He ordained Prince Rāhula,” he says, “But because...,” and so forth. “Therein” means in that [process of] going-forth and full ordination.
“Not the master” means that neither the preceptor for going-forth nor the instructor is the master.
