In the phrase “with a heart of arisen spiritual urgency,” the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state already attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). For the construction is: “having become one whose heart is possessed of arisen spiritual urgency. “All” means the entire speech.

*Tattha* (therein) refers back to the preceding statement. *Avisesena* (without distinction) means by way of generality, without making a distinction such as "wealth," "something else," "blameworthy," or "blameless.

Regarding the phrase *na ca buddhānaṃ* (and not for the Buddhas), the word *ca* (and) indicates that it is not only improper, but furthermore, that this is not the habitual practice (*āciṇṇa*) of the Buddhas. *Yaṃ* (which) refers to that which...
"Excellent. Here, in the phrase "likewise, Nanda," he says "just as it is said" (*yatheva kira*) and so forth, showing that the word *tathā* functions to indicate the object of comparison.
The construction is: "Just as they prophesied for the Bodhisatta, so too did they prophesy for Nanda and for Rāhula, it is said.
However, in the Pāḷi [of the Mahāvagga], it says: "Venerable Sir, when the Blessed One went forth, there was no small amount of suffering for me..."
The construction is as follows: "When Nanda went forth, there was no small amount of suffering; likewise, when Rāhula went forth, there was excessive suffering.
"Nemittaka" means those who speak of signs of good and evil fortune; thus they are called *nemittaka*. "Of the son" refers to the eldest son, Prince Siddhattha.
"For the sake of going forth" means for the cause of going forth, for the reason of going forth, or on account of the sign of going forth.
*Tato* means from the time of the Blessed One’s going forth. *Tampi* means Nanda as well. *Iti* means of such a kind.

The meaning is that it was like a great frustration of desire on account of the Blessed One’s renunciation. *Tampi* means Rāhula as well. *Tenā* means by reason of that renunciation. *Assa* refers to the king.
*Uppajji* is the connection [with the verb]. *Ito* means from the arising of sorrow, or from the requesting of a boon.

"He" refers to the king. "Yatra hi nāma" means "one who indeed. The construction is: "Even I, being one such as this—devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dhamma, and devoted to the Saṅgha—even I am not able to do that.
"Others" means others than myself. "Suffering" refers to the suffering of separation from kinsmen.
"A cause for deliverance" means a cause for deliverance from the censure, defamation, and abuse of men.
*“Tattha”* means in the statement beginning with *“not permitted.”* *Janetī* means she who gives birth, the mother; *janetī* means he who gives birth, the father.
By this, [the text] excludes the parents who raised [him]. The construction is: “or the mother has died. *So eva vā* means “or the son himself.
*“I am permitted,” he says* means he says “I am permitted,” whether by truth or by falsehood. Or the mother...
The construction is: "she herself has gone forth. *Pitassa* means "of whose father. *Assa* means "of the son. *Vippavuttho* refers to the mother’s absence due to some reason.

In the phrase "of the junior mother and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the senior mother and others. *Posanakā* means those who nourish or raise [the child]. *Tesupi* means "even in the case of those [other] parents who nourish [the child]."

"But not permitting the son," is the connection [of the phrase]. "Of the living one alone" means of that very person who is living, or of the monk who is ordaining him; the meaning is that it is not for the sake of traveling to another country or similar purposes. "Of them" refers to the mother and father. "A great wilderness" (*kantāra*):
it is called a wilderness because it must be crossed by means of water; primarily, a waterless wilderness is what is meant, as well as these five:
the wilderness of wild beasts, the wilderness of thieves, the wilderness of non-humans, the wilderness of famine, and the wilderness of desert sands.
“Crossed the wilderness” means by way of having traversed it. A great wilderness is a “mahākantāra.
Regarding the phrase “as far as,” he says “to whatever extent,” because here the word *yāva* has the sense of measure (*pamāṇa*).
42. Discussion on the Basis for Punishment for Violating the Training Rules (*Sikkhāpada-daṇḍakamma-vatthu-kathā*)

106. *Nāsanavatthu*: This refers to the basis for the removal of the [monastic] emblem; it is said to be the cause. The construction is: "of the latter five. *Daṇḍakammavatthu*: This is the cause for disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*). 107. Regarding *appatissa* (disrespectful):

here, by showing that there is no listening with reverence toward the words of the monks—that is, they do not place the monks in the position of seniority—it says, "the monks in the position of seniority," and so forth. By the term "those of the same livelihood" (*samānajīvika*),...

Regarding the phrase *asabhāgavuttikā*: here he shows that the word *sabhāga* is a synonym for *samāna* (equal), and the word *vutti* is a synonym for *jīvika* (livelihood). Regarding the word *parisakkati*:

since the root *sakka* is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—specifically in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* as the sixteenth root ending in the letter *ḷ*—to have the sense of "going," he says that the prefix *pari-* combined with the word *sakka* has the meaning of "going," hence the expression “*parakkamati*” (exerts oneself). As for “*kinti*” (how):
*kimeva*: here the word *iti* has the sense of the word *eva*; the meaning is, "by what means indeed? *Akkosati ceva*:
he reviles by means of birth and so forth. *Bhedeṭi*: he causes to be split. Regarding the phrase *āvaraṇaṃ kātuṃ*, the word *āvaraṇa* here is a synonym for the word *nivāraṇa* (obstruction);
thus he says, "to cause an obstruction. *Yattha*: in which courtyard or dwelling place.
"By the number of years" means by the calculation of years. "Of that" refers to the dwelling in the surrounding courtyard (*pariveṇa*). "In the vicinity" means in the immediate proximity.
"Oral" means that which is to be swallowed through the door known as the mouth. By the phrase "even while speaking," he indicates an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) through vocal activity;
by the phrase "even while putting down," he indicates it through bodily activity. "Of one who behaves improperly" refers to the performance of penance (*daṇḍakamma*).
“Of one who behaves improperly. “In such a measure of disciplinary action” means in such a measure of disciplinary action consisting of being made to fetch water and so forth.
“This” refers to the rice gruel, food, and so on. “You shall receive” means you will obtain.

To demonstrate the logical justification for the statement “in such a measure of disciplinary action,” he said, “For by the Blessed One,” and so forth. Regarding “disciplinary action” (*daṇḍakamma*): it is called *daṇḍa* because they are punished (*daṇḍenti*) or subdued (*dameti*) by means of it.
“Kamma” means that which is to be done; it refers to disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*), such as restrictions and so forth.

“In accordance with the offense” means in conformity with the transgression committed. “That too” refers even to the fetching of water, wood, sand, and so on. “And that indeed” refers to that performance [of the task].
“He will desist” means he will desist by way of body. “He will abstain” means he will abstain by way of speech. Regarding the phrases beginning with “on hot stones,” etc.:
By the word "and" (*vā*), other actions such as self-mortification and tormenting oneself are also included.
43. Discussion on the Matter of Obstructing Without Asking Permission. 108.
Regarding the phrase "without asking permission of the preceptor": here it means having not asked the preceptor for permission. What is absolutely not to be done?
He said, “Of you,” and so forth. *Daṇḍakammamassa* means “this is his disciplinary action. *Assa* refers to the novice (*sāmaṇera*).

Those who dwell together with their preceptor (*upajjhāya*) are called *saddhivihārikā*. Those who dwell near, that is, in the presence of their teachers of dependence (*nissayācariya*) and others, are called *antevāsikā*;
these are only those who have received full ordination (*upasampanna*).

Regarding "apalāḷentī" (*they dissuade*): since the root *laḷ* is stated in the *Dhātupāṭha* (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, the section on roots ending in *ḷ*) to mean "to serve," the meaning here should be understood as "they cause [them] to turn away from serving—that is, from *laḷana*—the Elder.
However, showing the intended sense in this context, he says "of you," and so forth. "Apalāḷetabbā" means "from another who is *laḷana* (serving)."

They must be removed. The construction is: "one who has been ordained as a novice within the assembly. "Disadvantage" refers to the fault of living in dependence upon one who is immoral. The construction is:
"Just as you, having come to bathe, committed an act of defilement by being smeared with excrement, so too, by living in dependence upon one who is immoral, you have committed an act of immorality.
The word "immoral" (dussīla) depends upon both the preceding and the following words.
Therefore, it is stated between two clauses. In this context, with respect to the preceding clause, it refers to an action already performed;

with respect to the subsequent clause, it refers to an action not yet performed. "He" refers to one who has received full ordination as a *sāmaṇera*. "To the preceptor" is said with reference to the *sāmaṇera*;
"to the dependence" is said with reference to one who has received full ordination.

"In the three ways of expulsion" means in the three types of expulsion known as expulsion from communal residence (*saṃvāsa*), expulsion by mark (*liṅga*), and expulsion by disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*). "He" refers to the novice (*sāmaṇera*).

"Various offenses" refers to offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*), serious offenses (*thullaccaya*), and offenses requiring expiation (*pācittiya*). "For" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "Even an ant or a termite":
here, it is called *kuntha* because it is crushed or harmed by creatures that eat living beings; or it is called *kundha* because it supports the earth (*kuṃ pathaviṃ dhāreti*).
*Kimiyeva pillikaṃ potakaṃ*: having elided the *m* of *kimī*, it becomes *kipillikaṃ*. For the word *pillika* is a synonym for *potaka* (a young one).
*Kimīnaṃ* or *kimīsu pillikaṃ* means "the young of the worms" (*kipillikaṃ*). "Only the state of being destroyed" refers to the very condition of being fit to be destroyed by that [magical] mark.
"At that very moment" means at the precise instant of his death and the breaking [of the charm]. "Of him" refers to the novice monk (*sāmaṇera*). And the taking of the lodging...
"It subsides" means that there is an interruption of the rains-retreat; this is the intended meaning.

"One who is beset by faults" means one who is indeed troubled by the fault of losing his characteristic marks and by the fault of being expelled for disciplinary action. "Having missed" means having failed. The connection is:

"of the novice monk while he is still dressed and robed as before. "Therefore" is because the formal proclamations (*kammavācā*) for going for refuge and for full ordination (*upasampadā*) are identical. By the monk...

The construction is: "By this [act] as well, those very things are undertaken, as if they were already undertaken. *Evaṃ* means "thus" in the sense of wishing for it, or in the sense of having undertaken it.
*Daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ* means for the purpose of strengthening the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). *Paṭiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ* means for the purpose of establishing the novice.
*Lacchati* means "he will obtain. The connection is: "It should be given by the Saṅgha. *Apaloketvā* means...
"Having requested permission from the Saṅgha"—by this he indicates one whose rains-residence has been cut short.

"In the case of taking what is not given" means that even by the mere act of taking a blade of grass, one ceases to be a *samaṇa*; such is the construction. "By way of misconduct" means because of practicing in a distorted manner.
"In speaking" means in the act of speech. "Having known" means having indeed known; the particle *eva* (indeed) is to be supplied here.
Therefore it was said: “not without knowing. The construction is: “those five training rules. “Of him” means of the novice (*sāmaṇera*).

“For the purpose of establishing” means for the purpose of establishing the training rules. “This one” refers to the one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. “The distinction” means the distinction from the *pācittiya* offenses of the monks.

“By way of the opposite” means by such phrases as “one who is not worthy, not a perfectly enlightened Buddha,” and so forth; and by such phrases as “twice-declared,” and so forth; and by such phrases as “one who has entered upon a wrong course,” and so forth.
The connection is that the novice (sāmaṇera) should be restrained by one who censures him on account of his opposition.

"For the purpose of the formal act of suspension (nāsanā) involving a rod against Kaṇḍaka" means for the formal act of suspension involving a rod against the novice named Kaṇḍaka. "That view" refers to the view of speaking in dispraise.
"Transgression" (accaya) means an overstepping or a fault. "He should be made to confess" means [he should say] "Venerable sir, a transgression has overcome me," and so forth.
It should be made to confess. "That is appropriate" means that the statement, "he should be expelled for the destruction of his characteristic marks," is fitting.
"Hi" (for/indeed) means truth, or because. "Idha" refers to the Khandhaka, or to the statement, "one should expel the novice.
To clarify the statement "the same method applies," he said, "For [regarding] eternalism and annihilationism," and so forth. [This concerns] one who holds a particular view.
The construction is: "a novice" (*sāmaṇera*). "In this context" refers to among the ten grounds for expulsion.

By the word "lust" (*kāma*), he shows censure by attributing the faults of redundancy and meaninglessness [to other views]. By the word "but" (*pana*), he shows esteem through the abandonment of those faults.
The connection is: "a novice who does not live the holy life" (*abrahmacārī sāmaṇero*). "It is fitting to ordain him" means that the act of ordination is appropriate. A violator of a nun...

The connection is with the word "novice" (*sāmaṇera*). Regarding the phrase "even for the going forth" (*pabbajjampīti*), it was stated "let alone for full ordination" (*pageva upasampadaṃ*) in order to show that the particle *pi* here carries the sense of censure. "This matter" (*etamatthaṃ*) means a matter of this kind.
47. The Discussion on the Matter of the Eunuch (*paṇḍaka*).
109. Because the words *dahara* and *taruṇa* are synonyms, it is said: "the young... the youthful. The word *moḷigalla* denotes a person with a stout body;
since it is an un-derived (*anipphanna*) term for the first day [of the lunar fortnight], he says: "at *moḷigalla*, that is, at those with stout bodies.
Regarding *hatthibhaṇḍa*, when it is said "those whose goods (*bhaṇḍa*) consist of elephants," they are called *hatthibhaṇḍa*; thus he says: "the elephant-keepers."
In the *Abhidhāna* (in the 367th verse of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*), however, the reading is “*hatthimeṇḍo*” (a bull elephant).
A *paṇḍaka* is so called because he falls (*paḍati*) into a state of deficiency. Explaining in detail the meaning that was stated in brief, [the author] says “*tattha*,” etc.
Therein, “of whom” refers to the *paṇḍaka*. “By impurity” means by the seminal fluid. “Of one who has been sprinkled” means...
“Āsiñcitabbaṃ”: by this he shows the etymological meaning of *āsitta* as "one who should be poured upon" with this impurity in the mouth.
"Ayaṃ": this refers to the paṇḍaka. "Ajjhācāraṃ": sexual misconduct. "Usūyāya uppannāya":
by this he shows the etymological meaning of *usūyā* as "one who envies" (*usūyati*). "Upakkamena": by means of effort. "Bījāni": seeds (testicles). By this means, from this...

The phrase "the seeds have been removed" shows the meaning of the term *opakkamika* (caused by external means). Regarding the term *pakkhapaṇḍaka* (a half-month eunuch), the meaning is shown as follows:

one who functions [sexually] during one half of the month is a *pakkhapaṇḍaka*; one for whom the feverish passion is suppressed during one half of the month is a *pakkhapaṇḍaka*. To show this meaning, he says, "But some," and so forth.
In that context, regarding the first explanation of the term, *pakkhe* should be understood to mean "in the period" (*kālapakkhe*). Regarding the latter explanation of the term:
The meaning should be understood as "in the dark fortnight" (*pakkhe*) or "in the bright fortnight" (*juṇhapakkhe*).
The phrase "by the power of unwholesome karmic fruition" (*akusalavipākānubhāvena*) should be connected specifically with the phrase "becomes a paṇḍaka. The word *assa* means "of the paṇḍaka.

A "neuter paṇṍaka" (*napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*) is called "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) because, unlike a man, he is unable to excessively "crush" (*puṃseti*) or subdue his enemies; thus, he is not a male (*na pumā*).

They say that by treating [the term] as "neither woman nor man" (*na-itthī* = *na-pumā*), the neuter gender (*napuṃsaka*) is also expressed through the etymological method (*niruttinaya*) of the words "neither-man-nor-woman" (*napumanaitthi*).
A *paṇḍaka* who is precisely a neuter is a "neuter *paṇḍaka*" (*napuṃsakapaṇḍaka*). "Among them" refers to among these five types of *paṇḍakas*.

"Even among them" refers even to the three types beginning with the "accidental" (*opakkamika*). By the phrase "in whichever faction," he excludes the state of being a *paṇḍaka* in each respective faction.
*Assa* means "of a paṇḍaka. *Ettha* means "among the five types of paṇḍakas. *Sopi* means "he too [the paṇḍaka]. *Ito* means "from this section on paṇḍakas.
By the phrase "The same method applies," he extends the rule specifically to the loss of the characteristic mark (*liṅganāsanam*).
48. Discussion of the Case of One Living in Communion by Theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*)
110. *Pārijaññapattassa*: that which perishes is *parijāni*, namely sovereignty, wealth, and so forth. The state of that is *pārijañña*, the exhaustion of sovereignty, wealth, and so forth.
One who has reached that is *pārijaññapatto*; [the word refers] to him. There is also a reading with the vowel *u*:
*pārijuññapattassa*. Regarding the term *khīṇakolañño*: those born in a clan (*kula*) are *kolaññā*; here the suffix *ṇya* is applied, and there is the insertion of the letter *n*.
To show the meaning of the term *khīṇakolañño*—meaning "one whose lineage is exhausted"—he said, "From the mother’s side and the father’s side," and so forth.
In that context, *mātipakkhapitipakkhato*: the mother’s side is *mātipakkho*; the father’s side is *pitipakkho*; both the mother’s side and the father’s side are *mātipakkhapitipakkhā*.
Regarding the phrase *phātiṃ kātuṃ*, here the root is *phā*.

"For the purpose of increasing" he said, "let him increase. By the phrase "being questioned," he shows that the word *yuj*—with the prefix *anu*—has the meaning of "questioning" in the expression "being investigated" (*anuyuñjiyamāno*).

"One living in communion through theft": *theyya* is derived from *thenana*; by changing the letter *n* to *y*, it becomes *theyya*. He is one whose communion (*saṃvāsaka*) is for the sake of theft (*theyyāya*). Thus: "one who lives in communion through theft."
A *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who dwells in communion through theft). And here, "communion" (*saṃvāsa*) does not consist merely of counting the years [of seniority] and so forth;
rather, even the taking of the outward signs (*liṅga*) through theft is indeed called "communion. Therefore, showing its threefold nature, he said "three," and so forth.
In that context, one who steals the signs is a *liṅgathenaka*; the same method applies to the others as well. Regarding this meaning:

Explaining in detail, he said, “In that regard,” and so forth. Therein, “he” refers to one who lives in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). Regarding the phrase “merely the outward mark (*liṅgamattasseva*)”:
here, by the word *matta* (merely), he excludes [the requirements of] communal living and so on.
“A foreign land (*videsam*): this refers to a region separated from one’s own country. Here, the prefix *vi-* expresses the sense of separation. Alternatively, *vi-*...

“To a distant place. Here, the word *vi-* signifies distance. *“Musā”* is a second-case indeclinable used in the sense of what is unreal; the meaning is “untrue speech. *“Paṭibāhati”* means he wards off others.
Regarding the phrase *“one who is a thief in communal residence,”* one might ask: what is meant by “communal residence”?

Is it not the performance of formal acts (*kamma*) together and so forth? To this he replies: “the counting of the monks’ seniority (*vassa*), etc.”—that is, “the counting of the monks’ seniority, etc.”
By the word "etc. (ādi), this includes such acts as receiving salutations according to seniority, declining seats, and appearing together at the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies.
By the phrase "distinction of action" (kiriyabheda), it shows that "co-residence" (saṃvāsa) is so called because, by means of this [distinction], one is made to dwell together;
thus, it indicates that co-residence is defined by the distinction of action. "In this matter" (imasmiṃ atthe) means in this subject, in this instance, or in this place.

The meaning is as follows: by this [phrase], he shows that in the context of a *pārājika* offense and so forth, "co-residence" (*saṃvāsa*) refers to performing formal acts together (*ekakamma*) and the like.
By the phrase “of both the gender and the co-residence,” he shows the nature of the "one who belongs to both" (*ubhayatthenaka*) here.

"Here" means in the context of one who lives in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*). Regarding the expression "by kings... or by fears," the word "fear" (*bhaya*) should be construed with each preceding term individually.
The meaning is: "due to fear of kings, fear of famine, fear of wilderness, fear of disease, and fear of enemies.
"For the purpose of taking robes" means for the purpose of bringing robes; this is the reading itself. The particle *vā* combines the sense of cause (*hetu*) or the sense of recipient (*sampadāna*).
This verse is considered to have violated the established meter because its grammatical case endings are out of order.
The faults of ornamentation have not been omitted. "Liṅga" means the mark of a recluse (*samaṇaliṅga*).
"Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*). "Does not accept" means does not consent to. "As long as" refers to for whatever length of time.
This, however, is the construction here: whoever here, out of fear of a king... or for the sake of obtaining robes, takes up the mark, he—having become pure in mind—
As long as one does not consent to living together [with the Saṅgha], so long is this person not called a "one who lives in communion through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*).
"Therein" means in those verses. "Here" means in this teaching (*sāsana*). "Thus" refers to when the outward signs (*liṅga*) are being assumed.

"In that person" refers to the individual. "Without having followed" means without having entered [the path]. "Having discarded the signs" means having destroyed the ascetic signs (*samaṇaliṅga*) that one had personally assumed.
*Pabbajitālayaṃ* means the shadow (or shelter) of one who has gone forth. *Pubbe* refers to those with whom one previously lived together.
*Sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni* means all meals given specifically for the sake of various religious sects (*pāsaṇḍa*).

*Sattavāho* means that which carries beings. *Veraṃ* means that from which one must abstain; one who practices that is a *veriko*. *Kāyaparihāriyāni* means things to be maintained by the body. *Taṃ* means you. *Hīnāyāvattabhāvaṃ* means the state of turning back toward a low condition, namely, the state of being a householder.
"Having disrobed" means having effected a separation from the state of going forth (*pabbajjā*). "That matter" refers to the matter designated as disrobing. "His" refers to the great novice.

In the phrase "or great," the word *vā* (or) has the sense of censure; it indicates that he is even more so in the case of one who is young. The construction is: "he is incompetent. "He" refers to the novice.
Regarding the term "cattle-herding calves, etc.": here, "calf" (*vaccha*) means a young bull. For he dwells near his mother, thus he is called a calf (*vaccha*).
It is called a "calf" (*vaccha*) because it cries out at the time of separation from its mother. By this term, both young bulls and full-grown bulls are included in a general sense.
A "cow" (*go*) refers to a field or land. A calf and a cow together are "cattle" (*vacchagava*); the protection of these is "cattle-herding" (*vacchagorakkha*).

These are the "cattle-herding and other [occupations]" (*vacchagorakkhādīni*), meaning those occupations beginning with cattle-herding, such as agricultural work and so forth. By the phrase "well-ordained" (*sūpasampanno*), a householder is also [included].
If he confers full ordination, it shows that he is well-ordained. "At the very time he was not yet ordained" means at the very time he was a novice.
Regarding the "determination in the Vinaya," this refers to the determination concerning one who lives in communion by theft as stated in the Vinaya.
One is a "thievish companion" because of having discarded the outward signs of a monk.

One is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who dwells in theft) because one remains within the outward signs (*saliṅga*). This person also is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* because of having an aspiration for the saffron robe (*kāsāya*). One is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* because of having abandoned the burden of the saffron robe. One is not a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* because one remains within the outward signs.
One is neither a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* because of having an aspiration for the saffron robe.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by means of sexual intercourse and so forth," it includes killing living beings and other such acts. One is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* [due to the saffron robe].

Because the burden has been laid down. "Ovaṭṭika" means performing [the act] with the lower part turned downward. "He protects for the time being" means that he protects for the duration because it was worn as a test.
"The mark" refers to the mark of a recluse (samaṇaliṅga). He becomes one who dwells in communion by theft because he has accepted the mark of a householder.

Whether he tests it or accepts it, he indeed protects it, because the white cloth contains within it the state of being a kāṣāya. Explaining the very same point already stated—that "this is the same method for a bhikkhunī as well"—he said "She too," and so forth.
The connection is that he is a novice who went forth in old age. "In the Pāḷi as well" means even in the sequence [of the text].
Just as a hawk goes taking a piece of meat, so too he goes holding the bowl after it has been presented to him with alms-food.
He is not one living in communion by theft because there is no counting of years [of seniority].
48. Discussion on One Who Has Gone Over to Other Sects (Titthiyapakkantaka) 110.
“He goes forth” means he has gone over (*pakkanto*). By the word “entered,” he shows that the root *kam* has the sense of taking a step;

he excludes the senses of desire and longing. “He” refers to one who has gone over to other sects (*titthiyapakkantako*). “Therein” refers to the case of one who has gone over to other sects. “One who is fully ordained” (*upasampanno*).
The connection is: "the bhikkhu goes. "Of them" means of the sectarians (*titthiya*).

Because he had already previously adopted a conviction, thinking, "I shall become a sectarian," it is said, "as soon as the insignia were taken. Regarding "grass-cloths and so forth": here, "grass" (*kusa*) refers to a blade of grass.

"Cloth" (*cīra*) means a row or a line; this is the meaning. A cloth made by stringing blades of grass together with a cord is a "grass-cloth" (*kusacīra*); that is the first among those [types of clothing].
“Those” refers to the grass-cloth garments (*kusacīra*) and so forth. By the word “and so forth,” bark-garments (*phalakacīra*) and others are included.

They say that a garment made from *kusa* grass is a “grass-cloth garment” (*kusacīra*). “Naked” means one who goes about unclothed (*acelaka*). An “Ājīvika” is so called because he lives having undertaken the ascetic practice of nakedness;
thus he is an Ājīvika. “Of them” refers to the Ājīvikas. “Having been exhorted” is the grammatical connection.
*Kinti kiṃ vataṃ*: What indeed is this vow? *Luñcāpeti* means he causes [them] to be plucked out or removed.
*Morapiñchādīni*: here, *piñcha* refers to a wing. For it is called *piñcha* because by means of it one *piñchati*, that is, flies through the sky.
In the *Dhātupāṭha*, it is stated: "The root *pichi* means 'to go'. A peacock's wing is *morapiñcha*; those things of which that is the first are *morapiñchādīni*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*),...
It includes items such as owl feathers. "As long as he does not accept" means as long as he does not accept the tenet.

"Him" refers to the bhikkhu who is investigating. "Tenet" refers to the tenet of a non-Buddhist sect (*titthiya*). "He protects" means he protects him from being classified as one who has gone over to a non-Buddhist sect.
The intention is that by the absence of such a tenet, he does not become one who has gone over to a non-Buddhist sect. "One whose robes are uncut" means...
In this context, the syllable *ā* has the sense of anger (*kodha*) or of being broken (*aḍḍa*); the word *chidda* has the sense of being defiled (*dūsana*).
Therefore, the meaning of *acchidda* should be understood as "not defiled by anger or by being broken. There is also a reading, *acchinna*. One whose robe is unbroken is an *acchiddacīvara*.
A *titthāyatana* is the dwelling place of those belonging to other sects (*titthiya*); it means the residence of the heretics.
49. The Story of the Animal (Tiracchānagatavatthu) 111.
As for the question, "Even though that nāga experiences sovereignty and prosperity equal to the splendor of the devas, why does he fear the nāga realm? the text says, "Kiñcāpi," and so forth.
Therein, the connection is with the words "even though he experiences. Here, the word *kiñcāpi* indicates a concession (*sambhāvanā*), while the word *pana* [indicates a contrast].
It is an indicator of the sense of reproach. "By a wholesome resultant" means by a rootless wholesome resultant (*ahetuka-kusala-vipāka*). "Of him" refers to the nāga.

"Of his own kind" means of a female nāga (*nāgī*) of the same species. The construction is: "food consisting of frogs that move about in water" means that food known as frogs, which have the habit of moving in water, becomes manifest.
"He" refers to the nāga. "Is distressed" means he is troubled by what is unpleasant. "Is ashamed" means...

Here, because the verbal root *har* has the meaning of "shame," he says "he is ashamed" (*lajjati*). This root ends in the vowel *e* and belongs to the *bhūvādi* class (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, it is the root ending in *r*, number 16).
Regarding "he loathes" (*jigucchati*), he says "his own person" (*attabhāvaṃ*) while demonstrating the object of the root *gup*.
Since the word "of that bhikkhu" (*tassa bhikkhuno*) must be construed with the word "having gone out" (*nikkhante*), it is the genitive case used in the sense of the locative.

He said, "In that monk. Alternatively, because of the possessive connection (*sāmiyogatta*) in the phrase "of that monk," he stated "in the act of departing" (*nikkhamane*), indicating that the suffix *-māna* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvatthe*).

By this, he shows that in the word *nikkhanto*, the suffix *-anta* is not used; rather, it is spoken by including the suffix *-māna* within the meaning of the suffix *-anta*. "Relaxed" (*vissaṭṭho*) means released from mindfulness. In that...
"In a bhikkhu. "By means of the monkey’s drowsiness alone" (*kapimiddhavaseneva*) means precisely by means of the monkey’s drowsiness.

Alternatively, the construction is: "sleeping as if sleeping by means of the monkey’s drowsiness. "He lay down again" (*paṭinipajji*) means he lay down once more. Regarding "he let out a cry" (*vissaramakāsi*):
here, the prefix *vi-* indicates a distorted or abnormal state, while the word *sara* denotes sound; thus, he says, "he made a distorted, loud noise."

Regarding the phrase “having elided the letter *a*”: by this, it is shown that in the expression “*tumhe kho'tthā*,” one should analyze the words as “*tumhe kho atthā*” and demonstrate the elision of the letter *a* following the letter *o*. There is also a reading “*akārassālopan*” (the elision of *a*);
if this is the case, the meaning should be understood as “having made the elision of *a*. By this, having made the word-break as “*tumhe kho atthā*,”...
The reading "tumhe khvatthā" is shown by changing the letter *o* to *va* when followed by the letter *a*.
Why does he say that [these things] do not flourish in this Dhamma and Vinaya? He says: "Because of the incapacity for jhāna... [etc.]". Regarding the phrase "the meaning is 'bhavathā'":
here he shows that the verbal root *as* expresses the sense of existence (*satta*), and *thā* is the suffix. Regarding the term "sajātiyā": here it means a common birth (*samānā jāti*).
Regarding the phrase "of these," when it was said "a female of the same species," she replied, "only a female nāga. In the expression "human women, etc.," the word "etc.
includes female animals, female ghosts (petī), and female deities. By saying "And here," he shows that the teaching beginning with "Monks, there are these two conditions" is an incomplete teaching.
"Here" refers to the case of the animal. "Frequently" means...
"Abhikkhaṇaṃ" means repeatedly or again and again.

Regarding the term "tiracchānagata" (an animal), one might ask: is it intended here as one included among the states of misery (apāya), such as one with a miserable rebirth (duggati) and a rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi)? To this he says, "Let him be a nāga," and so forth.
50. The Discourse on the Foundation of the Matricide and Other Offenses.

112. Regarding "nikkhantiṃ": because of the construction with the genitive case in the phrase "of this evil deed" (*imassa pāpakammassa*), the suffix *-ti* here has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvatthe*);
thus he says "departure" (*nikkhamanaṃ*). "Carrying away" (*apavāhanaṃ*) means the removal [of the being] from the taking on of rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).

"By whom" (*yena*) is connected to "by whom it was deprived of life while being a human" (*manussabhūtena yena jīvitā voropitā*). "Having become a human woman" (*manussitthibhūtā*) means having existed as a human woman; that is, having attained the state of a human woman.
"Or beings who have reached [that state]. By this, he excludes female animals and so forth. "A progenitor" (janikā) by this term excludes a foster mother and the like.
Regarding "even by oneself" (sayampi), the word "even" (pi) indicates that it is not only by the mother, but also by the son.
"By one who is human" (satā) means by one who is a being; the construction is: "by one who is of human birth, having become precisely of human birth, [the life] was taken."
It is called *ānantariya* because it produces its fruit in the immediately following existence; this refers to the act of matricide.

By this, he shows that one does not become an *ānantarika* (one guilty of an immediate offense) merely by killing a woman who is not one’s mother, nor even by killing one’s own mother if she belongs to another caste (*jātibheda*).
Furthermore, his going forth and full ordination are not prohibited. To demonstrate this, he says, "But by whom... and so forth. In that context, "to nourish" means to cause to grow.
*Posāpaniyā*: that very *posāvanikā*, having changed the letter *pa* to *va* and the letter *ya* to *ka*, becomes *posāvanikā*;
and she who is both *posāvanikā* and a mother (*mātā*) is *posāvanikamātā*. *Assa* means "of the son. This word depends on what precedes and follows it.
In that regard, in the preceding word there is a connection of state (*bhāva*), while in the subsequent word there is a connection of substance (*sāma*). In every respect, this is the same method.
He said, “Even if,” and so forth. The term “prostitute” is stated by way of illustration, because the son of any woman whatsoever must be accepted [as such].
Indeed, the sole criterion is the lack of recognition that “this is my father. “By this”—that is, by this son—he “is reckoned as a patricide”;
likewise, even in the case of a matricide, one who kills his mother without knowing “this is my mother” is still reckoned as a matricide.
This shows that it "enters into reckoning.
(114) Showing in detail the meaning already stated in brief, he says: "In the human species," and so forth.

"One who has not gone forth" means one who remains a householder. Regarding the phrase "and this going forth," he shows by the word "and" (*ca*) that full admission (*upasampadā*) is also excluded. "Assa" means...
“Of one who kills an arahant”: *avasesaṃ* means that which remains after the arahant; *assa* refers to the killer of a noble one (*ariyaghātaka*). The meaning should be understood as:

“He does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) because he is an animal, but his admission into the order (*pabbajjā*) is prohibited. “In this regard” refers to the karmas such as killing one’s mother.

Regarding “for the sake of killing” (*vadhāya*), he says “for the purpose of killing” (*vadhatthāya*), explaining that it is the dative case used in the sense of the accusative. By the word “to kill” (*māretuṃ*), [he clarifies] “for the purpose of killing.”

Here, he shows that the root *han* has the sense of "injuring. By the word "are led away" (*nīyanti*), he shows that in the phrase "they are brought down" (*onīyanti*), the prefix *o-* conforms to the meaning of the verbal root.
The connection is: "the statement which was spoken. The construction is: "the meaning of that statement.
By the phrase "and this particle *sacā ca* was spoken," [he indicates] that in the etymological explanations (*nirutti*) due to being oppressed by fear...
And because it is unwholesome, by means of speaking carelessly and speaking loudly, this particle shows that it was uttered by thieves.

By the phrase "or rather, the reading is simply 'sace ca'," he shows that even though they spoke in that way, because it was recited correctly at the time of the council and because it was recorded in writing, the reading exists exactly as it is. Therein...
"In those places. This is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "Of that" refers to the reading "If today we...
It shows the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) with the elision of the vowel *e* in "If today we... There is also a reading with the euphonic combination by eliding the vowel *a*:

"If today we... (115). "One who is natural" (*pakatatta*): she whose self (*atta*), which is her own nature (*sabhāva*), is by nature defined as virtue (*sīla*) is "one who is natural"; [the word refers to] her. By physical contact...
Because it constitutes a *pārājika* offense for nuns, it is said that "he brings about the destruction of their virtue. The connection is with the phrase "a nun who does not desire [it].

"Desiring" means desiring to wear white garments. Since she ceases to be a nun, the construction is: "therefore, he is not a defiler of a nun. The connection is with the phrase "a nun fallen from virtue."

The construction is: "He who, like Devadatta, splits the Saṅgha, he splits it. *Uddhamma* means devoid of the Dhamma. *Ubbinaya* means devoid of the Vinaya. "Of the four formal acts" refers to the four formal acts beginning with the *apalokana*.
The construction is: "He who, like Devadatta, sheds blood, he sheds it. Regarding the phrase "with a malicious mind":
here, not just any malicious mind is called a "malicious mind," but rather a murderous mind; thus he says, "with a murderous mind."

"In the body" means within the interior of the body. For because the Tathāgata possesses an indestructible body, it is impossible for blood to be produced by the injury of another through the cutting of the skin.
The construction is: "and he who makes him comfortable," as Jīvaka did; thus, "makes him comfortable. "And blood" refers to putrid blood.
54. The Discourse on the Matter of the Hermaphrodite (Ubhatobyañjanakavatthu) 116.
Regarding the term *ubhatobyañjanaka* (hermaphrodite), in order to show that this is a compound with an external referent (*bāhiratthasamāsa*), he says:

“And from the action that produces female characteristics,” and so forth. Therein, by the phrase “from the action... [etc. ...and from the action,” he demonstrates the nature of both. From both actions.
The phrase "they occur" (*pavattanti*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. "Sign" (*byañjana*) means the characteristic mark (*nimitta*). "Of him" (*assā*) refers to the person.

Regarding the expression "he does and he causes to do," the author says "by means of the male sign" (*purisanimittena*) and so forth, demonstrating here both the direct action (*suddhakamma*) and the caused action (*kāritakamma*) of the verbal root *kar*.
In that context, by the word "transgression" (*vītikkama*), he shows the direct action; by the word "another" (*para*), he shows the caused action.
“Having exhorted” means having urged. Showing its twofold nature, he said, “twofold,” and so forth.
Therein, one characterized by the female state is a hermaphrodite with female characteristics (*itthi-ubhatobyañjanaka*). The same method applies to the other case as well.
“Therein” refers to among the two kinds of hermaphrodites. “Female sign” means the female organ. The same method applies here too.
"Regarding 'the male characteristic' (*purisanimitta*)," here too: "manifest and concealed" means manifest by nature and concealed;
again, "concealed and manifest" means concealed by way of lust and manifest. "Causes another to take" means causes another person specifically to take.
"This" refers to the reason. "Of these" refers to the two types of hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*). [In] the *Kurundi*:

"But it has been said"—the construction is "what was said? *Tattha* means "in the case of one who possesses both sexual organs. *Vicāraṇakkamo* means "the sequence of investigation. There is also a reading:
*“Tattha vicārakkamo”* (therein, the sequence of investigation). The sequence of investigation is to be understood from the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī-aṭṭhakathā*;
but what is to be understood here? To this he says: "This is to be understood here. In that context, *idaṃ* (this) refers not to the cause for going forth and full ordination.
"Idha" means in this *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the statement "Then at that time," he spoke thus to show that the word "then" (*tad*) functions as an indefinite demonstrative.
“‘At which time’ means: the training rule had not yet been laid down; that is, the training rule ‘Monks, one should not be ordained without a preceptor (upajjhāya)’ had not yet been laid down.

By the phrase ‘devoid of a preceptor,’ the meaning of the negative particle *a-* in the word *anupajjhāyaka* is shown to be ‘absence. The connection [of the sentence] is: ‘one who desires ordination while being devoid of a preceptor. By the words ‘Thus,’ and so forth...”
It shows the fault. "Without having had him take a preceptor" means without having him take a preceptor by saying, "Venerable sir, please be my preceptor.
The construction is: "of the Sangha acting as the formal agent for one who is being ordained. "But the formal act" refers to the formal act of ordination (*upasampadākamma*).
By the phrase "the same method applies," it extends [the rule] to the statement that while there is an offense for the one performing the ordination, the formal act itself does not become invalid.
56. Discussion on the Basis for Offenses Regarding Alms-food, etc. 118.
"Whatever alms-food is obtained in the hands" is the construction [of the phrase]. "For that purpose" means for the sake of that alms-food.
In the expression "just as, for example, the heretics," the word *seyyathāpi* has the sense of comparison (*upama*), and the word *titthiya* refers to the heretic known by the name Ājīvaka.
Showing that this is so, he said: “Just like the heretics known as Ājīvakas.
Therefore, making a comparison with the heretics designated as Ājīvakas, he said they were complaining [about] “the curry and condiments,” and so forth. “Hi” means truly, or because.
“Tet” refers to the Ājīvakas. However, the formal act (*kamma*) does not fail, even when the bowl and robes are absent, by means of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) for one who is complete...
The intention is that because [the bowl and robe] have been specifically mentioned as "bowl and robe," the formal act (kamma) does not become invalid.
Regarding the word "borrowed" (yācitakena), he says "taken after having asked" to show that what is taken after being asked is "borrowed.
With the words "for such [an object]" and so forth, he demonstrates the fault. "Therefore" means because there is an offense; "of him" refers to the one seeking full ordination (upasampadā).
The construction is: "by teachers, preceptors, and so forth, who are indifferent. "Having relinquished" means having relinquished by means of a royal grant (*brahmadeyya*).

Because bowls and robes that have not reached the state of being determined (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*) are not actually bowls and robes, it is said: "the bowl and robe that have reached the state of being determined.
"Like a withered leaf" refers to the status of a novice monk (*samaṇuddesa*); for he is called "like a withered leaf" by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhivasena*).
Alternatively, just as a withered leaf is neither green nor yet dry, so too he who is looking toward the going-forth is neither a householder nor yet a novice;
therefore, because he is looking toward the state of being a novice, he is called a "withered leaf.
The connection is: "of the withered leaf that has fallen. "Alms not yet touched" means a portion that is not to be touched by the monks.
*Piṇḍapātaṃ*: "Equal to the portion obtained by novices" means it proceeds equally with the portion received by the novices. *Assa*: [refers to] the withered leaf. The construction is:
"Just as it is fitting for [the teacher] to perform all the duties of looking after a novice, so too it is fitting for him [the novice] to perform [them].
57. The Discussion on the Subject Matter of Those Whose Hands are Cut Off, etc.

119. Regarding the cases of "one whose hand is cut off" (*hatthacchinna*) and so forth, he says "of whom" (*yassā*) and so on to demonstrate the meaning of such expressions as "one whose hands are cut off. "At the wrist" (*maṇibandhe*) means at the joint of the forearm.
For it is called the "wrist" (*maṇibandha*) because one binds there various kinds of ornaments known as *maṇi*. "At the elbow" (*kappare*) means at the elbow-joint (*kapoṇiya*). For that...
It is called a "kappara" because one scrapes or injures the backs of others with it.
The construction is: "one whose hands have been cut off is called 'hand-cut'"; this same method applies to the remaining cases as well. Or, the construction is "one foot.
This same method also applies to the passage below: "one or two hands. Or, "two out of the four hands and feet."
"One hand, one foot" means two. "Ears" (*kaṇṇā*) refers to the apprehension of sound; for they are called "ears" because sound flows through them (*savati*).
"Attached to the ears" (*kaṇṇābaddha*) means bound to the ear-cavities. "To fasten together" (*saṅghāṭetuṃ*) means to effect a joining, that is, to effect a binding.
"In the form of a goat's hoof" (*ajapadake*) means in a place shaped like a goat's hoof. "Nose" (*nāsā*) refers to the nostrils. They...
For it is called *nāsā* because one makes an indistinct sound through it; *nāsikā* is simply the same as *nāsā*.
*Saṇṭhāpetuṃ* means to place well, that is, to place in its natural state. *Nakhasesaṃ*: one whose fingers have been cut off has only the nails remaining, thus he is *nakhasesa*;

[the text refers to] that. It is called *aṅguṭṭha* because it arises at the tip (*agge*) or the front (*pure*). By the phrase "in the manner already stated," [it refers back to] "having only the nails remaining."
The phrase “without showing” refers back [to the previous description]. “Named *kaṇḍara*” means named *mahāsira*.
For they are called *kaṇḍarā* because they bear (*dhārenti*) the body (*kaṃ*), with the letter *dha* changed to *ḍa*. “In which” refers to the *kaṇḍaras*;
this is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*). The construction is: “He whose fingers are connected like the wings of a bat is one named *phaṇahatthaka*.”
This concludes the section on the *phaṇahatthaka*. Since those with six fingers and so forth are also to be included among the *phaṇahatthakas*, he says, "He who has six fingers," and so on.
Even one who has six fingers is called a *phaṇahatthaka* by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*).
Regarding the term *khujja* (hunchbacked), he says "one whose body is hunched" in order to show the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) of the word *khujja*, namely, one whose body is hunched.
Why did he say "humpbacked"? He said "of the chest," and so forth. The construction is: "but for one whose [chest] is crooked, this too is called humpbacked.
"Crooked" means bent. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Brahmujugatta" means straight-limbed; "straight-limbed" (*ujugatta*) refers to limbs that are straight.
Because this Great Man has straight limbs like the straight limbs of Brahmā, he is "Brahmujugatta," the Great Man.
Explaining in detail the matter that was stated in brief, he said: "Of the dwarf-legged one," and so forth.
"Yesaṃ" (of whom) refers to both types of bodies. "Bhūtānaṃ" (of spirits) refers to non-human beings such as *pisācas* and *petas*. The construction is: "There is a body-form as it were.
"Parivaṭumo" means having a body that is rounded all around.

Regarding "galagaṇḍī": here, showing the etymological meaning as "one who has a goitre (gaṇḍa) on the neck (gale)," he says "yassā" and so forth. "Etam" refers to this word "galagaṇḍī. "Tattha" means in the context of the exclusion of those with goitres. Regarding the word "yam":
when "sipadī" is said—meaning "that which has a loose (sithila) foot (pada)"—only the "load-bearing foot" (bhārapāda) is to be understood;
thus he says, "the load-bearing foot is what is meant. One whose foot is the burden is a "bhārapāda. These two [terms] apply to those suffering from diseases of the feet that cause them to swell.
It should be seen. "One with pustules arisen" means one with boils arisen. "Upanāha" means a tight binding. "In a water-trap" means in a ditch filled with water.
"With water-sand" means with sand heated by water. The construction is: "to cause [the flesh] to wither so that the veins become visible.
"Such as this" refers to the nature of the oil-tube for the calves which makes the veins visible. "Likewise" [refers to the same].
The meaning is: "having acted in the same manner as one acts at the time of going forth.
Regarding the term *pāparogī* (one with a foul disease), he says "arisā" and so forth to show the specific nature of that foul disease.
Therein, "arisā ca bhagaṇḍaro ca pittaṃ ca semho ca kāso ca soso ca" forms a *dvanda* compound; those for whom these are the primary [diseases] are "those whose beginning is the fistula... and so on.

“Sosādayo. By the word “ādi” (and so forth), the ailments mentioned below are included. Therein, by the terms “bile” (*pitta*) and “phlegm” (*semha*), the diseases originating from them are to be understood.
With the phrase “constantly afflicted” (*niccāturo*), [the author] shows the meaning of the constant application of the suffix *ī* when it occurs in the sense of a present participle (*mantu-atthe*).
Regarding the phrase *parisadūsano*: here the word *iti* functions as a synonym for a name (*nāmapariyāyo*).
Thus, the meaning is: "one who is called a defiler of the assembly. The construction is: "He who defiles the assembly by his own deformity is one called a defiler of the assembly.

Having begun with the six defects of the body, he spoke [the passage] beginning with "too tall" (*atidīgho vā*) while elaborating on the state of being a defiler of the assembly. Regarding the phrase "too tall," here it is not only...
It is not intended that [the length] be merely two finger-breadths or so long for others; rather, it is intended to be twice as long or more.
Thus he said, "of others," and so forth. "In the region of the navel" means in one's own region of the navel.

For just as the nature of what is excessively long is to be understood from the description of another's [limbs], so too should the nature of what is excessively short and so on be understood in the case of those who are excessively short. "Mahodara" means having a large belly.
“Kappasīso vā” means like one with an elephant’s head or a yoke’s head; here, the word *kappa* signifies the meaning of a yoke (*yuga*).
“Kaṇṇikakeso vā” means endowed with hair resembling [the color of] *kaṇṇika* flowers. By the phrase “jātipalitehi,” he excludes the graying caused by the wind of old age (*jarāvāta*).
Regarding “pakatitambakeso,” here the word *pakati* (natural) excludes hair that has become tawny through some external application.

He turns back. "One with a whorl on the head" (*āvaṭṭasīsa*): it is called a *āvaṭṭa* because it revolves again and again; it is a hair-whorl (*kesāvaṭṭa*). One who has that on his head is "one with a whorl on the head.
"With upward-pointing tips" (*uddhaggehi*): with tips directed upwards. "As if bound by a net" (*jālabaddhena viya*): as if bound by a web. "Or with eyebrows joined together" (*sambaddhabhamuko vā*):
or one whose eyebrows are joined to one another. "Monkey-faced" (*makkaṭabhamuka*): [the face] of a monkey.
"One with eyebrows like a monkey" means one whose eyebrows are like those of a monkey. "With the corner of the garment" means with the edge of the hem. "One with crooked eyes":
here, *cakkala* refers to that which moves in a circular form (*cakkākārena lāti pavattati*), or that which takes up a circular form (*cakkākāraṃ vā lāti gaṇhāti*).
"Kekara" means wrinkled; for it is called *kekaroti* because it makes something deformed (*kucchitaṃ karoti*). "Just like a crab" means like a crab.
*Mūsikakaṇṇo* means "rat-eared. *Jaṭukakaṇṇo* means "bat-eared. *Aviddhakaṇṇo* means "unpierced-eared. *Hi* means "truly" or "because.
*So* refers to the one with unpierced ears. *Kaṇṇabhagandaro* means one who has a fistula (*bhagaṇḍara*) in the ear;
he is thus called *kaṇṇabhagandariko*. *Gaṇḍakaṇṇo* means one who has a tumor (*gaṇḍa*) on the ear. *Paggharitapubbenā* means "with oozing pus."
"One whose ear is pierced" is *ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo*. "By means of a cow's feeding-tube" refers to a tube made for the purpose of giving food and drink to cows.

"One with excessively tawny eyes" (*atipiṅgalakkhi*) is one whose eye is extremely tawny like that of a cat. "One with honey-colored tawny eyes" (*madhupiṅgalakkhi*) is one whose eye is tawny like the color of honey.
Regarding the term "one with eyelashes free of dust" (*nippakhumakkhī*): here, "eyelash" (*pakhuma*) is what is meant.
The hair grown on the eye is called *pakhuma* because it grows on both sides of the eye;
thus, one whose eye has no such hair is *nippakhumakkhi*. One whose eye has a flow of tears from it is *assupaggharaṇakkhi*.
One whose eye has blossomed (*puppha*) is *pupphita*; one whose eye is blossomed is *pupphitakkhi*.
"Akkhipākena" means by a disease that afflicts the edges of the eyeballs.
"Cipiṭanāsiko" means one with a flat nose. "Sukatuṇḍasadisāya" means resembling the mouth of a dog.
"Paṭaṅgamaṇḍūkasseva" means just like the facial appearance of a frog named Paṭaṅga.
The construction [of the compound] is as follows: “resembling the rim of a mortar” means resembling the rim at the mouth of a mortar.
“Resembling the hide of a drum” means resembling the hide stretched over the face of a drum.
“Eḷamukha” means one whose mouth constantly drips with saliva (eḷa). “Uppakkamukha” means one whose mouth is festering or putrid. “Saṅkhatuṇḍaka” means... [text fragment].
"Saṅkhatuṇḍaka" means one whose lip is like the snout of a conch (saṅkha).
"Like the teeth of an *aṭṭhaka*" means like the teeth of a plow named *aṭṭhaka*. The connection is with the phrase "to close the teeth.
"Between the teeth" means in the gaps between the teeth or in the middle of the teeth. "Like the tooth of a *kalandaka*" means like the tooth of a black animal (*kāḷaka*).

*Mahāhanuko*: one who has a large jaw; thus he is "large-jawed" (*mahāhanuko*). *Cipiṭahanuko*: one who has a flattened jaw; thus he is "flat-jawed" (*cipiṭahanuko*), meaning his jaw is not prominent.

*Nimmassudāṭhiko*: one who has neither beard nor fangs; thus he is "beardless-and-fangless" (*nimmassudāṭhiko*). *Bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo*: one whose shoulder-tops have fallen away; thus he is "fallen-shoulder-topped" (*bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo*).
*Godhāgatto*: one whose limbs are like the limbs of a monitor lizard; thus he is "monitor-lizard-limbed" (*godhāgatto*).

"Godhāgatta" (like a lizard’s leg). "Sabbampetaṃ" means this entire statement beginning with "kacchugatta" (scabby legs). "Ettha" refers to the statement beginning with "kacchugatta. The construction is:
"the detailed explanation (vinicchaya) should be understood.
"Bhaṭṭhakaṭika" means one whose buttocks have fallen away; that is, one for whom the buttocks have dropped off. "Accuggatehi ānisadamaṃsehi" means by means of the protruding flesh of the buttocks.
The connection [is as follows]: *Vātaṇḍika* means one whose scrotum is filled with wind (*vāta*); thus he is a *vātaṇḍika*.
*Saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuka* means one whose knees touch each other because they are drawn inward; thus he is a *saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuka*. *Vikaṭa* means one whose feet move sideways.
To show the meaning of *upaḍḍhapiṇḍika* along with its classification, he says, "That is twofold," and so forth. Therein, it is twofold.
The construction is: "he is endowed with half-calf-muscles. Alternatively, the construction is:
"he is endowed with half-calf-muscles" means he is of two kinds—either endowed with large calf-muscles that have descended low, or endowed with large calf-muscles that have ascended high.
"With a back-foot" (*piṭṭhikapāda*) means one whose foot is situated upon his back.
*Piṭṭhikapāda*: *Gaṇḍikaṅguli* means one whose finger has arisen as a goitre (*gaṇḍa*); thus, he is called *gaṇḍikaṅguli*.
"All these people" refers to this entire assembly. "One who corrupts the assembly" is a *parisadūsana*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by means of the eyes, etc.," other factors that create obstacles for the clarity of the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*) are also to be understood.
The construction is either "with two eyes" or "with one eye. "Both [versions]" refers to the statements of both Aṭṭhakathā masters.
Because the Pāḷi does not say "they ordain the blind," but rather says "they ordain the one-eyed," the word "alternately" (pariyāyena) is used.
For in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, by the term "one born blind" (*jaccandha*), it refers to one who is one-eyed in both eyes.
It has been said. *Kuṇī*: "Kuṇa" means crookedness or contraction; one who possesses this is called *kuṇī*. *Khañja*:
"Khañja" means that which moves with a deficiency in gait; thus it is *khañja*. *Kuṇḍapādaka*: here, *kuṇḍa* is a name for the lame person (*khañja*) himself.

For the lame person is called *kuṇḍa* because he stumbles (*kuḍati*), that is, he obstructs his movement. Why [is he called] *kuṇḍapādaka*? Why [is he called] *piṭṭhipādamajjhena*? [Because he walks] by the middle of the back of his feet.
"He walks" (caṅkamanto) is said because "his feet are contracted in the middle. For by this, he shows the cause for both the club-footedness and the walking with the middle of the back of the foot.
This same method applies to the subsequent sentence as well. "All these people"—this refers to all this multitude.
Regarding "one whose side is struck" (pakkhahato), showing that the meaning here is "one whose one side (pakkho) is struck (hato), that is, destroyed," he says:
“‘One hand,’ and so forth. There is also a reading “pakkhapāto,” but that is not a valid reading at all. For the word *pakkha* denotes a part or division, not a synonym for a cripple (*paṅgula*).
One who moves about using a chair is called a *pīṭhasabbi*; he is so called because his habit is to move about by means of a chair (*pīṭhena sabba-ti gacchati sīlena*).
By the phrase “weak due to old age,” it is meant that aging is *jarā*, and one who is weak because of that is “weak from aging” (*jarādubbala*).
It shows the meaning of the word. "He becomes strong" means he becomes strong due to the absence of adventitious diseases.
By the phrase "no vocal expression proceeds," it is shown that only the mouth moves and functions; here, no vocal expression is produced, and thus he is called "mute" (mūga).
The construction is: "He for whom vocal expression does not proceed is one who is called mute. "Mammena" means...
"Slip-of-the-tongue": this is a designation for one who repeats even a single syllable four or five times.
"Badhīra" means deficient in hearing. For "badha" (slaughter) is the destruction—that is, the loss—of the faculty of hearing;
he who "īrati" (goes toward) that [loss] is called "badhīra. The construction is: "He who does not hear at all in every respect is what is meant by 'badhīra'. By this...

This shows the loss of confidence. "By way of both faults" is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*), because it is also stated by way of three faults in the case of the banishment of those who are blind, mute, or deaf.
"Those" refers to the thirty-two persons beginning with those whose hands have been cut off.
The construction is: "There is a person who has not attained reinstatement; the Saṅgha reinstates that person. "Reinstates" means he causes him to enter the Saṅgha.
58. Discussion on the Basis for Living with the Shameless (Alajjīnissayavatthukathā) 120.
When joined with the remainder of the text as “exhortation for the shameless,” the genitive case is indeed appropriate in the sense of agency (*sāmivacana*).
Without showing that method, it was stated that “the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. By the phrase “in common with the bhikkhus,”...

"Bhikkhusabhāga" means that which has a portion (*bhāga*) consisting of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) in common with the monks; it shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as "the state of being one who shares a portion with the monks" (*bhikkhusabhāgatā*).
By the phrase "the state of being conscientious" (*lajjibhāva*), he shows the actual form of the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*). "A new place" (*navaṭṭhāna*) means a recently established location.
It is to be construed with the words "by the monk who had gone [there]."

"Thera" means the elder who provides formal dependence (nissaya). "Desirous of receiving" means desirous of receiving formal dependence. "Conduct" refers to the conduct of one who has entered upon formal dependence.
"On that very day" means on the very day he had gone [to the teacher]. It is stated, "there is no offense," because the intention was formed and the rising of the sun was not known.
Even though the rising of the sun was not known, it is stated, "at the rising of the sun," because the intention was not formed.

“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). By the phrase “two or three days,” four, five, or even six days are also to be understood, because they share the same result in terms of the state of being allowed to dwell independently according to the method of applying characteristics (lakkhaṇahāranaya).
Therefore he said, “I will dwell for seven days. “One who has obtained a privilege” (laddhaparihāra) means one by whom a privilege—namely, the removal of an offense—has been obtained.
59. Discussion on the Bases for Dependence, such as the "One Going on a Journey" (Gamika), etc.

121. Regarding the phrase “dependence on what is to be done” (*karaṇīya-nissaya*): the taking of dependence is expressed by the term *nissaya* through the elision of the latter member of the compound.

By saying “that which is to be done belongs to this [person],” it shows that the dependent is a qualifier placed after the word it qualifies (*visesanaparanipātabhāva*). [The phrase] “by one not obtaining dependence”...
Regarding the question, "What here is meant by 'not obtaining a support'?", he says "by oneself," and so forth. "Vutthapubba" means previously dwelt in.
By the word "api" (even) in the phrase "even by one dwelling for a single night," he shows what need there would be for two nights or more.
The construction is: "either while resting, or while seeking a caravan. "Of one going by boat" means of one who has set out on a journey by boat.

Regarding the phrase "by one who is being asked": because there is a possibility of multiple agents here, it is specified as "by that sick person. By the word "with pride," he excludes such things as the inability to ask. Regarding the phrase "it is comfortable":
since there might be the suspicion that it is comfortable merely by way of the suitability of the dwelling and so forth, he says, "by way of the attainment of serenity and insight.
The word "hi" means "truly. "This remedy" refers to this remedy for living in comfort. For [the defilements] that have become firmly established...

The construction is: "by means of insight" (*vipassanāya*). Or, the construction is: "tranquility is still tender" (*samatho vā taruṇo hoti*). "Of this very one" (*etasseva*) refers to the bhikkhu who possesses tender tranquility and insight.

Regarding the phrase "relying on him" (*tassa nissāya*), the construction here is: "relying on his instruction" (*tassa ovādaṃ nissāya*). Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative;
for the meaning is: "relying on that provider of support" (*taṃ nissayadāyakaṃ nissāya*). As long as there is the full moon of Āsāḷhī...

The construction is: "for that much time. Regarding the phrase "the full moon of Āsāḷhī," because of the use of the particle *yāva*, the ablative case should be understood as having the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*) rather than exclusion (*avajjha*). "In which" means in which place.
In the passage from the Canon, "even by clan," the word "even" (*pi*) indicates that it is not only by name, but also by clan.

This indicates that one should announce [the name]. Therefore, it should be announced either by announcing the name, such as "of the Venerable Pippali," or by announcing the clan-name (gotta), such as "of the Venerable Mahākassapa.
For this reason, it is said: "Of Mahākassapa," and so forth. By this, in passages such as "What is the name of your preceptor (upajjhāya)?
My preceptor, venerable sir, is named the Venerable Mahākassapa," the clan-name is treated as if it were the personal name itself.
"Included" is thus established.

Regarding the phrase "in a single proclamation," he says "in a proclamation from one [side]" in order to exclude its status as a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or a compound with an external referent (*bāhirattha-samāsa*).
In that context, "from one" means either at a single moment or by a single stroke; for he will later say, "at a single moment."

And [the words] “all at once” (*ekapahārena*). By this, he shows the *asamānādhikaraṇa-bāhirattha-samāsa* (a compound with a non-co-referential external meaning) as “those for whom the proclamation is done together” (*ekānusāvana*).
“By one” means by one teacher of the proclamation (*anusāvanācariya*). “Of one” means of one person seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*).
By the word “at one moment” (*ekakkhaṇe*), he shows the meaning of the term “together. “To ordain” means to ordain two persons seeking full ordination.
“By the same method as before” means by the very method previously stated, beginning with “one [teacher] for one [candidate], another for the other,” and so forth.

“To perform the proclamation together” means to perform the proclamation at a single moment for three candidates seeking full ordination by three teachers, in this manner: “one for one, another for another, and the remaining one for the remaining one. And in the phrase “that indeed,” here the word *taṃ* (that) [refers to...].

The phrase “the act of proclamation” (*anusāvanakiriyam*) is stated in order to show that the term “to perform the proclamation” (*anusāvane kātum*) has the scope of meaning pertaining to that very act.
Regarding the expression “two or three,” the word “or” (*vā*) here has the sense of an indefinite option. If one proclaims two [names] with a single teacher, they should be proclaimed as:
“This is Buddharakkhita and this is Dhammarakkhita. If one proclaims three, [they should be proclaimed similarly].
“‘This one is Buddharakkhita, this one is Dhammarakkhita, and this one is Saṅgharakkhita’—thus they should be announced.
Just as two or three [novices] may be announced together by a single preceptor (ācariya), so too it is said that a single [novice] may be announced by two or three preceptors.
By means of a single person acting as a preceptor—that is, having become a single preceptor—...
Or [it has] that meaning. By the phrase “with a single stroke,” he shows the meaning of the word “together.
“Two or three formal acts (kammavācā)” means two formal acts by two preceptors, or three formal acts by three preceptors.
In the case of the proclamation by a single upajjhāya, one, two, or three preceptors are permitted; however, in the case of a proclamation by different upajjhāyas, there must be different preceptors.
Showing that it is indeed permissible in this way, he said, “But if,” and so forth.
“The Elder Tissa” refers to the Elder Tissa who served as the master of the formal ritual (kammavācā). “Of the Elder Sumanā” refers to the Elder Sumanā who was his preceptor (upajjhāya).
“This” refers to the proclamation by one teacher without a preceptor. “This is the prohibition” refers to the prohibition: “But not by one without a preceptor.”
63. Discussion on the Procedure for Ordination (Upasampadāvidhikathā) 126.
*Taṃ upajjhanti* means "they approach him as their preceptor" (*taṃ upajjhāyaṃ*). Indeed, "upajjhā" and "upajjhāyo" are identical in meaning;

there is only a difference in phonetic form (*byañjana*), just as in the case of "sabhā sabhāyaṃ. Here, the word *upajjhā* belongs to the *rājādigaṇa* [of nouns ending in -ā] (the grammatical derivation is as follows).
In the *Saddanīti* (sutta 1140), the word *upajjhāya* belongs to the *purisādi* group.

The word *sabhā* is feminine, while the word *sabhāya* is either masculine or neuter. Regarding the phrase "they become bloated," he says "their limbs become swollen" because the verbal root *vitthāyati* is a nominal verb (*nāmadhātu*).
For the word *vittha* is a nominal term (*nāmasadda*) because it denotes a substance, and [the state of being] stiffened is due to a transformation (*vikāra*).
*gatta* is the broad term for these [words]. Having elided the letter *ddha*, the suffix *āya* is then applied. *Yaṃ* refers to whatever kind of obstacle has arisen. *Tava sarīre* means in your body.
By the word *nibbatta*, it shows the meaning of "producing" (*janana*) from the verbal root *jan* in the phrase "born" (*jāta*).
By the word *vijjamāna*, it shows the meaning of "manifestation" (*pātubhāva*) from the verbal root *jan* in the sense of "existing. *Santam* means being found or existing.
The construction is: "Iti-ādi kathetabbaṃ" (thus, etc., should be told).
64. Discussion on the Four Supports, etc. 128.
"Immediately after being fully ordained" means immediately after having become fully ordained, not at another time.
The meaning [of the passage] is as follows. Regarding the term *ekaporisa*: here the word *porisa* refers both to the span of an outstretched arm and to the measure of a person.
*Porisā* means "the measure of a man" (*purisa*); the suffix *-ṇa* is used in the sense of measure. *Chāyā* means the absence of sunlight. *Metabbā* means "to be measured.
The phrase beginning with "rainy season" (*vassāno*) is an illustration of the manner in which "the measure of the seasons (*utu*) should be explained."

To prevent [the reader] from misunderstanding the meaning of "the measure of the season" (*utu-pamāṇa*), he said "And here," and so forth. It is called *utu* because dissatisfaction (*arati*) recurs again and again;
it is called *pamāṇa* because by means of it the year is measured (*pamiyati*) and delimited. The connection is: "by how many days it is incomplete. "Of which" refers to the portion of the day.
One should supply the missing words of the text as follows: "of that season which is incomplete, of that season..."
To show another interpretation of the words “the season should be announced; the portion of the day should be announced,” he said “or else,” and so forth.
Therein, “this is the season called such-and-such” means either “this season is called the rains,” or “called the winter,” or “called the summer.
“Forenoon” (pubbanho) means the first part of the day (ahassa pubbo). In this regard, only the latter method [of explanation] applies.
It is more praiseworthy. Why? Because in the former method, there is no mention of specifying the portion of the day when the weather is complete;
however, in the latter method, the measure of the weather—whether complete or incomplete—must be specified.

Only the portion of the day of ordination should be specified as either "forenoon" (*pubbanha*) or "afternoon" (*sāyanha*). As for "recitation" (*saṅgīti*), here it means that [the verses] should be sung together as one.
"To be recited" (*kathetabba*)—showing the meaning of the word *saṃgīti* (recitation), he said: "Having brought all this together into one," and so forth.

Therein, *kiṃ* means "what [season]? *Idaṃ nāma* means "this very [season]. *Vadeyyāsi* means you should speak it for the purpose of informing newcomers of their status as senior or junior, and so on.
129. *Dutiyaṃ* means a companion: either a bhikkhu, a sāmaṇera, or a male layperson. *Akaraṇīyāni* means [actions] that should not be done by those who are fully ordained (*upasampanna*).
[These are] things not to be done. Regarding the term *paṇḍupalāsa*: here, *paṇḍu* refers to a color that is a mixture of white and yellow;
the word *palāsa* denotes a leaf, not something green, nor does it denote the *kiṃsuka* tree. To demonstrate this, he says: "a leaf of pale-yellow color.

Thus, the compound *paṇḍupalāsa* is appropriate both as a compound and as an analysis. At the time of compounding, that which possesses what is pale (*paṇḍu*) is "pale" (*paṇḍu*); that very same thing being a leaf (*palāsa*) is *paṇḍupalāsa*.
It should be done. Regarding the word *bandhana* (binding), since it means "that which binds flowers, fruits, and so forth," the term *bandhana* is a synonym for the stalk;
thus he said, "from the stalk. Regarding *puthusilā* (broad stones), here the word *puthu* is a synonym for "large"; thus he said, "large stones. 130.
*Tassa* refers to the monk who is subject to the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). *Sāmaggī* means the concord of the Saṅgha. *Tenā* refers to the one subject to the act of suspension.
"By a bhikkhu. "In sharing" means for the sake of sharing both material goods (*āmisa*) and the Dhamma. Here, sleeping together is also included because it constitutes an offense.

"There is no offense" should be understood as follows: there is no offense of *pācittiya* because he has not been suspended (*anukkhittaka*); and there is no offense of *dukkaṭa* because the characteristic of shamelessness (*alajji-lakkhaṇa*) is absent.
Thus ends the exegesis of the Mahākhandhaka,
adorned with one hundred and seventy-two rules, within the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya.
2. The Chapter on the Uposatha (Uposathakkhandhaka) 68.
Discussion on the Permission for Assembling, etc. 132.
In the Uposathakkhandhaka, it is called a *tittha* because they cross over and descend there; that is, a water-ford (*udakatittha*), or like a ford (*tittha*).

"Crossing-place" (*tittha*) means "tenet" (*laddhi*); thus it is said: "A crossing-place is called a tenet. For a tenet is called a "crossing-place" because it is a place where many proponents of tenets descend [into understanding].
"Other" means other than the tenets of the Sāsana (the Buddha's teaching). "Of these" refers to those wanderers (*paribbājaka*). "From this" means from this tenet of the Sāsana.
"Which" refers to whatever kind of doctrine (*dhammajāta*). "Of them" refers to those wanderers belonging to other sects.
Regarding the phrase "they obtain": here, since the pronoun *te* (they) refers to the human realm, he says, "those humans. Regarding the term "mute pigs":
because a fat-bodied pig lacks even the capacity for sound, it is called a "mute pig"; thus he says, "fat-bodied pigs. "His" refers to the bhikkhu.
"That" refers to the intentional lie (*sampajāna-musāvāda*). "What? means what offense? It is the word "dukkaṭa" (an offense of wrong-doing).
Thinking that there might be the apprehension that it is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) action, he said, "the *dukkaṭa* offense.

And the construction is: "Furthermore, that *dukkaṭa* offense does not arise by way of the characteristic of lying. To the question "By what does it arise?", he said, "But by the word of the Blessed One.
By the word means by the statement: "What happens in the case of intentional lying? It is a *dukkaṭa*. [It is] originated by non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
It originates from non-action through the non-performance of an offense that ought to be committed.
"By a human" means by a person (*manussa*). "Speech" (*vācā*) means by speech; for there is the elision of the letter *ya*. "Words" (*giraṃ*) means sound.
"To others" (*pare*) means to other individuals. "Verbal" (*vācasikaṃ*) means originating from speech. This, however, is the construction here: a bhikkhu, by someone nearby...
While standing, one does not speak with words; nor, regarding persons standing at a distance, should one utter a loud voice—thus too one would incur an offense of speech alone.

Regarding the term *antarāyiko*, it is said that the suffix *-ṇika* is used here in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*), hence "one who creates an obstacle" (*antarāyakaro*). [The question] "For what purpose?"...
Regarding the phrase *iminā kissa*, it shows that here the fourth case (*catutthī*) is used in the sense of purpose (*tadatthe*); however, it is also appropriate in the sense of cause (*hetvatthe*).
*Sabbattha* means in all instances, such as in the phrases “for the attainment of the second jhāna,” and so forth. *Itīti-ādi* is the conclusion.
