*Uddesato ca* means from the brief enumeration (*uddesa*), such as “Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs”; and *niddesato ca* means from the detailed exposition (*niddesa*), such as “The Pātimokkha: this is its beginning,” and so forth.
136. Regarding *devasikaṃ*, it is said that the suffix *-ika* occurs here in the sense of repetition; thus he says "day after day.
In the third and seventh fortnight of a season—meaning, among the eight fortnights of a single season, in the third and seventh fortnights.

The word "from the statement" (*vacanato*) is a reason by way of indication for the word "is appropriate" (*vaṭṭati*). "In such a condition" (*tathārūpe paccaye*) refers to a condition characterized by conduct that is contrary to the rule.

Regarding the condition (*paccaye*). "It should be followed" means it should be carried out with consent. Regarding the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "also from the statement," the particle *pi* includes the previously mentioned indicative reason.
"This" refers to the statement: "On whichever fourteenth or fifteenth day it may be, it is permissible to recite [the Pātimokkha].
71. Discussion on the Authorization of the Boundary (*Sīmānujānanakathā*)
138. "The signs are to be proclaimed" means the signs are to be announced. For *ākāra* is a suffix used for the sake of emphasis (*nikāra*).
The construction is: "A sign has been made; this mountain is the sign. This same method applies to what follows as well.
By the phrase "this same method," he extends the meaning to such passages as: "What is the sign in the eastern direction? A rock, venerable sir; this rock is the sign. This same [method applies].
The same method applies to the others as well. However, in the case of forests and water, one should say, "This is the forest," and "This is the water.
Regarding the river, one should say, "This is the river. As for the phrase "But here," it means "but in this intermediate direction (uttarā anudisā)";

the word "hi" indicates the fruit (the result). "Therein" refers to the statement, "The boundary markers (nimitta) should be proclaimed. "The circle of the boundary" (sīmamaṇḍala) means the form of the boundary (sīmabimba). "By that which is connected" (sambandhantena)...
By means of the preceding sign being connected with the subsequent sign.
By this, he shows that it is not permissible to enumerate signs by skipping one (ekantarika) and so forth, because there is no connection between the signs even through such an enumeration.
When there is a connection between the preceding sign and the subsequent sign, then even over a period of time—such as by enumerating one sign today and another sign tomorrow—it is permissible.
They say that it is permissible to designate [the site] by describing its characteristic marks (*nimitta*).
Regarding the term "mountain" (*pabbata*): here, *pabba* refers to a joint or a layer; because such [layers] exist in this [place], it is called a mountain.
Since a heap of sand might be confused with a mountain of pure soil, it is said: "But a heap of sand is not permissible. "The other one as well" refers to [a place other than] a heap of sand.
There is yet another threefold mountain. "The size of an elephant" means the size of an elephant measuring seven and a half *ratana*s.
"In the four directions" means in the four directions of the monastery. Regarding the phrase "with four or three," the word "or" (*vā*) here should be understood as including even more than that.
The construction is "or with a single sign. "From this" means from the sign of the mountain. "Therefore" means because [it was done] with one.
It is not permissible by way of a sign; therefore [it is said]. "That" refers to the mountain. "Therefore" means because only a single sign has been described.
The construction is: "that mountain which exists, [is called] 'the mountain'. "Inside" means inside the mountain.
Regarding the phrase "or a third part," here the word "or" (vā) should be understood to include even the first part or a portion thereof. "Of that" refers to that much [of the mountain].
Regarding the "locality" (*padesassa*): he says "if," etc., showing that the designation is agreed upon by including all the mountains beyond the third part and so forth.

The construction is: "In the case of a stone-marker (*pāsāṇanimitta*), the determination should be understood thus. It is called a "stone" (*pāsāṇa*) because it "binds" (*pasati*) by means of its solid mass.
Even an iron ball is included within the reckoning of "stone" because it is similar to it. Regarding the phrase "even an iron ball": [the commentary continues].
By the word "pi" (also/even), copper, bronze, brass, iron, gold, silver, and so forth are also included.
"Whatever it may be" refers to anything among stones, coral, gems, and the like. Its measurement as thirty-two *palas* should be understood by way of its shape, not by weighing or counting.
The construction is: "a stone that is even smaller. The construction should be made as: "whether it be a back-stone (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*) or a protruding stone (*uṭṭhitapāsāṇa*)."

—In the subsequent sentence, because the word *tasa* (that) is used as an indefinite demonstrative, the particle *eva* in the phrase “only a stone slab” (*pāsāṇasaṅkhaṃyeva*) indicates the meaning “not a mountain peak” (*na pabbatasaṅkha*).
“Of a great backstone” (*mahato piṭṭhipāsāṇassa*) means of a backstone that is large in length, width, and height, like Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala backstone. “That” (*taṃ*) refers to the backstone.
"It is not permissible to mark" means it is not permissible to designate [it]. "Hi" is a particle indicating that a fault has been found.
"Taṃ" refers to the stone slab. "Sīmāya" means from the boundary. "Vihāropi" means not only the boundary markers, but the monastery as well.
The connection is: "the stone slab must not be marked. Regarding the word "kittetvā," the term "stone slab" (piṭṭhipāsāṇa) should be supplied here.

The construction is: "In this way, the analysis of the forest-sign (vananimitta) should be understood. It is called a *vana* because it is frequented (*vaniyati*) by creatures such as peacocks and cuckoos;

or alternatively, it is a *vana* because they frequent (*vananti*) or resort to it. Those for whom the bark itself is the core are "bark-core" trees (*tacasāra*), such as the palmyra palm and the coconut.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), bamboos and so forth are included. Those for whom there is a core within are "inner-core" trees (*antosāra*).
"Sāka, sālā, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it includes *khadira* and other such trees.

"Of those mixed with heartwood" (*antosaṭhamissakānaṃ*) means of those [trees] mixed with trees that possess heartwood. Regarding the phrase "a forest of trees" (*rukkhānaṃ vanaṃ*), the relationship here should be understood as one between part and whole.
By this, in the expression "a forest of grass" (*tiṇavanaṃ*) or "a forest of trees" (*rukkhavanaṃ*), the meaning is either "a forest of grasses" or "a forest of trees."
It shows [this]. It is also appropriate to understand the meaning as "grass alone is the forest" or "the tree alone is the forest. "Four or five trees" means *catupañcarukkhā*;
a forest where that is the measure (*matta*) or limit (*pamāṇa*) is a "forest measuring four or five trees" (*catupañcarukkhamattaṃ vanaṃ*);
"from that" means from that which measures four or five trees. "A portion" means a portion of the forest. "In the middle of the forest" means in the center of the forest.
The meaning is "in the forest. For they indeed construct monasteries (*vihāra*) right between the trees. "A portion of the forest" means a single part of the forest. "Therein" means in the forest.

The word "standing forest" (*ṭhitavana*) is the object not explicitly stated for the verb "having praised" (*kittetvā*), but it is the object explicitly stated for the verb "should not be praised" (*na kittetabba*).

The construction should be understood as: "In this way, the determination regarding the tree-sign (*rukkhanimitta*) is to be known. It is called a "tree" (*rukka*) because it is "restrained" (*rūkkhiyati*)—that is, it is kept under control—by those who desire its fruits and so forth.

It is called a *rukkha* (tree) because it is protected (*rakkhiyati*), or because it grows in the earth (*ruhati*). "Living" (*jīvamānaka*) means, according to worldly convention, that which is living in the sense of being designated as green with roots, sprouts, and so forth.
"In thickness" (*pariṇāhato*) means by way of its broadness. "The size of a needle-shaft" (*sūcidaṇḍakapamāṇa*) means the size of the shaft of a needle or a stylus;
that bamboo should be understood to be the size of the little finger. "From that" (*tato*) means from a tree whose height is eight finger-breadths and whose thickness is the size of a needle-shaft.

"In bamboo, reeds, bowls, and so forth" means: bamboo, reeds, and bowls are "bamboo-reed-bowls"; those which have these as their beginning—such as potsherds and the like—are "bamboo-reed-bowl-beginnings," [referring to] in them.
"From that" means from the bamboo and so forth. "Even at that moment" means even at the very moment of the sign.
"Not a reason" means not a sufficient ground. "This" refers to the emerging of the nine new roots and branches. To speak...
"It is appropriate" means that it is appropriate to speak by way of both a general name and a specific name.

By this, he shows that even in the case of mountains and so forth, it is appropriate to speak of them by the general name "mountain" (*pabbata*) as well as by specific names such as "Vaṅka Mountain" or "Vepulla Mountain.

The construction is: "In the case of the sign of the path, the analysis should be understood in this way. It is called a "path" (*magga*) because it is traveled (*maggiyati*) by travelers who have lost their way.

It is called the "path" because one searches for it. The construction is as follows: whatever kind of path there may be—whether a foot-path or a cart-track—that goes through two or three villages after piercing [the forest], such a foot-path or cart-track is suitable.
"Having gone up" means having set out. The construction is: that foot-path which descends is not suitable. "Avaḷañja" means...
They are not for enjoyment. It is called *jaṅgha* because it produces going; it is the region between the knees and the ankles.
A caravan (*sattha*) is so called because it is together with goods (*attha*), that is, merchandise; a caravan traveling by foot is a *jaṅghasattha*.

A cart (*sakaṭa*) is so called because it carries a load, meaning it is capable of bearing it; a caravan traveling by that [cart] is a *sakaṭasattha*. Thus, there is both the *jaṅghasattha* and the *sakaṭasattha*.
And by the caravans with their pack-animals and wagons. "Hi" means "truly," or "because. "Etam" refers to the sign.
"Koṇam" means a corner of the monastery. The construction is: "having gone along the path. "Parabhāge" means beyond the four paths that surround the monastery.
"Dasasu nāmesu" refers to those mentioned in the commentaries on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and other such texts.

In such instances as “*maggo*, *pantho*, *patho*, *pajjo*,” and in those occurring among synonyms and so forth, [it refers] to the ten names for the path, beginning with “*maggo*, *pantho*, *patho*, *addhā*.

By the phrase “by whichever name,” it is shown that it is appropriate to designate even mountains and the like by any one of their many names, such as “*pabbato*, *giri*, *selo*, *addi*, *nago*, *acalo*, *siluccayo*, *sikharī*, *bhūdharo*,” and so on.
The construction is: "In this way, the analysis regarding the sign of an anthill (vammika-nimitta) is to be understood.

It is called an "anthill" (vammika) because it is vomited up by termites, or because it vomits forth creatures such as *sarabū* beetles, house-lizards, and so on. "Born on that very day" means born on the day that the sign was designated.
"From that" means from an anthill measuring eight finger-breadths in height, the size of a cow's horn.

The construction is: "In this way, the determination regarding the case of a river (*nadī*) is to be understood. It is called a *nadī* because it roars (*nadati*) and flows (*sandati*), or because it goes while roaring (*nadanto eti*).
"Of which" refers to the river; the connection is with the word "current" (*sota*).

By the phrase "every half-month" and so forth, it indicates that [the rain] falls three times in one fortnight and six times in one month during the rainy season. The connection is with the words "as soon as it has ceased."

By the word “*īdise*,” he refers by extension to the meaning of “every half-month” and so forth. “Three circles” (*timaṇḍala*) means the three circles consisting of the circle of the knees below and the circle of the navel above.
“Anywhere whatsoever” means whether at a ford or not at a ford. The construction is “it is moistened by water”;
the sense is that it becomes soaked. This is considered a river not only when there is a [visible] sign, but also...

Regarding the phrase "even when crossing to the other side of a river" and so forth, he said "of a bhikkhunī," etc. This should be connected specifically with the expression "even when going across a river.
As for the words "but which [river]," the construction is: "but the river, having been crossed. "That" refers to the river. "Vatim" refers to the canonical text (pāḷi).
"At the foot of a tree" means at the root of a tree. The construction is: "the water flows indeed, having completely overspread the obstruction. "In what manner" means by whatever mode.
The connection is with the phrase "it ceases.

"In a time of poor rainfall" means in a season like summer that is characterized by poor rainfall. By the words "by way of being waterless," the qualification "by way of being an obstruction" is excluded.
"It" refers to the watercourse. The construction is: "having been completed, it flows constantly."
"It is not permissible to make a sign" means it is not permissible because it has been carried away by people and because one did not go there oneself.

"But that which... refers to a watercourse. "At the beginning" means at the first stage. The connection is: "in the course of time it becomes a river. "That" refers to the watercourse. The construction is:

"In this way the determination regarding the sign for water should be understood. It is called *udaka* (water) because it flows (*udeti*) or issues forth; it is simply that which has gone into the earth.
“Water” is the connection [of the term]. “And that” refers to water situated on the ground. The construction is: “water standing in pits... oceans, etc., which does not flow away.
“Lifted up” means taken by lifting it up. “That word” refers to the statement.
“Even in a pit dug by pigs” means even in a pond dug by pigs. “At that very moment” means at the very moment of praising that sign. A pit, in the sense of being small...
“A pit. “That” refers to the making of a sign. “To make” means to make it oneself.
“And to have made” means to have others make it. Why is it not permitted within a boundary for receiving gains (*lābhasīmā*)? Because a boundary for receiving gains causes oppression to others.

Thus, showing this matter by way of its underlying principle, he said: “The boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*),” and so forth. “In this” means within the boundary of common affiliation.
It should be understood that the eight signs are mentioned with reference to the eight directions. The word "sā" (it) refers to the boundary (*sīmā*). The construction is: "by one sign or [another].
When describing three signs, one should observe the direction in which the signs are situated and describe them as "in the eastern direction," and so forth.
When describing a hundred signs, one should observe the eight directions of the boundary.
In each single direction, many signs should be described. "Shaped like a crossroads" means shaped like a crossroads at the junction of three roads;
the intention is that it is triangular. "Square" means a regular square.
"Shaped like a crossroads" [in another context] means shaped like a crossroads at the convergence of four roads. [Other shapes include] those shaped like a half-moon, a drum, and so forth.

However, it should be understood that [the boundary] exists by way of the fixed shape of the signs (*nimitta*). "That" refers to the boundary (*sīma*). The connection is: "It should be bound at a time when there is no movement by those desiring to bind it.

Regarding "monasteries with boundaries already bound" (*baddhasīmavihārānaṃ*): those in which a boundary has been bound are "bound-boundaries" (*baddhasīmā*); these themselves are the monasteries, thus "monasteries with bound boundaries," of them.
Regarding "bhikkhus wandering in the directions" (*disācārikabhikkhūnaṃ*): it means bhikkhus who wander in the various directions.
“Therein” means in that single village-field; the connection is that [the robe] should be sent to the monks. “Together” means from one place.
“Others too” means others besides the village-fields within the boundary-marked area. The construction is: “But the Elder Mahāpaduma said.
“From there” means from those various village-fields. “Should come” is stated by way of seeing the master. Therefore he said: “Coming also...”
“Not coming [to the boundary] is also permissible. Because they share a single boundary, it is said: “They should come from within the marks. The connection is:
“When they have thus assembled, the boundary should be bound. “Having made a limit” means having established the lower limit.
Regarding the phrase “ordination, full admission, and so forth,” the mention of “going forth” (*pabbajjā*) here is stated with reference to the request for the shaving of the head (*bhaṇḍukamma*).
“Fragmentary boundary” (*khaṇḍasīmā*) means a boundary that has come into being as if cut or severed at the edge of a monastery; that is the fragmentary boundary.
Regarding the phrase “the procedure (*vatta*) must be known,” he says “if indeed,” etc., while explaining the procedure in detail.
“The boundary” refers to the fragmentary boundary. “In such a way” is connected with “in whatever manner it is being tied. Showing its measurement:

He said, “She,” and so forth. “She” refers to the *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmented boundary). Regarding the act of rehabilitation (*abbhānakamma*), it is stated that there are “twenty-one bhikkhus,” referring to twenty bhikkhus together with the one who is subject to the formal act. “From that” means from the group of twenty-one bhikkhus.

In the phrase “even when taking [them],” the word “even” (*pi*) indicates that this applies even when taking fewer than a thousand, let alone more. Even when taking more than a thousand, at the edge of the monastery...
"Broken" means as if it were a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*). "That" refers to the broken boundary.

"Therein" refers to the locative case used for the substratum, namely within both the broken boundary and the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*). "Then" means immediately thereafter. "In this way" means when being formally appointed by means of this ritual proclamation regarding non-separation (*avippavāsa-kammavācā*).
"Indeed" (*hi*) indicates the result. "The boundary" (*sīmā*) refers to the boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*). "They will not be able" means—
Without first abolishing the non-separation [of robes], they will not be able to abolish the boundary.

"Boundary-stone markers" (*sīmantarika-pāsāṇa*) refers to stones placed between, in the middle of, two boundaries. The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even those measuring four finger-breadths" indicates that even those measuring one finger-breadth are permissible.
"On all sides" means on all sides of the fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*). "By those walking around" means by those walking in succession along the perimeter of the fragmented boundary.
The connection is with the word "by the bhikkhus. "From that" means from those boundary-stone markers;
having first designated the markers for two boundaries, he says "If, however," etc., showing that after that, whichever they desire may be bound among them.
Although it is permissible to bind [the boundary] as one wishes, it was stated "in this way" in order to show the practice of the ancients.
"Even though," and so forth. "Of both as well" means the connection is that the formal act (*kamma*) belongs to both those standing within the two boundaries.
"Hi" means truly, or because.

The word "ca" indicates the commencement of a sentence. The construction is: "This is what is called a boundary (*sīmā*). "Therein" refers to the five [locations], such as the stone slab on the back and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "in their respective places": it is said that boundary-stones do not remain in their places only with reference to a boundary-stone that has been merely placed on top of a rock slab.

However, having pierced the rock slab and buried the boundary-stone therein, they place it so that it cannot be moved from its position. This being the case, they certainly remain in their respective places.
It should be seen thus. "Not by a boundary" means that because water which supports the earth is made the limit of the boundary, the boundary does not burn away.
"In a hut or a house": here, both *kuṭi* and *geha* are names for a dwelling (*agāra*).

For a dwelling is called a *kuṭigeha* in the sense of "cutting" (*kuṭana*) away the suffering of cold and so forth, in the sense of "severing" (*chindana*), and in the sense of "grasping" (*gahaṇa*) various materials.
A *kuṭigeha* is a hut that is itself the house; [it means] even in that. "Without having plastered the wall" refers to a wall made of bricks or wood.
If the wall were made of stone and served as a boundary marker (*nimitta*), the wall should also be plastered.
"Having made it inside" means having made it within the wall of the hut-house. "In front" means in the courtyard (*āliṇda*) of the hut-house.
"At the place where water falls after flowing out" means at the spot where water falls after having run out.

"In this way, for a boundary thus determined"—this is the construction. "Without pointing out the wall"—this should be understood in the same manner as before. "Inside" means inside the cave or inside the wall. "In the space" means in the space for twenty-one monks. "In this way" means when it is being determined in this manner. "Inside" means inside the wall.
"It does not descend below" means it does not descend because of the level of the sky below. [Objection: But surely there is a descent by following along the pillars?
If it were so, why does it not descend? It should be understood that this is because there is no space for twenty-one monks above the pillars.
Showing the manner of descending below, he said, "But if," and so forth. *Tulānaṃ* refers to specific types of trees standing horizontally above the pillars.
*Uṭṭhahitvā* means having risen up from the ground. *Tulārukkhehi* [means by the pillar-trees].

“By trees reckoned as scales. By the phrase “a single connection,” it is shown that there is not only a single connection with the scale-trees themselves, but also a mutual connection between the four walls in the four directions.
“It descends even below” is said because there is sufficient space for twenty-one monks on top of the walls. “If at the top of the pillar…” [etc.]
By the word "occurs," it is shown that when there is space for twenty-one monks at the top of each pillar of a palace built with many pillars, one descends below. "In the spouts, etc.
means in the pegs (nāgadantaka), etc. By the word "etc.," it includes wall-cracks and so forth. "And the wall" refers to a wall made of brick or wood. If...
The walls and pillars are made of stone; they are to be inscribed. "Attached to the wall" means fixed upon the walls or at the points where they are attached to the walls.
Regarding the phrase "of the lower palace," it connects with the word "standing" (*ṭhita*). Alternatively, the construction is "of the pillars of the lower palace.
To show the manner of ascending above the boundary that was designated below, he said: "If..."
“...and so forth. “In the place where water falls without dashing” means at the edge of the roof-covering.
“Therein” means on that surface. The construction is: “they bind it as if they were binding a boundary on a back-slab stone.
“By that very delimitation” means by that very delimitation of the surface. Regarding the phrase “even on the Tālamūla mountain,” here *tālamūla* is [the name of]—
Having been large at the base, it gradually becomes slender; the same applies to a mountain of similar shape. "Canopy-shaped" means having the shape of a ceiling-curtain (*ullocaka*).
Alternatively, it has the shape of a tree with branches extending out in the four directions, or the shape of a crooked tree.
Just as a mountain may be canopy-shaped, so too it may have the shape of a *mudiṅga* drum or the shape of a *paṇava* drum.
The construction is as follows: therein, the *mudiṅga* drum is thick in the middle and thin at the base and the rim.
The *paṇava* drum is thin in the middle and thick at the base and the tip. Their shape is either the shape of a *mudiṅga* or the shape of a *paṇava*.
"Below" means below a mountain shaped like a *mudiṅga*; "in the middle" refers to one shaped like a *paṇava*.
"Or in the middle. "Two peaks" means two summits. "Between the peaks" means the space between the summits.
"Having built up" means having built up with bricks or stones. "Or having filled" means having filled with earth or sand.
"Resembling a snake’s hood" means similar to a snake’s expanded hood; the meaning is "a humped mountain. "A mountain reaching into the sky."
A cliff designated as "space" that is not enclosed by walls. "The measure of the boundary" means the measure of the boundary together with the interior hollow.
"The tip" means the point designated as the summit. "But if there is an inner cave beneath the mountain"—this is the connection.
"Of the upper one" means of that which stands above the inner cave. "From the other side" means from the outside. "Of it" [refers to the mountain].
The connection is with "outside the mountain. "From within" means from the interior.
The connection is with "there is a cave. To the question "How large? he says: "standing beyond the delimitation of the boundary. To the question "How small? he says:
"the measure of the very last boundary. "That" refers to the small cave. It is "too small" because it lacks even the measure of the very last boundary.

“Beyond” means beyond the boundary. “Outside” means outside the boundary. By the phrase, “If it is the measure of the boundary, it is indeed a boundary,” he shows that if it is not the measure of the boundary, it is certainly not a boundary.
“That” refers to the fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*).
“Having filled” means having filled it with bricks, clay, and so forth. “Having built a watchtower” means having constructed a turret.

"Having bound. Regarding the term *umaṅganadī*: here the letter *u* is a substitution for the letter *o*; therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: because it descends into and enters the earth (*pathavī*), and then moves (*maṅgati*) through it, it is called *umaṅga*. Since it is both *umaṅga* and a river (*nadī*), it is the *umaṅganadī*. "Therein" means in the *umaṅganadī*.
"Standing on the surface of the earth below" means standing by means of psychic power (*iddhi*) upon the surface of the earth beneath the boundary (*sīmā*).
"Sīmāmāḷaka" means a pavilion within a boundary that is a broken-off section. "Vaṭarukkha" means a banyan tree (*nigrodha*). "Tato" means from the banyan tree. "Niggatapāroha":
a *pāroha* is a specific type of root by which the tree, having grown large, ascends; it is a particular kind of root. "Niggatapāroha" means one from which a *pāroha* has emerged.
"Having cleared the great boundary" (*mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā*): here, "clearing" (*sodhana*) refers to those things belonging to the great boundary...
Bringing [the robe] within arm’s reach of the monks, or taking it outside the boundary (*sīma*). "Outside" means outside of two boundaries.
There is also the reading *bahiṭṭhā*; the meaning is that it should be made to stand outside.

"Without striking" means without striking the ground of the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) or the trees and so forth growing there. "In this way" means just as with a fragmentary boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), so too in that manner.
“Sīmāmāḷaka” means a fragmentary boundary enclosure.
“Sīmāmāḷake” means in the courtyard of two boundaries. “Of the sīmāmāḷaka” means of the sīmāmāḷaka that is the place where the formal act was performed.
“Of a branch standing in the air” means of a branch standing in the air that has grown up in the sīmāmāḷaka at a place where the formal act was not performed.
“Of him” refers to the connection with either the monk’s feet or his lower and upper robes.
“In the former manner as well” means even in the case stated previously, such as “there is a banyan tree at the boundary marker. “Therein” refers to that former manner.

“It is not permissible to have [the tree] removed and then [re-]establish it” means that if the branches of a tree rising from two boundaries, or a sprout emerging from it, extend across both boundaries...
It is not permitted to have it lifted by striking it against the surface of the earth or the trees growing there; for it stands fixed [there]. Regarding the word "to be brought":

since the verbal root *nī* (to lead) here takes two objects and the secondary object (*apadhāna-kamma*) alone is explicitly stated, the primary object (*padhāna-kamma*), namely "the bhikkhus," must be supplied.
"He goes up" means he rises into the sky, which is the atmosphere (*abbha*). "There" refers to the mountain. Why?
"It should be brought back," he said, beginning with "for while it is being bound," and so forth. Therein, "while it is being bound" means while it is being bound by the formal act (*kammavācā*).
By this, he shows that the unbound boundary descends into a region lacking a [previously established] measure. "Whatever" refers to anything such as a mountain and so forth.
"Anywhere" means in whatever place. "By a single connection" means by a single connection with the bound boundary.
The phrase *iti* means "therefore"; it is to be construed as "it should be brought.
(140) *Tiyojanaṃ* means three *yojanas*. By the word *pamāṇaṃ* ("measure"), the sense of "exceeding" or "surpassing" is excluded from the word *parama*.

*Etissā* refers to the boundary (*sīmā*). It is to be connected with the words "by a monk who is performing the formal act of designation" (*sammanantena bhikkhunā*). *Koṇaṃ* refers to that which is measured from a corner.
The construction [is as follows]: *hi* means "truth" or "because. *Āpattiñca* means "and an offense," namely, an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

*Pārayati* means "it covers over" or "it extends across. Because of the statement in the *Kaccāyanasāra* (verse 45), "Words denoting a measure take the gender of the object denoted," the word *pārā* is stated in the feminine gender with reference to the boundary (*sīma*) which is the object denoted. *Nadiyā* is used in the sense of the accusative case.

It is a word expressing a part [of a whole]. For the meaning is "a river. The connection is with the boundary that is being submerged by the river. "There" means within the boundary on the far bank of the river.
By showing the word-division as "yattha assa," he says, "wherever in the river," and so forth.
With the word "nadīyaṃ" (in the river), he indicates the scope of the relative pronoun *yaṃ*. In the phrase "dhuvanāvā," the word *dhuva*—

The meaning of "permanent" is expressed by the phrase "a ship for constant traveling. By this, he shows the etymological meaning of *dhuvanāvā* as "a ship for constant traveling," where it is permanent (*dhuvam*) and eternal (*niccam*).
"It would be" (*assā*) means "it exists" or "it might exist. Showing the measurement of the ship, he says "which" (*yā*), and so forth.
Therein, "which" refers to the ship. Regarding the term "by the man with the oar" (*pājanapurisena*), here "oar" (*pājanam*) is a specific instrument for the movement of the ship.
For it is understood that a boat goes by means of this, therefore it is called a "pājana" (oar); by changing the letter *ja* to *ca*, the form "pācana" is likewise appropriate.
The meaning is: "together with the man who has taken hold of it. The connection is: "that boat was led away.
"Upwards or downwards" means against the current of the river or down with the current. "By thieves" means by robbers. Even though...

The construction is as follows: even if [the boat] has been swept away, it must nonetheless necessarily be recovered; it is indeed a constant vessel. It is connected with "cut" by means of the wind or the *mālu* breeze.
By "waves" (*vīcīhi*) is meant by ripples (*taraṅgehi*). For a ripple is called a "wave" (*vīcī*) because it gathers (*cinoti*) or increases in a variegated manner.
Even though it has been carried to the middle of the river, it must nonetheless necessarily be brought back; it is indeed a constant vessel.
The construction is: "it becomes. *Ogatā* means having descended and gone. *Thalam ussāritā* is connected to *nāvāpi*: "the ship has been drawn up and brought to dry land.
Or, *visaṅkhatapadarā* means having planks free from being constructed [as a fixed structure].
*Dhuvanāvāva hoti*—the intention is that at the time of describing the sign, because it is a ship that moves constantly, it is indeed called a "moving ship" (*dhuvanāvā*). *Tatra* means...

Regarding the statement “on a boat”: although neither the sign (*nimitta*) nor the boundary (*sīmā*) actually proceeds with the formal act (*kammavācā*), it is nevertheless stated that “it proceeds with the formal act” because the boundary is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*) with it.
Therefore: because even those coming by boat were permitted by the Blessed One, for that reason.
*Yattha* means at the place where the boundary is designated as the river’s further shore. *Rukkhasaṅghāṭamayo* means made from a collection of trees.
*Padarabaddho* means bound with wooden planks. *Sañcaraṇayoggo* means fit for walking upon.

Because the word "atthi" (is) is used in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) in place of "assa" (of it) in the Text (*Pāḷi*), the meaning of the word "assa" should be understood as "hoti" (is). *Taṃkhaṇaññeva* means at that very moment.
"At the very moment the sign is mentioned": the connection is "having cut down a tree, it was made.
"A footpath bridge" (*ekapadikasetu*): that which is suitable for travel by a single person is "one-footed" (*ekapadika*), and that itself is a "bridge," thus "a footpath bridge.
Showing an improper bridge, he said, "But if... and so forth. "By that" means by the bridge. The construction is: "it is not possible to cross."

"Where" means at that place where the boundary is determined as being on the opposite bank of a river. "Only at the landing-place facing [the monastery]" means precisely at the landing-place directly opposite the boundary.
By saying "if," etc., he shows that it is permissible even if one ascends slightly above or descends below the landing-place facing [the monastery], whether by a permanent boat or a permanent bridge.
"Slightly" means a small distance, such as one or two *usabhas* (the length of a yoke).
“Upwards” means above the facing bathing place; “downwards” means below that.
“Within the distance of a *gāvuta*” means within the interior of a space measuring one *gāvuta*.

In order to show the procedure for the formal authorization (*sammanana*) by means of the procedure for announcing the boundary markers (*nimitta*), he said, “And furthermore,” and so forth. [In] two...
Because it is impossible to stand on both banks, it is said, "standing on one bank. "From that" means from the sign (*nimitta*).
"Himself" is said with reference to the bearer of the Discipline (*vinayadhara*) who describes the sign. "Encircling" means surrounding.
"Of that" refers to that extent of the boundary. "In the place facing it" refers to the sign standing on the riverbank below the current.
"In the presence. "From that" means from the sign (*nimitta*). "Of that" refers to that extent of the boundary. The connection is:
"There is a sign on the riverbank in the presence [of the monks]. "Should be connected" means it should be linked.
"Then" means after the sign has been proclaimed. "Having placed the monks within all the signs and within arm's reach"—all of this constitutes one [unit].
This was said with reference to the fact that it has been authorized so as to encompass the entire village precinct.

If, however, it has been authorized only in one part without encompassing the whole village precinct, then even monks standing outside the boundary marker must be brought within hand’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) before the authorization can be valid.
"The formal act" (*kamma*) refers to the formal act of authorizing the boundary. He spoke the words "excepting a river" while showing the reason for this statement: "the river..."
"But it does not come under the designation of a 'delimited boundary' (baddhasīma).

Regarding the phrase "it is an island" (*dīpako hoti*): here, "island" (*dīpo*) means an intermediate island. For it is called an "island" because it shines (*dippati*) in the midst of water, and because water flows on two sides (*dvidhā*) there;
that very thing, in its sense of being small, is an "islet" (*dīpaka*). Indeed, the letter *ka*— [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "Kakāro hi".]
*Khuddakatthavācaka*. "That" (*taṃ*) is an indicator. "By oneself" (*attanā*) means by the one who upholds the Vinaya.

"On this side and on the other side" (*orimante ca pārimante ca*) refers to both the near shore and the far shore for one standing in front of a landmark on the bank of a river with a downward current.
The connection is: "having designated a landmark on the opposite bank. To the question, "What is the landmark in the place in front of what? he says: "on the near bank of the river."
"In the place facing the sign. "From there" means from the sign. The connection is: "the sign exists facing [one].
"On the far shore and on the near shore" means on the far shore and on the near shore, facing the sign of one standing on the opposite bank and upstream.
"By the sign first mentioned" means by the sign first mentioned on the near shore and upstream.

By means of a sign (*nimitta*). "Having one boundary" (*ekasīma*) means that which has this as its single boundary; it refers to an island (*dīpaka*). Having regard for the phrase "and the two shores," it should be connected as "one boundary.
Alternatively, there is a reading as "a single boundary" (*ekasīmā*) in the constant feminine gender, irrespective of the context of excrement.
In the expression "either above or below," the word *vā* (or) signifies an indefinite option. "Then" (*atha*) means when that [condition] is predominant.

The application [of the rule] is as follows: "Directly toward the boundary-mark defining the monastery's limits" means that if the island is lower, it is directly toward the boundary-mark defining the monastery's limits situated on the near shore below the stream.
"Sikhara" means a horn; for it is called *sikhara* because it takes (*rāti*) the peak (*sikhā*), that is, the summit. "From there" refers to the island.
"By means of a sign on the opposite shore. This connects with the phrase "having recited the signs of the opposite shore.

This is a more detailed analysis than that given below the definition of the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*) for an island. Even for the more detailed [analysis] above, it should be understood by following this same method;
therefore, it has not been shown here. "Mountain-shaped" (*pabbatasaṇṭhānā*): it is called "mountain-shaped" because its location is level with a mountain.
In the phrase "both upwards and downwards," the particle *pi* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "Both peaks" means that which is a peak upwards and that which is a peak downwards;
thus, they are both peaks. "Shaped like a drum" means having the shape of a drum, which is thin at the base and at the tip, but thick in the middle.

"By the very first method" means by the first method among all the methods— namely, the method illustrating the boundary of the dwelling— which consists of the method of upward increase, the method of downward increase, and the method of both upward and downward increase.
"Shaped like a drum" means having the shape of a drum that is thick at the base and tip and thin in the middle.
