Regarding the phrase *anupariveṇiyaṃ*: here, it is stated as "in this or that cell" (*tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pariveṇe*) in order to show that the prefix *anu-* has the sense of repetition (*viccha-*) and that the word *pariveṇa* undergoes a change of gender.
For the word *pariveṇa* is neuter in gender, whereas here [it is used in the masculine].

However, having applied a reversal of gender, it is stated in the feminine form. By the phrase "without making a convention," he indicates that the word *asaṅketena* functions as an adverbial modifier (*kiriyāvisesana*) for the verb.
By the phrase "by means of the formal proclamation" (*kammavācāya*), he shows the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the verb "having abolished" (*samūhanitvā*).
Regarding the word *yataḥ*, showing that the suffix *-to* here functions in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇatthe*), he says "because" (*yasmā*). "Within arm's reach" (*hatthapāse*).
This shows that for one sitting outside the reach of hand-contact, the Uposatha has not been performed. "Assa" means for the bhikkhu.
"By way of the basis" means by way of the occasion (aṭṭhuppatti). The connection is: "in the open air in front of the Uposatha hall, or in a pavilion, etc.
"Those that have reached a sign or those that have not reached a sign" refers to those mentioned below among the eight signs.
Or those who have attained the signless state, or mountains and so forth, or others that are to be praised.
"If one does not arrive earlier, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means: if one does not arrive earlier when the Uposatha is being proclaimed, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
"He is in the middle of the monastery" is the construction. "Therein" means in the ancient residence; "there" means in the ancient [residence].
"In the residence. "Spacious" means sufficient for the Saṅgha’s sitting and standing. "Therein" refers to the residence vacated later;
the construction is "the sitting and standing place for all. "Therein" refers to the elder’s dwelling. "That" refers to the elder’s dwelling. "Herein" refers to your dwelling;
the connection is "there is no space for all. "Therein" refers to that [place] named so-and-so.
“[Regarding] the dwelling: ‘It is allowable’—this is how the construction should be understood. ‘Of him’ means of the Elder. 74.
Discussion on the Permission for the Non-separation Boundary (Avippavāsa-sīmā) 143.
“Named Andhakavinda”: this is the name of that village. “That” refers to Andhakavinda. “The Elder” refers to the Elder Mahākassapa.

“From there” means from Andhakavinda. By this, he shows that in the phrase “from Andhakavinda,” the ablative case is used in the sense of departure (*nissakka*). “Uposatha” is the accusative case used in the sense of the purpose; for the meaning is “for the sake of the Uposatha.
Showing the reason for coming from Andhakavinda to Rājagaha, he said, “For Rājagaha,” and so forth. Therein, “hi” means because.
Taking the monastery at Andhakavinda as the limit, it is said that there were "eighteen great monasteries. "Of these" refers to those eighteen great monasteries.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of giving a gift of harmony to the Saṅgha": here, the act of giving a gift of harmony to the Saṅgha fulfills one's own duty for the Uposatha.
Therefore, it is stated in the Pāḷi: "coming for the Uposatha. By the words "in Sippini,"...
“Crossing a river”: here he shows the name of the river. “Manaṃ vūḷho”:
here, showing that the particle *manaṃ* has the sense of “slightly,” he says “īsakam” (slightly). By the word “appamattaṃ” (carefully), he shows the meaning of the word “īsakam.

By the phrase “vūḷhabhāvo,” he shows that the abstract sense (*bhāvattho*) is to be understood even without the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*). “Caṇḍena” means “by one who is fierce. “Tattha” means...
"In the river. "Not paying attention" means not directing one's mental application (*ābhoga*) toward it as being a "fierce current.
"But not swept away" means not carried off by a great flood. "Struck by the water" means overwhelmed by the water. "His" refers to the Elder. "Wet" means soaked. 144.
"The previous formal proclamation" refers to what was stated previously: "That boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha as one where [a monk] is not separated from his three robes."

The formal proclamation (*kammavācā*). "This very one" means that this very formal proclamation is prescribed as an addition by inserting the phrase "except for the village and the vicinity of the village.

"This" refers to the final formal proclamation. The connection is as follows: because the community of nuns (*bhikkhunī-saṅgha*) dwells within the village, therefore only the former [proclamation] is permissible.
"If it is thus" means if this is the final formal proclamation for the community of nuns.
“Turning” (*vaṭṭana*) might occur; such being the case—this is how it should be construed. “He” (*so*) refers to the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*).

“By this formal act” (*etāya kammavācāya*) means by the final formal act (*pacchimakammavācā*). “He would not receive” (*na labheyya*) means that because of residing within the village, he would not receive the privilege of the three robes (*ticīvaraparihāra*).
To the question, “Does he not receive it at all? he says: “And there is an exemption for him” (*atthi cassa parihāro*). “For him” (*assa*) refers to the community of nuns. Even both...
"Regarding the *sīmā*": there are two kinds of *sīmā*, namely the *sīmā* for common residence (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*) and the *sīmā* for non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).

"Therein" means among the monks and nuns. "Of that" refers to the *sīmā* of the monks. "The same method applies": even when [the *sīmā*] of the nuns overflows or enters within the *sīmā* of the monks, the procedure for the formal act (*sammanana*) of the monks' *sīmā* is exactly the same.
"These" refers to the monks and nuns; for because they share a commonality, they are expressed in the masculine gender.
It has been stated. And here, in the phrase "excepting the village and the vicinity of the village," inclusion is to be understood;
why? Because villages, market towns, and cities share the same defining characteristic.
"Enclosure space" means a space suitable for an enclosure. "In those" refers to the villages and their vicinities. "Exemption" means the removal of the offense of being separated from one's robe.
“*Iti*” and so forth is the conclusion. “*Ettha*” means within the boundaries of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) and non-separation (*avippavāsa*).
“*Attano dhammatāya*” means by its own inherent nature. “*Yattha*” means in whatever place. “*Hi*” means truly, or because. “*Tassa*” refers to the boundary of non-separation.
“*Visuṃ*” means separately from the boundary of common affiliation. “*Tattha*” means in those two boundaries. “*Avippavāsāya*” means for the sake of the boundary of non-separation.

That [term] refers to the village. "Sā" (that) refers to the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*). The connection is: "when the boundary has been authorized," meaning when the non-separation boundary has been authorized.
Alternatively, it may be construed as "after it has been authorized. "Enters" (*nivisati*) means he enters or goes into for the purpose of dwelling. "That too" (*sopi*) refers to the village.

"Only as a designation for a boundary" (*sīmasaṅkhyaṃyeva*) means only by way of the conventional expression "non-separation boundary. "Monks who have resolved upon their robes" (*adhiṭṭhitatecīvarikā bhikkhū*).
The intention is that they obtain an exemption. The construction is: "Just as a village settled later also comes to be counted within the boundary, so too [is it here].
The construction is: "Houses were built with the thought, 'We shall enter,' and there was even a dwelling with the thought, 'We shall enter.
"Even a dwelling" means even a sense of expectation. "Entered" means entered the houses. "Having abandoned the house itself" means having abandoned the house.
Thus it is. By this, he shows that when the house is abandoned, everything is indeed abandoned.
The construction is: "Is there even a single family that has entered or not yet arrived?
Here, the phrase "even a single family that has entered" refers to the new village, while "even a single family that has not arrived" should be understood as referring to the old village.
"In that regard" means in the statement, "the procedure (vatta) must be known. "In the non-separation boundary" means in the great boundary (mahāsīmā).
For it is precisely this [great boundary] that is frequently employed in the formal act regarding non-separation; therefore, it is called the "non-separation boundary.
"The other" refers to the non-separation boundary. "Therein" means in those two boundaries. "Standing in places free from fear" refers to the courtyard of a shrine (cetiyangaṇa) and so forth.
It was stated [thus] because there is no space within a fragmented boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).

For when they establish a fragmented boundary, they exclude the site of the shrine terrace (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) and so forth, and establish it by delimiting the edge of the monastery in another secluded place. "To abolish" means to abolish the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*).
They will certainly not be able to obstruct it; for, having understood it as non-separation itself, [they act] regarding the fragmented boundary.

Because they have not fully understood [the Dhamma], they will simply be unable to maintain [the boundaries]. "The breaking of the boundary" (*sīmasambheda*) refers to the merging of a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) and a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīma*).
"Or by the disappearance of the Dispensation" (*sāsanantaradhānena vā*) means by the disappearance of the Teacher’s command. "But thoroughly" (*sādhukaṃ pana*) means, however, without doubt.
76. Discussion on Village Boundaries, etc.

147. Because the *uposatha* act has been treated separately, the state of being in common communion (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) should be understood by way of the remaining acts, either according to the method of the cow and the bull-calf (*gobalibadda-naya*), or by the method of elimination (*pārisesa-naya*). "That" refers to the state of being in common communion and performing the *uposatha* together.

By the word "unrestricted" (*aparicchinna*), he shows the intended meaning of the verbal root *sthā* (to stand/place) in the phrase "having set aside" (*aṭhapita*). "Whether a village or a town" (*gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā*).

Regarding the question, "By what is the city included here?", he says: "And by the mention of 'village' here," and so forth. Therein, "here" refers to the text "whether a village or a town," and it is connected with "by the mention of village.
Alternatively, "here" refers to among villages, towns, and cities, and it is connected with "the city as well.
To show the definition of the village and the others in detail, he says: "Therein," and so forth.
"In this and that" means in villages, market towns, and cities. "Village-chiefs" (*gāmabhojakā*) means those who enjoy (*bhuñjanti*) the village;
they are called village-chiefs. "Tax" (*balī*) means a levy. For it is by depending on that [village] that the village-chiefs live;
thus it is called "tax. The construction is: "even that which he gives after demarcating a single portion. "In the village-field" means the king's command is cast forth.
"Ettha" means a field; "gāmakhettaṃ" is a village-field, which is simply the village itself; [the word] "tasmiṃ" refers to that. "Ayampi" means this location as well.
"Sopī" means that location as well. The construction is: "a separate village by name. The construction is: "that separate village is indeed the village boundary (gāmasīmā).
A village given after being demarcated separately is called a "separate village" (visuṅgāmo). "Tasmā" means because it is a separate village, therefore. "Sā ca" means...

And there is the boundary of a separate village (*visuṅgāmasīmā*). The other [boundaries]—that is, those other than the boundary of a separate village—are the natural boundaries of villages, towns, and market towns; such is the construction of the meaning.
"In this way" refers to the textual passage beginning with "O monks, by one that has not been formally authorized.

"That" refers to the delimitation of the boundary. "In an undelimited [area]" means in an area not delimited by kings. By the phrase "in a forest region," the etymological meaning of *agāmaka* (non-village) as "where there is no village" is indicated.
It shows the similarity of form. "Like a forest of extinguished fires" (*vijjhāṭavisadisa*): that in which the burning of fire has departed is "extinguished" (*vijjhā*);

that in which thieves and others greatly harass (*ābhuso ṭavanti*) or oppress people is a "forest" (*āṭavi*). That which is both such an extinguishing and a forest is a "forest of extinguished fires" (*vijjhāṭavi*);
"like" that is "like a forest of extinguished fires. Here, according to the former method, it may be either near to villages and so forth, or not near.
Or, a forest region that has not been demarcated by those [boundaries] should be taken. In the latter method, a forest region that is far from the path frequented by people should be taken;
this is the distinction between these two. "Of him" (assā) means of the bhikkhu. "On all sides" (samantā) means all around.
"This boundary" (ayaṃ sīmā) refers to this seven-abhantara boundary. "Therein" (tattha) means within the seven abhantaras. "Standing on all sides" (samantā ṭhitassa).
Or for one sitting, it is that which is born within the inner enclosure, measuring twenty-eight cubits on the inside.
"Any river whatsoever becomes non-boundary" is the connection [of the text]. "Having attained the characteristics of a river-boundary" means having reached the defining marks of a river-boundary.
By this, he shows that a river not possessing the characteristics of a boundary, even when dammed, remains a non-boundary. This is stated with emphasis.
By the phrase “by its very own nature,” the sense of being a bond for monks is excluded.
“Therein” means in the river. “Therein” means in the lakes and oceans. “By whatever” means by anyone whatsoever, even down to an animal.
The connection is: “having been dug up, it is not made [by others], but is self-arisen. This is a qualification included within the reason. Having dug up...
For the meaning is "not made by anyone. Regarding *sayaṃjāto*, it means "arisen of itself"; thus the particle *eva* (only) should be construed [with *sayam*].
Therefore it is said: "not made by digging with anything whatsoever. As for *sobbho*, the analysis of the word (*padavibhāga*) should be made as *saṃ* + *ubho*.
Therein, the word *saṃ* expresses the sense of "all around," and the word *ubha* expresses the sense of "filling. Therefore, it is filled (*ubhati*) by water coming from all around.
The etymological meaning of *sobbha* (pit) should be understood as "that which is filled (*pūriyati*) therein. Therefore it was said: "It remains filled with water coming from all sides.

In the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), the locative case refers to the receptacle—namely, in rivers, oceans, and lakes. Since the word *yam* (which) has location as its referent, he says "which place" (*yaṃ ṭhānaṃ*).
"Of the medium-sized" means of one who is medium in strength; for he will later say "by one of medium strength. "From all sides" (*samantato*)...
By the word *iminā samantā* (“by this ‘all around’”), he shows that here the ablative case is used in the sense of an ablative of departure (*nissakkatthe*).
By the phrase *udakukkhepenā* (“by the throwing of water”), he shows that here the ablative case is used in the sense of an instrumental (*karaṇatthe*).

It is called *udakukkhepo* because water is thrown (*ukkhipitvā*) and cast (*khipiyati*) therein. By the word *paricchinnan* (“delimited”), he indicates an ellipsis in the text. Regarding the term *akkhadhuttā* (“gamblers”).
*Akkha* means a die. For it is called *akkha* because one moves (*akati*) or goes crookedly (*kuṭilaṃ gacchati*) by means of it;

they run (*dhavanti*), transgressing the boundary and going intent on the game, thus they are *dhutta*; those who are cheats (*dhutta*) at dice are *akkhadhutta*. *Dāruguḷa* means a ball made of heartwood.
By the phrase "or sand," he shows that this is an illustration for the term "splashing water" (*udakukkhepa*). *Yattha* means where.
"In which place" means a location. "Of that" refers to the throwing of water.
"Therein" means in rivers, oceans, and lakes. "The mouth-door" refers to the opening designated as the mouth of the ocean and so forth.
"Everywhere" means in every river. Showing the doctrine of the Elders (Theravāda), he said: "But that which... and so forth. "A yojana... and so on.
The construction is: "the statement 'it is permissible' was spoken by the Elder Mahāsiva. Regarding the phrase "even there," it means even in the case of a river measuring a *yojana*.

Expanding upon the manner in which it is prohibited, he said, "For by the Blessed One," and so forth. "The measure of the river" means precisely the measure of the river's depth, not the measure of its length and breadth;
this is also the meaning of the statement, "neither a *yojana* nor half a *yojana*."
It should be understood as being said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*).

Although the measurement of length and width has not been stated, it should be understood that one must take only such a river as is sufficient for performing the work according to its length and width from the source up to the mouth.
This connects with the phrase "the river which. "Of this sutta" refers to this sutta beginning with "the three circles" (*timaṇḍala*). "From the source" means...
“From the perspective of its attainment. “Therein” means in the river. The connection is that it must be established by all the bhikkhus. “From there” means from a single splash of water.
To the question “To what extent is it full? he says: “level with the ford” (*samatitthikā*). It is “level with the ford” because it fills up to the level of the ford.
Regarding the phrase “even having put on the bathing robe,” the word “even” (*api*) indicates “even without having put it on. Thus, even one who does not wear the bathing robe...
Because of the inseparable connection with the cloth, the meaning should be understood as "having put on another [garment].
Regarding the question, "When it is being performed while standing in a boat, is it permissible to do so even when the boat is moving? he says, "But when it is moving," and so forth.
With the words "For what reason," etc., he shows the cause. *Hi* means because. *Taṃ* refers to the mere splashing of water. This being so... there is the formal proclamation (*anusāvanā*).
Therefore, the construction is: "it is not permissible to do so on a boat that is moving. By the words "therefore" (*tasmā*) and so forth, he shows the benefit obtained.
To show that it is not only on a boat, he says "within a river" (*antonadiyam*) and so forth.
"Of a tree" means of a tree grown within a river. The connection is: "or the branch is established [there]. [The word] *sīmam*...

"Or having cleared the boundary" means: having cleared the boundary by bringing [the monks] within hand's reach or by excluding those standing within the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*) or the village boundary (*gāma-sīmā*).
The connection is with "or a branch or a sprout that has entered a *jāta-rukkha* (a tree growing from a stump). "Of it" refers to the *jāta-rukkha* on the outer bank of the river.
"Therein" refers to the stake (*khāṇuka*).

“Of that” means of Pāsāṇadīpaka. “In the manner previously described” means in the manner previously described at the site of the river-sign by the passage beginning with “every half-month. “It” refers to Pāsāṇadīpaka. “Again, it” refers to Pāsāṇadīpaka alone.

“Hi” means truly, or because. “Obstruction” (āvaraṇa) refers to the text (pāḷi). “That” refers to the obstruction. The connection is: “by means of the obstruction, or by means of the construction of a wall acting as a cause, it is cut off.
The connection is: “some portion of the obstruction is overwhelmed. “Therein” means in the portion of the obstruction.
“Hī” means truth, or because. “The lower embankment has been bound”: this shows the manner of constructing a pond after having destroyed the river.
“Therein” means in the river or in the pond. “Discarded water” means water discarded by someone through a water-channel for the purpose of protecting the pond.
“When it does not rain” means that even during the rainy season, due to a period of drought, the rain does not fall.
The river Sāti has its channel diverted. "At another time" means at a different time. "Having overflowed" means having fallen upon the villages and market towns.
"Flows on" means that during the rainy season, in the manner previously described, it flows for four months without interruption.
"The monastery boundary" refers to a bound boundary connected to a monastery.
The word *api* (even) in the phrase *samuddepi* refers to the river. *Tattha* means in that place. *Otaritvā* means having descended below;
there is also a reading *osaritvā*, which has the same meaning. *Saṇṭhahanti* means they stand level with the water. *So* refers to that place. *Udakantato* means from the edge of the water.
*Tattha* means in the ocean. *Bādhati* means it oppresses. *Tesu* refers to those boat-rafts. *Taṃ* refers to the backstone.
“Waves” (*ūmiyo*) means ripples. For they, having surged up by way of succession, destroy (*miyanti*) or harm sentient and insentient beings, or else they cast them inside;
thus they are called “waves. “Therein” (*tattha*) means on the back-slab (*piṭṭhipāsāṇe*). “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly, or because. The construction is:
“The back-slab was covered by water alone. “It” (*so*) refers to the island-mountain. Having said “at a distance,”...
Showing its measure, he said: "On a path where fishermen do not come. "Fishermen" (macchavadhā) refers to fishers;
for because they kill fish, they are called "fish-killers. There is also a reading "macchabandhānaṃ";
the etymological meaning should be made as "those who bind fish," hence "fish-catchers. "On a path where there is no coming" means having gone to a place where...
"Having returned on that very day, not at a place that is a path for those coming. "Anāgamana-patho" means a place where there is no path for those coming;
it refers to a location. There is also a reading "agamana-pathe," but that is incorrect.

Why? Because a path for those not going is not intended here. For what is intended is precisely a path for those who, having gone, do not return. "Of them" refers to the fish-killers. "Of the limit of their journey":

"Of the limit of going. "On this side" (*orato*) should be construed as "a small island or a mountain situated on this side. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among the small islands and mountains situated on this side.
"Having overflowed" (*ottharitvā*) means having overflowed with the natural water. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the ocean which has stood after overflowing.
The connection is: "even by those who are making [it], it must be made. "Where" (*yattha*) means in whatever lake. "This" (*ayaṃ*) refers to this lake; it is not a natural lake (*jātassara*).
[The word] "hoti" [is used]. The construction is: "This lake is counted simply as belonging to the village fields. "Tattha" means in the lake. "Yattha pana" means, however, in which lake.
"Tassa" refers to the natural lake (jātassara). "Tattha" means in that place. The construction is: "If there is deep water.
"Tattha" means on the platform (aṭṭaka). "Ettha" means in the natural lake; the construction is: "on the back-stones and the small islands situated [there]."
"A pond sufficient for a communal act" means a pond that is large enough to perform a formal act (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha.

Having said "it dries up," it was stated "waterless" in order to explain that very point. "Therein" refers to the pond. If he goes to the village territory merely because the water has dried up, [the question arises] when he goes;
thus he says, "But if there," and so forth. In that context, "therein" refers to the pond. "Ponds and so forth" refers to...
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), water channels and so forth are included. The phrase "when they dig" (*yadā khaṇanti*) should be connected as a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*).
Even though it says "that place," one should not understand it as referring only to the spot where digging occurs;
since it is stated generally as "here" (*ettha*), the entire pond must be understood. It is not merely a non-natural pond, but rather a village field.
He said: "It goes only as far as the village boundary.
It does not include a natural pond (*jātassara*). "Having filled" means having filled it with clay and so forth. "Embankment" (*pāḷi*) means a barrier.
"The whole" means that entire natural pond. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "and even salt water," it is indicated that not only a pit (*sobbha*) is reckoned as a natural pond.
It goes; rather, it indicates the salt-water [ocean]. "In a place that is a location for water" means in a place that is a site for water.

Regarding the phrase "overlapping one boundary with another boundary," since the words "boundary" and "boundary" here require a connection, it is said "of one's own and of others" in order to show their relationship. By the term "bound boundary," the word "boundary" [is explained].
Although it was stated in general terms, he shows that specifically only a "bound boundary" (baddhasīmā) should be understood. Expanding upon this very point, he says, "If indeed," and so forth.
"With intermingled branches" (saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā): because their branches are close to one another, they are those whose branches are intermingled;
thus, they are "with intermingled branches. This term "with intermingled branches" is merely illustrative; for even the roots are likewise intermingled.
It should be seen. "In those two" means in the two trees. "And the monastery boundary" means the ancient monastery boundary.
"Having made inside" means having made it within the boundary. Now, regarding the word "atha pacchā," he shows the meaning of the word *atha* by means of the word *pacchā*.
To the question "Who did this?", he says: "The group-of-six monks did this. "By that" refers to the instrument.
Showing the manner of completely covering over, he said “of others,” and so forth. “Of that” means of the bound boundary (*baddhasīmā*).

“A portion” means a single area sufficient for the monks to perform a formal act (*kamma*); that is, an area sufficient for even a single monk to stand and perform the observance-day ceremony (*uposatha*) by determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Those who bind [the boundary] while including within it a portion insufficient for performing a formal act are [violating] the boundary.
"They are called 'merging boundaries' (sīmaṃ sambhindanti). The 'vicinity of the boundary' (sīmāya upacāro) means the vicinity of the boundary that is to be bound later.
By the phrase 'expanding, he creates a confusion of boundaries,' it is shown that if there is a stone that does not expand [the area], it is permissible to make it the marker for both boundaries."
77. Discussion on the Breach of the Uposatha, etc. 149.

Since the preliminary duties for the fifteenth-day [Uposatha] have already been transmitted in the Canon, he speaks of the preliminary duties for the fourteenth-day [Uposatha] by saying, "Today is the Uposatha of the fourteenth.

The construction is as follows: "The explanation regarding 'illegitimate and incomplete' and so forth should be understood thus. *Adhammena vaggaṃ* (illegitimate and incomplete): [the following is the explanation].

In this context, "non-dhamma" (adhamma) refers to performing a *pārisuddhi-uposatha* in one monastery by four monks without having performed a *suttuddesa-uposatha*, and performing a *suttuddesa* by three monks without having performed a *pārisuddhi-uposatha*.
"A faction" (*vagga*) refers to the conveying of consent and purity (*chandapārisuddhi*) to a single person when not all have assembled. [End of] *Chandapārisuddhi*.
He comes only into the midst of the Saṅgha, not into the midst of a group, nor into the presence of an individual.

Regarding the phrase "by an illegal procedure, with a complete assembly": here, "illegal" is as already explained. "Complete assembly" means the gathering of all members. Regarding the phrase "by a legal procedure, with an incomplete assembly":
here, "legal" refers to the performance of the Uposatha by reciting the four Pātimokkha suttas, and the performance of the Uposatha by means of the three *pārisuddhi* (declarations of purity).
The section (*vagga*) is exactly as previously stated.
78. Discussion on the Reciter of the Pātimokkha. 150.
"This introduction" (*imaṃ nidānaṃ*) means this introduction to the Pātimokkha. Regarding the phrase "but it has been heard" (*sutā kho pana*): here, "it was heard" (*suyyittha*) [is intended].

"Sutā" means those things which have been heard, or "sutā" in the sense of "they will be heard," such as the recitation of the *pārājika* rules and so forth. The compound "sutā" should be formed by the grammatical rule of *sarūpa-ekasesa* (retaining only one of identical forms), meaning both "those that have been heard" (*sutā*) and "those that are to be heard" (*sutā*).
"The remainder" (*avasesa*) refers to what remains after the recitation of the *nidāna* and other sections, namely the recitation of the *pārājika* rules and so forth.

By the word "sutenā" (by what is heard), because of the technical rule of grammar stating, "When [an operation] is impossible in the sense, it is applied to the word," according to this maxim (*paribhāsa*), in the phrase "sutenā," it is the word itself [that is intended].
It should be understood. "By that method" means by that method of the introduction and the enumeration.
"Fear of wild men" (*aṭavimanussabhaya*) means the fear of a person living in the wilderness; the meaning is "fear of forest-dwellers.

In the cases of "obstacles from kings" (*rājantarāya*) and so forth, the distinction should be understood in this way—this is the construction. "Forest fire" (*davādāha*) means that which burns a grove (*dāya*).
By changing the *d* of *davadāho* to *r*, and the *y* of *yakārassa* to *v*. "Nanti" means [he kills] a monk (*bhikkhu*). Or "a single nun" (*bhikkhunī*)—this is the construction.

"The first recitation" (*paṭhamo uddeso*) refers to the recitation of the introduction (*nidāna*). "Therein" (*ettha*) means in the five recitations. "In which" (*yasmiṃ*) means in the recitation. "That too" (*sopi*) means the recitation as well.
"It should be announced by the word 'heard' alone" (*suteneva sāvetabbo*) means it should be announced to the Saṅgha by the phrase "heard"; thus is the word "alone" (*eva*) used.
He shows [this] by saying, "not in detail.

Regarding the word *anajjhiṭṭhā*, he says, "uncommanded" (*anāṇattā*) or "unasked" (*ayācitā*), demonstrating here—by means of the prefix—that the root *is* (to wish/desire) has a meaning other than that of wishing or desiring.
Here, the term "uncommanded" refers to the state of not being commanded by the Elder.

It has been said. Regarding the phrase “unasked,” it should be understood as referring to the state of being unasked by one who has obtained [permission] through formal agreement (sammuti) while still a novice.

“In this context” refers to the statement, “They speak the Dhamma without being requested. “One who requests the Dhamma”: one who requests for the purpose of a discourse on the Dhamma is a *dhammajjhesaka*;
[the phrase refers to] such a person. Or, having asked permission, or having been requested by that senior of the Saṅgha (*saṅghatthera*).
“Vāti” means “or. “By way of the sequence of turns” (*vārapaṭipāṭiyā*) means according to the order of the turns.
Regarding the phrase “*dehīti vā*,” here the particle *iti vā* should be connected with both the word “*bhaṇa*” and the word “*kathehi*.

The construction is: either “*bhaṇa*,” or “*kathehi*,” or “*dehi*” should be said. “By all three methods” (*tīhipi vidhīhi*) refers to the three ways of recitation known as *osāraṇa*, *kathana*, and *sarabhañña*.
And here, *osāraṇa* is that by which the discourse (*sutta*) is brought down and uttered; *kathana* is that by which the meaning (*attha*) is told;
and *sarabhañña* is that by which both the discourse and its meaning are recited with a melodic tone (*sara*).

"Recite" (*osārehi*) means utter the discourse. "Tell" (*kathehi*) means tell the meaning. "Melodic recitation" (*sarabhañña*) is the reciting of both the discourse and its meaning with a melodic tone. "Him" (*naṃ*) refers to the co-resident pupil (*saddhivihārika*).
"Having resolved upon the recitation" means having resolved, "I shall perform the recitation. "In this place" refers to the location of the exhortation.

"Dependents" refers to the co-residents (saddhivihārikas) and others. "He" refers to the senior of the Saṅgha; he is the object of the action in the phrase "should be spoken to," and the agent in phrases such as "speaks.
"Commenced" means commenced by the Saṅgha. "Setting aside" means setting aside the hearing of the Dhamma. "Concluding" means...
Having recited the first sutta. "By one who speaks again" means by one who subsequently explains the meaning (*attha*).

"Without stopping at all" means without halting midway between the sutta and its meaning. "Should be spoken" means the various types of meaning (*atthajāta*) should be explained. "For one who speaks... [etc.
...the method" means for one who, having first explained the meaning, then recites both the sutta and the meaning with the proper intonation (*sara*).
The meaning is that even when [the person] returns, the same method applies.
"Even in the course of conversation while sitting nearby" means even during talk with one seated in close proximity. "By him" refers to the senior monk of the Saṅgha (*saṅghatthera*).
"It is proper to speak" means it is proper to speak specifically. "By him" refers to the monk who has learned [of the matter] from the people. The senior monk of the Saṅgha says:
The connection is "or she remains silent. The construction is "it is said that she asks.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in the case of rejoicing, etc.," he includes such things as preaching the Dhamma. The connection is "the senior of the Saṅgha gives permission.
"In all places" means in all monasteries and inner houses.
*Sajjhāyanti*: reciting by oneself with mastery; the meaning is: reciting with mastery even without being requested by anyone.
*Thero*: an elder who is a co-resident (*saddhivihārika*). *Vissamissāmīti*: "I shall rest" means I shall go free from fatigue. *Āpucchitabbaṃ*:
one must take leave of both the first elder and the elder who has returned later. By one...
The connection is with the phrase "authorized by the senior of the Saṅgha. The phrase "to another" means to a senior other than the senior who has given the authorization;

this is the connection. "Him" refers again to the senior who has returned. Regarding the statement "one should appoint oneself," the accusative case is used here in the sense of the subject (the nominative);

thus he says, "one should appoint oneself. To the question, "What is the purpose of being appointed? Is he to be questioned without looking at the assembly? he says, "But by the one questioning," and so forth.
153. *Meti* means "to me. *Itoti* refers to the person; the connection is with the word *uppanno* ("arisen").
Regarding the phrase *puramhākaṃ*, having analyzed it as *pure amhākaṃ*, he says "firstly for us" because the word *pure* has the sense of "first.
The word *paṭikacceva* is a synonym for "even beforehand"; he shows its meaning by the phrase "even earlier. *Bhūtameva* means "only existing," or "only as it truly is."
82. Discussion on the Refutation of Illegal Acts (Adhammakamma), etc. 154.
"Illegal act" (*adhammakamma*) means an act that is not based in reality. Regarding "refute" (*paṭikkosituṃ*), since the root *kus* here has the sense of removing, he says "to prevent.
"View" (*diṭṭhi*) means a settled opinion. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to four or five [monks]. "In what way" (*yathā*) means by whatever manner.
The construction is "being spoken. "They do not hear" means other monks do not hear.

"Dependent on the elder" (therādhīnaṃ) means they are bound by the elder; this is the meaning. "Subject to the elder" (therāyattaṃ) means dependent upon the elder; the meaning is that it belongs to the elder.
"In this" refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
83. Discussion on the Request for the Recitation of the Pātimokkha, etc. 155.
"And ninefold" means: threefold according to the day, threefold according to the agent, and threefold according to the manner in which it is to be performed—thus making nine divisions or nine types.
"Fourfold" refers to [the four types of assemblies] beginning with "one that is contrary to the Dhamma and incomplete," and so forth.
It is fourfold. "Twofold" means twofold by way of monks and nuns.
"Ninefold" means fivefold in the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and fourfold in the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha, thus ninefold. "In this" refers to the passage:
"Whatever monk there is who is competent and capable. "Well-expert" (suvisada) means very proficient or pure. "Even this much"—the particle *pi* [indicates inclusion].
This shows that regarding censure (*garahā*), what indeed could be said when [the offense] is greater?

Regarding the phrase "neighboring residences" (*sāmantā āvāsā*), he says "a neighboring residence" (*sāmantaṃ āvāsaṃ*) because here the ablative case is used in the sense of the accusative. "Whoever is able" means whoever among many novices is able.
84. Discussion on the Permission to Take Note of the Counting of the Faction (*pakkhagaṇanādi-uggahaṇānujānanakathā*).
156. *Katinaṃ pūraṇī* means "filling how many lunar days" (*tithi*). *Ko divaso* means "how long is the day?
*Ayyāyattaṃ* means "dependent upon or bound by the masters," that is, the monks. *Saṃharitvā* means "having again collected the voting sticks" (*salāka*).
This reading does not exist in certain commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and manuscripts. Regarding *kālavato*: here, because the suffix *-vantu* has the sense of *-sva*, he said, "at the very time."
The word *eva*, moreover, is appropriate in the sense of "certainly. *Pageva* means "even at dawn. 158.
*Sāyam-pi* means "also in the evening. By the word *pi* (also), it includes other times for seeking refuge as well. 159. Regarding the phrase *āṇāpetum*:
this was stated in order to show those monks who are to be commanded, having set aside those monks who are not to be commanded.
“Some kind of work,” and so forth. The construction is: “always performing some kind of work. In the phrase “among preachers of the Dhamma, etc.,” the word “etc.
includes those who lead groups and others. “In turn” means by rotation. “A broom” refers either to a stick-broom (*yaṭṭhisammuñcanī*) or a hand-broom (*muṭṭhisammuñcanī*).
It is called a *sammuñcanī* because by means of it one sweeps or thoroughly cleanses; it is a term for a broom made of palm leaves.
"First. "That too" means even the breaking of branches.

"In the manner already stated" means in the very same manner as stated regarding the sweeping. "Should be brought back again" means the seats belonging to the Saṅgha should be brought back to the Saṅgha’s dwelling place.

"Even with mats" means even with mats made of bamboo and so forth. "Or a bowl" means either a lamp-bowl included among bowls. "That" refers to the oil and so forth. "Should be sought" means they should be sought by means of blameless seeking.
86. Discourse on the Bases such as Disintegration (Disaṃgamikādivatthukathā). 163.
Showing the distinction between the four verbal forms beginning with *saṃgahetabbo*, he said “*saṃgahetabbo*” and so forth.

Since the word *saṃgaha* is also used in the senses of “conciseness” (*saṅkhepa*) and “grasping” (*gahaṇa*), the Pāḷi [text] was used here to show that it means “in the sense of favoring” (*anuggaha*).
It was said, "He should be assisted. Therefore it was said, "by way of acting accordingly.
"He should be entreated" means that a learned bhikkhu, having been approached by the bhikkhus, should be made to speak—that is, he should be requested by the Saṅgha.
"He should be attended upon" means that a learned bhikkhu should be established by the bhikkhus through service and honor. "An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for all."
Having said that, in order to support that very point, it was stated: “In this case, neither the elders nor the youths are exempt. “By him” means by the learned bhikkhu.
“Even though this is so” means even when there is no such consent. “Evening and morning” (*sāyaṃpātaṃ*) means both evening and morning.
“Attendance” (*upaṭṭhāna*) means the place of attendance, or for the purpose of attending. “By him” means by the learned bhikkhu.
"Tesam" refers to the great elders (*mahātherā*). "Assa" refers to a learned (*bahussuta*) bhikkhu. "Saddhiṃcarā" means those who walk together with oneself;
thus they are called "companions. "Athāpi" means even if. The construction is: "or even one who is endowed with virtuous conduct speaks. "Eso ca ahañca" means "we two.
For when the formation of a single remainder (*ekasesa*) is to be made from the words *nāmam*, *tumhe*, and *amhe*, the word following [the first] is to be taken.
The construction is: "Let them dwell," so they say.
Regarding the statement "that residence must be gone to," for what purpose should one go there? Should one go every day? To this he says:

"It should be gone to every half-month for the purpose of performing the Uposatha. And that residence—only during the proper season; that is, only during the winter and summer seasons. Only during the proper season.
He said, “But during the rains,” and so forth, showing that the meaning is the state of what must be known. “Yaṃ” (which) refers to the *kamma*.
“Tattha” (therein) refers to the statement beginning with “dwelling for the rains. “So” (he) refers to the monk who recites the *Pātimokkha*.
“Aññasmiṃ” (in another) refers to another *Pātimokkha*-reciter. “Two months” means from the full moon of the month of Sāvaṇa until the full moon of Assayuja.
One should reside for two months. This was said with reference to one who has entered the earlier rains-residence (*purimavassa*) and then departs during the later period (*pacchimikā*).
If, however, having entered the later rains-residence, one departs immediately thereafter, one should reside for three months.
87. Discussion on the Giving of Purity (*pārisuddhi*).
164. "Communicates by means of any limb or member" means that being unable to utter a reply, one communicates by means of any limb or member.
"In both ways" means by both modes consisting of body and speech; the connection is "one communicates by means of body and speech.
"All" refers to all those who are ill. "Within arm's reach" means within the arm's reach of the Saṅgha.
"If they are far away" means if many who are ill are situated far from one another. "On that day" refers to the day on which the Saṅgha is not sufficient [to perform the Uposatha].
"He departs right there" means that the suffix *tha* is used here in the sense of the ablative; thus he says "from there," meaning "from the place where the purity (pārisuddhi) was offered.
By the word "goes," he shows the meaning of the root *kam* as "taking a step"; "somewhere" [is added].

This is his offense. Regarding the phrases "the novice admits," and so forth, he says, "‘I am a novice,’ thus he admits," etc., demonstrating the elision of the word *iti*, which here has the sense of the manner of admission. "Only what is real" means only that which exists.
"In all cases" refers to all instances such as "one who has renounced the training admits," and so on.
"At the very least, there must be four bhikkhus"—this is the connection. "In all cases" refers to all instances such as "one who has reached the Saṅgha disrobes," and so forth.

"In this case" refers to the bringing of the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity). By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even for many," he shows that whether the *pārisuddhi* is brought by one person for one, by many for one, or by many for many, it is indeed considered brought. "He" refers to the one who brings the *pārisuddhi*.
"Bhikkhu. "Yes" means [the response] of the bhikkhus. "Of that very person" means of the one who brings the declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*).
"But the other" refers, however, to the purity of the others. Regarding the term *biḷālasaṅkhalikā*: here, *biḷāla* means a rat-eater.
For he is called a *biḷāla* because he is able—capable—to catch a rat from its hole (*biḷāsayam*). *Saṅkhalikā* is a specific type of fetter used for binding living beings.
The name [is as follows]. Because it is connected by way of the relationship between that which is related and that which is related to it—namely, the cat’s chain—it is called “the cat’s chain.
This is merely an illustration, since the chain of whatever [animal] may be taken is intended.
The meaning is: “purity like that cat’s chain. Herein, this is the application of the simile: just as, first of all, by means of the chain...
Just as one bracelet reaches only the second bracelet and not the third, even so the purity (pārisuddhi) given first reaches only the second and not the third.
"Having come" means having come within arm's reach of the Saṅgha. In the phrases "he does not announce the Sutta in the Pāḷi," etc., the sense is that of the instrumental case (hetvatthe).

It is a word used in the singular sense. "He does not announce it by means of the Sutta" is the meaning. Regarding the statement, "There is no offense for the one who brings the purity," here the author says, "If...
[he] incurs an offense," demonstrating the positive sense (*anvayattha*) by way of implication (*atthāpatti*). "Of him" refers to the monk.
"Of both" refers to both the one who gives the purity and the one who brings it.
88. The Discourse on Giving with Desire (Chandadānakathā).
165. The construction is: "The determination regarding giving with desire should also be understood.

"The Uposatha has been performed" means that the Uposatha has been performed both for the one who gives the declaration of purity (*pārisuddhi*) and for the Saṅgha. "Another" means other than the Uposatha formal act (*kamma*). "Whatever formal act," however—
The connection: "Also a formal act" means any formal act other than the Uposatha formal act.

And in this regard, if on that very Uposatha day there is both a Uposatha formal act for oneself and for the Saṅgha, then only purity (*pārisuddhi*) should be given. If, however, there is another formal act, then only consent (*chanda*) should be given. If there is both a Uposatha formal act and another formal act, then both purity and...
And consent (*chanda*) must be given. It is with reference to this that it was said: “When one gives purity on the Uposatha day, one must also give consent.
“In the boundary” means either in a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*). “To sit” means to enter and take a seat;

for it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*, specifically the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* under root 16, beginning with *sakāra*) that the root *ās* signifies “sitting. “Or unanimity” means either physical unanimity (*kāyasāmaggī*).
167. Regarding the phrase "he remembers the Uposatha, or he does not remember," the word *pi* (also/even) is stated here to show the sense of non-restriction or optionality, as in:

"sometimes he remembers, sometimes he does not remember. By the word *ekantaṃ* (absolutely), it shows the sense of certainty (*sanniṭṭhāna*) of the word *eva* (indeed) in the phrase "he does not remember at all.
"He does not invalidate the legal act" means that even one who has attained sanity, or one who has not [yet] attained it, being insane, does not invalidate the legal act.
91. Discussion on the Uposatha of the Saṅgha, etc. 168.
Regarding the phrase “having swept,” it is stated that in the expression “that place,” the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
“This” refers to the statement beginning with “that place is to be swept. “By that” means by that reason. Thus say the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
The construction is: “‘Sammajjanī... ... it is said.
*Sammajjanī* means the act of sweeping. *Padīpo* means the lighting of a lamp. *Udakan* means the setting out of water. *Āsanena* means by the preparation of seats.
The word “iti” (thus) is to be supplied [from the preceding context]. *Uposathassa* refers to the ninefold *uposatha*.
The connection is with the term *pubbakaraṇaṃ*. "These" refers to the four formal acts (*kamma*). "Is called" means it is spoken of.
This [word] is expressed in the singular number because it depends on the proximate form *ākāra*, due to the non-difference between the act—referred to as "these"—and the form *pubbakaraṇa*.
However, the word "declared" (*akkhātāni*) is expressed in the plural number because it depends on the act, namely "these four."
It should be understood as "spoken.

"The announcement of the desire, the purity, and the season" refers to the announcement of the desire (*chandakkhāna*), the announcement of the purity (*pārisuddhikkhāna*), and the announcement of the season (*utukkhāna*).
"Counting the bhikkhus" means the announcing after having counted the bhikkhus. "Exhortation" means the announcing of the exhortation requested by the bhikkhunīs. "These" refers to...
These are five. "After the preliminary duty" means after the performance of the preliminary duty.
And here, the phrase "to be done after the preliminary duty" is a qualification of the manner in which they are to be performed, not of their purpose. However, this is the distinction:
it is called the "preliminary duty" because it is to be performed prior to the assembly of the Saṅgha, that is, prior to the performance of the Uposatha.
Because it is something that must be done, it is called "prior duty.
*Uposatha* means the day of the observance. *Yāvatikā ca bhikkhū* means as many bhikkhus as there are.

*Kammapattā* means those who have reached, are fit for, or are suitable for the observance ceremony. And those bhikkhus, as many as they are, should remain within hand’s reach, standing within a single boundary.
The construction is: "they exist. "Similar offenses" means offenses similar in their underlying matter (*vatthu*).
"To be avoided" means they should be shunned. "Persons" refers to persons such as householders and so forth. "In that" means in that Uposatha boundary hall (*sīmāmaḷaka*).

"These four" is the remainder of the text. The construction is: "by those monks who have arrived. By the word "also" (*pi*) in "even on the fifteenth," it is shown that it is not only permissible to determine [the date] according to the method found in the Canon, but also by saying, "Today is my Uposatha, the fifteenth."
92. Discussion on the Procedure for the Rectification of Offenses (Āpattipaṭikammavidhikathā).
169. The connection is as follows: [the rule] “... by the Blessed One... it should be performed” is to be understood.

By means of the three reasons beginning with the statement, “For one who has an offense...,” even though it was not explicitly formulated as “The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense,” it is established by implication according to the literal meaning.
This shows that it is indeed established. The triad of reasons should be connected with the word "to be known" (*veditabba*).

In the phrase "in cases such as thullaccaya," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the offenses of *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*. The connection is: "The statement 'I confess that' is indeed well-spoken.
"That" refers to the offense. "In your presence" (*tumhamūle*) means in your vicinity; for there is the elision of the *niggahīta* vowel.

It is indeed a sentence, not a compound. The terms "tumha" and "tuyha" are merely examples of the forms in which the nine newly ordained elders might speak; they do not indicate a failure to convey the intended meaning.
By the word "pi" (also) in the phrase "vuttampi" (it is also said), he shows that it is well-stated not only according to the method of the Pāḷi, but also by this method.
The connection is with the words "this too is to be spoken," namely, the manner of speaking.
"But it is easy to understand. The connection is: "The statement 'Yes, I see' is indeed well-spoken.

The word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "Vuttampi" (It is also said) includes the method of the Pāḷi text. The connection here is: "But what should be said regarding 'you should restrain yourself in the future.

Because the plural form must be used for elders (*garū*), it is stated as "saṃvareyyātha" (you [plural] should restrain). The connection is: "by the one who has spoken thus, namely the confessor of the offense."

“Tatra” means “when [it is said] ‘one who is free from doubt’” in the reading. The construction is: “when the sun is covered by clouds. The connection is: “that monk should say. “Having proclaimed the matter” means having proclaimed the matter consisting of the food.

“Those” refers to the offenses. Regarding the phrase “a similar offense,” he says “that which both persons... and so forth, showing that between the two types—similarity of the matter (*vatthusabhāga*) and similarity of the offense (*āpattisabhāga*)—only similarity of the matter is intended here.
The connection is: “whatever offense. “Those whose portion is the same” (*samāno bhāgo etāsaṃ*).

"Of the same class" (*sabhāgā*). "It is permissible to confess" means that even if it is of the same class as the offense (*āpatti-sabhāgā*), it is permissible to confess because the underlying matter (*vatthu*) is of a different class.

"Well confessed" (*sudesitā*): the intention is that by this, the monk is indeed cleared of the offense. The connection is with the word "another" (*aññaṃ*) referring to a *dukkaṭa*. The particle *pana* indicates censure;
it is used here because [the confession] proceeds in a manner censuring what was well confessed. Although it was indeed well confessed, nevertheless (*kiñcāpi... pana tathāpi*).

The construction [of the sentence]. *Taṃ* refers to the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). *Nānāvatthukaṃ* means having different bases (*vatthu*) by way of the teaching and the acceptance [of the confession]. 170.
Only one of the same class (*sabhāga*) should be mentioned, not one of a different class (*visabhāga*). *Hi* means "truly" or "because. *Tassa* refers to the one of a different class.
*Ito* means from the assembly of the Saṅgha. 95. Discussion on the Set of Fifteen Non-offenses, etc.
172. Regarding the phrase "They did not know," it is stated—"thinking 'they have entered the boundary' or 'they are entering'"—for the purpose of showing the manner of their knowing.
"Entered" means they had entered. "Of them" refers to four or more monks. As for the expression "those who are incomplete but perceive themselves as being complete," he asks:
why are they incomplete, and why do they perceive themselves as being complete? He says: [the answer follows].
“Of them,” and so forth. Therein, “of them” refers to other bhikkhus. “Because of having entered the boundary” means because of having gone inside the boundary;

this connects with the phrase “having become a faction. “A perception of unity” (*samaggasaññā*) means a perception that they are united; those who possess such a perception are “those with the perception of unity.
(175) To show the similarity between the term *kukkuccapakata* and the term *icchāpakata*, it is said:
“*Yathā*” and so forth. “In the prior stage” means in the period preceding the observance-day ceremony (*uposathakamma*).

“Even having made a determination” means even having made the determination that “it is indeed allowable. By the word “*abhibhūtā*,” the sense of overcoming is shown here through the prefix *pa-* attached to the verbal root *kar* (to do), indicating it is “prepared” (*pakata*).

176. Just as a *dukkaṭa* was stated previously in the sections on the fifteen [offenses] regarding the perception of a group or non-group, why is it said here to be a *thullaccaya*? It is because of the strength of the unwholesome state (*akusalabalavatā*).
100. Discussion of the Summary on Entering the Boundary (Sīmokkantika-peyyāla). 177.
The connection is that everything should be understood according to the summary for residents and visitors (*āvāsika-āgantuka-peyyāla*). Together with the manner in which it should be understood...

Showing by way of a simile, he said “Just as,” and so forth. The connection is that [the procedure] is to be brought in from the *āgantuka-āvāsika-peyyāla* (the abbreviated formula for visiting monks regarding resident monks).

In the previous *peyyāla*, it refers to the *āvāsika-āgantuka-peyyāla* (the abbreviated formula for resident monks regarding visiting monks). However, in the *āgantuka-āgantuka-peyyāla* (the abbreviated formula for visiting monks regarding visiting monks), it is to be applied;
this is the connection. And here, *peyyāla* means the protection consisting in the attainment of both the similar method and the knowledge that recognizes it.

The etymological meaning of *peyyāla* should be understood as follows: it is called *peyyāla* because it "suffices" (*alati*) or "enables" (*samattheti*) [the text] by means of repetition (*peyyaṃ*, *peyyaṃ*, *peyye vā*, or *peyyāya vā*).

178. Why is it said that while it is the fourteenth day for the resident monks (*āvāsika*), it is the fifteenth for the visiting monks (*āgantuka*)? To this he says, beginning with "of those who... (*yesaṃ*). Therein, "of those" (*yesaṃ*) refers to the visiting monks.
"From another kingdom" (*tiroraṭṭhato*) means from a kingdom other than the kingdom of the residents. "From another district" (*tirojanapadato*)... [text continues]
“Even in a single kingdom from another district”: they performed the fourteenth-day observance by way of a difference in perception.
“It should be followed” means it should be carried out with consent. “It should not be objected to” means it should not be prohibited by saying, “It is not the fourteenth day.
“Not unwillingly”: here the verbal root *kam* has the sense of “to wish,” and the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
He said: "It should not be given against one's will.
101. Discussion on the Display of Gender, etc. 179.
By the phrase "the manner of the residents," he shows that the compound *āvāsikākāraṃ* is a genitive (*chaṭṭhī*) compound. "In all cases" means...
In all these cases, such as “the mark of a resident,” etc., the connection is: “by which”—that is, by well-arranged beds, chairs, and so forth—he “takes. “Of them” means of the residents.
“The establishment of conduct” means the stability of conduct. The construction is: “That form, consisting of well-arranged beds, chairs, and so forth, is called the ‘appearance’.
The connection is: “which”—that is, the well-arranged beds, chairs, and so forth—he “causes to go” (or conveys). In that regard:

* Tattha means "in this or that place. *Līne āvāsike* (when the resident monk is absent) is the grammatical connection. The construction is: "That well-arranged bed, chair, and so forth, is called a sign (*liṅga*).
By the word "invisible" (*adissamāne*), he shows the meaning of the term "absent" (*līne*).

By the word "makes known" (*jānāpeti*), he shows the cognitive sense of the term "indicates" (*gamayati*). *Yaṃ* refers to the well-arranged bed, chair, and so forth. *Te* refers to the residents (*āvāsikā*).
The construction is: "That well-arranged bed, chair, and so forth, is called a *nimitta* (sign). "By which" means by the well-arranged bed, chair, and so forth.
"Those" refers to the residents (*āvāsika*); the construction is: "that [set of items] consisting of the well-arranged bed, chair, and so forth, is called an *uddesa* (assignment).

By these words, they are scattered and made manifest; thus it is an *ākāra* (form). It causes one who is sluggish to proceed and awakens them; thus it is a *liṅga* (mark). They are fixed; thus it is a *nimitta*.

“Nimitta” means that by means of this, things are known after being delimited; “uddesa” means that by means of this, things are pointed out or referred to—this shows the etymological meaning of the words.
“All this” refers to everything beginning with “the mode of the resident” and so forth. “According to what is appropriate” means in accordance with the application found in the Pāḷi.
“Therein” refers to among the modes of the newcomers and so forth. “Unknown” (aññāta) means that it should not be known as “this is ours”; that very thing is “unknown” (aññātaka).
“Sitting mats and so forth. Not knowing “this is ours” occurs because [the items] do not belong to oneself and belong instead to others;
thus he said, “belonging to others. “Water without sprinkling” means water devoid of pouring.
“Of the plural” refers to the genitive plural in the word “dhotānaṃ. “The singular” refers to the singular in “dhotassa. In the latter reading...
It is called *dhota* because one shakes off impurity (*mala*) by means of it; that which is both *dhota* and water is *dhota-udaka*; that very sprinkling is *dhota-udaka-nisseka*.

(180) Regarding the phrase "the view of those who belong to the same community" (*samānasaṃvāsaka-diṭṭhi*), he says, "The view that 'these are those who belong to the same community,'" showing it as a compound with the elision of the particle *iti*.
"These" refers to the resident monks. By the word "conviction" (*laddhi*), [he indicates] that they do not ask.
It shows the action. "The state of being of a different affiliation" means their state of having different affiliations due to their differing tenets (*laddhi*).
By the word "to crush," he shows the meaning of the prefix *abhi-* in the phrase "they do not overcome. And by the word "to overcome," he shows that same meaning.
He says that what is called "crushing the state of being of a different affiliation" is the causing of them to relinquish their tenets.
“They do not cause that view to be relinquished. 103. The Discussion on the Chapter Concerning Where One Should Not Go and Where One Should Go.
181. Regarding the term *sabhikkhuka*: the literal meaning is “that residence in which monks are found (*saṃvijjanti*)”; thus it is called *sabhikkhuka*.
Pointing this out, he said: “In whatever residence,” and so forth. “Yaṃ” refers to the residence. “Tadaheva” means on that very same Uposatha day.
By this, he shows that if one is able to go on that very day, one must go. By the word “akatvā” (without having done), he shows that, however, having done it, one may go.
“Aññatra” is a particle; he says “vinā” because it is a synonym for the particle “vinā.”
The construction is: “It is permissible for a Saṅgha consisting of four including oneself, or five including oneself, to go.

Herein, it should be understood that the phrase “four including oneself” is stated with reference to the Uposatha ceremony, while the phrase “five including oneself” is stated with reference to the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
“In the monastery” means within the monastery boundary (vihārasīmā) or the great boundary (mahāsīmā); for this [refers] to the monastery boundaries.

It is stated without distinction. "The boundary" (*sīmā*) refers even to a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*). "One should not go" means that one should not go because of the gravity of the offense for the Saṅgha.
"Therein" means within the partial boundaries and so forth. "For him" means for the bhikkhu. "It is permissible to go" should be understood as follows:

it is permissible to go from the place where the *uposatha* is performed by a group (*gaṇa*), but it is certainly not permissible to go from the place where the *uposatha* is performed by the Saṅgha. [This concerns] those who have neglected the *uposatha*.
The construction is: "It is proper for one to go to another residence. "Even by one who dwells in the forest" means even by one who lives alone in the wilderness (*arañña*).
"There" means in another monastery. "Uposatha" refers to both the *saṅgha*-uposatha and the *gaṇa*-uposatha.

(182) "That" refers to the residence. "There" refers to that residence. The construction is: "One should know, 'I am able to go. "There" means in that residence. This is to be connected with "nor has it been performed. The construction is: "One should know, 'It will not have been performed.'"
105. Discussion on Pointing Out Persons Who Should Be Avoided.
183. “Merely coming within arm’s reach” means merely coming within arm’s reach of the Uposatha assembly and so forth.
The construction is: “This giving of a deferred purity (pārivāsiya-pārisuddhi) is not permitted. “Of that” refers to the giving of the deferred purity.
Regarding the term *anuposathe*, he says "on another day" to show that the vowel *a-* here has the sense of "other than.
In that context, "on another" means on a day other than the two [regular] Uposatha days. The construction is: "that which is performed as concord of the Saṅgha, such as that.
"Of the Kosambaka bhikkhus" means of the bhikkhus residing in Kosambī. The construction is: "that concord which is like concord. By the word "excepting" (*ṭhapetvā*),...
The word "except" (*aññatra*) indicates the meaning of the particle. "But those who... refers to the connection: "but the bhikkhus are in concord.
"On the very day of the Uposatha" means on the Uposatha day itself.
Thus ends the commentary on the Uposathakkhandhaka.
3. The Chapter on the Entrance into the Rains Retreat (Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka). 107. The Discussion on the Permission for the Entrance into the Rains Retreat. 184.
In the Chapter on the Entrance into the Rains Retreat, regarding the term "not permitted" (*ananuññāta*), which here means "not laid down," the verbal root *ñā* is used in the sense of permitting.
He shows this by means of the word “unprepared” for the purpose of establishing the sense of the root *ñā* (to know). “Tedhā” means “those here.
The word “here” (*idha*) is used in reference to the teaching, the world, a location, and as a mere filler; however, showing that it is used here as a filler, he says:
“The word ‘here’ is a mere particle. “Saṃhananaṃ” means a compacting together; the meaning is destruction. Thus, this is the meaning.
He shows this by the word "destruction" (*vināsa*). Since the word *sakuntaka* is a synonym for a bird, he says "birds" (*sakuṇā*).
And "birds" (*sakuṇa*) refers to those who move through the air (*vihaṅgama*); for they are called "birds" because they are able to go in the sky.

Regarding the phrase "they will perish" (*saṃkasāyissanti*), here [the root] is "to perish" (*kase*) in the sense of "wasting away" (*acchana*), as found in the lists of verbal roots (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, root number 16, beginning with *sak*).
Because it is stated that the root *kas* preceded by the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "dwelling," he says, "they will dwell.

This root ends in the letter *-e*. "Permanent residence" (*nibaddhavāsa*) means constant dwelling. "In that which is named the rains" (*vassānanāmaka*) means in that which is designated by the season called the rains.

Since the rains last for four months, it is said, "for three months. Regarding the term "entrance into the rains" (*vassūpanāyikā*), here the root *nī* has the sense of "going"; thus he says, "the goings toward the rains" (*vassūpagamanāni*).

*Apārājju*: "The day after the full moon" is *aparajju*. The suffix *-jjū* is applied in the sense of "day after" (*aha-atthe*). In terms of meaning, it refers to the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada-divaso*).

This word *aparajju* belongs to the first group of nouns (*paṭhamanta-nipāto*). *Assa* means "of the full moon of Āsāḷhī. This is an external compound (*bāhirattha-samāso*) involving terms that do not share the same grammatical core (*assamānādhikaraṇa-visayo*).
It is to be construed as "when [the full moon] has passed. *Aparasmiṃ divase* means "on the following day," namely, on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada-divase*).
*Āsā* means on the full moon day of the month of Sāvaṇa. *Tasmā* means because it has passed into the following day, and because it has passed into the [new] month; therefore.

By the phrase "on the following first-day (pāṭipada) of the month," the text shows the meaning that the earlier period (*purimikā*) should be entered upon the first day immediately following the Āsāḷhī that has passed into the next day. *Āsāḷhiyā* means on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī. In the latter method as well...
The meaning should be understood as follows: on the first day (pāṭipada) immediately following the full moon of Āsāḷha, the later rains residence (pacchimikā) is to be entered.
"Of Āsāḷha" means the full moon of Sāvaṇa, which is designated as "Āsāḷha" because it occurs in proximity to the full moon of Āsāḷha.
The connection is that the rains residence is to be entered on that very first day. In the phrase "once" (*sakiṃ vā*) and so forth, the word *vā* has the sense of an indefinite alternative.

“Having uttered” (*nicchāretvā*) means having pronounced; the sense is “having articulated. In some instances, a sound following a cluster of uncontacted consonants undergoes contact, as in the case of words such as *nikkhamati*.
Therefore, by changing the following letter *ca* to *cha*, it is stated as “*nicchāretvā*.
108. Discussion on the Prohibition of the Rainy Season Wanderings, etc.

185. "An offense is to be understood": an offense is to be understood when one crosses the precincts by departing without regard [for the rains-residence], or when one causes the dawn to rise elsewhere by departing with regard [for it]. "Offenses are to be understood according to the number of monasteries":

here, if on the day of entering for the rains one should cross a monastery with the intention of not entering the rains-residence there, offenses are to be understood according to the number of monasteries.
Expanding upon that very point, he said, "If indeed," and so forth. "On that day" means on the day of entering the rains residence (*vassa*).
Regarding the phrase "a hundred offenses": in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), it is stated that because the word *sata* emphasizes the number, it takes the singular form.
"Only one offense" means that there is only one offense precisely for the act of overstepping the boundary of one's own monastery. By some obstacle...
The connection is with the word *anupagatena*.
To show the etymological meaning of the word *vassa*—namely, that its meaning is "that which has rain"—he says "named after the rain.
By the phrase "the first month," he shows the actual form of the other member of the compound. "The first month" refers to the first among the four months of the rainy season.
"Month. "Wishing to draw forward" means wishing to pull [the time] further back. The meaning is: specifically the month of Āsāḷhī, not the month of Sāvaṇa.
He says "month" because the word *juṇha* is associated with the moonlight. He says "month" because it is the month associated with the moonlight.
For that month which shines and glows, being associated with the moonlight, is called *juṇha*. Therefore, "month" is used in its general sense.
Even when [the date] has been stated, the month associated with the full moon (puṇṇamī) alone should be taken. "Some kind of decline" means some kind of diminution of virtue and so forth.
"In another [time] as well" means in a time other than the entering of the rains retreat. "Lawful" (dhammika) means consistent with the Dhamma.
109. Discussion on the Permission for a Seven-Day Task.
187. The construction should be understood as: "In matters to be done within seven days, such is the decision.

Regarding the phrase "by way of what is to be done within seven days" (*sattāhakaraṇīyena*), he says "that which is to be done within seven days" (*sattāhabbhantare yaṃ kattabbaṃ*) in order to show that it is a locative compound (*sattamīsamāsa*) and that the suffix *-anīya* has the sense of the object (*kammattha*).
Therein, by the term "within seven days" (*sattāhabbhantare*), he shows the locative compound; by "to be done" (*kattabbaṃ*), [he shows the passive sense].

By this [phrase], it indicates the object of the action (*kammattha*). By the phrase "within seven days" (*sattāhabbhantare*), it shows that the compound *sattāha-abbhantara* means "the interior of seven days," indicating the elision of the final member of the compound.
Regarding the expression "to go when sent" (*pahite gantuṃ*), the words "by messengers such as bhikkhus" are stated in order to show the agent and the object of the verb "sent" (*pahita*).
Therein, by the phrase "by bhikkhus, etc.," it shows the agent (*kattā*), and by the word "messengers" (*dūte*), it shows the object (*kamma*). "Seven days" (*sattāhaṃ*)...
Here, showing both the elision of the latter member of the compound and the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, he says:

"only within seven days. "In that very place" means in that very location to which [the body] was sent. By the phrase "he must not be raised up," he demonstrates the function of the particle *eva* in the expression "only within seven days."
189. When it is said that "it possesses flavor" (*rasavatī*) because flavor exists therein, one should understand it as referring to a house where food is kept;
thus he says, "It is called a 'house of food' (*bhattageha*). "House of food" means a kitchen where food is cooked.

Regarding the phrase "this sutta is ancient" (*purāyam suttanto*), having analyzed the compound as *purā ayam*, he states that the word *purā* signifies "as far as," saying, "as far as this sutta [extends]. It does not fall apart (*na palujjati*).
Here, since the root *luj* has the sense of destruction, he said, "it does not perish. "To be prepared" (*parisaṅkhata*) means that which is to be prepared.

"In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in all instances where [the word] is sought. "By this very allowable expression" (*imināva kappiya-vacanena*) means by this very allowable statement consisting of three sentences.
"Of these" (*etesam*) refers to these three sentences. "By a synonym" (*vevacanena*) [refers to the phrase]: "to sacrifice a sacrifice, and to study a sutta..."

"By way of [the phrase] 'to learn and to see the ascetics. "In seven" means in the seven categories consisting of male lay followers (*upāsaka*), female lay followers (*upāsikā*), monks (*bhikkhu*), nuns (*bhikkhunī*), female trainees (*sikkhamānā*), male novices (*sāmaṇera*), and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*). 110.
The Discussion on the Permission Granted Even Without Being Requested by Five.
193. By the phrase “even though he has been sent,” [the author] shows that the word “even” (*pi*) in the statement “one should go even when not sent” has the sense of inclusion.
Having analyzed and shown the reason why one must go into the presence of five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, he says:
“A bhikkhu is ill,” and so forth. “By ten” means: “The Saṅgha desires to perform an act, or [an act] has already been performed...”
