He said, “From the beginning,” and so forth. That is indeed easy to understand. The construction is: “One should go to the presence of a female novice by means of five [modes].
“From another” (*parato*) means from another person, or in another [person]. The connection is: “It is stated in the Andhaka-ṭṭhakathā. The construction is:
“Whosoever there may be, whether they be relatives or strangers, for them also. “That” refers to the statement.
112. The Discussion on Permission for One Who Has Already Set Out (Pahiteva-anujānanakathā) 199.

Regarding the term *bhikkhugatika*: when it is said that "one for whom a bhikkhu is the only resort (*gati*) or support (*patiṭṭhā*)" is a *bhikkhugatika*, it refers to a man who is dependent upon bhikkhus;
thus he says, "a man who dwells together with bhikkhus. *Palujjati* means to perish or be destroyed. *Bhaṇḍaṃ*... [text fragment]

Regarding the term *chedāpitaṃ* (caused to be cut): here the word *bhaṇḍa* has the sense of "requisites" (*parikkhāra*) and not the sense of "capital wealth" (*mūladhana*). Therefore, he says, "the material component-requisite" (*dabbasambhārabhaṇḍa*). Regarding *chedāpitaṃ*:
he explains the root belonging to the *cur-ādi* class as *chindāpitaṃ*, using a root from the *rudh-ādi* class. Regarding *dajjāhaṃ*: this is a sandhi involving the elision of the vowel *e*;
thus he says, "I would give" (*dajje ahaṃ*). There is also a reading *dajjehaṃ*; for in that case, it is a sandhi involving the elision of the vowel *a*.
*Dajjeti* means "he should give" or "I give. *Saṅghakaraṇīyenā* means "by means of a matter to be done for the Saṅgha.
To show this meaning, he said, "whatever [is to be done]," and so forth. Therein, the construction is: "whatever is to be done.

*Cetiyachattavedikādīsū* refers to the umbrella and the railing of a shrine (*cetiya*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), plastering with lime and so on are included. *Tassā* refers to that matter to be done for the Saṅgha.
The connection is: "it should be gone for the purpose of accomplishing.

"Therein" refers to the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka (the Chapter on Entering the Rains). The word "by one who is uninvited" (*animantitena*) functions as the agent (*bhāvakattā*) for the word "should go" (*gantun*).
"Should go" (*gantuṃ*) means either to go or the act of going; it is the agent for the word "is not permitted" (*na vaṭṭati*). "Right from the very beginning" refers to [before] hearing the Dhamma.
The construction is: "An agreement was made that they must assemble first. "Bhaṇḍaka" means belongings such as robes and so forth.
"It is not permitted to go" should be understood to mean that it is not permitted for one to go by oneself. Therefore it is said, "But if," and so on.
"Therein" refers to that monastery. By the word "is permitted," it is implied that there is neither a breach of the rains-residence nor an offense.

[The text] shows this. Regarding the word "even for the sake of" (*atthāyapi*), by means of the particle *pi*, it refers to the purpose [of thinking], "I will wash the belongings. "That" (*naṃ*) refers to the resident pupil (*antevāsika*).
"It is allowable" (*vaṭṭati*) means that it is allowable as long as seven days have not elapsed since the teacher’s command;
neither is there a breach of the rains-retreat nor an offense. The intention is that once seven days have elapsed, there is indeed a breach of the rains-retreat, but no offense.
113. Discussion on the Absence of Offense Regarding Interruption by Rain During the Interval (201).
"Not far" means nearby. "Therein" means in the village. "By way of a seven-day period" means once every seven days.
"The dawn must be made to rise" means the dawn must be made to rise within the monastery. "Right there" means in the village itself. "They" refers to the monks. Again...
This was said with reference to human beings. "Of those very [people]" means of those monks who have interrupted the rains residence. "That" refers to the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) and so forth.
"By the number of years" means by the calculation of the years.

"Rains-residence robe" (*vassāvāsika*) is the robe that should be given to those who have completed the rains residence. "Therein" means in that monastery. "To whom it has been delivered" refers to those to whom it has been assigned.

The connection is as follows: "dwells" means he dwells in a village monastery where [goods] have been left behind. "Property left behind" is the connection. "Here" means in the place where the bhikkhu resides. The construction is:
whatever property subject to distribution, such as robes and so forth, exists there—that is what is referred to. "Right there" means precisely in that village monastery where he dwells.
"From this" refers to from the field, the site, and so forth. The connection is: "in the hands of the kappiyakārakas (those who prepare what is allowable)."
“Also in the case of its arising there”: this refers to the conditions for the arising of that monastery, such as the field or land that was given.

In order to demonstrate the logical justification for the statement, “Having gone to that very place and having made an announcement, it should be divided,” he said, “For that which belongs to the Saṅgha,” and so forth.
“Inside the monastery” means within the boundary (sīmā). “In both cases” refers to the two locations designated as inside the boundary and outside the boundary.
The connection is: "the goods are in a state of being liable to division. 114.
Discussion on the non-offense regarding the interruption of the rains during a schism in the Saṅgha. 202.
Regarding the word *bhinnō* ("split"), in order to show that the suffix *-ta* does not denote the past tense here, he says: "when the Saṅgha has been split (*bhinne saṅghe*)."
“There is nothing to be done. As for the phrase “but the Saṅgha,” this is the agent (kattā) in the clause “it will be split,” and the object (kamma) in the clause “it is suspected.
By the word “will be split” (*bhijjissati*), he shows that the suffix *-ta* in the word “split” (*bhinno*) functions in the sense of the future.
Regarding the statement “the Saṅgha has been split by the bhikkhunīs,” one should understand: “In what way has the Saṅgha been split by the bhikkhunīs?”
He said: "It should not be regarded as 'the Saṅgha has been split by the bhikkhunīs'. "This" refers to the state of not being split by the bhikkhunīs.
"But these" refers to the bhikkhunīs. "That" refers to the Saṅgha. "This" refers to the statement: "The Saṅgha has been split by several bhikkhunīs. 115.
Discussion on entering the rains residence among those starting with Vaja.
203. By the phrase “the dwelling place of cowherds,” it is shown that cowherds live in the cow-pen like cattle.
Since the word *upakaṭṭha* is a synonym for “near,” he says “of the nearby [cow-pen]. “Therein” means in the hut. “Here” means in this hut.
Because it is not a monastery (*vihāra*), it is spoken of in a general sense as “here. “Three times” is stated according to the highest limit.
It has been stated. For since it was said below, "once, or twice, or thrice," it should be understood that even once is permissible.
"That too" refers to the cart standing in the vicinity of the hall. By the word "abode" (*ālaya*), he shows that the verbal expression "I enter the rains retreat here" must not be made.
And "abode" (*ālaya*) refers to the thought in the caravan: "I shall dwell here for the rains."
"Joining up. "On the caravan itself while it has set out on the road" is a locative used in a sense of disregard (anādare).
"Right there" means on the caravan itself. The connection is: "the caravan passes by. "There" means at the intended place. "It scatters" means it goes separately.
If it scatters in a place where there is no village, one should return to the previous village; not to another village.
"One must go. "From there" means from the village.
"One must enter" means one must enter after having said three times, "I enter the rains residence here. "Right there" means in the ocean itself.
"The shore" means the bank; for it is called a *kūla* because it keeps back (*kulati*) the water. "And this" refers to the monk who has entered the rains residence on the boat.
"Anutīram eva" means either by gradual succession, or by following along the bank. "Aññattha" means in another place than the village first reached.
"Tattheva" means in that very same village first reached.
"Iti" and so forth is the conclusion. Regarding the phrase "and he is permitted to invite," here the word *ca* (and) serves to connect the sentences. In the preceding [cases]...
And as for the word *ca* (and) here, it has the sense of exclusion; the word *pana* (but/however) indicates a distinction. "It is a non-offense" means that there is merely a non-offense.
116. Discussion on places where one should not enter the rains residence (*vassa*).
204. "Just as in the hollow of a tree" means in the cavity of a tree. For it is called a *susīra* because one (*su*) moves (*irati*) well (*saṃ*) into the cavity;
thus it is called a *susīra*. "A roof of planks" means covered with wooden boards. "The entrance door" means the door for entering and exiting.

The term *pavisaṇa* (entrance) is formed by applying the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*virūpekasesa*) to both "entering" (*pavisana*) and "exiting" (*nikkhamana*). "At the top of a stump" means at the top of a tree-stump (*khāṇu*).
"Upari" means above. Regarding "viṭabhī": that which goes down, piercing one another, is a "viṭa"; by changing the letter *pa* to *bha* and adding the feminine suffix *ī*, it is called "viṭabhī.
"Tattha" means on the platform (*aṭṭaka*). "Yassa" refers to the monk; it connects with "natthi" (there is not).
"Pañcannaṃ chadanānaṃ" refers to the five types of roofing materials, namely: grass, leaves, bricks, stone, and plaster.
"Of coverings. This is stated by way of generality, as it includes coverings such as mats and so forth.
"Door-fastening" means that which is to be fastened by means of a door. "A hut for the dead" (chavakuṭikā) is called a hut made in a cemetery, the place where corpses lie.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "beds with spikes and so forth," one includes spiked stools. "Therein" means in the hut for the dead.
"Another hut" means a hut other than a decayed hut. "Enclosure" means a wall. "Door" means an entrance for coming in and going out.
"What is called a 'parasol-hut'? means this is a hut made with a parasol. "Having made a hut with a large bowl" is the connection [of the sentence].
117. Discussion on Improper Agreements (*Adhammikakatikākathā*)

205. “Another also”: this refers to another [rule] under the agreement (katikā) that “one should not grant the going-forth during the rains-retreat. “There is an agreement” is the grammatical connection. “Of that”: of the unrighteous agreement. “Stated”: as stated in the commentary on the fourth *pārājika*. 118.
Discussion on the Offense of Wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for Making a Promise. 207.
Regarding the statement, “In making a promise, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*”), does the offense of wrongdoing apply only when one has promised the rains-retreat (*vassāvāsa*)?

He says, "not merely," and so forth, because it happens. "Of this very" means of the *vassāvāsa* (the rains residence) itself. In the phrase "even by such [means] as this," the word "even" (*pi*) should be connected with the word "in the promise" (*paṭissave*).
Thus, the meaning is "even in the promise. "Of this and that" refers to the action. The construction is:
"And that, moreover, is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of deception. In the phrase "even the first," the word "even" (*pi*) connects to the term "even afterwards" (*pacchāpi*).
He combines them. For the meaning is that the first [offense] is a *pācittiya* and the subsequent one is a *dukkaṭa*.
The construction is: "In such cases as 'that very day it is not to be done,' etc., this is how the decision (*vinicchaya*) is to be understood.

Regarding the phrase "the earlier date is not recognized": here, "earlier" (*purima*) means belonging to the past; that itself is the "earlier date" (*purimikā*), namely the lunar day of the first of the month (*pāṭipada*). [This applies] when there are two residences within different boundaries (*nānāsīmā*).

Regarding one who enters for the rains residence: when, on the second day, he has merely stepped out from the precincts of his first dwelling with the intention, "I shall dwell [here]," this is said—"the earlier period is not recognized"—with reference to the cessation of his claim to the first lodging.
"Without having caused the dawn to rise" means without having allowed the dawn to rise in the monastery where he entered for the rains residence. "On that very day" means on that same [day].
The connection is with the words "even for one who has departed" on the very day of entering the rains retreat (*vassūpagamana*).

Pointing out that the word "even" (*pi*) has the sense of censure, he says, "What need is there to mention," and so forth. "Attachment" (*ālaya*) means the clinging of the mind. "By way of forgetfulness" means by one who has lost mindfulness.
"Does not enter the rains retreat" means that he does not enter the rains retreat after making the verbal declaration: "I enter the rains retreat for these three months in this monastery."

"Seven days" means within seven days; this is connected with the phrase "if [the guest] has not arrived. "From the ninth day" means from the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the former Kattika month, or from the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the latter Kattika month.
"Or let him not come, there is no offense" means that because he has completed the rains residence, whether or not he comes, there is no offense. This is the meaning.
Thus ends the exposition of the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka.
4. The Pavāraṇākkhandhaka. 120.
Discourse on Living in Discomfort.
209. Regarding the phrase *allāpo* in the *Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka*:

here, showing that the prefix *ā-* has the sense of "commencement" and that the verbal root *lap-* has the sense of "speaking," he says "the first speech. *Ālāpo* means speaking or talking at the beginning, or from the beginning;
or it is that by which one speaks (*lapati*). [The form] is short before a conjunct consonant. Furthermore, it is repeated speaking, or that by which one speaks.
"Conversation. Regarding "by leaping with the hands," he says "by raising the hands," because here the verbal root *lagh*, preceded by the prefix *vi*, has the sense of lifting up.

"Living together like cattle": here "cattle" (*pasu*) refers to all four-footed animals. For they are called "cattle" (*pasu*) because they "afflict" (*pasanti*) one another—that is, they harm each other—or because they are "harmed" (*pasīyanti*) by humans and others. "Living together like cattle" means a dwelling together that is similar to that of cattle.
“Living together like animals” means living with animals; that is, the living together with animals. Expounding upon this meaning, he said, “For even animals,” and so forth.

“In that way” means just as they do not do it; such is the sense. “These too” refers to the bhikkhus. “Therefore” means because they did it. “Of them” refers to the bhikkhus. “In all cases” means in all instances of living with sheep and living with enemies.
*Mūgabbataṃ* means "the vow of a mute," like the practice of one who is mute; the meaning is "a vow consisting of empty words.
*Titthiyasamādānaṃ* means that which is to be undertaken by the sectarians (*titthiya*). *Vatasamādānaṃ* means a vow to be undertaken.

Regarding the phrase *aññamaññānulomatā*, in showing here the abstract sense of the word *tā*, he says "the state of being conformable" (*anulomabhāvo*). By this [term], as in the case of "deities" (*devatā*) and so forth—
It excludes the sense of "condition" (as in *tāpaccaya*) and the sense of a "collection" (as in *janatā* and similar terms).
Demonstrating the logical connection for the statement "to speak to one another," he says, "Let them speak to me," and so forth. The construction is: "They should speak to the monk who is speaking.
By the phrase "the state of emerging from offenses," he indicates that the compound *āpattivuṭṭhānatā* is a genitive (*pañcamī*) compound.

This shows the meaning of the suffix -tā as denoting existence. By the phrase beginning with “*vinayan*” (discipline), it shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as follows: *purekkhāra* means placing something before oneself;
the state of that is *purekkhāratā*; thus, *vinayapurekkhāratā* means the state of having discipline as one’s priority.
Here, they say that in grammatical treatises (specifically in the *Moggallānabyākaraṇa*, sutta 5.134), the word *pura-* takes the ending *-e*.
Showing the logical justification for this, he said: “‘Vadantu’ and so forth” (Moggallānabyākaraṇa, Sutta 5.134). 210.
“Inclusive of all” means that because it is stated in general terms as “the Saṅgha should invite,” it includes all [forms of invitation] such as the threefold recitation (*tevācika*) and others.
“Motion” (*ñatti*): it is called a motion because by means of this speech one makes the Saṅgha know [the proposal]. While expanding upon its inclusive nature:

He said, “When this was said,” and so forth. *Tevācikaṃ* means that which has three utterances (*tevāca*); thus it is *tevācikaṃ*. Or, it is *tevācikaṃ* because it is to be performed by means of three utterances.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. *Samānavassikaṃ* means those who have the same year (*samānavassa*) are *samānavassā*;
that which is to be performed by them is *samānavassikaṃ*. *Aññaṃ* refers to that which consists of two utterances (*dvevācika*) or one utterance (*ekavācika*).
211. Regarding "they remain" (*acchanti*): here, showing that the root *ās* has the sense of sitting down, he says, "they are simply seated.
By the phrase "they do not rise," he shows the specific result [of that action]. Regarding "in the meantime" (*tadantarā*):

although one should have said "tadantara," it is stated with the addition of the letter *m* due to the euphonic refinement (*vācāsiliṭṭha*) of speech; thus he says, "tadantarā. Of that time of his own invitation...
“In the interval. To show the restrictive sense of the phrase “as long as they perform the *pavāraṇā*,” it is said: “for that much time.

Because of the usage of the particle *yāva*, it should be understood that in the expression “in the interval thereof” (*tadamantarā*), the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*) is used in the sense of an inclusive limit (*abhividhi-avadhi*).
121. Discussion on the Divisions of *Pavāraṇā*

212. "On the fourteenth" means on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pubbakattika, which had been postponed because [the Saṅgha] was harassed by those who cause quarrels. The construction is: "Today is the *pavāraṇā* on the fifteenth; the preliminary duties (*pubbakicca*) must be performed.

In the phrase "in the *pavāraṇā* formal acts," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (specifying a particular type). It should be connected with such passages as "an illegal, incomplete *pavāraṇā* formal act," and so forth. Regarding "illegal and incomplete":
here, "illegal" means that although they have formed a Saṅgha, they do not perform the *pavāraṇā* of the Saṅgha, but instead perform the *pavāraṇā* of a group (*gaṇa*).
The performance [of the invitation ceremony] by a group (*gaṇa*), even though they have become a group, without performing the *gaṇa-pavāraṇā* but instead performing the *saṅgha-pavāraṇā*;
and what is called "a faction" (*vagga*) is the failure of all those dwelling within a single boundary (*sīmā*) to assemble together.
"In discordance but with unanimity" (*adhammena samaggaṃ*): here, "in discordance" (*adhamma*) is exactly as described above. "Unanimity" (*samagga*) means the assembly of all together.

"In accordance with the Dhamma they proceed in discord": here "Dhamma" means the performance of the Saṅgha’s Pavāraṇā by the Saṅgha having become a Saṅgha, and the performance of the Gaṇa’s Pavāraṇā by the Gaṇa having become a Gaṇa.

"Of those very same" means of the four requisites themselves. By the phrase "virtue and observances" (*sīlañca vatañca*), he demonstrates that the compound term *sīlabbata* is a dual construction (*dvandavākya*).

Rejecting the meaning of the word *bhusa* as "the Kaliṅga kingdom," he says "powerful" (*balavanto*). By the phrase "of one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavassa*), he shows the referent of the pronoun *assa* (his) in that context.
By the word "having taken" (*gahetvā*), he shows the sense of grasping for the verbal root *dā* preceded by the prefixes *pari-* and *ā-* in the phrase "they completely consume" (*pariyādiyantī*).
The particle *hi* means "truly. The syntactical connection is: "the defilements (*kilesā*) cause [this]."
“*Tesam*” refers to the defilements (*kilesā*). Regarding the phrase “having attained the imperturbable” (*āneñjappatta*):

here, *iñjana* means shaking or movement; that which is not shaking is *aneñja*; that very state is *āneñja*. To show the meaning as “having attained that,” he said, “having attained the immovable” (*acalanappatta*).
As for the word “and” (*ca*) in “decay and” (*vayañca*), it has the sense of including what is not explicitly mentioned; thus he said, “both decay and arising.”

Regarding the phrase "of the destruction of clinging" (*upādānakkhayassa*), he says, "the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative," showing that it means "one who is intent upon the destruction of clinging.

By the words "arising and passing away" (*uppādañ ca vayañ ca*), he shows that in the expression "arising of the sense bases" (*āyatanuppāda*), the word "arising" (*uppāda*) should be understood as including "passing away" (*vaya*) as well, because they are inseparable.
He says, "by way of cause and method," explaining that the particle *samma* has the sense of "knowing" (*ñāya*).

“Of one with a peaceful mind”: since the word *santa* here also occurs in the sense of exhaustion and so forth, he says “of one whose mind is extinguished (*nibbuta*)” to indicate that it functions here in the sense of being quenched.
“By way of attraction and repulsion”: attraction (*anunaya*) is so called because it leads the mind repeatedly toward an object;
it is lust (*rāga*). Repulsion (*paṭigha*) is so called because it strikes against an object; it is hatred (*dosa*). Attraction and repulsion together are “attraction-and-repulsion.”
"By them": the connection should be understood as "there is attraction toward the desirable and repulsion toward the undesirable.
148. Discussion on the Prohibition of Double-layered Sandals, etc. 245.
Regarding the phrase "explaining something else," here the word *añña* (other) is twofold, according to whether it is a pronoun (*sabbanāma*) or a noun (*suddhanāma*). Of these two, here—
It is simply the name "pure" (*suddha*); however, that term applies to fools, children, and to *arahatta*. Here, however, showing it as referring to *arahatta*, he said:
"They declare *arahatta*. "By which" means by its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "One is known as an *arahant*"—this is the meaning of the word *arahā*. "That" refers to the intrinsic nature.
"From the commentary on the sutta itself" means from the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* itself. "Not brought forward" means...
"Not led upward. Regarding the phrase "certain foolish persons" (*ekacce moghapurisā*): the word *ekacca* is a synonym for "others," and the word *moga* is a synonym for "empty";
thus he says, "but other empty persons. By the expression "as if laughing," he shows that the word *maññe* (I think) here has the sense of "as if.
"Only non-existent" means only what is not found. Regarding the term "one-sided" (*ekapalāsika*).
The word *palāsa* denotes a leaf. A *paṭala* is like a leaf; therefore, it is called "a single *paṭala*.
Regarding the phrase "to be carried by eighty carts," one should understand the meaning to be "that which is to be carried by eighty carts," having connected the word *asīti* with the word *sakaṭa*.
By the statement "two cart-loads are one *vāha*," he shows that there are forty *vāhas*.
Regarding the phrase "and a troop of seven elephants," he says "six female elephants," etc., in order to show the actual nature of a troop (*anīka*).
A collection of seven elephants is a "seven-elephant troop" (*sattahatthika*). Because there are seven troops, there are forty-nine elephants.
Among those, there are seven male elephants and forty-two female elephants. In the word *dviguṇā* ("twofold"), the term *guṇa* has the sense of a "layer" (*paṭala*).

He said: "Two-layered. Regarding the term *guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*, since "double-layered" (*dviguṇa*) and "triple-layered" (*tiguṇa*) have been mentioned separately here, he says, "It is spoken of starting from four layers," in order to show by way of elimination that it possesses the state of being "layer upon layer" (*guṇaṅguṇa*).

"Layer upon layer sandals" (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhanā*) means sandals with layer after layer; the meaning is sandals with many layers. Having joined [the syllables] together with the letter *u*, the letter *ga* should be recited.
And it should be written [as such]. However, nowadays the letter *u* is not seen in manuscripts. 149.
Discussion on the Rejection of the Interpretation "All Blue," etc. 246.

"All blue" (*sabbāva nīlikā*) means that all sandals (*upāhanāyo*) are blue; because they are blue in all parts, they are called "all-blue" (*sabbā-nīlikā*). Alternatively, it is also [interpreted as] "all-blue."

It should be done. In that context, "and among those" means among those such as the blue-flowered plant (*nīlikā*) and others. "Having the color of the *ummāra* flower" means its color is like the color of the *ummāra* flower;
the same applies to the remaining terms. Regarding "having the color of the *addāriṭṭhaka*": here, *adda* means moist;
*ariṭṭha* refers either to the *pheṇila* tree or a crow. Therefore, *addāriṭṭha* means the moist *ariṭṭha*, which is the *pheṇila* tree, or a crow.
That very [stone] is *addāriṭṭhaka*; because its color is like the color of *addāriṭṭhaka*, it is called "the color of *addāriṭṭhaka*.

Regarding the phrase "in these": it refers to those that are entirely blue and so forth. Regarding "having wiped": it means having rubbed clean. Regarding "even by a small amount": the word "even" (*pi*) is used in the sense of emphasizing the possibility. The meaning is:
"What kind of talk could there be when the entirely blue and other colors have been broken down?"

By the phrase “those for whom the blue parts are large,” it shows that this is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound with an external referent (chaṭṭhībāhiratthasamāsa), meaning “those whose blue parts are large. And *vaddhikā* is a binding (*naddhi*).
For it is called *vaddhikā* because it extends (*vaddheti*) from the surface of the sandal; and it is also called *vaddhikā* because one binds the surface of the sandal by means of it.
“In all cases” refers to all [types] such as those with yellow bindings (*pītakavaddhikā*) and so forth. “By this too” refers to...
“Blue,” “with a binding,” and so forth, refer to sandals as well. “On the sole” means on the sole of the sandal.
By the phrase “having bound with a strap,” he shows the meaning of the word *khalakabaddhā* (strap-bound) to be that they are to be bound with such a strap.
“Yonaka sandals” are the sandals of people of the Yavana race. “Having wrapped around” means having wrapped all around. “Above... [up to] the shank.”
By this, he shows the distinction from [the previous simile of] the bundle tied up. “With cotton-wool (*tūlapicu*)” means with the wool known as *tūla*.
By the phrase “resembling a partridge’s wing,” he shows the etymological meaning of *tittirapattikā* as being like the wing of a partridge (*tittira*).
A *tittira* is a particular kind of bird. “In the place of the ear-ornament (*kaṇṇika*)” means at the place where two growths meet together. “Meṇḍa…” [and so forth].
By the phrase "made," it shows the meaning of the word *meṇḍavisāṇavaddhikā* (ram’s-horn-earrings): these have ear-rings similar to the horns of a ram (*meṇḍa*).
"In that same way" means just as they were made by attaching ear-rings shaped like the horns of a ram or a goat.
By the phrase "scorpions... made," [it is shown]: a scorpion’s sting is a *vicchikāḷa*; these have ear-rings like that.
This shows the meaning of the word *vicchika-aḷikā*. The term *aḷa* in expressions such as *aḷacchinna* (“cut at the toe”) refers to the big toe, but here it refers to the tail;
therefore, it is said, “in the shape of a tail. *Talesu* means “on the soles of the sandals.
By the phrase “morapiñchehi... sibbikā,” it is meant that they are sewn all around or encircled with peacock feathers.

This shows the meaning of the expression "stitched with peacock feathers. Regarding the phrase "variegated sandals," he says "variegated" (*vicitrā*) because the word *citra* here has the sense of being "manifold" or "diverse.
"In these" refers to those such as the leather-bound sandals and so forth. "To be used" means to be employed.
The root *vaḷañj* means "to use" or "to enjoy" (according to the *Dhātupāṭha*, specifically in the *Saddanīti Dhātumālā* under the jakāra class). This is the third [root] beginning with *t*.
“Among those,” however, means among the *khallaka* (leather straps) and so forth. The construction is: “when they exist.
To show the meaning of the term *sīhacammaparikkhatā*—meaning “encircled by a lion’s skin”—he said, “at the edges,” and so on. *Pakkhibiḷāla* is a *tuliya* (a type of bird).
For it is called a *pakkhibiḷāla* because it possesses wings and because its face resembles that of a cat (*biḷāla*).
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by the skin of a bat" (*luvaka-camma-parikkhatā*), he shows that the word *luvaka* is a synonym for a bird or a cat.

There is also a reading: "surrounded by the skin of an owl" (*ulūka-camma-parikkhatā*). "Among these as well" refers to those such as the one surrounded by a lion's skin; the connection is with the phrase "any kind of sandals. 247.

Regarding "taken off" (*omukka*), showing here that the prefix *ava-* has the sense of separation, he says: "removed after having been fastened. The meaning is "old sandals worn over other sandals" (*guṇaṅguṇūpāhana*).
151. Discussion on the Prohibition of Sandals within the Monastery (Ajjhārāme upāhanapaṭikkhepakathā) 248.
Regarding the phrase “by whatever craft,” etc.: that by which they live further (*abhi*) is *abhijīvana*.

What is that? It shows the meaning as “craft” (*sippa*). “Of that” means of the craft. “Here” means in this teaching (*sāsana*). The word “which” (*yaṃ*) is a grammatical inversion (*vacanavipallāsa*).
He said: "Ye tumhe" means "you who. "Hi" signifies truth. The phrase "yaṃ-nipāto" is to be construed as: the particle *yaṃ* occurs in the sense of the word *yadi*.
"Ācariyā eva" (only teachers)—by the word *eva*, he excludes the status of being merely a teacher. "Hi" signifies truth. "So" refers to one who is *avassika* (a student who must live with a teacher).
"Taṃ" refers to the six-year period. "Nissāya vassati" means that during the four-year period of the *avassika*, [he lives under] the six-year [rule].
Because he has been ordained for ten years, he dwells depending on him. To show the measure of a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), he said, "of the preceptor," and so forth.
"Greater" means older than oneself. They have the preceptor as their measure or limit; thus, they are "those who have the preceptor as their measure" (*upajjhāyamattā*). 249.

To show the etymological meaning of "foot-nail disease" (*pādakhīlābādha*)—an affliction occurring due to flesh resembling a wooden pin (*khīla*) protruding from the foot—he said, "from the foot," and so forth. The connection is "protruding from the foot."
251. Regarding the passage beginning with *tiṇapādukā*, he says “by whatever kind of grass” and so forth, showing the etymological meaning and other aspects of the term *tiṇapādukā* (grass sandals).
This is indeed easy to understand. By the phrase “well-established on the ground,” he shows the meaning of *asaṅkamanīyā* (not to be stepped over) as that which should not be transgressed.

252. *Aṅgajāteneva* means by one’s own *aṅgajāta* (genital organ). *Aṅgajātaṃ* refers to the genital organ of cows. Regarding *ogāhetvā*, he says "having grasped firmly," because here the prefix *o-* has the sense of firmness (*daḷhattha*).
153. Discussion on the Prohibition of Vehicles, etc. 253.

Regarding *itthiyuttena* (drawn by a female), he says "drawn by a cow" (*dhenuyuttena*), because according to conventional usage (*rūḷhivasena*), even a cow is called a "female" (*itthī*). *Purisantarena* (by another man).

In this context, a vehicle for which a man stands between [it and the driver] is a "purisantara-yāna" (a vehicle with a man in between). Since "one who stands between" (purisantaro) means, in terms of actual meaning, a charioteer, he said "by a man as charioteer" (purisasārathinā), connecting it with the word "by the vehicle" (yānena).

Regarding the phrase "at the play on the Gaṅgā and Mahī," since both the Gaṅgā and the Mahī are "Gaṅgā-Mahī," he said "at the play on the Gaṅgā and Mahī" (gaṅgāmahīkīḷikāya) to demonstrate that this is the meaning.
For there, men and women play in water-sports on vehicles.
Regarding the phrase "a handcart yoked by men," he says "there" and so forth, showing: "I allow you, monks, both the vehicle yoked by men and the handcart.
Therein, "yoked by men" (*purisayutta*) means a vehicle that is to be yoked by a man. "Handcart" (*hatthavaṭṭaka*) means...
"Hand-rolled" (*hatthavaṭṭaka*) refers to a vehicle that is to be turned by hand. "By the jolting of the vehicle" (*yānugghātena*) means by the vehicle’s moving over uneven ground;
for the verbal root *han* has the sense of "going. To show this meaning, he says, "of one mounting the vehicle," and so forth.

By the phrase "on account of that" (*tappaccayā*), he indicates that in the expression "by the jolting of the vehicle," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*). "A chair-litter" (*pīṭhaka-sivika*) [is so called] because of the chair...
*Saḷhakataṃ sīvikaṃ*: a litter made of *saḷhaka* grass. *Paṭapoṭalikā*: a bundle made of cloth. 154.
Discussion on the Prohibition of High and Large Beds.
254. A high bed is an *uccāsayana*; a large bed is a *mahāsayana*. This applies to couches (*āsandi*) and so forth.
The construction is: "the definition (vinicchaya) should be understood. "A seat exceeding the [proper] measure" means a long seat.

For it is called *āsandī* because one sits upon it (*sadati*) by resorting to it (*āgamma*), or because it gives (*dadāti*) [support] extensively (*āyataṃ*) or well (*suṭṭhuṃ*). "Fierce forms" (*vāḷarūpāni*) refers to fierce forms such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
It is called *pallaṅka* because it is marked (*aṅkīyati*) or characterized (*lakkhīyati*) by having fierce forms delineated on its legs. *Gonaka* means "cow-hide."
*Gonaka*: It is so called because one rises up from it with long hairs (*dīghaloma*). *Kojava*: It is so called because it moves or goes upon the ground, that is, upon the floor (*kuyaṃ*).
"Of that" refers to the *gonaka*. The connection is that its hairs are said to exceed four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in length.
*Vānacitrauṇṇāmayattharaṇa*: That which has variegated forms produced by weaving—that is, by sewing—is *vānacitra*; that which is produced from wool is *uṇṇāmaya*.
A woolen spread (*uṇṇāmayattharaṇa*) is a spread made of wool; it is a "variegated woolen spread" because it is both variegated by weaving and a woolen spread.
A white spread (*setattharaṇa*) is so called because it is covered (*sevīyati*) with white threads (*setatthika*); thus, it is a white spread.
According to this meaning, it should be understood as *paṭikā*, since it "spreads out" (*paṭati*) or attains whiteness. This word *paṭikā* also applies to the crescent moon and to stones.
It occurs. *Ghanapupphaka*: because there is dense (*ghana*) or hard (*kathina*) flower (*puppha*) here, it is called *ghanapupphaka*.

By this, he shows that it is a *paṭalika* because there is a layer (*paṭala*) here known as a dense flower. *So* refers to the spreader (*attharaṇa*). *Āmalakapaṭa*: a cloth made after displaying the *āmalaka* flower. *Tūlikā*:
a stuffed mattress (*tūlikā*) made by filling it with cotton (*tūla*). *Vikatikā*: [images] by means of the forms of lions, tigers, and so forth.
It is called a *vikatikā* because it is made with various patterns. In the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
“*Uddalomī* is a woolen rug with hair on both sides; *ekantalomī* is a woolen rug with hair on one side. Here, however, it is said:
“*Uddalomī* is a woolen rug with hair growing out from one side; *ekantalomī* is [a woolen rug] with hair growing out from both sides.”
It is called "a woolen covering" (*uṇṇāmaya-attharaṇa*). Therefore, two commentaries differ from one another.

Here, I shall explain the meaning of the words according to the method of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*. It is called *uddalomi* because it has arisen with two rows [of wool], or because there is hair (*loma*) here counted as two fringes (*dasā*).
By applying the insertion of the nasal *ṃ*, there is also the reading *undalomi*.
This is the meaning. Because there is hair numbering ten [rows] on one side, it is called *ekantalomi* (single-sided-haired). Regarding the phrase *koseyyakaṭṭissamayaṃ*:
here, *koseyya* means silk thread (*kosiyasutta*). *Kaṭṭissa* refers to the grass known by the name *kaṭṭissa*.

By this, having formed a compound through the elision of the dissimilar (*virūpekasesa*)—namely, *koseyyañca kaṭṭissañca kaṭṭissāni*—the spread (*attharaṇa*) made from *kaṭṭissa* grass is called *kaṭṭissa*.
It shows the meaning. "Pure silk" (*suddhakoseyya*) means pure silk not sewn with jewels; by this, he shows that even pure wool (*suddhakaṭṭissa*) is permissible.
He says "of sixteen," etc., showing the meaning of *kuttaka* as "that where sixteen dancing girls stand and perform a dance.

"With antelope skins" (*ajinacammehi*) means with the skins of the *ajina* deer; it connects with the word "made. "Succession" (*paveṇī*) refers to [garments] such as the double-layered cloth (*dupaṭṭa*) and triple-layered cloth (*tipaṭṭa*).
Because it is made by way of tradition (*paraṃparavasena*), it is called a "lineage" (*paveṇī*). For antelope skins are more delicate;
therefore, having made double layers, triple layers, and so forth, they are made according to the lineage. Hence it is said, "an antelope-skin lineage.

By the phrase "the skin of a *kadalimiga* deer," its skin should be understood as the "kadalimiga" [deer] through the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*), or by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
He says "vāti" to show this. Since the word *pavara* means "supreme," he says "the supreme bedspread. He says "that kadalī-deer-skin supreme bedspread" [to specify].
Regarding the term *sauttaracchada*, he says "together with an upper coverlet," showing that the letter *sa-* here functions as the word *saha*.
By the word "above" (*upari*), he excludes meanings such as "best" for the word *uttara*. By the word "together" (*saddhiṃ*), he [indicates the function] of the word *saha*.
It excludes that which has the same meaning. By the phrase “white...
is not permitted,” it shows that even if there is a permissible underlaying cloth beneath it, a red canopy is not permitted. Why? Because a red canopy is not permissible.
Regarding the term “red pillows on both sides,” this was stated in order to show the nature of both; namely, “the head-pillow and the foot-pillow. The head [approaches]...
It is called a *upadhāna* because one rests (*tiṭṭhati*) upon it; or, it is called a *upadhāna* because it supports (*dhāreti*) great (*upa*) comfort;
it is a pillow (*bibbohana*). The construction is: "If it is of the proper measure, that pillow is allowable.
155. Discussion on the Prohibition of All Leather, etc.

255. *Dīpipotaka* means "like a young leopard," thus *dīpipotaka* refers to a fawn. *Bhittidaṇḍakādīsu* means "in connection with wall-poles and the like. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), pillars and other such items connected to walls are included.
256. The construction is: he who is unable to enter a village without sandals is called "sick.
157. The Discourse on the Story of Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa.
257. "By this" means by the reading "in Kuraraghara. "Of him" refers to Mahākaccāna. It is called "Papāta" because there is a great precipice (*mahātaṭa*) here;
therefore, it has the name "Papāta. "By this" means by the reading "on the mountain Papāta.
"Of him" refers to Mahākaccāna. He is called "Kuṭikaṇṇa" (Pointed-Ear) because he possesses an ornament worth a *koṭi* on his ear.

Showing the meaning of the words, he said: “But [the value] of a koṭi,” and so forth. That by which one adorns oneself is *piḷandhana*; it means an ornament. The fourth consonant is produced from the teeth (*dantaja*).
By the phrase “producing confidence,” he shows the etymological meaning: it is called *pāsādika* because it generates confidence (*pasādaṃ janeti*).

“Worthy of inspiring confidence” (*pasādanīya*) means that which should be inspired with confidence; the sense is that it is fit to be made confident. “The statement of the meaning” (*atthavacana*)...

“Meaning” (attha) is so called because it is expressed by this; thus it is “a word for meaning” (atthavacana). In the original text (pāḷi), the reading “inspiring confidence” (pasādanīya) does not currently exist in the manuscripts.

Previously, there was only the reading “beautiful to behold” (dassanīya) before the word “charming” (pāsādika). Herein, regarding the phrase “the highest taming and tranquility” (uttamadamathasamatha):
the word *damatha* has the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and the sense of restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*), while the word *samatha* has the sense of concentration (*samādhi*).
Showing the purpose for the tranquility of the mind, he said, “And the supreme taming,” and so forth. By the word *ca* (and), he indicates a copulative compound (*dvandava*).

Regarding the phrase “of the various wrigglings and writhings” (*visūkāyika-vipphanditānaṃ*): it refers to the various movements consisting of views and thoughts that arise as the opposites of *visūkā* (straightness).
By the term “the faculty of energy” (*vīriyindriyaṃ*), it is shown that in the expression “the faculty of the restrained” (*yatindriyaṃ*), the word *yata* denotes energy.
He shows this. Regarding the word *nāga*, he says "devoid of transgression" (*āguvirahita*) while demonstrating the etymological meaning:
"one for whom there is no *āgu*—that is, evil—is a *nāga*. To the question "From what day [has this been so]?", he says, "From the day of my going forth.

Demonstrating the meaning of *kaṇhuttara* as "where black clay (*kaṇhamattikā*) is on top," he says, "surpassed by black clay. By the word "above" (*upari*), [he indicates the sense of] the word *uttara*.
It shows the meaning. By the phrase “with the hooves of oxen,” it shows that because they resemble the hooves of oxen, they are called *gokaṇṭaka* (ox-thorns).
The construction is: “They [the ox-thorns] were guarded against. Thus the ground becomes rough; this is the connection. “By these” refers to the four grasses beginning with *eragu*.
“That” refers to the *eragu* grass. “By that” refers to the *moragu* grass. “The appearance of a person” (*jantussa vaṇṇo*).
Regarding the connection: as for the phrase "he prepared a lodging," what is meant by "preparing a lodging"?
He says: "He prepared either a mattress or a grass mat. And having prepared it, he informed Soṇa. What did he inform him? He says:
"Friend," and so forth. The connection is: "The Teacher wishes to dwell [there]."
258. Regarding the phrase “*tassa soṇassā*,” this indicates that the word *taṃ* here is used in the accusative case in the sense of similarity (*sāmyatthe*). “*Taṃ*” means “your.
“*Aṭṭhakavaggikānī*” refers to those chapters for which there is a group (*vagga*) consisting of eight units or a collection of eight.
These are the sixteen discourses beginning with the *Kāmasutta*. “*Yo*” refers to the person; it is to be connected with the word “endowed” (*samannāgato*).
The word *api* (also/even) in *ariyopi* indicates that it is not only one who is endowed with purity who does not delight in evil, but rather it shows that even a noble one (*ariya*) does not.
Regarding the passage from "May it occur to you" (*paṭibhātu taṃ*) up to "it is said to be pure" (*suci ti vuttaṃ*), this exists only in certain manuscript copies of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
As for the phrase "this indeed he is" (*ayaṃ khvassa*), the word *assa* here is a verb; thus he says, "he would be" (*bhaveyyā*). "He would show forth" (*paridasseyya*)—[refers to] the five.
Having selected the excellent [qualities], he showed them. The construction is: "May this be the time for that word which my preceptor makes known to me.
Regarding the phrase "with the holder of the Vinaya as the fifth," he says "with the teacher of the proclamation as the fifth," rejecting the meaning of "with the preceptor as the fifth."
A "shoe-receptacle" (*upāhanakosa*) is a place for putting shoes away; it is a small box. Regarding sheepskin and goat-skin, there is nothing that is called "unallowable" (*akappiya*).
However, regarding deer-skin, some things are permitted and some are not. Showing this by way of analysis, he said, "Regarding deer-skin," and so forth.
"Of these very [animals]" refers specifically to the skins of the six animals beginning with the *eṇi* deer. "But of others" refers to [skins] other than those of the six deer.
But as for the remainder: the connection is that their hides are not permitted.
In the verse, the construction is: "the monkey, the black lion, the sarabha, the kadalimiga, and whatever other wild beasts (vāḷamiga) there may be—these.
"Of them" refers to the monkeys and so forth. "Therein" refers to the verse, or among the monkeys and others. By the phrase "lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas," [wild beasts are indicated].

It shows that they are of the same form. He says "not only" and so forth to indicate that there are only these many wild beasts. "Of these very ones" means of the lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas alone.
The connection is: "the hide is not permitted. "Of which" refers to the six, such as the eni-deer and others. "Those" refers to the six, such as the eni-deer and others. The construction is:
"Indeed, it is true that the hide of all these wild beasts is not permitted. Or, having brought [the matter] forward... [text ends].
“Not given” means it has not been given after being brought forth or placed in the hand or at the foot.

By the phrase “does not come into reckoning,” he shows the meaning as “that which comes into reckoning” (*gaṇanūpaga*). “And what is determined” (*adhiṭṭhitañca*) means, however, that which has been determined.
“When” (*yadā*) refers to the time. “From that” (*tato*) refers to from that time.
Thus ends the explanation of the *Cammakkhandhaka*.
6. The *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*. 160.
Discussion on the Five Medicines, etc.
260. In the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*, he says “arisen in the autumn season” (*sāradika*) in order to show the meaning of what has arisen during the autumn season.
By the phrase “by a bile affliction” (*pittābādhena*), he shows the actual nature of the illness. Elaborating on the cause of the bile affliction, he says “for in that [case],” etc.
“By that” means by that reason. “Of them” refers to the monks. “Having entered into the interior of the stomach” (*koṭṭhabbhantaragata*).
It has gone inside the stomach; the intention is that it enters within the interior of the intestines.
"For the purpose of food" means the function of food, or the task to be performed by food.
261. "They do not cover" means those medicines do not cover over the foods. Why? Because the foods have not been digested.
Thus, in order to show this meaning, he said, "They do not wear out. They cannot cover [the body], nor can they pacify diseases of wind.
Here, it should be understood that by the phrase "they do not wear out," he shows the cause for their inability to cover;
and by the phrase "nor can they... pacify," he shows the result of that same [cause]. By the word "siniddhāni" (moist), he means "they moisten."
This shows the meaning of "snehikāni" (greasy). Regarding the phrase "bhattacchannakena," it refers to that which covers over the meal;
he says "by that which makes the meal unpalatable" (*bhattārocakena*), meaning that which does not produce a desire for the meal.
262. The construction should be understood as: "the explanation regarding *acchavasa* and so forth is to be known. In the text, [it says] "received and cooked..."
Having used the word "associated" (*saṃsaṭṭha*) as an adverbial modifier of the action, it was stated—
"in cases such as 'received at the proper time,' etc."— to show that it must be connected with the phrase "to consume.
Regarding the expression "to consume by means of using oil," he said "for a period of seven days" to indicate for how long a duration one may consume it by means of using oil.
161. Discussion on Root and Other Medicines. 263.
Regarding the phrase "the determination of root medicines and so forth": the word "also" (*pi*) refers back to the determinations concerning *accha*, *vasanti*, and so on.
"Herein" (*idha*) means in the Chapter on Medicines (*Bhesajjakkhandhaka*). "Whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) refers to the determination. "Pisanasīlā": that wherein one grinds is *pisanā*.
That very stone is a *pisana-silā* (a grinding stone). By this, it shows the meaning: "it sits having become immovable," thus it is called *nisada*.

*Pisana-potaka* means: that by which one grinds is *pisana*; that very thing being a young one (*potaka*) is a *pisana-potaka*. By this, it shows the meaning: "the young one of the *nisada*," thus it is called *nisada-potaka*. *Hiṅgu-jātīyo* means species of asafoetida.
Regarding the term *sāmudda*, he says “on the seashore” and so forth to show the etymological meaning: that which exists in the ocean (*samudde*) is *sāmudda*.
By the word “shore,” he shows that the locative case here functions in the sense of proximity to the ocean.
“Natural salt” means salt by its own nature, not salt cooked with various ingredients; this is the meaning. “On the mountain... [text continues]
By the word "arises" (*uṭṭhahati*), he shows the meaning as *sindhava* because it arises on the mountain named Sindhū.
Showing the etymological meaning of *ubbira*—that which rises up, emerging from the ground—he says, "a sprout arises from the ground.
According to this method of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), only the third consonant (*o*) in *oṭṭhaja* is appropriate; however, in the manuscripts, only the fourth consonant (*u*) appears.
It is seen. There is also a reading, “ubbhidaṃ. “Bila” means a hollow or cavity.
Therefore, explaining the meaning as “a hollow cooked together with raw materials,” he said, “cooked together with raw materials.
In the *Abhidhāna*, however, there is the reading “bilālaṃ” in verse 461. “Taṃ” refers to that hollow.
264. The construction is: "Does the body odor of anyone [arise] like the body odor of horses? Regarding the phrase "tassāpi" (of her too), it refers to the nun as well.
By the word "api" (also/even), he includes those afflicted by itching and other such monks. Since the word *chakaṇa* is used for the dung of horses, it is stated as "cow-dung.
"Ordinary powder" (*pākatika-cuṇṇa*) means even unboiled dye-powder. "This too" (*etampi*) refers to the ordinary powder as well.
The connection is: "He does not eat that raw meat. The connection is: "He does not drink that raw blood. "Non-human" (amanussa) refers to a spirit (bhūta) resembling a human.
"That" refers to the raw meat and blood. 265. He says, "'Ointment' (añjana) is a general term," meaning "the word 'ointment' is a term that includes all [types of ointments].
"A term that includes all" means a term that encompasses all kinds of ointments. "This" refers to this very word "ointment. It is called "ointment" because it anoints the eye.
It is called *añjana* because one anoints (*makkheti*) with it; or, it is called *añjana* because it anoints (*añjati*) the eye and makes it clear.

The third letter is born from the palate (*tālujo*). "In a bowl" (*kapalle*) means occurring in a bowl. For indeed, lamp-soot that occurs when a bowl is turned upside down over the flame of a lamp is called "lamp-soot" (*kapalla*).
To show this meaning, he said: "lamp-soot taken from the flame. [The phrase] "with ointments and powders" (*añjanūpapisanehi*).

Here, in order to show the meaning of the term *añjanūpapisana*—which refers to that which is to be ground together with the ointments—he said: "by those ground together with the ointment. By the word "together" (*ekato*), he shows the very meaning of the word "with" (*saddhim*).
The particle *hi* means "indeed. The construction is: "Any powder whatsoever for grinding with the ointment is not unsuitable. Then...
The construction is: "it is not allowable" (*na vaṭṭati*) means it does not exist [as a fault], [but rather] "it is indeed allowable" (*vaṭṭati yeva*).
In this method, the verbal form "is not allowable" (*na vaṭṭati*) functions as the agent because it depends on another action. For even among verbs, the status of both agent and object is obtained.
The terms beginning with "sandalwood" (*candana*) are easy to understand.
Rejecting the fault of over-extension regarding the term "made of bone," he said, "except for human bone.
Regarding the term "suitable for a probe" (*salākaṭṭhāniya*), showing the etymological meaning as "that wherein a probe stands," he said, "wherein," and so forth.
Therein, "wherein" means in that hollow shaft or similar object. "Probe" (*salāka*) refers to an ointment-applicator.
“*Odahantīti ṭhapenti*”: they place [it]. “*Aṃsabaddhako*”: it is called *aṃsabaddhaka* because one binds it to the shoulder (*aṃsa*) by means of this.

“*Yamakanatthukaraṇī*”: it is called *natthukaraṇī* because the nose-treatment (*natthu*) is performed with this; a twin (*yamaka*) nose-treatment instrument is a *yamakanatthukaraṇī*. The connection is: “all that is an oil-preparation (*telapāka*).

By the phrase “*Ati viya khittamajjānī*,” he shows the meaning of the words: “*atikhittāni*” means they are thrown in or put in too much; those very things which are marrow (*majja*) are “*atikhittamajjānī*.”
*Paṇṇasedaṃ* means sweat with leaves. *Aṅgārānaṃ* means with coals. *Tattha* means in those [materials], such as dust, sand, and so forth.
*Vātaharaṇapaṇṇāni* means leaves such as *uddāla* and others that remove wind. *Tattha* means in those leaves. *Nānāpaṇṇabhaṅgakuthitaṃ* means "various leaf-braids";
it is called "various leaf-braids" (*nānāpaṇṇabhaṅga*) in the sense that various leaves themselves are to be braided together; by that...
“Boiled” means boiled with various leaf-decoctions. “With hot water” means by means of hot water. “Therein” means in the water-pool. “In each joint” means in each knot.
“By which” means by the foot-ointment (*pajja*); the construction is: “to prepare that foot-ointment.
By the phrase “medicine suitable for the feet,” he shows the etymological meaning as “that which is beneficial (*hita*) to the feet. “With sesame paste” (*tilakakkena*).
Here, because the word *kakkasa* denotes flour, it is said "with flour" (*piṭṭhehi*). Placing [it] with a mouthful is "mouthful-sized" (*kabaḷikaṃ*).
Because a ball of seven [grains] is similar to a mouthful of rice, it is called "a ball of seven. "Like a pin" means like a wedge.
"With salt" means with salt made of salt-crystals. It obstructs expansion, thus it is "expansion-obstructing" (*vikāsikaṃ*), which is a rag for obstructing oil.
“Wound-treatment” (*vaṇakamma*) means either treatment for a wound or work on a wound.
Regarding the question, “At the very moment one is bitten by a snake, should one take [the flesh] oneself and consume it? he said, “Not only,” and so forth.
“This” refers to the great carrion; “should be consumed” is the connection. “But in other cases” refers to those other than when one has been bitten by a snake.
"But. The construction is: "If it is feces that has reached the ground, it may be accepted.
269. Regarding "disease arising from a love potion": a *vasīkaraṇa* is so called because one brings [another] under control (*vasaṃ karoti*) by means of it;
it is a medicinal drug. That which is drunk is a *pāna*; that very thing is a *pānaka*. A love potion that is a drink is a *vasīkaraṇapānaka*.

The disease arising from that is "the disease arising from a potion for subjugation. By this [phrase], "the affliction given by the mistress of the house" (*gharadinnakābādha*), the meaning of the term is shown as follows:
the affliction arising from the potion for subjugation given by the mistress of the house (*gharaṇī*) is called "the affliction given by the mistress of the house.
"To be stirred with cold" (*sītāya āloḷetabbaṃ*) means *sītāloḷaṃ*, which is water. The word *sītā* refers to the furrow of a plow.
He speaks primarily of the furrow-path (*phālapaddhati*); figuratively, he speaks of the clay adhering to the plough when it is in the furrow.
Therefore it is said: “it should be stirred by the ploughshare. In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, showing that same meaning, he says: “by the plough,” and so forth.
“One who eats what is fully cooked” means one who specifically eats what has been thoroughly prepared. Regarding “mūtaharītaka,” here “mūta” is used in its general sense.
Showing that even when this is said, only cow urine should be taken, he says: "Harītakī infused with cow urine.
By this, he demonstrates the meaning of the term *muttaharītakī* as "harītakī infused (*paribhāvita*) with that urine. The phrase *taṇḍulakasaṭo* means the thick sediment of rice-washing water;
it is washed and smooth, and that itself is the "bean-boiled drink"—this is the construction. "With meat broth" (*maṃsaraseṇa*).
By this, it is shown that "meat broth" is called *paṭicchādanīya* (to be covered/concealed) because it must be covered with meat.
163. Discussion on the Permission for Sugar and Other Items.
272. *Hi* means "truly. *Pakkattā* means "because of the state of being cooked," [referring to] the beans (*mugga*). *Te* refers to those beans.

274. "In an improper hut" (*akappiyakuṭiyam*) means inside an improper hut. "For him" (*assa*) refers to the monk; the connection is that it is not permitted for him. "Even that" (*tampi*) refers even to a warm offering of food (*uṇhayāgu*).
By the word "even" (*pi*), it is shown that it goes without saying that he should not cook meat. "Rice with the grains separated" (*uttaṇḍulabhatta*):

it is "separated from the grains" (*uttaṇḍula*) because it has been parted from the cooked rice; for the vowel *u* expresses the sense of separation. The meaning is "rice from which the grains have not [yet] been separated [from the husk]. (Alternatively, it means rice that is not yet fully cooked.)

"Food consisting of husked rice" means food from which the husks have been removed. The construction is: "It is permissible to apply fire once to milk, buttermilk, and so forth, when they have been boiled.
A collection of beings such as cats and mice is called a "lump of creatures" (*ukkapiṇḍaka*) by way of conventional usage;
thus he said, "cats, mice, lizards, and mongooses. Because his pride has been subdued through the state of being one who eats leftovers (*vighāsāda*), he tames body and speech.
He said "vighāsāda" because [the word] *damaka* means "one who eats scraps.
(276) Then, showing the scope of the term *tasa*, he said "yatthā" and so forth. "Yattha" means in which place. "Nīhaṭaṃ" means having been taken out, it was carried away.
(278) Regarding "vanaṭṭhaṃ pokkharaṭṭhaṃ": here, that which stands in the forest is "vanaṭṭha"; that which stands in a lotus pond is "pokkharaṭṭha."

In order to show the etymological meaning of the word *pokkharaṭṭha*, he said, “In the forest,” and so forth. By the phrase “in a lotus thicket,” he shows that the word *pokkhara* denotes a lotus (*paduma*).
The construction is as follows: that fruit which does not produce a sprout from its seed is called “seedless.
167. Discussion on the Prohibition of Surgical Operations.
279. Showing that it is called *durupaya* because it is afflicted by suffering (*dukkhena rupati*), he said, "it grows through suffering" (*dukkhena ruhati*).

Regarding the terms *satthakamma* (surgical treatment) or *vatthikamma* (enema treatment), he said, "as in the case of a concealed [wound]," etc., demonstrating the literal meaning: surgical treatment is the procedure to be performed with a knife (*satthena*), while enema treatment is the procedure to be performed by means of a bladder (*vatthi*). "With a needle..."

By the phrase beginning with “or,” he shows that the word “surgery” (*satthakamma*) here is merely illustrative. The phrase “or by a knife” (*satthena vā*) should be connected with the phrases “cutting or tearing.
The phrases “or by a needle, or by a thorn, or by a small dagger” should be connected with the phrase “or piercing.
[The phrase] “or by a stone splinter... [is to be understood in the same way].

The phrases "or with the nail" are to be construed with the phrase "or with scratching. "This" refers to the act of cutting with a knife and so forth. "And here" refers to the acts involving a knife or a probe.
"But there," however, refers to the narrow passage (the anus). "By that" means by means of alkaline substances and the like.
Regarding the anal passage, it is the tube smeared with medicinal ointment by which they perform the alkaline treatment, or the bamboo tube...
The construction is as follows: "They introduce oil," meaning that either a tube smeared with medicinal ointment or a bamboo tube is indeed permissible.
280. "On that day" means on that very day. "Some gift" is the construction. "By this [woman]" means by Suppiyā; the construction is: "Will there be something else whatsoever that is not to be given?
Regarding the phrase "Yatra nāma," here the suffix *tra* is used in the sense of cause (*kāraṇatthe*).

He says, "Because of the name," [to explain] how it comes to be so. By the word "investigating" (*vīmaṃsī*), he shows that here the verbal root *ikkh*, preceded by the prefixes *paṭi* and *ava*, has the sense of investigating (*vīmaṃsana*).
"The flesh of such-and-such" (*asukamaṃsaṃ*) means either the flesh of such-and-such [a thing] or the flesh of such-and-such a being.
169. The Discussion on the Prohibition of Elephant Flesh and Other Meats.
281. "Forest-cocks" (*araññakokā*) means: it cries out (*kukati*) in order to seize (*ādā*) creatures such as rabbits and cats;

thus it is a "cock" (*koka*). Being born in the forest, it is a "forest-cock" (*araññakoka*). "Like village dogs" (*gāmasunakhasadisa*) means similar to the village dog. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the forest-cocks.
"But the dog" (*yo pana sunakho*) is connected with the word "arisen" (*uppanno*). "By a village bitch" (*gāmasunakhiyā*): the genitive case is used here in the sense of comparison (*sāmyatthe*).
*“Kokena”* is an instrumental expression used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahādiyoga*). Those words are to be construed with the word *“by means of a connection”* (*saṃyogena*).

*“Tassa”* refers to the dog. *“Ettha”* refers to human flesh and so forth. *“Sajātikatāya”* means because of the state of being of the same class (*samānajātikabhāvato*). *“Anupaddavatthāya”* means for the sake of a place free from danger; it is to be connected with the phrase *“are prohibited”* (*paṭikkhittāni*).
Regarding the offense: in the case of human flesh, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*).
In the remaining cases, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "But prepared specifically for [him]" means meat prepared specifically for a bhikkhu.
170. Discussion on Rice Gruel, Honey, and Balls of Food, etc., 282.
"Alone" (*ekako*): here, the suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of being without a companion; thus he says, "I have no second. "He" refers to the brahmin.
"Having made [it]" means having made a travel-provision (*paribbaya*); the construction is "he had it prepared.

"By the verse of thanksgiving" means by the verse that expresses the thanksgiving. Regarding the words "of those who aspire" (*patthayataṃ*) and "who desire" (*icchataṃ*), because they function as the recipient (*sampadāna*) in the sense of "sufficient for the purpose," it is said:

"The connection is with this [phrase] 'it is sufficient indeed to give'. "That alone is to be taken" means that, in the sense of the agent (*kattubhāva*) of the abstract noun "giving" (*dātuṃ*), that very [agent] is to be understood.
The meaning is that this reading alone should be accepted. 283.
The construction is as follows: "That gruel which generates an invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is called 'gruel for eating' (*bhojja-yāgu*). *Yā* refers to the time.

By the phrase "starting from" (*ādiṃ katvā*), it is indicated that in the expression *yadaggena*, the word *agga* has the sense of "beginning," and functions as an instrumental case used as an adverbial modifier of the action.
He shows this. By the phrase "merit that produces rebirth in heaven" (*sagganibbattakapuñña*), he indicates a metaphorical application of the term "heaven" (*phalūpacāra*) to the merit itself.
"It" refers to the sugar. 284. "Of such a nature" (*tathārūpena*): by its own inherent character. The meaning is: by a nature corresponding to the sugar. 173.
The Discourse on the Foundation of the Village of Pāṭaligāma.
285. Just as everything is spread out, so too is it "all that has been spread out"—this is the construction.

286. Regarding the phrase "Sunidha and Vassakāra," the particle *ca* (and) indicates a copulative compound (*dvanda*). "For the purpose of cutting off the entrance" means for the purpose of closing the gateway for the toll (*suṅka*).
By the term "house-sites" (*gharavatthūni*), the word *vatthu* is used in the sense of a cause or a material object.
Having rejected [the previous interpretation], he explains it for the purpose of breaking the ground. The construction is: "Those deities, it is said, incline [the world].

"According to what is appropriate" means according to whatever is suitable to their respective wealth and power. "In the world" means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*). "Sound" refers to the noise of fame.
"By that very [cause]" means by that very cause of the sound’s emergence. By the phrase "a place of resort," the word *āyatana* here [in the expression] "the noble *āyatana*" is [explained].
This shows that the meaning is "a place of assembly. The connection is: "as much as is called a place of buying and selling. By the phrase, "For merchants...
it is called a place of buying and selling," he shows the etymological meaning (*vacan-attha*) of *vaṇippata*: it is so called because merchants (*vaṇija*) fall together and assemble there.
It should be understood that when one ought to say *vaṇijapata*, the letter *ja* is elided. In the Pāḷi, [the word] is "of them" (*tesam*).
In order to show that a portion of the text must be supplied, it is said: "of those who trade in the noble abodes.
The genitive case in *tesaṃ* is used in the sense of similarity (*sāmyatthe*), or in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇatthe*), or in the sense of the ablative (*vibhatta-apādānatthe*).
*Idaṃ* refers to the city. Regarding the term *puṭabhedanaṃ*, he demonstrates its etymological meaning by stating: "it is called *puṭabhedanaṃ* because they break open their packages (*puṭaṃ*) here."
He said, "The place for breaking up a bundle. Explaining the statement, "The word *vā* has the sense of 'or'," he said, "In that case," and so forth.
Therein, "there" (*tattha*) means in Pāṭaliputta, or in the three types of breaking: by water, by a boat, and by enmity.

By the phrase "mutual breaking" (*aññamaññabhedā*), he shows that in the term *mittabhedā* (breaking of friendship), the word *mithu* is a synonym for "mutually" (*aññamañña*). [This applies] to the words *uḷumpa* and *kulla*.
Even though the meaning is the same, he says “a raft,” etc., in order to show the distinction in the instruments used. Water is called *ulu*;
that which protects from it is a raft (*uḷumpa*). Water is called *kaṃ*; that which moves upon it is a boat (*kulla*).
Regarding the word “ocean” (*aṇṇava*), one might ask what this ocean is the name of; thus he says “ocean,” etc. “Ocean.”
The construction is: “This is a designation for a body of water. *Aṇṇo* means water; because that [water] exists in this [place], it is called *aṇṇavo*.
It is stated, “Here, ‘rivers’ are intended,” because the word *sara* occurs both in the section beginning with the vowel *a* and in the section on *kaṇḍa*.
“Here” means in this verse. “This” refers to the category of things (*atthajāta*).
“Yet there are noble ones”: the connection is that those noble ones are “crossing over.
Regarding the phrase “leaving behind the quagmires,” the word *visajja* here ends in the suffix *-tvā*, and the word *pallala* denotes a low-lying place;
thus he says, “leaving behind... low-lying places. The construction is: “But this person binds a raft. The intended meaning is: “The wise people have crossed over.”
287. Regarding "Ananubodhā" (through non-awakening), the word is in the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) in the sense of cause; thus he says, "by means of not awakening.
Regarding "sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ" (wandered and transmigrated), this is stated with reference to the object (*kammattha*) of the suffix *-ta*; thus he says, "by me and by you.
By this, he shows that the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kattuttha*). With the words "Or else," etc., he shows the abstract state (*bhāvattha*) of the suffix *-ta*.
Regarding the term *saṃsitaṃ*, he says "it is *saṃsaritaṃ*" because here the letter *r* is elided from the verbal root *sar*.

By the phrase "the rope of craving" (*taṇhārajjū*), he shows that the rope of craving is called the "guide to existence" (*bhavanetti*) according to the etymological sense of the word *bhavanetti*—namely, that it leads from one state of existence to another.
(289) Regarding the colored garments and ornaments, they are described as "blue" by way of their common characteristic; thus he says, "This [term] 'blue' is inclusive of all."
“Tattha” means “in the passage beginning with ‘blue’. “Tesam” refers to the Licchavis. The construction is: “Their natural color was not blue.

“Etam” refers to the statement beginning with “blue. Regarding “paṭivattesi,” he says “he struck” because here the verbal root *vat* (to speak), through the influence of the prefix or by way of an intensification of meaning, carries the sense of striking.
By the phrase “sajanapadam,” the word “āhāra” in the expression “sāhāram” [is explained].

He shows that it means "the country. For since the country must be brought [as tribute] because of its status as a surrounding appendage to the city, and since the king’s men bring tax from it, it is called "food" (āhāra). The construction is: "You should give Vesālī together with its country.
Regarding the phrase "they snapped their fingers," he says "they moved their fingers," because the verbal root *phuṭ* has the meaning of "moving."
“By a woman” (*itthikāya*): she is indeed a woman; she is called a "woman" (*itthikā*) in the sense of being smaller than a man.
By her. 178. The Story of the General Siha (Sīhasenāpati-vatthu). 290.
Regarding the phrase “the Dhamma and the Dhamma-conformity” (*dhammassa ca anudhamman*): here the word *dhamma* has the sense of a cause; thus he says, “the conformity with the cause.”

The word “by others” (*parehi*) is the agent (*kattā*) for the word “said” (*vutta*). The phrase “for the reason stated” (*vuttakāraṇena*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the word “with reason” (*sakāraṇo*).
The construction is: “Even some slight statement of yours. The word “by the wise” (*viññūhi*) is the agent (*kattā*) for the word “to be censured” (*garahitabba*).
The phrase “the reason for censure” (*garahitabbakāraṇaṃ*) is the object (*kamma*) for the phrase “does not occur” (*na āgacchati*). [They are] those who do not wish to misrepresent.
Here, the prefix *abhi* has the sense of overcoming, and the root *khā* preceded by *ā* has the sense of explaining; thus he says, "not wishing to explain after having overcome [them].
Regarding the term *anuviccakāraṃ*, he says "having investigated" (*anuvicitvā*), because here the word *anuvicca* consists of the root *vic* with the suffix *tvā*.
By the word “having reflected” (*cintetvā*), he shows the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) for the verbal root *vic*.
By the word “to be made” (*kātabba*), he shows the etymological meaning of the word *kāra* as that which is to be done (*katabba*). “A banner” (*paṭāka*) means a victory banner (*dhajapaṭāka*).

By the word “they should wander about” (*āhiṇḍeyyuṃ*), he shows the sense of going (*gati*) for the verbal root *yā* preceded by *pari* and *ā*. In the canonical text (*pāḷi*), there is also the reading “they should carry around” (*parihareyyuṃ*).
“Āhiṇḍeyyuṃ” means they wander about. “Muddhaja” is the third syllable.
Regarding “opānabhūtaṃ,” he says, “standing like a prepared well,” in order to show the meaning as “one who has become like a well (opāna).
By the word “udapāno,” he shows that the word *opāna* has the sense of a well (*udapāna*). For a well (*udapāna*) is so called because all people descend there and drink.

"Opāna" is what is called [a water trough]. "Imesaṃ" refers to the Nigaṇṭhas. "Hi" means truly, or because. The construction is: "Since a gift must indeed be given to those who have arrived, therefore do not interrupt it.

294. The construction is as follows: "Dependent action" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is a designation for "causal action" (*nimittakamma*). "Whoever" (*yo*) refers to any person whatsoever.

Regarding the phrase "outside the monastery enclosure" (*bahārāmakoṭṭhaka*): here, the locative case is used in the sense of proximity;

refers to the bricks and so forth that are to be resolved upon with the thought, “Let us build a kitchen-shed.”
The connection is: "It is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā. "In that way" means just as it was stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.

"In those two" refers to the two types of cow-pen enclosures (*gonisādika*). "Where" refers to the hut (*kuṭi*); the connection is that "the monastery (*ārāma*) is not enclosed.

“Gonisādā” means a cowshed (*gosālā*), because cows enter it and sit there at their pleasure. “Like a cowshed” means a hut (*kuṭi*) resembling a cowshed.
The connection is with the words “people say. “This” refers to the hut. Regarding the word “even” (*pi*) in the phrase “even when spoken,” it refers back to the sentence:

It was stated again; asking "What was stated?", he said: "For a bhikkhu... [etc.]... it occurs.
"Also" (api) means other than those. "That" (taṃ) refers to the statement. "Indeed" (hi) means truly, or because. Or else, it means "only belonging to the Saṅgha" or "only belonging to the bhikkhu."
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Therefore, it is well-spoken"—this is the connection. A *gahapatisantaka-kuṭi* is a hut belonging to householders.

The phrase "having announced the formal act" (*kammavācaṃ sāvetvā*) is merely an illustration, because it is permissible even by means of a simple request (*apalokana*) without reciting the formal act.
A *sammuti-kuṭi* is a hut that is to be authorized either by means of a formal act or by a simple request. The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the section.

Whatever material thing has been stored is all connected by the term "stored. The connection is: "stored" means placed in a house sufficient for two persons to lie down together on an improper ground.

saying "it is not allowable," he states the positive concomitant (anvaya) of the negative [rule] by saying, "But that which is time-limited for seven days," and so forth.
"Therein" refers back to the preceding statement; for the meaning is "in that statement. The connection is: "the novice gives."

"Whatever [food] such as rice and so forth" is the construction for "raw meat. "What is called 'stored near the mouth'" means that the means (upāya) for an offense, being stored near the mouth, is what is called "storage" (sannidhi).
"Therein" refers to the *Mahāpaccarī* or to those things stored within the vicinity of the mouth.
"The bhikkhu cooks and consumes" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Mixed with raw meat" means contact with raw meat.
"Jahitavatthukā" means those for which the material basis has been abandoned; this is how it connects with "ussāvanantikā katā" (completed by formal proclamation).
