By the phrase "by whichever bricks and so forth," and by the word "etcetera," pillars, stones, and clay are included.
He includes [them]. "In others than those" means in things other than the bricks and so forth established by them.
"When enclosed by a wall, etc. means when a boundary defined by the precincts (upacāra-sīmā) of a monastery has been enclosed by a wall or the like.
By the word "etc. in "wall, etc.," he includes a fence. "It is permissible to obtain a kitchen hut" refers to one that is [constructed] in the manner of a cow’s footprint (gonisādikā).
The meaning is that, by virtue of the absence [of a formal authorization] in the other three types of *kappiyakuṭīs*, it is permissible to obtain any kind of *kappiyakuṭi*.
Therein, "in each respective place" means in this or that location. "But the others," however, refers to those other than the *ussāvanantika* and *gonisādika* [authorizations].
"Two" refers to both types of authorization for a householder (*gahapatisammuti*); the connection is that they remain as having their basis abandoned. "A wing, a side-entrance, or a courtyard."
It is called a *pakkhapāsaka* because it looks at and binds [the roof] so that it does not fall onto the two sides.
A *maṇḍala* is a specific kind of wooden beam placed above the ends of the rafters and the *gopānasīs*. Both the *pakkhapāsaka* and the *maṇḍala* together constitute the *pakkhapāsakamaṇḍala*.
"In which place" means in whatever location. "Having given to one who is not fully ordained" means by way of relinquishing without expectation to one who is not fully ordained.
Having given [it]. They say that even a distribution made with a sense of expectation is permissible, just like the assignment of robes (*cīvaravikappana*).

"Therein" (*tatra*) refers back to the preceding statement. "He" (*so*) is the Elder Karavīkatissa; the connection is "having seen, he asked. "The Elder" (*thero*) is the Elder Mahāsiva. "On a rough day" (*lūkhadivase*) means on a day when there is no moisture.
"From there" (*tato*) means from speaking; the connection is with "the other" (*paraṃ*). "Him" (*naṃ*) refers to the Elder Mahāsiva. "In front" (*pamukhe*).
"At the mouth of the womb. "That" refers to the entire jar. "Outside" means outside the monastery.
"He" refers to the Elder Mahāsīva. 180. The Story of the Householder Meṇḍaka, 296.
Regarding the phrase "outside the door," one asks, "Outside whose door? and he replies, "Outside the door of the granary. "The *āḷa*-pot."
Regarding this, he said "a pot for cooking *āḷaka* rice" (*āḷakataṇḍulapacanaka-kathāli*) in order to show the meaning of the term *āḷakathāli*, which refers to a pot used for cooking;
the food cooked in it is called *āḷakathālika*. "A vessel of condiments" (*byañjanabhaṇḍika*) means equipment for condiments;

This shows that the word *bhiñjanaka* is a synonym for *bhaṇḍika*. Regarding the term *dāsakammakaraporisa*:

here, *dāsaporisā* (male slaves) and *kammakaraporisā* (male laborers) together form *dāsakammakaraporisa*; this is a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*) with elision of the latter member in the first part of the compound.
Demonstrating this meaning, he says, "male slaves and male laborers. The word *porisa* [in this context] is also [treated as] by means of the word *purisa*.
“Samāna” means “a man is indeed a person” in its sense. Regarding the phrase “with constant food,” the word *dhuva* here is a synonym for “constant”;
thus he says, “at all times. This is to be connected with the phrase “with sour milk.

From the passage beginning with “But in the case of Meṇḍaka” up to the passage ending with “right at that moment with sour milk,” this [text] exists only in certain manuscript copies of the Aṭṭhakathā.

"Herein" means in the *Meṇḍakavatthu* (the Story of the Goat). "In the juice of the cow" (*gorase*) refers to the juices produced from cows, consisting of milk, curd, buttermilk, fresh butter, and ghee.
"Provisions for the journey" (*pātheyya*) means that which is beneficial for the road. "Knowing" means knowing that he desires provisions for the journey.

"Or by the practice of wandering for alms" means either by the practice of wandering for alms from places where one is not known or where one has not been invited. The word "even" (*api*) implies "let alone" (*pageva*).
This shows that it is by means of the practice of wandering for alms. It is to be connected with the phrase "with whatever provisions.
182. The Story of the Foul-Haired Ascetic Keṇiya. 300. Regarding the word *kājehi*:

here, in order to show the counting of the *kājas*, he says, "with five hundred *kājas*. Because two *kuṭas* were taken with one *kāja*, it is said, "a thousand *kuṭas*. *Vo* means "you. It is to be connected with the phrase "well-pleased."

*Tattha* means in the text "eight drinks," or among the eight drinks. By the phrase "a drink made from mangoes" (*ambehi katapānaṃ*), he shows a compound with the middle term elided (*majjhelopasamāsa*).
*Tattha* refers to those that are raw and cooked. The connection is: "by one who makes it, it must be made. "By cooking in the sun" means by means of cooking caused by the sun.
"It is allowable only before midday" means that because it was made by the bhikkhu himself, it is allowable only before midday.
Therefore it was said: “By those not fully ordained,” and so forth. The connection is with the phrase “ambapānaṃ kataṃ” (amb-fruit drink made).
“In all drinks” means in all drinks such as jambu-drink and others. “Among them” refers to among those seven drinks beginning with jambu-drink.

The word *pana* indicates a specific distinction. “With jambu-fruits” means with jambu-fruits, whether raw or ripe. “Aṭṭhikehi” means that which has bone (*aṭṭhi*) within it is an “aṭṭhika” fruit. “With the juice of the species” (*jātirasena*).
“Like juice from an unripe [fruit]”: by this, he shows that it should not be mixed with honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth.
“But that,” namely, the drink of *madhuka* flowers; “grapes” means grape fruits; “sālu” means a tuber; “the juice of the fruit of the seven grains” means rice-washing water.
By the phrase “the juice of ripe *ḍāka* vegetables,” it is indicated that the juice of unripe *ḍāka* vegetables is permissible.

It illuminates. *Hi* means "truth" or "in detail. *Rasa* means "cooked juice. The construction is: "the juice of cooked [foods] lasting for a lifetime, such as ghee and so forth, which have been received and set aside. The connection is: "cooked juice of foods lasting for a lifetime.

As for the phrase "even of those lasting until the end of the day," the word *pi* (even) indicates that this applies even more so to those lasting for a lifetime. *Yaṃ pānaṃ* means "whatever drink..."
"The drinking of the juice of madhuka flowers. "Sā" means the juice of madhuka flowers. "Tenā" means by means of the madhuka flower. The construction is:
"from whatever time they have ceased making liquor, from that [time]. The juice of sugarcane, when free of sediment, is permitted after a meal because it is allowed for seven days.
"These four juices" refers to these four, namely: fruit, leaf, flower, and sugarcane juice.
The tastes. "Sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their mouth" means that sacrifices have the fire-oblation as their opening;
the sense is that the fire-oblation is the best among them.

Showing this, he said, “*Katikamakaṃsū*. *Kati* refers to the agreement (*katika*) known as a promise. Regarding the word *uḷāraṃ*, the term *uḷāra* here signifies “excellent.

Regarding “*paṭibhāneyyakā*,” showing that they are so called because they are engaged in ready wit (*paṭibhāna*), he says “endowed with ready wit.

"Pure craft" (pariyodātasippa) indicates the meaning. It is called *sippa* because it is practiced or cultivated by those seeking a craft;
or, it is called *sippa* because it lies for the benefit of craftsmen or proceeds [toward that end]. The first letter is from the word *oṭṭhaja*.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the nāḷi-measure and the sower," he says "by both the nāḷi and the sower" in order to show that it is a *dvanda* compound. By this, it is shown that the *yakāra* is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*padasaṇdhi*).
[The text] shows this. There is also a reading, “nāḷiyā vā pasibbakena,” but that is not the correct reading. To explain what is meant by “āvāpaka,” he says, “āvāpaka nāma yatthā,” and so forth.
In that context, “yattha” means “in which bag. By this, he demonstrates the etymological meaning of “āvāpaka”:
it is called an *āvāpaka* because they bring [the seeds] here and sow—that is, they place them—within it. In the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), the root *vapa* means “to deposit seeds.”
This is stated in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* (under the root *pakārantadhātu*). Here, however, it should be understood as "inserting.
Therefore it is said, "they insert. "Only to carry about" means only to carry after having taken possession of.
"Wages" means hire. "He" refers to the bhikkhu. "That" refers either to the hoof-trimming kit that has been taken possession of, or "another's" means belonging to someone else.
304. This is the gift of the tenth portion. "Ten sections" means ten portions. 185.
The Discourse on the Four Great Authorities (Catumahāpadesakathā). 305.
Regarding the phrase "this is not allowable," etc.: the construction is that these four great authorities are [indicated] by the words beginning with "this is not allowable."
*Apadesā* are locations where one points by making them a basis (*apassaya*); or alternatively, *apadesā* are reasons by which one points after making them a basis.
"Great bases" (*mahāpadesā*) are great bases. The construction is: "and having taken that," meaning having taken that discourse (*sutta*) known as a great base.
"Rubbing away" (*parimaddantā*) means rubbing repeatedly; the sense is "examining."
*Idam* refers to the cause. *Tam* refers to the nine great fruits and secondary crops.
*Tāni* refers to the minor fruit drinks. *Hi* means indeed. *Tesam* refers to the six types of robes. *Tattha* refers to among the six types of *anuloma* (permissible) robes.

By the phrase “cloth produced from living beings,” he shows that it has the nature of silk cloth (*koseyya*). “Two cloths” refers to Chinese cloth (*cīnapaṭa*) and Somāra cloth. The construction is: “*Dukūla* is the *anuloma* of hemp (*sāṇa*).”
“Of those very two” means of those two alms-bowls. “Of those very three” means of those three water-vessels. “Of those very two” means of those two waist-bands.
“A white parasol” is a parasol made with white cloth. “Of those very three” means of those three parasols. “Mixed flavor” means a blended flavor.
Here, the root *bhid* has the sense of the word “broken,” as in the phrase “it was broken here.”
The meaning of *bhid* (to split) is "division," which is defined as making twofold;

however, it should be understood that when the prefix *sam-*—which subverts the root-meaning—is added to the root *bhid*, it subverts the sense of division and instead expresses the sense of "contact. *Challim-pi* means "even the bark.
*Sakaleneva* means "by the bark alone. The construction is: "whatever is entirely unmixed with milk-rice (*pāyāsa*). *Tāni* refers to the *takkola* (black pepper), *jātiphala* (nutmeg), and so forth.

"In *laṭṭhi*, *madhuka*, and so forth" means in *laṭṭhika* (liquorice), *madhuka* (bassia), and so forth. Alternatively, the reading "in *laṭṭhi*, *madhuka*, and so forth" is simply not a valid reading.
"Whatever" refers to the substance. "In whatever manner" means by whichever mode; it is connected with "when being washed" or "when being scraped.
Having stated "of blended flavor," "intermingled" is said to demonstrate that very same point. "Its own nature" means for as long as the time lasts.
The nature of what is allowable (*kappiya*). "Therefore" means because it brings [the medicine] near; "therefore" [means] for that reason. "By that" refers to what is used for seven days.
"Received on that very day" means received on that same day. The connection is with "by what was received two days prior for seven-day use.

"In this regard" refers to the section on the mixing of medicines. "Offenses are to be understood" means the offenses are to be understood according to their respective order. "In all cases" refers to the entire chapter on medicines (*bhesajjakkhandhaka*).
Thus ends the exegesis of the Bhesajjakkhandhaka.

306. Regarding the phrase “the Pāveyyakas” in the Kathina-kkhandhaka: here, in order to show the meaning of the word *pāveyyakā* as “those who dwell in the kingdom of Pāvā,” he says, “residents of the kingdom of Pāvā. “Therein” means in the kingdom named Pāvā. “Those who have one father” means those whose father is one;
they are brothers with one father (*ekapituka-bhātaro*), and [the text refers to] them. “This” refers to this term “Pāveyyakas.”

“Name. Regarding the word “among them,” it refers to the Pāveyyakas. The phrase “not merely by dwelling in the forest” is stated in order to show the function of exclusion (*byavaccheda*) of the qualification “by way of undertaking the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).
For a qualification is of two kinds: that which effects exclusion, and that which makes [the meaning] manifest. “Among them” refers to the Pāveyyakas.
The connection is with the words “even though they possess the state of being alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*), etc. The particle *pi* (even/also) refers back to the forest-dweller (*āraññaka*).
This refers to the statement beginning with “all those who dwell in the forest. As for the phrase “but these,” it refers to the Pāveyyakas.
Regarding the term *udakasaṅgahe*, he says “held together by water” (*udakena saṅgahite*) to show that it means that which is to be held together by water.
By the expression “on dry land and in low ground,” he demonstrates the actual form of the word *udakasaṅgahe*.
“Muddy with water” (*udakacikkhallo*) means mud stirred up by water; thus it is called “muddy with water.

Regarding the phrase “filled with *oka*,” he says “filled with water” because here the word *oka* is a synonym for water. For water is called *oka* because it accumulates (*ucayati*) and exists in a state of aggregation (*samavāya*).
“Of them” refers to those from Pāveyya. “Dense” means without intervals. “In them” refers to the robes. “By that” [refers to the aforementioned].

Because of the thickness of their robes and because the water did not leak through, even when questioned by the Blessed One, "Did you spend the rainy season in comfort, remaining free from disputes?", those bhikkhus, instead of answering as they were asked, removed the word "comfortably" and said, "We spent the rainy season without disputing.
Thus it is said: "We spent the rainy season without disputing."
"‘In this regard,’ etc. Here, the word ‘and’ (ca) should also be connected with the phrase ‘due to the absence of comfort.
For the meaning is: due both to the absence of comfort in the lodging and to the dissatisfaction arising from not having obtained a vision of the Blessed One.
‘The discourse on the Anamatagga’ refers to the discourse on the *Anamataggiya Sutta* in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. All those [monks] from Pāvā..."
"Bhikkhus" is the connection [of the address]. "That" refers to the discourse on the *Anamatagga*.

"From that" means from the discourse on the Dhamma; "furthermore" is the connection. "The Blessed One addressed" is the connection. "A single robe" refers to the *saṅghāṭi*. "With the inner and the upper" (*santaruttarena*): together with the inner (*antara*) is "inner-together" (*santara*);
that which is both inner and upper is "inner-and-upper" (*santaruttara*), by that. "Would be" (*assu*) means they would exist. "They would have been" (*abhavissaṃsu*).

For this is the meaning. The fact that the locative case (*sattamīvibhatti*) and the past tense (*kālātipattivibhatti*) possess an identical meaning has indeed been stated in the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*).
The word *ca* has the sense of introduction (*upanyāsa*). The construction is: "This is called the *kathinatthāra*.

The connection is with the phrase "being desirous of granting permission" (*anujānitukāmo hutvā*). Therein, in the passage beginning with "I allow you, monks," since the vowel *o* is merely a particle (*nipāta*), how is the meaning [to be understood]?
He said, "It will be," meaning "for those for whom the kaṭhina has been spread. This is the connection with the phrase "of the monks for whom the kaṭhina has been spread.
Saying "evañhi" (for thus), etc., he shows the quality obtained. The word *hi* indicates that quality obtained. "From the other" means from another.
Since it was said, "That shall be yours" or "That shall be for you," rather than saying "that is yours" or "that is for you," the form *vo* is merely a particle.
This is the intended meaning. By the phrase “*vo* is simply a genitive case ending,” he shows that the meaning is “for you” (*tumhākam*).

This being the case, one might ask: “In the subsequent passage ‘*so nesaṃ*’ (‘that for them’), what will the meaning be? To this he says: “But in the case of ‘*so nesaṃ*’... and so forth. The construction is:
“for those of you who have performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, [it is] yours. The word *kaṭhina* expresses the sense of firmness; it is an un-derived primary noun (*anipphanna-pāṭipadika*).
The meaning is: "firm" in the sense of being capable of encompassing the five benefits, beginning with wandering without having asked for permission.
Regarding the phrase "therein": it refers to the five benefits beginning with wandering without having asked for permission.

To show that "wandering without having asked for permission" means wandering (*caraṇa*) is "wandering" (*cāra*), and that wandering without having asked for permission is "wandering without having asked for permission," he says: "wandering without having asked for permission. By the phrase "wandering without having undertaken [the precepts],"...
Regarding the term *asamādānacāra*: here it is shown that by applying the substitution of *an* for the suffix *tvā* in the first member of the compound, it is expressed as *asamādānacāra*.
Regarding *yāvatatthacīvara*: here he says that the sandhi occurs through the elision of the vowel *ā*, thus stating, "as much robe as is needed" (*yāvatā cīvarena attho*).
There is also a reading *yāvadatthacīvara*; in that case, the letter *da* is merely a phonetic junction (*padasandhimatta*). The word *yāva* expresses the sense of limitation.
The word *abhivijjhati* is not a designator [of the meaning]. It forms a compound with the word *attha*.

Regarding the phrase "whatever robe-offering (*cīvaruppāda*) there may be," he says "within the boundary established for the Kathina" (*kathinatthārasīmāya*) in order to show the scope of the word *tattha* (there).

"By the offering arising there" (*tatruppādena*) means by the arising—that is, by the root source—there in the boundary established for the Kathina. By the expression "the robe arises" (*cīvaraṃ uppajjati*), [he explains] "robe-offering" (*cīvaruppāda*).
The phrase *cīvaruppāda* (robe-offering) indicates that it is a compound where the subsequent term qualifies the preceding one (*visesanapara*), meaning "the arising of robes" or simply "robes.

*Keti* means "how many? This is said with reference to the statement "according to the number of groups" (*gaṇavasena*). Alternatively, *keti* means "who are they?"—that is, those who have completed their rains-residence (*vutthavassa*).
This is said with reference to the statement "according to the number of those who have completed the rains-residence" (*vutthavassavasena*). "Even a hundred thousand people may receive [them]."

The word “also” (*pi*) indicates that they obtain even more than that. “Those whose rains-residence is broken” (*chinnavassā*) means those who have entered the first [rains-residence] and then had their rains-residence broken.
“In another monastery” means in a monastery other than the one where the *kathina* robe was spread.
All these monks—those whose rains-residence is broken and so forth—are “completers of the quorum” (*gaṇapūrakā*) for the monks who have entered the first rains-residence.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Of the others only" means only those who have entered the preceding rains-residence and have performed the first invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*).
"Full of years" means having completed twenty years, or having completed the full period of training. "He" refers to the novice (*sāmaṇera*).
Thus, "even here" means in these three cases as well.
The construction is: “Is it permissible for a *kathina* robe-cloth given by anyone to be used? The connection is: “Any robe-cloth given by anyone whatsoever is permissible.
“That” refers to the rule (*vatta*). “Not knowing” means on account of not knowing; for the suffix *-anta* is used here in the sense of a cause. “Of him” means of the donor of the *kathina*.
“In this way” means by the method that will be explained below. The connection is: “a cloth sufficient for one [monk].”
“Of that” means of the *kathina* robe-cloth. The connection is: “so many needles are required. The construction is: “thus it should be explained. The connection is:
“the one who spreads the *kathina* must also know the duty (*vatta*). The word “also” (*pi*) refers to the donor of the *kathina*.
In explaining the duty in detail, he said: “from the weaver’s house,” and so forth. “By the very thread brought” means by the continuity of what has been brought.
"Khalimakkhitasāṭaka" means an unwashed cloth. For it is called "khalimakkhitasāṭaka" because it has been smeared with *khala*, *takka*, and sour gruel (*kañjika*).
"Kathinatthārasāṭaka" means a cloth given for the purpose of spreading the kathina.
"Tadaheva" means on the very day it was given. "Tasmiṃ" refers to the kathina-spreading cloth that was first given.
"And other things" means other than the *kathina* robe-cloth. By the word "and," it is shown that he does not bring only the *kathina* robe-cloth, but also other things.
"He" refers to the donor of the *kathina*. "The other" refers to the first donor of the *kathina*. "Having exhorted him in such and such a way" means:
"That which belongs to this person is more beneficial to the Saṅgha than that which belongs to you; because it is so beneficial to the Saṅgha, even by you..."
Having exhorted him in whatever manner is appropriate, saying, "It should be desired; for one who desires thus, there is great merit," [the connection is:
"by which monk? The construction is: "The kaṭhina-cloth should be spread by that monk to whom the Saṅgha gives the kaṭhina-cloth.
The connection is: "of which monk? The construction is: "It should be given to him who has worn-out robes."

“Mahāpariso” means one who has a great assembly; thus he is called the Elder Mahāparisa. He said “Api ca,” etc., to show that the statement “the younger [monk] is capable, it should be given to him” is not absolute.
“Api ca” means “certainly. “Tadatthāya” means for the sake of that worn-out robe.
“Assa” means of the monk. “Pelavo” means sparse. “Tenāpi” means even by the one who performs the *kathina* ceremony.
The procedure for that [is as follows]. "The formal act (kammavācā) for the giving" means the formal act for the purpose of giving.
The construction is: "But when the kaṭhina has been thus given, [the robes] must be finished. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even by one," he shows that it is even more so with many.
"Praised by the Buddhas" means praised by the Buddhas. "At the end of a hundred thousand past aeons..."

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: *tassa* means "of Padumuttara. The construction is: "He indeed took up the *kathina*. *Taṃ* refers to the *kathina*; the connection is that "the Teacher performed it" (*akāsi*).
To the question, "What should be done with the *kathina* once its completion is finished? he said: "But when the completion is finished," and so forth.
The connection is: "Having taken up the *kathina*, it should be spread out. The phrase "by that monk who is spreading the *kathina*" is to be connected with "should be addressed."

In the word *suddhakattā*, it is the simple agent (*kattā*); in the word *anumodāpetabbaṃ*, it is the causal agent (*kāritakattā*). To the question "What should be said?", he says: "The robe has been spread... please give your approval.
In the phrase "by those monks who are the approvers," the word is the unexpressed agent (*avuttakattā*) for the word "should be addressed" (*vacanīyo*);
in the phrase "should be made to approve," it is either the unexpressed object (*avuttakammaṃ*) or the causal object (*kāritakammaṃ*). In the word *kathinaṃ*, it is the root-object (*dhātukammaṃ*).
Or the prescribed ritual action (*vuttakamma*) should be brought forward. To the question "What should be said?", he replied: "The [robe] has been spread... [omission] ...we rejoice.
"By the others" means by the those who offer the rejoicing (*anumodaka*). "Of all" refers to both those who spread the robe and those who offer the rejoicing. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly.
"This" refers either to the fact that all have spread the robe, or to the statement: "Of two... [omission] ...and of the one who offers the rejoicing."
The construction is: "When the *kaṭhina* has been spread in this way, moreover... By "by whom" is meant by the monk.

"Without having deliberated" means without even deliberating whether one says, "We give it to the one who spreads the *kaṭhina*," or "We give it to the Sangha. "Even the remaining robes" means even those robes remaining from the robe used for spreading the *kaṭhina*.
This is to be connected with "should be given by the Sangha. By the word "having informed," [it is implied] that there is no need for a formal act (*kammavācā*).
It shows the absence of any duty. "By the standing rule for the rainy season residence" means by the rule that operates during the period of the rainy season residence (*vassa*).
"Valuable goods" refers to valuable goods such as beds, pillows, and so forth. "Within a single boundary" means within a single precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
Regarding the phrase "and just as": here the word *yathā* has the sense of the word *yaṃ*. For the meaning is "by whatever method. "The great ground" (*mahābhūmika*)...
"Of great scope": by virtue of possessing twenty-four aspects, it is said to be "of great extension. "From that" means from the characteristic of non-existence.
"Also in the commentary"—the word "also" (pi) indicates that this is not the case here alone.
"Therein" refers to among the twenty-four aspects. "By the mere scratching"—here, for the purpose of grasping the measure, [it is done] with the fingernails and so forth.
“Likhanaṃ” means scratching; showing that “ullikhita-mattaṃ” (the mere amount scratched) refers to the measure, he said:
“by the mere taking of the measure in length and breadth. Elaborating on that same point, he said:
“The measure,” and so forth. The construction is: “he scratches while showing [it]. “Pañcakaṃ” means a piece of five measures, or a group of five.
By the word "vāsa" (or etc.), it includes other types such as those consisting of thirteen [parts] and so forth.
"Merely by placing a false thread upon the robe" means merely by placing a false thread on top of the robe. "Merely by sewing lengthwise" means merely by sewing along the length.
"Merely by binding a seal-strip" means merely by binding a seal-strip. "Two pieces of cloth" (*cimilika*) means two rags (*pilotikā*). "The first piece of cloth" refers to...
The construction is: "having joined together another, one's own original lining (*pakaticimilikā*), [the cloth] was set aside from the *kathina* lining.
Having supplied the elliptical phrase "that first lining," it should be connected with the words "having made the belly-lining of the *kathina* robe-cloth" (*kathinasāṭakassa kucchicimilikaṃ katvā*).
"Of the original robe" (*pakaticīvarassa*) means of one's own original robe. "An original robe with a fastened border" (*pakatipaṭṭabandhacīvaraṃ*).
"Binding-cloth by means of a plain cloth-strip. "By the mere act of placing it along the back" means by the mere act of placing it over a longwise-woofed robe;
for when one wears a longwise-woofed robe, because it stays at the back, it is called "along the back.
"By the mere act of placing it across the belly" means by the mere act of placing it over a crosswise-woofed robe; for a crosswise-woofed robe...
Because it remains in the belly at the time of putting on the robe, it is called "following the belly.
"Merely by placing the visiting cloth (*āgantuka-paṭṭa*) upon" means merely by placing the visiting cloth over the robe. "Or" (*vā*) means "alternatively.

"Befitting" (*sāruppa*) means suitable for ascetics. "By way of indirect talk" (*parikathāya*) means by means of a discourse produced through a circuitous or figurative method. "Excessively exalted" (*ati-ukkaṭṭha*).

"Is permissible" means that only what is most excellent is permissible. "Similar to what has been dipped" refers to the connection with the *kathina* robe being similar to the cloth that has been dipped.
"Therein" refers to the two kinds of storage. "On that very day" means on the very day it was given.

"By means of what is to be relinquished after a night has passed" means by means of what becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) once a night has elapsed. "By another" means other than the three robes (*ticīvara*). "With a border and a fringe" means made together with a large border (*mahāmaṇḍala*) and a half-border (*addhamaṇḍala*).

309. Having thus shown the characteristic of the plane of disadvantage in twenty-four aspects, he now says “*ahatena*,” etc., while showing the characteristic of the plane of benefit in seventeen aspects.
Therein, it is called *ahata* because it has not been worn out—that is, it did not go through use—or because it is not to be worn out or harmed by use; thus, he says “*aparibhūtena*” (unused).
By the phrase “*ahatasadisenā*,” he shows that in the expression “*ahatakappenā*,” the word *kappa* has the sense of “similar.

Regarding the term “*pāpaṇikenā*,” he says “fallen at the shop door” (*āpaṇadvāre patitaṃ*), demonstrating that a shop (*āpaṇa*) where goods are spread out (*pasārita*) is a “shop” (*pāpaṇa*), and what has fallen therein is “shop-fallen” (*pāpaṇika*).
By the word “*pilotika*,” he shows the actual form of the suffix *-ṇika*. [The phrase] “by the very reversal of what was stated” means:
By the [terms] stated as “by means of a sign,” etc., it is precisely through perversion. “Therein” (tattha) refers to the Parivāra. “Indeed” (hi) means truly, or because.
“Here” (idha) refers to the Kathina-khandhaka. The connection is: “it is deficient by that statement being spoken. 310.
“Therein” (tattha) refers to the passage beginning, “And how, monks, is the kaṭhina suspended? “The progenitors” (janettiyo) means mothers.
The exegesis (*yojanā*): She honors her children by means of this Dhamma, thus she is a mother (*mātā*); or, she is honored by her children in accordance with the Dhamma, thus she is a mother;
being like her, they are called "matrices" (*mātikā*). This is what is shown. *Kathinubbhāra* and *kathinuddhāra* are identical in meaning.
*Etā* refers to these types of words. *Tāsu* refers to the eight matrices. *Assa* refers to the lifting of the kaṭhina (*kathinubbhāra*).

188. The Discourse on the Sevenfold Taking (Ādāyasattakakathā) 311. Regarding the phrase "they will not return": here, the prefix *pati-* has the sense of repetition (*punattha*), and the verbal root *i-* has the sense of going (*gatyattha*). Demonstrating this, he said, "they will not come back again" (*na puna āgamissanti*). Thus, the connection is: "it is cut off for one who departs.

"And this" (*etañca*) refers both to the limit of departure (*pakkamanantika*) and the suspension of the Kathina (*kathinuddhāra*). "To them" (*tāham*) means "to those, I [say]. "To you" (*te*) means "to you."
"Another" means other than one's own dwelling. "Thus it occurs" means this reflection arises. "That" refers to the impediment of the monastery. The construction is:
"was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun. The connection is: "the two impediments are severed at once. "Neither before nor after" means simultaneously.
To the question, "Why was that severance of the impediments not stated in detail? he says: "But that," and so forth. "But that" refers to the severance of the impediments.

The connection is with the words "it is not stated. "In this" refers to this suspension of the kaṭhina. To the question "Why is this suspension of the kaṭhina called 'ending with destruction'?", he says "Because," and so forth. "Of him" refers to the bhikkhu.

The connection is with the words "is cut off" in the phrase "in the case of the disappointment of hope. "But this" refers to the suspension of the kaṭhina that occurs through the disappointment of hope.

The connection is: "it becomes manifold. "Of that" means of the bhikkhu. The construction is: "It is said" refers to this "termination of the kaṭhina due to the cutting off of hope" being what was stated.
"But here," however, means in this place. "Therein" means in the case of crossing the boundary.
312–325. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion. "In seven" means among the eight *mātikās*, in the remaining seven in number, excluding the one concerning the cutting off of hope.
Or in a group of seven. "Those very ones" means the seven themselves. "From that" means from the alternative. "Whichever" refers to the removals of the kaṭhina.
"By the others" means by those other than the cutting off of hope. The connection is: "those obstacles which have been stated.

To show the etymological meaning of *catta*—namely, "that by which the residence is abandoned"—he said, "by which mind," and so forth. *Taṃ* refers to that mind. By the phrase "the same method applies," [he indicates this].

"Vantaṃ" (vomited) means that by this [act], the residence (*āvāsa*) is vomited out. "Muttaṃ" (released) means that by this [act], one is released from the residence; thus it extends the etymological meaning.
"In all cases" means throughout the entire Kathina-khandhaka.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the Kathina-khandhaka.
8. The Chapter on Robes (Cīvarakkhandhaka) 202.
The Discourse on the Matter of Jīvaka 326.
In the Chapter on Robes, rejecting the meaning of "apadakkhiṇa" as "not to the right," he said: "They are clever and skillful."

Regarding the word *abhisaṭā*: here, showing that among the various meanings of the verbal root *sar* (to go), it carries the sense of "going" (*gati*) in this context, he says, "gone toward" (*abhigatā*).

"Gone toward" means they are to be approached face-to-face. Now, since the Pāli text says, "of those people who were desirous, of those who were desirous," why is it said instead, "by those people who were desirous, by those who were desirous"? To this he replies, "But in the sense of the instrumental case," and so forth.
By this, he shows that the sixth case-agent (*chaṭṭhī-kattā*) is indeed identical to the third case-agent (*tatiyā-kattū*).
When it is said "one who dwells in a market town (*nigama*) is a *negama*," he says "a group of householders" to indicate that a *negama* is a group of householders.
"Those who dwell in the city" are the *nāgaras*. The connection is: "having given [it], they caused [it] to be established. "Gardens, groves, vehicles, and so forth."
Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other types of objects of enjoyment and use are included. "In the place of a courtesan" (*gaṇikaṭṭhāne*) means in the location of a courtesan.
A "courtesan" (*gaṇikā*) is one who beautifies the city; for she is called a "courtesan" because she is to be approached by a multitude (*gaṇa*) of people seeking her.

And in the phrase "with a hundred as a substitute," the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇattha*). It refers to that which is designated as a substitute (*paṭinidhi*) for going [to her] at night.

The meaning is indeed “by means of a hundred. Regarding the word *gilāna* (sick), he says “the state of being sick” (*gilānabhāva*) because it should be understood that here the abstract sense is conveyed even without the abstract suffix (*bhāvapaccaya*).
By the word “should make known” (*jānāpeyya*), he shows that the root *vid-* has the sense of making known (*ñāṇattha*) in the phrase “one should inform.
Regarding the term *kattarasuppe*, the word *kattara* is a synonym for “old”; thus he says “on an old bed. They sleep.
A *suppa* is that wherein dogs and such are found; a *kattara-suppa* is a weeding-hook.
328. "That" refers to Jīvaka. The connection is: "Other princes, it is said, speak thus. "Nimmātiko" means one who has no mother.
In phrases such as "yathā ca," the construction is: "as they send, so [they do]. The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*sampiṇḍana*).
The meaning is: not only did they speak thus, but furthermore, no one sent anything at all.
"Of others" means of those other than Jīvaka. "His" refers to Jīvaka. "Thus" (iti) means in this manner. "He" refers to Jīvaka.
"All that" refers to both his speaking the words "without a mother, without a father" and his failure to send a gift—all of that.
"Yaṃnūna" means "it would be well indeed. The construction is: "It would be well indeed if I were to learn the craft of surgery.
"Tassa" refers to Jīvaka. "Etadahosi" means this occurred; the sense is that a reflection arose.
"Parūpaghātapaṭisaṃyuttāni" means connected with approaching another, or connected with striking (*upahanana*) excessively (*bhusena*). "Mettāpubbabhāgaṃ" means the preliminary stage of the craft.
“Loving-kindness precedes this” means that loving-kindness is its preliminary stage (*mettā-pubbabhāga*). Thus, the construction is: “It was so.
Because the previous reflection was not definitive, he said “Moreover,” etc., in order to show its definitive nature. “Moreover” (*api ca*) means definitively. “This one” (*ayaṃ*) refers to Jīvaka.

“From here” (*ito*) means from the auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*). “This one” (*ayaṃ*) refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*). “In the midst of the four assemblies” (*catuparisantare*) means in the middle of the fourfold assembly. “Of expanded virtues” (*patthitagunaṃ*)...
"Pattharitaguṇaṃ" means one whose virtues are spread abroad. "Ṭhānantaraṃ" means a distinction of status. "Ahampi" means not only this lay follower (upāsaka), but I too;
such is the meaning. "Bhagavā" is a term of address. "Patthanaṃ" means a desired boon. "Codiyamāno pi" means even when being urged or exhorted.
By the word "pi" (even/also), there is a reference to what was previously considered. "Esa" means this Jīvaka.
329. Regarding the word *disāpāmokkho*, in order to show its etymological meaning as "one who is pre-eminent (*pāmokkho*) among the directions (*disāsu*)," he says, "in all directions," and so forth.
And at that time—meaning at the very moment Jīvaka was thinking—[the merchants] arrived; this is the connection [of the sentence].
"Them" refers to the merchants; "he asked" is the connection. "From where? means from the city. "From Takkasilā" means from the city of Takkasilā.
*“Tattha” means in Takkasilā. “Āma” is a particle used in the sense of acceptance; for its meaning is “yes, it is so. “Te” refers to the merchants.
“Tathā” means they did exactly as Jīvaka had said; this is the sense. “So” refers to Jīvaka. “Pitaraṃ” refers to Prince Abhaya.
“Tehi” means by those merchants. “Taṃ” refers to Jīvaka; the connection is that he questioned him. “So” refers to Jīvaka. [The question was: “Why, dear father, have you come here?”*
The construction is: "He asked. "From that" means from the one who asked. "He" refers to Jīvaka. The construction is: "I have come to learn.
Regarding the phrase "and he learns much," and so forth—it is said, "he learns much" because he has learned the craft itself without performing any other work.
In this context, the construction is: "Just as they learn, so too does he not learn. He...
*Panā* means Jīvaka; the connection is that he *karoti* (performs) or *sikkhati* (learns). *Ekaṃ kālaṃ* means at one time. Since this is so, why does he learn much?
To this he says, "Even though this is so," and so forth. *Medhāvitāya* means by way of the wisdom of quick grasping and retention;
the connection is "much craft. The construction is: "the craft learned by this Jīvaka is not forgotten."
The construction is: "Whatever craft the teacher knows, this Jīvaka knows that much.
"Yaṃ" refers to the craft; "ayaṃ" refers to Jīvaka; "bhavissati" (will be) is the connection. "Naṃ" refers to Jīvaka. "Yathā" means in whatever manner.

"Kammavipākaṃ" means a disease born of the ripening of karma. The word "naṃ" is the object of the causative verb in the phrase "sikkhāpesi" (he caused to train); "bhesajjayojanaṃ" (the application of medicine).
*Pada* means the act of placing the foot. *Bhesajjayojanaṃ* means the application of medicine to a disease.
*So pana* refers to Jīvaka. *Iminā*—the connection is that it was not learned by this Jīvaka, but was learned [by others].
*Ekena dvārena* means through one of the four gates. *Āhiṇḍanto* means wandering about. Regarding the phrase *parittaṃ pātheyyaṃ*, here the word *paritta*...
Because it functions for the purpose of protection as well, he said "a small amount" (appamattakaṃ) to show that it functions here for a minor purpose.
The construction is: "Why did he give such a small amount of provisions? "His" (tassa) refers to the world-renowned [physician].

"This one" (ayaṃ) is Jīvaka; the connection is with "he will receive. "From there" (tato) means from the receiving. "When the provisions were exhausted" (khīṇe pātheyye) is to be construed as: "when the provisions had become exhausted."
203. The Story of the Housewife of the Treasurer, etc.

(330). Regarding the phrase *yā nāma*: it refers to a housewife. Concerning the expression *kimpi māya*, he says, “*kimpi me ayaṃ*,” explaining that here there is a sandhi involving the elision of the vowel *e*.

By this, he excludes the sandhi involving the substitution of the letter *y*. There is also a reading, *myāyaṃ*; if that is the case, it is simply a sandhi involving the substitution [of *m* for *me*].
There is no elision-conjunction (*lopasaṃdhi*). The construction is: "Will this wife of mine give some gift to be given?
*Tassa ca* means "and of him," though there is also a reading as *katassā*. *Rogūpasamassa ca* means "and for the subsiding of my illness";
by these words, he shows the meaning of the word *saṃyamassa*. By the word "benefit" (*upakāraṃ*), [he explains] the sense of "I perceive" (*upajānāmi*) here.
This shows the meaning of *upasadda*. *Adhippāya* means the intention (*āsaya*) of the housewife.
Regarding the statement, “Let all this ornament be yours,” one asks: did the king say this according to his true nature, or did he say it after thinking something over?
To this, he says, “The king,” and so forth. In that context, *imaṃ* refers to this ornament. *Pamāṇayutte* means proportionate to the reason. *Naṃ* refers to Jīvaka.
"Of the plays as well" (*nāṭakānam-pi*) means of the five hundred plays as well. "He too" (*so-pi*) refers to Jīvaka. "Of those" (*tesam*) refers to the plays of Abhayakumāra.
"To me" (*me*) is connected with "it is not fitting" (*na patirūpam*). "Of my grandmothers" (*ayyikānam*) means of my maternal grandmothers. The construction is: "What service has been done for me?
By this, he shows that the office and the service are identical in meaning. "The King, being pleased, gave [it] and said" is the connection.
205. The Discourse on the Story of the Rājagaha Merchant 332.
“By the changing of postures” means by repeatedly shifting from one posture to another.
The construction is: “The brain of this merchant, who had lain motionless for three weeks. The construction is also: “Perhaps he might lie down.”

[He] addressed the merchant. "By that very reason" means for that same cause. Regarding "sīsacchavi," which means "that which covers the head," he said "head-skin" (*sīsacamma*) to indicate the skin that conceals the head.
"Of him" refers to the merchant. Regarding "in three weeks," since the latter term must be understood by multiplying it with the former term, he said:
"by each of the three sides, [taking] one week at a time."
333. "Having had the people removed" means having had the people depart.
207. The Story of King Pajjota. 334.
"Born because of a scorpion" means born for the sake of a scorpion; the meaning is that he was born in dependence upon a scorpion.
The construction is: "And all medicine is repulsive to scorpions.
Regarding the term *paññāsayojanikā*, he says "he is capable of going" in order to show that the suffix *-ṇika* functions here in the sense of being able to go.
"Of this king" refers to the king named Candapajjota. "Only a female elephant" means only the female elephant named Bhaddavatikā.
“Vīsayojanasataṃ” means one hundred and twenty yojanas.
The construction is: “for one son of good family who was seated to eat. “Tassa” refers to that son of good family;
the connection is with “he informed. “So” refers to that son of good family; the connection is with “he commanded, ‘Bring it! “Itaro” refers to the man. “Taṃ” refers to the bowl.
"In whatever [existence]" means in whichever state of existence. "In each of those places, may I be endowed with vehicles"—this is the construction.
"He" refers to that man. "This king named Pajjota was born"—this is the construction.
By saying "having given all the *sabbi* to drink," he shows that this is merely an illustration; thus he says, "and having given all the *sabbi* to drink," etc. And the *sabbi*...
"Having made him drink," means having instructed the attendants on the proper method for food and conduct. "Olumpetvā" (having dipped) refers to the root *lup*, which has the sense of placing;
thus he says "odahitvā" (having placed). "Virecesi" (he purged) means he purged both upwards and downwards.
208. The Discourse on the Pair of Fine Kasi Cloth Garments.
335. *Sivathikaṃ*: It is called *sivathikaṃ* because jackals (*sivā*) come and stand there for the purpose of devouring corpses (*kuṇapa*).
By this term, it is shown that *siveyyaka* (wool from a charnel ground) arises in a *sivathika*, with the elision of the syllable *tha*.
*Tattha* means in Uttarakuru. *Taṃ* refers to the dead body. *Hatthisoṇḍakasakuṇā* means birds having the appearance of elephants.
Because they have trunks like those of elephants, they are called *hatthisoṇḍakā* (elephant-trunked); and because they are birds, they are called *hatthisoṇḍakasakuṇā* (elephant-trunked birds).
"They bring for the king" means they bring for the sake of the king, or they bring into his presence.
"This" refers to the pair of Siveyyaka cloths. Showing that it is called *siveyyaka* because it was woven in the kingdom of Sivi, he says "Or rather," and so forth.
"Tenā" means "for that reason. The construction is: "They say 'it is from Sivi,'" etc., as the ancients have said.
209. Discussion on the Thirty-Fold Purgative. 336. Regarding the phrase "kiṃ pana":
here the word *kiṃ* has the sense of indefiniteness. The meaning is: "Is it coarse? Or is it not coarse? [The text continues: "The drinking of oil..."
The connection is between the words "moistens" (*temeti*) and "does" (*karoti*). "In all places" (*sabbattha*) means throughout the entire body.

"Sinews" (*sirā*) refers to the *kaṇḍarā* (tendons). "He comes" (*ayati*) refers to Jīvaka. "For the purpose of removing gross humors" (*oḷārikadosaharaṇatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of taking away gross bodily humors (*doṣa*).

"When the natural state exists" (*pakatatte*) connects with the sense that when the inherent nature (*sabhāva*), known as the "natural state," is present. The construction is: "O Venerable Blessed One" (*bhagavā bhante*). "From where? (*kuto*) means from whose presence.
The construction is: "He thought, 'Is it permissible? From "there" means from that thinking. "Soṇa" refers to Koḷivisa-Soṇa; the connection is with the word "is eating.
"From there" means from the presence of Soṇa. "His" refers to Soṇa. "He" refers to Soṇa. "Of the Elder" refers to the Elder Moggallāna. In the phrase "the bowl," this is the agent (sāmī);
in the phrase "he gave," it is the recipient (sampadāna). The connection is with the words "another alms-food."

The connection is: "The king, too, desired to eat. The construction is: "Into both of those two alms-meals—the one Sujātā gave and the one Cunda the smith’s son gave at the time of his final *parinibbāna*—the deities infused nutritive essence (*oja*).
"In others" means in alms-meals other than those two. "They desire" means they have a preference for it. "He" refers to King Bimbisāra. "Only yours" means...
"It is yours alone. "That" refers to the word of the Blessed One. The connection is: "The king did it. "Those" refers to the eighty thousand sons of good family.
"For this very purpose" means for the purpose of establishing Soṇa in Arahatship, not for the purpose of favoring the king; this is the intended meaning. 210.
The Discourse on the Request for Boons.
337. "One by whom the duty of eating has been performed" means one who has finished his meal; the connection is with the words "when that [person] is present.
"In the very manner stated" means in the manner stated in the case of Rāhula. "This cloth" refers to this cloth from Sivi; the connection is with the word "arisen.
The word "so long" (tāvā) is to be supplied. "In the interval" means during the period between the time this cloth arose.
“Some bhikkhu” is the connection. “By that” means by reason of being a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*). “This one” refers to Jīvaka.
Regarding the phrase “householder’s robe,” rejecting the interpretation that it means “the robe of householders,” he says: “a robe given by householders.
“Connected with the benefits of giving cloth” refers to the benefits of giving cloth, such as [the passage] beginning, “He is a giver of cloth, a giver of beauty.”
[The term] is connected with the benefit (*ānisamsa*). Because it is stated by way of distribution (*vicchā*), the universal noun (*sabbanāma-sadda*) “*itarītarena*” has an indefinite meaning;
thus he says, “by whatever [robe], whether of little value or of great value. “*Pāvāra*” means the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
For it is called *pāvāra* because it is chosen (*variyyati*) or desired (*icchiyyati*) for the purpose of wearing. By the phrase “of various kinds such as cotton,” he shows its specific nature.
"Only a natural *kojava*" means a *kojava* that is naturally suitable for monks.

Because it is suitable for dancing while sixteen dancing girls stand upon it, and because its back is large, it is called "large-backed" (*mahāpiṭṭhiya*); such a *kojava* is a "large-backed *kojava*" (*mahāpiṭṭhiyakojava*).
It is said that its hairs are more than four finger-breadths in length.
211. The Discourse on the Permission for Blankets, etc.
(Kambalānujānanādikathā) 338. *Kāsīnaṃ*: Of the people of the Kāsī country, or of the people residing in the kingdom of Kāsī. *Pasenadissa*:
He is called Pasenadi because he conquers (*jināti*) an opposing army (*paccuṭṭhaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ senaṃ*); the letter *ja* is changed to *da*. *Esa*: This one.
"This is the King of Kāsi. By the word "sahassa," he shows that *kāsi* is a conventional number. "Worth that" means worth that [quantity] of *kāsi*.
To the question "Why is it called 'half-Kāsi'? he says "But this," and so forth. "This" refers to the blanket.
"Panā" indicates the sense of a reason; for its meaning is "because."

339. To show that "bhaṅga" (a mixture) means that the five types of thread, such as linen and so forth, must be mixed together and pounded, he said, "What is called *bhaṅga*," and so on. "Made of *vāka* grass alone" means produced solely from the *vāka* grass known by the name *bhaṅga*.

340. "Those" refers to the monks; the connection is with the phrase "they reportedly observed. "Of this" connects with the word "meaning. "They did not stay" means they did not remain; the sense is "they did not dwell.
Regarding the term "nākāmā," here the verbal root *kamu* has the sense of "desiring," and the letter *ya* is elided.
He said: "Not without consent. "Should be given" means a share should be given. "In the vicinity" means near the cemetery.
The phrase "If, however," and so forth, is stated to show that the statement "they must give a share even against their will" is not absolute.
"Here" refers to this cemetery. The construction is: "They give [the portion], saying, 'Let those who have arrived take it. "By whom" refers to the monk. "They entered together with equals" means...
In this context, the word *sadisa* (similar) is a synonym for *sama* (equal); thus he said, "They descended together. *Samaṃ* is a neuter noun.
Or, showing it as *samānadisāya* (in the same direction), he said, "or in one direction"; here, however, the elision of the letter *y* is to be understood.
*Bahimeva* means precisely outside of the charnel ground. *Katikaṃ* refers to an agreement (*saṅgara*) established by what has been done.
213. Discussion on the Appointment of a Robe-Receiver (Cīvarapaṭiggāhakasammutikathā) 342.
The construction [of the sentence] is to be understood as follows: "In such cases as 'one who does not fall into favoritism' (*chandāgati*), etc., this is the method of exposition.
The connection is with "the robe of relatives, etc. "In a certain person" refers to a particular individual. The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative. By one or another of these three—
The meaning is: "He goes astray through favoritism for a reason. The word *api* (even) is used in the sense of reproach;

the connection is "even for one who has arrived [late]," which implies, "how much more so for one who arrives later. *Avamaññanti* means they treat with contempt. *Vo* means "of you. The construction is: "How could there be nothing?
*Muṭṭhassati* means one whose mindfulness is lost. The connection is "even for those who have arrived, [the distribution of] robes..."
The word *pi* has the sense of respect (*sambhāvanattha*). The meaning is "much more so those who arrived first.
The construction is: "This is called the place for receiving robes. *Santasanto vā* means "or repeatedly. *Idañcidañca* refers to "this and that robe.
*Tasmā* means "because he goes" and "because he knows," therefore [he does]. *Yo* refers to the monk. The connection is with the word "is able" (*sakkoti*).
The construction is: "A monk of such a kind is to be appointed. "Even by means of an announcement" (*apalokanena*) means:

"I announce the Saṅgha to appoint the monk named so-and-so as the receiver of robes"; this is connected with "is to be appointed. "But where" (*yattha pana*) means: in whichever resident monastery (*dhuravihāra*).
By the phrase "only at the place where it was received," he shows the scope of the pronoun *tat* in the expression "right there" (*tattheva*). "Having discarded" (*chaḍḍetvā*).
In the phrase "having abandoned by this," it shows the meaning of the verbal root *ujjha* as "relinquishing.

Regarding the term *cīvarapaṭiggāhaka*, he says "he who... and so forth, demonstrating its etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as "one who receives a robe" (*cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhātīti cīvarapaṭiggāhako*).
Therein, the construction is: "He who receives [it] is called the robe-receiver (*cīvarapaṭiggāhaka*). [The term] *cīvarapaṭisāmika*...
This shows the meaning of "one who stores robes" as one who, having taken the robe from the place where it was received, places it and keeps it in the storehouse (*bhaṇḍāgāra*).
Regarding the phrases "he who does not follow favoritism" and so forth, the construction here is: "among these [qualities] and those [to be mentioned] below.
214. Discussion on the Authorization for the Storehouse, etc.
343. The construction is as follows: whichever *vihāra* or *aḍḍhayoga* there may be, that *vihāra* and so forth should be formally authorized (*sammanitabbo*).

In the phrase “by means of *ārāmikas*, *sāmaṇeras*, etc.,” the term is an ablative (*apādāna*) in the sense of separation; however, it is also appropriate as an instrumental (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, a border monastery (*paccantasenāsana*) should not be authorized due to dangers such as thieves and the like.
“In the very midst of the *vihāra*” means specifically in the midst of the storehouse (*bhaṇḍāgāra*) of the *vihāra*.
*Yassa* means "of the storehouse. This word is the genitive (*sāmī*) with respect to the word "in the roofing, etc.," and the dative (*sampadāna*) with respect to the word "there is not.
*Yassa pana* means "but of that storehouse. *Yattha katthaci* means "in whatever place. *Yena* means "by which cause [of falling].
*Mūsika* means "a mouse" (one who eats after having gnawed). By the word "etc.," one includes the monitor lizard, the mongoose, and so forth. *Upa-*... [text continues]
"Ants" (*upacikā*) are so called because they cover themselves with soil or gather it up. "That" refers to the rain and so forth. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because.
"Thus" (*evaṃ*) and so on constitute the conclusion.
By the phrase "by the receiver of robes and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the storer of robes and the keeper of the storehouse. "Therein" (*tattha*).
Regarding those [terms]: the connection is "it must not be accepted by the robe-acceptor. "Meanwhile" (*tāva*) refers to the robe-storer and the storekeeper, or else it means "first" by them.
"Whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) refers to the robe. "In the same way" (*tatheva*) means exactly as one accepts it after having set it apart individually.
"By the robe-storer too" (*cīvaranidahakenāpi*): the word "too" (*api*) implies that it is not only by the acceptor, but also by the storer.
He summarizes. "In that very way" means exactly as the storekeeper explains. "From those" refers to those robes;
it is an ablative of separation (*vibhatta-apādāna*), or rather, a selection (*niddhāraṇa*) from among those robes. "That very same" refers to the robe specified by the Saṅgha.
"Thus," etc., is the conclusion. The connection is with "authorized by the Blessed One. "Storehouse" means a place for keeping goods.
“A house. “The storekeeper” means one appointed to the storehouse. “Because of abundance” means for the purpose of being appointed due to an abundance of requisites.
Since this is so, he asks, “For what purpose was it permitted? and says, “Moreover,” and so forth. The connection is:

“it was permitted for the sake of assistance. “Hīti” indicates the detailed explanation. The construction is: “they would not even know. The connection is: “two or two robes. “To provide support” means—
"In order for the Saṅgha to perform an act of inclusion.
Regarding the phrase "he must not be ordained," the author says "others too" and so forth, pointing out other persons who likewise cannot be ordained by way of enumerating the categories.
The word "hi" indicates a detailed explanation. "Therein" refers to the four [cases]. The connection is: "but the Saṅgha grants [it]. And "because of being helpful" refers to the Saṅgha.
And because of being helpful. Here, it should be understood that in the first three [cases] there is only one cause, whereas in the last two there are two causes.

"Being present" (*sammukhībhūta*) means existing face-to-face with one another; or, "present" (*sammukha*) means having come together. Having become present, it is "being present" (*sammukhībhūta*). Due to the connection with the word *bhū*, the letter *a* becomes *i*. Within the boundary of the vicinity (*upacārasīmā*),...
The Saṅgha is established. To demonstrate this meaning, he said: "by one standing within the boundary of the precincts" (*antoupacārasīmāyaṃ*).
"A clamor" (*kolāhala*) refers to an indistinct noise produced by many people gathering together in one place. To show its nature, he said: "of us," and so forth.

By the phrase "among those distributing robes" (*cīvarabhājakesu*), he demonstrates the manner of resorting to an improper course; this is indeed easy to understand. "Become like a scale" (*tulābhūto*)—
“Becoming like a scale” means having become equal to a scale, or having attained the state of being equal to a scale.
“Impartial” (*majjhatta*) means one whose self-nature (*attasabhāva*) stands in the middle;
thus, he is impartial. “This” refers to the robe. “Dense” means without intervals. “Thin” means sparse. Here, by the word “having selected,”...
This shows the selection according to the measure of the cloth. By the word “tulayitvā” (having weighed), it shows weighing by value.
“Having made praise and blame” means having made both praise and blame, and having made both the small measure and the large measure;
the sense is that some robes are of little value while others are of great value. “Worth ten each” means...
"Worth ten, ten kārṣāpaṇas" means: having bound together a robe worth nine [kārṣāpaṇas] with one worth one, and that worth eight with two worth one;
such is the meaning. "In equal pieces" means having set aside pieces of equal measure;
by this, he indicates that in the phrase "of various colors" (*vaṇṇāvaṇṇa*), the word *vaṇṇa* has the sense of "measure. "Ten monks each" means...
This is stated by way of illustration (*upalakkhaṇavasena*), since it is possible to count [the items] in other ways as well.
"Bundle" (*bhaṇḍika*) means a bag connected with robe-material. "Peg" (*kusa*) means a wooden stick.
"Masters of themselves" (*attissarā*) means masters of themselves by their own selves. The connection is with "the performance of duties for others. "Half-portion" (*upaḍḍhabhāga*)...
A half-share from the portion obtained by the bhikkhus. "But those who" refers to the sāmaṇeras.
"An equal share" means a share equal to the share of the bhikkhus. "And this" connects with the statement "a half-share," meaning it was so stated.
"Exactly the same" means of equal measure for both the bhikkhus and the sāmaṇeras. "Produced there and belonging to the rainy-season residence" means in that monastery.
The *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-cloth) is produced by means of its origin and its root. "Reinforcement" (*phātikamma*) means the work of augmentation; the meaning is:
"having performed whatever manual labor—such as sweeping, binding, and so forth, as prescribed in the Vinaya—is necessary so that there is no deficiency in the monastery.

"This" refers to the taking [of the cloth] after having performed the reinforcement. "Indeed" (*hi*) signifies truth. "In this case" (*ettha*) refers to the taking of the *tatruppāda-vassāvāsika* (the rainy-season robe-cloth produced on the spot).
"Of all" means of all the bhikkhus and sāmaṇeras without exception. "Even with regard to the robe-stores" means even with regard to out-of-season robes (akālacīvara) kept in the storehouse.
By the word "even" (pi), one refers to the robes produced there for the rainy season residence (vassāvāsika).
The connection is: "the sāmaṇeras raise a shout. "Apaharita" means devoid of greenery. "Raṅgachalli" means a dyed surface. "This" refers to [the fact] that they raised a shout.

The connection is: "the equal distribution is stated. "And those" refers to the novices (*sāmaṇera*). "They do it by skipping over [the proper time]" means that they do not perform it at the times when it ought to be done, but rather perform it at whatever moment they desire. "Those" refers to the novices.
"An equal share must be given" means that an equal portion must be given merely by the fact of their having promised, "We shall do it."
The connection is that this was said [with the intention]: “to give his own share. To the question, “With reference to what was it said?
he replies: “From the storehouse... with reference to this. *Pahatāya* means either “to be struck” or “to be driven away. *Tasmā* means “because it was said with reference to this, therefore.
*Anīhaṭesu* means “when they have not been brought out from the storehouse. *Imassa bhikkhuno* refers to this monk who desires to cross over.
"Of the bhikkhu. "By means of a scale" means by means of a measure.
"Among those" refers to the cloths; the connection is that "one cloth" [was weighed]. "When all have been set down" is the syntactical link. "By this much" means by twelve *gghanaka*s.
"Having heard that" means having heard those words of the bhikkhus. "In all cases" means in every instance belonging to the Saṅgha or a group.
He said, "What is called 'not throwing' (anukkhepaṃ nāma)," etc., showing that it is "not throwing" because it is thrown or cast in by way of not being provided.
The connection is with "worth as much as. The construction is: "worth [something] by that much of a value. "Deficient" (vikallakā):
the state of being deficient is deficiency; it is the state of being insufficient for the robes and the person; that itself is "deficiency" (vikallakā). "Therein" (tatthā) is a remainder of the text.
The meaning is: "among those two, [the robes] are deficient. *Atthi* means "they exist"; this is a particle. The connection is: "and they must be given by those who cut [them].

"Must be given" (*dātabbāni*) means "must be cut" (*chinditabbāni*). For the word *dā-* has the sense of "cutting off" (*avakhaṇḍana*). "To give" (*dātuṃ*) means "to cut off" (*avakhaṇḍituṃ*). "Thus," etc., is the conclusion.
"In this" (*ettha*) means "in these [robes] that are deficient. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the robe. "Then" (*atha*) means "after [the donor] has been satisfied."
*Therein*: in the portion belonging to one bhikkhu. *Suitable for a recluse* (*sāmaṇaka*): appropriate for a recluse (*samaṇa*). *He*: the bhikkhu. *By that*:
by means of that requisite (*parikkhāra*). *This too*: the setting aside of another requisite suitable for a recluse.
By the word "too" (*pi*), it refers back to the previous cutting of cloth.
“They gather in a group. The construction is: “there are eight or nine bhikkhus. “Of them” means of those eight or nine.
“In this way,” etc., is the conclusion. The construction is: “this is the state of insufficiency.
Again, showing the deficiency of the robe itself, he said “or else,” and so forth. Herein, in the first method, there is a deficiency of both the robe and the person.
[The former] exists [in the case of] the robe itself at the end; this is the distinction between these two.
215. Discussion on the Dyeing of Robes.
344. "But that which has been used by a householder" means a cloth that has been used by a householder; "something ripens" is the grammatical connection.
“Sītudaka” means cool water. This is a reversal of gender (liṅgavipallāsa). Regarding “Uttarāḷumpa,” one should divide the words as “uttara uḷumpa”;
by eliding the letter *u* after the vowel *a*, and lengthening the preceding vowel, it is called “Uttarāḷumpa. “Uttarāḷū” means northern water.
For the word *uḷu* is a synonym for water; that which protects (*pāti*) or guards (*rakkhati*) that [water] is “Uttarāḷumpa.”
Showing its actual form, he said: "a support for dye. *Rajanaṃ* means a dye-skin. *Hi* indicates the fruit. *Rajanaṃ* means dye-water.
*Hi* indicates the detailed explanation. *Thevo* means a drop of dye. *Na visarati* means it does not flow out.
Regarding *rajanāḷuṅkaṃ*, the derivation of the word should be understood here in the same manner as before. *Rajanauḷuṅkaṃ* refers to that which is designated as dye...
A "dye-tub" (*rajanauḷuṅka*) is that which is made for the purpose of holding water.

He said, "that very thing together with its handle," showing that a bowl joined with a handle is a "handle-bowl" (*daṇḍakathālaka*). A "dye-vessel" (*rajanakuṇḍa*) is a large jar used for pouring dye.
"Elsewhere" (*aññatra*) means another place. Since the word *patthinna* is a synonym for "stiff," he said "stiff" (*thaddha*). "Ivory and saffron robes" (*dantakāsāvāni*).
Here, by the word "tooth" (danta), its color is to be understood; that [color] belongs to these, thus they are "tooth-colored" (dantāni).
These are both "teeth" and "yellow robes" (kāsāva), hence "tooth-yellow robes" (dantakāsāvāni). Demonstrating this meaning, he said: "tooth-colored. The grammatical connection is:
"they wear tooth-colored yellow robes."
216. The Discourse on the Allowance for Tattered Robes (Chinnakacīvarānujānanakathā) 345.
"Bound by a long boundary" means bound by a long limit. "Shaped like a crossroads" means the shape formed by the convergence of four roads.
Regarding the phrase "you are able," here the prefix *upa-* combined with the root *saha-* has the sense of capability.
He said, "Are you able? However, the prefix *pa-* has the sense of overcoming, as in such words as *pasahati* ("he overcomes").
The construction is: "Who indeed" means that Ānanda, who will indeed understand—that Ānanda is wise. The construction is: "*Kusī*" is the name, the designation. By the word "etc.
(*ādi*) in "downwind etc.," it includes the surrounding area and so forth. The construction is: "*Aḍḍhakusī*" (Half-Kusī).

Regarding *gīveyyaka*: here, in order to show the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as "that which is woven with thread on the neck" (*gīvāyaṃ suttasaṃsibbitaṃ*), he says "in the place that wraps around the neck," and so forth.
By the term "*āgantukapaṭṭa*," he shows the actual form of the suffix *-eyyaka*.
This same method applies to "*jaṅgheyyaka*" as well. "This name" refers to "*gīveyyaka*" and "*jaṅgheyyaka*."
*Nāmaṃ* means "name. *Iti* means "thus. *Etaṃ* refers to this [phrase] beginning with "anuvivaṭṭaṃ. The construction is: "The name 'anuvivaṭṭa' is this.

*Vivaṭṭassa* refers to the middle section. Regarding *bāhantaṃ*, in order to show the meaning of the word—that the ends placed above the arms are called *bāhanta*—he says "of the arm," and so forth. *Tesaṃ* refers to those two ends. *Etaṃ* refers to this [term] "bāhantaṃ."
217. Discussion on the Allowance of the Three Robes (Ticīvarānujānanakathā) 346.
Regarding the phrase "when they have been reduced to the state of having their belongings cast off" (*ukkhittabhaṇḍikabhāvaṃ āpādite*):

here, in the term *ubbhaṇḍita*, *ukkhitto bhaṇḍo* means "cast-off belongings"; thus, the word-meaning is shown as *ubbhaṇḍitā* meaning "those who have reached the state of having their belongings cast off. Those [monks] were thus *ubbhaṇḍita*.
“Bhikkhus addasa” (the monks saw) is the construction. “By way of insertion into a seat” (bhisisaṅkhepena) means by way of placing [something] into a seat;
the sense is “by way of entering,” which is what is meant by “in the form of a seat. “There” (tattha) refers to Dakkhiṇāgiri. “Those monks going” (gacchantā te bhikkhū) is the construction.
By the phrase “of the measure of eight” (aṭṭhapamāṇāsū), he shows that here the suffix -ka has the sense of measure in the expression “antaraṭṭhakāsu.”
In some manuscripts the word *pamāṇa* (measure) is not seen; it should be understood as having dropped out. "At night" (*rattīsu*) is the connection [to the previous context].
Regarding "the Blessed One" (*bhagavantaṃ*), since this is used in the accusative case to express the sense of the dative, he says "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*).

Regarding "cold-naturesd" (*sītālukā*), he says this while showing the etymological meaning: "those for whom cold is their nature (*pakati*) are 'cold-natured' (*sītāluna*); they themselves are 'cold-naturesd' (*sītālukā*)."
“*Sītapakatikā*”: the construction is that those sons of good family who are by their very nature afflicted by cold are called “cold-sensitive” (*sītālukā*). Regarding the word *ekacciyaṃ*:

here the word *ekacca* is a synonym for “one,” as he says, “a single cloth. By this, he shows that the suffix *-iya* is used in the sense of identity, taking the form *ekacca* (one) and adding the suffix *-iya* in its own sense.
By the word “cloth” (*paṭṭa*), it is shown that *ekacciyaṃ* is that which is connected with this “one” (*ekacca*).
Having established the literal meaning, he demonstrates the form of the suffix *iya*, which occurs in the sense of being "connected" (*niyutta*). "Iti" means "thus. The connection is:
"The Blessed One permits. "The others" refers to the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the inner garment (*antaravāsaka*), as distinct from the outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*).
218. Discussion on Excess Robes, etc.
348. Regarding the term *acchupeyya*: here, *acchi* refers to the pupil of the eye; that which is like this is *acchic-chiddo*.
That which is to be approached or brought near to that is *acchupeyya*. By the phrase “should cause to stick,” he shows the intended meaning.
“Therein” means in the refuse-rag (*paṃsukūla*). “All this” refers to the entire statement beginning with “the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) is double-layered.”
"Having extracted" means having removed. "Interwoven" means sewn together by being bound to one another. 351. "Leading to heaven" (*sovaggika*):
here, heaven (*sagga*) is so called because beautiful things such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth are its summit (*agga*).

There is an elision of the vowel *u* in the first member of the compound, and with the substitution of *u* for *u*, it becomes "suvaggo. That which has giving as its cause for attaining such a beautiful heaven is "leading to heaven" (*sovaggika*). GIVING.
Showing this meaning, he said: “The cause for attaining heaven. With the word “removes” (*apaneti*), he shows the sense of removal belonging to the verbal root *nud*.

Regarding the term “healthy” (*anāmayā*): here the word *āmaya* is a synonym for disease; thus he said “free from illness” (*arogā*). That which has no *āmaya* is “healthy” (*anāmayā*). 353. “To those who have attained jhāna”:
this is said because the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is suppressed in ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) who have attained jhāna.
356. "Shown by way of combination" means *sandidṭṭho*. "Shared by way of combination" means *sambhatto*. "Spoken to face-to-face" means *ālapito*. "By these" means by these two. 221.
Discussion on robes and so forth that do not fall under the final alternative.
359. "Made from rags" (*katapaṃsukūlo*) means rags have been made. By this, it is shown that the word "from rags" (*paṃsukūlato*) functions as an adjective for the following word.
...shows. "By the application of a patch" means by the fixing of a patch. In the phrase "by means of thread alone," the word *eva* (alone) excludes a piece of cloth (*pilotika*).
"Having pulled repeatedly" means having drawn it out repeatedly; for the root *abhi-dhā* has the sense of drawing.
By the statement "the corner of the outer robe is long," [it implies] that here, in the term *vikaṇṇa*, the word *kaṇṇa* is understood as meaning an uneven edge.
What does it show? "From that" means from the dripping. "Decaying" means taking on folds.
Showing the etymological meaning of *aṭṭhapadaka* as "sewn with an eight-padded [patch]," he said, "to sew the edge of the bowl with a piece cut in an eight-padded pattern.
Therein, "to sew the edge of the bowl with a piece cut in an eight-padded pattern" refers to sewing by means of an eight-padded drawing.

Having shown the seam here and there, one should sew the edge of the bowl. There is also a reading, “by means of an eight-padded patch” (*aṭṭhapadaka-cchannena*), which means by means of the shape of eight wooden planks.
By the phrase “the visiting bowl should also be given,” it indicates that [the bowl] is brought in subsequently as a visitor.
The phrase "it is given" (*dīyati*) indicates the etymological meaning of *anvādika*. There is also a reading with the fourth vowel:

it should be understood as *anvādhika*, meaning that which is placed or deposited subsequently (*anu-pacchā*) as something adventitious (*āgantuka*). "But this," however, refers to the *anvādhika* itself.
(361) "Of the remaining kinsmen" means of those kinsmen other than mother and father. "He surely causes to fall into ruin" means that while perishing, he causes [them] to fall.
“*Vassiko*”: it is designated and grasped [as such]; thus, when it is said "*vassika-saṅketa*," he says "four months.
*Hi* means "truly" or "because. The connection is with "the forest-dwelling bhikkhu.
*Tenā* means "by that forest-dwelling bhikkhu."
222. Discussion on the Origin of Robes Belonging to the Saṅgha. 363.
“In another place” means in a location other than where it was given. The construction is: “Even those robes that have been taken away belong to you alone.
“Of them” refers to the robes. “Another” means one other than the one who has resided for the rains alone. For five months, all of that belongs to that very bhikkhu.
"Is" is the connection. "That which is a robe"—the connection is that all of that is a robe. "Whatever [robe]" means even a robe.
"He"—meaning the bhikkhu—"takes"—this is the connection. "For the purpose of the rainy-season residence" means for the sake of the bhikkhu’s dwelling during the rains.
"From a deposit set aside" means from a deposit set aside by attendants who have applied it for interest. "From what is produced thereon" means...
“In that monastery” means from its site, such as the coconut grove and so forth. “This” refers to what will be stated hereafter. “In this” refers to the statement:

“Those robes belong to him alone until the suspension of the Kathina. “Which” refers to the robe. The word *pana* indicates a specific distinction. “This” (*idaṃ*) is merely a poetic ornament for the phrase.
“Here” (*idha*) means in this monastery; some also say it is merely a verbal expression. “Even for one who has not spread the Kathina” (*anatthatakathinassāpi*).

The word *pi* (also/even) indicates, all the more so, one for whom the kaṭhina has been spread. In the phrase "during the fifth month," the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).

"From that" means from the fifth month. The construction is as follows: does he give this *vassāvāsika* robe-material to the Saṅgha that has already spent the rains-residence in the past year, or rather to that of the future year?
"At the time of the back [of the rainy season]" refers to the period starting from the first day of the summer months until...
The full moon day of Assayuja is the time for the back (of the rainy season).
"From the rains" means from the month of the rains. "In this" refers to among these robes. "Some monks" is the connection [to the context].
"That matter" refers to the reason for that robe belonging to the Saṅgha. "Right there" means in the very place it was taken. "He" refers to the one who took the robe belonging to the Saṅgha.
"Bhikkhu. "Therein" means in the monastery and so forth.

"Him" refers to the bhikkhu who is taking the robes. Showing the duties in detail, he said "Therefore, etc. The connection is: "those [robes] are to be distributed by that bhikkhu. "Of him alone" means of him alone while he is making the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhahantassa*).
The connection is: "each single portion. In this context, the construction is: "I myself am [the one] in this place. "They become wrongly grasped" means...
The intended meaning is that they belong to the Saṅgha alone. There is a distinction: if one takes them with a sense of ownership, thinking, "These robes are mine," they are wrongly taken;
if one takes them without a sense of ownership, thinking, "These come to me," they are rightly taken.
Regarding the phrase "when the kusa grass has been cast down," he says "in one portion" and so forth, showing that the suffix *-ta* here denotes the present time.
