"Already taken" means that when a single portion has been identified as "this belongs to him" by way of a blade of grass that has fallen into one section, it is "already taken" because it is thereby known to belong to all [the monks in that group]; this is the intended meaning.
"From here" means from the very robes and alms-food. "Being prepared separately" means while the robes and the alms-food are being prepared separately.
He says, "She was giving very slowly," because she was giving very slowly; the intention is that she is spoken of as "giving" in the present tense because the act of giving was uninterrupted.
"Because the giving was interrupted" means because the state of the act of giving had been cut off.
The connection is: "But this case has arisen. And these elders refers to these elders, such as Nīlavāsi and others, who were preeminent among those who uphold the Vinaya.
223. The Discourse on the Case of Upananda the Śākyaputta.
364. "In this" means in the case of Upananda. "His" means of Upananda. "Residents of the village" means those who dwell in the village.
“Ayanti upanando” means: he is called *mukhara* because his mouth (*mukha*) is harsh (*khara*); thus, *mukhara* [is formed] with the elision of the letter *k*.

Alternatively, *mukhara* means “one who has a mouth,” where the suffix *ra* occurs in the sense of possession (*mantutthe*), expressing censure. “A light offense” (*lahukāpatti*) refers to an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭāpatti*). “Of that very person” (*tasseva*) refers to the monk who was taken hold of.
The construction is: “when there is the laying down of the burden” (*dhuranikkhepe sati*).
“Having a single intention” (*ekādhippāyo*) means it is intended or desired for the sake of one person;
it is the share of one individual. Therefore, he said, “only as the share of one individual. “In whatever way” (*yathā yathā*) means by whichever mode. “He” (*yo*) refers to the individual share.

“In that same way” (*tathā tathā*) is to be supplied [from the context]. “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the statement beginning with “But here” (*idha pana*). “In each dwelling” (*ekekasmiṃ āvāse*)...
The connection [is as follows]. The word "or" (*vā*) includes other cases such as every two days and so forth. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to each individual portion.
"A single person" (*eko puggalo*) means a single person who resides permanently. "In this way" (*evaṃ*) means when half [of the portion] is being given.

Regarding the phrase "or where" (*yattha vā pana*), it is stated "thus in the former case" (*evaṃ purimasmiṃ*) in order to show the scope of the word "that" (*ya-*) here. The connection is with "in the former residence" (*purimasmiṃ āvāse*). From that...
Here, showing the scope of the word *tasa*, he says: "more than [the portion] from the monastery where one has resided. And this phrase:

"In that case, half of the share of the robe-cloth should be given" refers to the statement *idañca*. "By monasteries within a single boundary" means by monasteries situated within a single precinct-boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"Monasteries with different boundaries" means monasteries situated within different precinct-boundaries. "The taking of lodgings" (*senāsanaggāha*)...
The taking of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*) occurs within the boundary of the preliminary precinct (*purima-upacāra-sīmā*). "Therein" means in the monastery for tranquility (*passambhana-vihāra*).

"The remainder" refers to what remains after the robe (*cīvara*). "In all places" means in all monasteries. "Of one who has gone within the boundary" means of one who has gone within the precinct boundary;
this is to be connected with the word "monk. The robe falls solely to the one who took the lodging, whereas the remainder—namely, all things such as food and medicine—belongs to everyone.
The intention is that it reaches one who has come from another residence and is within the boundary.
224. Discussion on the Matter of the Sick: 365.
Regarding "having laid him down on a bed," here "laying down on a bed" means having him lie down upon a bed; thus he said.
"‘Lay him down on a couch’: ‘soiled with urine and excrement’ means defiled by urine and feces.
‘Whoever’ (yo) means anyone. ‘Me’ (maṃ) means me. To show this meaning, he said:

‘by performing my instruction and admonition. The sense is: by performing my instruction (ovāda) and my admonition (anusāsani). ‘In this context’ refers to the passage beginning: ‘Monks, whoever should attend upon me...’"

Showing that the meaning of the Sutta is not to be taken literally because it is of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), he says, “And of the Blessed One,” and so forth. “Of whom” means of the sick person.

Regarding the phrase “the preceptor and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) includes five persons: the teacher (*ācariya*), the co-resident student (*saddhivihārika*), the resident pupil (*antevāsika*), the one who shares the same preceptor (*samānupajjhāyaka*), and the one who shares the same teacher (*samānācariyaka*).
The connection is with the words “or he may go about alone. The word “even” (*pi*) in the phrase “even the senior of the Saṅgha” indicates that this applies even to him, let alone others.

366. Regarding the phrase "abhikkamantaṃ vā" (or to one approaching): since it is said that "one who approaches" (*abhikkamanto*) means "one who comes toward," he says "or to one increasing" (*vaḍḍhantaṃ vā*), meaning in the sense of growth.
The connection is with the words "he does not manifest illness" (*ābādhaṃ nāvikaroti*). By this, he shows the actual form of the suffix *-anta*.
The connection is with the words "this food" (*idaṃ nāma bhojanaṃ*). Regarding the word "saṃvidhātuṃ": here, the verbal root *dhā* is preceded by the prefix *sam-vi*.
The root *kara* has the sense of all roots, and the root *kara* also has the sense of all roots; therefore it is said, "one should prepare medicine.
"Assa" means "of the attendant of the sick person. Rejecting such meanings for the word *antara* as "middle" and so forth, he says, "it is called the cause.
225. Discussion on Property Belonging to the Deceased.
367. Regarding the phrase *kālaṅkata*, he says “by the act of dying” (*kālakiriyāya*) to show that here the act (*karaṇa*) is what is meant by “done” (*kata*).

“Having obtained permission” means having obtained permission [with the words]: “Venerable sir, such-and-such a monk has passed away; I seek the Sangha’s permission to give his three robes and his bowl to those who attended him while he was ill.”
369. Regarding "the gain for those who attend to the sick" (*gilānupaṭṭhākalābha*), it refers to what is to be obtained by those who attend to the sick.
The connection is with the phrase "all the bhikkhus. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that case where [a person] has passed away.
What do they say? The construction is: "They say, 'All [the requisites]... [belong] to the owners. Between the two opinions, the latter opinion is approved by the commentator of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
They say: "That which is the matter. Explaining the very meaning already stated—that "whatever exists should be given"—he said:
"In another... should be given. "That" refers to the requisite.

"Equal" (*samaka*) means that the measure of this portion is equal; thus it is "equal. "Merely by way of arrangement" means merely the assigning [of tasks], such as "do this and do that. "The senior's portion" means a double portion.
"Yo pana" means "but a certain monk. "Ettha" means "among many monks. "Yena" means "by anyone whatsoever"; it is connected with the words "given" and "prepared. "Ekadivasampi" (even for one day):
the word "pi" (even) indicates that this applies even more so for two days and so forth. "Sopi" (he too):
the word "pi" indicates that it is not only one who has been an attendant for many days, but he as well. "Samīpaṃ" means "into the presence of the sick person."
“He is coming” means he is approaching nearby.

“Because of expectation” means because of the expectation of a share. By the words “I will come again and look after it,” he shows that [the gift] should not be given to one who goes away thinking, “I will not come again to look after it.
“Having laid down the burden” means having laid down the burden of attending.
The construction is: "Let there also be a woman. "Of that bhikkhu" means of that bhikkhu who has passed away.
"Even if it is worth a thousand [pieces of gold], it must be given only to those who attended to the sick"—this is the construction.

"Other" means other than the bowl and robes. "They" refers to the attendants of the sick. "The remainder" means what remains after the bowl and robes. "Than that" means than that which is abundant and of great value.
“Requisites for the three robes” means the set of three robes. “All this” means all these requisites.
“He receives” means the attendant of the sick person receives.
“He” refers to the one who has passed away. “Of anyone” means of either a householder or one who has gone forth. “To him alone” means to the very person who received the gift.
"By consent indeed" means by the consent of the monks themselves. "In each respective place for the Sangha alone" means for the Sangha residing in each respective monastery (*vihāra*).
This was said with reference to requisites placed within the monastery.
If they have been placed in a village or in the forest, the entire Sangha is the owner. Why? Because the inheritance belongs to the Sangha alone. "Even of many" means...
Starting from three, there are also many. In relation to such statements, even within the Teaching (sāsana), the three grammatical numbers—singular, dual, and plural—are seen in their meaning;
however, since there is no distinction between the dual and plural in terms of sound (sadda), it should be understood that the dual number does not exist [as a distinct category].
"Only what has not been taken" means: because it belongs to oneself alone and because it is common to others as well, it is "only what has not been taken."
If all have died, they may give with consent; it is indeed well-given. "That" refers to the property. "Among them" means among all of them. 227.
Discussion on the Prohibition of Garments Made of Kusagrass, etc. 371.
By the phrase "made of akkanāḷa," he shows the etymological meaning: that which is produced from *akkanāḷa* is called "akkanāḷa."
Regarding the term *makacimayo*: here, by the word *makaci*, the meanings of the word *potthaka*—such as "book" and so forth—are excluded.

By the word *maya*, it indicates, in the same manner as before, that a taddhita suffix has been applied to denote "made of. "The rest" refers to the kusa-grass robes and so forth, other than the bamboo-reed books.
"Among them" refers to the kusa-grass robes and the others.
372. "Of one with a triple-layered robe" (*tipaṭṭacīvara*)—this is said with reference to the gift of a double-layered robe (*dvipaṭṭacīvara*) in its middle part.

"Of those" (*tesam*) refers to those [robes] that are entirely blue and so forth. "A bodice" (*kañcuka*) means a covering. For it is called a "bodice" (*kañcuka*) because it is worn on the body (*kaciyati*), that is, bound to the body.
"Also a turban" (*veṭhana*) refers to a head-dress (*uṇhīsa*). For since it is that by which the head is wrapped, it is therefore called a "turban" (*veṭhana*).
It is said [thus]. Regarding the phrase "made of tree bark" (*rukkhachallimaya*): here, by the word *rukkhachalli*, the meaning of the term *tirīṭa* as "bark" is indicated.
For it is called *tirīṭa* because the bark (*vakkala*)—being a constituent part of garments—goes to or attains concealment (*tirobhāva*), that is, the state of being covered;
or alternatively, because it goes forth (*eti*) and functions as a tree that is concealed (*tiropati-channa*). [This is stated] in the *Abhidhāna*.
In the 442nd verse of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, however, there is a reading as "tarīṭa" without the vowel *i* after the letter *t*.

Regarding "pādapuñjana": it is called *pādapuñjana* because by means of it the foot (*pāda*) is honored (*pujiyati*) or cleansed (*sodhiyati*); it is the third consonant produced from the palate (*tālujo tatiyakkharo*).

Regarding the phrase "when there is a suitable substitute for one who goes away" (*sante patirūpake gāhake*): here, a "suitable substitute" (*patirūpaka*) refers to a person with whom a monk has established a close relationship while he was still present.
This shows that if there is no one suitable to receive it, it is indeed properly distributed when the Saṅgha distributes it without having given it away.
"Seven persons" refers to seven types of individuals: four who are departing, insane, deranged in mind, or afflicted by pain; and three who have been suspended (ukkhitaka).
230. Discussion on the arising of robes when the Saṅgha is split.
376. Regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha is split," it is specifically the splitting according to two factions that is intended here, and nothing else;
thus he says, "two factions. The construction is: "they give robes to one faction. With reference to the two factions, it is said, "of the entire Saṅgha.
"This" refers to the robe. "Of that very robe" means of that [specific] portion.
"Only the robe. "In which place" means in whatever location. "The water for the offering is the measure" means that the water for the offering itself is the measure, not the gift to be given.
Therefore, the intention is that those who receive the water for the offering become the owners of the gift.
The construction is "by both sides. "Beyond the ocean" refers to Jambudīpa; for it is [farther] than the island of Siṃhala.
The further shore of the ocean is called "the other ocean. "The other side" refers to the side not yet obtained, in contrast to the side already obtained of both the water and the robe.
232. Discussion on the Summary of the Eight Robes.

379. The connection is with the words "now he says. "By way of the person-as-the-basis" (puggalādhiṭṭhānanayena) means that it is stated by way of the basis of the agent—the person who is the giver—by means of a verb expressing the agent, namely, "he gives within the boundary" (sīmāya deti).
"In this regard" (ettha) refers to these eight headings (mātikā). The construction is: "the eighth heading among those eight. "Therein" (tattha) refers to the eight [headings].
Regarding the *mātikās* (matrices). "In all cases" means in all instances such as "he gives by prior agreement," and so forth.

However, in the exposition of the *mātikā* beginning with "within the boundary... it should be distributed," the construction should be understood as follows: "the decision (*vinicchaya*) is to be known thus. Regarding the phrase "he gives within the boundary," the connection is that "fifteen kinds of boundaries are to be known here.
"Therein" refers to among those fifteen boundaries. The connection is that "the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*) is delimited. "Such an extent of place" refers to...

Because the place that qualifies for a boundary (parikkhepa) has not been stated exclusively [in the previous section], he says "Furthermore" (*apica*) and so forth, in order to show the place that qualifies for a boundary exclusively.
Or, the connection is with the phrase "of those cast out from a permanent assembly. The word "at the limit" (*pariyante*) depends on what precedes and follows it;
therefore, it should be construed with all three ablative cases. And "that," namely, the *upacāra-sīmā* (the precinct boundary).
Thinking, "When the bhikkhus increase, the residence also increases," it was said: "when the bhikkhus increase. This is to be connected with "of all the bhikkhus.
"Just as stated" means just as stated in the discourse on the boundary (sīmākathā).
Furthermore, in the phrase "apica kho," the word *api* expresses a question; for the meaning is: "by whom was it established? [The answer is: by kings and royal ministers.
The connection is with the word "establishing" (*ṭhapenti*). "Boundary of gain" (*lābhasīmā*) means the limit of gain. "Which" (*yaṃ*) refers to the gain.
"Within this interval" (*etthantare*) means within this interval of a *gāvuta* and so forth. "Called a boundary of gain" (*lābhasīmā nāma*) means a boundary delimited by gain.
"Therein" (*tattha*) refers to among many countries. "And intermediate islands" (*antaradīpā ca*) means other islands than the great island; the intention is that they are small islands.
“In this very boundary” means in the *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary or partial boundary) itself. “Of those very [monks]” means of those who have entered that *khaṇḍasīmā*.
Showing the meaning and result of this, he said “of others,” and so forth. The construction is: “of a monk standing in a tree or on a mountain, or one situated below in the middle of the earth.
This is to be connected with “of one standing within this *upacārasīmā* (proximate boundary). “Within the *samānasaṃvāsasīmā* (boundary of common affiliation)...”

Regarding "at the great boundary" (*mahāsīmāya*). Regarding "in a broken boundary or in the interval between two boundaries" (*khaṇḍasīmasīmantarikāsūti*): this refers both to a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and to the interval between two boundaries (*sīmantarikā*).

In that case, it extends even to the locations of two villages. However, what has been given within the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*) does not extend to the village location, because it has been stated:
"excluding the village and the vicinity of the village."
The island marked by the *jambu* tree is Jambudīpa. Those whose hands and feet are copper-colored (*tambo*) or red (*lohito*) are the *tambapāṇino*.
There were seven hundred people, beginning with Prince Vijaya. Their dwelling place was Tambapaṇṇi; that very island is Tambapaṇṇidīpa, [the reference being] "in that.
The connection is that it is a portion belonging to all of them. "Right there" means in Jambudīpa itself. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion.
"But he who speaks" is the connection [of the sentence]. "From that," meaning from the speaking; "to another" is the connection. "Him" refers to the Elder Mahāsiva.
"Even three leagues away"—the word "even" (api) indicates that it applies even to those less than that distance. "All this"—meaning all this, such as the receiving of gains and so forth.
"Thus they said" is the construction.
Because it proceeds according to what is desired by the *katikā* (agreement), it is abundant; therefore, in order to show here the agreement of desire, it is said:

“by means of an agreement for equal gain. Therein, in the reading “he gives by means of an agreement,” the connection is: “it is to be distributed by the monks who have assembled. “Of that” refers to the monastery.
“Dwelt in by the Buddha” means presided over by the Buddha in the sense of sovereignty.
“Was inhabited” means it was inhabited by the Buddha. “By this much” means by this mere announcement.
“Seated” means he is actually seated, or as if seated. “In that monastery too” means even in that ancient monastery and so forth.
“In this very way” refers to [the proposal]: “The Saṅgha approves of making this ancient monastery have an equal share with that new monastery,” and so on.

It is just so. "Here" means in an old monastery (*porāṇaka-vihāra*). "Therein" means in a new monastery (*nava-vihāra*). "In this way" means that just as one monastery is to be constructed together with another monastery, so too [is it done];
such is the meaning. Regarding the term *bhikkhāpaññatti*: here, *bhikkhā* (alms) is established and fixed by way of constant practice; thus it is called *bhikkhāpaññatti*.
Showing this, he said: "In the place where his own relinquishment is established. The word *tassa* refers to the reading: "Where permanent services are performed for the Saṅgha.
The construction is: "The meaning should be understood in this way. *Yattha vā* means "or in which place. *Anena* means "by the giver of the robe. The connection is:
"or fixed meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) and so forth were caused to be provided. By whom? [By the one mentioned previously.]

"Panā" means by the giver of robes. "The entire monastery" (sakalopi vihāro) refers to the entire monastery together with its arama grounds. "Therein" (tattha) means in the case of the giver of robes.
"These" (ime) refers to the monasteries such as those where the duties of the *pākavatta* are performed. "Dhuvena kariyantīti" means monasteries that are maintained permanently.
"He" (so) refers to the giver of robes. "Yattha" means in whichever place. "Sabbattha" means in all the many monasteries.
*Te hīti*: by the majority of the monks. *Dhuvakāresūti*: the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa). *Ekatthāti*: in one particular place of distribution (*dhuvakāra*).
By the phrase, "If he says, 'Take it according to the number of monks,'" it is shown that if he does not say this, it is not permissible to take it after dividing it according to the number of monks;
the intention is that it is permissible to take it according to the number of monasteries (*vihāra*).
“Tathā” means “in the same way as he says, ‘Take it by counting the number of bhikkhus’”—this is the meaning. “Ettha” refers to the items to be distributed. “Taṃ” refers to the bed and chair;
the connection is that they are to be given after asking. “Pucchitvā” means having asked the donor;
“vadati” means the donor speaks. “Saṅghassāpi”: the word “api” (also/even) indicates that it is not only for the donor [but also for the Sangha].
The connection [of the sentence] is: "It should be divided by the Saṅgha standing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).

"Standing within the boundary" means standing within the precinct boundary. "Even though not having arrived" means even though not having reached the place of distribution. "Of a lazy nature" means of a nature characterized by indolence. "Persistence" (*ṭhitikā*):
it is called *ṭhiti* because one persists (*ṭhīyati*) by way of continuity; that itself is *ṭhitikā*. Alternatively, it is so called because it begins from the point where one has stood.

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that “it should be given,” the word-play (*vacanattha*) should be understood as follows: it is called *ṭhiti* because it stands (*tiṭṭhati*) there by way of continuity; that very thing is *ṭhitika*.
“Setting aside the *ṭhitika*” means setting aside the *ṭhitika* consisting of twenty years. “Of them” refers to the elders.
“Of those who have arrived one after another” refers to those who have arrived at the place of distribution. Or [it refers to] at the door of one’s own monastery. One’s own...

The construction is: "It blows only within the monastery. "Boundary" (*sīmā*) refers to the precinct boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*). The construction is: "When the Elder’s seat has been ascended. "By the number of years" means by the counting of years.

"Individually" (*pāṭekkaṃ*) means separately. The connection is: "all the robes indeed. To show the meaning of what was poorly spoken and wrongly grasped, he said: "In every place they have gone to, they belong only to the Saṅgha. "One" means one among the ten types of robes.

The construction is: "There is either a flower or a fold on the cloth. "By that" means by the flower-fold. "A single thread" means a single strand. "Therein" means in those places where it remains fixed. It must be accepted by both [the donor and the recipient] because there is no fixed ownership.
The construction is: "Whatever robe belongs to the bhikkhu himself.
It is also permissible for paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearers), because it was said, "We give to the Saṅgha," or "We give to you," rather than saying, "We give to the bhikkhus" or "We give to the elders."
It is also permissible for those who wear rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*). For "senior monks" (*bhikkhuthera*) does not refer to oneself alone, but includes many others;
therefore, it is permissible. When it is said, "for the Saṅgha," it refers exclusively to the Saṅgha itself;
therefore, even when it is said, "for the Saṅgha," it is not permissible, let alone when it is said, "for you."
"From that" means from many pieces of cloth. "It is not permissible to take" means it is not permissible for *paṃsukūlika* (rag-robe wearers) to take them.
"That" refers to the cloth. "Therein" means among the requisites. "Thread" means yarn.
Having thus demonstrated the legal decision regarding what is given by entering within the boundary (*sīma*) with the words, "We give this to the Saṅgha," [the text continues] outside the boundary...
Showing that [the robe] has been given, he said, "But if," and so forth.
"And bound on one side" means bound on one side without exceeding twelve cubits. "But those who" refers to the monks.
Regarding the phrase "he gives to both Saṅghas," although it is stated by way of four sentences, he indeed gives to both Saṅghas.
Showing the names, he said: “Even when it is said, ‘I give to both Saṅghas,’ and so forth.
Because it is included by the mention of “both Saṅghas,” that is, because the individual is included by the mention of “both Saṅghas.
By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends the method by which, having made twenty-one divisions, one [share] is to be given to the Cetiya. There is no portion that reaches the Cetiya.
Because it was not included by the mention of both Saṅghas.
"Therein" means among the two Saṅghas, individuals, and cetiyas. The rest is easily understood.
"Formerly" means during the time when the Buddha, the Blessed One, was living. "Then" means when the Buddha, the Blessed One, was still present.
"An image" (*paṭimā*) means a likeness; for it is called an "image" because it is made by the Blessed One as something resembling himself.
"A shrine" (*cetiya*) means a stupa; for it is called a "shrine" because it is to be honored and worshipped by gods and humans, or because it is to be built up with bricks and so forth.
"Therein" refers to among the objects to be given. "Which" is a demonstrative pronoun referring to the action.
The construction is: "giving what. Regarding the word "therein" (*tattha*), it means in that act of giving.
To show the meaning of the pronoun "who" (*yo*), which expresses an indefinite [subject], he says: "either a renunciant or a householder.
Because the sequence of the earlier and later actions is not fixed due to their variable nature, it is stated: "or even having eaten first, one may perform the duty afterwards."

By the phrase “even having carried it a long distance, it should be honored,” it is shown that there is no offense of sending by messenger on foot. The connection is with the words “of the monk who carries. The word “gacchato” (of one going) is used in the genitive case in a sense of disregard. “That” refers to the food brought for the Saṅgha. Regarding “of the Saṅgha that has spent the rains”:
one who has spent the rains is called *vassaṃvuttho*; this is a compound where the *ta* suffix is not elided (*aluttaka-tanta-samāso*).
That very Saṅgha is the “Saṅgha that has spent the rains”; [the text says] “of that. The word *yāvatika* is a synonym for “as much as”; thus he said, “as many as.”
"Even for one who has gone off in another direction": the connection is that [the robe] must be given even to one who has departed for another region.
"They say": other teachers, distinct from the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), say this.
"This": this statement. "To those who have arrived": to those who have arrived at the place where it was given. "Of all": of all those who have spent the rains retreat wherever they may have been.
Of all [monks]. Therein means in the monastery. Therein means when that [invitation] exists, or among those monks. "Dwelling for the rains" means those who dwell for the rains;
of them. "In the month of robes" means in the month of Kattika, characterized by the robe [season].
"The last day of winter" refers to the full moon day of Phagguna, which is reckoned as the last day of winter.

*Vassāvāsikaṃ* means a robe that should be given to those who have resided during the rains. Showing the manner in which it should be assigned, he said, "to one who has completed the residence for the past rains," and so forth.
Therein, *atītavassāvāsassā* means either of one who has completed the past rains, or of the Saṅgha that resided during the past rains.
*Taṃ* refers to the robe.

"Having set aside" means having set aside [the portion] for the monastery. "Of those who have arrived" means of those who have reached this place. "From here" means from the time of the distribution of robes. "Those" refers to the monks who have resided during the rains retreat.
Regarding the word *ādisa*, he says "having pointed out" (*ādisitvā*) while showing that it is a form ending in the suffix *-tvā*.

The construction is to be understood as: "this meaning is to be known. "In that" refers to the reading beginning with "or with rice-gruel. "Or for the sake of today's" means for the sake of the merits arising today.
"Of them" refers to the inviters; it is connected with "of the monks who have entered. "By whom they were invited" means by whichever monks they were invited.
Or, it is connected with "whose bowl [is filled]. "It does not reach them" means it does not reach any of them; why? Because they were not invited.
"It does not reach them" means it does not reach those [invited monks]; why? Because [the food] was [taken] from the house where they were invited.
"Because he has been expelled. "He" refers to the donor.

"Even before this" means even prior to this [incident]. "His" refers to the donor. "Having caused to dwell" means having caused to reside. "He" refers to the donor. "Who" refers to the bhikkhu; the connection is with the word "dwells. "Those" refers to the medicines. "This" refers to the robe-cloth (*cīvara*).

By the phrase "and for his pupils," the co-residents (*saddhivihārika*) should also be understood, because they have the habit of dwelling near [their teacher] through recitation and other such duties.

One who has come to receive a recitation (uddesa) and one who departs after having received it—even though these two do not habitually dwell at the end [of the teacher's bed]—are called "pupils" (antevāsika) by way of conventional usage (rūḷhi).
By this, he shows that one who has come to receive formal dependence (nissaya) and one who has previously received dependence in the presence of an elder are both called "pupils.
This applies to those who, having performed their duties, wander about while receiving recitations, cross-examinations (paripucchā), and so forth.

The construction is: "it applies to all resident pupils (*uddesantevāsika*). By this, one should also include co-resident pupils (*saddhivihārika*), dependent pupils (*nissayantevāsika*), those who have received full ordination as pupils (*upasampadantevāsika*), and those who have gone forth as pupils (*pabbajjantevāsika*), because they too are monks who maintain a fixed residence. "In all cases" means throughout the entire *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.
Thus ends the construction of the commentary on the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.
9. The Campeyya Khandhaka. 234.
The Story of the Monk of the Kassapa Clan. 380.
Regarding the phrase "at the Gaggarā lotus pond" in the Campeyya Khandhaka, [it should be understood that] here the word *gaggara* functions as a proper noun.

Pointing this out, he said, "by a woman named Gaggarā. By this, he shows that the word *gaggara*—having made the name *Gaggarā* the basis for its application—denotes the female substance (*itthidabba*).
The phrase "bound by a cord" (*tantipaṭibaddho*) means bound by a cord. The construction should be understood as:
"In such cases as 'he even made an effort regarding the rice-gruel' (*ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā*), this is how the analysis is to be known. "Of that bhikkhu" refers to the one named Kassapa-gotta.
Of that bhikkhu. "Right there" means in Vāsabha village itself. 382.
The connection is with the phrase "performing an illegal act by a faction," and so forth; this refers to the distinction [between these cases]. 236.
Discussion on legal acts deficient in the motion (ñatti), etc.
Regarding the phrase *aññatrāpi dhammā*: here, the word *dhammā* is an ablative used in the sense of the accusative; thus he says, “*aññatra dhamman*.
Since the particle *aññatra* can occur with any of the second, third, or fifth cases when employed, it also functions as an accusative.
Therefore, it is stated, “or rather, this very reading [is correct]. By the phrase “by means of a real object (*bhūtena vatthunā*),”...
This shows the true meaning of the word *dhamma*. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends the reference by way of the linguistic nature (*saddasabhāva*) alone, not the meaning.
Therefore it was said: “But here,” and so forth. “The Teacher’s instruction” (*satthusāsana*) means the Teacher’s command.
Since the Teacher’s command consists in the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the proclamation (*anusāvana*), he says: “the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation.”
With the phrase “both censured and done,” he shows the dual compound (*dvandava*) for the term *paṭikuṭṭhakataṃ*.

That which is to be censured is *paṭikuṭṭha*; that which is to be done is *kata*, namely the action (*kamma*). Demonstrating this very meaning, he says, “that which [is done] among others,” and so forth. Therein, *yaṃ* refers to the action.
387. "In the Pāḷi" means in the Vinaya-pāḷi. "That" refers to the formal act (*kamma*); the connection is that "it is not performed. "In this" refers to the Aṭṭhakathā.
"And that," meaning "and that detailed exposition," is connected with "has come down.

To the question, "Why has it come down specifically by way of the *ñattidutiya* (second-motion) and *ñatticatuttha* (fourth-motion) formal acts, when it ought also to have come down by way of the *ñatti-apalokana* (motion-and-announcement) formal acts? he says: "Because, however... and so forth.

The construction is as follows: while there is either omission or alteration in the *ñattidutiya* (motion-and-second) and *ñatticatuttha* (motion-and-fourth) formal acts, there is none in the *ñattikamma* (motion-only act).
The intention is that in a *ñattikamma*, because no other business can arise once the motion has been established, there is neither omission nor alteration.
"Those" refers to the *ñattikamma* and *apalokanakamma* (informal acts). "Of all formal acts" refers to all of them.
Of the four types of legal acts (*kamma*). "From another" means at another time, at the conclusion of the assembly.
237. Discussion on the Fourfold Assembly and so forth. 388.

Regarding the phrase "that which is called a legal act," this is the construction. "Of them" refers to the Saṅgha. "One who has reached the point of the legal act" (*kammappatta*): here, by means of the legal act, or of the legal act...
Rejecting the meaning "attained by means of," he said, "attained through action" (*kammaṃ patto*).

According to the method of the Pāḷi, the meaning "attained among actions" (*kammesu patto*) is also appropriate. Furthermore, according to worldly usage, the meaning "attained by means of action" or "attained from action" (*kammena kammassa vā patto*) is likewise entirely appropriate.

389. *Parisato* means "from the assembly" (*parisakāraṇā*). *Tattha* refers to the textual passage beginning with "If, monks, [a legal act] is to be performed by a quorum of four," or else to the twenty-four types of persons.

*Kammanānāsaṃvāsaka* is one who has been subjected to an act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*). *Laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka* is one who follows the views of those who have been suspended (*ukkhittānuvattaka*).
By the word "having been" (*hutvā*), [the text indicates that the status applies] in the twenty-four instances such as "with a nun as the fourth."

This shows that it has the status of an adverbial modifier (*kiriyāvisesaṇa*). "Bhikkhunīcatuttho" means "one for whom a bhikkhunī is the fourth"; the meaning of the word should be understood through such expressions as "the Saṅgha consisting of a group of four," and so forth.

(393) By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "parivāsādī," it includes *mūlāyakaṭṭhana*, *mānatta*, and *abbhāna*. "Of these" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the formal acts (*kamma*) beginning with *parivāsa*. "From here on" (*parato*) means in the subsequent *Cūḷavagga*.
394. Regarding "of one who has performed a censurable act": this refers to an act performed after having become censurable. Regarding "of a regular monk" (*pakatatta*):
here, the meaning is shown as "one whose self-nature (*attā*)—consisting of natural virtue (*pakatisīla*)—is his," thus "a regular monk.
It is said, "of one who has not committed a *pārājika* offense," because even one who has not fallen into a *saṅghādisesa* offense possesses unimpaired virtue.
This shows that even one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense remains a regular monk (*pakatatta*). For he is indeed called "one whose virtue is unimpaired" in this context;
however, elsewhere, because a *saṅghādisesa* constitutes a failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*), one who commits it is indeed called "one whose virtue is impaired.
Regarding the term *ānantarika*: here, [the commentary] explains both the connection of the word *anantara* and the meaning of the suffix *ṇika*.
Showing this, he said: "of one sitting immediately after himself. Therein, by the word "his own" (*attano*), he shows the connection with the word "immediately after" (*anantara*);
by the word "sitting" (*nisinnassa*), he shows the meaning of the suffix *-ika*.
239. Discussion on the Two Expulsions, etc.
395. "By way of the basis" (*vatthuto*) means by way of the causal basis. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the textual passage beginning with "Monks, there are these two...

By the phrase "spoken with reference to" (*sandhāya vuttaṃ*), he shows that the Sutta beginning with "one who has not attained" (*appatto*) has a meaning that requires further interpretation (*neyyattha*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakammaṃ*).
Again, "that" (*taṃ*) refers to the very same act of banishment. The connection is: "this monk has not attained."
"Why is it 'not attained'? he asks, and says "Because," etc. "By its individual characteristic" means by a characteristic that occurs without being separated [from the object].
What is meant is: by a characteristic belonging to oneself, which exists separately from oneself.
"If it is not attained, why is it 'well-extracted'? he asks, and says "But because of this," etc. "Of him" means of the bhikkhu; "he would make" means...
The connection [is as follows]: if the Saṅgha expels him by means of an act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) and so forth, then he is "properly expelled"—this is the connection.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu. Since it is permitted, the construction is: "therefore, he is properly expelled. To the question, "By how many factors is it permitted?
he says: "Even by a single factor."

396. Regarding *osāraṇā*: here, because the verbal root *sar* with the prefix *o-* has the sense of "entering," he says "entry. Regarding the word *tattha* (therein), it refers to the reading beginning with "*osāraṇā*. Regarding the phrase "*osāreti*":
here, rejecting the sense of entry by way of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) and so forth, he says "by way of the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*).
In the expression "*sahassakkhattumpi*," the particle *pi* has the sense of censure; [it implies] even one time and so forth.
This shows what kind of discussion it is. "Sātisārā" means "with fault. "Tathā" means "just as the preceptor and the teacher are with fault, so too [is the case].

The connection is that the rest of the community of performers is also with fault. Since it is stated that "the thirty-two beginning with those whose hands have been severed are well-ordained," it should be understood that the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is valid even for the blind, the mute, and the deaf, provided they have not already left the order.
There are thirty-two [offenses], beginning with those involving the cutting off of hands.
397. "By way of a non-existent basis" means by way of an untrue basis, or by way of a non-occurring basis.

"Therein" refers to the textual passage beginning with "But here, monks. Regarding the term *paṭinissajjitā*, one should understand that the suffix *-ta* functions here in the sense of the object (*kamma*).
Pointing this out, he said, "It should be relinquished.
241. The Discourse on Upāli’s Questions: 400.
"Therein" refers to among Upāli’s questions. The construction is: "One question was asked together with [the rules concerning] *tassapāpiyasika* and so forth."

The connection [of the following] also applies to the monks (*bhikkhu*). By the word "also" (*pi*), it is shown that these [cases] are not to be applied only to the *Upāli-pañha*, but rather also to the prohibition of monks.
242. Discussion on the Act of Censure (*tajjanīya-kamma*).
407. “In this case, monks, a monk who is quarrelsome,” and so forth—this is the connection with what was said.

Regarding the phrase “in that [passage],” it refers to the text beginning with “In this case, monks. As for the term *anapadāna*: here the root *dā* preceded by the prefix *apa* has the sense of “cutting off”;
thus he says, “*Apadāna* is called a delimitation (*pariccheda*). There is no *apadāna*, meaning no cutting off or limit to the offense.
The meaning of the phrase "of this" (*etassa*) should be understood as "without a source" (*anapadāna*). The connection is that "that very same text has been stated.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tattha*), the construction is: "it is not possible to understand any determination of the meaning according to the text.
Thus ends the analysis of the commentary on the Campeyya Khandhaka.
10. The Kosaṃbakakkhandhaka. 271.
The Discourse on the Quarrel at Kosaṃbī. 451.
The connection should be understood thus: "In the Kosaṃbaka-kkhandhaka, this sequential narrative (anupubbikathā) is to be known in this way. [From] the Vinaya according to the Pāḷi.
And because he upholds both that [Vinaya] and its meaning, he is a *vinayadhara*; likewise, because he upholds the *suttanta*, he is a *suttantika*.
"Among those" refers to those two monks. The connection is: "The monk who was a *suttantika* went out. "Remnant of water for rinsing the mouth" (*ācamanaudakāvasesa*):

that by which one rinses or washes is "rinsing" (*ācamana*); that very water is "water for rinsing" (*ācamanaudaka*); the remainder of that very [water] is "remnant of water for rinsing" (*ācamanaudakāvasesa*).
“Remaining rinsing water” is the meaning. “That monk” refers to a monk who specializes in the Suttantas. “In this regard” means regarding the setting aside of the remaining rinsing water.
By saying, “If there is [any], I shall confess it,” he demonstrates his own tractability and desire for training.
“Those” (tē) connects with “how” (kathaṃ). Alternatively, “those” (tē) connects with “there is not” (natthi). “Unintentionally” means without mindfulness.
Thinking that there might even be a side of non-offense due to what has already been done, he said, "There is no offense. But here, it is indeed an offense. "He" refers to the Suttantika.
"The Vinayadhara too"—the connection is that the Vinayadhara, moreover, reported [this]. "Even while committing [an offense]"—the word "even" (pi) has the sense of reproach.
"They"—the connection is that they spoke, referring to the dependents of the Vinayadhara. "Of him"—of the Suttantika. "They"—referring to the dependents of the Suttantika.
The connection is: “The *nissitakas* reported. “He” refers to the *suttantika*. “A speaker of falsehood” means one whose habit is to speak what is unreal or to utter words that are untrue.
“This one” refers to the *vinayadhara*. “Those” refers to the *nissitakas* of the *suttantika*; the connection is: “they said.
“From that” means from the cause of increasing the quarrel. The connection is: “the *vinayadhara* did [this].”
453. By the phrase “it is not yet split,” he shows that in the word *bhinno* (split), the future tense is used for the suffix *-ta* in the sense of an event that is certain to occur.

Demonstrating this very point along with a simile, he says “Moreover (*apica*),” and so forth. “*Taṃ*” refers to the crop. By the phrase “it will split,” he demonstrates the etymological meaning of the expression:
“because it will split, it is called ‘split’ (*bhinno*)”. And “*so kho pana*” refers to the Saṅgha. By way of quarreling...
The connection is with the word "will split" (*bhijjissati*). "By way of the sense of agitation" (*sambhama-atthavasena*) means by way of the sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
For the word *sambhama* functions in three senses: respect, fear, and spiritual urgency; here, however, it functions in the sense of spiritual urgency. The intended meaning is:
"by way of the sense of spiritual urgency when the Saṅgha of monks has split. This refers to the [word] "fear" (*bhaye*) mentioned below.
It should be understood that this was spoken with reference to the meaning of "confusion" (sambhama), which is included by the word *ca* in the verse beginning, "In anger, in praise...
Here, in the reading, "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split!

The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split!", the term *āmeḍita* refers to what is uttered (*ita*) repeatedly (*ā*) due to the delirium (*meḍa*) of being afflicted by fear and so forth; thus it is called *āmeḍita*.
"454. *Hīti* is the opening word. The connection is with the phrase "the Blessed One might say. *Ukkhepakā* means those who cast out or remove.
*Ukkhittānuvattakā* means those who follow one who has been cast out. *Etesaṃ* refers to those who follow the cast-out person.
Again, *etesaṃ* refers to the casters-out. *Pakkho* means a friend or side. *Tantimeva* means the text itself, or the activity itself."

455. "The monk" (*yoti bhikkhu*). The connection is with "he arouses a thought" (*cittam uppādeti*). "To you" (*tumhe*) is said with reference to those who speak according to the Dhamma (*dhammavādino*).
"What do you say? (*kiṃ bhaṇatha*) means "what words do you speak. The connection is with "having thus asked. "And of them" (*tesañca*) refers to those who speak according to the Dhamma.

"And of the others" (*itaresañca*) refers to those who speak contrary to the Dhamma (*adhammavādino*). "These" (*ime*) refers to these monks on one's own side. "Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.

“It invalidates the formal act (kamma)” means that it invalidates the act because of the statement: “Monks, if one should perform a formal act with a fourth member who belongs to a different community (nānāsaṃvāsaka), it is not a valid act and is not to be performed.
“Of the others as well” refers even to those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī).

Even one who sits on the side of those speaking according to the Dhamma but adopts the views of those speaking contrary to the Dhamma (adhammavādī) becomes a member of a different community from those speaking according to the Dhamma.
This method is not stated here because it is established by the meaning of the method already explained. "Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu; "enters" is connected with "takes. "Having sat down" is the construction. "These" refers to these bhikkhus on one's own side.
"The others" refers to the other bhikkhus on the opposing side. "Of them" refers to those who speak according to the Dhamma. Where...
"Or on that side"—that is, on whichever side of those who speak according to the Dhamma.
"He takes them as 'these are speakers of the Dhamma'" means that he perceives the monks belonging to each respective side, whether they are truly so or not, as "these are speakers of the Dhamma. 456.
Action performed by the body is bodily action; action performed by speech is verbal action. Therein, bodily action...
“Giving indications”: monks give indications by striking with the body. “Giving indications through verbal action”: monks give indications by speaking harshly.
Therefore it is said, “striking with the body,” and so forth. “Giving indications” means causing [the offense] to proceed.
By the phrase “through anger,” the sense of “through affection” is excluded. “Unrighteous acts” (*adhammiyāni*) means those things which ought to be done through unrighteousness.
By the word “kiccāni,” he shows the actual form of the suffix *iya*. Regarding the term “asammodikā,” he says “asammodikāya” because there is an elision of the letter *y* here.
By the word “kathāya,” he shows the actual form of the suffix *ṇika*, having formed the word “asammodikā” from the sense that it “produces non-concord.
Regarding the phrase “releasing the range,” here “range” (*upacāra*) refers to the hand of those striking one another.

The meaning is "having left that place where one has reached. Regarding the term *āsanantarikā*, he says "one seat as an interval" (*ekekaṃ āsanaṃ antaraṃ*) to show that it is called *āsanantarikā* because one seat is the interval—that is, the intervening space—between this act of sitting.
By the word "having done" (*katvā*), he shows that it functions as an adverbial modifier of the action.
457–8. The construction is: "This, it is said, is the intention of that bhikkhu. "These" refers to the bhikkhus who are overcome by anger;
"the Blessed One, however, spoke" is the connection. By the phrase "Anattho ato," he shows the elision of the vowel *o* in the compound *anatthato*.
In order to show the meaning of those words, he says "from this" (*etasmā*), and so forth. By the phrase "Or else" (*atha vā*), [he explains] "anatthado."
It shows that it is stated as "anatthato" by changing the letter *da* to *ta*, just as in the case of [the term] "Sugata" and others.
"Anatthado" means one who gives what is harmful (*anattha*). 464.
Regarding the word "puthu": here, the word *puthu* is a synonym for "great," therefore he says "mahā. "Assa" refers to the quarrelsome person.
Regarding "of the people" (*janassa*): here, the word *sama* is a synonym for "similar," thus he says "one who is similar" (*ekasadiso*);
this is a compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). The construction is: "this person is a maker of strife. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those persons who are makers of strife.
The connection is: "there is also this one other reason. "No one thought so" (*na maññittha*) is to be construed as: "not even a single person thought so. By this...
In this context, by the word *amaññaruṃ*, the substitution *ru* for the case ending (*āvibhatti*) is shown.
Regarding *parimuṭṭhā*, he says "those whose mindfulness is completely lost" (*parimuṭṭhasatino*), showing that it means "those for whom mindfulness is completely lost.
Because it is stated in the eight-syllable verse that "the fifth [syllable] is light everywhere," the fifth syllable, the letter *ra*, is short.
It occurs. Therefore it is said: "The short vowel substitute has been made for the letter *rā*. In the phrase *bhāṇino*, it means "of those speaking words.
Regarding the term *mukhāyāmaṃ*, here the word *āyāma* is a synonym for extension (*vitthāra*), and since extension means spreading out, he says "to spread out" (*pasāretuṃ*).
By using the suffix *-tuṃ* which indicates the sense of the dative case (*sampadāna*), he shows that the dative sense is expressed by the accusative case. [The word] *nītā*...
Showing that the act of the one who recites the *kammavācā* is a subordinate action, he says, "this state of shamelessness.
Because it is a verb with two objects (*dvikammakadhātu*), the primary object, "his own," must also be supplied. "That" refers to the quarrel.

By the word "knowing" (*jāna*), he shows both the meaning and the grammatical construction of the word "wise ones" (*vidū*). The etymological derivation (*vacanattha*) should be made as: they see (*vidanti*) or they know (*jānanti*), thus they are "wise ones" (*vidū*).
The intention [is as follows]. "Accompanied by danger" (*sādīnava*) means occurring together with danger (*ādīnava*), that is, with fault (*dosa*).
"This" (*ayaṃ*) refers to quarreling (*kalaha*). Regarding the phrase "and those who harbor resentment toward it," in order to show the referent of the word "it" (*taṃ*), it is said:

"animosity" (*āghāta*). "Those" (*ye*) refers to people. "Harbor resentment" (*upanayhanti*) means they bear a grudge or bind [themselves] to it. Regarding the term "Sanantana," since the word *sanantana* is a synonym for "ancient" (*purāṇa*), he says: "the ancient one" (*porāṇo*).
By the word “aññe” (others), he excludes here the meanings of the word *para* such as “behind” and so forth.
By saying “saṅghamajjhe” (in the midst of the Saṅgha), he shows the referent of the word *ettha* (here) in the phrase “mayam ettha yamāmase” (we here restrain ourselves).

Since the verbal root *yam* has the sense of restraining (*upayamana*) and the letter *e* is merely a particle, he says “upayamāmā” (we restrain ourselves). [The meaning is: “We go constantly and continuously into the presence of Death.”
By this, he shows the form of the word *na jānantī* (“not knowing”). The construction there is: “among that great mass of people, those who are wise.
*Evaṃ hi* means “just so. The construction is: “Knowing thus, those wise ones proceed. *Medhagā* are quarrels;
they are so called because they go on or persist while causing injury (*medhantā*) or harm. Some say the suffix *ṇvu* is added to the root *medha*. According to their opinion:
The reading should be *medhakā* with the first syllable long. *Tesampīti*:
even for those [two], namely Prince Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu. *Saṅgatīti*: meeting. *Voti*: for you.
For you whose parents' bones were not shattered, whose lives were not taken, and whose cattle, horses, and wealth were not seized.
The construction is: "Why is there no meeting for you with them?

Regarding the phrase "all dangers," he says "both manifest dangers and concealed dangers" while showing that the word "all" indicates both the reason already stated and a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). By the word "having overcome," [it means] "having mastered."
This shows that the word *padassa* functions as a suffix (*paccaya*). "By him" means by the wise companion.
Regarding the phrase "like a king" (*rājāva*), one should analyze the compound as *rājā iva*;

thus, taking the word *rājā* as an illustration (*upalakkhaṇa*) and showing that the word *iva* indicates the sense of comparison, he says "just as" (*yathā*), and so forth. [The words] *raṭṭha*, *vijita*, and *saddā*.
These are reciprocal expressions. Because the relationship between the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*visesya*) is understood through their mutual application, it is said:
“the conquered kingdom. By the phrase “like an elephant in the forest,” he shows the analysis of the words. In order to show the meaning of those words, he says:
“‘Mātaṅga’ is said to mean an elephant,” and so forth. By the expression “is said to mean an elephant,” [it is implied that] its great limbs (*aṅga*)—that is, its body—are large.
By the meaning of the word *mātaṅga*, it is shown that an elephant is called a *mātaṅga*; this is because the word *mahanta* (great) undergoes the substitution of *māta*.
The word *nāga* applies to five meanings: a serpent, an elephant, a *nāga*-tree, something supreme, and a designation (*nāma-paññatti*).
Here, showing it in the sense of "supreme," he says: "‘Nāga’ is a designation for what is great. [The phrase] *mātaṅgaraññeva*...
Having shown here that the word *iva* functions to indicate a simile, he says "Just as... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the application of the meaning.
By the phrase "And just as Pālileyyaka," he indicates the actual form of the Mātaṅga elephant by way of illustration.
275. The Discourse on the Journey to Pālileyyaka.
467. *Pālileyyaka* refers to the elephant-nāga dwelling in the Palila thicket of forest.
Since the two terms "elephant" (*hatthī*) and "nāga" are stated as synonyms (*pariyāya*), he says "great elephant" (*mahāhatthī*) to indicate the superior sense.
The construction is: "the tips were broken off by those elephants and others who went further and further ahead. *Obhaggobhagga* means having been broken down.
Showing that "obhagga" means fallen down, he said, "having broken it again and again, it was felled.

By the word "uccaṭṭhānato" (from a high place), he shows the meaning of the prefix *ava* by way of its downward direction. "Etassa" refers to the elephant-nāga. "Tete" refers to the elephants and so forth.
"Tehī" refers to those elephants and so forth. The construction is: "by those drinking. "Kaddamodakāni" means waters mixed with mud.

Regarding the phrase *īsādantassāti*: here, he says “of one whose tusks are like the pole of a chariot” (*rathaīsāsadisadantassa*) to show that *īsādanta* means “one whose tusks are similar to a pole.

By the term “chariot-pole” (*rathaīsā*), he excludes the plow-pole. Regarding *yadeko*: this means “that which is one. He says “because” (*yasmā*) to indicate that the word *yam* has the sense of a reason.
“Of this elephant” (*assa nāgassa*) refers to the noble elephant (*hatthināga*). “By the elephant” (*nāgena*) refers to the Buddha-elephant (*buddhanāga*).

Regarding the phrase "for as long as he desired," the question arises: for how much time did he remain there? To this, it is said: "for three months. "By this much" means by this duration of dwelling for three months. The connection is: "it became widespread. "Everywhere" means throughout the entire surface of Jambudīpa.
By the expression "the residents of Kosambī," the author shows the etymological meaning of *kosambaka*, namely, those who dwell in Kosambī.
276. The Discourse on the Eighteen Bases (Aṭṭhārasavatthukathā).
471. By the phrase "taking up what has been obtained" (*laddhiggahaṇa*), he shows the etymological meaning as "that which is taken up" (*ādīyate*) or "having taken up" (*ādāya*).
475. "On that very day" means on the very day of performing the concord of the Saṅgha. 476.

"Without going from root to root" means without having gone from one root to another. By the phrase "departed from the meaning" (*atthato apagatā*), [he indicates] from the standpoint of the meaning...
The phrase "apetā atthāpetā" indicates the meaning of the word [as "those who have departed from the meanings"].
By the phrase "byañjanamattaṃ upetā," it indicates the meaning of the word "byañjanūpetā" as "those who have approached or entered into the mere letter.
Regarding the expression "atthesu jātesu," he says "vinaya-atthesu uppannesu" because here the word *jāta* is a synonym for "arisen."
And that phrase should be applied to all the following phrases, beginning with "in the affairs of the Saṅgha.
To show that "one of great benefit" means one for whom there is a great benefit consisting of assistance, he said, "one of great assistance.
Regarding the phrase "blameless in the first instance," he said "firstly" (tāva) to indicate that the word "first" (paṭhama) here is used in a figurative sense. From virtue...
By virtue of his moral discipline. *Upekkhitācāro* means one whose conduct is observed from a state of equanimity (*upekkhā*).
There is also a reading, *apekkhitācāro*. *Upaparikkhitācāro* means one whose conduct has been thoroughly examined;

thus he is called *upaparikkhitācāro*. Regarding the word *visayha*: here, the verbal root *sah-* preceded by the prefix *vi-* has the sense of overcoming, and the suffix *-tvā* is applied; showing this [the author] says:
He said: "Having overcome. "Not departed" means not separated from the cause. The connection is: "the monks speaking. To show that meaning, he said:
"Because," and so forth. "He" refers to the monk; the connection is "he does not diminish.

Since "through envy" already includes going to a wrong course due to hatred (*dosa*), by the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*), "by way of going to a wrong course" refers specifically to the remaining wrong courses.
"Sota" means a bhikkhu. "Chambhati ce vā" means he is indeed paralyzed; the meaning is that he becomes rigid.
"Vedhati ca" means he trembles. "Yo ca" refers to the bhikkhu. "Īdiso" means such as this—that is, he does not possess this kind of speech characterized by envy or by following a wrong path.
"Kiñca bhiyyo" is a combination of particles; the meaning is: what more than what has been stated should be told?
The construction is: "The meaning of this verse should be understood. "Ya" (who) refers to the bhikkhu. "Hi" (indeed) means truly.
Regarding "kālāgataṃ" (timely), he says "arrived at the appropriate time for speaking," thereby indicating both the time to be grasped and that it is a *sattamī-tappurisa* compound.
Regarding "vacaṃ" (speech), he says "speaking," showing that the word does not primarily denote the speech itself, but rather the person possessing the speech who is the primary referent.
Regarding the word *āceraka*: here, it is the teacher’s (*ācariya*) that is *āceraka*, and it is his own (*sassa*) that is *saka*.
Demonstrating this etymological meaning, he says, “in his own teacher’s doctrine. Because it occurs within a verse, the substitution of *ācera* for the word *ācariya* must be made.
By the word “doctrine” (*vāde*), he shows the actual form of the suffix *ṇika* when it functions in the sense of “this belongs to that” (*idamatthe*). “They are able to measure” (*alaṃ pametuṃ*).
Here, the word *alaṃ* has the sense of capability, and the word *pama* has the sense of weighing; thus he says, "capable of weighing.

Regarding the phrase "in what is to be told" (*kathetabe*), the word *tave* usually expresses a state (*bhāva*) elsewhere, but here it expresses the object (*kamma*); thus he says, "in what is to be told.
"Skilled in the points where one has gone astray" means skilled in the points where one has erred.
The connection is: "This verse was spoken. "That" refers to what is to be told. The construction is:

"This is the meaning here" means that this very thing is the meaning of the verse in this context. By the word "gacchantī" (going), he shows the sense of motion for the verbal root *vaj* in the word "vajantī" (proceeding).
By the phrase "attano ācariyavādaṃ" (his own teacher’s doctrine), he shows the meaning of the compound "sakaṃ ādāya" (taking his own). [The term] *ācariyavādo*...
Because it is to be taken up and grasped, it is called "ādāya" (having taken). "Tadanurūpaṃ" means suitable for that matter.
The connection is: "the bhikkhu while answering. "By the eight qualities of a messenger" refers to:

"He is one who hears, one who makes heard, one who learns, one who retains, one who understands, one who makes understood, one skilled in what is appropriate and inappropriate, and one who does not engage in quarreling."
By these eight limbs of a messenger being thus stated, he says, "To whom [is] the work of a messenger?

[The answer is] "To the Saṅgha. These are the duties of a messenger; those very duties are the "work of a messenger" (*dūteyyakamma*); [it refers to] among those. "This" is the indicator of the matter (*atthajāka*);

the construction is: "it has been stated" (*vuttaṃ hoti*). Alternatively, "this" (*idaṃ*) means this very sense. "It has been stated" (*vuttaṃ hoti*) means it has been spoken. In the latter method, there is a reversal of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).

It should be understood as follows: they bring [offerings] and sacrifice, that is, they honor, thus they are *āhava*, the donors; their bringing [of offerings] is *āhūna*. That which is to be brought and sacrificed, to be honored, is *āhuti*;
[the phrase] "that *āhuti*" refers to this. In the expression "in the affairs of the Saṅgha," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Therefore it was said: "of each respective affair. Regarding the term *karavaca*: here, although one should say *vacokara* (one who performs speech), due to the nature of the verse, the word order has been reversed.

Because it was said, "one who acts upon the word," he says, "acting according to the instruction. By the phrase "by means of acting upon the instruction," he shows the referent of the pronoun *taṃ* in the expression "he does not conceive by that.
The construction is: "The monk who incurs [the offense] becomes guilty of an offense. In the phrase *tassā ca*, the substitution of *ssā* for the locative ending *smā* should be made.
*Yathā* means "in whatever manner"; the meaning is "by way of the formal act of the Vinaya" (*vinayakamma*). *Yesu* means "in as many matters as there are.

The connection is: "both these are the Vibhaṅgas. *Assa* refers to "of the bhikkhu. Regarding the phrase "of the basis for emerging from an offense" (*āpattivuṭṭhānapadassa*), the word *pada* has the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇa*), and it is used in the genitive case with the sense of the locative;
thus he says, "in the cause for emerging from an offense. By the word "skilled" (*kusala*), [it implies] one who is proficient.

"A wise person" (*paṇḍito*): by the meaning of the word "one who knows" (*kovidoti*), it shows that he is called "learned" (*kovido*) because he knows—that is, understands—what is contemptible and evil.

The construction is: "The monk goes while performing [the duties]. By the word "duties" (*vattaṃ*), it shows the scope of the pronoun *taṃ* here as referring to the procedure of reinstatement (*osāraṇa-tanti*).
By the word "which" (*yā*), it shows that the pronoun *etaṃ* in the phrase "this too" (*etampi*) functions as an indefinite demonstrative.
"In all cases" means throughout the entire Kosambaka Khandhaka.
Thus ends the commentary on the Kosambaka Khandhaka.
Thus [ends] the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The exposition of the Mahāvagga is completed. By me,
named Jādilañchita, it has been recited for many.
The method of exposition for the Mahāvagga-Khandhaka is completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Exposition of the Pācittiya and other rules.
Having thus completed the method of exposition for the Khandhaka of the Mahāvagga,
I shall now provide the method of exposition for the Cūḷavagga.
1. The Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammakkhandhaka) 1.
Discussion on the Act of Rebuke (Tajjanīyakamma).
1. The construction is as follows: "In the first chapter on formal acts within the Lesser Section (Cūḷavagga), the meaning should be understood thus. Regarding the phrase "of the Lesser Section":
The term *pada* refers to the phrase "in the Kammakkhandhaka," indicating a relationship of part to whole (*avayavi-sambandha*).

The word *tāva* means "starting from" the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka, or "first among" the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka and so forth. Both the particle *ceva* and the particle *ca* indicate that the phrase "Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka" constitutes an *asamāhāra-dvandva* (a copulative compound where the members are not joined as a collective).
The name of the supports (*nissaya*) is applied to those who rely upon them by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra-vasena*).
Showing that the co-residents (*saddhivihārikas*) and pupils (*antevāsikas*) were also named Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, he says, “Their dependents as well,” and so forth.

By the word *pi* (“also”), he includes those who are in the vicinity. By the phrase “very strong,” he shows that it has the sense of intensification, since the two words “strong” and “weak” are used here as synonyms for the purpose of comparison. Where one should say “strong-strong,” [the repetition indicates]...
This was stated by lengthening [the vowel] due to the mellifluousness of speech (*vācāsiliṭṭha*). "Reply" (*paṭivadatha*) means speak in a concealed place.
By this, he shows that the verbal root *mant* in the phrase "respond with this" (*iminā paṭimantetha*) has the sense of speaking secretly.

Regarding the meanings of the suffixes expressing the instrument or the act of speaking, he says "more capable" (*samatthatarā*) while demonstrating that "those whose purpose is sufficient" (*alamatthā*)—meaning those who are sufficient for their aims—are "those more excellently sufficient" (*alamatthatarā*).

Regarding the discussion on the twelvefold set of illegitimate legal acts (*adhammakamma-dvādasaka*), the construction should be understood as follows: "The determination regarding such cases as 'performed in the absence [of the parties]' is to be known.

Demonstrating that "in the absence" (*asammukhā*) means being devoid of the [four] presences, he says: "performed without the presence of the Saṅgha, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the person. Regarding the phrase "without having questioned":
By the phrase *iminā appaṭipucchā*, he shows that the suffix *tvā* has become the vowel *ā*. By *tasseva*, he means "of the very one who was accused.
Regarding the term *adesanāgāminiya*, in order to show that the vowel *a* here has another meaning, he says: "one who is subject to a *pārājika* offense... or [the like].

The word *ettha* refers to the act of condemnation (*tajjanīyakamma*). The phrase *nava padā* means "in nine places"; this is the nominative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). In the preceding cases...
The construction is: “among the nine locations mentioned in the three triads. This should be connected with the word “each one.
“By these two terms” means by these two words [“each one” and “by these”]. “Twelve triads” means twelve, having combined the nine triads with the three preceding triads.
“In the white sides as well” means even in the white sides, by way of the absence of negation.
6. By the phrase “of those who have gone forth,” he excludes what is incompatible for householders. In the expression “together with grief, etc.,” the word “etc.

includes “together with joy. At this point, in all the manuscript commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), starting from the reading “he should not be ordained” (meaning “he should not be ordained by acting as his preceptor”) up until “he should not be associated with,” [the text continues].

There is a reading stating, "Having reconciled one another, no quarreling should be allowed. For now, the explanatory text for the eighteen duties of proper conduct (*sammāvattanavatta*) has been written;
that text should not be written in this place. Why? Because it does not follow the sequence of the Canon (*pāḷi*).
Indeed, in the Commentary itself it says: "We shall explain the eighteen duties of proper conduct in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*."
Because it will be explained [later], and because it has been commented upon according to the wording in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*. Therefore, that reading is not an ancient reading;
it should be understood as a reading inserted later. The connection is:
"Of three monks, O bhikkhus," and so forth, as it was said. "Even by each one" means even by any one of the three factors.
By this, he shows the state of being worthy of the formal act (*kamma*) through the manner of producing the constituent parts of the sentence. *Hi* means "truly. The construction is:

"It is stated that the specific factor for a *niyassa* (restraint) is the fact of being a frequent offender. Here, it should be understood that the word *iti*, which expresses a manner, is indicated by elision (*lutta*).
This same method applies to the following [formal acts] as well. It is called *tajjaniya* because one is corrected (*tajjīyati*) by means of this disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*).
That which is subject to censure is itself the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*).

Because by means of this disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) a fool is made dependent and is separated [from his companions], it is called *niyassa*; the doubling of the letter *s* occurs because it belongs to the *div*-class (the sixth class of roots), as in the examples "nassaṃ" or "vassaṃ.
That which is itself the act of dependence is the act of dependence (*niyassakamma*). One is expelled from the village and so forth.

"By this disciplinary act" refers to the act of banishment (*pabbājanīya*); that very act is the "act of banishment. "In three" refers to the three factors consisting of being a quarrelsome person, one who repeatedly commits offenses, and a defiler of families;
[the phrase] is to be construed as "by whichever factor [among these]. The construction is: "If it is permissible to perform all the disciplinary acts [simultaneously].
If this were the case, then the statement made in the *Campeyyakkhandhaka* would be contradicted—this is the connection [of the argument].
"By way of the diversity of word and meaning" means by way of the difference between the words and the meaning. Elaborating on that very point, he said:

"For one deserving a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure), etc. Therein, the construction is: "The meaning of the words beginning with 'Of three, monks,' etc., is the fulfillment of the constituent factors (*aṅga-sambhava*).
"Therefore" means because it does not conflict; therefore, it is "done by the Saṅgha."
“Connection. The construction is: “of that bhikkhu who is deserving of a formal act such as *tajjanīya* (censure), by means of this characteristic.
Having thus shown the purpose of concluding the formal act, he said, “But for whom...,” etc., in order to show the presence of the necessary factors.

Therein, “for whom” refers to the bhikkhu; the connection is with the word “exists” (*atthi*). In the phrase “among quarrelsome persons, etc.,” the word “etc. includes those who repeatedly commit offenses and those who corrupt families.
"He includes. The connection is: "If the Saṅgha so desires, it may perform [the act].

"Worthy of the formal act" (*kammāraha*) means worthy of the formal act (*kamma*), or worthy regarding the formal act. "In this" refers to the *Kammakkhandhaka*. "By the former" refers to the previously recited *Campeyyakkhandhaka*.
"The latter" refers to the subsequent *Kammakkhandhaka* as recited by others. "It accords" (*sameti*) means it goes together with, or is consistent with.

*“Therein”* refers to the legal acts (*kamma*); the connection is with the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*). Alternatively, it refers to the constituent factors (*aṅga*); the connection is with the phrase “by way of one who creates strife.
*“But then”* means “even though it has been spoken in that manner. The connection is with the phrase “by the one reciting the formal motion (*kammavācā*).
*“Indeed”* (*hi*) indicates the result. *“By a true basis”* means by a factual ground. *“Of another legal act”* means of a legal act other than the act of censure.
Of the formal act. Why? The construction is: "Why should a formal act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*) be performed against one who is foolish, incompetent, and prone to many offenses?
"This too" refers to the formal act of censure as well. "In all cases" means in all formal acts.
This concludes the discussion on the eighteen grounds for which a formal act should not be suspended.
8. *Pannaloma* means "with fallen body hairs. *Etam* refers to the procedure (*vatta*). *Netthāram*:

here, when there is a conjunction of uncontacted consonants, the letter *th* replaces the following letter *t*; therefore, the reading with the second [dental] consonant is appropriate. *Yena* refers to the procedure.
*Nissāraṇā* means "from the point of departure. The construction is: "it should be fulfilled for either ten days or five days."
"Hī" means "truth. "Ettakena" means by this much, that is, by a period of ten or five days.
2. Discussion on the Act of Subordination (Niyassakamma).
11. Regarding the phrase "apissu bhikkhū pakatā," since particles have multiple meanings, here the word "api" has the sense of "always" (nicca).

The word *pakata* has the sense of "overpowering" in such expressions as "overcome by remorse" (*kukkuccapakatā*), but here it is shown to have the sense of "engaged," as he says: "they are constantly engaged.
3. Discussion on the Act of Banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*).

27. *Ettha* means in the case of the story of Assaji and Punabbasu. Regarding *kāyiko*: here, he states "bodily play is called *kāyikā*" in order to show the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) that one who plays with the body is *kāyiko*.

By the phrase "the same method applies," he extends the explanation to the etymological meaning of *vācasiko* (verbal) as "one who plays with speech," and *kāyikavācasiko* (bodily-verbal) as "that which is both bodily and verbal. And here, the latter etymological meaning—
This is a collective dvanda compound; furthermore, grammarians maintain that even in a collective dvanda, the masculine gender may be used in certain instances, as in examples such as "Dhamma-vinaya.
To show the etymological meaning of the word *kāyiko*—namely, "one who transgresses the training rule prescribed for the door of the body"—it is said:
"Transgression of the training rule prescribed for the door of the body is what is meant. [One who] transgresses the training rule prescribed by means of the body...

The etymological meaning of *kāyika* (bodily) is indeed appropriate here. By the phrase “it is called ‘upahananaṃ’,” he shows that *upahananaṃ* means injury (*upaghātaṃ*), and that very injury is what constitutes the etymological sense of *upaghātika*.
By the word “*nāsanaṃ*,” he shows that the root *han* has the meaning of harming (*hiṃsana*).
Bodily wrong livelihood consists of such things as the preparation of medicinal oils and elixirs by means of prohibited medical practices and the like.
The construction is: "by name. By this, he shows the actual nature of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*).
4. Discussion on the Act of Reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*): 33.

In the case of the Sudhamma story, the meaning should be understood as follows: the construction is "in this way. Regarding the term *anapaloketvā*, since the word *loka* preceded by *apa-* has the sense of "asking permission," he says: "without having asked permission."

34. *Kinti* means "what indeed. *Khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ* refers to hard and soft food. *Vā* means "by you. *Gahapati* is a term of address. *Therānaṃ atthāya* (for the sake of the elders) is the syntactical connection.
*Paṭiyattaṃ* means prepared. By the phrase *etaṃ avoca*, he demonstrates the elided sandhi (*niggahitādesa*) in the expression *etadavoca*.
As for the word *yadidaṃ*, because it is joined with the word *tilasaṃguḷikā* (sesame balls), [it functions as a demonstrative].
He said, "The feminine gender," referring to "this which... *Tilasaṅkhalikā* means a ball mixed with sesame seeds.

By the words "that does not exist," he shows that the pronoun *yaṃ* (which) in the subsequent sentence depends upon the pronoun *taṃ* (that) in the preceding sentence. "A certain man" is the connection.
*Pūviyo* means a cake, or trade by means of cakes. "By that" means for that reason. "Him" refers to the householder.

“Thera” refers to the Elder Sudhamma. Regarding the phrase “whatever it may be,” he says, “the expression ‘any little thing’—namely, even a word about a sesame ball,” showing that *kiñci* here means *yaṃ* (that which).
“Idam” means this matter. “So” refers to the chick. “Kākavassitam” means the cawing of a crow;
the connection is that [the chick] did not even do that. In the phrase “tayāpi,” the particle *api* refers back to the chick.
The construction is: "It shows this meaning—that neither the word of a bhikkhu was spoken nor the word of a householder was spoken.
39. The discussion on the twelvefold [set] beginning with illegitimate legal acts (*adhamma-kamma*).
