The connection is with the preceding legal acts. "Therein" refers to the constituent factors (*aṅga*). Just as when the assembly is being scrutinized, there is the acquisition of gain by householders...
The construction is: "they do not obtain. Since the root *sakk* preceded by the prefix *pari* has the sense of "exerting effort," he says, "exerting effort" (*parakkamanto*).

"Therein" (*tattha*) refers to among the non-benefits (*anattha*) and so forth. "Destruction of benefit" (*atthabhaṅga*) means the destruction of the benefit of householders. "Disappearance" (*avasana*) means the disappearance of householders.

Regarding the word "of householders" (*gihīnaṃ*), he says "in the presence of householders" (*gihīnaṃ santike*), because here the genitive case is used in the sense of equality. As it is being done...
The construction is: "He is truthful; thus he does not act [in that way]. The particle *api* in the phrase "even by a single factor" has the sense of emphasizing possibility;
it shows that what need is there to speak of [the case] with more than that number of factors. "In this regard" refers to the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma* (act of reconciliation).
It is called *paṭisāraṇīya* because one's own fault must be made to be remembered (*sārāpetabba*) by means of this disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*); that very act is the *paṭisāraṇīyakamma*.
5. Discussion on the Act of Suspension for Not Seeing an Offense (Āpattiyā adassane ukkhepanīyakamma-kathā) 46.

Regarding the phrase "you should discuss" (*saṃsatha*): here, showing the meaning of the verbal root *saṃs* as "to speak," he says "you should announce. The meaning is: "you should discuss," that is, "you should speak. 50.

Regarding the phrase "he is a maker of quarrels" (*bhaṇḍanakārako hoti*) and so forth: since this is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the cause, he says "on account of quarrels and so forth," etc.

The cause is such things as being quarrelsome; the offense incurred because of that is the fruit; the intention is that a formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) should be carried out for one who does not acknowledge that offense.

"Of that" refers to the offense. 51. "In this regard" means in the formal act of suspension. "Therein" means among the forty-three rules of conduct (*vatta*). "He should be censured" refers to this point.
Rejecting the sense of motion for the root *dhaṃs*, he said, "He should not be reproved.
For in such passages as "he shakes off the dust," the root *dhaṃs* functions in the sense of motion.

Regarding the phrase "not a bhikkhu [reproving] by bhikkhus," he said, "another bhikkhu [reproving] by other bhikkhus," thereby precluding the meaning that it is that very same bhikkhu [reproving] by those very same bhikkhus. "Not one with the banner of a householder" means:

Regarding the phrase "the banner of householders" (*gihīnaṃ dhajo gihiddhajo*), it is said that this refers to white garments and so forth; thus he says, "white garments," and so on. "The triad of terms beginning with 'not [those of] other sects'" refers to the three statements:
"Those of other sects are not to be associated with; monks are to be associated with; one should train in the training of the monks.
By the word "not to be disparaged" (*na apasādetabbo*), [it is implied] "not to be reviled" (*na āsādetabbo*); here, [this is understood] through the verbal root preceded by the prefix *ā*.
This shows the state of equality with the six elements beginning with earth (*pathavī*). Regarding the phrase "either inside or outside," he asks "inside or outside of what?

and replies, "of the monastery (*vihāra*). The construction is that all the remaining [terms] follow in the same way. "By this" refers to the act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) for not acknowledging an offense.
"Of that" refers to the offense. "Here" refers to when the act of suspension has been carried out for not relinquishing a pernicious view (*pāpikā diṭṭhi*).

It is called *ukkhepanīya* because by means of this disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*), one is lifted up, cast out, or removed from [the community] regarding matters such as the failure to see an offense.
That very act is the *ukkhepanīyakamma*.
Thus ends the explanation of the *Kammakkhandhaka*.
2. The Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikakkhandhaka) 1. Discussion on the Duties of One Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikavattakathā) 75.
Regarding the word "pārivāsika" in the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation: they are called *pārivāsika* because they are living their probation (*parivāsa*).
Pointing this out, he said: “Those who are undergoing probation. Therein means: in the derivative compound phrase “those who are undergoing probation.
Among them means: among the four kinds of probation. “Heretic’s probation” (titthiyaparivāsa) means:

the probation of heretics; or, the probation to be given to heretics; or, the probation to be undergone by heretics—thus it is a “heretic’s probation. “Unconcealed probation” (appaṭicchannaparivāsa) means:

"Unconcealed probation" (*appaṭicchanna-parivāsa*) means probation for what has not been concealed. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the probation for what has not been concealed. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to the statement.
"But this" (*ayaṃ pana*) refers to this probation for what has been concealed. "Here" (*idha*) refers to the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.

"The rest" (*sesā*) refers to those remaining other than the probation for what has not been concealed. "The three" (*tayo*) refers to the three beginning with the probation for what has not been concealed; they are "to be given."

[The word] "connection" [is used]. To the question "To whom should it be given?", he says "by whom," and so forth. "And those who have fallen into [an offense]" means those who ought to fall into one.
"Among them" refers to the three kinds of probation (*parivāsa*). "But these" refers to the three. "Here" refers to the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka*.
"Therefore" means because they are intended here; therefore. "Among these" refers to the three kinds of probation.
Regarding the phrase "of regular bhikkhus," he says "excepting," etc., to show who is intended here as a "regular.

In the expression "those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha), etc.," the word "etc. includes those deserving the trial period (mānattāraha), those undergoing the trial period (mānattacārika), those deserving rehabilitation (abbhānāraha), and so forth.
The word "also" (pi) refers back to the "regular" and the "irregular" (pakatipakatatta). "They" refers to the regulars. [The text continues with] "that salutation, etc."
The construction is: "they perform. Regarding "they accept," here "acceptance" means receiving; thus he said, "they receive. "Therein" refers to acts such as salutation;

this locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "Proper conduct" (*sāmīcikamma*)—the construction is that this is a designation for the training in higher ethics (*ābhisamācārika*).
"Salutations and so forth" refers to salutation, rising from one's seat, and the gesture of joining the palms (*añjali-kamma*). "Fanning, giving of wind, and so forth" refers to...
Regarding "by the giving of wind, etc., set in motion by being struck with a fan": here, *abhihāra* means the act of bringing (*abhiharaṇa*).
To show the meaning of the compound *āsanābhihāra* as "the bringing of a seat," he says, "the bringing of a seat.
Furthermore, since even the act of arranging [the seat] is itself called "bringing" because it is arranged after having been brought [there], he says, "or else, the arranging itself."
By the phrase "water for washing the feet" (*pādadhovana-udaka*), he shows that the etymological meaning is: water for washing the foot is *pādodaka*.
By the phrase "foot-rest" (*pādaṭṭhapanaka*), he shows that the etymological meaning is: a stool for placing the foot is *pādapīṭha*.
By the phrase "or a foot-scrubber" (*pādaghaṃsanaṃ vā*), he shows that the etymological meaning is: a scrubber for the foot, a foot-rubbing stone, is *pādakathalika*.

This shows [the meaning]. The connection is: "even for co-residents (*saddhivihārika*), there is the act of salutation and so forth. By the word "also" (*pi*), it is shown that what kind of talk could there be for one who consents to others?
"Those" (*te*) refers to the co-residents. "Gone forth through faith" (*saddhāpabbajita*) means those who have gone forth out of faith.
"Noble sons" (*kulaputta*) refers both to those who are noble by birth and those who are noble in conduct. The connection is: "they do so, indeed after having requested permission."
"Non-acceptance even when forbidden" means that there is no offense from the time one is forbidden onwards; thus he said, "from the time of being forbidden.
Regarding the phrase "mutually according to seniority," here the word *mithu* is a synonym for "each other," and the word *yathā* is a synonym for the pronoun *yaṃ*;
it also has the sense of "desire. Thus he said, "whichever one is senior among each other. For they are called *mithū* because they meet (*mithati*) and come together with one another.
“Tena tena” means by that monk; in the word “sāditun,” it is the agent in the sense of the abstract state (bhāva). The connection is: “I allow [it] to be accepted.
By the phrase “vuḍḍhapaṭipāṭiyā,” he shows a locative *abyayībhāva* compound meaning “according to the sequence of seniority” (*yathāvuḍḍhaṃ*).
In the preceding word, however, it is a nominative *abyayībhāva*. “Pāḷiyā” means in a row. “Tattheva” means in the place of the junior-most member of the Saṅgha.
"Even at the *pavāraṇā*"—by the word "even" (*pi*), it is shown that it is not only on the *uposatha* day, but also at the *pavāraṇā*.
This is to be connected with the phrase "being distributed by the Saṅgha.
Regarding "feeding" (*oṇojana*): it is called *oṇojana* because one "feeds down" (*avanudate*). The verbal root *nud*, preceded by the prefix *ava*, changes its *n* to *ṇ* and its *d* to [ṇ].
By adding the letter *ja*, it is called *oṇojana*. The root *nud* has the sense of "removing"; therefore it is said, "it is called 'distribution' (*vissajjana*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "uddesabhatta, etc.," one includes *salākabhatta* and other such types of food. "Of him" (*assa*) means of the one on probation (*pārivāsika*).
"Those" (*tāni*) refers to two or three portions of *uddesabhatta* and so forth. "Below" (*heṭṭhā*) means below himself. "Take" (*gāhetha*) means [take] the more junior monks.
“Have them take it. *Bhattapaccāsā* means that the expectation itself is for food; the sense is “expectation of food.
By the word “to be distributed,” the meaning “to be served out” (*oṇojana*) is shown. The construction is: “when they are being taken and distributed in this way.
“Those” refers to the designated food and so forth. “But if he does not take it” means if [he does not take it] from the Saṅgha.
"He does not accept by means of the rainy-season assignment. "He does not relinquish" means if he does not relinquish it to another. "Specifically" means having designated [a recipient].
"Of him" refers to the one on probation (*pārivāsika*). "For" (*hi*) means because. The construction is: "of him who is seated in the position of the most junior member of the Saṅgha.
"At the mealtime" means at the place where the food is taken. "He" refers to the one on probation; the connection is "do not be weary. "This" refers to...
*Oṇojanaṃ*. "Of him" (*assā*) refers to the one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*); it is connected with "authorized" (*anuññātaṃ*).
"By monks who have arrived and are arriving" (*āgatāgatehi bhikkhūhi*) is the connection. *Catussālabhattaṃ*: a hall with four openings is a "four-hall" (*catussālā*), which is a dining hall;
the meal given there in succession is a "four-hall meal. "This" (*etaṃ*) refers to the four-hall meal. "In the text" (*pāḷiyā*)...
Of the monks’ canonical text (*pāḷi*). "Having stepped down" means having descended. "Within arm's reach" means within the arm’s reach of the food-giver.
"Crow" refers to a *kulala* (a hawk or falcon). The phrase "by monastery attendants and novice monks" functions as the causative object for the verb "to have brought.

"By oneself" means by the one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) without being commanded by another, but acting on his own initiative. "Even in the case of a large basket of alms-food" means having placed it inside a large basket.
"Even when the meal has been given. "But where," however, means "but at the place where the serving is taking place.

76. Regarding "In this regard, this is the proper conduct": here, showing that the word *tatra* (therein) functions as an indefinite demonstrative, he says, "Now, this proper conduct which has been described.
It is called "proper conduct" (*sammāvattanā*) because one must conduct oneself properly by means of it. "Therein" (*tattha*) means "in this proper conduct."

Regarding the phrase "he should not grant full ordination": here, since even the recitation of the formal act (*kammavācā*) while acting as a preceptor (*ācariya*) constitutes granting full ordination itself, it is said, "even having acted as a preceptor, the formal act should not be recited.
Regarding the phrase "in the absence of another": this means when there is no one other than himself who can recite the formal act.
Regarding the phrase "support (*nissaya*) should not be given": here, support should not be granted to newcomers alone.
Showing that even a formal support (nissaya) should not be given, he said, "Support should not be granted to newcomers," and so forth;
this is to be connected with the phrase "by whichever bhikkhus [it] has been taken.

"Another novice" means a novice other than those novices who were taken by giving them the status of a preceptor (upajjhāya) at the time of being regular members (pakatatta). "Those who have become positions of authority..."
It is the basis for the state of being the authority over all conventional designations (*sammuti*). "To one who is capable" means to one who is capable of instructing the bhikkhunīs.

By this, it is shown that even one who has not received formal authorization may, when commanded by one who has received such authorization, be permitted to instruct the bhikkhunīs regarding the heavy rules (*garudhamma*) or other matters.
This is to be connected with the phrase "the bhikkhunīs who have arrived are to be addressed. "Vā" means "to you."
"Sā" means "that monk. "Vo" means "to you," which connects with "he will give.
"Sukkavissaṭṭhiyā" means "on account of the offense of emission of semen. The construction is: "A grave offense such as bodily contact and so forth must not be committed.

Regarding the nature of the offenses and the bases for offenses, there is a distinction between what is more blameworthy and what is even more blameworthy according to the categories of offenses (āpattikkhandha).
Explaining in detail, he said, "In seven," and so forth. "More grave" means that the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) is more grave than the offense of *dubbhāsita* (ill-spoken).
"Of those" refers to the seven offenses. "By the same method as before" means by the same method as the preceding offenses.

"Distinction" refers to the difference between the bases (*vatthu*) [of the offenses]. Thus, according to the categories of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), the relative gravity—more grave or more grave still—of the bases of offenses has been shown.

Having shown this, he now says, "But in the case of a training rule involving an offense by transgression of the rules," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that very point to them by way of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
"Both" refers to both that which is designated as the basis (*vatthu*) and the offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding the term "formal act" (*kamma*): here, the name of the cause—the formal act—is applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) to its effect, namely the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
Since the formal act (*kammavācā*) that has become effective is called "the act" (*kamma*), he says, "The formal act of probation (*parivāsakammavācā*) is spoken of.
Regarding the term *kammavācā*, its etymological meaning should be understood as either "an act when there is an act" or "that which is to be spoken by means of an act.
*Kasikamma* is the work known as farming. *Gorakkhakamma* is the work known as cattle-herding. By the phrase "the act has been performed," [the nature of] the act...
"Those who perform [the act] are the 'doers'"—this indicates the meaning of the term *kammika*. "Those" refers to the monks who are the doers; they are not to be censured—this is the connection.
That which is to be said because of this fault is "what is to be said" (*vacanīya*); that which possesses what is to be said is "one who has what is to be said" (*savacanīya*);
the meaning is that such a person should not be made [to be so]. Expanding upon that very point, he said: "For the sake of an obstacle," and so forth. Up to...
The construction is: "That legal case is not settled until [the monk] has not departed even a single step from this residence.
"Tesaṃ" means "to you. Regarding "anuvādo," it is said that one speaks to others here by way of instruction; thus, it refers to the position of seniority. Therefore he says:
"The position of seniority in the monastery must not be given [to you]. Showing the nature of the position of seniority, he says: "By the reciter of the Pātimokkha..."
“Or,” and so forth. *Me* means “to me. *Taṃ* means “to you. Regarding “should not be reproved”:

here, as to by whom he should not be reproved, he says, “either on account of the matter or on account of the offense. “Should not be reminded” means he should not be made to remember [the offense]. Regarding “should not be associated with by the bhikkhus”:
here, showing that he should not be associated with by the bhikkhus through their own quarreling, he says, “mutually...”
"Having joined [the group], one should not cause a quarrel.
"Being the senior of the Saṅgha" means even while being the senior of the Saṅgha; this is the sense. Since it was appropriate to go in front, he asked, "What is to be gone behind?
and so forth, saying, "Twelve cubits," etc. "The limit of the seat" means the seat itself is the limit.
The lowest limit is the end of the seating area; showing that meaning, he said: "It is called the seat of the junior members of the Saṅgha.
*Svāssa* means "that would be for him. *So* refers to the limit of the seating area. *Assa* refers to the one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). *Tattha* means "in the limit of the seating area.

*Ayaṃ* refers to the one undergoing probation; the connection is "he does not obtain [it]. *Gahitāvasesā* means "remaining after the beds have been taken. *Maṅgulagūthabharitā* means "filled with foul excrement."

"Filled with the excrement of ill-omened things. "Of him" means of one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*). "A ground struck by dust" (*rajo-hata-bhūmi*) is so called because it is a ground where dust has fallen and settled.
"Filled with bats and mice" means full of bats and mice. "A leaf-hut" (*paṇṇa-sālā*) is a hut roofed with leaves. "Of him" means of the one on probation.
"All dwellings" (*āvāsā*)—this is how they are to be construed. "By these" refers to those who are in their natural state (*pakatatta*).
"In those" means in the residences (*āvāsa*). "To go" means to the residence. "Requisites" means the gains for the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*).
"On one side" means on one side of the residence, not standing in the midst of the monks' assembly.

"He" refers to the one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*); "giving" is the connection [to the verb]. "That very thing" means limited only by the seating and so forth. In a place where relatives have offered [the meal]...

The connection is with the word "having been invited. "Therein" means in that family. "Having made arrangements" means having prepared [the meal]. "Of him" means of the family, or it may mean [of the monk]. "Being ashamed" means being modest.
"By whomsoever" means even by one who is on probation (*pārivāsika*). "Accepted" means the acceptance of the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice (*āraññika-dhutanga*).

"In that manner" means in the same way that the forest-dweller’s practice should not be undertaken. "Even the alms-food-eater’s ascetic practice" (*piṇḍapātika-dhutanga*); here the word "even" (*pi*) [indicates inclusion].
He looks toward the forest-dweller’s factor (*āraññikaṅga*). “But he who” means, however, one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*).
The construction is: “for me, [it is] for not announcing. Or, the construction is: “when [he is] not announcing.

Regarding the phrase “by this reason,” it shows that in the expression *tappaccayā*, the word *paccaya* has the sense of “reason,” and that the ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of a reason.
The meaning of the phrase *tappaccayā* should be understood as: "the cutting off of that night itself is the condition.

The word *sāmaṇerehi* (by novices) is the indirect object (*kāritakamma*) of the verb *pacāpetvā* (having caused to cook). Here too, there is no prohibition against one who eats after having had [food] brought out from its original place or having had it cooked in the monastery.
Why? Because it is stated: "*tappaccayā*" (on account of that). *Gāme* means in a large village, at all times.

The meaning is: in a village that is not secluded from several hundred bhikkhus. "A village residence" (*gāmakāvāsa*) means a village itself is called "village-residence" (*gāmaka*) in the sense of being small;
a residence built therein is a "village-residence," and that [is what is meant].
The connection is with "having gone" and "one who is a *pārivāsika* newcomer. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in some monastery; "all the bhikkhus" [is the subject].

The connection [is as follows]. Therein, "in each case" means in each respective place where [the monks] are staying. "He does not see some [of them]; because he does not see them, he does not report it;
thus there is a breach of the night"—this is the intended meaning.
"Of one or of many newcomers" is the connection. "In this regard" refers to the statement: "It should be reported to a newcomer."

"In the phrase. "By the very method stated" means by the very method stated in the phrase, "It should be announced to the newcomers. Revealing that stated method, he said, "If," and so forth. "Of them too" means of the newcomers as well.
"Of him" refers to the one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). "Even though [the newcomer] does not know" is a genitive used here in a sense of disregard.
"And this person" refers to the one undergoing probation. "At the time they have gone" means at the time when the newcomers have departed.

*Yepi*: even those who have arrived as guests. *Okkamitvā*: having descended; the meaning is "having entered. *Ayañca*: and this one, namely the *pārivāsika* (one on probation); the connection is with the word "knows" (*jānāti*).
*Nesaṃ*: of those [guests]. *Yopi*: even he who is a guest. *Assa*: of that *pārivāsika*. *Aññātattā*: because of not knowing the fact of their arrival.
The word "rehabilitation" (*abbhāna*) is the object (*kamma*) for the verb "performs" (*karoti*).
In the word “hoti,” the agent (kattā) is implied. “Exceeding nights” means nights in excess of those during which the offense was concealed.

“This” refers to the procedure for practicing the duties of one on probation (pārivāsika-vatta). “The unerring procedure” (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā) means a procedure that is not transgressed; the sense is a procedure that is certain.

The connection is with the phrase “even as the bhikkhunī goes. “To make known” means to cause to hear. “By way of place and non-place” means by announcing from one location to another. The connection is with the statement “the Elder Karavīkatissa said.”
“On the Uposatha day”: by this term, in the phrase "on the Uposatha," the word *uposatha* excludes meanings such as the recitation of the Pātimokkha and so forth.
“Also on the Pavāraṇā [day]” means even on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony. “To go” means to go to the place where the bhikkhu is staying. “Even by means of a messenger”:
here, having rejected a messenger who is not intended, it is stated—“an unordained person... should be made to announce”—in order to show the messenger who is intended.
“Dwelling in solitude” (*suññavihāra*) means a dwelling secluded from other monks. “Where” (*yattha*) means in whichever residence. “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly, or because.
“Therein” (*tattha*) means in that dwelling in solitude. The construction is: “But when the ten kinds of obstacles exist, one must certainly go.
“By those of different affiliations” (*nānāsaṃvāsakehi*) means by those who differ in legal acts (*kamma*), in affiliation (*saṃvāsa*), and in formal acquisition (*laddhi*).

81. Showing the actual nature of the *āvāsa* (residence) and so forth, he said, “The ‘residence’ is called...,” and so on. “By the third phrase” means by the third phrase, “whether in a residence or in a non-residence.
“In these” refers to the residences and so forth. “From the covering” means from the edge of the roof-covering. “Inside the residence” means inside the residence as delimited by the walls.
“Without distinction” means generally, without making a distinction such as “one who has been suspended” (*ukkhitaka*) or “one who is on probation” (*pārivāsika*).
"By 'water-fall' (*udakapāta*): it is called a water-fall because water falls there from the roof; by that [means].
"In places bound by a five-colored roof" means in these residences where the roof is bound with a fivefold measure; this is the connection.

"The one on probation (*pārivāsika*) and the one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*) are excluded together with the regular monk (*pakatatta*)"—this is the construction. Regarding "even when in different precincts (*nānūpacārepi*)," the word *api* (even) implies [the inclusion of] being in the same precinct (*ekūpacāre*).
This shows what kind of talk [is prohibited]. "Therein" means in a residence where it is covered by a single roof, and so forth; the connection is "if he lies down.
"In that case" refers even to one who has been on probation for sixty years.
Regarding the phrases "he must rise" and "he must be invited": here, does "he must rise" mean that upon seeing a regular monk (pakatatta) who is senior to himself, he must rise?
"He should be invited" means he says, "even one who has been ordained on that very day," and so forth. "Obuddha" means obstructed.

Regarding "at a single seat" (*ekāsana*), the word *eka* here is a synonym for *samāna* (equal); thus he says, "at a seat for those of the same year of ordination" (*samānavassikāsane*), which means "the seat of those with the same year of ordination.
Regarding "seated on the ground" (*chamāyaṃ nisinne*), the word *chamā* here is a synonym for "ground"; thus he says, "seated on the earth" (*bhūmiyaṃ nisinne*).
"By another" means by one who is undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). "He walks back and forth together with a companion"—this is the construction.
By the phrase "on a single walking-path," he shows the analytical statement for the compound *ekacaṅkama*, which is a coordinate compound (*tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa*).
Regarding the expression "walking on the ground," he says "walking on the ground" (*chamāyaṃ caṅkamante*) because the accusative case is used here in the sense of the locative.
"Ayaṃ pana" means "but this," which will be explained below. "Ettha" refers to the reading: "while walking on the ground.
"Caṅkamante" means while [others] are walking in their natural state. "Na caṅkamitabbaṃ" means it should not be walked upon by one who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika).

The construction of the meaning is: "What need is there to mention [a place] endowed with a heap of bricks and surrounded by a railing? "Pabbatantaravanantaragumbantaresu" means among mountains, forests, and thickets.
In the midst of mountains, in the midst of forests, or in the midst of groves; or in mountain clefts, forest clefts, or grove clefts.
"The precinct" (*upacāra*) means a precinct of twelve *hattha*.

82. "The other" refers to the group of nine novices (*navaka*). "Of him" means of the novice. "There is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rules of conduct" means that because he is unaware [of the rule], there is no offense for breaking the rules of conduct.
An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This same method applies everywhere. "Neither later nor earlier" means not later and not earlier;
the sense is "in a single stroke. The construction is: "Two who are on probation (pārivāsika) for the same duration.

He said, "If two," and so forth, showing the fault of two who are on probation living together. "Of them" refers to the two who are on probation. "In this case" refers to those on probation and so forth.
“Among five bhikkhus”: the construction is that there are four [cases], beginning with one deserving to be sent back to the beginning (*mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha*).

“The giving of probation, etc.”: by the word “etc.,” one includes sending back to the beginning, the granting of the *mānatta* penance, and rehabilitation (*abbhāna*). “In these very cases”: namely, in the cases of the giving of probation and so forth. “This one”: the one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*). 83.
Showing the connection for the passage beginning “Then the Venerable Upāli...,” he said: “But this... and so forth.
The construction is: “of the elder Upāli who had gone into seclusion. Alternatively, taking the genitive as a term of disregard, the construction should be made as:

“of the elder Upāli, [who was] one who had gone into seclusion. “In this” means: in the duties of one undergoing probation (*pārivāsika-vatta*). “He” refers to the elder Upāli. “His” refers to the elder Upāli. “Therein” means:
among the three ways of breaking the night. “This which is” connects with “dwelling together” (*ekato vāsa*). That dwelling is co-residence (*sahavāsa*).

The word *nāma* is to be construed [with the preceding term]. Regarding *vippavāsa* (separation): showing that it means dwelling while being separated from one who is in good standing (*pakatatta*), he says, "dwelling alone.
In the phrase "of guests, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) should be understood to include resident monks (*āvāsika*).
84. *Tattha tattha* means "in this or that place. *Dvīsu padesu* means "in two places," that is, in two sections consisting of sentences.
"Even by a single word" means even by a single phrase. "Parivasiyittha" means he has completed the probation;
one for whom the probation has been completed is "one who has completed his probation" (*parivutthaparivāso*), and it refers to him. "Hi" means truly. "Esā" is connected with "this monk.
"In the pure portion" means in the section concerning purity. "Of suffering" means of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*). "End" means the final limit or destruction.
2. Discussion on the Duties for One Subject to Be Sent Back to the Beginning (Mūlāyapaṭikassanārahavatta). 86.
“Excluding one who is subject to being sent back to the beginning for a ninth time” is the construction. “Of these five, they are those who are regular (pakatatta)” is the connection.
“Of them” refers to those subject to being sent back to the beginning, those subject to the trial period (mānatta), those undergoing the trial period, and those subject to rehabilitation (abbhāna).
The connection is: "the characteristic of those deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) and so forth, of the four [categories].
"Therein" means in the duties of one deserving to be sent back to the beginning. "From this" means from the duties of one deserving to be sent back to the beginning.
87. The construction is: "Just as one on probation (pārivāsika) does not count as completing the quorum of a group, so too these do not count."
4. Discussion on the Practice and Observance of the *Mānatta* (Probation). 92.

Regarding the phrase "in a group that is deficient," it is said here that "group" (*gaṇa*) is as defined in the training rule concerning eating in a group (*gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada*); thus he says, "four or more. "In all cases" refers to the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation (*Pārivāsika-kkhandhaka*).
Thus ends the commentary on the Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation.
3. The Samuccaya Khandhaka. 1.
Discussion on the Emission of Semen.
Regarding the phrase "therein" in the Samuccaya Khandhaka: it refers to the four kinds of *mānatta*. The *mānatta* that is granted is the *mānatta* for unconcealed offenses.
The construction is with the word *nāma*. This same method applies to the subsequent sentences as well.

In the phrase "of a concealed offense" (*paṭicchannāya āpattiyā*), the instrumental case expresses the sense of cause, or the ablative case expresses the sense of reason. "Half a month" (*addhamāsaṃ*) refers to a period of fifteen days.

"Having gathered together" (*odhāya*) means having made into a collection. By the phrase "having brought together into one," he shows the meaning of the word "having gathered. "Among them" (*tesu*) refers to the fourfold [types of concealment].
Regarding the *mānattas*: "this" refers to the *mānatta*. From the phrase "for one who has not concealed... [etc. ...by way of statement," this is the indicative cause (*ñāpakahetu*).

By this, it shows the meaning of the statement that the *mānatta* to be given for an unconcealed offense is called "unconcealed *mānatta*" (*appaṭicchannamānatta*). "That" refers to the unconcealed *mānatta*.
"Here" means in this textual tradition (*pāḷi*). "Beyond that" means more than those three. "Those which have various bases" (*nānāvatthukāyo*) means those whose bases are manifold.
"Tāsanti" means they are afraid of various grounds.
"Māḷakasīmāyameva" means in the boundary-mound itself; the meaning is "in the courtyard of the boundary.

"Tattheva" means in that very same boundary-mound. "Vedayāmahaṃ" means I make known; the meaning is "I inform the Saṅgha of my state of practicing the *mānatta* penance. "Vedayati" means [he makes known].
He makes it known; the intention is: "May the Saṅgha remember me thus.

"In the manner already stated" means in the very manner stated in the Pārivāsikakkhandhaka. "It should be laid down" means it should be laid down by saying, "I lay down the mānatta, I lay down the duty.
"From the courtyard" means from the precincts of the boundary. "He too" refers even to one who goes together [with him]. By the phrase "it was not announced in the courtyard," for whom—

It is shown that even if it has not been announced to him [the resident monk], it may be deposited in the courtyard (*māḷaka*). The connection is with the words "it should be said by the one announcing.
It is stated, "monks who are like-minded (*sabhāgā*) are residing," because for one living together with those who are dissimilar, the duty (*vatta*) is difficult to fulfill.
By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by four or five," one includes more than that as well. From a place suitable for an enclosure...

[This is] from the place defined as the "enclosure" (parikkhepa) specified in the Cīvarakkhandhaka. The phrase "having passed two stone-throw distances" is stated for the purpose of avoiding the vicinity where the sound of the monks' recitation and so forth can be heard within the monastery.
If one is not released from the vicinity of hearing, one must pass even further than that. "Having entered" refers to [the area of] monks who have set out on the road.

Having entered [the village] for the purpose of abandoning the vicinity of hearing the sound of voices. The phrase "by a thicket or by a fence" is stated for the purpose of abandoning the vicinity of sight.
Here, "vicinity" (upacāra) means that very place where, standing, one sees or hears.
"Another" means other than four or five bhikkhus. "This one" refers to this one who is practicing the *mānatta* penance.
By the phrase “having entered within a twelve-fathom precinct,” it is shown that if one goes without having entered and without knowing [of the danger], there is no violation of the night-limit.
In this regard, even for those who have seen forms or heard sounds, the announcement must be made even if they are standing outside the twelve-fathom precinct.
For those who have neither seen nor heard, the announcement must be made to those who have gone inside the twelve-fathom precinct.
It must be seen. "If there is something to be done" is stated for the purpose of showing the reason for the one who goes;
even when there is nothing to be done, it is permissible to go. "He too" refers to even a single bhikkhu.

By the phrase "having announced it in his presence," it is shown that if it is not announced, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) due to the breach of the rule. When depositing [the robe] after having announced it in the presence of one person, what is lacking?
He says, "And this," and so forth, because in a *gaṇa* there is neither a fault regarding the feet nor separation. Therein, "and this" refers to one who is practicing the *mānatta* penance.
The construction is: "by whatever reason he dwelt, by that same reason. And having observed the presence of monks:
since they would depart without informing him when he was still in his natural state (*pakatatta*), therefore, within the twelve-fathom precinct of the monks—
The meaning is: "having observed the presence [of others]. Here, by the phrase "having informed the group," he shows the absence of the fault of wandering in a deficient group.
By the phrase "and having observed the presence of the monks," he shows the absence of the fault of being separated [from one's robes].
"Yam" refers to whichever monk was not previously informed. "Ayam" refers to the depositing [of the robe] after first informing the person who is to be seen.

By the phrase “the exemption for one who has laid down the duties,” it is shown that [the announcement] must be made to all those who have entered within the boundary (upacāra) while the duties have not been laid down.

The word “this one” (ayaṃ) refers to the one practicing the *mānatta* penance; it is to be construed with the word “standing” (*ṭhito*). “By him too” (*tenāpi*) means by the one practicing the *mānatta* penance as well; “it should be requested” (*yācitabbaṃ*) [is the meaning].
The construction [is as follows]: "He" refers to the bhikkhu who has not relinquished his observance. "Therein" refers to the statement, "He is to be rehabilitated.
The construction is: "This method of rehabilitation has been stated. "And this" refers to the method of rehabilitation. "Of those" refers to the offenses.

"In this way," etc., is the conclusion. The connection is: "But the concealed *mānatta* penance must be granted. By the phrase beginning with "of the concealed," [it is shown that] it is for one who has concealed [the offense].

This shows the meaning of the expression “the *mānatta* to be given for an offense that was concealed” (*paṭicchannamānatta*). “It” refers to the *mānatta* for what was concealed. 2. Discussion on the *Parivāsa* (Probation) 102. “Of that” means of the *mānatta* for what was concealed.

“Having combined” means having combined it right here in this discussion on the *parivāsa*. The construction is: “We shall show it right here in this discussion on the *parivāsa*. For the word “right here” (*idheva*) looks back to what precedes and forward to what follows.
Explaining the *parivāsa* intended here in detail, he says, "For this [is]...
and so forth. The construction is: "The *parivāsa* intended here is threefold. Regarding that, "in the three kinds of *parivāsa*.
Explaining the statement "for an offense concealed," he says, "For someone... and so forth. As in the case of the Elder Udāyin, for an offense concealed for one day...
The construction is as follows: "This is an offense; likewise, for someone, there is an offense concealed for one day.
And just as the offense mentioned further on belongs specifically to the Elder Udāyī, so too the construction is: "for someone, there is an offense concealed for two days or more.
Following this stated method, the principle should be applied to subsequent cases as well. Therefore, because [there are offenses] concealed for one day and so forth...
There is an offense beginning with one; therefore, it must be known—this is the construction [of the sentence].

Expanding upon the state of being concealed, he said, “For this,” and so forth. In that context, regarding the reading “in ten ways”: *āpattisaññī* means one who has the perception (*saññā*) that “this is an offense. *Pahu* means capable; the verbal root *hū*, preceded by the prefix *pa*, signifies capability.
In that context, regarding that *mātikā*: *yaṃ* refers to the offense; *sopi ca* means the bhikkhu as well; *tattha* means in that [context].
Regarding the offense: "He" refers to the bhikkhu. "Therein" means regarding the offense.

"He stands on the side of the shameless" means that because he stands on the side described as "deliberately concealing an offense," he stands on the side of the shameless. Regarding the term "regular" (*pakatatta*):
here, rejecting the meaning of "one who has not committed a *pārājika* offense," [the commentator] says: "The three kinds of acts of suspension..."
"Uncommitted": this refers to the state of not having concealed [the offense], or to the statement, "he incurs... [and so on] ...thought out by those who are skillful.

In the verse, by the word "with remainder," it excludes the *pārājika* (defeat). By "grave," it shows that here only what is equivalent to a *saṅghādisesa* (formal meeting of the community) is intended.

"Disrespect" means disrespect toward the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Fault" (*vajja*) means an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). "By one who has been suspended" means by one acting as the agent of the suspension.
"Of whom" refers to a bhikkhu; "there is not" is the connection [with the verb]. "Due to being of a timid nature" means due to having a timid character.
The construction is: "of whichever bhikkhu dwelling in a mountain hermitage. "In a mountain hermitage" means in a monastery built at the foot of a mountain or within it.
"In this" means in such a case. The construction is: "only when an obstacle exists. The construction is: "for him it remains uncovered."

"Even for one who covers [the bowl] with the perception that there is no obstacle, it is 'uncovered'": the intention is that even for one covering it with the perception that there is no obstacle, because it is strictly an obstacle, it remains "uncovered.

"Of him" means of the bhikkhu. "Jaw-wind" is the wind that causes disease of the jaw. "It pierces" means it pierces the jaw. "By this" means by the bhikkhu. For those who perceive abundance, even if covered, it is strictly non-abundant and thus remains "uncovered."
Regarding the phrase "and desiring to conceal," this fourfold set should be understood here:
one who desires to conceal conceals; one who desires to conceal does not conceal; one who does not desire to conceal conceals; and one who does not desire to conceal does not conceal.
With reference to the first case therein, it is said: "This is of plain meaning. In the same way, a fourfold set should be understood for the remaining matrices (mātikās) as well.

In the four tetrads, it is concealed only in the first phrase and not in the remaining phrases. To show the meaning that has not yet been explained, he says, "But if," and so forth. Regarding the term *purebhatte vā*:
it means either *purebhattaṃ* (before the meal), or that which precedes the meal (*bhattato*), or that which precedes the meal (*bhattassa*).
This is stated because, in an indeclinable compound (*abyayībhāva-samāsa*), the application of the suffix *am* for the seventh case-ending is not invariably fixed.
“Before the meal”: this same method applies here to the phrase “after the meal” as well. Having shown the meaning of the second clause, he says “But for whom...
and so forth, in order to show the meaning of the third clause. The construction is: “for whichever bhikkhu is staying in a place where there are no other bhikkhus.
The genitive cases in “of one who is waiting” and “of one who is going” are used in a sense of disregard.
Explaining the meaning of the fourth phrase, he says, “But whoever,” and so forth. Therein, “but whoever” refers to a bhikkhu; the connection is with the word “discloses.
“Sabhāgaṃ” means one who is without enmity. “Ayaṃ” refers to the bhikkhu. The construction is: “as ‘upajjhāya’ or as ‘ācariya.
“Lajjāya” means for the sake of shame, by reason of shame, or on account of shame. “Hi” means truly.
Or, "here" (*idha*) means in the place where the offense is announced. "To one who is not an enemy and is similar" (*averisabhāgassa*) means to one who, being without enmity, is similar [to oneself].

"Desirous of making known" (*pakāsetukāmo*) means desirous of making it known to others. "Also to the preceptor" (*upajjhāyassāpi*): by the word "also" (*pi*), he indicates that what kind of talk should take place in the presence of another as well.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in the place where the offense is announced. "A *saṅghādisesa* offense similar to the basis" (*sabhāgasaṅghādisesaṃ*) means a *saṅghādisesa* offense whose factual basis (*vatthu*) is similar.

“Of one who is pure” means: of one who is pure from a *saṅghādisesa* offense that is similar in nature to the basis [of the rule]. Showing the manner of disclosure, he said, “And while disclosing,” and so forth.
“Thus these,” and so forth, is the conclusion. “From that” means: because it is to be known;
“the other” is the connection. “Concealed for one day” means: concealed for the duration of one day. Up to...
"Fourteen days": the calculation (*yojanā*) should be made according to the number of days; thus it is called "calculation.
"Concealed for a fortnight" means concealed for a fortnight. "Concealed for more than a fortnight" means concealed for more than a fortnight.
"Concealed for a year" means concealed for a year. "Or from that" means or from more than sixty years. "Even further" means even beyond that.
"Than that" means than three offenses. "Beyond" means exceeding [that number]. "By way of counting" means by way of counting the offenses.

"Or by way of describing the bases" means by way of describing the bases of the offenses. "Or by way of the mere name" means by way of the name itself, namely, "offenses involving formal meeting" (*saṅghādisesa*). Here, the word *matta* has the sense of restriction; by it, the basis is excluded.
*Tattha* means in the phrase "by way of mere name. *Sajātisādhāraṇaṃ*: its own genus (*jāti*) is *sajāti*;
that which is common (*sādhāraṇaṃ*) to that is *sajātisādhāraṇaṃ*. *Sabbasādhāraṇaṃ*: common to all [offenses] or common by means of all offenses is *sabbasādhāraṇaṃ*.
*Tattha* refers to the two kinds of names. Regarding the phrase *sabbasādhāraṇanāmavasenāpi*, here the word *api* (also) implies: "Venerable sir..."

This shows that it is permissible to say, "Venerable Sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses concealed for one day," both by way of the commonality of the name of the class (*sajātisādhāraṇanāmavasena*) and by way of the commonality of both [the class and the number] (*ubhayasādhāraṇavasena*).
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. And all this—beginning with the probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth—is a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*).

The construction [is as follows]: it is called a *vatthu* (basis) because one dwells there due to being dependent upon it. *Go* refers to speech or knowledge; that which protects (*tāyati*) this is *gotta* (clan).

*Tattha* means "among those four kinds, beginning with the *vatthu*. *Tattha* (in that case) means "among those utterances. By way of [the offenses] such as emission of semen, bodily contact, and so forth...
Regarding the phrase "even by speech," the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes such expressions as *duṭṭhulla* (grave offense) and so forth. "But here" means in this particular place.
"Whoever it may be" refers to either Tissa or Phussa who has committed the offense.

"It should be announced in this way" is to be construed as: "It should be announced according to the method that will be explained below. What should be announced? It should be announced as follows: "Venerable sir, [I am such-and-such]... may the Saṅgha bear this in mind"—this is the construction.
“I announce myself” means “I announce myself. The meaning is: “I make the Saṅgha know my status as one undergoing probation (pārivāsika),” or “I make it known to the Saṅgha.
“He announces himself” means “he makes me known. The meaning is: “He makes the Saṅgha know my status as one undergoing probation;
let the Saṅgha bear this in mind regarding me. Here, in many manuscript copies of the Aṭṭhakathā, [the phrase] “of the three... [is found].
There is a reading: "or by one announcing more than [three], may the venerable ones bear it in mind. In certain manuscript commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), there is only this much:
"by one announcing three, may the venerable ones bear it in mind. This same reading occurs below in the discussion on *mānatta* as well.
Therein, by the phrase "more than [three]," it refers to one who announces more than three, having regard for the Saṅgha.
If he wishes to speak in the singular, he should say, "May the Saṅgha remember me.
Then, having regard for several monks, if he wishes to speak in the plural, it shows that he should say, "May the Venerable Ones remember me," just as in the case of three [monks].
And this is stated solely according to the rules of grammar (saddasattha), not...
It should be understood as referring to the failure of the formal act of discipline (*vinayakamma*).
By the phrase "the determination of the night within the monastery itself," it shows that one must undergo the probationary period (*parivāsa*) even within the inner boundary (*upacārasīma*).
"Inner boundary" refers to the enclosure of a walled monastery, or, in the case of an unwalled one, the area suitable for such an enclosure.
"Esā" refers to the monk who is on probation. "Assa" refers to the monk who has arrived.

"Tato" means from the day the offense was concealed. "For the purpose of dispelling remorse" means for the purpose of dispelling the remorse [of thinking], "Should I have to undergo probation for a period equal to the number of days the offense was concealed, or should I not? "Parivutthattā" means because of having completed the probation.
*Parivasitattā*: because of having completed the probation (*parivāsa*). *So*: that monk who has completed the probation. *Idaṃ*: this *mānatta* (penance) which is to be granted.
*Taṃ*: that concealed *mānatta*. *Chārattaṃ*: "six nights" means six nights combined; it is a *digu* compound in the sense of a collection.

Although one should say "cha-rattaṃ," it is stated thus by lengthening the letter *cha* for ease of pronunciation; furthermore, this is the accusative case used in the sense of immediate connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
The connection is: "It is permissible to grant the *appaṭicchannāpatti* (unconcealed offense).
By this, it is shown that even by combining the previously mentioned *paṭicchannamānatta* (concealed penance) with this *paṭicchannamānatta*, it is permissible to grant it.
Even so, it is called *paṭicchannamānatta* in relation to the *mūlamānatta* (root penance). The construction is: "How is it permissible to grant it?"
"Assa" means of one who is requesting the *mānatta* discipline. "Tadanurūpaṃ" means appropriate to that request.
Regarding the phrase "if two [days] have been concealed," here "two" is merely an illustration, for more than that may also be accepted.

"Sabbattha" means in all cases, whether there is one or many [concealed days]. "Tadanurūpameva" means exactly appropriate to the granting of that *mānatta*. "Idha pana" refers, however, to the *mānatta* for concealed offenses.
"However. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion. The construction is: "that *mānatta* which is given. "In this case" means in the case of concealed *mānatta*.

"The remainder" means those remaining after the unconcealed probation (*appaṭicchanna-parivāsa*) and the concealed probation (*paṭicchanna-parivāsa*). "Therein" refers to the two remaining types of probation. The connection is:
"at the end of an unrighteous (*adhammika*) practice of *mānatta*, the probation (*parivāsa*) permitted [by the Buddha] [is required]. In what?

"Permitted regarding the matter" means he said, "regarding this matter. "This" refers to the pure confession (*suddhanta*); "should be given" is the connection [to the verb]. "That" refers to the knowing or not knowing.
"Therein" refers to the two types of pure confession;

"is called the minor pure confession" (*cūḷasuddhanta*) is the connection. "Who" refers to the bhikkhu; "speaks" is the connection. "From the day it was announced" means from the day the offense was announced.
The connection is: "While living in probation, one must live out the probation" (*tanti cūḷasuddhantaṃ, parivasantena parivasitabbaṃ*).

"He took up" means he took up the probation. "Another" means other than the month already taken up. By the statement "there is no duty to grant probation," he shows that there is also no duty to take up probation;
for it is because [probation] is to be granted only to one who takes it up, or because it is to be taken up only by one who grants it. "It climbs even upwards" means...
Because one must undergo probation for a period other than the time of taking up the probation, it "ascends" even upwards;
because one must also undergo probation for a period less than the time of taking up the probation, it "descends" even downwards. This refers to ascending and descending.
"Of that" means of the probation until the end of the purification (*suddhantaparivāsa*). "Depending on just one, there come to be two, three, or many."
He said: "Because there is no plurality without one.
Having thus shown the *Cūḷasuddhanta* (the Shorter Case of Pure Conduct), he spoke the words beginning with "But whoever... while showing the *Mahāsuddhanta* (the Greater Case of Pure Conduct).
"That" refers to the *Mahāsuddhanta*. The construction is: "for as many days as the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*) may be, for that much time. "It does not ascend above [that]" means...
Because there is no time for ascending further, one does not ascend higher. "In this" refers to the *suddhanta-parivāsa* (purification-period probation).
"This is called the *suddhanta-parivāsa*" is the conclusion.
