Regarding the word "for the sake of schism" (*bhedāya*), he says "for the sake of a schism in the Saṅgha" (*saṅghabhedāya*) while rejecting the schism of another. The word "even in the case of illness" (*gilānepi*); here the particle *pi* indicates: "What then of other [cases]?
"In that very place" (*tattheva*) means in the very location where the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is being settled. "On one side" (*ekato*).
By this, he shows the identity of the word *ekajjhaṃ* with the word *ekato*; the difference lies in the suffixes *jjha* and *ta* respectively from the root *eka*.
By the phrase "because it is similar to the covering with grass" (*tiṇavatthārakasādissattā*), he shows the metaphorical application (*sadisūpacāra*).

That which is to be covered over with grass is "grass-covering" (*tiṇavatthāraṃ*); that which is like the covering with grass—namely, excrement and urine—is "the grass-covering method" (*tiṇavatthārakaṃ*).

In this context, *adhikaraṇa* (legal dispute) alone is primarily intended, while *samatha* (settlement) is used by way of metaphorical application (*phalūpacāra*), with the suffix *-ka* having the sense of similarity.
Making that meaning clear, he said, “For just as...,” and so forth. The construction is: “excrement or urine being struck.
The word “being struck” (*ghaṭṭiyamāna*) is a qualifying attribute containing a causal factor; it is to be connected with the word “afflicts” (*bādhati*).
The construction is: "of that which is well-covered, [namely] excrement and urine. The word *suppaṭicchāditassa* ("well-covered") is also a qualification included within the causal factor;
it is to be connected with the phrase "it does not cause affliction. The connection is: "that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) which leads to...
*Mūlānumūlaṃ* means both the root and the secondary root. *Taṃ* refers to that legal issue.

"By this act" means by the act of covering over with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*). The construction is: "Just as excrement covered over with grass becomes well-pacified, so too, what is covered over by the covering with grass becomes well-pacified. "Thus" (*iti*) means therefore. 213.

Regarding "grave offense" (*thullavajja*): since here even a grave transgression (*thullaccaya*) is considered a grave offense, it is intended here as being equivalent to a *pārājika* or a *saṅghādisesa*.

He said: "It is both a *pārājika* and a *saṅghādisesa* offense. Regarding the term *gihipaṭisaṃyutta*, he said "of householders" (*gihīnaṃ*) and so forth, showing the meaning of the expression as "that which is connected with householders is *gihipaṭisaṃyutta*.
The word "by the inferior" (*hīnena*) should be construed with the word "reviling and disparaging" (*khuṃsanavambhana*).
In the phrase "in the case of lawful requests" (*dhammikapaṭissavesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause or occasion (*nimitta*).
214. "They have emerged at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*)"—this is the connection. "Therein" means in the place where the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) has been settled.
"Even though their minds are directed elsewhere" means even though their minds are directed toward or placed upon a point other than the decision regarding the legal issue.
"From the circle of ordination" means from the boundary-marks of the ordination zone (*upasampada-sīmā*). "But those monks," however, [refer to] the disclosure of what was seen (*diṭṭhāvikamma*).
The connection is with those who are "doing," or "coming," or "sitting. "By them" means by the monks who are deciding the legal case (*adhikaraṇa*).
"Therein" refers to the place where the legal case has been decided. "Having given their consent" means having given their consent to the Saṅgha.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "pariveṇa, etc.," dwellings (*āvāsa*) and so forth are included. "Them" refers to the monks.
8. Adhikaraṇakathā 215. Regarding the term *vipaccatāya*:
here, that which falls into or proceeds by way of a transformation (*vikāra*) is *vipacca*, namely mental suffering (*cittadukkha*). That very thing is *vipaccatā*.
Showing that it is for the sake of that, he said, "for the sake of mental suffering" (*cittadukkhattha*). [He also said] "harsh speech" (*pharusavacana*).
By this, he shows that the word *vohāra* is a synonym for speech (*vacanapariyāya*).

Regarding the phrase "whatever there [is] therein" (*yo tattha*), he says "among those who are repeating" (*tesu anuvadantesu*) in order to show the scope of the pronoun *ta*. The construction is: "whatever is the reproach" (*upavāda*).
The construction is: "the term 'repeating' (*anuvadanā*). "Showing the manner" means showing the manner of the repeating, or [it refers to] the cause of the showing. "Again and again" (*punappunaṃ*).
Regarding the phrase *iminā anusampavaṅkatā*, here the prefix *anu-* indicates the sense of "not cut off.
*Tattheva* means "in that very [act] of following along. *Sampavaṅkatā* refers to being bent, inclined, or leaning in a thorough manner.
Regarding *abbhussahanatā*, showing it to mean "excessive exertion," he says "Why? and so forth. Regarding *anubalappadāna*, here [it means] again and again...
Showing the meaning of *balassa padānaṃ*, he said, “of the preceding word,” and so forth.
Regarding *kiccayata*, here—as in the case of “*mā paṇḍiccayaṃ*” and similar expressions—the augment *ya* is added for the sake of increasing the syllables;
thus he said, “*kicca* itself is *kiccaya*. By the phrase “both of these are synonyms for the Saṅgha,” [he shows that] the term *kiccakaraṇīya*...
This shows that it expresses the agent; for the Saṅgha, in the sense of the word "it acts," is called both "the duty" (*kicca*) and "that which is to be done" (*karaṇīya*).

Its state—when expressed as "the state of being a duty" (*kiccayatā*) or "the state of being that which is to be done" (*karaṇīyatā*)—is understood precisely as the formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*). Therefore it is said:
"Both of these are synonyms for the formal act of the Saṅgha. If it were a term expressing the action itself, [it would mean] "that which is to be performed."

Since the *saṅghakamma* (formal act of the Saṅgha) is obtained precisely when it is stated as "a duty" (*kicca*) or "what ought to be done" (*karaṇīya*), the suffix *-tā* would have the sense of "itself.
For if that were the case, one should not have formulated the etymological meaning as "the state of being a duty is *kiccayatā*, the state of being what ought to be done is *karaṇīyatā*";
yet such a formulation has been made. Therefore, it should be understood that [the word *kamma*] does not denote the formal act itself. "Of that very same" means of the *saṅghakamma* itself.
*Therein*: in the four formal acts, beginning with the act of seeking permission (*apalokana*). *The Saṅgha within the boundary*:

the Saṅgha residing within the precinct boundaries (*upacārasīmā*) and so forth. *Having cleared*: here, "clearing" refers to the removal of those within the boundary from the presence of the Saṅgha, the bringing of the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give consent, and their exclusion from the boundary.
To show this meaning partially, it is said: "of those entitled to give consent..."
"Having brought forth the desire (chanda). It is called *apalokana* because one looks toward [the Saṅgha] or requests permission by means of it; that very act is the *apalokanakamma*.

"In the manner already stated" refers to the manner stated beginning with, "having cleared the Saṅgha within the boundary. It is called *ñatti* because by means of it one informs the Saṅgha, the group, or the individual through such words as "Let the Saṅgha hear me";
that very act is the *ñattikamma*. The *ñatti* itself constitutes the second [part of the formal act].

A *ñattidutiyakamma* is that very formal act which consists of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñatti-dutiya*). Here, although the motion (*ñatti*) is placed first, it is the proclamation (*kammavācā*) alone that is second;
however, following the method of reverse enumeration—as in the expression “with contact as the fifth” (*phassapañcamā*)—it is called “a motion followed by one proclamation.
Regarding the phrase “with contact as the fifth,” although in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* it says “contact... [the same principle applies].

It should be understood that while "contact (phassa) exists, feeling exists, perception exists, volition exists, and consciousness exists," contact is mentioned first [in the Sutta], yet in the *Dhātukathā*, it is stated as "with contact as the fifth" by employing a reverse order of expression.
This same principle applies to the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatti-catuttha-kamma*); for "by one proclamation" means it must be proclaimed after the motion.
*Anusāvanā*: by means of those [proclamations]; and "by three proclamations" means that following the motion (*ñatti*), it must be announced again and again, or three times;
thus, they are called *anusāvanā*, and [the phrase refers to] them. "Therein" means among the four types of formal acts (*kamma*).

Regarding "having informed," he said, "it should not be performed by way of a motion and so forth," thereby showing the result of this [term]. And "even a formal act consisting of a motion" (*ñattikamma*)...

By the word "also" (pi), it is shown that not only the act of seeking permission (apalokana-kamma) is included, but likewise the act consisting of a motion (ñatti-kamma). Regarding the phrase "but the act consisting of a motion and a second [proclamation]" (ñattidutiyakammaṃ pana): here the word "but" (pana) indicates a distinction or indicates an alternative view.
"Therein" (tattha) means among the two types of acts. "Heavy" (garukāni) means not light. "The remainder" (avasesāni) means those remaining after the six types of acts; such acts are light acts.
The connection is with the word “the rest. There is also a reading “*avasesā*,” in which case the connection is with the word “conventional designations” (*sammutiyo*).

The particle *pi* in the phrase “even after having announced” (*apaloketvāpi*) includes the sense of “even after having proclaimed the formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution” (*ñattidutiyakammavācaṃ sāvetvāpi*). In order to exclude other possibilities, he says:

“But it must certainly not be performed by way of a formal act consisting of a motion alone or a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution. The connection is with the words “a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution must be performed. “In this context” refers to the Section on Settlement (*Samathakkhandhaka*).
"But in detail, it has already been presented"—this is the connection. "Of these" refers to the four types of kamma. "But whatever matter is not explicitly stated"—this is the connection.
"Therein" means among the four types of kamma. "That" refers to that matter. "Thus" means while explaining it precisely within the section on kamma itself.
"For" (*hi*) indicates the quality already attained. "Easy to understand" means it can be easily comprehended.
216. “By way of the canonical text (pāḷivasena) alone” means that the intention is not by way of the commentary (aṭṭhakathā).
220. “By which” refers to the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda). This shows the etymological meaning of *vivāda*: it is called *vivāda* because they dispute by means of this.

The word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “and by means of the methods of settling” (*samathehi ca*) has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). By this, it is shown that it is not only disputes (*vivāda*), but also legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
It combines [the terms], or alternatively, "by means of the methods of settling" (*samatha*) refers to the methods of settling themselves.

By this, he demonstrates the etymological meaning of *adhikaraṇa* as that which is "administered" or "settled" by means of the methods of settling. "A dispute itself is the legal issue" is *vivādādhikaraṇa*.

By the phrase "in this manner and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes such etymological explanations as "they speak by means of this arising of consciousness" (*anuddhaṃsana*), or "it is a reproach" (*anuvāda*).
222. "By way of intentional speech" means by way of a statement spoken with reference to what is blameworthy according to worldly convention (*lokavajja*).

Expanding upon the meaning of that intentional speech, he says: "In which," and so forth. Therein, the construction is: "in which [matter] such as digging the earth, etc., there is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
"In that" refers to the factor of a wholesome mind within the legal issue arising from an offense. "Therefore" means because it is not possible to say [otherwise], therefore.
The phrase "this" refers to the statement, "There is no wholesome legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*)," which is the connection to what was previously said.
Having shown what was not stated with reference [to that], he says "but this was said with reference to... while demonstrating what was stated with reference [to it].

Therein, the connection is "but this" means "but with reference to the cause. The construction is "that which is a legal issue arising from an offense. "Worldly transgression (*lokavajja*)"—[is the term used].
In this compound, the words are in apposition (*tulyādhikaraṇa*). That which is to be avoided in the world, or by means of the world, is *lokavajja* (worldly offense).

*Taṃ* refers to the legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). *Tattha* means in the context of the legal issue of offenses. *Vikappa* means various ways of conceiving, or various modes of reasoning.
*Yaṃ pana* refers to the legal issue of offenses. In the phrase “*paṇṇattivajjaṃ*,” the words are in apposition. It is [an offense] according to the rule established by the Blessed One.
"That which is to be avoided because it is the cause [of unwholesomeness] is a fault by rule (paṇṇattivajja). ‘That’ refers to the legal issue of an offense (āpattādhikaraṇa);

the connection is that it is unwholesome (akusala). ‘Something slight’ (kiñci) means a minor matter; the connection is that it is incurred by one who does not know whether it is an offense or not an offense.
‘Therefore’ (tasmā) means because it is indeterminate (abyākata); ‘therein’ (tattha) refers to the legal issue of an offense consisting of a fault by rule."
The construction is: the statement “The legal issue arising from an offense... [etc. ...is wholesome” has been spoken.
If one commits [an offense] with a wholesome mind, then surely the legal issue arising from an offense should be called wholesome?
To this he says: “But if,” and so forth. “This” refers to the legal issue arising from an offense. One might say: “This is called... [etc. ...wholesome.”
The construction is as follows: *eḷakaloma* (sheep’s wool) and *padasodhamma* (the training rule on foot-washing) are *eḷakalomapadasodhammāni*;
those which have these as their beginning are *eḷakalomapadasodhammādīni*; those which have these as their origins are *eḷakalomapadasodhammādisamuṭṭhānā*;
the connection is “of those offenses (*āpattīnaṃ*) as well. *Tattha* means “in those offenses originating from *eḷakaloma*, *padasodhamma*, and so forth.”

"A factor of an offense" means the cause of an offense. Having thus shown what is not a factor of an offense, he says "but by way of bodily and verbal intimation," etc., in order to show its actual factors.
Therein, "of those that proceed by means of movement" means those that proceed with movement as their cause.
Alternatively, "movement and proceeding" refers to the moving body and the proceeding speech; thus, they are "those that proceed by means of movement."
Of those body and speech [actions] that have arisen through movement. "And that" refers to either one of the two, body or speech.
Regarding the term "indeterminate" (*abyākata*), the word "iti" here signifies completion.
The construction is: "This meaning should be understood in this way. "By that" means by the mind. By the phrase "this... together with," he perceives [the object].
Here, he shows the beautiful meaning of the compound *saṃsadda* together with its grammatical form. By the phrase “having transgressed...
having made allowable,” he shows the meaning of the word *cecca* together with its qualification. By the phrase “by means of an effort...
having sent forth,” he shows the meaning of the word *abhivitaritvā*. Since the word *yaṃ* in the Canon refers to the object of transgression, he says: “*yaṃ*...”
"An offense-dispute is a transgression. By the word "commits," he indicates the remainder of the reading. Thus, the construction is:
"of that bhikkhu, [the offense] is from transgression.

In the section on the indeterminate (*abyākata*), the word "also" (*pi*) refers back to the section on the unwholesome (*akusala*). "Of that" refers to the mind. Regarding the words "not knowing," and so forth...
The meaning of the terms should be understood by way of the opposites of those stated in the section on the unwholesome (*akusalavāra*).
The meaning of the terms beginning with "that which is a legal issue arising from an offense" (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) is exactly the same as in the section on the unwholesome. 224.
The connection is that the meaning should be understood in this way in such cases as "this dispute is not a legal issue" (*vivādo no adhikaraṇa*).
9. Discussion on the Methods for Settling Legal Issues (Adhikaraṇa-vūpasamana-samatha-kathā) 228.
"In a formal act performed by a quorum of four" refers to formal acts such as the authorization of a boundary (*sīma-sammuti*).

"In a formal act performed by a quorum of five" refers to formal acts such as full ordination (*upasampadā*) in border regions. "In a formal act performed by a quorum of ten" refers to the formal act of full ordination in the central regions.

Regarding "a procedure requiring a group of twenty": this refers to the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*). "Attained to the formal act" (*kammappattā*) means having reached, being fit for, or appropriate to the formal act.
230. "It should be accepted" (*sampaṭicchitabbaṃ*) means it should be received. And having accepted it, "it should be passed over"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
"Property" (*bhaṇḍaka*) refers to property such as robes and so forth. "For the purpose of suppressing pride" (*mānaniggahatthāya*) [refers to] the pride of those who have fallen into quarreling.
For the sake of restraint. "Katipāhaṃ" means several days; the sense is two or three days. 231.
Regarding the phrase "and endless discourses," the word *ananta* here is identical in meaning to the word *aparimāṇa*; thus he says "innumerable.
By the word "utterances" (*vacanāni*), he shows that the term *bhasse* is a synonym for speech. Regarding the *ubbāhikā* (committee).
"Should be appointed": "By whom should he be appointed? To this he says, "Having obtained leave," and so forth.
By this it is shown that he should be appointed either by an act of mere intimation (*apalokana-kamma*) or by an act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñatti-dutiyakamma*).

It is called *ubbāhikā* because, having set aside the endless talk [of others], it excludes or prohibits [the speaker] from speaking further by means of this authorization; [it is] by that [authorization]. Furthermore, by those thus appointed...
The connection is with the words "should be decided by the bhikkhus. The construction is: "having sat down separately" and "having sat down within that very assembly.
"By others" means by others than the formally authorized bhikkhus (sammata-bhikkhus).
233. Regarding the phrase *tatrassa*: having analyzed the words as *tatra* and *assa*, the word *tasa* refers to the assembly (*parisa*) and is well-established in its referent.

Since the word *assasadda* is a verb (*ākhyātika*), he said, "it might exist in that assembly. Although it was stated in general terms as "it has not come down in the Sutta," because it will later be specified as "not in the Suttavibhaṅga," he said, "the Mātikā has not come down," meaning it was stated with reference to the Mātikā.
"The Vinaya too" means the Khandhaka-vinaya as well. By the word "too" (*pi*), it refers back to the Suttavibhaṅga. "By the shadow of the phrasing" (*byañjanacchāyāya*)...
Here, since the word *chāyā* refers both to a reflection (*paṭibimba*) and to radiance (*pabhā*), he says, “merely the phoneme.

The intention is that, without taking as the meaning something that falls within the category of a phonemic reflection or a phonemic radiance, one takes only the mere reflection and radiance of the phoneme.
By the word “negates” (*paṭisedheti*), he shows that the word *paṭibāha* has the sense of negation alone, and not the sense of crushing (*maddana*). [He explains] the mode of negating...
Pointing this out, he said: “In the acceptance of gold, silver, fields, land, and so forth,” etc. *Kiṃ* means “how” or “for what reason”; *kasmā* means “from what cause.
*Ime* refers to these monks who accept gold and the like. *Kārethā* means “you should cause [them] to do”; for *eyyātha* is a substitute for *etha*.
In this question, the seventh case ending (*sattamīvibhatti*) occurs. *Sutte* means in the Sutta Piṭaka. Another...
The connection is: "the Dhamma-preacher says. "Of these" refers to those who wear [the robes] hanging down. "In this case" refers to wearing them hanging down. 234.
Regarding "more numerous monks," since they are indeed superior by being double, triple, and so forth, he said: "even if there is only one more, they are 'more numerous.
By the phrase "what need to say more," etc., he shows that the word *pi* (even/also) in the expression "even by one" has the sense of censure (*garaha*).
The Discourse on the Taking of the Threefold Voting Stick (Tividhasalākaggāhakathā) 235.
Regarding the term *saññatti*: here, *saññatti* means the act of making known (*saññāpana*); showing that it is for that purpose, he says, "for the purpose of making known" (*saññāpanatthāya*).

*Gūhitabbo* means that which is to be hidden; that itself is the *gūḷhaka*. The connection is: "the taking of the voting stick (*salākaggāha*) is to be performed. It is to be uncovered (*vivaritabbo*).
“Open” (*vivaṭo*) means that very same thing as “open-mouthed” (*vivaṭako*). It is called “whispering into the ear” (*sakaṇṇajappo*) because it is whispered or spoken into one’s own ear;
that itself is the meaning of “whispering-into-the-ear” (*sakaṇṇajappako*).

By the phrase “having applied the perception of the sign,” he shows that here the word “mark” (*vaṇṇa*) refers to shape (*saṇṭhāna*); the meaning is: “having made marks [sticks] of good and bad shapes.”
The connection is: "After that, [the procedure] should be understood as being performed from the point of making it dissimilar. The construction is: "All those voting sticks (*salākā*)...
"Having done" means having cast [them]. "By the method stated" refers to the method stated beginning with the words, "In an assembly crowded with shameless people," and so forth.
By the term "up to the third time" (*yāvatatiyaṃ*), it shows the meaning here to be that it should be drawn out again and again.
"Atirekajāte" (when it has arisen in excess) is to be connected with "by those who speak contrary to the Dhamma.
The word "api" (even) in "yāvatatiyampi" (even up to the third time) shows that if it is less than that—only once or twice—what indeed would the discussion be?
The construction is: "But in the case of whispering into one's own ear, the decision should be understood as follows. "If the senior of the Saṅgha accepts [the charge]"...

The connection [is as follows]: "He" refers to the senior of the Saṅgha (*saṅghatthero*). "Having reached the latter stage of life" means having reached the final period of existence. "This" refers to the voting tally (*salāka*) of those who speak what is not Dhamma. "His" refers to the senior of the Saṅgha.
"The other tally" refers to the tally of those who speak according to the Dhamma, distinct from the tallies of those who speak what is not Dhamma.

"He" refers to the senior of the Saṅgha. "That" refers to the tally of those who speak according to the Dhamma. "Therefore" means because of the reason for not understanding. "In the manner already stated" [refers to the previous explanation].
The method is exactly as stated in the *Gūḷhaka*. "Vivaṭattha" means that its meaning is open (*vivaṭa*).
Regarding the discussion on the *tassapāpiyasikā* (further penalty) procedure [238]:
"Near to a *pārājika*" means close to a *pārājika*. In the phrase "in the case of taking what is not given, etc.," by the word "etc. (*ādi*),...

The phrase *manussaviggaha* (a human being) includes the offense of a *pārājika* regarding superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*). Regarding the word *nibbeṭhayamānaṃ*, it means "without a binding";
the connection is with the words "that [person], namely, the nun. By this, he shows that in the expression *nibbeṭhentaṃ*, the word *anta* is a synonym for the word *māna*.
Regarding the phrase *ativeṭheti*, as to "by what does one wrap excessively," he says: "By such words as 'Come now, Venerable Sir,' etc. By that...
"By the accuser": the one who has been accused says, "He spoke to me. "Of this":
of that wicked person who performs acts such as insulting and then confessing. "He will be virtuous": if the wicked person should become virtuous.
"Cessation": the subsiding of the state of being wicked. "If not": if he does not become virtuous.
"Thus he has been expelled" means that by means of that *pāpiyasikā* (act of further penalty) procedure, he will have reached expulsion.
"In all cases" means in the entire *Samathakkhandhaka*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Samathakkhandhaka*.
5. The Section on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka). Discussion on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukathā). 243.
Regarding "boxers" (muṭṭhikamallā) in the Section on Minor Matters: they are so called because they strike with their fists and injure one another.

*Muṭṭhikamallā*. By this, [the commentator] shows the reverse order of the words in the Pāḷi. Regarding *gāmamudavā*: here, those who are devoted to the adornment of their physical appearance are *mudavā*, meaning "those for whom there is joy (*modana*)";
thus, showing that those dwelling in the village and possessing such joy are *gāmamudavā*, he says:
"citizens devoted to the adornment of their physical appearance. This is a compound word, as in expressions such as *vaṇṇavā ahesuṃ* ("they were possessed of beauty").

It should be understood as follows. Regarding the term "pillar" (*thambha*): here it does not refer to a pillar placed anywhere at random, but rather specifically to a pillar set up after being buried at a bathing place (*nhānatittha*).
Thus he said, "pillars set up after being buried at a bathing place. Regarding "brick, stone, wood, or plaster walls" (*iṭṭhakā-silā-dāru-kuṭṭānaṃ*):
this refers to walls made of brick, stone, wood, or plaster. Regarding "in the form of an eight-padded cross" (*aṭṭhapadākārena*): this means in the shape of an eight-padded board.

The lines of the *rājīyoti*. “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the wrong place; it connects with the word “having scattered” (*ākiritvā*). “A lute-player’s hand” (*gandhabbahatthako*) means like the hand of a lute-player (*gandhabba*) holding a lute (*vīṇā*);
thus he is a “lute-player’s hand. Because it was made of wood, it is said: “with a wooden hand.
“By that” (*tena*) refers to the lute-player’s hand; it connects with the word “having taken” (*gahetvā*). “Powder of *kuruvindaka* stone” refers to [the powder] of that which is so named.
"Powders of stone. "That," refers to the bundle of formed pellets; "having taken" is how it connects [to the sentence].
"Grasping each other" means grasping one another firmly by the body; showing this, he says, "body against body with one another.
"Like the teeth of a makara" means like the teeth of the fish named makara. "In the shape of the base of a bowl" means in the shape of the stand for receiving saliva.
In the phrase "even for one who is ill," the word *api* (even) indicates that it is even more so for one who is not ill.
244. *Danta*: crocodile teeth. *Akata-mallakaṃ*: an unmade bowl. *Kapāla-khaṇḍaṃ vā*: the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (or).
Because it is devoid of the blossoms of cough (*kāsa-phulla*), it is called a *ukkāsikā*, a cloth-wick. It is so called because it has no blossoming of cough.
“Ukkāsā” (coughing) is the same as “ukkāsikā. “Of anyone whatsoever” means of one who is either sick or not sick, or one who is weak from old age or strong and young.
“On the back” means on the back; this is the reading itself. “Puthupāṇi” refers to the broad area of the palm;
that which is performed by it is “puthupāṇika,” meaning hand-massage. Therefore it is said: “Hand-massage is so called. “Of all” means—
For all those, whether they are bathing or not bathing.
245. "From the ear" means from the ear-hole. It is called a *vallikā* because it resembles a creeper such as the *muttolambaka*.

A "hanging thread" (*palambakasutta*) is so called because one hangs by means of it after having released oneself; that very thread is the "hanging thread. A "bracelet" (*valaya*) is a wrist-ornament (*niyura*).

246. *Dumāsikaṃ* means that which is connected with two months. *Duvaṅgulaṃ* means that of which there are two finger-breadths; it refers to hair. *Ubhayenapi* means by both, namely, by that which is designated as "two-month" and "two-finger-breadth.
The construction is: "This too has been stated as the upper limit.
*Tato* means from the "two-month and two-finger-breadth" [measure].
"Osaṇṭhentī" means: showing here that they smooth [the surface] by rubbing it down and then set it level, he says, "having rubbed it down, they cause it to settle.
"In those made of ivory, etc."—by the word "etc.," he includes those made of bone and so forth.
"With the hand-spread" means with the spread (surface) known as the hand. "With mud" means with a resin resembling mud. "With water-oil": herein, both water and...
By saying "and oil," and by saying "with oil reckoned as water," he indicates the meaning [of the term].
With this he shows the etymological meaning of the word *udakatela* (water-oil) as "oil mixed with water. *Uṭṭhaloma* means "with hair standing up.
*Temetvā hatthaṃ* means "having moistened the hand with water-oil. *Uṇhābhitattarajokiṇṇasirānampi* means "even for those whose veins are covered with dust and heated by the heat..."
"Scorched by heat and with heads covered in dust": scorched by heat and with heads covered in dust;

or alternatively, those whose heads are scorched by heat are "scorched-headed," and those whose heads are covered in dust are "dust-covered-headed"; thus, "scorched-headed and dust-covered-headed" means those who are both scorched-headed and dust-covered-headed, [the compound] being formed by the elision of the latter member of the first term; [this applies] to them as well.
"Allohatthenā" means "with a copper hand," or this is the reading itself.
247. The construction is: "all those copper plates and so forth, upon which the reflection of the face is perceived.
"In whatever place" refers to the connection with "in any mirror or in a bowl of water. "Sañchavi" [means...]
The construction is: "Has skin now appeared? Am I indeed old?
Regarding the phrase "smearing the face," he asks, "With what do they smear it? and answers, "With facial ointments that produce a clear complexion.
By the term "manosilā," he shows that *manosilā* itself is *manosilikā*. "Those" refers to the marks. "And with yellow orpiment, etc. [is said].
By the word "pi" (also), it is shown that not only with realgar (*manosilika*), but also with yellow orpiment (*haritala*) and so forth.
248. Regarding the passages beginning with "Monks, one should not dance," the construction should be understood as follows:
"niccāpentassa vā" means either dancing oneself or causing others to dance. "Sādhugītaṃ" means a beautiful song associated with [themes such as] impermanence and so forth.
Or [the singing] of virtuous people. The connection is: "Even the *dantagīta* (tooth-song) is not permitted. "That which" refers to the song.
"In the prior stage" means before the act of singing. "Even for one who causes others to sing" means even for one who has others sing it.

"But that which" is a reference to the action. The construction is: "Whatever he strikes, there is no offense regarding that striking. "All" means the entirety of dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
"Passato" means both seeing and hearing; for hearing is included under "seeing" either by way of a single-remainder compound or by way of a general designation.
"Vihārato" means from staying in a place free from dancing, singing, and instrumental music. "Vihāraṃ" means a dwelling place where there is dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
"Asanasālāyaṃ" means in a dining hall situated within a village.
249. *Sarakiriyan* means the activity (*kiriya*) of sound (*sara*). By this, he shows the meaning of the word *sarakutti*: here, the making (*karaṇa*) of sound is *sarakutti*.
The connection is with the phrase "not having attained concentration" (*aladdhaṃ samādhiṃ*).

Regarding the term *pacchimā janatā*, since a collection cannot exist without its constituent parts—that is, there is no whole (*avayavin*) apart from its parts—the suffix *-tā* also carries the sense of the base noun itself; thus he says, "the last person. (*Pacchimo*)... [text fragment] ...he says.
"Jana" means people. "That and that duty" refers to the various duties such as the recitation of the Suttantas and so forth.
"Having destroyed the syllables" means having destroyed the syllables by speaking them otherwise than they should be spoken—for instance, by pronouncing long vowels as short, and so on.
As for the word "pana" (but/however) here, it is a particle indicating a distinction; the meaning is that a specific difference from chanting (gīta) should be understood.
"Suttantavatta" means the recitation of the Suttanta as a duty (*vatta*). This same method applies here to "Jātakavatta" and "Gāthāvatta.

As for "that," it refers to the duty. However, if it is not permissible to make it excessively long by destroying that [duty], then, since this is the case, he said "by way of a square duty (*caturassena vattena*)" and so forth, in order to show how the Suttantavatta and the others should be performed.
In that context, "by means of the fourfold conduct" (*caturassena vattena*) means by means of the complete conduct of recitation. "Circular" (*parimaṇḍalāni*) means round on all sides;

the meaning is that they are full orbs. By the phrase "spoken with melody" (*sarena bhaṇitaṃ*), he shows the etymological meaning of *sarabhañña* as "that which is to be spoken with melody. The connection is: "It is said that there is [this] in *sarabhañña*."
The methods for reciting the *taraṅgavatta* and so forth do not exist today. There is only the number "thirty-two" (*dvattiṃsavattāni*), but not the things numbered.

Therefore, it is stated in the commentaries (*ṭīkā*) that "the methods for reciting the *taraṅgavatta* and so forth have lost their practical application. *Atthi* means "they exist" (*saṃvijjanti*). For this word *atthi* is a particle (*nipāta*). *Tesu* refers to "among those thirty-two rounds. *Yaṃ*... [refers to]... (Note:

The duties (*vatta*). In order to show the common characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) of all these, even including those whose practical application has been lost, he said, “of all,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is with “the characteristic of all thirty-two duties.
Having said “without destroying,” he said “without making a modification” in order to make that same meaning clear. Therein, the making of a modification—
The meaning is that the characteristic consists not in speaking by adding more syllables than the number of measures (*mattā*) by which a word is completed,
but rather in proceeding in a square manner appropriate for a recluse. Regarding the phrase "wool with the hair outside" (*bāhiralomiṃ uṇṇim*),
he says "wool-hairs" (*uṇṇalomāni*), taking the term *bāhiralomi* as a bahubbīhi compound.
“Having placed outside. By the term “woolen cloak” (*uṇṇapāvāra*), he shows the elision of the final member of the compound *uṇṇī*.
Alternatively, by means of the word *pāvāra*, he shows the form of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-paccaya*) by taking it as *uṇṇī*—meaning that which has wool (*uṇṇā*) [as its material].
In stating, “For one who wears it thus, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*),” he speaks to show the method of implied meaning (*atthāpatti-naya*): “the hairs [should be] inside...”
“Having prepared it, it is permissible to wear it. 251. “Of one who cuts off the *aṅgajāta* itself”:

the construction is “of one who cuts off the *aṅgajāta* itself. Alternatively, the construction is “for one cutting off the *aṅgajāta*, there is a *thullaccaya* offense. “Of one cutting off [the organ] when it has become the mark in cases such as being bitten by a snake or an insect,” is the construction.
252. “It has arisen”: it has arisen by way of acquisition (*paṭilābha*). In order to make its state of having arisen manifest, he said:
“*So*,” and so forth. Therein, *so* refers to the merchant of Rājagaha; the connection is with the verb *kīḷati* (“he plays”). *Tassa* refers to the merchant.
This word [tassa] is a genitive in the sense of comparison (*sāmi-attha*) with respect to the word *jāle* (“in the net”), and it is a dative with respect to the phrase *uppannā hoti* (“arises”).

*Taṃ* refers to the sandalwood block. *Assa* refers to the merchant. This word [assa] is a genitive in the sense of comparison with respect to the word *purisā* (“men”), and it is connected with *adaṃsu* (“they gave”).
"In the word *pade*, the recipient (*sampadāna*) [is indicated]. *Vikubbaniddhi* is psychic power (*iddhi*) that proceeds by way of performing various transformations (*vikāra*).
*Adhiṭṭhāniddhi* is psychic power that proceeds by way of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
'Householders offer'—this is the connection. 'Having made a sauce' means having added a sauce. *Taṃ*—"
"Gold plates, etc. The word "even" (*pi*) indicates that touching them is permissible, let alone receiving them.
The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by means of communal use" has the sense of "but" (*pana*). Thus, the meaning is: "but by means of communal use.

The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "householder vessels" has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). Thus, the meaning is: "householder vessels are also permitted. [This refers to] bronze, copper, and brass.
Because they share a common nature, it is said: “The bronze bowl... is included. 253. The construction is:

“‘To be engraved’—this is what was stated. Regarding “a natural circle,” one might ask: “Is even a mere makara-tooth [ornament] considered a non-cut circle? Therefore, he says: “Only a circle cut by a makara-tooth. 254.
“Having struck together” means having struck each other after turning [the bowls]. It is permissible to place three bowls one above the other.
The connection [is as follows]: A "ground-support" (*bhūmī-ādhāraka*) is a support made of ivory and the like that is close to the ground.
A "wooden support" (*dāru-ādhāraka*) is a support made from a single piece of wood. A "staff-support" (*daṇḍa-ādhāraka*) is a support made from many staffs, starting from four staffs.
"Therein" refers to among the supports consisting of a piece of wood similar to the tip of a lathe and the three-staff support. "Having taken it thus" means...
The construction is: "Having taken the bowl, it should be placed on only one [surface]"—thus it is said.

"Right there" means right at the edge of the plastering (*miḍḍha*). "Wide" means broad. "On the outer side" means on the outer surface of the wall. "Made" means made for the sake of the wall's stability. "Therein" means at the edge of the border (*paribhaṇḍa*).
"That cloth which, having been spread out, the bowl is placed upon—that cloth is called a *coḷaka*"—this is the construction. "But in that case," however...
But in Coḷaka: "Where" means on which sand. "It does not break" means the bowl does not break.
"Bowl-shelf" (pattamāḷaka) means a stand made for the purpose of placing the bowl. "Utensil-basket" (bhaṇḍakukkhaḷikā) means a basket for putting utensils such as bowls into.
"Anywhere" means on anything at all, such as a wall-peg or the like. "Of one who hangs it" means [hangs] the bowl.
"Of one hanging [it] from a bag. The construction is: "or made for the purpose of sitting or lying down. "By another" means by something other than the bowl.

"By a canopy-like cloth" (*aṭṭakachanna*) means by something resembling a canopy; the sense is "by something similar to a canopy. "Therein" means on the bed or bench placed under the canopy-like cloth.
"Shoulder-sling" (*aṃsabaddha*) is that by which it is fastened to the shoulder; that itself is the "shoulder-sling" (*aṃsabaddhaka*); by that.
"Having fastened" is the connection [to the preceding]. "It is not allowed to place a sunshade" is the connection. "Filled with food" means a bowl full of food.
The construction is: "either when the sunshade has been placed after being tied up, or when the sunshade has been placed after having erected a stand.
"Any kind of bowl, whether full of food or empty" is the connection.
255. "Of whom" means of a bhikkhu. It is not that only a bhikkhu who has an alms-bowl in his hand is one "with bowl in hand";
rather, the construction is: "provided there is an alms-bowl anywhere on a limb of the body, whether in the hand, on the back, or on the foot.
This same method applies to the subsequent sentence as well. By these sentences, [the terms] "with bowl in hand" and "to push open the door" [are explained].
And he shows that [the term] is merely illustrative. The connection is "or having opened a needle-case.
The word "or" (*vā*) in "or with a key" refers back to the phrase "with a part of the body.

"A gourd-vessel" (*lābukaṭāha*): it is called a *lābu* because it hangs down; a vessel made from a *lābu* is a *lābukaṭāha*. By the word "temporary" (*tāvakālika*), [it is shown that it is for] only a single occasion.
This shows that after taking and consuming the material food (*āmisa*), it should be discarded.
*Ghaṭikapāla* means a vessel’s rim or fragment. *Abhu me* means "there was loss for me"; the sense is that it arose.

Although one should say *abhu me*, it is stated thus by way of the insertion of the nasal stop (*niggahita*). *Utrāsavacanaṃ* is a word that is the cause for speaking out of fear. *Dinnakamevā* connects with "the material food given by others."
"Having scraped" means having scraped with the mouth. "Discarded scraps" means food that has been thrown away. "Among these" refers to the scraps of meat and so forth. "A non-leavings, clean bowl":
it is called "non-leavings" (anucchiṭṭha) because there is no leavings (ucchiṭṭha) therein; it is a clean bowl (suddhapatta), that [is what is meant]. "With a hand full of leavings":
it is called "leavings" (ucchiṭṭha) because leavings are present therein; that very hand is a "hand full of leavings" (ucchiṭṭhahattha).
"By him": the connection is "having sprinkled with the left hand. "Therein": in the clean bowl (*suddhapatta*). "Even by this much":
even by the mere taking of a single globule of water. "It": the clean bowl. "But the hand": even the hand that has been soiled by food remainsders;
here, the word *pana* has the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*). The construction is: "whatever bone or whatever scrap [he may find]. "Therein": [refers to the aforementioned context].
Regarding "in fish, meat, fruits, and so forth": *taṃ* refers to a piece of bone. Regarding *yaṃ pana*: the connection is with "a piece of bone and so forth";
the meaning is "desiring to eat it again. *Tattheva*: right there in the bowl. *Katvā*: having placed [it].
The connection is with "any bone-thorn and so forth."
256. "A sheath for a knife" means the act of wrapping a knife. The construction is: "or a *pipphalika* is called a 'staff-knife' (*daṇḍasatthaka*).
It is called *pipphalika* because one pierces (*pipphāleti*) with it; that very thing is the *pipphalika*. "And another" means something other than a *pipphalika*. The construction is:
"any staff attached to a knife made by joining it together is called a 'staff-knife' (*daṇḍasatthaka*). By this...
This shows the meaning of the term *daṇḍasatthaka* (stick-sword) as a knife joined with a handle.
"Stained with impurities" means stained with this [specific] impurity. "With what has been scattered" means with seeds such as those of liquor that have been scattered.
"With that" means with the liquid consisting of stone powder. "To smear" means to smear the needle. That liquid, when smeared with honey and flour, breaks apart.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Madhusitthakapilotika" means a rag (*pilotika*) smeared with honey-dregs (*madhusitthaka*).
"Therein" means on the ladder. The cord by which they bind the kathina is called the "kathina-cord"—this is the construction.
"Therein" means in the kathina made according to the measurement of a tall monk. "On the staff" means on the kathina-staff. "Of him" refers to the tall monk.
“Of a *kathina* robe made according to the prescribed measure. “Of another monk” means:
of a short monk as opposed to a long monk. The construction is: “of a mat made according to the measure of a staff-*kathina*.
By the phrase “making double,” he shows that “the lid” is the name for a specific action known as making double. “The binding cord” refers specifically to...
It is called a *vinandhanā* because one is bound (*bandhiyati*) by means of it; that very rope is the *vinandhana-rajjū*.
To show this same meaning, it is said: "a rope for binding. The same method applies here to the term *vinandhana-suttaka*.
"By that thread" means by the *vinandhana-suttaka*. "Therein" refers to within the small ladder (*khuddaka-nisseṇiyaṃ*), [referring to] certain intermediate threads.
The connection [is as follows]: "Making a designation by means of a measure" means making a designation by means of a measure from another sutta. The construction is:

just as making a designation by means of a black thread, so too is making a designation by means of a turmeric thread. Regarding the phrase "receiving with a finger," since the word "receiving" (*paṭiggaṇhantī*) is stated here with the instrumental case "with a finger" (*aṅguliyā*), and because the object is not stated, in order to show that object—
It is called a “needle-mouth. An *aṅgulikosa* is a finger-sleeve. 257.
Regarding “a bowl, a box, etc.,” here a “bowl” (*pāti*) is a particular kind of vessel made in the shape of a receptacle for holding items such as needles.
“Having scattered” means having thrown in. “Having shaken” means having cleared it out. “A thick handle” means a handle without gaps.
"Having placed within the *kaṭhina*" means having placed it inside the *kaṭhina*.
"Having bound with a cloth" means having bound it with a piece of cotton cloth.
The construction is: "for a monk who does not possess a water-strainer. The connection is: "but he who requests [it]. "In the middle of the staff" (*majjhedaṇḍake*).
"In the middle of the Daṇḍaka forest. "Water" means water that is not allowable (*akappiyaudaka*). "That" refers to the water. "Which" refers to the filter (*parissāvana*).
It is called a "filter" because by means of it water flows, goes, and proceeds, having become purified. The construction is as follows:
that which one spreads over the water and uses to take up water with a jar is called a "spreader" (*ottharaka*). Expounding this very meaning, he said:
“*Taṃ hi*,” etc. *Taṃ* refers to the water-strainer; it is connected with the word *bandhitvā* (having tied). *Tesu* means in those four stakes.
*Sabbapariyante* is connected with *mocetvā* (having loosened at the entire edge of the water-strainer).
*Ottharitvā* means having immersed [it]. *Cīvarakuṭikā* is a small hut made of robes; it was constructed for the purpose of protection against mosquitoes.
It is called "a hut made of dung. 260.
"With bodies overflowing with phlegm and other humors" means with bodies in which phlegm and other such humors abound. "Door-post" means a door-jamb.
"Wherein" refers to the door-post. "Therein" refers to the door-sill. "Therein" refers to the door-lintel. Smoke issues forth.
By this [word] *ati-dhūmanetto*, it means "having a hole for smoke. Therefore it is said: "the hole for the exit of smoke.
By the word "with fragrances" (*gandhehi*), he shows the instrumental case of the word "to perfume" (*vāsetuṃ*).

By the phrase "the place for placing water" (*udakaṭṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ*), he shows that in the expression "water-place" (*udakaṭṭhānaṃ*), the compound is formed by eliding the middle term (*majjhepadalopa*), such that the placing of water is the "place for water. Therein...
In a place near water. "A storehouse" (*koṭṭhaka*) here does not mean just any place where anyone has a storehouse;
rather, it refers specifically to a gatehouse, or a storehouse belonging to the gate itself—thus he says "gate-storehouse" (*dvārakoṭṭhaka*).
261. "Preparation" (*parikamma*) refers to the preparation of the back and so forth. That by which something is covered is a "covering" (*paṭicchādi*); it is simply a cloth.
*Paṭicchādi* means a covering for the body. Regarding the phrase "there is no water," he says "there is no bathing water" in order to exclude drinking water.
262. The construction is: "a water-lifting bucket like the scale of leaf-sellers. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "with long leather thongs etc.," ropes and so forth are included.
That which is called "operated by a hand-held jar" is wheel-shaped, having many spokes (*ara*). Spoke by spoke...
A machine that revolves by being turned with one or two hands to which jars have been fastened.
An *arahatthaghaṭi* is a machine where jars are to be fastened to hands that are not fixed; that very machine is called an *arahatthaghaṭiyanta*.
A leather vessel is a vessel made of leather. "It is unenclosed" means the cesspool has no wall. "The piling up of water is permissible."
The connection [is as follows]. In that water-scooper (*udakapuñjana*). There is also a reading, “*udakapuñjanī*.
This being the case, the meaning is: “by means of that water-scooper.

“To remove” (*paccuddharituṃ*) means to take away. 263. “With lashed side-panels” (*āviddhapakkhapāsakaṃ*): it is so called because the side-panels (*pakkhapāsaka*) are lashed (*āviddha*) all around (*ā*). “In the circle” (*maṇḍale*) means in the circle of the nave (*kaṇṇikamaṇḍala*).
“Kata-kūṭa-cchadanaṃ” means that which has a constructed peak and roof; it refers to a sauna (jantāghara).
“Etan” refers to the name “nillekhajantāgharaṃ. By the phrase “cattāro māse,” he shows the analytical explanation (*vākya*) of the *digusamāsa* compound “catumāsaṃ.
264. Regarding “namatakaṃ,” in order to show the distinction from the *namataka* mentioned previously, he says “with sheep’s wool,” and so forth.

"Have been washed" means they have not been washed [previously]. "By way of treating it like a piece of leather" means by means of fixing, designating, and removing [the status of a bowl] as if it were a piece of leather;
the meaning is that it may be used [as such]. "In a box" means in a casket made in the shape of an octagon or similar form.
"This" refers to the name "soiled foot-wiping cloth. "Even those made of wood"—the word "even" (api) indicates that they are not only made of copper, bronze, or silver. "Right there" means...
In Maḷorikā itself. "Because of going for the sake of collecting in a bowl" means because of going to collect [food] in a bowl. "Hi" means truly, or because.
It should be understood that previously the bowl was permitted for the purpose of protecting the alms-bowl, whereas now it is for the purpose of eating.
"A single monk goes" is the connection. "The remainder" refers to what remains of the fruits and cakes that were to be taken. In that...
"At that moment" means at the moment of eating.
"Even with each single limb"—the word *pi* (even) has the sense of inclusion; the meaning is that it applies even more so with limbs in addition to those.
The connection is: "of the lay follower who was thus endowed, [the bowl] was turned upside down. "His" refers to the lay follower.
"Should not be accepted" means it should not be accepted by the Saṅgha. "Of such-and-such a lay follower" is the connection [to the previous phrase].

"At the time of turning [the bowl] upright" means at the time of turning the bowl upright. "Having caused him to request" means having caused the lay follower who has turned the bowl upside down to make the request.
"Within arm's reach" means within the arm's reach of the Saṅgha.
268. Regarding the word *purakkhatvā*: here, showing that the word *pura* has the sense of "in front" and that the word *kara* has the sense of "substitution," he says, "having placed in front.
"He" refers to Prince Bodhi; the connection is with the verb *santharī* ("was spread").
"I shall obtain" means "I will obtain. The construction is: "This Prince Bodhi is incapable of obtaining a son. Thus, he shows the fault in stepping [upon it].
He said, beginning with “If,” and so forth. “Afterwards” means subsequent to entering [the Order]. “This one” refers to the Blessed One. “This” refers to the reason.
“At that time” means prior to the promulgation of the training rule (sikkhāpada), or before the promulgation of the training rule. “Out of contempt” means out of contempt for householders.
“For the sake of auspiciousness” means for the sake of auspiciousness such as freedom from illness and so forth. Regarding the term “dhota-pādaka”: here, by means of washed feet...
Showing the meaning of the term *dhotapādaka* as "that which is spread out in the place for stepping upon," he said, "What is called *dhotapādaka*," and so forth.

Therein, by the phrase "the spread-out covering (*paccattharaṇaṃ atthataṃ*)," he demonstrates that the suffix *-ika* (ṇika) in the word *dhotapādaka* functions in the sense of "having been spread out."
269. "In the shape of a lotus pericarp" means having the form of a lotus pericarp. The construction is: "The foot-rubbing [tool] that has been made is called *kataka*.
"That" refers to the *kataka*; the connection is "is indeed prohibited. It should be understood that the word "that" (*taṃ*) has dropped out in some manuscripts.
"Because of the application of abundance" means because of the application toward the state of having many requisites. "A stone-foam cloth" means...
"Even a stone fan. "Fan" (*bījanī*) means a square fan. "That" refers to the whisk; the connection is "let it be made.
Here too, the word *taṃ* (that) has been omitted [in the compound]. The construction is: "let it be made with bamboo, ivory, or reeds, or with peacock feathers, or with leather products.
The connection is "every kind of whisk. In the Canon text, *tālavaṇṭaṃ* means "made together with a handle."
*Tālaṃ* means a palm-leaf fan; by the word *tāla*, a round fan made of that material is to be understood, because of the relationship between the cause and its modification (*vikārī-vikāra-bhāva*).
*Makasabījanī* means a fan for driving away mosquitoes; the construction is that even fans with handles made of ivory or horn are suitable as mosquito-fans.
The phrase “by a fan made of wool” (*vākamayabījaniyā*) functions as either the locus (*ādhāra*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the word “included” (*saṅgahitā*).
270. The construction is: "For whom" refers to a bhikkhu whose eye is weak.
"Another" means that some other affliction, such as a bodily fever or the like, arises; this is the construction.

The phrase "But during the rains" should be connected specifically with the phrase "for the purpose of protecting the robe. "For the purpose of protecting the robe" means for the sake of protecting the robe from being soaked by rain.
The connection is with the phrase "when there is fear of wild beasts and thieves. An *ekapaṇṇacchatța* is an umbrella made from a single leaf, such as a palm leaf.
"In all places indeed" means in all villages and forests alike.
By the words "a sword, a horse," he demonstrates the rule of non-restriction (*anavakāsa*) for the word *asi* (sword). *Asi* means a blade; *assa* means...

“Of the thief” (*corassa*) is connected with “eighty. Regarding the word “vijjotalati,” he says “it shines forth” (*vijjotati*) because here the suffix *-ala* serves merely for the grammatical formation of the word.
By the phrase “only four cubits long,” he shows the meaning of the expression “of appropriate measure. “From that” (*tato*) means from the length of four cubits.
“Of all” (*sabbesaṃ*) refers to both the sick and the healthy. The word “but it is possible” (*sakkā pana*) [is connected] with the word “is not allowed” (*na vaṭṭati*).

The agent [is implied] in the word “should be given”; the object [is implied] in the word “to be given. The intention is that they should be given only after having been formally appointed, not without such appointment.
273. “Has come” means that which has come out from the stomach. The connection is: “vomiting from the throat, food. “Having retained” means having established it [within].

The connection is: “while remaining unretained. “Which” refers to the hard and soft food; the connection is “fallen. “That” refers to the hard and soft food; the connection is “having taken, one may consume. “This” refers to the statement.
274. Regarding “I shall make a sound”: it is said that what is made (*kariyati*) or uttered here is called a “sound,” thus he says, “I shall make a sound.
“Sound” refers to a loud noise such as, “This monk is making me angry! By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in “with the nails, etc.,” he includes spitting at the face.
“For the sake of protection” means for the sake of guarding with compassion. “Cutting the nails” [is mentioned].
That by which one cuts the nails is a nail-cutter, such as a knife and so forth.
Regarding the term *vīsatimaṭṭha*, it is explained that it means the polish (*maṭṭha*) of twenty nails; thus he says, "even on twenty nails," and so on.
*Likhita-maṭṭhe* means polished after having been scraped. *Kārāpenti* means they have them done by a barber. *Nakhatō* means from the nail or from between the nails.
"Or: *apakaḍḍhitun* means having pulled out, to remove.
275. *Khurakosaṃ* means a case for holding a razor. *Kattariyā*: it is called *kattari* because one cuts (*kantiyati*) with it;
it is a particular instrument made of iron, and [the shaving is done] by means of that. By the word 'having cause to cut' (*chedāpentī*), [it is implied] 'having cause to shave' (*kappāpentī*) here."
He shows the intended meaning of the word *kappa* (allowable) by way of its purpose.

Regarding the phrase "making [them] grow their beards," he says "making [them] have long beards" (*massuṃ dīghaṃ kārāpentī*) while rejecting the interpretation that it means "having grown the beard, they cause it to sprout.
"Eḷakamassū" means "one whose beard is like that of a sheep"; thus, it is called "golomika" (sheep-wool-like). This connects with the term "four-cornered" (*catukoṇa*).
Regarding the phrase *iminā caturassaṃ*: here it is shown that the word *aṃsa* has the meaning of "corner.
For in the expression *caturassaṃ*, where one should have said *caturaṃsaṃ*, the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is elided and the following *sakāra* is doubled, thus it is called *caturassaṃ*.
*Lomasaṃharaṇaṃ* means the removal of body hair. *Lomarājiṭṭhāpanaṃ* means the application of lines of hair.

"In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means "in all [instances]," such as the wearing of a beard and so forth; this is the grammatical connection. "On account of the conditions of boils, wounds, and sores" (*gaṇḍavaṇarudhiābādhapaccayā*):

a boil (*gaṇḍa*), a wound (*vaṇa*), and a sore (*rudhi*) constitute "boils, wounds, and sores"; these very things are the afflictions (*ābādhā*), hence "afflictions of boils, wounds, and sores," and [the phrase refers to] the conditions for those.
A "wound" (*vaṇa*) is a large wound. A "sore" (*rudhi*) is a small wound. "With gravel and so forth" (*sakkharādīhi*) means with gravel, honey, and flour.
*Saṇḍāsa*: it is called *saṇḍāsa* because it thoroughly (*suṭṭhu*) bites (*ḍaṃsati*) the hair. "That" refers to the hair; "situated" (*ṭhita*) is the connection [to the verb].
Where situated? He says: "on the eyebrow," and so forth. Having become what is it situated? He says: "having risen up, it is situated as disfigured" (*vibhacchaṃ*).
The construction is: "it is situated having become disfigured. It specifically devours (*bhakkhati*) what is beautiful (*sobhana*), thus it is *vibhaccha*; that which is not beautiful.
“*Vigaccha*,” it is also read; it is called *vigaccha* because it goes (*gacchati*) to what is unsightly, or because it causes one to go there.
In this context, it should be understood that the former reading alone is the original text. The construction is: “whether grey or not grey, such hair.
Regarding the term *kaṃsapattharikā*: here, they are called *kaṃsapattharikā* because they spread out or display [wares] in a bronze shop (*kaṃsa-āpaṇe*).
When it was said [that they should be taken], he replied, "the bronze-vessel merchants.
A *bandhana* is that metal by which one binds [an object] so that it does not fall, such as the handle of a vessel; the term *bandhanamatta* means just that amount of binding.
278. "By one going out" means by one departing from the monastery. "Where" means in whatever place. By the word "recalling,"...
This shows that one should wander for alms without having wandered [previously]. "Bahurajjuka" means that which has many ropes (*rajjuyo*);
thus it is *bahurajjuka*. By this, he shows the etymological meaning of "kalāpuka" as that which is to be made by a bundle (*kalāpa*), a collection of many ropes;
the vowel *i* is changed to *u*. Regarding "deḍḍubhaka," here the word *deḍḍubha* should be understood as referring to its head by way of metaphorical designation (*ekadesūpacāra*).
*Deḍḍubhakaṃ* means "like a *deḍḍubha*"; the suffix *-ka* is applied in the sense of similarity. Therefore it is said: "resembling the head of a water-snake.

By the phrase "shaped like the body of a drum (*murajavaṭṭi*)," it is shown that the word *muraja* refers to the body of the drum because it is a derivative of that [word], and thus it demonstrates the etymological meaning as "that which resembles a drum. "Having wound" means having wound many ropes together into one.
The term *maddavīṇasaddo* is a synonym for *pāmaṅga*. It is called *maddavīṇaṃ* because it is like a *maddavīṇā* lute; thus it is said to be “shaped like a *pāmaṅga*.
By the phrase “how much more so many,” he shows that the particle *pi* in the expression “even one (*ekampi*)” has the sense of emphasis (*sambhāvanattha*).
“Woven with fish-bones” means woven after showing [the pattern] like a fish-bone. “Of various kinds such as *kuñjaracchika*” means of various kinds such as *vāraṇaacchika*.
An elephant (*kuñjara*) is so called because it causes the earth (*kuṃ*) to decay (*jarāpeti*), and it is also called an elephant because it delights in thickets (*kuñje nikuñje ramati*).
That which is like its eye is "elephant-eye" (*kuñjaracchika*); those things of which that is the first are "elephant-eye and the rest" (*kuñjaracchikādi*);

their varieties are "the varieties of elephant-eye and the rest. By the word "and the rest," ox-eyes and so forth are included. [The phrase] "shaped like a key or a cocoon" (*kuñcikākosakasaṇṭhānaṃ*)...
By this, he shows the meaning as "like a pig's intestine" (*sūkarantaka*).
For a pig's intestine has a hollow in the middle, like a key-case (*kuñcikākosaka*). "It conforms to a pig's intestine" means it conforms by way of a pig's intestine.

"Only on the fringes" means only on the ends of the waist-band (*kāyabandhana*). "In this place" refers to the fringes. By the phrase "it is not permitted above four," [he indicates] the *muraja* fringes.
This shows that it rolls upward from there. "Having wrapped" means having wrapped the rope with cloth.
"In the shape of a grape" means in the shape of the head of a *varaka* (a type of bird). "Being sewn thus" means being sewn in this manner. "Hi" is a particle indicating the fruit [of the action].

"Pāsanta" refers to the end of the cord (*pāsakoṭi*). 280. The construction is: "that which is worn after making a hanging loop is called 'elephant-trunk' (*hatthisoṇḍaka*). "Of women in Coḷa" means in the kingdom of Coḷa.
Of the women who dwell there. Like an elephant’s trunk, it is worn as an *hatthisoṇḍaka*. Like a fish’s fin, it is a *macchavālaka*.
It has four corners (*kaṇṇa*) on this garment, thus it is a *catukaṇṇaka*. Like a palm-leaf fan, it is a *tālavaṇṭaka*.
It has a hundred folds (*vali*) on this garment, thus it is a *satavalika*. By the word “many times,”...
In the phrase "satavalika," it is shown that the word *sata* has multiple meanings.
By the expression "on the left or right sides," it is shown that the previously mentioned lower garment (*nivāsana*) is that which is worn from the waist downwards.

That which is worn after being folded together is the *saṃvalliya*. A wrestler (*malla*) and a laborer (*kammakāra*) are "wrestlers and laborers" (*mallakammakārā*); these are the "and so forth" (*ādayo*).
“Of those who” refers to the Malla laborers and so forth. By the word “and so forth,” gamblers and others are included. The construction is:
“Whatever they wear as an undergarment (*nivāsana*), none of that undergarment is permitted. This connects with the phrase “one or two corners.
“Corner” refers to a corner of the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*). By the word “likewise,” it is implied that [the robe] is worn after lifting up one or two corners of the inner robe.
This refers by extension to the meaning of “hanging over. The connection is: “having shown the inner border (antokāsāva). The construction is: “by one who, not being ill, wears two [robes].
“With the same quality” means having made the outer border (bahikāsāva) possess the same quality as the inner border. “Thus,” etc., is the conclusion. “And which” refers to that which is worn.
“Here” refers to the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka. And that which [is mentioned] in the commentary on the Sekhiya rules.
"Prohibited" is the connection. "All that is worn" is the construction. "Having made it without alteration" is the connection.
"Both corners" refers to both corners situated below and both corners situated above. "That" refers to the circular wrapping.
"Therein" means that in the expression "the way of dressing by householders," there exists whatever other way of dressing [is prohibited]; this is the connection. "Therefore" [is the conclusion].
Since it is called "the layperson's way of wearing [the robe]," the connection is: "therefore, it should be worn evenly all around.
The construction should be made with the words beginning, "The way they wear it, and the way they place it. "Of that very" means of the long cloth itself. "Of that very" means of the cloth itself.
"One who makes [another] recite" means one who causes another to take up or to recite the text (*pāḷi*). "In that way" means in the manner in which they wear it.
281. The construction is: "of the king going to some place.
By the phrase "men carrying the requisites and goods," it is shown that those men are called "shaven-head-wrappers" because they wrap the shaven head with a cloth.
"Intention" refers to the intention of the people who were complaining. In the expression "the intermediate sky," the word *antara* here denotes the sense of "middle."

He said, “In the middle. By the words “having attached,” etc., he shows the meaning of the term *antarākāja* as that which is to be carried by being attached within the interior of a carrying-pole (*kāja*).

By the phrase “beneficial for the eyes,” he shows that in the expression *acakkhussa*, the suffix *-ssa* occurs after the word *cakkhu* in the sense of “beneficial to. “By a carpenter’s measuring-finger” means by a finger-measure appropriate for builders.
283. By the phrase “in grass, forests, and so forth,” he shows that in the expression “setting fire to a grove (*dāya*),” the word *dāya* denotes a forest.
By the phrase “giving fire,” he shows that the verbal root *lip*, preceded by the prefix *ā*, signifies the giving of fire through the influence of the prefix.
Regarding the term *paritta*, showing that it means “that by which one protects oneself on all sides (*samantato tāyati anena*),” he says: “either by clearing away the grass or by digging a moat.”
“Or for protection. “In this case” means in the act of performing a protective rite (*paritta*). “Is permitted to give” means it is permitted for him himself to give.
“To remove” means to take away. The connection is with “the fire, whether reached or not reached. “In that manner” refers to the manner of giving the fire and so forth.
The connection is with “by the monk who extinguishes it with water.”
284. Regarding the phrase *sati karaṇīye*: here, the word *karaṇīya* is a synonym for *kicca* (duty), which is why he says, "in the duty of gathering dry sticks and so forth.
By the expression "gathering dry sticks and so forth," he shows the nature of the duty (*kicca*).

By the term "measured by a man" (*purisappamāṇa*), he shows that in the word *porisiya*, the suffix *-ṇiya* occurs in the sense of measurement (*pamāṇatthe*). That which is "measured by a man" (*purisappamāṇa*) is [the height] above...
The measure of that man is the span of his two arms. The construction is: "having seen," or "having been" [there], he saw.
In the phrase "even if very high," the particle *pi* has the sense of inclusion (*sambhāvana*). For the meaning is: "how much more so, then, a low tree. 285.
Regarding the term *kalyāṇavākkaraṇa*: here, *karaṇa* means that which is made or uttered; it is sound. It is speech itself that is the *karaṇa*.
"Those who possess beautiful vocal expression" (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇā*) means those for whom there is beautiful vocal expression;
showing this, he said "possessing sweet sounds. "Like the Veda" means like the sacred scripture (*suti*). "The method of recitation" means the means for recitation. "His own" (*sakā*):

this belongs to "himself" (*sassa*), which is the Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*); therefore it is said, "by the Fully Enlightened One. For by the Fully Enlightened One, [it was spoken] in the Magadhi dialect.
Thus was the Dhamma spoken; therefore, that Magadha idiom is called "one's own" (*sakā*). Regarding the term *nirutti*:

it is called *nirutti* because meaning is extracted (*nīharitvā*) by means of this linguistic formulation (*saddapaññatti*). In the verbal root *vac*, the letter *va* becomes *u*, and thus all conventional usage (*vohāra*) is obtained.
However, since it is stated here as "by one's own" (*sakāya*), it refers specifically to the Magadha usage. Therefore it has been said:

“Māgadhavohāro” means “the Magadhan usage. There is also a reading, “sabhāvaniruttī” (the natural language). For if this is the case, it refers specifically to the Magadhan language, which is the root tongue occurring by way of the nature of all beings.

286. The connection is: “Lokāyata is the name for the teacher of the heterodox sects. “For this very reason” means: for this very reason, namely, [the argument] that “Why is a crow white? Because its bones are white. Why is a crane red? Because its blood is red.”

288. Regarding the phrase *antarā ahosi*: here the word *antara* has the sense of "intervention" (*byavadhāna*). Thus he says, "She was *antaritā*, [meaning] concealed. By that word, the meaning is that the discourse on the Dhamma was interrupted. 289. Regarding the phrase *ābādhappaccayā*:

here, showing that the condition for the illness—namely, that which is reckoned as its medicine—is the "condition for the illness" (*ābādhapaccaya*), he says "of whom," etc. By this, he rejects the interpretation that the illness itself is the condition, i.e., that "the condition for the illness" means the illness is the condition.

293. What is called a matter of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭavatthu*) includes such things as planting a flowering tree through improper speech and so forth. What is called a matter of an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiyavatthu*)...
Digging the earth and so forth for the purpose of planting trees, laying flower garlands, and the like.
"Paharaṇī" means that by which one strikes; thus it is called *paharaṇī*. "This" refers to this name, "*paharaṇī*. The connection is:
"of any iron implement reckoned as a weapon. "That" refers to the iron implement reckoned as a weapon. It has already been stated: "A *kataka* is shaped like the pericarp of a lotus," and so forth.
It has already been stated. "Of Dhaniya alone" means of Dhaniya specifically. For it is said, "of Dhaniya alone," because a hut made entirely of clay built by others was not evident.
Alternatively, the construction is: "like a hut made entirely of clay belonging to Dhaniya.
"In all instances" means throughout the entire Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka.
Thus ends the commentary on the Section on Minor Matters (Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka).
6. The Section on Lodgings (Senāsanakkhandhaka): The Discourse on the Permission for Monasteries (Vihārānujānanakathā).
294. Regarding the phrase "it was not laid down" (*apaññattaṃ hoti*) in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*, the root here is not *ñap* (to know), but rather *ñā* (to permit);
and that [root] has the sense of granting permission. Therefore, he says, "it was not permitted" (*ananuññātaṃ hoti*).

By this, he excludes meanings such as "understanding" (*avabodhana*) from the root *ñā*, and shows it only in the sense of granting permission. Because items such as the *aḍḍhayoga* (half-roofed house) are mentioned separately, by the word "vihāra" (monastery)...
By way of exclusion, it is said that only the remaining dwellings are to be understood; thus he says: "The remaining dwellings, excluding the half-roofed houses and so forth.
A *suvaṇṇavaṅka* house is a house covered with a roof of golden rafters. A brick cave is a cave constructed of bricks. The same method applies to the others as well.
Regarding the phrase "of both those who have arrived and those who have not yet arrived," the word "and" (*ca*) here indicates a copulative compound (*dvanda*). He arrives... [text continues].
“Āgato” means one who has arrived; “anāgato” means one who has not arrived; thus, “saṅgho” (the community) refers to those who have arrived and those who have not arrived.

“Āgatānāgato” is a collective dvanda compound in the masculine gender; [the word] “tassa” (of him) refers to that. By the phrase “appaṭihatacārassa,” he shows the etymological meaning of “cātuddiso” as one whose movement is unimpeded in the four directions.
295. The construction [of the sentence] should be understood as: "The analysis is to be known thus in the verses on rejoicing (anumodanagāthā).
"By way of discordance of the seasons" means by way of the discordance of cold and hot seasons. "A wind with spray" means a wind that has come together with water droplets;
for here the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "together," while the word *phusita* denotes a water droplet. "Only straight rain from clouds" [is affected] by the wind.
Because they have been swept away, they fall straight down like showers of rain from a cloud. In the text, the suffix *-to* in the word *tato* functions in the sense of the nominative case;
thus, the meaning is "that dwelling. In the phrase *vāḷamigāni ca*, the word *ca* means "and wild beasts"; this is an instance of a change in grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
"All these" refers to all seven phrases beginning with "cold. They are to be joined as follows: "That dwelling is cold... and so forth.
The meaning is that [phrases] such as "it repels... and "...it repels the rains" are to be connected accordingly.
By the word "vihārena," he shows that in the Pāli text, the suffix *-to* in the phrase *tato* functions in the sense of the agent;
thus, the meaning is "by means of the dwelling. *Paṭihaññati* means it is repelled. In the phrase *sukhatthaṃ*, there is an elision of the latter member of the compound.
He said: "For the sake of dwelling in happiness. The two phrases, "for the sake of shelter and for the sake of happiness," should be connected with the elliptical word "there is" (*hoti*).
For the meaning is that the gift of a monastery is both for the sake of shelter and for the sake of happiness. "This" refers to this underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
"Is stated" means it was spoken. The construction is: "The gift of a monastery is for the sake of happiness. And [it is] for the purpose of meditating and for the purpose of insight.
The connection is: "there is happiness. "For its sake" means for the sake of that happiness.
"Also by the following word" refers to the word "giving of a monastery" (*vihāradāna*), which stands after the two words "to meditate and to practice insight" (*jhāyituñca vipassituṃ*).
"Here" means in this monastery. The connection is: "the giving of a monastery" means the gift of a monastery, or a monastery to be given; it is "praised. It is "stated" [in the following].

It is stated in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*. In the supporting text (*sādhakapāḷi*), the construction is as follows: he who gives a dwelling place becomes a giver of all things, a giver of strength and so forth.
In the phrase "so ca" (he, and), the word "ca" has the sense of restriction; for the meaning is "he alone.
By the word "vihāre" (in a dwelling), he shows the scope of the pronoun "ettha" (here) in the expression "vāsayettha" (one should cause to dwell). "Vāsaye" means "one should cause to dwell."

Regarding the phrase "their food" (*tesaṃ annañca*), he says "suitable for them" (*tesaṃ anucchaviyan*) in order to show that the word "their" (*tesaṃ*) should be connected with the elliptical remainder of the text, "suitable" (*anucchaviyaṃ*).
Therein, the construction is: "food suitable for them and garments suitable [for them].
Alternatively, showing that "their" (*tesaṃ*) is a dative case used in the sense of a locative, he says "among them" (*tesu*), meaning "among the bhikkhus."

The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase *ujubhūtesu*: here, by treating the locative case (*bhummavacana*) as having the sense of the dative (*sampadānatthe*), the interpretation "one should give to those upright monks" is indeed appropriate.

By the expression "those whose minds are not crooked" (*akuṭilacittesu*), [the commentator] shows that in the word *ujubhūtesu*, the word *uju* has the sense of "not crooked," and that the word *bhūta* forms a compound with the external object. Those whose minds are upright are called *ujubhūtacitta*.
The meaning of the word *ujjubhūtā* should be understood as "having become straight. *Nidaheyya* means "having dug [the ground], he would place [it].
By the phrase "without violating the clarity of mind," he shows either the fruit of that very meaning—namely, "with a serene mind"—or the exclusion of any other meaning.
The particle *hi* indicates the result. Thus, for that donor of the monastery who possesses such a serene mind, those bhikkhus...
The construction is: "teaching the Dhamma.
(296) *Āviñchanachidda*: it is called *āviñchana* because one inserts a finger into it and pulls (*añchati*) or draws (*ākaḍḍhati*) from it, or because it is by means of that.
