It is derived from the verbal root *achid* preceded by the prefix *ava*; the vowel of the prefix is lengthened, and the vowel of the root is changed to *i*.
Having [made it], it is called "the drawing-in" (*āviñchana*); that very opening is the "drawing-in opening. Regarding "the drawing-in rope":
it is called "drawing-in" (*āviñchanā*) because one inserts it into the door-opening and draws it in or pulls it; that itself is the rope, thus "the drawing-in rope.
The construction is: "any rope whatsoever is not unsuitable. Alternatively, the construction is: "it is not unsuitable" means it does not fail to exist; rather, it is indeed suitable.
Regarding the phrase "three *tāla*s," it is said that here the word *tāla* is a synonym for a key, thus [the text] says "three keys.

By this, [the commentator] excludes the meanings of tree and musical instrument from the word *tāla*. "Whatever" refers to the apparatus (*upakaraṇa*). "Of that" means of the apparatus. "Railing and window" (*vedikāvātapāna*):
it is called a "window" (*vātapāna*) because one drinks the wind through it; a window made in a railing is a "railing-window. "Wheel-base" (*cakkalika*).
In this context, it is called a *cakkala* because it revolves and turns in the shape of a wheel; it is a bundle of rags for the feet.
Showing that one must be bound by means of that, he says, "to bind a bundle of rags for the feet.
By the phrase "having made a mattress the size of a window," he demonstrates the meaning of the term *vātapānabhisi* as a mattress made to the measure of a window.
297. The connection [of the sentence] is to be understood as: "It is permissible because of the statement, 'Even a high chair'. The construction is:
"A long bench on one side with legs only eight finger-breadths wide is permissible"; the intention is that anything greater than that is not permissible.

The word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even if it exceeds the measure" indicates that if it conforms to the measure, it is certainly permissible. "Seven-limbed" (*sattaṅga*) refers to [the three directions].
"Without support," "four feet"—thus it has seven parts, hence it is called "seven-limbed. The word "this too" (*ayam-pi*) refers back to the *āsandi* (stool) by means of the particle *pi*.
The connection is: "it is called an *eḷakapādapīṭha*. An *eḷakapāda* is so called because its feet are like those of a goat (*eḷaka*);
that very foot-stool is an *eḷakapādapīṭha*. An *āmalakavaṇṇikapīṭha* is the color of an *āmalaka* fruit.
The shape is the color of an *āmalaka* fruit; that which is fashioned from it is "of *āmalaka*-color" (*āmalakavaṇṇika*). That very seat is an "*āmalaka*-colored seat" (*āmalakavaṇṇikapīṭha*).
By the word "by way of appearance" (*ākārena*), he shows that the word "color" (*vaṇṇa*) has the meaning of "shape. "These" refers to the seats. "Therein" refers to the seat.
"Made of *muñja* and *pabbaja*" means made from both *muñja* grass and *pabbaja* grass.
“Of people” means of carpenter-people. “For the purpose of protecting the skin” means for the sake of thoroughly protecting it from the destruction of the skin.
By the word “etcetera” in the phrase “of *simbali* trees, etc.,” all trees that produce cotton are included.

By the word “etcetera” in the phrase “of milk-creeper vines, etc.,” all creepers that produce cotton are included. By the word “etcetera” in the phrase “of *poṭakī* grass, etc.,” [all such grasses are included].
The phrase "all those producing cotton" includes all species of grass. Regarding the word "by three": it refers to trees, creepers, and shrubs. One might ask:
"Since there are many types of living organisms (bhūtagāma), is there not some class of living organisms free from these three?
Why, then, are all living organisms included? To this he says: "Because there are no [others] among trees, creepers, and grasses," and so forth. Since there are none [else], they are thus included.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Therefore" means because it does not exist.
The construction is: "All of this is cotton. The connection is: "Even hair is permitted for a bolster. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even hair," one refers back to "cotton.
"Any flower whatsoever" means every kind of flower. Having reached the leaves, it is not only the *tāmāla* leaf that is forbidden; all other leaves are likewise forbidden.
The intention is that even a clean one is permissible. "Fivefold" means of five types, by way of wool, cotton, bark, grass, and leaves.
By the phrase "measuring half the body," it shows the meaning of "half-body-sized" (*addhakāyika*) here as: "those made to the measure of half a body.
Those pillows upon which they place [the head] starting from the waist up to the head are [meant].
The construction is: "Those pillows are called 'half-body' [pillows]. "Of which" refers to the pillow. "In width it is one *muṭṭhi-ratana*" is the connection.
By this, he shows that the measurement of the width for that [pillow] where the entire head together with the neck can be placed is one *muṭṭhi-ratana*.
Regarding the phrase "of two ears out of three ears," this refers to both sides of the pillow.
This was said with reference to the measurement of cloth to be placed at the two ends.
However, this [pillow] is made by doubling the cloth placed at both ends of the bolster so that the edge touches the edge, resulting in three corners.
Among those three corners, the distance between two corners is one span and four finger-breadths; the middle portion extends from edge to edge.
It is a "fist-jewel" (muṭṭhiratana) in size; however, this pillow is three-cornered.
Having made it circular or square and so forth, it should be sewn such that from corner to corner, the width at its broadest part is one fist-jewel in measure. It must be sewn in this manner.
More than this is not permitted, but less is certainly allowed. "Head-pillow" refers to the head.

It is called a *sīsūpadhāna* (head-pillow) because they place it upon or support it there. They are called *bibbohanāni* (bolsters) because they specifically, or exceptionally, carry (*vahanti*) comfort.
"Above" means above the bolsters. The construction is: "but those which are made of allowable cotton.
The word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even though large" indicates that small ones are even more so. — Vinayadhara Upatissa Thera.
The connection is with the words "he said. By the term "one who holds the Vinaya," he shows the distinction from the Elder Phussadeva.
"Or unallowable cotton" means unallowable cotton for a mattress; for there is no such thing as unallowable cotton for a pillow.
Regarding the phrase "five mattresses," he says "by five" while rejecting both the status of a complete sentence and the status of a *digu* compound that does not denote a collective whole.
"Mattress-fills filled with wool and so forth. By this, he shows the meaning of the term "five mattress-fills" (*pañcabhisī*) as mattress-fills filled with these five things beginning with wool.
In terms of meaning, however, it is indeed appropriate to treat the compound as an *asamāhāra-dvigu* (a numeral compound not denoting a collective aggregate).
Why is there a count of five? He says: "By way of counting the stuffing," and so forth. For (*hi*), because their count is stated by way of counting the stuffing, therefore...
The construction is: "there are five kinds of mattresses. "Therein" refers to the five beginning with wool (*uṇṇā*). The connection is: "is included by the mention of wool.
"Only a blanket" means a blanket made of wool. A mattress made by inserting wool or made of wool is a "wool mattress" (*uṇṇābhisi*).
The same method applies to the cotton mattress (*coḷabhisi*) and the others.
"Limitation of measure" (*pamāṇaniyama*) means the restriction of measure, such as "it must be this much in measure. A cushion to be spread upon a bed is a "bed-cushion" (*mañcabhisi*).
"Of these" refers to the bed-cushions and so forth. The construction is: "that which is this cotton" (*tūla*). "Even on a skin" means even on a cushion made of leather.
The connection is that by this, what was stated in the *Kurundi* commentary is established.

“Mañcabhisim” means a mattress to be spread upon a bed. By the phrase “they gather it for the purpose of spreading,” he shows that in the word “attharanti” (they spread), the meaning must be understood through the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect.
For gathering is the cause for spreading, while spreading is the effect. “Upari” means above the surface of the mattress.
“Phusitāni” means drops. “Bhittikammaṃ” is work that must be done on a wall, like the application of various colors, similar to painting.
Regarding “ikkāsa,” he says “either tree resin or gum” because it is the name for resins and gums.
By the phrase “clay mixed with husks,” the literal meaning is that clay mixed with husks is “husk-clay.”
It shows [this]. "Mustard-powder" means mustard flour. By the phrase "having become drop by drop," it shows here a metaphorical application (*kāraṇūpacāra*) for what is overflowing;
for while the cause is "overflowing," the place [of the effect] is "having become drop by drop.
"To be heaped up" means to be cleared away. "Mud from a cesspool" means feces made of dung from a latrine.
“Clay. By this, he shows that in the phrase “dung-clay,” the word *laṇḍa* is a synonym for excrement.
299. Regarding the rule, “Monks, a painted image [is not allowed],” since the text states, “a female form or a male form,” one might ask:
is it only the forms of women and men that are prohibited? To this he says, “not only,” and so forth. Even the form of an animal...
The connection is that it is not permissible either to do [the act] or to say, “Do it.
“Door-keeper” means the form of a door-keeper. “Inspiring confidence” means those things by which one should be inspired with confidence; the meaning is, those worthy of inspiring confidence. 300.
“A single courtyard” means having the same level ground as the monastery site. “A chamber to be roofed with a flat tile” means a chamber to be covered with a flat tile.
*Tattha* means "on the tree to be pierced. By the word *kata*, he shows the meaning of the suffix *-ṇika* in the phrase *kulaṅkapādaka*.
The connection is: "to set up that imported wall-base. *Vassaparittāṇatthaṃ* means "for the purpose of protection against rainwater.
By the word *madditamattikaṃ*, [he shows] the meaning of the word *sudhā* in the phrase *uddasudha*.
It shows the plaster of the wall and turns away from the plaster of the food.
"In front" means in front of the monastery (*vihāra*). "That" refers to the location; the connection is "they strike.
The construction is "of that location which has been made. It is also called "paghāna" by way of the long vowel [reading *paghāna*]. By this, in the previous reading—

It illustrates the state of being joined (*rassabhāva*). There is also a reading “*pakuṭṭan*” (*pi pāṭho*); due to the presence of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), there is also the reading “*pakuṭṭan*.
By this, he shows the absence of a conjunct consonant (*nisaṃyogabhāva*) in the previous reading. “*Vaṃsan*” means bamboo (*veḷu*). “*Tato*” means from the bamboo.
By the phrase “*osāretvā katan*,” he shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as “that which is done after having reinstated is a reinstatement (*osāraka*). “*Chadanapamukhan*” means...
By this, he shows the form of the suffix *ṇika*. "Fitted with a wheel" (*cakkalayutta*) means joined with a wheel.

301. "A vessel for giving water" (*pānīyadānabhājana*): that by which one gives water is a "water-giving [vessel]," and that very vessel is a "water-giving vessel. With the phrase "a ladle and a bowl," the construction is: these two are the counterparts to the water-pot.

303. "A door-bolt" (*dvārathakanaka*): that by which a door is bolted is a "door-bolt. Just as there is a door-bolt at village gates, so too a door-bolt fitted with a wheel is a "door-bolt. This is the construction.
305. *Assatariratha*: A *assatara* is one who is superior (*visesa*) or pre-eminent (*atisaya*) among horses;
or else, it is one who surpasses (*tarati*) or exceeds (*atikkamati*) ordinary horses. That which is to be yoked to these chariots is a *assatarī*;
those very chariots are called *assatariratha*. Showing this, he says: "Chariots yoked to *assataras* are *assatarirathas*. In that context, "yoked to *assataras*" means...
By this, he shows that the word *assatarī* contains the taddhita suffix *-ī*.
Regarding the phrase *āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā*, it is stated as *āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalāni* because it must be connected with the phrase *sataṃ kaññā sahassāni*.
By this, he shows that the vowel *ā* occurs in place of the prefix *ni-*. Those maidens (*kaññā*) who have jewel-earrings fastened (*āmutta*) upon their ears are called *āmuttamaṇikuṇḍalā* maidens.

Rejecting the meaning that he has attained final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the aggregates (*khandhaparinibbāna*), he said, "He has attained final nibbāna through the nibbāna of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*).

Regarding the term "become cool" (*sītibhūta*), he said, "By the absence of the heat of the defilements," implying that he became cool precisely because of the absence of the heat of the defilements, and not because of anything else.

By the phrase "by the absence of the substrate of defilements" (*kilesūpadhi-abhāvena*), [it is explained] that in the term "without substrate" (*nirupadhi*), there is an absence of both the substrate of the aggregates (*khandhūpadhi*) and the substrate of volitional formations (*abhisankhārūpadhi*).
He rejects the [wrong] meaning.

Regarding the term "attachments" (*āsattiyo*): showing that they are called attachments because they repeatedly cling to sense objects or to states of existence, he says, "to form and so forth," and so on.
"Longings" (*patthanāyo*) refers to cravings. By this, he shows the essential nature of the attachments. "Having cut" (*chinditvā*)...
In the phrase "having cut with this," the term *cheda* indicates the sense of cutting.

Regarding the phrase "having removed the distress from the heart" (*vineyya-hadaye darathe*), he says "having removed the distress of the defilements from the mind" (*citte kilesa-darathaṃ vinetvā*) in order to show that the word *vineyya* has the form of a gerund (*tvā*-suffix), that the word *hadaya* denotes the mind (*citta*), and to illustrate the nature of the distress (*daratha*).
Therein, by the word "in the mind" (*citte*), he explains the meaning of the word *hadaya*.
By the word "defilement" (kilesa), he shows the essential nature of distress; by the word "having disciplined" (vinetvā), he shows the presence of the suffix -tvā.
"Vayakaraṇa" means the capital or principal. For that is called "vayakaraṇa" because by it the principal (vaya) is made (kariyati).

By this, he shows the meaning of "veyyāyika," which is the making of the principal (vayassa karaṇaṃ vayāyikaṃ); here the suffix -āyika is used in the sense of the instrument (karaṇatthe), and thus "veyyāyika" simply means that which pertains to the principal.

307. Regarding the phrase "one whose speech is acceptable" (*ādeyyavāca*): here, "acceptable" (*ādeyya*) means that which should be accepted; thus, "one whose speech is acceptable" (*ādeyyavāca*) refers to one whose speech is such.
Demonstrating this, he said, "his speech," and so forth. In that context, "his" (*tassa*) refers to Anāthapiṇḍika.
"Possessing wealth" (*sadhana*) means having existing wealth, or being wealthy oneself. "Having little wealth" (*mandadhana*) means having meager wealth. "He gave" (*adāsi*) means Anāthapiṇḍika gave.
*Iti* means "thus"; it connects with *datvā* (having given) and *katvā* (having done). *So* refers to Anāthapiṇḍika; it connects with *agamāsi* (he went).
*Kahāpaṇe santhari* (he spread out kahāpaṇas); this is the connection. [The word] *koṭiyā* functions as either the instrument or the locus.
*Paṭipātetvā* means having caused them to be laid out. The construction is: "whatever trees or whatever lotus ponds stood there in that place."
“Tesam” means “of those” trees and lotus ponds; it is stated in the masculine gender by referring to their commonality (*sāmañña*).
“The measurement of the enclosure” means the measurement of the circumference. “Assa” refers to Anāthapiṇḍika. The construction is:

“even though the householder was thus giving away so much wealth. Regarding the phrase “he had a gatehouse built,” he says “the gatehouse palace” (*dvārakoṭṭhakapāsāda*) here in order to exclude other types of gatehouses.

Regarding the phrase "monasteries and so forth" (*vihārādayo*), here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the fourteen requisites mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as the *pariveṇas* (cells) and others.
In connection with the building of monasteries for our Blessed One, he says "of Vipassī," etc., showing the building of monasteries for all seven Buddhas.
Therein, the construction is to be understood as: "He caused a monastery to be built for the Blessed One Vipassī."
The construction is as follows: having purchased a piece of land measuring three *gāvutas* by spreading out golden rods, he had a monastery built.

This same method applies to what follows as well. It should be understood that a piece of land measuring eight *karīsas* is equal to ten ox-lengths (*usabha*) of a rod, which amounts to two hundred rods.
Having stated, "In this way, [the lifespan] gradually decreases," [he addressed] all people...

Inspiring [the listener], he said, “For all successes,” and so forth. Therein, the construction is as follows: since all successes decline, therefore it is indeed enough to become dispassionate toward all successes, and it is indeed enough to be liberated from all successes.
For the word “toward all successes” (*sabbasampattīsu*) must be connected with the word “to be liberated” (*vimuccituṃ*) by changing its grammatical case.
308. Showing that *khaṇḍa* and *phulla* function as the locative bases (adhikaraṇa), he says:

“*Khaṇḍa* means a place that is cut; *phulla* means a place that has burst. Therein, by the phrase “a place that is cut,” he shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) of *khaṇḍa* as: “it is cut (*khaṇḍati*) or it is being cut (*chijjati*) therein.
By the phrase “a place that has burst,” he shows the etymological meaning of *phulla* as: “it bursts (*phullati*) or it splits open (*phalati*) therein.”

Regarding the phrase "he will attend to it" (*paṭisaṅkhārissati*): here, it is stated that "the ordinary sense is being made" (*pākatikaṃ kariyati*) in order to show that the prefix *pati-* retains its original meaning and that the word *saṅkhārissati* is derived from the verbal root *kar*. 310.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Sāriputta; the connection is "he comes. "This" refers to the nursing of the sick and so forth.
“Assa” means of the Elder. In the phrases beginning with “aggāsana,” the word *agga* can be understood both in the sense of “first” and in the sense of “supreme.
Therefore it is said: “the seat of the Elders,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “antarā satthīnaṃ,” here *antarā* is an ablative used in the sense of a locative.
And since the word *satthi* refers to the thighs, which are a part of the feet, he says: “in between the four feet.”
315. Regarding the phrase "he established," one might ask: by making what sacrifice did he establish it? To this he says: "by making a sacrifice of eighteen crores.
"Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion. 316.
Regarding the phrase "with an unfinished meal," the word *vippakata* here is a synonym for "incomplete"; thus he says: "when it was incomplete..."
Regarding "in eating": the analysis (*viggaha*) should be made as "that which has been scattered, or will be scattered, is 'prepared' (*pakata*);
it is not 'unprepared' (*avippakata*). In terms of meaning, however, it is said to be "being done but not yet finished.
"In this place" means in that location. "Too close" means too near to the monk who is eating. "Of him" refers to the monk who is eating. "Or having drunk," etc.
"Having drunk gruel" means having drunk it. "Or having eaten" means having eaten solid food (*khajjaka*).

"Even with empty hands" means even with empty hands; by the word "even," he shows that it is all the more so when one has hands carrying food. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "He" refers to the monk who has empty hands.
"Offense" refers to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "Who" refers to the monk who has left his meal unfinished. "He" refers to the monk who arrives later.
"And this monk" means this monk who has left his meal unfinished. "By him" means by that junior or senior monk who has left his meal unfinished.
To the question, "Is it permissible for a junior to command a senior?", he says: "Indeed, the senior," and so forth.
"Indeed" (hi) means truly, or because. "He" refers to the senior monk. "From there" refers to [the place] from which water is to be fetched.
"By command. "That" refers to the action.
"He" refers to the bhikkhu. By the phrase "of such a kind," its restriction is to be understood. A spittoon for spittle should be placed for one with a cough.
A chamber-pot should be placed for those with fistula or dysentery. For others, other [utensils] should be placed.

Thus it is said: “There are... [etc. ...there are. Regarding the phrase “in which”: it refers to whichever sick person. The connection is: “even he who prepares the medicine. Regarding the term *lesakappa*:
since the words *lesa* and *kappa* are identical in meaning here, it is stated as “by a slight amount, such as a mere headache, etc.
Regarding the phrase “having counted the bhikkhus”: showing that this means “having known the number,” he says “the limit.”
"Having known. In this context, by the word "delimitation" (*pariccheda*), he shows the intended meaning of the word "group" (*gaṇa*).
By the word "having known," he shows the meaning of the verbal root *i*.
[This concludes] the discussion on the taking of lodgings.

318. Having rejected the act of lying down, which consists of stretching out the body, [the author] says "beds and seats" (*mañcaṭṭhānāni*) while pointing to the "lying down" (*seyyā*) that is designated as a dwelling place (*senāsana*).

By the phrase "by way of delimiting the lying down" (*seyyāparicchedena*), he rejects the sense of "value" (*aggha*) for the word *aggha* in the expression "worth of a bed" (*seyyagghena*) and clarifies it as having the sense of "delimitation. And here—
The fact that the word *aggha* is joined with its fourth vowel has already been stated above in the commentary on the *Samuccaya-kkhandhaka* in the *Yojanā*.

"Time" (*kāla*) refers to the time for receiving bedding. "Being taken" (*gāhiyamānā*) means being caused to be taken. Regarding the phrase "they were in excess" (*atirekāni ahesuṃ*), by this it is meant that they "were extended" (*ussārayiṃsu*);
here the meaning of "extended" (*uddhaṃ sārayiṃsu*) is "they went beyond [the limit]" or "they occurred."

[The text] shows this. Regarding the phrase "excessive" (*atirekāni*): they are excessive in comparison to the limit set for the monks, as they exceed the limit set for the beds. Regarding the term *anubhāga*:
showing that it is a portion (*bhāga*) to be given subsequently (*anu*, i.e., later), he says, "to give yet another portion.
By the statement beginning with "if [the beds] are too small," it is meant that if the monks are somewhat few, there may be two or three beds for each monk.
It should be given. From whatever [portion] among the *mandas*, two or three dwellings (*vihāras*) should be given; this meaning should also be understood.
"Therein" refers to the statement, "it should not be given against one's will. The construction is: "when a share has been taken. The construction is:
"that monk by whom both the secondary share (*anubhāga*) and the first share have been taken."
“Outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*): by this, he shows the meaning of “outside the boundary” as that which has gone out from, or is seated outside, the boundary.
Because the residence (*āvāsa*) is excessively extensive due to the expansion of the precinct boundary, it is said:
“even for one standing at a distance. “Even in the season” means even in the winter and summer seasons; for in that season, the cold and heat are intense.
Because it occurs specifically during that [particular] season, the name "seasonal time" (utukāla) becomes well-known for that very reason.

Therefore, it is said: "even in the winter and summer seasons. By the word "even" (pi), the rainy season is implied. Acceptance on the day of the first rains-retreat (vassūpanāyika) is the "first" (purimaka); acceptance on the day of the second rains-retreat is the "second" (pacchimaka).
Acceptance at a time between the two days of the rains-retreat is the "intermediate" (antarāmuttaka). In a single monastery...
Within the boundary of a single monastery (*vihārasīmā*). "The owners of the lodgings" (*senāsanasāmikā*) refers to the givers of the lodgings;
the connection is with the word "giving. "That" refers to the lodging. "The residents do not look after it" is the connection. "Therein" means in that lodging.
"Even though it is decaying" means even though it is perishing. "The Blessed One said" is the connection. "Of that" refers to the lodging. "On another day" (*aparajju*) means on a subsequent day.

"Gatāya" means having passed. The construction is as follows: when the *pavāraṇā* has passed—that is, when the day of the *pavāraṇā* has elapsed—one must have the *antarāmuttaka* robe-material taken on the following day.
"That" refers to the *antarāmuttaka*.
"By one taking" means by one causing it to be taken. "By him" means by the one who is taking it. "In the eighth month" means [after] four months.
"In the winter month" and "in the four summer months" refers to eight months; sometimes it may be five summer months, or nine months.
"Broken" means a place that has been cut; "blossomed" means a place where fruit has formed. "Should be repaired" means it should be restored to its original condition.
"Having spent the day" means having spent the day in the surrounding courtyard (*pariveṇa*). "There" means in the dwelling place (*senāsana*) that was taken up.
“Night and day” (*rattindivaṃ*) means both night and day; it is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), and this is used in the accusative case to denote uninterrupted duration.
“It is not obtained” means it is not obtained by the senior of the Saṅgha. “This” refers to the lodging.
Showing that the lodging must not be taken by means of an intermediate release, he said: “But in which...,” and so forth. After the lapse of three months.
"By the lapse of three months" means by the passing of three months; "by the passing of three months. "Hi" means truly, or because.
"But in which" refers to the lodging. "At once" means only a single time. "This" refers to this discussion.
"Therein" refers to the two kinds of taking possession of lodgings. "During the season" connects with "they come during the season. Of them...
"Then it should be given" is the connection. "What is called 'the wrong time'? means there is no wrong time for rousing [them from sleep].

"One [bed] or one bed-place should be set aside"—this is the construction. "Or one elder comes"—this is the construction. "With their belongings removed" (*ubbhaṇḍikā*) means with their belongings lifted up.
"When there are many" means when there are many monks, starting from three. "It suffices" means it suffices for each individual monk. "Therein" means...

"In the courtyard" (*pariveṇe*). "Of that very [person]" (*tasseva*) means of the owner of the courtyard itself. "If they are not sufficient in this way" (*evaṃ apahontesu*) means if they are insufficient according to the value of the courtyard.

"By the value of the mansion" (*pāsādagghena*) means by the measurement of the mansion designated as the monastery (*vihāra*). "By the value of the chamber" (*ovarakagghena*) means by the measurement of the inner cell (*gabbha*).
"By the value of the bed" (*seyyagghena*) means by the measurement of a bed measuring four or five cubits. "By the place for the couch" (*mañcaṭṭhānena*)...
By way of the space occupied by a bed measuring two cubits in width and four cubits in length.
Since the space for one bed can accommodate two stools, it is said, "by way of the space for one stool. This is stated on the basis of being able to sit;
if it is not possible to sit, [the bedding] should not be given. Therefore it was said: "merely the standing space of a bhikkhu..."
"It should not be entered. "Etam" refers to the mere space where one stands. "Hi" means truly, or because.
It is said, "one bed-space or [space] for three people should be given," because a single bed-space is insufficient for three persons to occupy a single seat.
"Hi" means truly. By the phrase "in the cold season," it is implied that even during the hot season, throughout the entire day...
This indicates that it is not possible to dwell in the open air [at all times]. However, during the season of feverish heat, it is possible to dwell in the open air throughout the entire night.
Although it is possible then, one should understand that because it is not to be given during the seasons of cold and heat, it must not be given even during the season of feverish heat.
Showing the manner of sitting for three people in a single place on a couch or in a single place on a chair:
He said, “By the Great Elder,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is with the words “to be spoken by the Great Elder. “One who values sleep” means one who has a strong attachment to sleep.
“It burns me with cold” means the cold oppresses me. “By him” means by the Great Elder. “And by the second elder” — the word *api* (also) refers back to the Great Elder.
“In the very manner stated” means in the manner stated by the passage beginning with “having coughed,” and so on. “Thus,” and so forth.
The conclusion: "But in Jambudīpa, some monks are teaching" is the connection.

"Any place at all, whether a bed-place or a chair-place" is the construction. The words beginning with "this" are spoken for the purpose of stating the subsequent statement by way of concluding the preceding statement.
The construction is: "The assignment of lodgings during the rains retreat is to be understood in this way. "The duty of a guest" means the duty for one who has arrived as a visitor.
"Elsewhere" means in another place. The construction is: "by a guest who, having gone there, desires to dwell.

"On the very day of entering the rains" means on the very day of commencing the rains residence. "Therein" refers to that other place. He spoke [the following] to show the reason why one should not go:
“Or a place for dwelling,” and so forth. *Hi* means because. *Tatra* means in another place. *Tenā* means by reason of the cause of distress or failure.
*Tasmā* means because he would not dwell in comfort; therefore. *Taṃ vihāraṃ* means that monastery in which he desires to dwell. *Tattha* means in that monastery;
the connection is that while dwelling there, he will dwell happily. *Uddesatthiko* means one who seeks the recitation (of the scriptures).
Or by way of a brief indication. "The suitability of the meditation subject" means the state of being suitable for the meditation subject, or the suitability of the meditation subject itself.
"Therein" refers to another monastery. The connection is that it "should be struck" by one who is going there. Showing the manner in which it should be struck, he said:
"Not therein," and so forth. "Therein" means in one's own place. To the question "Why should it not be spoken? he said: "You," and so forth.
The construction is: "there is no, nor does there exist, *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) and so forth, or rice-gruel, snacks, and so forth.
The connection is: "the requisites for the uposatha hall. The construction is: "accept this palm-leaf fan and this needle for your monastery.
"*Gamiyavatta*" means the duty (*vatta*) of monks who are traveling. The word "by the young ones" (*daharehi*) [is connected] with "having had [it] lifted up" (*ukkhipāpetvā*).

In the two phrases “having caused to take up” (*gāhāpetvā*), there is the *kāritakamma* (causative action); in the phrase “alms-bowls and robe-cloths” (*pattacīvarabhaṇḍikāyo*), there is the *dhātukamma* (root action) in the phrase “having caused to throw up” (*ukkhipāpetvā*);
and in the phrase “oil-tubes, walking-sticks, and so forth” (*telanāḷikattaradaṇḍādīni*), there is likewise the *dhātukamma* in the phrase “having caused to take up.
“By showing himself” means by making himself manifest to people. “Thoughts” (*vitakka*) refers to thoughts characterized by an abundance of conditions for sensual desire.
The word “saparivāraṃ” (with a retinue) is an adverbial modifier for the word “gacchantañca” (and while going). For this is the case, the connection is: “and while going with a retinue.
However, the word “naṃ” (her) is an adjective modifying the agent. For this is the case, the connection is: “that nun, together with her retinue.
And the word “disvā” (having seen) is likewise an adverbial modifier. For this is the case, [the connection is: “and while she was going...”
The connection is: "having seen that monk together with his retinue. The connection is: "people say. "Among them" means among those people.
The connection is: "one wise person. The construction is: "this time is called the time for entering the rains retreat.
"Where" means in a place. The connection is: "his," referring to that one wise person, [is] "the speech. "Those people entreat" means...
Connection: "Elsewhere" means another place. "Friends" (*mittā*) are so called because they feel affection for one another (*mejjanti*).

"Companions" (*amaccā*) are so called because they dwell together (*amā saha vattanti*) in pleasure and pain. "Friends and companions" (*mittāmaccā*) refers to those who are friends and also companions. "Having consulted together" means having deliberated equally or properly.
"Right here" means in the village itself, or in the monastery itself. Why is it permissible to accept [the invitation]? Is it not...?
He said, "All this is both improper and blameworthy," [but then] stated, "Indeed, all this is both proper and blameless.
For since all this is both proper and blameless, the construction is: therefore, it is permissible to accept everything.
The connection is with the words "but it is said in the Kurundi. "Both" refers to the statements found in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā and the Kurundi.
The connection is that both of these are statements.
Expounding upon the duties of a resident monk (*āvāsika*), he said, "Even beforehand," and so forth. Therein, "even beforehand" means even prior to the arrival of the visiting monks (*āgantuka*).
"The road to the meditation hall and the monastery" refers to both the path leading to the meditation hall and the path leading to the monastery.
“Muddavedikāya” means on the platform surrounding the shrine (cetiya). Why must all this also be done? He says: “Because they desire to dwell during the rains,” and so forth.
“Hi” means truly, or because. The connection is: “Those desiring to dwell during the rains will dwell in comfort.
The connection is: “by the resident monks who have performed the preparatory work. From whichever family it is normally obtained...
The construction is: "In that family, one should ask for the *vassāvāsika* (provisions for the rains retreat). "Never given before" means not given previously. "For" (*hi*) means because.
"Afflicted" means having approached, or being severely oppressed. "Therein" means among people. "They" refers to the people.

"When the *vassāvāsika* is being taken" means when the lodging for the rains retreat is being caused to be taken. "Of the monks who have been made to take" means of the monks who have been caused to take [the provisions].
*Vassāvāsikaṃ* means a robe-cloth that should be given to those dwelling for the rains-residence (*vassa*).

*Gāhaṇakālo* means the time of causing [the robe] to be taken. *Upakaṭṭho* means near. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in *chātakādīhi*, illnesses and so forth are included. *Yaṃ* refers to the robe-cloth. *Tato* means from the robe-cloth. *Taṃ* refers to the speech.
*Tadanurūpena* means in accordance with the speech of those people. *Tesaṃ tesaṃ* refers to those people.
The connection is "the rainy-season robe.
"Of whom" means of the bhikkhu. "He" refers to that bhikkhu. The construction is "speaking thus. "That" refers to the robe.
"Having retreated" means having gone back; the meaning is having departed from the monastery. "There" means in the village. "Having placed it as a deposit."
Having placed either a permissible item (*kappiyavatthu*) or an impermissible item (*akappiyavatthu*) in the hands of monastery attendants (*ārāmika*) and others.

"In the monastery" (*vihāre*) means of the monastery, or for one dwelling there during the rains retreat. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even without having asked," the meaning "even after having asked" is indicated.
"Of those families" (*tesaṃ kulānaṃ*). "Duty" (*vattaṃ*) refers to the duty of looking after them and so forth. "Of those" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the families. And "having come" (*āgatañca*).
The connection is that they say, "He has come as a paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer). "By him" means by the paṃsukūlika.
"They do not wish to give" means that even when it is announced to the Saṅgha, they do not wish to give it to the Saṅgha.

"A bhikkhu who is like himself" means a bhikkhu who is similar to himself. "This" refers to the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe). It is not permitted for the paṃsukūlika; why? Because it is a robe belonging to a householder.
The phrase beginning with "iti" is the conclusion. "Saddhādeyye" means regarding what is to be given out of faith, namely the gains pertaining to the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsika*).
"Tatruppāde" means regarding the gains arising in that monastery. "Bhaṇḍapaṭicchādanaṃ" refers to the robe-material used for covering.
For it is precisely because the body is covered by this robe-material that it is called "bhaṇḍapaṭicchādanaṃ."
It is said: "Have it taken" means have it taken by the monks. "Should be caused to be taken" means it should be caused to be taken by the monks.
"But the object" refers to an object other than the cloth, whether allowable (*kappiya*) or unallowable (*akappiya*).

Why is it indeed permissible? One might ask: "Is not an unallowable object impermissible? To this he says: "For [in the case] of those who make allowable," and so forth. For therein, because it has been authorized, [it is permissible].
Therefore, the construction is: "it is indeed permissible. The connection is with the phrase "arisen from a given cloth.
The connection is with the phrase "which cloth was given. "In this" refers to the cloths given into the hands of the preparers of what is allowable (*kappiyakāraka*).
The connection is with the phrase "by those who offer that cloth. It becomes a heavy article (*garubhaṇḍa*); because it is a heavy article, [it is excluded] from other requisites.

The intended meaning is that it should not be offered. "By way of the individual alone" means by referring to a specific person, as in: "The monks are distressed for robes; would it please the Saṅgha to set aside this much portion of rice for the monks to make robes?
and so forth—thus, by way of the individual alone. "By way of the Saṅgha" means by way of the Saṅgha, as in: "The Saṅgha is distressed for robes," and so forth—it is not [by way of the individual].

"Should be done" is the connection. Having thus shown that a *apalokana*-kamma (a formal act of notification) should not be performed with respect to a person, he now says, "Even by way of gold and silver," etc., showing that it should not be performed with respect to the object (*vatthu*).
"By way of allowable goods" means by way of whatever allowable goods remain after the robes and rice; for as regards robes and rice...
Because they are mentioned separately, in the phrase "by way of allowable goods," only those remaining allowable goods are to be understood here.
"But that" refers to the *apalokana-kamma* (an act of notification). To show the manner in which it should be performed, he said "Now," and so forth. "Subhikkhaṃ" means where alms-food is abundant.
"Sulabhapiṇḍaṃ" means where alms-food is easily obtained. By these two terms, [the meaning] is mutually [reinforced].
It shows the reason: because there is an abundance of alms, alms are easily obtained; because alms are easily obtained, it is said that there is an abundance of food.
Thus, having observed the requisite of robes, one should observe the lodging—this is the connection.
"At the time" means at the time of the formal appointment. "It is stated" means it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Why must two be appointed? Is it not possible to appoint even one?
"It is appropriate," he said, and so forth with "for thus" (*evaṃ hīti*). Therein, the construction is: "Because one will cause [the other] to accept it, therefore two should be appointed.
For by means of one who has obtained the consent (*sammuti*), it is possible to cause another to accept; however, it is not possible for oneself to cause oneself to incur [the offense].
Therefore, when two have been appointed—the junior to the senior, and the senior to the junior—both [should act] toward one another.
The intended meaning is "they shall cause [them] to enter. "Should be appointed" means they should be appointed together as one.
Regarding the phrase "eight or sixteen," the word *pi* (also/even) indicates that it is permissible to appoint more than that number together as well.

In this regard, the statement in the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka* concerning the appointment of officials—that eight persons were appointed together—is the proof for this. It is indeed an act of censure (*niggaha-kamma*).

For it should be understood that the Saṅgha does not perform [legal acts] for the Saṅgha. "Of them" refers to the eight and sixteen persons; the connection is that formal authorization (*sammuti*) is indeed permissible.
To the question "How should it be observed?", he says: "A cetiya-hall," and so forth.
"An assembly hall" (*āsana-ghara*) means a shrine room for images. Halls built near paths or lotus ponds are spoken of by way of their vicinity (*upacāra*).

“Road” and “lotus pond. For those halls are constructed anywhere on a road facing a village that has entered within the boundary of the precincts, as well as lotus ponds dug within the boundary of the precincts; thus it should be understood—this is the construction [of the meaning].

Having shown what is not a dwelling place (*asenāsana*), he says “monastery” (*vihāra*) and so forth to show a dwelling place. “At the foot of a tree” means at the foot of a tree that has a covered door-frame attached.
The same method applies to the bamboo thicket as well. The connection is "by one who causes [the robe-material] to be taken, those things which are to be taken.

"Belonging to the Saṅgha" means arising from that source. "In those two" refers to the two requisites for robes. "Which" refers to the requisite for robes. "Of that" refers to the requisite for robes.
"From the place where it stands" means from the location where it remains by way of continuity. "The other" means the other than the requisite for robes previously taken.
"Appatāya" means "due to lack of power"; it is connected with the word "being seized. "Pariveṇagghena" means "by way of the boundaries of the pariveṇa.
"They receive" means that the monks who own the pariveṇa receive it. "Tad" refers to the pariveṇa. "Vijaṭetvā" means having disentangled it;
the meaning is "having divided it into two or three portions. "Pakkhipitvā" means having placed [the share] into its respective portion.
"It should not be done thus" means it should not be done in the manner that the Elder Mahāsiva stated.
Showing the reason why it should not be done, he said, "For people," and so forth. "Therein" refers to the courtyard; the construction is: "it was said that one should enter.
"In this" refers to this place of grasping. "He protests" means he objects. Showing the manner of his protestation—
He said, "Do not, friend," and so forth. The construction is: "Thus he spoke" (*iti vuttaṃ*) and "thus he protested" (*iti paṭikkosati*). For one *iti* word is indicated as being elided.
"His" refers to the Great Elder. "The gathering" means the gathering of monks. "Him" refers to the Great Elder.
"Should be spoken thus" means it should be spoken according to the method that will be explained below. "‘Hold [this] as a requisite,’ thus it should be spoken."
The construction is as follows: “It reaches, friend,” is how it is to be construed.

By the phrase “it has been taken,” he shows that it is “taken” because it was spoken by way of the present tense, as in “take it” or “I take it. Showing the state of not being taken by way of the past and future tenses, he says “But if,” and so forth.
“Mere arising of mindfulness” means the mere production of mindfulness regarding the taking. “In this case” refers to...
In the context of receiving requisites for lodgings (*senāsana-paccaya*).
"Yopi" means "yampi" (whatever). This nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative; thus the construction is: "whatever requisite he relinquishes.

And "paccayaṃ" refers to the requisite of robes (*cīvara-paccaya*). "Ayampi" means "this [other] requisite as well. The particle *pi* (also/even) [indicates inclusion] in the phrase "in the courtyard of great gains" (*mahālābha-pariveṇe*).
He collects the requisites. "In that very cell" means in that very cell taken by the paṃsukūlika.
"Of another" means of a bhikkhu other than the paṃsukūlika. The construction is as follows:
the paṃsukūlika will tend to the lodging thinking, "I am living here," while the other will tend to the lodging thinking, "I am receiving the requisites. By these two...
"By means of two reasons" refers to the two reasons consisting of the taking up of robes. "When those who wear rag-robes take [them]" is the connection.
"Here" means in the monastery. "By him" means by the wearer of rag-robes. "Below" means beneath the dwelling; the connection is "another nun standing below.
"By him" means by the wearer of rag-robes; the connection is "some words. "Of the wearer of rag-robes who has completed the rains residence" [is the connection].

The construction [of the sentence]: “It is allowable” means it is allowable for a wearer of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*). “In that dwelling place” means in the dwelling place taken up by the wearer of rag-robes.
“But of whom” refers to those people. “Of them” refers to those people.

“Having made a stupa” means having made a shrine (*cetiya*). “Of it” refers to the stupa. “By that monk” refers to the monk who receives the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering). “That” refers to the dining hall. The connection is: “it is allowable to have it built. “All this” refers to this entire statement.
"From the dawn of the first day of the month" means from the sunrise of the first day (pāṭipada) reckoned as the day of entering the rains residence.
"One who wanders with thoughts" means one who is intent on wandering with such thoughts as, "Where indeed shall I dwell?

"He requests a lodging" means he requests a lodging from the assigner of lodgings. "Taken" means taken by the Saṅgha. "Where" means in that place. "Should be spoken by those who have entered the rains residence."
[This is] the connection. They repeatedly release or clean the shrine courtyard (*cetiyāṅgaṇa*) and so forth; thus they are called *sammuñcaniyo*.
In the root *muc*, in the sense of cleaning, the suffix *ya* occurs in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇatthe*). The first syllable is produced from the palate (*tālujō*).

If staffs are easily available, two or three bamboo brooms (*yaṭṭhisammuñcaniyo*) should be tied together for each person. If tally-sticks (*salākā*) are easily available, five or six handful-brooms (*muṭṭhisammuñcaniyo*) [should be used].

The meaning is "they should be bound. "Five by five torches" means that in forest dwellings, five by five fire-torches should be struck and split for the purpose of detecting dangers; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "having established a fixed routine," he said, "by those performing the routine," in order to show the routine that must not be neglected.
And so forth. Therein, the connection is that those performing the duties (*vatta*) should not perform such unrighteous duties (*adhammika-vatta*).

For it is true; the construction is that all these—recitation (*uddesa*) and so on—are conceptual proliferations (*papañca*). They are called *papañca* because they cause one to proliferate, meaning they cause one to remain long in *saṃsāra*.
"The vow of the mute" (*mūgabbata*) means the vow of the mute, or that which is to be performed by the mute, or [a vow] like that of a mute even by those who are not mute.

The vow (vata) is indeed what ought to be done. Having thus shown the duty that should not be performed, he now says, "What is called the Dhamma of the scriptures," etc., in order to show the duty that should be performed.

"Even the threefold" means even the three modes by way of the scriptures (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha). Whether it be the constituent part of the Dhamma of the scriptures (avayava-pariyatti-dhamma) supporting the whole of the Dhamma of the scriptures (avayavin-pariyatti-dhamma), or the whole of the Dhamma of the scriptures supporting the constituent part of the Dhamma of the scriptures, [it does so].
Therefore, it should be understood that the Dhamma of the scriptures establishes itself by means of itself. "Recite" means recite the scriptures.
Regarding the instruction, "Having purified them... ordain them," here "purifying" means examining all those of good family who observe proper conduct.
Regarding the instruction, "Having purified them, grant them dependence (nissaya)," here "purifying" means examining whether they possess the qualities common to monks.
“Hī” means truth. “Kulaputta” means one who is a son of noble conduct. The construction is: “as many ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) as you are able to undertake.
“Antovassaṃ nāmetan” is an accusative case used in the sense of a locative; the meaning is “within this rainy season,” and it is to be connected with such words as “should be” (bhavitabba).
“Sakaladivasaṃ” means throughout the entire day. “Appamattehi” [means by those who are heedful].
"Connection. "The duty of wandering alone" means the duty to be practiced by one who wanders alone. "In speech" means in words.
"Discourse on the ten bases" means discourse having the ten bases such as fewness of desires.
"Contentious, slanderous, and harsh speech": it is called "contentious" because it produces contention and strife; and it is "contentious speech."
The construction is: "You should dwell frequently with attention to divisive speech, harsh speech, and quarrelsome, divisive, and harsh speech;
you should be exhorted thus. Regarding the "rule for chewing tooth-sticks":

this refers either to the chewing of tooth-sticks as explained below in the commentary on the taking of what is not given, or to the procedure (*vatta*) for chewing tooth-sticks. [As it is said: "By one putting the bowl into its bag..."
By the phrase “it should not be told,” the prohibition against telling [the donor] is for the purpose of protecting the bowl, lest the bowl be broken through negligence while it is being spoken of.
The word “iti” in the expression “it should be pointed out” (ācikkhitabbā) signifies completion.
The connection is with the words “some donor. A “visiting monk” (āgantuka-bhikkhu) is one who has arrived after the robes have been taken up.
"Bhikkhu": the senior monk of the resident community (*āvāsika-saṅghatthera*). "The first portion" refers to the first portion previously received;
"having exchanged" means having exchanged the rainy-season gift (*vassāvāsika*) that is to be given later for the portion previously received.

The construction is: "It should be given to the guest at the place where [the portion] was obtained by the guest according to the length of residence. The word "to the guest" (*āgantukassa*) applies both to what precedes and what follows.
It looks back [to the previous rule]. Therefore, it is stated between the two rules. "Entered for the rains in the first year" means entered for the rains on the day of the first-year observance.

The repetition in the form "two, three, four" or "whatever was obtained, whatever was obtained" is stated as a distributive repetition (*vicchā*) either to indicate the inclusion of many monks or to express plurality. "But by that newcomer" means by one who has arrived later. "By those who have entered for the rains in the first year."

This method should be understood to apply even when there are many *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) gifts to be given on the final day of the invitation (*pacchimavassūpanāyikadivasa*), even though it was not stated [explicitly] regarding those obtained in small amounts;
this is because [the rule] was stated with reference to two [monks] by way of the first and second [cases].
"Even for two" means for both the first and the second. "The monks who have entered the rains retreat say so, being weary from begging for alms."
The connection [of the words] is as follows: *idha* means "in this place. *Vasanta* means "dwelling together. The construction is:

"It would be good if there were two portions. *Sādhu vata* means "may they certainly be excellent"; such is the meaning. *Yesaṃ* refers to "of those monks. *Tattha* means "in those places where one has been invited by kinsmen.

*Pavāraṇāya* means "on the day of the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*). *Tesu* means "among those monks. *Ye* refers to "those monks. *Tattha* means "in those places where one has been invited by kinsmen."
"Why must it be given after seeking permission? Is it not because they consent? To this he says, "Even though they consent," and so forth.
In that context, "hi" means "because. By the phrase "neither for the owner of the rains-residence," he indicates their state of having interrupted the rains-retreat.
"They do not even get to refuse" means that because the agreement and rule were established at the very outset, they do not even get to refuse; [this applies] to all of them.

"No amhākam" (not ours) is the construction. "Idha" means in this place. "Taṃ" refers to the agreed-upon rule of conduct (*katikavatta*). "Eko bhikkhu" (a single monk) is the connection. "Tesaṃ" refers to those monks.
"Tattha" means in that common location. The construction is: "of those monks who have returned after having stayed there.

"Iti vuttaṃ na labbhati" (it is said that it is not obtained) is the construction. "Imesaṃ" refers to certain [monks] who have reached the period of the rainy-season residence (*vassāvāsa*). "Gāhitasadisaṃ eva" (just like what was taken) is the construction.
It is exactly the same as when one has received [the robe] for the rains-residence.
"Of those very ones" means of some particular ones. "Even though he has departed" means even though he has gone to another place. "Hi" means truly, or because. The construction is:

the work performed by that monk, such as the setting out of drinking water and so forth, is "settled as wages," meaning it stands as payment for his labor. This is a formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*).
The connection is: "having made it, it was taken as belonging to the Saṅgha. "Belonging to the Saṅgha" is said with reference to the source of revenue for that [monastery].

"Even one who has left the order"—the word "even" (pi) indicates, all the more so, one whose rains-residence has been terminated. "By way of requisites alone"—that is, by way of requisites given through faith. "They say"—some say.
The connection is: "A monk who has gone away from his residence departs [from the rains retreat]. Regarding "among people": among the people who gave the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) requisites.
"In the presence of" means in the presence of the resident monk. "Having caused to accept" means having caused them to accept by saying, "We shall certainly give.
"From whom it was taken" refers to the monk from whom the lodging was taken. "Of the owner of the lodging" refers to the son, daughter, or others of the one who gave the lodging.
The connection is as follows: "We give for the lodging" means we give for the sake of the lodging. "Therein" means in the lodging. Only one cloth should be given. Why?

Because it must be given to the lodging itself, rather than to an individual. "By means of the standing for the rainy-season residence" means by means of the standing [of the robe] received for the rainy-season residence.
"In this very same manner" means that because it was given to the lodging itself, the procedure is exactly the same. "They belong to him alone" means they belong to the individual alone.
Because it was given, it belongs to him alone. The connection is:
"The second [seat] was taken for the Elder's seat. Because the first portion was taken by the novice, it is said:
"Having given the excellent portion to the novice. "Both" refers to both the Elder and the novice. "Himself" refers to the donor.
"By oneself alone. "The rains-residence fee" (*vassāvāsika*). "Whose" refers to either the elder (*thera*) or the novice (*sāmaṇera*).
"From this" means from the manner already stated. "Of the young novice" refers to a tender novice. "He" is the head of the household.

"Them" refers to the people who have received [the robe]. "Whose" refers to the monk. "Of them" refers to those people. "Should be explained as it truly is" means the reason for the time of disrobing and the details of what was done.
It should be explained as it truly is. "Only pure refuse-rag wearers" means those who are exclusively pure refuse-rag wearers, unmixed with others.
This is the conclusion regarding the duties of a resident monk (*nevāsika-vatta*).
The Story of Upananda.
319. "This is the meaning" (*ayam attho*) means that this meaning which is about to be explained is to be understood in this way;

such is the connection. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the village. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the lodging (*senāsana*); the connection is with the phrase "by one who is taking it up. "Here" (*idha*) means in Sāvatthī.
"Released" (*muttaṃ*) means that the lodging has been relinquished. "Even there" (*tatrapi*) means even in the village. "In both places" (*ubhayattha*) means in both Sāvatthī and the village.
"Herein" means in the case of Upananda. "How" means in what manner does it subside?
"Here" means in the Dispensation (Sāsana). "A certain person takes [it]" is the connection. "There too" means even in a neighboring monastery.
"His" refers to the bhikkhu. "Here" refers to the dwelling place (senāsana). "Mere attachment" means mere arising of consciousness. "Thus for him" means *iti assa*; thus for that bhikkhu.
The meaning [is as follows]. "In all cases" refers to every instance within the tetrad beginning with "taking by taking. The connection is: "he who goes.

Regarding "transgressing the boundary of the vicinity" (*upacārasīmātikkame*), this locative expression is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*) or to indicate a characteristic state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*).
"Therein" means that if he returns to another monastery, it is permissible; the intention is that the formal assignment of lodgings (*senāsanaggāha*) does not become nullified.
320. "A bhikkhu who is older or younger": he is either older or younger than oneself. The construction is:
"that bhikkhu is called 'one with three years' difference. A bhikkhu standing within three years [of seniority] from another bhikkhu is "one with three years' difference" (tivassantara).
"Therein" means among the bhikkhus. "All these" refers to those with a three-year difference, a two-year difference, and those of equal seniority.
The connection is: "These monks receive [it]. Regarding the phrase "which is sufficient for three":
even on a seat—excluding beds and stools—that is sufficient for three to sit comfortably, they are permitted to sit by twos;

this is how the construction should be understood. By the word "even" (*api*), beds and stools are being referred to. This is the "long western seat. "Even with one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannena*): [this is the meaning].
The word *pi* (even) indicates, all the more so, one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*).

"On the elephant's frontal globe" (*hatthikumbhe*) means on the mass of the elephant's head. By this term "elephant," it is shown that "elephant's frontal globe" is understood either through the metaphorical transfer of a part to the whole (*avayavūpacāra*) or by the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
"Like an elephant" (*hatthī viya*) means an elephant; [it refers to] a portion of ground, [or] that which stands upon an elephant.
"Elephant-clawed" (*hatthinakhaka*) means "the palace whose nails are counted as its feet. The construction is: "This name 'elephant-clawed' is the name of the palace built in such a manner.
The phrase "variegated with gold, silver, and so forth" should be applied to all the terms: "doors, beds, stools, and palm-leaf fans.
Whatever has been fashioned as decorative art (*cittakamma*), all of it is permissible.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "We give it to the palace" is the connection. "Separately" means apart from the palace.
"Only what has been accepted" means that everything is indeed accepted. "To use the eighteen kinds of coverings, such as woolen rugs (*gonaka*), etc. is the connection.

"By way of what is distinctively provided by householders" (*gihivikaṭanīhārena*): that which is specifically prepared according to one's desire by householders is "distinctively provided by householders" (*gihivikaṭa*); it belongs to the householders.

“*Gihivikaṭan*” means the removal, the bringing out, the removal of what has been brought out by householders; [the phrase] “by that” refers to this. “They may be used” means they may indeed be used for sitting upon.
“There too” means even on the Dhamma-seat. This concludes the discussion on items that must not be relinquished.
321. "These" refers to heavy articles (garubhaṇḍa). "Therein" means among the five [types] by way of heaps, or among the twenty-five heavy articles by way of their individual forms.
Having come, they delight there abundantly; thus it is called an *ārāma*. "Of those very same" refers specifically to flower-gardens and fruit-gardens.
By the phrase "a designated spot," he shows that the word *vatthu* has the meaning of a specific portion of ground. An *ārāma* dwells [there]; it is established.

"Herein" (*ettha*) means on the site of the monastery (*ārāmavatthu*). "Among those" (*tesu vā*): here, by the word "or" (*vā*), it is intended as an alternative that even a portion of ground other than the nine [new] divisions may constitute the site of the monastery.
"Monastery" (*vihāra*): it is so called because one brings about or carries out the four modes of conduct (*catuiriyāpatha*) therein.
"Of that" (*tassa*) refers to the monastery. "Of the four beds": the genitive case is used in the sense of specification (*niddhāraṇa*). "A certain bed" (*aññataro mañco*).
The construction is with the word *nāma*. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
By the phrase “a cauldron made of iron,” he demonstrates that in the term *lohakumbhī* (iron cauldron), it is a compound formed by the elision of the middle member (*majjhelopasamāsa*).

The literal meaning—“a cauldron consisting of iron” (*lohmayā kumbhī*)—is also entirely appropriate. By the phrase “this same method,” he indicates the meanings: “a vessel made of iron,” “a jar made of iron,” and “a basin made of iron.”
He extends [the application]. "Therein" means in the bowls of the reciters. *Arañjara* is so called because, being very large, it quickly decays (*araṃ khippaṃ jarati*) or destroys;
or else, it is *arañjara* because it is not able (*ala*) to hold water, having changed the letter *la* to *ra*.
Showing the conclusion by way of a verse, he said "Thus," and so forth. Therein, the connection is with "thus he proclaimed."
Two heavy articles consist of two groups; the third heavy article consists of four groups;
the fourth heavy article consists of nine sections; the fifth heavy article consists of eight divisions.
Thus, in this manner, the Lord with his five stainless eyes proclaimed the twenty-five kinds of heavy articles in five heaps—this is the construction [of the verse].

“In that regard” means among heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*). “For” (*hi*) indicates an expansion. The construction is: “All this heavy goods is said to be ‘not to be relinquished’. “Here” means in this context. The connection is: “But it has come down in the *Parivāra*. The construction is:
“Five heaps were spoken by the Great Sage. “In this” means in the *Parivāra*.
“Therein” refers to the statement “by way of exchange. The connection is: “This heavy goods is to be brought forward. Always.

"Standing" (*tiṭṭhanti*) means "stable" (*thāvara*); the root is *ṭhā*, with the suffix *vara*, and the change of the letter *ṭh* to *th*. By this term, monasteries (*ārāma*), monastery sites (*ārāmavatthu*), dwellings (*vihāra*), and dwelling sites (*vihāravatthu*) are to be understood.
Because they are not to be relinquished and are not subject to distribution, heavy goods that are not light are "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*).

By this term, the twenty-one types of heavy goods, such as beds and so forth, are to be understood. "In regard to stable things" (*thāvare*) is the locative case used for the support; it is connected with the word "included" (*pariyāpanna*).

Alternatively, the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*); thus, the meaning is "among the permanent things" (*thāvaresu*), which is to be connected with "fields" (*khette*) and so forth.

It is called a "field" (*khetta*) because the seed of grain (*pubbaṇṇa*) is sown (*khipati*) therein. It is called a "site" (*vatthu*) because the seed of non-grain (*aparaṇṇa*) dwells (*vasati*) or is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) therein.
A "tank" (*taḷāka*) is so called because an enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) is made there on a level plot of ground (*tale bhūmibhāge*) from one, two, or three sides.
*Saro* (arrow). The *mātikā* (matrix/table of contents) is that which is to be performed according to the opinion of the farmers.

The connection is: "to exchange with a monastery. To the question "Which ones are to be exchanged? he says: "These four as well. The word *pi* (also/as well) serves to include all the individual parts.
In that context—referring to the statement "it is permissible to exchange. *Dūre* (far away) means in a place distant from the monastic compound (*saṅghārāma*). Regarding the phrase *yampi*:
"Even a coconut fruit. "They take it away" means they take it for the Saṅgha.
"To others" is connected with "to people other than the Saṅgha. "Those" refers to the people. "It should be accepted by the Saṅgha" is the connection.
"It is pleasing" means it is desired or wished for that the Saṅgha’s monastery should be exchanged for the people’s monastery, or the people’s monastery for the Saṅgha’s monastery.
The connection is "a park for the bhikkhus. "This" refers to a park belonging to laypeople (*manussa*).

"Small" means smaller than a monastery (*saṅghārāma*). "Income" (*āya*): it comes (*āyati*), it goes toward increase through wealth; that which causes one to increase by means of wealth is "income," and that [is what is meant]. "Of equal measure" (*samakam eva*) means of exactly the same dimension;
the connection is "if he gives the income. The suffix *-ka* is used here in the sense of measure. The connection is "trees belonging to laypeople."

The connection is: "We give the surplus to the Saṅgha. "Having made known" means having made known to people the benefit of a gift given to the Saṅgha, [thinking], "What is given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit.
The construction is: "Are they not indeed possessors of the fruit?
"Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion. "By this very method" means by that same method according to which a monastery (ārāma) is to be exchanged for a monastery.
The construction is: "by means of a large or small monastery site. The connection is: "monasteries and monastery sites, as well as monasteries and monastery sites, should be exchanged.
"Both" refers to both types by way of house and palace. "Therein" means in the house. "But this," however, refers to the house known as a palace.
The connection is with "the houses of people. The construction is: "by means of a monastery site, whether of great value or of small value. The connection is:
"monasteries, monastery sites, parks, and park sites are to be exchanged. "In this way," and so forth, is the conclusion. The construction is:
"in the exchange of heavy goods for heavy goods, the legal decision (*vinicchaya*) should be understood in this manner. Regarding "in sand-castles": [the text continues].

In houses built for the purpose of playing with dust. "Suitable couches" (*kappiyamañca*) refers to couches that are allowable for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, and are not made of gold, silver, or similar materials.
The connection is that even couches made of gold, silver, and so forth may be given to a monastery (*vihāra*).

"Outside the boundary" (*bahisīmāya*) means outside the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the dwelling place of the senior monk of the Saṅgha. "Therein" (*tattha*)... [end of fragment]
In the dwelling place of that bhikkhu. By specifying the statement “of great value,” he says: “worth a hundred [pieces] or worth a thousand [pieces]. “A hundred beds” means many beds.
“Even among these” refers even to the benches, mattresses, and pillows. “Therein” refers to the benches, mattresses, and pillows.
The connection is: “a permissible bench, etc. Or, [it may refer to] something impermissible or of great value.
“*Kappiyaṃ vā*” means “or by means of what is allowable,” and it is connected with “having exchanged” (*parivattetvā*).

The word “*vuttavatthūni*” (the stated items) is the unstated object of the verb “*parivattetvā*,” while it is the stated object of the verb “*gahetabbāni*” (to be taken); thus, it is a word that depends on both the preceding and the following.

“*Pasatamattaudakagaṇhakānipīti*” (even those holding as much water as a *pasata*): here, a *pasata* is a closed fist. “*Sīhaḷadīpe*” (in the island of Sihaḷa): [it is so called] because it takes (*lāti*) the lion (*sīhaṃ*).
“Sīhaḷo” means one who seizes (*gaṇhāti*); having changed the letter *la* to *ḷa*, it refers to the king named Sīhabāhu. Because he was his son, Prince Vijaya was also called Sīhaḷa.
Since the island was seized by him as his place of residence at the beginning, it is called the Sīhaḷa Island; [the word] "in that" refers to this.
One who seizes the foot is a "foot-seizer" (*pādagaṇhano*), and he is precisely a "foot-seizer" (*pādagaṇhanako*). Regarding the phrase "what is called a foot": in this context of "a foot-seizer,"...
"Pāda" means: the connection is that a metal vessel which holds five *nāḷis* of the Magadha measure is called a "pāda.
By this, he shows the method of conventional usage (*vohāranaya*) wherein the name of the measure is applied metaphorically (*upacārato*) to that which possesses the measure.
"From that" means from the vessel holding five *nāḷis*. "These" refers to the iron cauldrons and so forth.

"Water-pitchers... and spoons, etc. means: the water-pitcher (*bhiṅgāra*), the alms-bowl (*paṭiggaha*), the ladle (*uḷuṅka*), the tongs (*dabbi*), the spoon (*kaṭacchu*), the plate (*pāti*), the tray (*taṭṭaka*), the cup (*sarako*), the casket (*samugga*), the charcoal pan (*aṅgārakapalla*), and the smoke-spoon (*dhūmakaṭacchu*).
These—beginning with the water-pitcher and ending with the smoke-spoon—are what they are "etcetera" for;
thus, they are called "water-pitchers... and spoons, etc. By the word "etcetera," other items are included.
Requisites are to be taken. "Distributable" means they are to be shared out. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "bell-metal, iron, and so forth," copper is included.
"Copper" refers to brass. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because.

"Personal use" (*pārihāriya*) means using something belonging to the Saṅgha by setting it aside from communal use and employing it as one's own private use, or by taking possession of it with the thought, "This is my own."

It is not permitted to eat while holding [the bowl] with the hand. “In the manner of a householder’s *vikaṭa* (raw food)” means precisely by way of the intention (*abhinīhārena*) that it is “a householder’s *vikaṭa*.

The construction is: “even in another vessel made of allowable metal, there is a collyrium-box (*añjanī*). Alternatively, in the phrase “in a vessel made of allowable metal,” the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*);
it should be connected with the words beginning with “collyrium-box. “Needle” (*sūcī*) refers to a needle for sewing robes and so forth.
*Paṇṇasūcī*: a needle for writing on leaves. *Aññampi*: other [items] besides the eye-salve box and so forth.

*Dhūmanettañca phālañca dīparukkho ca dīpakapallako ca olambakadīpo ca*: the smoke-inhaler, the hoe, the lamp-stand, the lamp-tray, and the hanging lamp—[these are] the smoke-inhalers... up to ...the hanging lamps.
Because they possess forms consisting of women, men, and animals, they are called "those having the forms of women, men, and animals. [These are] the smoke-inhalers... up to ...the hanging lamps.
"And those images of women, men, and animals" refers to smoke-funnels... [etc. ...images; this is a compound where the qualifying term is placed last.
The connection is: "metal objects that should be affixed to walls, ceilings, door-panels, and so forth," whether these or others.
"A metal peg" means a pin made of metal. "Having carried around" means having carried it about with the sense of possession, thinking, "This is mine."
Having removed those things belonging to the Saṅgha, articles for personal use, or household utensils. "Made of milk-stone" means made of stone that has the color of milk.
"Gold, silver, bronze, and crystal"—that is, gold... [as before] ...crystal; vessels made from these are "gold... [as before] ...crystal vessels.
"All" refers to all such items as gold, silver, and so forth. "Is allowable" means it is allowable for the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
The construction is: "In this way, the determination regarding the axe and so forth is to be understood. Or, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).
The connection is: "by which axe it is not possible. "From that" means from the axe. The word *mahattarī* is a non-derived primary form (*anipphanna-pāṭipadika*) synonymous with "great.
The connection is: "the great axe. "Of physicians" means of surgeons. By the word "and" (*pi*) in the phrase "and the adze for piercing veins," [it is included].
The phrase "even before" indicates that it was indeed large. The connection is: "the axe which was fashioned as a representative of weapons.
Alternatively, the construction is: "there is, moreover, an axe which was fashioned as a representative of weapons.

"Untouchable" means not to be touched; the sense is that it is unworthy of being touched. The word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "not even four finger-breadths" indicates that anything larger than that is, of course, even more so.
"Digging in and eating" is *nikhādana*. "Its mouth is four-cornered" is *caturassamukha*. "Its mouth is like a trough" is *doṇimukha*. The construction is:

"The sweeping-stick and the piercing-stick are also *nikhādana* when they are bound to a handle. It is called *daṇḍabaddha* because it must be bound with a handle, or because a handle is bound to it; thus it is *daṇḍabaddha*.
Having said "adaṇḍaka" (without a handle), it is stated "only the fruit itself" in order to show its meaning. That which has no handle is *adaṇḍaka*.
"Yaṃ" refers to the digging-in [of the handle]. "Pariharituṃ" means to carry away by taking possession as one's own private property, or to remove it from the status of belonging to the Saṅgha.
The tip (*sikhara*) is also included by the very act of digging-in, according to the method of applying the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*).
Because they have the same function. "By which" refers to those by which [the trees] whirl around and cut;

the connection is that these were given by people. "They" refers to the people; the connection is "they say. "Not" means "not ours. "In their natural state" (*pākatika*) means remaining in their original condition;
the meaning is, "we shall act so that they remain as they were first. "If they bring them" means if there is a request.

They take it away without having made [the payment]. "Even though they do not take it" means even though they do not take it again. The smith, the brazier, the coppersmith, the reed-worker, the jeweler, and the bowl-binder—the smith...
pe... the bowl-binder; of them. The anvil, the hammer, the tongs, and the balance—the anvil... pe... [and so forth].
*Tulā* (balance). "From the time it was given to the Saṅgha" means from the time it was given to the Saṅgha. That by which one cuts tin is *tipucchedana*;

that very knife is the *tipucchedana-satthaka* (tin-cutting knife). The construction is: "having set aside the large knife (*mahākattarī*), the large pair of tongs (*mahāsaṇḍāsa*), and the large forceps (*mahāpipphalika*).
He asks why they were set aside and says: "The large knife and the others are heavy articles (*garubhaṇḍa*). Regarding that:
The construction is as follows: since items such as the large knife (*mahākattarī*) are heavy articles (*garubhaṇḍa*), therefore I have stated, "excepting the large knife," and so forth.

The construction is that the determination regarding creepers (*vallī*) and the like should be understood in this way. "Creepers reckoned as rattan-creepers, etc. means creepers known as rattan-creepers and so on. Regarding the measure of "half a *bahuppamāṇa*":
here it is said—“A *byāma* is the length of both arms extended; two *passas* are its width.”
Because it is stated in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* (verse 269), the term "bāhu" here refers specifically to a *vyāma*.
Therefore, the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) should be understood as follows: "half of two arms" (*addhabāhu*) refers to two arms, each measuring one *vyāma*, when spread out across both sides;
"measuring half an arm" (*addhabāhuppamāṇa*) means that its measurement is such; [in length] it is two cubits.
"Vallī" (creeper) is what is meant. "Tatthajātakā" means those grown on that land belonging to the Saṅgha.
"Rakkhitagopitā" means protected by the Saṅgha itself and guarded by others. By this, it is shown that what is unprotected and unguarded does not constitute "heavy property.
"Sā" refers to that creeper. "Atirekā hoti" is the connection [to the previous context]. "Upanetuṃ" means to bring that creeper near. "Suttañca" (and thread).
“Makaci, vāka, coconut husk, hide, and thread... [and so on] ... “Hides; made from these, or from thread... [and so on] ... they are made of hide. The connection is:
