“Whether ropes or cords, they constitute heavy property. Regarding the phrase “single-stranded or double-stranded,” the word “or” here includes three-stranded and so forth.
The construction is: “thread given after twisting, and makaci, vāka, and coconut husk given after twisting.”
"Whatever bamboo" is the connection. "That too" means even bamboo is permissible; this is the connection. By the word "also" (pi), it refers back to "creeper.
"All this here" means all this [mentioned] is here in the bamboo, or among the bamboos; this is the connection. "Of equal measure" means of the same measurement as the bamboo already taken.
"Or exceeding" means more than that. "Worth its price" means worth the value of that bamboo.
*Phātikamma* means the act of increasing. *Tattheva* means right there, at the place of receiving.

*Gamanakāle* means at the time of going elsewhere from the place of receiving. By the phrase "having sent [someone], it should be given," one should also understand through the method of applying characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*) that it may also be given by coming oneself, because the function is the same.
Because the *muñja* and *pabbaja* grasses are mentioned separately in the Canon by means of the compound *muñjapabbaja*,

he says "having set aside the *muñja* and the *pabbaja*" and so forth, showing that by the principle of remainder (*pārisesa-naya*), the word "grass" must be understood as referring only to the remaining types of grass,
excluding those two. Furthermore, because they share the same fruit (or quality), even leaves are included under "grass" according to the method of figurative application (*lakkhaṇahāra-naya*).
Showing this, he said “*yatthā*,” and so forth. Therein, “*yatthā*” means in which place; “*iti*” means thus. The connection is: “and grass becomes a heavy commodity.
“*Tatthajātakaṃ vā*” means grown in that monastic compound (*saṅghārāma*). “*Bahārāme*” means outside the monastic compound. “*Tampī*” means even that grass.
By the word “*pi*,” creepers and bamboos are also implied. “*Aṭṭhaṅgulappamāṇopī*” means even [grass] measuring eight finger-breadths in length.
"Even eight finger-breadths in measure. An "empty book" (rittapotthaka) is a book that is void because it has not been written upon;
it may be made of cotton cloth and so forth, or even of leaves.

This is mentioned here by way of the discussion on leaves. "Or five colors" means the five colors by way of blue, yellow, red, white, and madder. "That too" refers to clay as well. By the word "too" (pi), it implies creepers, bamboo, and grass.

The construction is: "In this way, the determination regarding wooden articles (dārubhaṇḍa) should be understood. The construction is: "There is some wooden article, whatever it may be, that has been protected and guarded. The connection is: "But it is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra), it refers either to the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* or to the canonical text (pāḷi) beginning with "Now at that time" (*tena kho pana samayena*).

Regarding the word "among these" (imesu), it refers to the *āsandika* chairs and so forth. Regarding the word "here" (ettha), it refers to the benches (*pīṭha*), in connection with the phrase "a bench of straw" (*palālapīṭha*). "Covered with a tiger skin" means with a tiger skin.
*Avanaddhaṃ*: bound. *Vāḷarūpaparikkhittaṃ*: surrounded by the forms of beasts. *Ratanaparisibbitaṃ*: sewn all around with threads of jewels. *Etesupi*:

even in these cases, such as curved planks and so forth. Regarding the reading “*saṅkhathālakaṃ pana bhājanīyan*” (but a conch-shell bowl is to be shared), there is a reading “*tathā*” immediately following it;
that does not fit here, but later [the text says] “whatever has been made is indeed a heavy object (*garubhaṇḍa*)”.
It is appropriate [to place this] immediately after the recitation. For in that context, the meaning is as follows:

just as anything made by anyone constitutes "heavy goods" (garubhaṇḍa), so too, among the wooden posts, beams, stair-rungs, floor-boards, and so forth, any material form used as a component of a house—whether made of wood or stone—is indeed heavy goods.
“*Sabbam* (all)” means the entire water-pot, its stand, and its base-ring. “*Etesupi* (even among these)” refers to the supports and so forth.
Regarding “*tathā thambhatalā*,” the word *tathā* here extends by analogy (*atidisati*) to the phrase “precious goods alone.

“*Saṅghe dinnam* (given to the Saṅgha)” means given to the community of monks. “*Bhūmattharaṇam* (floor-covering)” means that which is to be spread upon the ground. “*Tampī* (that too)” refers even to the sheepskin.
The connection is that the mortar is indeed a heavy article. This same method applies to the pestle and so forth as well. "In these" refers to the bed-legs and so on.

"By means of a vessel permitted for use" means by means of a vessel permitted for the purpose of holding [food]. Regarding the term *dhamakaraṇa*, here the reading without the suffix *-ka* (nissaṃyoga) alone is appropriate, just as in expressions such as "he blows the conch, a conch-blower.
Therefore, it is called *dhamakaraṇa* because it blows—that is, it functions—by means of wind.
*Dhamo* is a sound caused by wind; the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) should be understood as "one who makes a *dhamo*" is a *dhamakaraṇa*.
"All this" refers to all these items, such as the permitted wooden staff (*vāsidaṇḍa*) and so forth. "Than that" means than the permitted wooden staff and so forth;
the construction is: "a larger wooden staff and so forth is heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*)."

“Just as it was produced” means exactly as it occurred. “By those” refers to the elephant tusks and so forth; it should be connected with the word “made. “Even though finished by carving” means even though completed through the work of carving.
The construction is: “The determination should be understood in this way regarding earthenware vessels. “Use and enjoyment” (*upabhogaparibhoga*) is a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
This term should be connected specifically with the phrase “pot, lid, and other such pottery vessels.”

Regarding the term *thūpikātī*: here the word *iti* has the sense of the word *idaṃ*. The construction is: "All this [is considered] heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*) from the time it was given to the Saṅgha.
The qualifying phrase "not exceeding the measure" (*anatirittapamāṇo*) must be connected with the qualified noun "water-pot" (*ghaṭako*). "In this" (*ettha*) refers to earthenware;
the suffix *-ttha* is used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāre*) or a specification (*niddhāraṇe*). [This refers to] earthenware.

The water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) partakes of the portion that is to be shared; the same principle applies to metal vessels—this is how it should be construed. "In this context" refers to the determination of heavy goods (*garubhaṇḍa*). 323.
Regarding the phrase "merely by placing the bundle": here, "placing the bundle" (*bhaṇḍikāṭṭhapana*) means the tying together of the bundle, as he said.
“By means of a measure equal to a pigeon’s nest. *Assa* means of the bhikkhu. *Citakadhūmo* is the smoke arising from a funeral pyre.
*Etasseva vihāro*—the connection is that it is the dwelling of that very bhikkhu. *Dhūmakāle* means at the time when the smoke has arisen.
By the word “having informed,” that which is informed during the time of smoke is *dhūmakālika*. The construction of the meaning is: “having become *dhūmakālika*.”
He shows that [the phrase] should be connected with the words "a completed dwelling" (*pariyositavihāra*) in the text.
"A dwelling whose construction is finished" (*katapariyositavihāraṃ*) means: this new work (*navakamma*) has its construction finished; thus it is "a dwelling whose construction is finished.
The connection is: "they give this new work. The construction is: "as long as the rafters have not been set up, so long it is called 'unfinished' (*vippakata*). From that...
"From the time of ascending the rafters": [this means] having persuaded someone, he will have it built;

that is, the owner of the monastery itself, having persuaded some bhikkhu, will have it built. "In a five-cubit monastery" is the connection. "A new construction of six years' duration" is the connection.
"Therein" refers to the *aḍḍhayoga*. "He" refers to the *aḍḍhayoga*. Showing the determination of its size, he said: "ten cubits or eleven cubits."
The connection is with "a new construction (*navakamma*) of ten or eleven years. "From that" means from twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*).
The connection is with "even in a palace similar to the Lohapāsāda. "From that" means from the nine-year-old new construction.

"A supervisor of new construction (*navakammika*)" means one who is engaged and occupied with new construction. "In the season" means in the winter or summer season. "To ward off" means [to prevent] others.

To prevent [the use] by monks who have arrived. "Of the owner of the residence" means of the donor of the residence. "His" means of the owner of the residence. "In the lineage" means in the family line. "Those" means yours.
"He" refers to the owner of the residence and so forth. The connection is: "[the residence] must be maintained by the monks. "They too" means even the relatives and attendants.
"Even in that" means even regarding the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha. The connection is: "many residences. The construction is: "one residence."
The connection is with the phrase "or one residence. The connection is with the words "arisen from" (uppannāni), [referring to] "from those" (tato) residences already assigned.
In the *Kurundi*, however, it is said that the construction is: "How was it said? (kinti vuttaṃ). "Having taken one bed-place" means having taken one bed-place as private property (*puggalika*).
"A third part" (*tibhāga*) means a third portion; this is indeed the reading. "Therein" (*ettha*) refers to the ruined monastery.
"Puggalikameva" means "only personal property" (puggalikaṃ eva) or "as if it were personal property" (puggalikaṃ iva). "Jaggā" means "look after" (jaggāhi). "Hi" is a particle indicating the result.
"Evaṃ jaggito pana" means "but when the monastery has been looked after in this way. "Tasmiṃ jaggante" means "while he is looking after it.

"Saddhivihārikādīnaṃ dātukāmo hoti" means that he desires to give [the goods] to his co-residents and others; that is, without giving them to the Sangha’s storehouse or to the dwelling place of the novices, [he keeps them] for himself alone.
He wishes to give to his *saddhivihārika* (resident pupil) and others.

The meaning of "it is allowable to give to the *saddhivihārika* and others" is that it is allowable to give to them because only a portion [of the monastery] has been taken as private property (*puggalika*), rather than the entire monastery having been taken as such.
The construction is: "it is said that he should be made to look after it. Here, although there is a reading "it is said" (*vuttaṃ*), that is not the correct reading.

Regarding the phrase “but it is stated in the *Kurundi*,” because it is in the nominative case (*ākāra*), the construction is as follows: this other statement as well, which is about to be spoken, is stated in that very same *Kurundi*. To the question “How is it stated?
he says: “Two monks,” and so forth. The connection is “two monks perform [the act]. By whom? By the monk. That very same...
"Owner" (*sāmī*) means that he who first took possession of that land is the owner; this is the meaning. "In a suitable place" means in a suitable location for a lodging.
"That" refers to the act of making it one's own property (*puggalikakaraṇa*). As for the phrase "but whatever building-work," the construction is as follows:
here, "building-work" (*vayakamma*) refers to the foundation of the work performed in that monastery. What is meant is that the foundation of the monastery must be given. "Of that" (*tassa*)—
"For one making it for the Saṅgha. "Right there" means in the very vihāra that has been built. "In the vicinity of the built dwelling" is a locative expression used in the sense of proximity;
thus, it means "in the vicinity of the built dwelling. "Those who approach for shade and those who approach for fruit" means those who go toward the shade and those who go toward the fruit;
the sense is that they bring shade and fruits. "Having informed" means having informed the Saṅgha.
"Owners" means owners of trees. "Should be removed" means they should be cleared away.

By the phrase "without taking even a single creeper belonging to the Saṅgha," it is shown that if one builds a monastery on land belonging to the Saṅgha after taking what belongs to the Saṅgha [as materials], it remains the property of the Saṅgha alone.
This applies to palaces with two or three stories, etc., regarding half of their portion.
Showing this, he said, “It is both a palace,” and so forth. “A palace above” is the connection. “His” refers to that monk who built the monastery;
“his lower palace” is the connection. “In the monastery” means in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha; the meaning is “in the vicinity of the monastery.

“In a place where it has not been done” means in a place where a mound (*caya*) or a front porch (*pamukha*) has not previously been constructed. “Either a mound or a front porch” [refers to] of the monastery belonging to the Saṅgha...
*Cayaṃ vā pamukhaṃ vā*: either a heap (*caya*) or a front (*pamukha*). *Bahikuṭṭeti*: outside of a wall (*kuṭṭa*), or beyond the wall. *Tassā* (of him):
the connection is that it belongs to the monk who has made the heap or the front. *Visamaṃ pabbatakandarādinti*: the connection is "on uneven ground such as mountains, ravines, and so forth.

*Apadeti*: without a reason for one who is capable [of doing otherwise]. *Kataṃ hotīti*: it has been made; that is, a heap or a front has been constructed. *Tatthāti*: regarding those heaps and fronts, the *saṅgha*.
The construction is: "It is said to be 'not one's own'.
The connection is: "to take a superior bed.

"Having returned again" means having departed and then returning again. "Of him" refers to the monk who has taken charge of the new building work (*navakamma*). "This" refers to the lodging (*senāsana*).
324. Regarding the discussion on the prohibition against using [things] elsewhere:
here, the word *ati* has the sense of "taking away," and the word *hara* has the sense of "consuming. Thus he said, "They do not consume [them] after having taken them elsewhere.
The construction is: "whatever bed, chair, and so forth. Therein means: in the Undriya Mahāvihāra.
*Tat* refers to beds, chairs, and so forth. *Tasmā* means because he permits; therefore.

*Tat* refers to beds, chairs, and so forth. *Aññatra* means to another monastery. *Arogaṃ* means healthy, due to not being afflicted by illness. *Tasmiṃ vihāre* means in that monastery. *Tasmiṃ* means in that monastery.
*Tato* means from that monastery. *Suyojitāni* means well-applied. Or it refers to the original gift.

The intention is that there is no restoration to its original state. "From an abandoned monastery" means from a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha that has been abandoned by monks without concern, and from a private monastery that has been abandoned by an individual with concern.
"At the time of the residents" means at the time when the residents are present. "From there" means from the abandoned monastery.

Regarding the phrase *phātikammatthāya*: here the word *phāti* has the sense of "increasing," which is why he says, "for the purpose of increasing. "In this context" refers to the reading *phātikammatthāya*. *Cakkalikaṃ*:
it is called *cakkala* because it moves (*lāti*) in the shape of a wheel (*cakkākārena*), or because it takes up (*lāti*) the shape of a wheel;
that very thing is *cakkalika*, meaning a foot-washer. By the phrase "made by wrapping with woolen cloth and so forth," its mode of construction is indicated.
It shows [the following]. "By which" means by the feet. "Water" refers to water that has soaked into the dwelling. The construction is: "the water is not visible.
"It is not permitted to step with sandals on" is the construction.
"On a plastered floor" means on a floor smeared with lime-plaster. "On a polished floor" means on a floor polished with a coating of cow-dung and clay.
"Pādāti" means bed-legs. "Tasmiṃ coḷake" means in that cloth. "Ṭhapentassā" means of one who is placing [them] on the bed-legs. "Tatthā" means among those monks.
"Nevāsikā" means those who dwell permanently; thus they are called "nevāsikā. "Ṭhapentī" means they place the bed-legs [on the cloth].
"Tathevā" means just as the residents use it, so too is it permissible for guests to use it; this is the meaning.
Regarding "a white wall," the word "or" (*vā*) here includes blue walls and so forth.
Because it is stated generally as "a door or a window," etc., doors, windows, and the like are not to be leaned against even if they have not been treated with plaster.
Or, it is to be construed with "by something such as cloth," and so on.

By the word “having washed” (*hutvā*), he shows that the phrase “with washed feet” (*dhotapādakā*) functions as an adverbial modifier for the verb “to lie down” (*nipajjituṃ*), and he excludes its status as a qualifier of the noun “monks” (*bhikkhū*). To the question, “In what place do they feel scruples about lying down?
he says: “in a place to be stepped upon with washed feet. This [phrase] refers to the place to be stepped upon...

By the term “designation” (*adhivacana*), he shows the meaning of the reading “on a foot-washing stand” (*dhotapādaka*) as follows: “a foot-washing stand” is so called because a washed foot stands (*tiṭṭhati*) in that place; thus, “on a foot-washing stand” is the meaning. “This” refers to the name “on a foot-washing stand.
Regarding the phrase “having spread,” he asks, “Having spread by what? and answers, “by a rug. By the phrase “belonging to oneself,” he indicates that it is not something belonging to the Saṅgha.
He rejects a bed-covering with another bed-covering. “Even from sleeping” (*niddāyato*) means even for the sake of sleeping;

it is connected with “contracted” (*saṃkuṭite*). Alternatively, “even from sleeping” means even while one is sleeping. In the phrase “a part of the body,” the genitive case has the sense of identity (*sāmyattha*);
in the phrase “an offense indeed,” it is the dative case. It is connected with “when they touch the hairs. “By way of usage” (*paribhogasīsena*).
This shows that there is no offense for one who touches a limb of the body with some purpose other than for personal use.
The application of the phrase "to touch with the palm of the hand, to touch with the sole of the foot, or to step upon it" should be understood according to what is available.
In order to show the meaning of the phrase "by way of use," he said: "for one who is carrying out a bed or a chair," and so forth.
The Discourse on the Permission for Community Food, etc., 325:
By the phrase “food for the Saṅgha,” he demonstrates that the term *saṅghabhatta* is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*).
The construction is: “They are unable to prepare food brought for the sake of the Saṅgha. Regarding the terms “designated food” (*uddesabhatta*) and so forth:

The construction is: "In this way, the meaning is to be understood. By the phrase "to prepare a meal for those monks obtained by means of an invitation (*uddesa*)," it shows the etymological meaning of *uddesabhatta* as "the meal that must be prepared for those monks obtained by means of an invitation.
"In the same way" means just as [monks] are obtained by being invited from the Saṅgha. "Having delimited" means by [specifying] "one or... and so forth.
“Having delimited. “Of those” means of the monks who have been invited.
By this, he shows the etymological meaning of *nimantanabhatta* as “the meal to be prepared for the monks obtained through an invitation.

By the phrase “having cut the tally-sticks,” he shows the etymological meaning of *salākabhatta* as “the meal to be prepared after cutting tally-sticks. “Pakkhika” means “fortnightly”; “uposathika” means “on the Uposatha day.”
The construction is: "having thus determined it as 'of the first day' (pāṭipadikaṃ). That which is to be done during the fifth and subsequent fortnights is "fortnightly" (pakkhikaṃ).

That which is to be done on the Uposatha day is "Uposatha-related" (uposathikaṃ). That which is to be done on the first day of the lunar fortnight is "of the first day" (pāṭipadikaṃ); that very meal is the "first-day meal" (pāṭipadikabhattaṃ).
Regarding the phrase "the meal of recitation and the invitation," here the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with"; [it refers to] "the meal of recitation, the invitation," and so forth.

The meaning is: "they have reached this conventional usage. Why did he authorize *saṅghabhatta* (meals for the Saṅgha) as well, rather than authorizing only *uddesabhatta* (meals by appointment) and so forth?
He says, "Because," and so on. Therein, the connection is with the words "because they will be able [to provide it].
"They" refers to people. "That too" refers to the *saṅghabhatta*. By the word "too" (*pi*), he implies *uddesabhatta* and the others.
Showing the detailed explanation of the *saṅghabhatta* (food for the Saṅgha) and so forth, he says “therein,” and so on. Therein, the construction is:
“In that [text], namely in the reading ‘*saṅghabhattaṃ*, *uddesabhattaṃ*’ and so forth, the determination should be understood thus.

Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) among the *saṅghabhatta* and the rest; the construction is: “For us who are eating, today ten or twelve days have passed.”
"From another" means from another place. "Therein" means in the meal for the Saṅgha. "Should be told" means people should be told.

"That" refers to the meal for the Saṅgha, the formal act (kamma), or the act performed [with the thought] "for us. "That" refers to the meal for the Saṅgha. This concludes the discussion on designated meals (*uddesabhatta*).
The construction is: "This method is to be understood thus. The connection is with the phrase "or sent by the king.
"If it exists" means if there is a standing supply (*ṭhitikā*). "By the assigner" means by the assigner of meals. "It must not be passed over" means that the assigned meal must not be bypassed.
"But they" refers to the alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*). "Setting aside the standing supply" means [setting aside] the standing supply in its place of storage.

"Setting aside" means "releasing. "Of them" refers to the Great Elders (*mahāthera*). "Even from a monastery situated a league away" means even from a monastery located with a distance of one *yojana* intervening. "From the place where they are staying" means from the location where they are currently residing.

"Even for those who have not arrived" means even for those who have not reached the place where the meal is being designated. "An expanded boundary" means that the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) has been expanded.
"Even when given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha" means: even when it has been given to the most junior member of the Saṅgha, as long as the second portion has not yet been assigned.
"By seniority" (*vassaggena*): *gaṃ* means that which is counted; *vassa* itself is *gaṃ*, thus *vassaggaṃ*;
by that seniority (*vassaggena*), meaning by the calculation of years, is what is intended. If the reading were *vassagghena* with the fourth vowel, then it would mean "by the limit of the year."
The meaning should be understood;
this [interpretation] alone is more appropriate. "In one monastery" means within the boundary (sīmā) of a single monastery.

Regarding the phrase "in that very place where the meal was designated," the word "very" (eva) here excludes the possibility of it being in another location. "One" refers to a single donor. "By him" refers to the monk who has been sent. He...
"Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the cause. "On that day" means on the day he was sent. "Forgets" means he forgets due to the lapse of mindfulness.
"In the dining hall" means in the dining hall designated as the place for the distribution of meals. The construction is: "whatever is the natural state.
To show the meaning of the statement "they become joined together," he said: "mutually twelve cubits apart."
“Without having abandoned”: a new *ṭhitika* (a portion of alms) is one other than the original *ṭhitika* placed at the place where the meal was assigned.
“Hi” means truly, or because. “Etam” refers to the assigned meal. Because it is stated with the specification “tomorrow,” it is not obtained on the second day.

*Kocī* means a donor. It should be distributed on the basis of those staying in one’s own monastery; that is, because they have not yet entered the monastery to which they are going, it should be distributed on the basis of those staying in one’s own monastery.
The connection is: "the meal that has been given should be distributed. *Sampattānam* means those who have arrived at the place where [the meal] was given.
*Tattha* refers to the place where it was given; [it means] "only for those who have arrived."

The connection [is as follows]: "Of that monastery" means of the monastery one has entered. "In this or that place" refers to those various places known as the village gate, the street, and the crossroads.
Regarding the phrase "those who have come within the precincts," here "within the precincts" (*antoupacāra*) means within twelve *hattha*s.

Among the three types of precincts—the precinct of the village gate, the precinct of the street and crossroads, and the precinct of the house—he shows the specific distinction of the precinct of the house:
He said: "And here, the vicinity of the house (*gharūpacāro*)... and so forth. "Here" refers to among the three types of vicinities. The connection is: "the vicinity of the house is to be understood.
A house that has one vicinity is called "one-vicinity" (*ekūpacāraṃ*). "Of these" refers to the four types of houses.

"Therein" refers to among the four houses. The connection is: "that which is the house of a single family. "One-entrance" (*ekavaḷañjaṃ*) means having a common use through a single door. "Therein" refers to within the one-vicinity.

The connection is: "but that which was made into a single house. "For the sake of dwelling in happiness" means for the sake of dwelling in happiness by putting an end to quarrels. "In this or that place" refers to each specific place demarcated by the walls. The connection is: "in whichever house they cause [them] to sit.
The construction is: "that which is called a 'dwelling' (*nivesana*). The construction is:
"as for the share of the assignment (*uddesalābha*) that arises, he receives it. The construction is: "even though they are seen, nevertheless..."

"But whoever" means "the monk. "Obtains" is the connection [to the verb]. "In another" means in someone other than himself. "By him" refers to the monk who is receiving the designated meal (*uddesabhatta*).
"While they are waiting for the time" means while the monks are waiting for the time of eating; "while they are seated" is the connection. "Some person says" is the connection. The construction is:
"Give the bowl for the designation of the Sangha," or "it is said. "That very same... [is the continuation].
By the word “method,” he refers by extension to what was said after placing a monk in the position of the bowl.
“In this regard” means in the case of the meal for recitation, or in such a statement. “Pleasing” means one of amiable character. “By him” means by the reciter. To the question “How does he know?
he says, “obtained by one of ten years’ standing. “Of him” refers to the reciter; the connection is with the word “statement. “Quietly” means...
“Gentle sounds. There is also a reading, “soundless,” which means “without noise. “Of all the juniors” means of all the junior monks.
“Even when asked about the shadow” is a locative used in the sense of disregard, or it is a genitive. “He does not receive” means he does not receive because [the time] has passed.
“Even for one who is sitting or even for one who is sleeping” is a genitive used in the sense of disregard; [it refers to] the monk.
"Even when sitting or even when sleeping"—this is the meaning. "Hi" means "truly. The construction is: "This is indeed what is called 'receptacle-goods' (bhājanīyabhaṇḍa).
"Therein" refers to the statement, "it reaches [the monk] only when he has arrived. "By way of the precinct" means by way of the twelve-fathom precinct.
"In that" refers to within the enclosure. "A certain lay follower sends"—this is the connection. "Of choice foods" means with choice foods. "Of water" means...
"Filled with water" is the connection [of the phrase]. "People who have come" is the connection.

"By whom" means by the bhikkhu. "Which" refers to the object (the meal). "Surrounded by the three robes" means surrounded by the three robes, or possessing the three robes as an accompaniment; this is the meaning of "a meal provided with the three robes. For the construction is:
"Is it not true that such a distinction of merit belongs to this bhikkhu? Indeed, even the water is a distinction of his merit.
To the question, "Why does he receive another *uddesabhatta* (meal by assignment)?

he says, "But the water," and so forth. The construction is: "those people who came having taken [it]. "Of them" refers to the great elders (*mahāthera*) and others. "By the young novices" means by the young novices; it is to be connected with "when they were received.

"Therein" refers to the *uddesabhatta*. "In front" means in front of the great elders. "In the bowl" refers to the bowl for the community's assigned portion (*saṅghuddesapatta*); it is to be connected with "even while not yet taken. "The *uddesabhatta* brought" is the connection.
"One says" is the connection. "He," meaning the person, "speaks" is the connection. The construction is: having spoken according to what pleases you, bring it.
"One who is sent as a messenger" means a messenger sent according to his own preference or according to the preference of the other party.
"Or a bowl received in succession" means a bowl obtained in turn from the Saṅgha; this—

This was said with reference to food offered by invitation (*nimantanabhatta*). "Whatever he desires" means whatever the messenger, having been dispatched, desires. "He"—referring to the fool—"should not be spoken to," is the connection [of the sentence].
"He might speak in accordance with the nature of the question" is the connection. "From that" means from the cause of speaking.
"Known as 'standing like a peak' (*kūṭaṭṭhitikā*)" means that, having mixed it with other meals for recitation (*uddesabhatta*), it proceeds in a straight line and then turns back like a peak.
This is what is called the "continuity of occurrence. Expanding upon that very point, he said: "Of a king, or... and so forth. Regarding the term *ekacārikabhattāni*:
they are to be traveled for (*caritabbāni*) and eaten (*bhakkhitabbāni*) by making each [meal] one for oneself; thus they are *ekacārikāni*.
It is meant that they are to be eaten by making each one for oneself, without mixing them with other designated meals (*uddesabhatta*); those very meals are *ekacārikabhattāni*.
The connection is: "Some monks had gone. Regarding the phrase "among them": among those same some monks.
"At that very moment" means at the very moment they were seated. "Again, at that very moment" means at the very moment they were being taken [as pupils].
When it is said, "exquisite food," they ask, "From what age onwards? and when it is said, "from such-and-such an age," this is how the construction should be understood. "Taken" (gāhite).
The connection is as follows: while the newcomers did not know the order of seniority (*ṭhitika*), they took up their bowls;

likewise, even when those who had arrived already knew the order of seniority, [the same occurred]. The same method applies to what follows. "Let only the monks come" means that without taking up their bowls, [he intended] for only the monks to come.
"Among those who do not know the standing order (*ṭhitika*) regarding guests": this refers to newcomers. "The king, having fed them": the king, having fed them in his own residence. "Of these":

the connection is with the phrase "even the alms-bowls of the newcomers. "That which has been brought": that food which was brought without having been eaten [by the king]. "It should not be included":
that food should not be included in the standing order because it is small in quantity. "Of these": of the newcomers.
"It becomes a debt" means it is a liability. A liability is that which has the nature of being repayable; therefore, the intention is that it must be returned.
"In this place" refers to the spot where one has eaten, without knowing the boundary of the standing area. "One should sit for so long" means one should wait and remain seated for that duration.
The opinion of the Elder Purima might be that even holding [the bowl] by its rim is similar to a debt. For if that were the case, there would be [a conflict] between the two...
The statement of the Elders is exactly the same.

"A single alms-meal" is the connection [of the phrase]. "Of such a kind" means accompanied by the three robes and worth one hundred [pieces of money]. "This" refers to the alms-meal; thus it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
"A single monk" is the connection. "One who eats in between" means he eats in the interval, that is, in the middle of the meal offered for recitation (*uddesabhatta*).
"One who has committed an offense" refers to one who has fallen away from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The construction is: "a novice who is of full age. The connection is:
"the standing period of that novice who has received full ordination has elapsed. "He" refers to the monk who carries the alms-bowl for the recitation. "Nearby" means in his own vicinity.
"If they carry it off by theft" means if those who carry the bowl steal that bowl. "There is an offense of debt" (*gīvā*) means:
The responsibility (gīvā) falls upon the bowl-distributor. "That monk" refers to the monk sitting nearby. "His" refers to the bowl-distributor.
There is a reading in the manuscripts as "this," but it is not good. "From there" means from the house where the designated meal was served.
In order to show the meaning of the word "well-prepared," he said: "Because the meal has been given, there is no responsibility."
The connection is: "one who accepts [food] up to ten portions (*uddesabhatta*) becomes [one who accepts]. The construction is: "having had food brought by means of ten bowls.
"Bhikkhudattiyaṃ nāma" means "that which is given by a bhikkhu. "So bhikkhu" refers to that bhikkhu who accepted [the food].
"Te bhikkhū" refers to those bhikkhus who were alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*). "Come, venerable sirs, be my companions" means: "Come, venerable sirs, be my companions."
"Having spoken"—this is the connection. "His"—refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*). "There"—in the house of the lay follower.

"Of that very one"—of the one who has consented. "The others"—the nine alms-food eaters (*piṇḍapātika*). "Of them"—of the ten monks. "Of that monk"—of the monk who has consented. "Of those who have finished eating"—of those who have already eaten.
The connection is that nine *piṇḍapātika* (alms-collectors) were said to be going there. "There" means in the house of the lay follower (*upāsaka*).
"In that place" refers to among the ten monks. The construction is: "having heard the Dhamma talk of one who was offering a thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) with a sweet voice.
"An unmade portion" means it was not made before; thus, it is an "unmade" (*akata*) portion or section, hence "an unmade portion" (*akatabhāga*).
The meaning is "the guest-portion.
The connection is: "a certain lay follower gives. "This" refers to the solid and soft food. The construction is: "it should be given to the owner of the bowl.
"Setting aside" means setting aside as usual. And having said, "Let the entire Saṅgha eat," and having said nothing further—
Even when [the guest] has departed, because it was previously stated, "Give all the bowls belonging to the Saṅgha," they should be divided and used.
"Having brought them in a bowl" is the connection [of the phrase]. "One morsel each" means one morsel for each individual monk.
"He remains" means he dwells. "For whose sake by you? connects with "was brought. The phrase "by one monk" [is to be understood as follows].
In the word “gāhetabbaṃ,” the object is in the causative sense; in the word “bhattaṃ,” he says the suffix *-tabba* expresses the passive object (*dhātukamma*).
“Without saying ‘What is being brought? means without asking the lay follower, “What item have you brought?
There is also the reading “Kiṃ āharissasi?,” which means, “What item will you bring? [He gave] rice gruel for the entire retinue and expensive fruits.
The construction is: "And likewise, a single common portion (*ṭhitikā*) must be made for the choice snacks. "A single common portion" means a portion that is exactly the same.
In the phrase "likewise for the molasses," the word "likewise" (*tathā*) refers back to the statement: "Only a single common portion is permitted.
Thus, the construction of the discussion on the *uddesabhatta* (food by assignment) is completed.
The Discourse on Invitations and Meals:
An invitation is of two kinds—personal and communal. With reference to the personal kind, it is said: "If it is personal, one is the master oneself.
Without saying things such as "Designate so many bhikkhus from the Saṅgha," [one says] "for so many..."
"Accept the meal for the bhikkhus"—having thus invited them, what is given is called a "sangha-invitation. "In this case" means in the context of an invitation.
"It is permissible even for alms-collectors (piṇḍapātika)" means that because it is spoken of using the appropriate term "alms-food" (bhikkha), it is permissible even for those who live on alms.
"In order of arrival" means according to the sequence received from the Sangha. "The person who has come speaks"—this is the grammatical connection.
“Having interrupted” means having interrupted the words, “And you may go.

“From the house where the invited meal was given” means from the house to which the meal for those invited was provided. “One brings it” is the grammatical connection. “Having filled” means having filled with food. “That” refers to the food.

“Even here” means even in the case of an invitation. “Therefore” means because of that reason of speaking. The word “so bhikkhu” (that monk) is the natural subject for the word “assā” (of him), [as in] “jigucchanīyo” (disgusting).
The word *tattha* (there) functions as an adverbializer (*vikatika*). *Assa* means "it would be" or "it exists. The construction is:
"To him who says, 'I have come for the sake of a bowl,' a bowl should be given. *Bhattāharaṇakapattaṃ*: that by which one brings food is *bhattāharaṇaka*;
that very bowl is the *bhattāharaṇakapatta*, [meaning] "the food-bringing bowl. *Paṭipāṭibhattaṃ*: food obtained in succession.
"By means of the fixed portion of alms-food" (*ālopabhattaṭṭhitikato*) means by means of the fixed portion of the food obtained with each individual mouthful (*ālopa*).

"By the contraction of the mouthfuls" (*ālopasaṅkhepena*) means by the contracting of that [food] in each individual mouthful. This method is the distinction from the meal given as a formal assignment (*uddesabhatta*).

"For whom have they been brought? (*kassa te ābhataṃ*) is to be construed as: "For whose sake have they been brought by you? "The meal for the Sangha" (*saṅghassa me bhattaṃ*) means: "For the sake of the Sangha, by me."
"Food has been brought. "The meal for the elders has been brought by me"—this is the connection with the phrase "the lay follower sent it.

"These three people": the senior of the Saṅgha, the one renowned for his mastery of the texts and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the distributor of meals—these are the three persons. "To be asked": "Shall I take [the food] from the Saṅgha? etc.
"Or rather, shall I come with those whom I know?"—this was asked. "Āruhiyittha" means they had ascended. "Attanavamehi":
those for whom the self (ātman) is the ninth are "attanavamā"; the connection is "with those bhikkhus. "Hi" means because.
"Ete bhikkhū" refers to these three bhikkhus, beginning with the senior of the Saṅgha. "Tenā" means by that bhikkhu who is unacquainted with the texts, the dhutaṅgas, and so forth.
"Should be practiced" is the connection. Alternatively, the construction is: "or having taken those bhikkhus whom you know to be dependent [on the laity].
"One should go to another village oneself" is the connection. "That very village" refers to the village where the invitation was received.
"There" means in the dining hall. "On festivals and so forth" means on festive occasions and the like. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it includes people [gathering] for some other reason.
He gathers together a large assembly. "Then" means at that time of being invited. "From the place of assembly" means from the place where the bhikkhus have gathered.
"According to one's ability" (yathāsatti) means in accordance with one's power; the meaning is "without exceeding one's power.
And here, since the word *satti* can also denote a weapon known as a *kunta*, he says "according to one's strength" (*yathābala*) in order to exclude that [meaning].
The connection is: "or the senior monk of the Saṅgha comes. Because there are many agents, it is stated in the plural as "they come.
"At one time" means on a single day; that is, on the day of arrival. "From the fixed time" means from the time when his residence in that very place has become settled.
"On the second occasion" means on the second day. "Those who have newly arrived" means...
"Those who have not come before" means those who are entirely new arrivals. "Therein" means in that particular place. "Of them" refers to the new arrivals.
"In this" refers to the place where they have not come before.

"Everywhere" means in all places, both their own locations and the locations of the arrivals. "By him" refers to the monk who has received an excessive amount. "Without making a distinction" means without making a differentiation.

The phrase "the discourse on *salākabhatta* (ticket-food)" is to be construed as: "but *salākabhatta* should be understood in this way. The word "from the statement" (*vacanato*) is a reason indicating the necessity for the word "should be given" (*dātabbā*).
"Or by means of a *salākā*" means either by means of a blade of *kusa* grass. "Of such-and-such a name" means of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) named so-and-so.
“Having bound together” means having written down; the sense is “having cut. To show the meaning of the word “having piled up,” he said:
“having mixed together again and again by way of upper and lower. The connection is: “to be given by the distributor of food. “Not many” means few.
“Even by way of village” means even by way of a village where, for the most part, the gains are equal. By the word “even” (pi),...
He regards the family. The connection is: "by one who causes [them] to take, they are indeed caused to take. The construction is: "there are sixty *salāka*-meals.
"Of these" refers to the two or three *salāka*-meals.
"That" refers to the village where there are many *salāka*-meals. "But that," however, refers to the single *salāka*-meal. "Among these" refers to the monks.
“By means of restraint” means by restraining even one person who is unwilling due to being far away. “That” refers to the ticket-food (*salākabhatta*).
“In the border village” means in a village situated on the outskirts. “With the perception that it has been taken” means with the perception, “It has been taken.

“Having returned to the monastery again” means not having returned to the monastery [before], but having first taken the ticket-foods in the border village and subsequently returning to the monastery.
It is permissible to take [the portion] for oneself and eat it. Why, then, must one return to the monastery?
Is it not the case that even without formally taking it, since it belongs to one’s own bowl, it is permissible to take and eat it? To this he says, “For not,” and so forth.

For (hi) because the alms belonging to the Saṅgha outside the boundary cannot be taken [as one's own], therefore one must return to the monastery; such is the construction of the sentence. Or, by way of a single wall—that is, by way of a single house-wall—...
"Or by means of the arms. "In streets and so forth" means in the streets and households; the locative case is used here for the purpose of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

"Where" means in whatever place. "If the tickets are not present" should be construed as "if they are absent. "Even after specifying" means even after specifying villages and so forth, saying, "The ticket-meals (*salākabhatta*) of such-and-such a village shall reach you."

Expounding upon this very matter, he said, “Therefore, etc. Therein, “by him” means by the monk who distributes the tickets (*salākā*). “Should be sent for” is the syntactical connection. “In a village reached by turn” means in a village that must be visited in rotation because it is too far away.
“There” refers to that village. “At a place more than a *gāvuta* away” means at a location exceeding one *gāvuta*.

“On that day” means on the day of receiving the ticket-food. The construction is: “it should not be given to one who does not go. “For” (*hi*) means because. “But for three days” indicates an uninterrupted connection (*accantasamyoga*).
This is a term of application. "That" refers to the tally-slip (*salāka*) of the village on this side of the river.
Regarding the question of how strictly the disciplinary action (*daṇḍakamma*) should be carried out, he said: "It must not fall short of sixty or fifty.

"The turn for the monastery" (*vihāravāro*) means the duty (*vāro*) for the purpose of guarding the monastery. "Of the monastery-warden" (*vihāravārikassa*): one who guards the monastery by turn, or having taken a turn, is a monastery-warden (*vihāravāriko*).
"It should be given to him" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Monastery attendants" (*vihāragopakā*) means those who guard the monastery. "Alteration" (*aññathatta*) means an alteration of faith.
"It should be given to other families" means that rice-gruel and so forth should be given to other families.
"Having caused a turn to be taken" means having had others take turns. "Of them" refers to the monastery attendants. "The tally-stick" (*salākā*) refers to the one who normally distributes it.

Having considered [the context], it is stated in the plural as “they become. “Only the *phātikamma*” means only that *phātikamma* which is to be given by the Saṅgha for the purpose of protecting the monastery.
By the word “also” (*api*) in “and also another,” he shows that it is not only the *phātikamma*, but also something else.
“Of the *atirekauttaribhaṅga*” means: that which has an extra *uttaribhaṅga* is an *atirekauttaribhaṅga*; [it refers] to that.

“*Salākā laddhā*” means that the voting sticks (*salākā*) themselves were obtained. “*Taṃdivasaṃ*” means on that day when the voting sticks were obtained. “*Ekasseva*” means for each one individually. “*Vijaṭetvā*” means having interlaced those two or three meals taken as individual portions into a single bundle.
“*Ekasambhogā*” means sharing together. The connection is: “by one who causes [them] to enter, he should give.

“*Sammukhībhūtassa*” means of anyone standing within the boundary of the precincts (*upacārasīmā*). “*Pāpetvā*” is the construction [meaning] “having caused to reach. “*Rasasalākaṃ*” means a sugarcane stick. It is also called “*rasālasalākaṃ*.”

This is the reading; this is the meaning itself. Having shown the procedure for what is to be recited in a small monastery (khuddakavihāra), he says “in a large monastery” and so forth to show that same [procedure] in a large residence (mahā-āvāsa).
The statement “it is even permissible to give a piece of chalk... [etc. was said with reference to a small monastery; therefore—
It is said, “In a large residence,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “by means of a tally for medicine and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (ādi) includes tallies for perfumes and garlands.
“Therein” refers to among the tallies. “The measure of the first alms” means the amount of alms that should be given from the top.
“Such meals” refers to meals having the same nature as the measure of the first alms. “And not” refers to such meals.
"If there are many" means if there are numerous [monks]. "Whether obtained or not obtained" means whether they have received it or not.
"When other voting sticks have been taken" means when other voting sticks have already been picked up. "Standing nearby" means standing close by without having extended one's hand.
"His" refers to the monk. "This voting stick" is said so that it may be established as "this is his voting stick."

It is permissible. "Unrighteous" means a formal agreement (*katikā*) that is not connected with the Dhamma. "Give to one who has not arrived" means give the voting ticket (*salāka*) to a monk who has not yet arrived.
"He" refers to the distributor of meals; "should say" is the connection [to the verb]. "By me, it was brought to me"—this is the connection. "Therein" means in the village.
"You should eat"—if he should say this, it is permissible; such is the construction. "Right there" means in the dining hall itself. "Therein" means...

"In that village. "Having brought [the food] to the monastery" means having brought the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food) to the monastery. "At the time of the distribution of tickets" means at the time when the monks are made to take the tickets.

"Therein" means in that particular direction or location. "By another" means by someone other than oneself; this is to be construed with the phrase "it is obtained. "But by him" refers to one other than the traveler. "In that" refers to the traveler. The construction is: "without even having crossed the boundary of the precinct (*upacārasīma*)."

*“Therein”* means in an abandoned monastery. *“Among them”* refers to the resident monks; *“having departed”* is the connection. *“He himself”* refers to the guest monk; *“whoever goes”* is the connection. *“That”* refers to the ticket-meal (*salākabhatta*);

*“does not reach him”* is the connection. *“By merit”* means from merit. *“And furthermore those”* refers to the tickets. *“But the basket”* refers to the ticket-basket. *“Therein”* means in the basket.
*“From this very place”* means from the very spot of pouring [the tickets]. *“One”* means one ticket. *“Should be said”*...
The one who gives the voting ticket must say, "The monks have gone"—this is the connection. "There" means in another monastery. "The senior elder also goes"—this is the connection.
The construction is as follows: when the monks have arrived at the alms-village without having eaten in the monastery they have reached, the bowls must not be given [to them].
“Food provided for one staying at the monastery” means food situated in the monastery.
Regarding the discussion on “fortnightly food” and so forth:
the connection is that “food is given. “On the fourteenth, fifteenth, fifth, and eighth days” refers to those specifically marked days.
The construction (*yojanā*). "By those intent on action" means by the accumulation of karma.

By these readings, he shows the meaning of the word *pakkhika* as that which is to be given during the fortnights. "That" refers to the fortnightly meal (*pakkhikabhatta*). In the word "is," it is the agent;
in the word "having caused to take," it is the base-object (*dhātukamma*); in the word "to be eaten," it is the expressed object (*vuttakamma*). "Of all" refers to the monks. "Of whom" refers to...
"Of the bhikkhus. *Manda* means "little. *Taṃ* refers to the *salākabhatta* (ticket-food). *Paṇītaṃ dentī* means they give it after having made it choice.
*Lūkhabhattaṃ* means food that is not succulent. The construction is:
"Whatever food one eats oneself, that very same is given. By this, it is meant that what is to be given on the Uposatha day is called *uposathika*.
This shows the meaning of the words. Regarding "on the uposatha day": this refers to the day of the uposatha. Herein, the distinction is as follows:

if on the fifteenth day donors give while saying, "It is for the fortnight (pakkhika)," it is called "fortnightly" (pakkhika); if they give while saying, "It is for the uposatha (uposathika)," it is called "uposatha-related" (uposathika).
Regarding "on the first day of the month (pāṭipada)": this refers to the day of the first of the month. Regarding "by means of the uposatha rite": by means of the uposatha rite acting as the cause.
By the phrase “the alms-giving to be given on the first day of the fortnight” (*pāṭipade diyyanakadāna*), the meaning of the word *pāṭipadika*—that which is to be given on the *pāṭipada*—is shown.
“Both of those” refers to both types of meals: the Uposatha meal and the *pāṭipadika* meal.
In the expression “these seven meals,” here the word “these” (*ima*) indicates that the word “thus” (*iti*) has the sense of the word “these. Regarding the phrase “seven meals”: in this...
The seven meals, beginning with *saṅghabhatta*, mentioned in the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* are [included].

The connection is: "and four other meals. Regarding the phrase "among those," it refers to the four meals. By the words "given to newcomers" (*āgantukānaṃ dinnaṃ*) and so forth, he demonstrates that the term *āgantukabhatta* (newcomer’s meal) is a compound formed by eliding the fourth case ending (*catutthī-majjha-lopa*). Elsewhere, however, [it is said]: "for a newcomer..."

By the phrase “brought for the sake of,” etc., he shows a genitive-middle elision compound (*chaṭṭhī-majjha-lopa-samāsa*). “Therein” means among the four meals. “Of all” refers to the monks. The connection is:
“one newly arrived monk sits down. “By him” means by the first-arrived one. “He” refers to the newly arrived one.

In the phrase “even having arrived,” the word “even” (*pi*) has the sense of censure; the meaning is: “but later, how much more so before. The construction is: “it should be taken by him. By the phrase “on the very day of arrival,” he shows that it should not be eaten on the second day and so forth.

"Somewhere" (*katthaci*) means at some place. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the meal for guests (*āgantuka-bhatta*). "Set aside" (*nibandhāpitaṃ*) means established permanently. "In the dining hall" (*asanasālāyaṃ*) means in the dining hall within the village. "If not present" (*asati*) means when they are absent.
The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the resident monk also" (*āvāsiko pi*) indicates that it is not only the traveler who [does not receive it].
The construction is: just as the guest meal is obtained for two, three, or seven days, so this traveler's meal (*gamiya-bhatta*) is not obtained. "On the road" (*panthaṃ*).
The path. "They block" means they obstruct. The connection is "or they block water. "These calamities" refers to thieves and so forth;
these are the calamities. "Having laid down" means having set out.
"Of this" refers to the one who is gravely ill. Again, "of this" refers to a future one who is gravely ill. "Suitable food" means...
Suitable food for the sick. "Mixed rice-gruel" (*missakayāgu*) refers to gruel cooked by mixing various types of rice.
"It does not cause distress" means it does not produce an adverse reaction.
"This too" refers even to the meal provided for the attendant of the sick person. "Therein" means in that family. "For him" means for the sick person. "Thus given" means...

They are given in the manner that will be explained below. Regarding the statement "it is permissible even for alms-collectors (*piṇḍapātika*)," because it is spoken of using the permissible designation "alms-food" (*bhikkhā*), it is permissible even for alms-collectors.
Regarding the statement "it is not permissible," because it is spoken of using the impermissible designation "meal" (*bhatta*), it is not permissible.
The connection is: "there are another three meals. "Therein" refers to among those three meals. "The principal meal" (*dhurabhatta*)—here [is the explanation].
Because the word *dhura* is semantically similar to the word *dhuva*, it has the sense of "permanent"; thus he says, "it is called *niccabhatta* (regular meal).
*Taṃ* refers to the *dhurabhatta*. *Tattha* means "in the two kinds. The phrase "*saṅghike*" (for the Saṅgha) is to be supplied as a remainder of the text.
In the phrase "*puggalikepi*," the particle *api* refers back to the word "*saṅghike*. *Pacchā* means after the initial statement, "Take almsfood."
Or [it refers to] another who has spoken the words.
Showing that the meal which, having been prepared in a hut, is to be given is "hut-meal," he said: "What is called 'hut-meal,'" and so forth.
"Yam" (which) refers to the meal; "caused to be bound" is the connection; "the monks residing in the lodging" is the connection. "Yam" (which)...
“*Panā*” means food; it is connected with “given. “*Tasseva*” means of that very person. “*Tasmin*” refers to that person.

To show that “*vārabhattaṃ*” (turn-food) is food given by taking turns, he said, “*Vārabhattaṃ nāmā*,” and so forth. “*Tampi*” means even that turn-food. To present them collectively by way of conclusion, he said, “*Iti imāni cā*,” and so forth.
“*Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ*” means in the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*); it is connected with “stated. “*Tattha*” means among the four types of food.
Showing that food arising in a monastery is "monastery-food," he says, "Monastery-food is called... and so forth.

"Food produced there" means food produced in that monastery by means of fields, land, and so forth, which have been given for that purpose. "That" refers to the monastery-food. "In what manner" (*yathā*) means by whatever mode;
it is to be connected with the word "when being received. "A group of eight" means that of which eight is the measure.
Or, *aṭṭhaka* refers to a person; food given to him is *aṭṭhakabhatta*. It is the same in the case of *catukkabhatta*.
Showing this very meaning, he said: “We shall give to eight bhikkhus,” and so forth. Regarding *mahābhisaṅkhārikena*:

a great preparation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) involving all [ingredients] such as boiled rice and the like is a *mahābhisaṅkhāra*; that which possesses this is *mahābhisaṅkhāriko*, by means of which—namely, with an extremely abundant cake (*atirasakapūva*).

The connection is with the words “having placed in a bowl. By the phrase “given after having set aside,” it shows the meaning of the term *guḷhakabhatta* (hidden-food): that which is to be given by being concealed is the “hidden food,” and that very meal is called *guḷhakabhatta*.
“In this world” means in this [human] world. The connection is with the words “some people give. [It is] for the purpose of knowing the limit of the bhikkhus.

By the phrase "giving with a ball" (*guḷaka*), it shows the meaning of the term *guḷakabhatta* (ball-food), which refers to the meal that is to be given after counting the monks by means of that ball.
Furthermore, it should be understood that in the former method there is a conjunction of the letter *ha* with the letter *ḷ*, whereas in the latter method there is none.

One knows the count of the monks by counting the balls of sugar (*guḷapiṇḍa*). The words "Thus," etc., constitute the conclusion. The connection is: "The distribution of robes (*cīvarabhājanīya*) has been stated."

“In all medicines” (*sabbi-ādīsu bhesajjesu*): this is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). The word “of all” (*sabbissā*) has a dependent connection with the word “even a hundred jars” (*kumbhasatampi*).
“It must indeed be given to those who arrive later”: it means that even if there is nothing to be given in the second portion, it must still be given to those who arrive later.
“Precisely at the place where all have assembled” (*sabbasannipātaṭṭhāneyeva*): precisely at the place where all the bhikkhus have gathered. “Distributable goods” (*bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṃ*).
The name "receptacle" applies only to that which has been attained, not to that which has not been attained.
And since one is generally attained at every place of assembly, it is therefore said:
"only at every place of assembly. "Just as it stands" means exactly as it was, without dividing anything at all. Having stated "misapprehended," for the sake of that meaning—
Showing this, he said: "In whatever place it has gone, it belongs to the Saṅgha alone. "Having reflected" means having redirected [the intention].
"All that" refers to everything placed in the bowl. "Stiffness" (*thina*): it is called *thina* because it remains in a state of density;
thus, "dense" is what is meant. "From the stated limit" means from the limit stated as "ten bhikkhus and ten water-jars."
In this verse, "the Pāḷi" refers to the Vinaya-pāḷi. "And the commentary" means the commentary on that very [text].
"Vicakkhaṇo" means one who sees or perceives various meanings (*vicakkhati*). "Evaṃ" means by the method already stated. Herein, the construction is as follows:
a wise (*vicakkhaṇo*) bhikkhu, having examined both the Pāḷi and the commentary, being indeed diligent (*appamatto*), [should apply himself].
"Divide the requisites belonging to the Saṅgha.
Thus ends the application of the discussion on the distribution of requisites.
"Half a portion" means half a portion from what is obtained by the bhikkhus. The rest is easy to understand.
Thus ends the explanation of the *Senāsanakkhandhaka*.
7. The *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka*:
The Discourse on the Ordination of Channa.

330. Regarding the phrase "renowned, renowned" (*abhiññātā abhiññātā*) in the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka*: here, the word *ñāta* preceded by the prefix *abhi-* has the sense of "well-known," hence he says "well-known, well-known.

"Kāḷudāyi and the rest" means Kāḷudāyi and others. The construction is: "the ten messengers together with their retinues and many other people were known as the Śākya princes. "Among us" refers to those counted within the Śākya clan.
“Among us” (*amhesu*) uses the locative case in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*); by this, he indicates an ellipsis in the text.
By the word “from the family” (*kulato*), he shows that in the phrase “from the family” (*kulā*), the ablative case is used in the sense of departure (*nissakka*).

Regarding the phrase “the duty of those living in the household” (*gharāvāsattha*), he says “that which is in the household life” (*gharāvāse yaṃ*) and so forth, demonstrating that it is the obligation of people dwelling in a house. Therein, “that which” (*yaṃ*) means whatever. Water (*udakaṃ*).
Regarding the phrase "should be led away" (*ninnetabba*), he says, "so that the water may be well-drained in all places," showing that here water must be led out, carried away, and removed.
*Susanti* means "drying up. "Grasses" (*tiṇāni*) refers to grasses that damage the crops.

By the word "should be pulled up" (*uddharitabbāni*), he shows that the root of the verb *dhū* here has the sense of shaking off or destroying. "Stalks" (*bhusā*) refers to the stalks and stems of the grain.

“Mixed with those” means mixed with straw and chaff. Regarding the instruction “it should be winnowed,” he says “it should be removed” (*apanetabba*) here in order to show that the root *phuṇ* has the sense of scattering.
In the phrase “you yourself recognize [this] by way of the household life,” the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayogatthe*).
The prefix *upa-ja-* follows the meaning of the verbal root; furthermore, the prefix *upa-* is elided and the case ending *hi* is dropped.
Therefore it was said: “You alone know the matter of household life. “I” refers to me, who am named Prince Bhaddiya.
“By you” refers to you, who are named Prince Anuruddha. By the phrase “I shall go forth together [with you],” he indicates the remainder of the text.
“The rest” refers to the statement: “I shall go forth together [with you].”

331. Regarding the word *nippātitā*, he says “*nikkhāmitā*” (driven out) to show that they have been made to depart after having gone forth from there. Regarding the word *mānassino*, he says “*mānassayino*” (those who rely on conceit) to show that they lie down upon (*sayanti*) or depend upon (*nissayanti*) conceit (*māna*).

332. Regarding the phrase “*yassantarato na santi kopā*” (in whose interior no anger exists), he says “*yassa citte*” (in whose mind) to show that the word *antara* here denotes the mind (*citta*), and that the suffix *-to* expresses the sense of the locative case (*sattamī*).
Why do anger and the like not exist? He says: “Because they have been eradicated by the third path.”
Because hatred has been eradicated by the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimagga), the intention is that there is no anger in the mind of that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
Thus, regarding the phrase "and having transcended existence and non-existence," he says "But because it is said... and so forth to show the meaning. Therein, the construction is:
"But because it is said [thus], therefore the meaning should be understood in this way. In this context, "non-existence" (vibhava) is said to mean evil (pāpa).
[The word] *sambandho* [connects the following]. Now, it might be asked: "In the Pāḷi, 'vibhava' does not exist; only 'abhava' exists.
Then why is it said, 'vibhavo means abhavo'? To this he says: "'Vibhava' and 'abhava' are one and the same in meaning.

By this, he shows that they differ only in sound. The connection is: "That which is called 'the state of being and non-being' (*bhavābhavatā*) is manifold. By the phrase "of many kinds" (*anekappakārā*),...

It shows the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*) for the word *iti*. The connection is: "one who has transcended by means of all four paths. "Of him" (*tassa*) refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).

333. *Ahimekhalikā*: like a girdle, it is a "girdle-like thing" (*mekhalikā*); a snake itself as a girdle is an "ahimekhalikā. Demonstrating that very meaning, he says: "having bound a snake around his waist. 334. Regarding *sammannati*:
here, although it should be stated according to the root belonging to the *curādigaṇa* as *sammāneti*, it is stated according to a root belonging to the *divādigaṇa*.
Showing that it is so stated, he says: "He honors. For the method of the Pāḷi is inconceivable.
"He honors" means he performs an act of honoring. "Yaṃ" refers to the action; "so" refers to the Teacher.
By this, he shows that in the phrase "yaṃ tumo," the word "tumo"—which is a conventional term—is here synonymous in meaning with the pronoun "so."
The Discussion on the *Pakāsanīya-kamma* and so forth (336):
By the phrase “resembling spittle,” he shows that the requisites obtained through wrong livelihood have the nature of spittle by virtue of their similar status.

Therefore, they are called “spittle” (*kheḷa*) because they are like spittle; [the term refers to] the requisites of wrong livelihood. Because one eats—that is, consumes—[them] when there is no spittle [of craving], they are so designated.

The meaning of the word *kheḷāsaka* should be explained accordingly. At present, in both the Canon and the Commentary, there is a reading with the first syllable of the lip [changed] as *kheḷāpaka*. 340. Regarding the term *patthaddhena*:
here, "stiff" (*thaddha*) in the sense of being excessively stiff is *patthaddha*; the meaning is "intensely stiff. Therefore it was said:
“By one who is motionless”: “resembling a painted figure” means here that a painted figure (*potthakarūpa*) is made of cloth, ivory, and so forth;
resembling such a painted figure is “resembling a painted figure,” by which [he is meant].
342. “Those known as kinsmen of the king”: here, they are called *rājañātā* because they are known by the king as “our elders”; those very ones are *rājañātakā*.
The meaning must be understood. Showing the intention regarding that meaning, he said: “The king knows us,” and so forth.
*Pahaṭṭhakaṇṇavālo* means one whose ears and tail are uplifted (*pahaṭṭha*). *Bandhaniccalo* means motionless, as if bound by ropes and creepers;
this is connected with *pahaṭṭhakaṇṇavālo*. By the word “having done” (*katvā*), [the phrase] “ran forward” (*abhidhāvī*) [is implied].
In this context, he shows that [the word] functions as an adverbial modifier of the action (*kiriyāvisesanabhāva*).
For instance, in the phrase *dukkhaṃ hi kuñjara nāgamāsado* (“O elephant, you have approached the serpent with suffering”), he says “O elephant!

(*bho kuñjarā*) while making it clear that the word *kuñjara* is a vocative address (*āmantanapada*). Since the word *nāga* applies to both serpent-nāgas (*ahināga*) and elephant-nāgas (*hatthināga*), he refers to him as the “Buddha-nāga” (*buddhanāga*).
Showing that the word *āsado* means "approaching" (*sadana*) or "going toward" (*upagamana*) with anger, he said: "It is called approaching with a murderous mind.
*Dukkhaṃ* means the cause of suffering both now and in the future. In the phrase *dukkhaṃ hi*, the particle *hi* is merely for the purpose of completing the meter;
alternatively, its meaning is "suffering indeed. By the phrase "of the slayer of the Buddha-elephant," [he refers to] the elephant...
"He strikes, thus he is a 'nāga-striker' (nāgahata)"—this shows the meaning of the word.
Regarding the phrase "he retreated while shrinking back," it is explained that he was called *paṭikuṭiyo* because his gait was crooked (*kuṭena*) toward the Tathāgata;
thus, showing that he retreated while being *paṭikuṭiyo*, [the commentator] said: "facing the Tathāgata himself with his hind feet..."

"‘Osakkī’—by this [word], it is shown that here the sense is ‘seeing,’ among the meanings stated in the *Dhātupāṭha* (Pāṇini 1539; *Saddanīti*, *Dhātumālā* 18, under the root ending in *d*) as ‘marking’ (*lakkhana*) and ‘seeing’ (*dassana*).

‘Not to be marked’ (*na lakkhitabbo*) means he is not to be characterized by other virtuous persons (*sappurisā*). Here, the suffix *ṇya* occurs in the sense of the agent or the object; [regarding] the letter *y*..."
By using the letter *ka*, it is stated that one is "unfortunate" (*alakkhika*).
343. By the phrase "food to be eaten," he shows here that the suffix *-yu* has the sense of the object (*kamma*) in the term *tikabhojana*.
"That" refers to the *tikabhojana*. "In accordance with the Dhamma" refers to the text of the *Mātikā-vibhaṅga* which states: "In eating in a group, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."
“Appropriate. The phrase “the discourse on the request for the five items” (*pañcavatthuyācanakathā*) refers to the discourse regarding the requesting of five items.

“A lifespan” (*āyukappa*): this is said with reference to a lifespan in the great hell of Avīci. In works such as the *Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, it is stated that a “lifespan in the great hell of Avīci” means one intermediate aeon (*antarakappa*).
In works such as the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated that it is “one incalculable aeon” (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*). “Supreme merit” (*seṭṭhaṃ puññaṃ*) means great.
“Merit. By this, he shows that the word *brahma* has the sense of “greatness,” as in “I am great through merit.

Since it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—namely, Pāṇini 7.3.5 and the *Saddanīti Dhātumālā* (root 16 of the *hakārantadhātu*)—that the root *br̥h* means “to grow,” the word *braha* is a designator for “greatness.
From the root *br̥h*, by applying the suffix *ap*, one gets “*brahā*”; by applying the suffix *man*, one gets “*brahmā*.”
The reading exists. "Only for the duration of a lifespan" means only for the duration of a lifespan in the heavenly realms.

Regarding the discussion on schism in the Saṅgha (Saṅghabhedakathā) 344: "He" refers to Devadatta; the connection is that he is said to have gone. "Right there" means right within the boundary of the monastery (*vihārasīmā*). "Separate" means separate from the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).
345. Regarding the term *āgilāyati*: here, the prefix *ā-* has the sense of overcoming (*abhibhavana*), and the root *gila* has the sense of affliction (*bādhana*).
Thus it is said: "Overcome by feeling, it afflicts. *Taṃ* refers to the back. It is called *ādesanā* because one teaches after having indicated another's mind;
that itself is the marvel, hence *ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*. It is called *anusāsanī* because one instructs by means of it; demonstrating this very meaning:
He said, "‘Even so for you,’ and so forth.

(346) Showing that *anu* here is a prefix (*upasagga*) with the sense of imitation (*anukiriyattha*), and that the root *kṛ* takes the suffix *anta* and belongs to the *gacchantādi* class, he said, “performing an imitation of me.
By the word “afflicted” (*dukkhita*), [he indicates] the root *kap* in the sense of “miserable” (*kapaṇa*).

He shows that it means "for the purpose of harming. Regarding the phrase "of the Great Boar" (*mahāvarāhassa*), he says "of the Great Nāga" (*mahānāgassa*) in order to reject the meaning of "boar" (*sūkara*) for the word *varāha*.
By the word "earth" (*pathavim*), he rejects the interpretation of the word *mahi* in the phrase "transforming the earth" (*mahiṃ vikubbato*) as referring to the great river of that name.
By the word "tearing apart" (*padālentassa*), he indicates the sense of tearing apart through the prefix *vi-* applied to the verbal root *kṛ*.

He shows this. Regarding the phrase "of one eating lotus roots" (*bhisaṃ ghasamānassa*), he says "of one chewing lotus roots" (*bhisaṃ ghasantassa*) because the word *māna* here has the sense of the present participle suffix *-māna*.
"Of one chewing" means "of one consuming. The construction is: "that lotus pond named 'River'.
By this, he shows that in the expression "tending the rivers," the term "river" refers to a lotus pond. "Tending" means "protecting an elephant herd."

347. By the phrase “one who hears is a hearer,” he shows the twofold nature of the Pāḷi. By the phrase “without doubt,” he shows the verbal root *dhi* (to hold) in the sense of being non-doubtful, and thereby excludes the verbal root *dis* (to see).
350. In the phrase “even by a thousand Buddhas,” the particle *pi* has the sense of censure; it shows that this is even more so for a single Buddha.
By the word “a being” (*satto*), he shows the primary referent of the word *koci*. The word “eight” (*aṭṭha*) indicates the meaning of the verb form.
Pointing this out, he says, "standing. Regarding the phrase "Devadatta—thus have I heard," he says "by the Blessed One" because the word "me" (by me) is spoken with reference to the Blessed One.
"That very same" means precisely what was heard. "This" refers to the statement, "Devadatta—thus have I heard.
"He recites" means he causes it to increase. By the word "having reached" (*patvā*), [it is implied] that "assailing" (*āsajjana*) here is the meaning of the verbal root *sad* in the sense of going.
And it shows the qualification of the action. Regarding the phrase "one who has reached the Avīci hell": Devadatta has not yet actually reached the Avīci hell;
however, because his reaching of the Avīci hell is certain in the future, he is said to have "reached the Avīci hell.
Thus he says: "The past tense is used in the sense of necessity. "Āsaṃsāyaṃ" means in the sense of what is necessarily to happen. For the ocean is indeed formidable.
Regarding the word *mahā*, it is said that here the term *bhesma* is a synonym for "terrifying"; thus he says, "terrible" (*bhayānaka*).

In the *Upāli-pañhā-kathā* (351), while demonstrating that the suffix *-to* functions here in the sense of the locative case, he says, "on the side of those who speak according to the Dhamma" (*dhammavādīpakkhe*).
By the word “anunayanto,” he shows the meaning of the prefix *anu* in the phrase “he announces.
“Anunayanto” means leading [the matter] again and again. Showing the manner of the announcement, he says:

“It is not for you alone,” and so forth. The construction is: “If this were unrighteousness (*adhamma*), or this were contrary to the discipline (*avinaya*), or this were not the teaching of the Teacher (*asatthusāsana*). By the word “bodheti,”...
“Sāvetī” (he proclaims) here shows the meaning of the verbal root *sudhātu*.

By the phrase “having proclaimed” (*anussāvetvā*), it is shown that in the expression “he proclaims, he causes voting tickets to be distributed,” the act of proclaiming occurs in the prior stage, while the act of distributing the voting tickets occurs in the subsequent stage.

“By this much” (*ettāvatā*) means by this mere proclamation and distribution of voting tickets. However, the Saṅgha is not yet split; the intention is that the Saṅgha is split only when, after having proclaimed and distributed the voting tickets, a formal legal act (*saṅghakamma*) specific to the faction has been performed.
The construction here is: "Having stood upon this, there might be an inquiry from some accuser. To the question "In what way might it be so?", he says: "In this manner, Devadatta," and so forth.
Therein, "in this manner" (*evam*) means when the Sangha, which was previously intact, has been split. "How" (*katham*) means in what mode. Again, "how" (*katham*) means for what reason.
"Of the king" refers to King Ajātasattu; [it refers to] the deed he caused to be done. "Because of having caused to be killed" refers to King Bimbisāra.

Because of having caused [him] to be killed. Regarding the word “therein” (*tattha*), the construction is: “Standing upon the statement beginning with ‘Upāli, a bhikkhu...’, I shall state the resolution.
Because of having failed (*viraddhattā*) means because of having transgressed. Explaining that matter in detail, he said “Therefore, then” (*tena hi*), and so forth.

In that context, “therefore, then” (*tena hi*) is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. “For thus” (*evaṃ hi*) means in this very way. “Of him” (*tassa*) refers to Devadatta. “But the prince” (*kumāro pana*)...
"But as for Prince Ajātasattu, what [fault] was not stated?"—this is the connection. "Of him" means of Devadatta.
"Therefore" means because, although he committed an act that would cause schism even before the actual schism occurred, his incapacity (*abhabba*) was subsequently established;

therefore, the decision regarding the grounds for causing a schism (*bhedakaravatthu*) should be understood in this way. This refers to the categories of *dhamma* and *adhamma*, etc., according to the method of the Suttanta and Vinaya.
Showing a distinction, he said: “By way of the Suttanta,” and so forth. Therein, “by way of the Suttanta” means by the teaching of the Suttantas;
it is said to be by the method of the Suttanta teaching. “Tathā” (thus) means otherwise than that.
“Tattha” (therein) refers to the two, namely, dhamma and adhamma. “Evaṃ amhākaṃ” (thus for us) means when it is done in this way for us. Thus [is it] by way of the Suttanta.

Having shown the distinction between what is Dhamma and what is non-Dhamma, he now says, beginning with “But by way of the Vinaya,” in order to show that same distinction according to the method of the Vinaya.
The connection is: “it must be done with a factual basis. This applies likewise to the phrase “with a non-factual basis.
