Having thus shown the distinction between the pair of Dhamma and non-Dhamma by means of these two methods, he now [proceeds] to the pair of Vinaya and non-Vinaya.

Showing the distinction, he said, "By way of the Suttanta," and so forth. Therein, according to the method of the Suttanta, it is called *vinaya* because it leads away (*vineti*) lust and the other defilements;
according to the method of *vinaya*, it is called *vinaya* because it leads away (*vineti*) body and speech—this is how the meaning of the word should be understood.

Having thus shown the distinction between the pair of "discipline" (*vinaya*) and "non-discipline" (*avinaya*) by way of these two methods, [he now addresses] the pair of "spoken" (*bhāsita*) and "unspoken" (*abhāsita*).
Showing the distinction, he said: “By way of the Suttanta method, there are four foundations of mindfulness,” and so forth.
Therein, the construction is: “The ‘eightfold path’—this statement was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.
Having thus shown the distinction between the pair of ‘spoken and unspoken’ according to the two methods, now, regarding the pair of ‘practiced and unpracticed’:
Showing a distinction, he said: “By way of the method of the Suttanta, ‘daily,’ and so forth. Therein, the word “daily” (*devasika*) should be applied to only three terms:
“entering [meditative attainment],” “surveying,” and [the third term]. “By way of occasion” (*aṭṭhuppattivasena*) means by way of the arising of a cause.
For a cause is called “occasion” (*attha*) in the sense that it is that from which a result arises; the arising of an occasion is “occasion-arising” (*atthuppatti*), and that very thing—

Regarding *aṭṭhuppatti*: having changed the letter *t* of *attha* into *ṭ*, one has *aṭṭha*; the state (*vaso*) of such an occasion (*aṭṭha*) is "the state of an occasion" (*aṭṭhuppattivaso*), by means of which [it is so called].
This term should be construed with both of the two phrases: "instruction in the Suttantas" and "discourse on the Jātakas.

"This" (*idaṃ*) refers to the attainment of the fruition-attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) and so forth. "Habitual" (*āciṇṇaṃ*) means bound (*ābandhitaṃ*), or repeatedly accumulated and increased (*punappunaṃ upacitaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ*), or made proficient (*paguṇaṃ*). "Wandering about" (*cāriyapakkamanaṃ*)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
"Going forth for the sake of conduct.

Having thus shown the distinction between the dyads of "practiced" and "unpracticed" by way of two methods, he now says, "By way of the method of the Suttas, there are four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth, in order to show the distinction between the dyad of "prescribed" and "unprescribed. This is exactly like the dyad of "spoken" and "unspoken."
Thus, by means of two methods of exposition from the Sutta and Vinaya, the distinction between five pairs has been shown.
Regarding the pair on offenses and non-offenses, the word "etc. (*ādi*) found in the subsequent sentence following the reading "not with the intention of releasing" must be brought forward.
For the meaning is: "in this manner, etc. In that context, the phrase "therein, therein" refers to each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
This term should also be carried over into the subsequent sentence.

In the pair concerning light and heavy offenses, "five classes of offenses" refers to the five bases of offenses consisting of *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*. "Two classes of offenses" refers to the two bases of offenses consisting of *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*.
In the pair concerning offenses with remainder and without remainder, "six classes of offenses" refers to the six bases of offenses remaining after excluding the *pārājika* offense.
The pair of "grave and non-grave" is exactly like the pair of "light and heavy. However, this is the distinction:
a grave offense is called "grave," while a light offense is called "non-grave. Thus, the distinction between the four pairs has been shown solely by way of the terminology of the Vinaya.

*Ettha*: in the statement beginning with “proclaiming what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma. *Catunnaṃ saṅghakammānaṃ*: of the four kinds of formal acts of the Saṅgha, such as the act of notification (*apalokanakamma*) and so forth.

By those who perform [them], acting as the cause; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the causal agent (*hetvatthe*). *Tattha*: in the statement beginning with “these [people] by means of these. *Apakassanti*:
here, showing that the root *kas* has the meaning of "going," he says “they draw away the assembly. *Vijaṭenti*: they untangle; the meaning is that they separate [them]. *Ekamantaṃ*.

“Ussādentī” means they create a protrusion at one end. Regarding “avapakassantī,” because of the two prefixes (*ava* and *pa*), the meaning should be understood as being excessive; thus he says, “drawing [it] out excessively.
Revealing this excessive sense, he says, “they act in such a way that [the parts] become completely separated. “Yathā” means “in whatever manner they are being acted upon.”
[The word] *sambandho* [means connection]. By the word “*visuṃ*,” it is shown that this is an unformed primary noun (*anipphanna-pāṭipadika*) expressing the sense of “separately” or “distinctly.
“*Vatthūsu*” means in the grounds for schism. “*Imaṃ gaṇhatha*” means “take up this doctrine.
“*Visuṃ*” means separately or distinctly. In order to reconcile the statement spoken in this Khandhaka with the Parivāra text, he says, “In the Parivāra, however,” and so forth.

In that context, "by five modes" means by these five reasons: "by means of the formal act (kamma), the recitation of the summary (uddesa), the proclamation (voharanta), the announcement (anussāvana), and the drawing of lots (salākaggāha).
"Of that" refers to the statement spoken in the Parivāra. "Here" means in this Saṅghabhedaka-khandhaka; the construction is:
"by this characteristic of schism in the Saṅgha as stated here. By the phrase "there is no difference in meaning," [it is shown that there is no distinction].

It demonstrates that there is a distinction in terms of the phrasing. "Of this" refers to the characteristic of schism in the Saṅgha. The construction is: "but that [distinction] is an absence of difference.
"In that very place" means in the Parivāra itself. "In all instances" means throughout the entire Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
Thus ends the analysis of the commentary on the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka.
8. The Chapter on Duties (Vattakkhandhaka).
1. Discussion on the Duties for a Visitor. 357.
Regarding the statement in the Chapter on Duties that "in the monastery" refers to the precinct boundary (upacārasīma), he said: "near the precinct boundary."
Regarding the word “having taken,” the object (*kamma*) “sandals” is evident, but the instrument (*karaṇa*) is not.
Therefore, showing the instrument, he said: “having taken with the handle of the sandals. By this, he excludes the instrument “with the hand.
Regarding the term “they retreat,” rejecting the meanings of “entering” and “departing,” he said: “they gather together.”

Regarding the phrase "sandals... [etc. ...should be asked," the expression "should be asked" is explained here by showing the manner in which they should be asked along with the object of the question:
"In what place? and so forth. Therein, by the words "In what... [etc. ...piece of cloth," he shows the manner of the inquiry.
By the words "The resident monks," he shows the object of the action. By the words "should be spread out," he shows that which is to be answered.

Here, he rejects the sense of "producing" (cajanattha) for the verbal root *saj*. Regarding the statement "the alms-resort (*gocara*) must be asked about," he says "the alms-round (*bhikkhācāra*) must be asked about," showing that here the word *gocara* is identical in meaning to the word *bhikkhācāra*. It is called *bhikkhācāra* because they wander for alms (*bhikkhā*) therein;
it refers to the village of the alms-resort (*gocaragāma*). "In which" means in whichever village. By the words beginning with "what," [he asks about] drinking water.
In the passage beginning with "should be asked," he shows the manner in which one should ask. "At what time? means at which time.
"Of one going out" means of one going out from the monastery. "Should be looked at" means should be observed.
By the phrase "if he is able," the word "if" (*sace*) here has the sense of "when" (*yadi*), and the word "able" (*ussahati*) means "he is capable" (*sakkoti*).
He shows that this is a method (*pariyāya*). The connection is with "for one who is able, the duty of cleaning the monastery.
2. Discussion on the Duties of a Resident Monk (*āvāsika-vatta-kathā*):
359. The construction is: "The determination regarding the duties of a resident monk should be understood thus. The connection is with "all must be performed."

“Of him” means of the senior guest. By the words “if he is wise,” etc., it is shown that if the junior does not say, “Please sweep the shrine courtyard first,” then one should simply perform his duties after setting aside the broom.

Because it is stated with the restrictive particle “only” in the phrase “only medicine should be given,” even if the junior does not say, “Please prepare medicine first,” medicine alone [should be provided].
[This] should be done. However, by the words beginning with “For he is wise,” [the author] merely shows that this is something which must be said to a guest.

Introducing the conduct not found in the canonical text (pāḷimuttaka-vatta), he says “Moreover,” and so forth. “By fanning” means by a fan (*bījanī*). For “fanning” (*bījana*) is the neuter gender, while “fan” (*bījanī*) is the feminine gender.
And by this commentarial statement, “he should be fanned” (*bījitabbo*) and “it should be fanned” (*bījitabbaṃ*), [it is shown that] it is fanned.

"By this" means by a brush; the etymological meaning of "brush" (*bījanī*) should be understood as "that by which one brushes. "Of him" refers to a more senior guest. "To be rubbed" means to be smeared [with oil].
"Indeed" (*hi*) signifies truth. "In this" refers to the shoe-brushing cloth. "Where" means in which monastery.
This is to be connected with the phrase "by the resident monk who was asked."

By the phrase, “...he does not obtain [permission] from his own presence,” it is shown that even if one does not come of one's own accord, one is not permitted to fail to perform the duties (*vatta*) toward a guest who has arrived in one’s presence.
3. Discussion on the Duties for Those Departing (Gamikavattakathā) 360.

The construction is: “In this regard, the determination (*vinicchaya*) regarding the duties for those departing should be understood thus. “Therein” refers to the Chapter on Lodgings (*Senāsanakkhandhaka*).

"Having settled all that" is the connection. The construction is: "Wherever there is a dwelling made upon a stone surface or on those stone pillars where termites do not ascend—that stone surface or those stone pillars—even for one who does not ask permission, there is no offense.
The phrase "on four stones," etc., is what has been stated; this is the connection.
The connection is that [the benefit] is made at the place where termites arise. "This" refers to the advantage (*ānisansa*).
The connection is that it applies to beds and chairs placed in a house that is subject to rain. 4. Discussion on the Procedure for Expressing Thanks (*Anumodana-vatta-kathā*).
Regarding the phrase "it was successful" (*iddham ahosi*): here, rejecting the meaning of increase for the root *idh*, he says "it was accomplished" (*sampannam ahosi*).
The connection is with "the elder of the Saṅgha being seated. The construction is "the junior elder being seated for the purpose of the expression of thanks.
The connection is also with "even when requested by the elder of the Saṅgha. The connection is with "the one who expresses thanks speaks. *Anu* means repeatedly.
One who rejoices through a Dhamma talk with the donors afterwards is an "anumodaka" (one who expresses appreciation). The construction is: "If he says, 'Go,' he is an anumodaka.
"Tassa" refers to the anumodaka. "People cause [it] to be done" is the connection. The word "ekenā" (by one) is the object of the causative verb in the word "kārenti" (they cause to do).
"Tassa" refers to the bhikkhu who has been caused to act. "Anumodanato" means for the sake of the expression of appreciation. "Upanisinnakathā" (a conversation seated nearby).
It is called *upanisinnakathā* because it is spoken by those sitting near (*upaniṣad*). *Anumodanāya* means for the purpose of expressing appreciation (*anumodana*).
*Ajjhiṭṭhova* means simply requested by oneself. *Ettha* refers to the occasion of the expression of appreciation.

By the phrase "one whose offspring has been born" (*sañjātavacca*), it shows that the suffix *-ita* is used in the sense of "having arisen," based on the analysis: "one whose offspring (*vacca*) has arisen (*sañjāta*) for him is a 'born-offspring' (*vaccita*)."
5. Discussion on the Duties Concerning the Dining Hall (Bhattaggavattakathā) 364.
Regarding "the duties concerning the dining hall" (*bhattaggavatta*): it is called a "dining hall" (*bhattagga*) because they take food there; it is the place of serving.
The duty to be performed therein is the "duty concerning the dining hall. The detailed exposition regarding that duty concerning the dining hall should be understood as follows.
The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: a "place for serving people" (*manussānaṃ parivisanaṭṭhānaṃ*) is where people, together with their wives and children, dwell and feed the bhikkhus.

By the word "having crowded in too closely" (*atiallīyitvā*), it is shown that in the phrase "having encroached upon" (*anupakhajja*), "crowding in too closely" (*atiallīyana*) refers to the act of harming (*khadadhātu*).

"While seats exist" (*āsanesu satīti*) means while seats are present. This is connected with "for the junior [bhikkhu] sitting down" (*nisīdantassa navakassāti*). "He incurs [the offense]" (*āpajjatīti*).
He incurs an offense. The construction is: "The elder incurs [the offense] by not giving permission when asked. *Saṅghāṭi* means the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) that has been put on.
*Pattadhovana-udaka* means water for washing the bowls for the purpose of eating. *Gahetabbaṃ* means it should be taken with the hand.
The construction is: "In the manner that it is being taken. *Mattāya* means by measure. In the case of *sabbi* and so forth, the word *eva* (indeed/only) is to be supplied.

“*Sabbiādīsūti*” means “among all kinds of ghee, oil, and *uttaribhaṅga* [curd-milk preparations]”; this is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). “*Yaṃ*” refers to that which begins with ghee.
“*Appahotīti*” means it is not sufficient for all the monks. “*Taṃ*” refers to that which begins with ghee; the connection is “prepare it.
The connection is “such [food] beginning with ghee.”

The construction is: "that which is the dining hall. "Hand-washing water" means the water for washing the hands of those who have finished eating. "In between" means in the middle of the meal. "By one who is thirsty" means by one desiring to drink. "In the throat" means at the throat.
Regarding "by one returning," he asks: "From what place is he returning? and answers: "from the dining hall. The construction is: "In what manner, or by what way, should one return?
He asks: "Why should junior monks return first? and answers: [as follows].
“*Sambādhesu hi*,” etc. “The place of exit” (*nikkhamanokāsa*) means the place from which one has already exited first. “In order” (*paṭipāṭiyā*) means according to the order of seniority.
“At the front” (*dhure*) means near the door of the house; for here the word *dhura* denotes proximity. The construction is: “if the novices are sitting inside the house.
“Between” (*antarena*) means by way of the interval between the monks, or through their midst. “Scattered” (*viraḷāya*) means thinly spread.
6. Discussion on the Duties of One Who Goes for Alms (Piṇḍacārikavattakathā) 366.
The construction [of the sentence] is: "The determination regarding the duties of one who goes for alms should be understood thus. The connection is with "or having taken cotton.
The connection is with "and whatever thing" (*yañca*), meaning "having taken whatever object. "Standing while doing" means "having become one who is doing."

Or standing. "That" refers to the action. By saying "not [looking] at the one giving alms," he rejects the interpretation that because it is stated using the feminine gender, one must not look at the face of a woman alone; thus he says, "whether she be a woman," and so forth.
By the phrase "at the time of giving alms," he shows that there is no fault even if one looks at another time. At one time, while she is giving alms...
"At no time should one look [at it]" rejects what is not desired.
7. Discussion on the Duties of a Forest-Dweller (Āraññika-vatta):
"The determination regarding the duties of a forest-dweller should be understood in this way" is the construction. Regarding the phrase "one should descend from the lodging": here—
Because one who is seated at the foot of a tree or in similar locations in the forest lacks a dwelling, the term "lodging" (*senāsana*) is said here with reference to a place for residing;
thus he says, "one must depart from the place of residence.
Regarding the phrase "having placed the bowl in its bag," he asks: "How should the bowl be placed in the bag? He replies: "If..."
"Outside," and so forth. Therein, "the bowl should be placed" is the connection.
Regarding the phrases "having washed" and "having prepared," one should connect them by changing the case endings to "the bowl [or] the water. "That too" refers even to the bamboo tube.
"Nearby" means near the forest dwelling (*araññaka-senāsana*). And just as fire-sticks (*araṇisahita*) are required for one living in the forest, so too...
The construction is: "Even for one who has set out upon a wilderness journey, a companion is to be desired. "Living in a group" means living together with a group;

this connects with the word "for a forest-dweller. "By that" means by the companion. By the phrase "the asterisms themselves are the words for asterisms," it is indicated that the asterisms such as Assayuja and so forth (as found in verses 58–60 of the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*) are for the purpose of knowing the directions.
And it shows that they are called "lunar mansion words" because they serve as the cause for one who knows the conventions (*samaya*).
8. Discussion on the Rules for Lodgings (Senāsanavatta).
369. The construction [of the sentence] is: "In the rules for lodgings, the determination (*vinicchaya*) should be understood thus. "The gate" means the main gate (*mahādvāra*).
*Mahāvaḷañjaṃ* means that which is to be used by great people. *Tattha* means at the gate. *Āpucchitvāva* means having asked permission from an elder;
it is connected with "of a fellow-monk who is more senior. *Vaṭṭatiyeva* means it is indeed permissible to dwell there as one pleases.
*Parivattitabbaṃ* means it should be turned around toward the face.
9. Discussion on the Conduct Regarding the Steam Bathhouse (Jantāghara-vatta), etc.
371. The construction [of the sentence] is: "The determination regarding the conduct in the steam bathhouse should be understood in this way.

*Bahijagati* means the outer veranda. 373. The construction [of the sentence] is: "In the matter of rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), the meaning should be understood in this way. *Nīharitvā* means having carried out the water.
“Ācamitabbaṃ” means it should be washed. For it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (dhātupāṭha) that “the root *camu* preceded by *ā* means washing.
“This is too open” means this place is too exposed; the sense is that it is not covered by anything. “Only for one who does not obtain water” means precisely for one who does not obtain water.
374. The construction is: “In the duties regarding the privy, the analysis should be understood in this way. “He” refers to one chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakaṭṭha*).
The making of a latrine. "In every case" means in every single instance.

Regarding the phrase "not with a rough stick," he says "or with a split stick," and so forth, showing that it is not only a hard stick that is called "rough," but also split sticks and the like which scrape the skin are indeed called rough. "Of one who has entered" means of one who has entered the latrine.
"A place common to all" means a place designated as a latrine that is shared by all monks, or one that is common to everyone.

"Therein" means in that place common to all. The construction is: "for the purpose of going regularly" refers to whatever place has been made for one's own regular use, or whatever place belongs to an individual.
Showing that *uhaḍati* here consists of the prefix *upa-* and the verbal root *haḍ*, he says “*uhaḍitā*.

Since it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—specifically in Pāṇini’s *Dhātupāṭha* (977) and in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā* (15, under the roots ending in *-da*)—that “*haḍa* [means] the voiding of excrement,” he says “smeared with excrement outside the latrine. [The word] “to be washed” (*dhovitabbā*)...
They should be washed with water. "Even this" means even when water is not available. "In all cases" means throughout the entire Vatta-khandhaka (Chapter on Duties).
Thus ends the commentary on the Vatta-khandhaka.
9. The Pātimokkha-ṭṭhapana-khandhaka (Chapter on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha).
1. The Discussion on Requesting the Recitation of the Pātimokkha 383.
Regarding the phrase "on the night of Nandimukhī" in the section on the suspension of the Pātimokkha (*Pātimokkhaṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*):
here, *nandi* means that which rejoices or is satisfied. This word ending in *-i* is neuter. In instances such as "Nandisena" and "Nandivisāla," this same word ending in *-i* is masculine.
[The word *nandimukha*] exists [as a masculine noun ending in -a]; however, here, in consideration of its face (*mukha*), it is a neuter noun ending in -ika.

Because the face of the bright quarter is turned toward her at the time of sunrise, this night has a "joyful face" (*nandimukha*); thus she is *nandimukhī*, meaning "the night. By that *nandimukhī* night, it is said:
"For even at the time of sunrise, the night appears as if it were joyful-faced (*nandīmukhā*). Regarding the phrase "internally rotten": here...
Introducing the meaning of "the putrid stench within the body," he said, "In the continuity of one's own mind," and so forth.
By the phrase "by way of the rain of defilements," he rejects the meaning of "by way of the rain of water. *Avassutaṃ* means soaked; the sense is "moistened.
Regarding *kasambujātaṃ*, here *kasambu* means refuse. For when a place is being mopped or swept clean, that [refuse] remains.
It is called *kasambu* because it makes a noise; the meaning should be understood as "born like that," hence *kasambujāta*.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated as "born thoroughly defiled" (*ākiliṭṭhajāta*) by way of its underlying intention, meaning "born exceedingly defiled.
There is also a reading: "born defiled due to being filled with faults" (*ākiṇṇadosatāya kiliṭṭhajāta*). By the phrase "even to the point of seizing him by the arms,"...
The connection is: "he shows by means of the recitation. The word *hi* is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. The word *tena* refers to that "vain man" (*moghapurisa*).
Because of the usage of the particle *yāva*, the fifth case ending in the phrase *bāhāgahaṇāpi* is used in the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).
The word *nāma* indicates censure; because of its usage, the future tense in the phrase *āgamessati* is employed in the sense of the past. (From the *Saddanītisuttamālā*)
(From Sutta 893). The construction is: “He will indeed wait. “Āgamessati” means he will endure [the delay] for a short while.

For it is stated in the *Dhātupāṭha* (in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*, root 18, the group of roots ending in *m*) that “from the root *gam*, with the prefix *ā*, [the form *āgameti* is used] in the sense of enduring for a short while (*īsaṃ adhivāsane*).
384. Regarding the phrase “not by a long descent,” he says “not immediately” in order to show that it is not by a long descent.

"Deep. For the word *āyata* is a synonym for "long. As in such passages as, "The Dhamma should not be sung with a long-drawn-out melody," it is meant that there is no precipice at the beginning of the long shore. "Right from the start" means right at the beginning of the shore.
By the phrase "deep by degrees," the intended meaning of the statement "not deep right from the start" is expressed.
[The text] shows this. "One whose nature is fixed" (*ṭhitadhammo*) means one whose inherent nature remains within the very boundary of the shore.

Regarding the phrase "he does not overstep the limit" (*velaṃ nātivattati*), [the author], demonstrating that the word *velā* functions here in the senses of "shore" and "boundary," says: "The retreating ravine is the boundary-limit (*mariyādavelā*).
Therein, by the term "retreating ravine" (*osakkanakandara*), he shows the sense of "shore," and by the term "boundary" (*mariyāda*), he shows the sense of "limit."
A *kandara* is so called because it is to be split (*darita*) by water; a *osakkanakandara* is a cleft where there is a subsiding (*osakkana*) by water—that is, a shore.
The meaning is that it does not overstep the shore, which is both a cleft and a boundary.
Regarding the phrase "it carries the shore," he says "it reaches the shore" (*appeti*) to show that the root *vah* here has the sense of reaching. In that context:

*Appetīti* means he causes to reach. By the word *ussāreti*, the meaning of the phrase *tīraṃ vāheti* (he drives to the shore) from the Pāḷi text is shown by the phrase *thalaṃ ussāreti* (he draws up onto dry land).
*Ussāreti* means having lifted up, he causes to go. Regarding *aññāpaṭivedho*:
here, *aññaṃ* refers to that which one understands (*ājānāti*) or has understood (*ājānittha*), namely either the path of Arahatship or the fruit of Arahatship.
Alternatively, the penetration of that [truth] is the penetration of final knowledge (*aññāpaṭivedha*); the long vowel in the middle is for the sake of ease in pronunciation.
What is called "penetration of final knowledge" is precisely the arising of Arahantship. Therefore it was said: "the arising of Arahantship.
(385) In order to show that the statement "The rain pours through what is covered" is a text spoken with intentional meaning from the *Udāna* collection, he said: "an offense," and so forth.
In this context, the connection is as follows: the statement "the rain leaks through what is covered" is what was spoken;
and the connection is that "this" refers to the incurring of new offenses. 4. Discussion on those worthy of hearing the Pātimokkha.
386. “Before or after” means before or after the motion (*ñatti*).
“In the field” refers to the field for the suspension of the Pātimokkha. Showing that field, he says “Therefore,” and so forth.

“He utters the letter *re*” means that among the thirty-six syllables, the one who performs the motion and suspension utters the letter *re*. “This” refers to the place where the thirty-five syllables are pronounced.
“Vutta” means when it has been stated by the one who proposes the motion (*ñatti*). The construction is: “even before the words ‘Let the Sangha hear me’ have been commenced. 5.
Discussion on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha that is Lawful and Unlawful.
387. “By that person” means by that person who has been accused. “That failure” refers to what is comprised by failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and so forth.
That is failure. "By way of being rootless in perception" means by way of the perception that [the act] was "done. "And done" means done exclusively;
"and not done" means not done exclusively. The connection is:
"it does not come because of the desire to provoke anger. "By that" refers to the reason such as its not coming. "He incurs" means...
The one who suspends the *pātimokkha* incurs [an offense]. "In this way" (*iccassāpi*) means: in this manner, for that very person who has suspended the *pātimokkha*.

"He takes it back" (*paccādiyati*) means he takes it up again (*pati ādiyati*); the meaning is that he takes it up again by saying, "The act was not done; the act must be done again," and so forth, or he begins it again.
6. Discussion on the Suspension of the Dhamma Pātimokkha 388.
"In cases such as setting out on a journey," etc., means: in cases such as setting out on a journey. By the word "etc.

(*ādi*), acts such as theft with a thieving mind are included. "Perception of form, etc. means perception of form, perception of gender, and perception of signs. "Regarding that" refers to suspicion; this is the grammatical connection.
7. Discussion on the Factor of Taking Up Oneself (Attādāna) 398.

Regarding the phrase "by one who wishes to take up [the matter] oneself" (*attādānaṃ ādātukāmena*), what is meant by "taking up oneself"? He says: "one who wishes to purify the Teaching," and so forth.
By this, he shows that a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) which one must take up for oneself in order to challenge another is called "taking up oneself. It is not the right time.
Regarding the phrase "to take up this self-appropriation," he says "fear of kings" and so forth to show that it is the wrong time.
Therein, "vassāratta" means the rainy season. For it is called "vassāratta" because the rain (*vassa*) rains (*rañjati*) excessively there during that time.
Even the rainy season is called the "wrong time" because it is difficult to bring a modest assembly from afar for the purpose of settling a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus.
The meaning is: "this is a time of fear of kings and so forth. "The opposite" means a time when there is an absence of fear of kings and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "this taking up of self is unreal," the word "unreal" (abhūta) here is a synonym for "non-existent";
thus he says, "this is non-existent," meaning this taking up of self does not exist. The connection is "taken up by me. The construction is "a person possessing virtue."
The connection is: "They go toward what leads to self-grasping. "This" refers to self-grasping.

Regarding the statement, "I shall not obtain it in this visible life; I shall obtain it in this visible life," he asks: "With reference to what was this said, 'I shall not obtain it' and 'I shall obtain it'?
To which he replies: "Sometimes indeed," and so forth. Therein, *appekadā* means "even at one time. The word *hi* [is used as an emphatic particle].
It is an expositor of details. "Of such a kind" means having the nature of being a close friend or associate. "That" refers to the obtaining of supporting monks;
this is the connection. The phrase "I shall not obtain" is what was said; this is the connection. The construction is:
"There will be quarreling and so forth, just as there was quarreling and so forth among the people of Kosambī. It is something that causes no regret even afterwards.
Regarding the phrase "it will be," it is said that for one who undertakes the formal act of admission (*attādāna*) endowed with the five factors, it becomes like something that causes no remorse;
even afterwards, it remains a cause for no remorse. Thus he says, "Subhadda, the elder who went forth late in life," and so forth.
In this context, "the rehearsal of the five hundred" refers to the rehearsal to be performed by the five hundred elders, beginning with Mahākassapa. [And] of the Elder Mahākassapa...
The construction is: "it becomes a cause for recollection later; it is as if it were so. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
"A cause for recollection" means a cause for repeated recollection by way of joyful gladness (*sammoda*). By this, he shows the meaning of the phrase "a cause for non-remorse" (*avippaṭisārakara*).
Regarding the word "later" (*pacchāpi*), showing that the particle *pi* has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated, he says: "of the Dispensation... (*sāsanassa*)...
And so forth. Therein, the connection is with the phrase "the splendor of the Dispensation.
The intended meaning is that it leads to the splendor of the Dispensation, just like the moon and sun when they are free from defilements.
8. Discourse on the Factors to be Reviewed by the Accuser.
399. In such passages as “*acchiddena appaṭimaṃsenā*,” the construction should be understood in this way.
Having first shown that which is “with holes and with flesh,” he says “*yenā*” and so forth, showing by way of contrast that which is “without holes and without flesh.

Therein, the connection is with “*yena katāni*” (by which they were made). It is called “*chiddo*” because it is pierced (*chijjati*). *Paṭi* means it is repeatedly rubbed or touched (*masiyati āmasiyati*).
The prefix *paṭi-* [is added], there is the elision of the letter *niggahita*, and this description of the action emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāva*).
"Together with the prefix *paṭi-*" means *sappaṭimaṃsa*; the meaning is "bodily conduct that proceeds in a contrary or inverted manner.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by groundless accusations, etc.," one includes grave verbal misconduct and so forth.
In the phrase "Is my mind full of loving-kindness? it is shown that only the state of loving-kindness that has reached absorption (appanā) is intended;
thus he says, "having severed the obstacles," and so forth. Therein, "obstacles" refers to obstacles such as those related to one's dwelling place.
By the expression "with hostility destroyed by way of suppression," he demonstrates precisely that state of loving-kindness which has reached absorption.

Regarding the question, "But friend, where was this said by the Blessed One?", he says, "In which city was this training rule [stated]? in order to show the scope of the words *idaṃ* (this) and *kiṃ* (what).
9. Discussion on the one who reproves being made to wait.
400. Regarding the passage beginning with “I shall speak at the proper time,” the author says “one to one,” etc., to demonstrate the proper and improper times for an accusation.
Therein, “one” refers to the accuser acting alone; “one” refers to the accused being alone. The construction is: “in the midst of the Saṅgha...
or in the dining hall, etc., at a time when [the parties] are surrounded. Therein, by the phrase “in the midst of the Saṅgha... or in the dining hall, etc.,” [it is shown that...]
By this he shows the absence of the occasion; by the phrase "at the moment he was surrounded by his attendants," he shows the absence of the time.
By these words, he shows that what was said—namely, "I shall speak at the proper time"—was stated after including both the occasion and the time within the term "time.
*Tacchena* means by truth. *Ham* is a particle that should be applied individually to each of the following phrases: "O elder! O elder! [The text continues: "O elder..."
The meaning is: "O fellow wanderer," "O wearer of rag-robes," or "O preacher of the Dhamma. "This" refers to the action (*kamma*).
"Dependent on a cause" means dependent on causes such as being advanced in years and so forth. The particle "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*) should also be construed with each [term].
And here, because the particle "hambho" expresses disrespect according to worldly convention, it is harsh.
"He speaks" means that because the honorific particle "Venerable Sir" (*bhante*) expresses respect, he speaks gently.

"Having made it dependent on the reason" means having established that "this is indeed the fault in this transgression. By the phrase "having established a mind of loving-kindness," he shows that the term "mind of loving-kindness" functions as an adverbial modifier for the verb "I shall speak. "Not with a mind of ill-will" (*no dosantaro*).
Here, demonstrating that the word *antara* denotes the mind (*citta*), he says: "not with a corrupted mind.
By the word "having been" (*hutvā*), he shows its status as an adverbial modifier of the action.
10. Discussion Concerning the Accuser and the Accused.

401. Regarding the word *ajjhattaṃ*, he says “in one’s own mind,” demonstrating that the word *atta* here denotes the mind (*citta*) and that the seventh case ending (*sattamīvibhatti*) does not undergo the substitution of *am*.
By the word “having produced” (*uppādetvā*), he shows the intended meaning of the phrase “having brought to mind” (*manasikaritvā*).
Regarding the term *kāruññatā*, since among the two suffixes, *ṇya* and *tā*, only one expresses the abstract state (*bhāva*), [it is the latter].

Showing that it means "one's own," he says: "the state of being compassionate" (*karuṇabhāvo*). In this context, the state (*bhāvo*) of a compassionate person (*karuṇassa puggalassa*) is compassionateness (*kāruñña*);

that itself is compassionateness-ness (*kāruññatā*). Alternatively, the word-meaning should be understood as follows: a compassionate person (*karuṇo eva puggalo*) is compassionateness (*kāruñña*), and the state of that is compassionateness-ness (*kāruññatā*).

"By this" refers to the term "compassionateness-ness" (*kāruññatā*). "And compassion" (*karuṇañca*) refers to compassion that has reached absorption (*appanā*). "And the preliminary stage of compassion" (*karuṇāpubbabhāgañca*)...
And the sense-sphere compassion that occurs by way of preliminary (parikamma) and access (upacāra) stages prior to the attainment of absorption (appanā).
By both [terms]—namely, by the two words "desire for welfare" (hitesitā) and "compassion" (anukampitā)—[this is meant].

And "loving-kindness" (mettaṃ) refers to loving-kindness that has attained absorption. And "the preliminary stage of loving-kindness" (mettāpubbabhāgaṃ) refers to that which occurs by way of preliminary and access stages prior to the attainment of absorption in loving-kindness.

And loving-kindness pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-metta*). "In the pure" (*suddhante*) means in a pure portion. "Having made a formal admission" (*paṭiññaṃ āropetvā*) means having made the accused person admit [the charge].
The construction is: "those which are these"—referring to those five qualities stated by way of the method beginning with "compassion" (*kāruññatā*).
By this, he shows that in the phrase "these five qualities," the word "these" (*ime*) functions as an indefinite demonstrative.

Regarding the phrase "and in truth and imperturbability," he says "and in verbal truth" in order to exclude here the meanings of "truth as abstinence" (*virati-sacca*) and "ultimate truth" (*paramattha-sacca*).
By the term "akuppanatāya" (by way of imperturbability), he shows the sense of the abstract suffix *ṇya* by treating it as "the state of being unperturbed" (*na-kuppa-bhāvo akuppam*).
"Hi" means "truly" or "in detail. "Another should not be provoked" means another should not be made to feel anger.
"In all cases" means in the entire *Pātimokkha-ṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Pātimokkha-ṭṭhapanakkhandhaka*.
10. The *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*.
The Discourse on the Story of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (402).
Having presented the objection, "Why does he reject [it]? in the *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka*, he says "Nanu... and so forth, showing her intention (*ābhoga*). With the words "Kāmaṃ...
and so forth, he provides the answer by way of an admission (*abhyupagama*) and a refutation (*parihāra*). In that context, the word *kāmaṃ*...
The word *pana*, however, has the sense of favor (*anuggaha*), while *tathāpi* has the sense of reproach (*garaha*). The connection is: "nevertheless, she rejects it.
*Taṃ* refers to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. The construction is: "having been requested, [it was] permitted. *Ayaṃ* refers to the going forth (*pabbajjā*).
"Having made it auspicious" means having made it obtained, that is to say, having made it pleasing.

403. Regarding the phrase *kumbhathenakehi*: here, they are called *kumbhathenaka* because they steal by lighting a lamp in a jar and using that light; thus he says, "having lit a lamp in a jar," and so forth.

*Nāḷimajjhagataṃ* means having gone into the middle of the stalk of the grain. *Gaṇṭhiṃ* means the node or joint. There is also a reading *kaṇḍaṃ*, which has the meaning of "the stem. *Yena* refers to the creature. For it should be understood that this word *yaṃ* (who/which) does not depend upon the word *taṃ* (that).
*Antorattabhāvo* means the state of being internally red (bloodied). *Etamatthaṃ* means this matter that is about to be explained. *Āḷiyā* means by means of a covering.
In the phrase "even when not tied" (*abaddhāyapi*), the particle *pi* is used for the sake of inclusion, meaning "how much more so when it is tied.

"Anything" (*kiñci*) means a small amount. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to the water. "Even that" (*tampi*) refers to the water as well; here the particle *pi* refers back to any water that might be standing where it is not tied.
The construction is: "these heavy rules (*garudhamma*) which have been laid down. "Right from the start" (*paṭikacceva*) means beforehand, or even at the very beginning. "Among them" (*tesu*).
Regarding the *garudhammas*: the construction is "even though they have not yet been laid down. The phrase beginning with "it was said first" is stated;
the construction is that it shows this meaning: "it will remain for exactly one thousand years. And the connection is that this statement, "one thousand years," has been spoken.

"From that" means from the thousand years. The word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) also" [indicates] the True Dhamma of penetration (*paṭivedha-saddhamma*).

It looks back. Since it is understood that when two true dharmas (saddhamma) are established, the true dharma of practice (paṭipatti-saddhamma) is likewise established, this was not explicitly stated.
"Those very same" means precisely five thousand years. The construction is: "One should not say either that 'when the teaching (pariyatti) exists, penetration (paṭivedha) does not exist.
"Characteristic" (liṅga) means the appearance of a recluse (samaṇa-vesa); the sense is the outward form of a recluse (samaṇākāra).
The Discussion on the Authorization for the Higher Ordination of Bhikkhunīs: 404.

Regarding the phrase "by this subsequent rule" (*anupaññatti*): in reference to the higher ordination obtained by Mahāpajāpatī through the acceptance of the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*), this present rule is called a "subsequent rule. The meaning is that one should grant the higher ordination by means of that subsequent rule. [Regarding] Mahāpajāpatī...
"Having made them *saddhivihārinīs*" means having made the five hundred Sākiyan women, with Mahāpajāpatī as their preceptor (*upajjhā*), her *saddhivihārinīs*;
this is the meaning. "Thus" (*iti*) connects to "therefore they became" (*tasmā ahesuṃ*). "By this exhortation" (*iminā ovādena*) means by this exhortation of the Blessed One.

410. "Of her" (*etissā*) refers to that bhikkhunī. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to the formal act (*kamma*). "In another" (*aññasmiṃ*) means in another formal act. "Another" (*aññaṃ*) refers to a formal act other than the one to be performed.
411. *Kaddamodakena*: by means of water that is stirred up with mud. In the phrase *kaddamādīsu pi*, the particle *pi* should be connected with the word *yena kenaci*.
For the meaning is: "by whatever [means] at all. *Sannipatitvā*: having assembled with the community of nuns (*bhikkhunīsaṅgha*).
*Apasādanīyaṃ*: an act that is to be performed for the purpose of censure. *Ettāvatā*: by this much, that is, by the mere announcement.
"Avandiyo" means one who should not be saluted; the meaning is that he is not worthy of being saluted. "Tato" means from the point of having to announce it three times.
"Na vandantī" means the bhikkhunīs do not salute him. "Disvāpi" means even upon seeing that bhikkhu.
"Tena bhikkhunā" refers to the bhikkhu who shows what is censurable; the connection is that he must ask for forgiveness. "Vihāre yeva" means among the bhikkhus.
"In the very monastery. "By that bhikkhu" refers to the bhikkhu who is to approach; "should speak" is the connection [of the sentence].
"From there" means from the time when he is to be spoken to. "He" refers to the bhikkhu who is showing what is to be disparaged. "In this" refers to the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka.
"In the Analysis of Formal Acts" (Kammavibhaṅga) refers to the section analyzing formal acts at the conclusion of the Parivāra.
“Shining forth” (*obhāsanti*) means they speak with what is base; showing this, he said, “they shine forth with what is not the true Dhamma” (*asaddhammena obhāsanti*).

Regarding “associating with bhikkhunīs,” he said, “with men by means of what is not the true Dhamma” (*purise asaddhammena*), showing here the object (*kamma*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). Here, by the word “men” (*purise*), he shows the object;
by the phrase “by means of what is not the true Dhamma” (*asaddhammena*), he shows the instrument. Regarding “entering the monastery” (*vihārappavesane*)...

Regarding "the entering of the monks' dwelling": in the phrase "to set aside the exhortation," he says "not [entering] the nuns' quarters" and so forth, showing the manner in which the exhortation is set aside. "For the sake of the exhortation" means for the purpose of receiving the exhortation.

"Do not do it" means you should not do it. 416. Regarding "young girls of householders": the construction is that they bind those who are young girls living as householders, as it were. "With a thick cloth-band" means...

“With a thick, woven cloth. Regarding the term *ekapariyaka*: he says “that which encircles once” (*ekavāraṃ parikkhipanakaṃ*) in order to show that a waist-band (*kāyabandhana*) made by wrapping [the cloth] around the waist once is called *ekapariyaka*.
In that context, “encircling” (*parikkhipana*) means fit for encircling the waist.
Regarding the phrase *vilīvena*, he says “with smooth betel-nuts” (*saṇhehi vilīvehi*), because here a singular number is used in the sense of the plural.
By the word “*katapaṭṭenā*” (with a made band), he indicates that there is a textual supplement (*pāṭhasesa*) in the Pāli, namely “*katenā*” (made).

“*Setavatthapaṭṭenā*” means with a band made of white cloth. “*Kataveṇiyā*” means by a made braid. By this, the etymological meaning of the term *dussaveṇī* is shown as “a braid made from this cloth.”

[The text] shows this. The same method applies to the preceding and following sections as well. *Coḷakāsāva* means that because the cloth itself is dyed with a decoction (*kasāva*), it is called "coḷakāsāva.
*Aṭṭhillena* means by a bone that has been gnawed by a rat. By the phrase "on the ankle-bone of the leg," [the author] shows the connection to the bone.
Regarding the expression "having the hand pounded," here "hand" refers specifically to the forearm, not from the elbow downwards.
Pointing [to it], he said, "the upper arm. "The back of the hand" means the surface of the hand. "The back of the foot" means the surface of the foot. 417.
"In the same manner as stated" means in the same manner as stated regarding the smearing of the faces of the group-of-six monks (Chabbaggiyas), and so forth. "On a limb" means on a part of the body.
"On a cheek" means on the region of the jaw. "Standing in light": here, "sāloka" means that where there is light (*āloka*) present, it is "sāloka."
Having done so, the door must be taken; therefore it is said, “having opened the door. “Discharging” means they ordain them. “Setting up a slaughterhouse”:
here the word *sūna* is a synonym for meat, thus he says, “selling meat.
“By him” means by the slave. This word is the indirect object (*kāritakamma*) of the verb “causing to do. By the phrase “both raw and cooked,”...
The phrase *haritakapakkikaṃ* indicates a compound expression (*dvandavākya*). Therein, *haritakaṃ* means green leaves;
*pakkam* means boiled leaves.
"Only as stated" means exactly as stated in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.
419. *Pāḷimuttakavinicchayo* means a decision (*vinicchaya*) that is separate from the decisions stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
Expounding upon this "decision separate from the Canon," he said, "If indeed," and so forth. The connection is: "anyone who dies says. *Mamaccayena* means "after my passing.
*Aññassa* means "to someone other than those [monks] mentioned, such as the preceptor (*upajjhāya*) and others. *Tesam* refers to the preceptor and the others.

"It does not exist" means it is not a requisite. "Indeed" (hi) means truly, or because. "Granting of an offense" (accayadāna) means a gift given with the thought, "Let there be [atonement] for the offense.
"It does not take root" means that the granting of an offense for anyone—whether one of the five classes of legitimate members, a renunciant, or a householder—does not take root among them;
the intention is that it takes root only in the Saṅgha. However, for householders...

The connection is with the phrase "the giving away of what has been transgressed. Regarding the word "grows" (*ruhati*): the meaning is that the giving away of what has been transgressed by anyone—whether a householder or one who has gone forth, whether a layman or another—takes root for them;
it becomes their own property. 420. Regarding the term *purāṇamallī*:
here, *mallī* is the wife of a wrestler (*malla*); thus, he shows that *purāṇamallī* means "an old wrestler's wife."
He said, “In former times,” and so forth. By the phrase “at the time of being a householder,” he shows the actual form of the suffix *ṇa* in the word “purāṇe.
“Of the wrestler” means of the fist-wrestler. Regarding the term “male organ,” since the word *byañjana* here is a synonym for *nimitta* (sign), he says “the male sign. “Mind” means a mind of lust.
421. *Yaṃ vatthu* means that which is the object; *aggaṃ* means the first portion. *Asappāyaṃ* means unsuitable for oneself.

*Hiyyo* means on the immediately preceding day. *Aññasmiṃ* means other than [those] bhikkhunīs. The word *bhikkhunīhi* is the causal object (*kāritakamma*) with respect to the word *paṭiggāhāpetvā*. *Hi* means truly, or because. 426.
By the phrase *“bhojanakālaṃ”* (at the time of eating), he indicates the specific time in relation to the expression *“kālaṃ vītināmesuṃ”* (they let the time pass).
"Pure" refers to the beginning [of the list]. "Tāsanti" refers to eight bhikkhunīs. "Abbhintarimā" means those included within [the group].
"Aññā" means other than the eight bhikkhunīs. The connection is: "she is junior.
By the phrase "except for the dining hall," it is implied that elsewhere in all cases one must not be bypassed according to seniority; here, the word "other" (añña) functions as the ablative.

It shows [the meaning]. In the phrase "in another" (*aññasmiṃ*), the locative suffix *-smin* indicates the meaning of the suffix *-ttha*. By the expression "in the section on the distribution of the four requisites" (*catupaccayabhājanīyaṭṭhāne*), it shows the actual form.
Regarding the statement "one may confer full ordination even by means of a messenger," one might ask: "Is full ordination ever permissible entirely by means of a messenger? To this he says:
“By messenger... it is permissible. This connects with the phrase “by whatever obstacle”; the intention is that it is not permissible when no obstacle exists.
“At the conclusion of the formal act (kammavācā), she is indeed fully ordained (upasampannā)” is the connection. “Right at that moment” means precisely at the instant of full ordination.
Regarding the phrase “even the construction work,” the word “even” (pi) refers to the storage shed (udosita) and the dwelling (upassaya).

432. *Tassa* means "of that woman. Regarding the phrase "until that boy reaches the age of discretion," one might ask how the state of being discreet (*viññubhāva*) is to be understood here; thus he says, "until [he is able] to eat," and so forth.
In the expression *ṭhapetvā sāgāraṃ*, the letter *sa-* functions as the word *saha-*, and *agāraṃ* is shown to mean "a bedchamber";
thus he says, "except for the mere extent of a bed within the house. Just as one should behave toward another man, so...

The construction is "it is thus. By the word "aññasmiṃ" (in another), the substitution of *ekāra* for the locative case-ending (*smiṃ*) of the pronoun "añña" in the phrase "aññe purise" from the Pāḷi text is demonstrated;
and by that demonstration, it shows that the prohibition of the *ekāra* substitution for the locative case-ending of pronouns in the Kaccāyana grammar (Kaccāyana Sutta 110) is not universal.
434. The connection is that this [passage] shows by means of the words, “Because she has gone away.
By the word “since,” it shows the causal sense of the pronoun *yaṃ* in the phrase *yadeva*. The connection is: “She was dressed in white garments.
By the phrase “for that very reason,” it shows precisely the causal sense of the word *tadeva*. By the phrase “not by the renunciation of the training,” it shows the fruit of that meaning.
[The text] shows this. "She does not receive ordination again" means that the nun who has left the order does not receive ordination again.
"She does not receive even the going-forth" means that a nun who has transferred to another religious sect does not receive even the going-forth, let alone ordination.
"Massaging the feet" means massaging the feet of the nuns. "Hair" refers to the hair of the nuns. "Therein" [means...]
Regarding the statement, “being scrupulous, they do not consent,” the connection is with the words, “some teachers say. The construction is, “they become impassioned.
“In this case” refers to the salutation and so forth of men. “This” refers to the salutation and so forth of men;

it is the object mentioned by the word “permitted” (*anuññāta*) that becomes the agent mentioned by the word “is allowable” (*vaṭṭati*). Alternatively, this refers to what is specifically permitted for men.

The construction is: "Saluting and so forth are permissible. For this being the case, the phrase "specifically permitted" (*odissa anuññāta*) is a qualification included for the sake of providing a reason;

the intended meaning is that it is permissible because it has been specifically permitted. "That" refers to the statement spoken in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means "truly" or "because. 435.
Regarding the phrase "sitting cross-legged," he says "having folded the legs crosswise" (*pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā*), while thereby rejecting the "seat-cross" (*āsana-pallaṅka*).
“...sitting down. In that context, *ābhujitvā* means having bound together. *Kūpa* means a cesspool. *Upari* means above the cesspool.
By the phrase “it is visible in all directions,” he shows that while it is indeed concealed, it is not covered over from above.
436. *Kuṇḍaka* means husks. *Ettha* refers to the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka.
11. The Pañcasatikakkhandhaka. 1.
Discussion on the Minor and Lesser Training Rules (Khuddānukhuddakasikkhāpada).
441. In the *Pañcasatikakkhandhaka*, the connection is that [the rule] beginning with “four...

pe ... minor rules” was stated. “By way of method” (*pariyāyena*) means by way of cause. Regarding the term *dhūmakālika*: here, the time of smoke is *dhūmakāla*; the meaning is “the time when smoke has arisen.
That which has this [time] as its limit is *dhūmakālika*, referring to the formulation of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). Thus, showing this meaning, he said “as long as,” and so forth.
443. This refers to the inquiry: “But, venerable sir, what are the minor and lesser training rules?
By the word “by you,” the sense of the pronoun *te* (plural) as “to you” or “your” is excluded here. “Offense” (*āpatti*) means an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
“Indeed” (*hi*) means truly, or because. “They” (*te*) refers to the elders. “The Saṅgha... does not abolish” and so forth.
The construction is: "this statement was recited. And the connection is: "the words 'Friend, confess that dukkaṭa offense' were also spoken.
But as for "the Elder," the connection is: "the Elder Ānanda said. Therein, "in the inquiry" refers to the asking. "In what manner" means by which mode.
"In four instances" refers to such passages as: "He sewed the Blessed One’s rainy-season robe after having stepped on it," and so forth.
In four places. "Therein" refers to the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka.
Thus ends the commentary on the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka.
12. The Sattasatika-kkhandhaka.
447. Regarding the phrase “they increase the *kaṭasi*” in the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka*:
here, showing that the word *kaṭasi* denotes a cemetery ground (*susāna-bhūmi*), he says, “they increase the ground by repeatedly depositing corpses (*kaḷevara*). In this context, *kaḷevara* means...
*Dehaṃ*. For it is called *kaḷevara* because it is gathered together (*sampiṇḍetvā*) and desired (*variya*) as a collection of parts and limbs (*avayave*).
Thus, the construction is: "While increasing the terrible cemetery, they take up renewed existence. 454.

Regarding the phrase "A wicked deed has been done by us, friends," he said, "Friends, a wicked deed has been done by us," showing that here the word *no* functions like the word *amha* (we) and serves as the genitive agent.
455. By the phrase “a word of endearment,” it is shown that in the expression “By which dwelling on the plane (bhūmi-vihāra) have you been established?
the word *bhūmi* is a conventional term (*ruḷhīsadda*) signifying a word of endearment. By the word “addresses,” it is shown that this is a form of address; the meaning is “Friend, O Plane!

The “raft-dwelling” (*kullavihāra*) is the dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*); and because that is associated with the first three jhānas, it is a “shallow dwelling,” as expressed by the phrase “by a shallow dwelling.”
457. "In Sāvatthī" means in the city of Sāvatthī. "In the Suttavibhaṅga" refers to the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanīya*).
Expanding upon the fact that it is prohibited, he said, "For there," and so forth. "There" refers to the Suttavibhaṅga; the connection is "it is prohibited.
"There" refers to the statement beginning with "if one who has stored up [food] perceives it as not having been stored up. Some teachers think thus.
The construction [of the sentence]. He said, “But whichever monk...,” etc., in order to explain what they think.

The construction is: “even that non-salted food which is called ‘raw meat’ (āmisa). “By that” means by the salt previously accepted. “That” refers to the raw meat. “Accepted on that very day” means accepted on that specific day.
“Therefore” means because it was accepted on that very day; therefore. “Of one who speaks” means of one who is speaking.

The connection is with the words "by the word of the Blessed One. Here, the construction is: "In the case of consuming food that lacks salt or is not sought after, they think there must be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"They" refers to certain teachers. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even by an offense of wrong-doing," he shows that it is even more so for an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "Here" refers to among those things to be used for life and those to be used for a limited time. That which is to be used for life was not received on that very day.

The construction is: "that which was received on that very day is indeed 'yāvakālika' (to be used within the same day). And the connection is: "and that which was received on that very day is 'yāvakālika'. The construction is:
"if you consider that to be an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). "Mixed with what is for life" means mixed with that which is for life, namely salt.
"Mere curry" means it is not permitted at an improper time; thus it is called "mere curry."

Regarding the word "here" (*ettha*): in the statement beginning with "Monks, by means of what is for the time being" (*yāvakālikena*), the construction is that [food] received on that very day is "for life" (*yāvajīvika*).

That which has the same destination as that which is for the time being is "of the same destination as what is for the time being" (*yāvakālikagatika*). Therefore, there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this is the connection. Regarding "here":
it refers to the consumption of food using salt received previously. [In the case of] what was received on that very day together with what is for the time being...

The construction is: "mixed with [other] flavors" and "lasting for as long as life. The construction is: "that aforementioned [food] lasting for as long as life is the very cause for the offense of expiation regarding eating at the wrong time.
The word "thus" (*evaṃ*) means "in that manner"; the connection is: "even though received today, it is [still considered] lasting for as long as life. The construction is:

"with what was received on another day and is [only] suitable for the proper time. The word "that" refers to the food suitable for the proper time that has been mixed with what lasts for as long as life.

The connection is with the words "even if not knowing. "This" refers to the aforementioned *yāvakālika* (food that may be eaten at the proper time). "From that" means from the *pācittiya* offense regarding the eating of stored food (*sannidhi-bhojana*).
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. The construction is: "In the Sutta-vibhaṅga of Sāvatthī"—this exposition is pure.
The connection is with the words "in Rājagaha, in the Uposatha-saṃyutta"—this statement was spoken. "In the Uposatha-saṃyutta."
In connection with the Uposatha, [it is said] in the Uposatha-kkhandhaka. To the question "With reference to what was this said?", he replies:
"It was said with reference to this: 'Monks, [you should not... ... 'a dukkaṭa offense. The meaning of *atisāreti* is "to proceed by transgressing" or "to go beyond.
And here, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). The connection is: "This is what was stated in the Campeyyaka section of the Vinaya-vatthu."
By the phrase “it is found in the Campeyyakkhandhaka,” he shows the meaning of the word *campeyyaka* as that which has come down in the Campeyya [chapter].
*Dhammikaṃ* means that which proceeds according to reality. For the connection is: “because it is found in the Suttavibhaṅga. *Dasāyeva* means “only on the border-cloth”;
this is the locative case used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra*). *Vidatthimattā* means having the measure of a span (*vidatthi*). *Dasāya vināti* means “he weaves the border-cloth.”
"Having avoided. The connection is as follows: for one who makes that measure—namely, the measure consisting of three spans (vidatthi)—the aforementioned *pācittiya* offense is incurred.
The formulation "for one who exceeds that, there is a *pācittiya* involving cutting" is indeed found in the text.
"In all cases" means throughout the entire Sattasatika-kkhandhaka.
Thus ends the Concordance for the Commentary on the Section of Seven Hundred [Khandhakas] within the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya.
"Composed of two sections" means it is comprised of two sections by way of the Mahāvagga and the Cūḷavagga.
"Divided into twenty-two parts" means there are ten in the Mahāvagga and twelve in the Cūḷavagga; thus, there are twenty-two types.
"The abandoner of the suffering of the five aggregates" refers to the Blessed One, whose nature is to abandon the suffering known as the five aggregates. "Even hope" means even desire.
Now, this is the application here: May the noble hopes of living beings likewise be fulfilled,

just as this commentary on those Khandhakas— which were spoken by the Blessed One and comprise twenty-two divisions arranged in two sections within the teaching of the Blessed One who has abandoned the suffering of the five aggregates— has been accomplished without obstacle.
Thus ends the *Yojanā* (Exegesis) on the commentary (*Saṃvaṇṇanā*) of the *Cūḷavagga* within the *Samantapāsādikā*,
the commentary on the Vinaya.
By me, who am marked with the name Jādila,
the method of interpretation for many [passages] of the Cūḷavagga and the Khandhaka has been completed.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Having thus applied the method of arrangement for the *Pācittiya* and so forth, for the *Parivāra*,
for the *Vagga*, and for the *Cūḷavagga* and *Khandhaka*, one should proceed with this system of arrangement.
Now, for the sake of the commentary, I shall provide the method of exposition for the sections.
This is the exposition of the section on the formal rules (paññattivāra) within the sixteen great sections.
Having thus provided the commentary on the twenty-two Khandhakas, this teacher,
now wishing to provide the commentary on the Vinaya that has been classified as the "Parivāra," first spoke the words beginning with "of the pure Parivāra" (*visuddhaparivārassa*),
desiring to make a formal promise by way of showing the connection (*anusandhi*). Therein, "of the pure Parivāra" (*visuddhaparivārassa*) means of the pure...
The connection is with the Blessed One who is surrounded by the fourfold assembly, or rather, who is endowed with a retinue designated as the "pure fourfold assembly.
For when the retinue is pure, the Blessed One—whether surrounded by that retinue or being that very retinue—is said to be "pure" himself.
By this, [the purity] of the "retinue" is indicated, which is included among the qualities to be taught for the one being praised.
Thus, praise is offered to the Blessed One, who is the very embodiment of the teaching (*dhamma*).

By the phrase "possessing a body consisting of the aggregates of the Dhamma" (*dhammakkhandhasarīra*), it is meant that he is endowed with a body comprised of the aggregates of the Dhamma, such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth;

by this, praise is offered to the Blessed One in accordance with the *Khandhakas* that have been described. For this is the natural way of teachers: namely, to praise [the teacher] in accordance with the Dhamma that is to be taught.
The praise of the Teacher. "Immediately" means at the immediately following time.

"This" refers to the Vinaya. "Appeared previously" means that which appeared in the Vibhaṅgas and Khandhakas previously taught. "Method" refers to the entire method known as the determination of the meaning of words.
"Having abandoned" means having relinquished. "Commentary on the non-obvious meanings" means the commentary on the meanings of those words whose meanings are not obvious.

This is the application here: In the dispensation of the Blessed One, whose body is the mass of Dhamma and who is surrounded by a pure retinue, there is a Vinaya collection known as the *Parivāra* that was compiled immediately after the *Khandhakas*.
Having set aside the method of that previously established Vinaya, we shall now provide an exposition of its meaning, which has not yet been fully elucidated.

1. Regarding the phrase *tattha tattha*: it refers to that portion of the Vinaya known as the Parivāra, which was mentioned as being subject to commentary in the statement, "I shall provide a commentary on its meaning not yet explained. *Saṅkhepattho* means the summarized meaning.

In the expression *yaṃ tena*, the author says "yo so" to show that the pronoun *ta-* functions here as an indefinite reference. In that context, *yo* is the indefinite reference, and for it [the author uses] "tenā."
The restriction (niyamana) is to be understood. The word *so* (he) is a poetic ornament (*padālaṅkāra*).
For, between two pronouns, the former is generally the principal element, while the latter is a verbal ornament (*vacanālaṅkāra*). Thus, the connection is: "He, the Blessed One, who laid it down.
Regarding "for the sake of long duration": it means for the purpose of its remaining for a long time, namely five thousand years; and the connection is with both "being requested" and "laid down."
The connection is: "requested by the General of the Dhamma. The construction is: "having been requested, he laid it down.
The connection is: "laid down by that Blessed One. By saying "by one who knows and sees," he indicates the object of the two words;
thus he says, "of this and that," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "at the time of laying down," he shows the object of the word "by one who knows."
“‘For ten purposes’—by this, the object (*kamma*) of the word ‘seeing’ (*passatā*) is shown.
Having thus demonstrated the method of construction by showing the object, he now says “Moreover,” etc., in order to show another method of construction by demonstrating the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Because the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) must be mentioned separately [from the others] in the phrase beginning with “by means of past lives, etc. (*pubbenivāsādīhi*), [the word *ādi* is used].
The supernormal powers of the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividha*), the divine ear (*dibbasota*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittavijānana*) are to be understood [here].
By these terms, [the text] shows that the two phrases "knowing" (*jānatā*) and "seeing" (*passatā*) function as the instruments for the five mundane higher knowledges (*lokika-abhiññā*).

"By the three true knowledges" (*tīhi vijjāhi*) means by the three true knowledges consisting of the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*). Alternatively, "by the six higher knowledges" (*chahi vā pana abhiññāhi*)...
Together with the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa), [he was endowed] with the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) reckoned as the five mundane higher knowledges.

"In all places" means in all three times and regarding all five knowable phenomena. "With the universal eye" means with the universal eye reckoned as unobstructed omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
"With wisdom" means with the wisdom of omniscience. "Through walls and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," mountains and other such obstacles are included.

He gathers [them]. "With the fleshly eye" means with the physical eye (*pasādacakkhu*). "With the wisdom of penetration" means with the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*). "With the wisdom of teaching" means with the wisdom of omniscience (*sabbaññutapaññā*).
For in actual meaning, the wisdom of teaching is indeed the wisdom of omniscience. Therefore it was said:
"By the power of that wisdom, he set forth the path of the Abhidhamma discourse for the gods. By these words, according to the various states (*avatthāvasena*)...

This shows the possibility of the formation of each of the two words individually. "By the Arahant" means: because he has slain (hatatta) enemies (arīnaṃ) and spokes (arānaṃ), and because he is worthy (arahatta) of requisites and so forth, he is the Arahant.

"By the Fully Enlightened One" means: because he has awakened (buddhattā) correctly (sammā) and personally (sāmaṃ) to all phenomena (dhammānaṃ), he is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha); the connection is with "by that Blessed One. "By whom was it brought?"—that is the first [question].
The construction is: "By whom was the *pārājika* brought forth?"—this is the meaning in brief. 2.
Regarding the response to the question, however, the meaning should be understood as follows: the construction is that the phrase "that which by him... [etc.
...is a *pārājika*" is merely a citation (*paccuddharaṇamatta*), not a demonstration of the meaning; it is merely a restatement (*patiuddharaṇamatta*), not an exposition of the sense.
The meaning [is as follows]. "In this" means in these locations. "One proclamation" (paññatti) means the first proclamation.
"Subsequent proclamations" (anupaññattiyo) means the proclamations established later.
"To this extent" means that it has been answered by the mere statement: "one proclamation and two subsequent proclamations."
The connection is with the word "exist. The connection is with the phrase "they ask the third [question]. To the question "Why is there no 'unarisen designation' (anuppanna-paññatti) in that case?
he says, "For this... and so forth. There, the construction is: because it does not exist elsewhere, therefore it does not exist.
By the phrase "designated when the fault has not yet arisen," the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) of "unarisen designation" is given as: it is to be designated when the fault has not yet arisen.
[The text] shows this. This is an *anuppanna-paññatti* (a rule concerning what has not yet arisen). Therefore (*tasmā*) means because it does not exist elsewhere; therefore.

Regarding the term *sabbatthapaññatti*, he says “in the Middle Country and so forth,” demonstrating that it is an *aluttasamāsa* (compound without elision) meaning “a designation in every place (*sabbattha*).
By the phrase “both in the Middle Country and in the bordering regions,” [he explains] the word “everywhere (*sabbatthā*).”

It shows the literal form (*sarūpa*). Having set aside the designation by partial application (*padesapaññatti*), he says “with the holder of the Vinaya as the fifth,” and so forth, showing the designation by universal application (*sabbatthapaññatti*) through the method of elimination (*pārisesanaya*).
Therein, “with the holder of the Vinaya as the fifth” means with the teacher of the proclamation (*anussāvanācariya*) as the fifth.
“In this very place” means in the Middle Country itself. “By these” means by the four training rules (*sikkhāpada*). “The remaining ones” means those remaining after the four training rules.

Regarding the term "common designation" (*sādhāraṇapaññatti*): here, "common" refers specifically to those [rules] belonging to both monks and nuns; thus he says, "of both monks and nuns. As for the phrase "but this":
it refers to the first *pārājika*, and the connection is with the word "designated" (*paññatta*).

"Merely a discourse on what has been settled" (*vinītakathāmattameva*) means merely a discourse that elucidates the matter already settled. "Of them" (*tāsaṃ*) refers to the nuns. "Merely the phrasing" (*byañjanamattameva*) refers to the word "common" (*sādhāraṇā*).
And the terms “both” (*ubhato*) and so forth are merely a matter of phrasing. “In this” refers to the words *sādhāraṇapaññatti* (common designation) and *ubhatopaññatti* (designation of both).
By the phrase “entered into the introduction” (*nidāne anupaviṭṭhaṃ*), he shows that the compound *nidānogadhaṃ* is a locative tatpuruṣa and that the word *ogadha* has the meaning of “entered into.
It is called *ogadha* because it remains and stays having sunk down (*ogāḷho*). [Objection: Is it not the case that in *nidānogadhe*...
If [the first recitation] were present, it should have been said, "by the first recitation"; why then was it said, "by the second recitation"?

To this he says, "because it is included in the introduction" (*nidānogadha*). The construction is: "even though it is included in the introduction" (*nidānapariyāpannaṃ samānaṃ pi*). The particle *pi* has the sense of censure;
it shows that [this fault] applies even more so when it is included in the second recitation. Expanding upon the expression "of the failure of virtue, etc. (*sīlavipatti-ādīnaṃ*):
He said, "The first," and so forth.
"By the two-fold" means by that which is called the two-fold aggregate of body and mind. But surely, since it was stated "by a single origination," one should have said "from the body alone";
why then was it said, "it originates from both body and mind"?
He said, “In this case,” and so forth. “In this” refers to the statement, “by a single origin. “Mind” means the mind of sexual intercourse.
“You have fallen into an offense” is to be construed as “you have fallen into [an offense]. “Yes, I have fallen” is to be construed as “yes, I have indeed fallen.
“At that very moment” means at the very instant of his admission. “That person” refers to that individual who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense.

“On account of that” (*tappaccayā*) means on account of one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. The construction is: “But as for the statement ‘It is not settled by which means of settling’ (*na katamena samathena sammati*), it was spoken.
“That” (*taṃ*) refers to the statement; the connection is that “it was spoken. The construction is:
“The stated *mātikā* is the *paññatti*; the *paññatti* designated as the stated *mātikā* is called the *vinaya*. *Mātikā*.
For it is so called "description" (*paññatti*) because it is made known (*paññapīyati*), established in brief, or because it makes known the mode [of being].
By the phrase "it is called the word-commentary," he shows that it is a "classification" (*vibhatti*) because by means of it there is a detailed distribution (*bhājiyati*).
"Transgression" (*vītikkama*) refers to transgression of body and speech; for it is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) because it does not restrain or close off body and speech.
It is said. Regarding the phrase "for whom it proceeds," in order to show the agent of the action of proceeding (*vattati*), he says:
"the Vinaya Piṭaka and the commentary. "Familiar" means committed to memory. "They"—referring to those persons; the connection is with the verb "they bear" (*dhārenti*).

"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "Of this"—of the first *pārājika*. Regarding the question "by whom was it brought? (*kenābhataṃ*), here the verbal root *bhṛ* (to bear) has the senses of maintaining and nourishing.
In order to show the meaning of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) [as found] in the list of verbal roots (Pāṇini 108), he says, "By whom was it brought?

With the words "Brought by tradition" (*paramparāya ānīta*), he shows that the term *paramparābhatam* is a compound in the instrumental case. Alternatively, he shows that this is a sentence formed by the elision of the letter *y*, corresponding to the question "By whom was it brought? (*kenābhata*).
Regarding the verses beginning with "Upāli, Dāsaka, and so forth," he says "Now," etc., to explain for what purpose and by whom they were composed.
"That" refers to each subsequent [verse]. "Therein" means within those verses. "This" refers to the statement.
"By this method" means by this method as stated in the question and answer concerning the first *pārājika*.

Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section on the formal rule (*paññattivāra*) in the *Mahāvibhaṅga*. 157. Regarding the commentary on the section on the offenses already committed (*katāpattivāra*) and so forth:

the phrase “*iti*” means from the section on the formal rule; the application is that the seven subsequent sections stated thereafter are indeed of plain meaning (*uttānattha*). The phrase “the section on the offenses already committed” (*katāpattivāra*)...
The section characterized by the term “katāpatti” (committed offense) is the first. This same method applies to the remaining sections as well.

“Tadanantara” means stated immediately after those seven sections. Regarding “samuccayavāra”: it is called *samuccaya* because therein offenses, failures, and so forth (*āpatti-vipatti-ādi*) are gathered together (*saṃ*) and combined (*uciyaṃti sampiṇḍiyaṃti*);
that very section is the *samuccayavāra*.
188. "Therefore, by those eight sections" is the connection with the phrase "stated subsequently.

The construction is: "one section on formal designation (paññatti) is stated by way of condition (paccaya). "By way of condition" means by means of the word *paccaya*. "Of that" refers to the condition (*paccaya*).
