"Those too" refers to the eight sections. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion. "Therefore, from the Mahāvibhaṅga, they have come subsequently" is the connection.
Thus, the construction is: "these thirty-two sections. *Hi* means "truly" or "because.
*Ettha* refers to within these thirty-two sections. 257.
Regarding the commentary on the section on origins (*samuṭṭhāna-sīsa*) immediately following that: the meaning is that it is stated immediately after those thirty-two sections.
The construction is: "should be known. "Decided as 'not-self'" means determined precisely as being not-self.
By this, [the author] shows that the root *ci* has the sense of "determination" in the phrase "by the determination that it is not-self.

Regarding the phrase "by way of the aspect of impermanence, etc.," in the expression "of similar phenomena" (*sabhāgadhammānaṃ*), those which have a portion (*bhāga*) in common with the aspects of impermanence and so forth are "similar" (*sabhāgā*); those very phenomena are "similar phenomena" (*sabhāgadhammā*).

It shows the meaning of the word. "Even a mere name" means even a mere name such as "impermanent" and so forth. By the word "even," it shows that, let alone a derivative name (nāmika) based on the nature of impermanence and so on, [the thing itself] is not perceived;
"is not perceived" means it does not appear. By this, he shows that in the phrase "it is not known," the root *ñā* has the sense of appearing.
Regarding "the abandoning of suffering," he shows that "one abandons suffering" is what is meant by "the abandoning of suffering."
He said, “The destroyer of suffering. It is called the destroyer of suffering (*dukkhaghātana*) because it destroys suffering; this refers to the True Dharma (*saddhamma*).

Regarding the phrase “the Khandhakas and the Mātikā,” although one should have said “the Khandhakas and the Mātikā,” the reading exists in the short vowel form for the sake of ease of pronunciation; thus he said, “the Khandhakas and the Mātikā.
Regarding the phrase “the origin is determined,” here, although one should have said “the origin is determined (*niyatakata*),” [it is stated as such].
In expressions such as “parosahassa,” the term is stated as “samuṭṭhānaniyatokataṃ” by way of the augment *o*;
thus he says, “the origin has been made fixed. By this means: by the reading “the origin has been made fixed.
“To be understood” (*paccetabbo*) means it is to be approached; the meaning is that it is to be known face-to-face. “By others”: by other training rules than the three training rules.
“In that regard” (*tattha*) refers to the words concerning the cause of schism (*sambheda-nidāna*). The connection is: “it is to be understood by means of the word ‘schism’.

“Indeed” (*hi*) means truly. The connection is: “having set aside those three training rules” (*sikkhāpada*). “Designated as the place of promulgation” (*paññatti-desasaṅkhātaṃ*) means designated as the place that serves as the locus of the promulgation (*paññatti-ṭṭhāna*).
By the phrase “these three,” he shows the agent of the action expressed by “are seen. By the phrase “are being manifested” (*paññāyanti*), [he shows the object].
It shows the meaning of "digging" in the earth element. "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the three categories known as the determination of origin, the non-distinction, and the cause;
this is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "But the other," however, means something different from the determination of origin, the non-distinction, and the cause.
"Āḷavī" means in Āḷavī. Regarding the phrase "among the Sakyas and the Bhaggas," it is expressed in the plural because these are names of countries (*janapada*).
The construction is: "the training rule which is prescribed in the two Vibhaṅgas, they recite.
By the word "vibhaṅgesu," it is shown that there is an elision of the letter *s* in the word *vibhaṅge*. "Of that" refers to the training rule.
"According to the method" means in accordance with the proper logic. "That" refers to the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*). "Listen from me" means listen from my presence. "Thus" (*iti*) has this meaning.
*Kathina* refers to the origin of the first *kathina*. *Together with what is not permitted* means together with that which originates from what is not permitted.
Regarding the phrase *sadisā idha dissare*, the word *idha* (here) pertains to the scope of both Vibhaṅgas by way of meaning and context;
thus he says, "here in the Ubhatovibhaṅga. By the word *sadisāni* (similar), [it is shown that] in the term *sadisā*, there is a substitution of the vowel *ā* for the syllable *nikāra*.
It is shown [as follows]: by the word "dissanti" (they appear), the substitution of the letter *e* for the suffix *anti* is shown here (in the Niruttidīpaniya, sutta 570).
The section on the Origin:
An Exposition of the First Pārājika Origin.
258. To the question, "For what purpose was the statement beginning with 'sexual intercourse' and 'emission of semen' spoken?", he says, "Now," and so forth.
Therein, "there" refers to the statements beginning with "sexual intercourse" and "emission of semen. "The head of the origins" means the head among the origins, or the primary origin among origins.
"The remaining ones" refers to the seventy-five training rules (sikkhāpada) remaining after the first pārājika. "By that" means by the first pārājika.
Explaining the statement beginning with “Contact with semen,” he says “Therein,” and so forth. “Therein” means in the statement beginning with “Contact with semen.
“At the end of the Khuddaka commentary” means at the conclusion of the *Khuddakaaṭṭhakathā*.

“Reversal of gender” means a change in grammatical gender. Regarding the phrase “produced by body and mind,” when it is said that they “occur in the body and mind,” they are called “productions”; thus he says, “produced by body and consciousness (citta) were made.”
Commentary on the Origin of the Second Pārājika: 259.
The connection is that this origin constitutes a single heading for the origins.

By the term "taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*), it is shown that here, within a collective name, a part is being used as a designation for the whole. "The rest" refers to the sixty-nine rules remaining after the second pārājika.
The training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "By that" means by the second *pārājika*. "Therein" refers to the statement beginning with "a human form" (*viggahuttarī*) and so forth.

To show the meaning alone, without paying attention to the phrasing of the words "human form" and so on, it is said: "the training rules regarding the human form and the superhuman state" (*manussaviggahauttarimanussadhamma-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the phrase "the second [offense] is undetermined" (*aniyatā dutiyikā*), this is stated in the Canon (*pāḷi*) in the feminine gender because it refers to the offense; however, in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is...
However, with reference to the training rule (sikkhāpada), it is stated as "the second" by way of the neuter gender.

Regarding the phrase "the originations (samuṭṭhāna) are made into triads," he says "the originations are made into triads" to show that where one should have said "originated by triads" (tikasamuṭṭhānā), the word order has been reversed and the letter *k* has been lengthened to produce the form "samuṭṭhānā tikā.
Commentary on the Origin of the Act of Matchmaking (sañcaritta).

260. Regarding the term “sañcarī,” this refers first to the offense of matchmaking (*sañcaritta*), which is the primary head of offenses arising from a single source; the remaining [offenses] are similar to it.

He says, “In the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated that they ‘neglect’ (*riñcantī*) and ‘recite’ (*uddesanti*),” having characterized the training rule concerning the washing of wool by means of the word “neglecting” as it appears there.

Furthermore, the construction is as follows: the triad of training rules stated as “up to the door-bolt for the purpose of setting the bolt,” “one should give a robe to an unrelated nun,” and “one should sew a robe.”
The connection is that the statement “and with a robe for a recluse” was thus spoken. The connection is that this refers to the statement “one should give a robe for a recluse.
261. Commentary on the Origin of the Formal Rebuke (Samanubhāsanā):
This formal rebuke is one head of origin; the remaining [offenses] are similar to it.
Commentary on the Origin of the Kathina: 262.
"Ubbhataṃ" (the robe has been hauled out) is one head of origin for the Kathina-offense; the remaining [heads] are similar to it.
"Saddhiṃ āvasathena" means together with the word "āvasatha" (lodging).
Commentary on the Origin of the Eḷakaloma: 263.
“Eḷakaloma” (sheep’s wool) is the name of one head of origin (*samuṭṭhāna-sīsa*). “Iti” means from what has been stated above.
“Pāḷi” refers to the matrix-text (*mātikā-pāḷi*). “Virajjhitvā” means having failed [to observe] the proper sequence. “Yathā” means in whatever manner. The word “pana” (but/however) [is used here].

"For the purpose of assistance. However, even though they write [it], the construction is "but nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "In this way" (*evaṃ*) means by that manner. "The sequence of the meaning" (*atthānukkamo*) means the progression of the meaning.

The connection is that the statement "or by a residence without monks" has been spoken. The connection is that it refers to the statement "one should spend the rains residence in a residence without monks.
The connection is that they have been stated by the words beginning with "a bhikkhunī," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the reading "a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) and a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*) [are included] with a female householder (*gihinī*)" is comprised.
264. Regarding the explanation of the origin of the recitation of the words (*padasodhamma*):
"Word" (*pada*)—this is one head of origins (*samuṭṭhānasīsa*) known as the origin of the recitation of the words; the others [arise] by means of it.
“Similar. The connection is that this statement, “And likewise by one who has set,” has been spoken.

The connection is that this refers to the statement, “One should exhort when the sun has set. The same method applies here as well for the phrase, “And [it was] said with reference to the lack of opportunity...”.
Commentary on the Origin of the Offense (Addhānasamuṭṭhānavaṇṇanā).
265. "On a journey" (*addhāna*): this is one head of origins known as the origin by way of a journey; the remaining [cases] are similar to it. 266.
"A caravan of thieves" (*theyyasattha*):
this is one head of origins known as the origin by way of a caravan of thieves; the remaining [cases]...
"They are similar to that. The construction is: "The statement 'by the arrangement [of the offense], it is the seventh' has been spoken.
"Immediately after that" means immediately after that training rule; the connection is with the word "arrived.
Commentary on the Origin Arising from Teaching the Dhamma.

267. Regarding the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the teaching on the Dhamma (*dhammadesanā*), there is no distinct heading for the origin; rather, all eleven training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are stated collectively as having the teaching on the Dhamma as their origin.
"Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion. "Of those" refers to those training rules. "Mixed origin" (*sambhinnasamuṭṭhāna*) means an origin through association (*saṃsaggasamuṭṭhāna*).
It is threefold by way of the origin of announcing [the offense] to one who has become [a monk], the origin of causing a thief to leave the order, and the origin of what is not permitted.

It is of three kinds. The word "that" (taṃ) refers to that which has a fixed origination; its connection is with the word "occurs" (hoti). Again, the word "that" (taṃ) refers to that which has a fixed origination;
its connection is with the word "to show. Again, the word "that" (taṃ) refers to the statement. Regarding the phrase "conducive to the Dhamma of the Guide" (nettidhammānulomika):

here, it is called a "guide" (netti) because it leads and guides body and speech; or, it is a guide because it leads and guides body and speech therein, or by means of it. "Dhamma" refers to the canonical text (pāḷi).
For since it holds (dhāreti) the meaning (attha), it is therefore called "Dhamma. The Dhamma that is itself a guide (netti) is "Netti-Dhamma";
that which is in conformity with it is "conformable to the Guide-Dhamma" (nettidhammānulomika). Thus it was said: "in conformity with the Dhamma of the Vinaya Piṭaka.
In this way, the application of the commentary on the section concerning the origins (samuṭṭhāna-sīsa) is completed.
Commentary on the Section on Questions Concerning the Intermediate Repetition (Antarapeyyāla-katipucchāvāra-vaṇṇanā) 271.

Now, the connection is with the word "vutto" (is stated). Because it is connected with the word "idāni" (now), it should be understood that the suffix *-ta* in the word "vutto" here denotes the present tense.
"Tattha" means in the matrix (mātikā) or in the questions. "Āgatāpattipucchā" means a question regarding an offense that has been encountered. The particle "hi" is an indicator of distinction.
The meaning is: "Indeed, I shall explain the distinction. "In this" refers to the second phrase, "How many aggregates of offenses (āpattikkhandhā) are there?

By the words "by way of a heap," he shows that the word *khandha* has the sense of a collection (*rāsa*). Regarding the term "bases of training" (*vinītavatthūni*), he says "questions on the Vinaya" because here the word *vinīta* is a synonym for *vinaya*.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the words *vinīta* and *vinaya* differ both in sound and in meaning?
But why is it called the "Vinaya-puccha" (Inquiry on Discipline)? He says: "That which is disciplined... [etc. ...one. These are three terms.
"One in meaning" means one precisely in meaning, not one in sound. "Bases of discipline" (*vinītavatthūni*) refers to the bases for the disciplining of offenses.
"In which" refers to those who lack reverence. "Being present" means while they exist. And here, when these are present, no offenses arise.

The phrase "they exist" or "they exist when [something] is absent" should also be understood according to the principle of what is established even without being explicitly stated. "In which" refers to the types of disrespect (*agārava*).
"Those" refers to disrespect and respect (*agāravagārave*). The connection is "because they do not exist.

"An inquiry into the state of failure" means an inquiry concerning the state of failure (*vipattibhāva*). It is called an "inquiry" (*pucchā*) because one inquires by means of it. "Roots of dispute and roots of reproach"—these inquiries are the "root-inquiries."
Regarding the connection: in the manuscripts, there is a reading together with the section [beginning] "These are," but that is not the correct reading.

"Root-questions" (*mūlapucchā*): they are called questions because they are questioned; the questions concerning the roots are "root-questions. In passages such as "the legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*), the word "stated" (*vuttaṃ*) is the connection.
"Of those very ones" means of the legal issues themselves. This is the summary outline (*mātikā*) here.

In the *Niddesa*, "in the *mātikā*" means in the *Pātimokkha*. "In the *Vibhaṅga*" refers to the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*); the construction is that [the terms] are stated according to how they have come down. This is the exposition (*niddesa*) here.
In the sub-exposition (*paṭiniddesa*), showing the meaning of the words beginning with "aversion" (*āratī*), he says "far away" (*ārakā*), and so forth.
Therein, by the word "far away," he shows the meaning of the prefix *ā-* in the term "aversion. "By these" refers to the classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*); "far away" means...
Regarding the connection: by the word "ramatī," it is shown that the *tip* suffix occurs in the sense of an abstract noun (*katvattha*).
"Rati" means "delighting. By this, it is shown that the *tip* suffix also occurs in the sense of an action (*bhāvattha*). "Vinā" means "without these aggregates of offenses.
By this, he shows the meaning of the prefix *vi-* in the word "virati. "Paccekam" means "one by one"; the prefix *pati-* indicates repetition (*vicchattha*).
"Visuṃ visunti" means individually. By this, he shows the meaning of the prefix *pati* in the word *paṭivirati*.

In the phrase "virati paṭivirati," the suffix *-ti* should also be understood as having the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvatthe*). "Vera" refers to those unwholesome states such as lust and so forth;

because they cause harm, they are to be desisted from, thus they are "viraṃ," which is the same as "veraṃ. For they are called "veras" (enmities) because they are the causes of enmity. "Etāya" means by this...
"Of abstinence. By this, he shows that in the phrase "non-doing" (*akiriya*), the suffix *-iya* functions in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The construction is: "that which is the cause for the category of offenses. "Of that" means "of the cause for the category of offenses. "From the opposite side" means "from the state of being contrary.
By this, he shows that in the phrase "non-doing" (*akaraṇa*), the prefix *a-* has the sense of contrariety. "Through the commission of the category of offenses" refers to the categories of offenses.

Regarding "transgressing and falling into [an offense]": by the word *velanato*, he shows the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as "it transgresses" (*velati*), thus it is *velā*; or else, "transgression" (*velanaṃ*) is *velā*. "The outlet" (*niyyānaṃ*) refers to the path.
For the path is called "the outlet" because it goes to, or proceeds toward, Nibbāna by way of making it its object.
By the word "binds" (*bandhati*), he shows the meaning of binding for the verbal root *sidh*. "He restrains" (*nivāreti*).

By this, the intended meaning of the root *bandh* (to bind) is shown. "This" refers to the name "bridge" (*setu*). "That bridge" means that bridge consisting of the categories of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
Here, although the reading "so setū" (that bridge) and "etāya paññattiyā" (by this designation) exists in some manuscripts, it is not the correct reading.

The construction is: "In those who show disrespect toward the Buddha, this determination (*vinicchaya*) should be understood. Regarding "yo" (whoever), it refers to anyone; as in the phrases "does not go," etc.
The connection [is as follows]: "Dharamāne" means while existing, while being present; this is the meaning. "Upaṭṭhānaṃ" means a place of attendance, or for the purpose of attendance.
"Etassa" refers to anyone at all, whether a householder or one who has gone forth.
"Dhammassavanaṃ" means a place for hearing the Dhamma, or for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. "Dhammassavanaggaṃ" means they take up the hearing of the Dhamma.
"Ettha" means at the head of the Dhamma-listening, that is, at the Dhamma-listening pavilion. Alternatively, it is called the "head of the Dhamma-listening" because it receives the Dhamma-listening;
it refers to the assembly of people gathered at the place for listening to the Dhamma. "Cittīkāraṃ" means a manner of showing respect.
The construction is: "he sits down distracted or without regard. "Kāyapāgabbiyaṃ" means he treats others with extreme contempt.
That by which one is oppressed is *pagabbha*, meaning overweening pride (*atimāna*); it is the third letter of the word *oṭṭha*. The state of being *pagabbha* is *pāgabbiya*;
bodily *pāgabbiya* is bodily impropriety (*kāyānācāra*). "The three trainings" refers to the three trainings beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
Negligence is heedlessness (*pamāda*), which is the absence of mindfulness; thus he said, "and in negligence and the absence of mindfulness."
“Maintaining through material things” (*āmisa-paṭisandhāra*) means the connecting of oneself and others with material things; likewise for “maintaining through the Dhamma” (*dhamma-paṭisandhāra*).

The connection [of the text] is that the meaning of the phrases beginning with “disrespectful toward the Teacher” (*satthari agāravo*) is [explained] by the passage beginning with “not living humbly” (*anīcavuttī*). “Not deferential” (*appatisso*) [is explained] by the passage beginning with “not living humbly.”

It shows the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*) of the word; however, the literal meaning (*saddattha*) should be understood as follows: one who does not listen to the Teacher’s words with focused attention is called "one without a protector" (*appatisso*).

Regarding the phrase "internally" (*ajjhattaṃ*), he says "in one's own continuity" (*attano santāne vā*) while demonstrating both that it refers to the state of being "internally" in the sense of "one's own" among the four types of internality (such as *niyakajjhatta*), and that there is no substitution of *am* for the locative case ending. [He also says] "in one's own faction" (*attano pakkhe*).
By the word "or," he rejects the interpretation that [the object] is within one's own mental continuum (*cittasantāna*).
In that context, regarding the phrase "for you" (*tumhe*), showing the scope of the pronoun *ta*, he says: "in that division into internal and external.

Regarding "for the abandoning" (*pahānāya*), showing both the instrumental function of the root *hā* and the sense conveyed by the suffix *-āya*, he says: "by means of the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*) and so forth."

"...for the purpose of abandoning by means of the methods. By the phrase "by the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*), etc.," the word "etc. includes the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) and so forth.

"That" refers to the root of dispute. By the expression "for the sake of non-occurrence," he shows here the meaning of the verbal root *sudhātu* preceded by the prefix *ava*, in the sense of "non-flowing" (*anavassavāya*).
Regarding the term *sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*: here, *saṃ* means "one's own" (*attano idaṃ saṃ*). He explains that one who clings to one's own view as being supreme is a *sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī*, saying:
"He clings to his own view alone. With the words "Whatever... and so forth, he shows the manner of clinging. Regarding the term *ādhānaggāhī*:
here, by the etymological sense of "that which is firmly established" (*ābhuso ṭhiyate ādhānaṃ*), the word *ādhāna* is a synonym for "firmness" (*daḷha*).
He said, “one who grasps firmly. One who grasps firmly is a *daḷhaggāhī*. 273. The construction is:
“Even though the description of the root of the dispute is the same. Then, however (*atha kho*), means: even though it is the same in that way, this is the distinction here;
such is the connection. The construction is: “of persons who are disputing. “Disputing in such a manner” means: in that way.

The connection is: "quarreling" and "reproaching. Having perceived the offense and pointing out the very meaning already stated—that "he has fallen into such-and-such a failure"—the text says, "You have fallen into a *pārājika*," and so forth. "In this" refers to the basis of reproach (*anuvāda-mūla*).

"Distinction" means the distinction from the basis of quarreling (*vivāda-mūla*). For those who quarrel, the roots of quarreling are anger, enmity, and so on; for those who reproach, [the roots are...]
It is meant that they are the roots of the expositions.

274. Regarding the phrase "loving bodily action": here, *mettaṃ* means that which possesses loving-kindness (*mettā*); thus it is "bodily action," meaning bodily action accompanied by a mind of loving-kindness.
Therefore it is said: "bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness. [This applies] to those present and those absent.
Showing the detailed explanation, he said, “Therein,” and so forth. Therein, “therein” means among those [who are] face-to-face and behind one’s back.
“Bodily action” means loving-kindness as bodily action; this is to be connected with “the giving to the elders. “By both” means by the junior elders as well.
“Among them” means among the junior elders. “Disrespect” means contempt. [This refers to] their own [faults] which are difficult to remove.

The construction is: "Patisāmana" means like "patisāmana. By the phrase "consisting of loving bodily action," he shows the essential nature (*dhamma-sarūpa*) of this *dhamma* in the statement "this too is a *dhamma*.

The particle "pi" (also/even) refers to the *dhammas* that will be mentioned later. By the word "saritabbo" (should be remembered), he shows that the suffix *-anīya* expresses the object of the action (*kamma*).
"Satijanako" means one who generates mindfulness in fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārīs*).
Showing the intended meaning of that word, he said: “He who does not,” and so forth. Therein, “he” (yo) refers to a person.

“It” (naṃ) refers to the bodily action of loving-kindness (mettā). The connection is: “recalling that person. “Of whom” (yesaṃ) refers to fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārīnaṃ). “Those” (te) refers to the fellow practitioners of the holy life. The connection is: “having become clear-minded.
By the phrase “he makes dear” (piyaṃ karoti), [the meaning of] the term “one who makes dear” (piyakaraṇo) is shown.
The phrase "he makes" (*karoti*) shows the meaning of the word *piyakaraṇa* (one who creates affection). This same method applies here to the term *garukaraṇa* (one who holds in esteem) as well.

By the expression "for the state of being to be included," he shows that the word *saṅgahāya* (for the sake of inclusion) is a designation of the object where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant.

*Saṅgaha* means that which is to be included; [the phrase means] for the purpose of that. "By them" refers to those fellow-celibates (*sabrahmacārī*). By the expression "for the state of being in harmony" (*samaggabhāvāya*), [he shows] the state of being in harmony (*samagga-bhāva*).
This shows the meaning of the word *sāmaggī* (concord).

*Paggayha-vacanaṃ* means speech after having exerted [the mind]. In the phrase *vihāre*, the locative case (*bhummavacana*) is used in the sense of a support; it is to be construed with *there asante* (when the Elder is absent).
*Taṃ* is to be construed with *kadā āgamissati nu kho* (when indeed will he come?). *Mamāyana-vacanaṃ* means speech occurring in the manner of "mine-making" (*mamāyana*).
[This is] the statement. "Lubricated with the moisture of loving-kindness" means they are moistened by the moisture known as loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Eyes" means the eyes. By the word "free from illness" (*appābādha*), he shows the meaning of the term "healthy" (*aroga*).

Alternatively, one is healthy by virtue of being free from constant illness, and free from illness by virtue of being free from adventitious illness; or one is healthy by virtue of being free from internal illness, and free from illness by virtue of being free from external illness, [and free from illness] by virtue of being free from bodily illness.
Or he is healthy, being free from illness due to mental affliction. "Applying the mind" means repeated attention. The construction is:
"He does not eat by discriminating against a person. Explaining its meaning in detail, he says, "For whoever," and so forth.
Therein, "whoever" refers to a person, and it is connected with "eats. By the phrase "I will eat this much... and so on, [he shows] the state of one who eats having discriminated the food.

[The text] shows this. By the phrase, “I shall eat this much, or that belonging to such-and-such a person...,” it shows the state of one who partakes of what has been specifically assigned to an individual (*puggalapaṭivibhattabhogibhāva*).
“This” refers to the person. “Brought” means brought from a village or similar place. By the word “even” (*pi*) in the phrase “even if not given,” it shows that giving is also permissible;
for indeed, giving is not prohibited for anyone. “Of all” means of both the immoral and the virtuous.

“Vuttaṃ” means stated in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). “Viceyya” means having investigated. By the word “pi” (also) in the phrase “dātumpi,” he includes that it is also permissible to give without investigating, as a general rule.
[Objection: If this is so, has not the classification of individuals (*puggalavibhāga*) already been made?
Why then does he say, “It is permissible to give after investigating,” with the words “na hi” and so forth? “Hi” means because. “Ete” refers to those such as the sick and others. This...

"Having investigated the footing" (*padaṃ vicinitvā*) refers to the action (*kamma*) regarding the word "footing. Regarding the word "giving" (*dentena*), it is the recipient (*sampadāna*). "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "Thus they go" (*iti ayanti*):
having brought this to mind, he is one who fulfills the qualities conducive to mindfulness (*sāraṇīyadhamma*).
In the passage beginning with "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍāni*), first of all, having shown brokenness, flaws, impurities, and stains, [the text proceeds] by way of their opposites.
Showing [the training rules] beginning with "unbroken" (akhaṇḍa), he says "of whom," and so forth. Therein, "of whom" refers to the bhikkhu; the connection is "his training rule is broken.
"In the seven classes of offenses" is the locative case used for the locus (*ādhāra*); the connection is "a training rule.
For because a training rule is formulated in dependence upon an offense, the offense is the domain of that training rule. Or, "at the beginning or at the end" refers to the training rules.
"At the beginning or at the end. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an indefinite alternative.

It is said, "the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is broken," because an offense arises when a training rule is broken. "Broken" (*khaṇḍa*) means cut. "In the middle" means in the midst of the training rules.
"Broken" refers to a training rule that has been broken. "Hollow" (*chidda*) means an opening. "Two or three training rules..."
"Connected" (*sambandha*). "Spotted" (*sabala*) means variegated. "Broken" (*bhinnāni*) refers to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) being broken. "Speckled" (*kammāsa*) means diverse.

Herein, the distinction between these two is as follows: that which is variegated in one place by a single dissimilar color is called "spotted," while that which is diverse in various places with various colors is called "speckled. [This applies to] the torn [robes] and so forth.
Showing that they are "unbroken" and so forth by way of their reversal, he says, “But for whom...,” and so on.
“Unbroken virtues” means unbroken precept-virtues (*sikkhāpada-sīla*). “But those” refers to the virtues. The word “these” is merely an ornament for the verse.
“Because of making one free” means because of making one free from the slavery of craving and establishing one in the state of freedom. By this, [it is meant] “they are the makers of freedom.”
It shows that this is stated by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*). The connection is with the words “they are called ‘free’” (*bhujissāni*).

“By the wise” (*viññūhi*) means by the Buddhas and other true persons (*sappurisā*). In the phrase “access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) or absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*),” the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction;
for the meaning is “both access concentration and absorption concentration. “They lead to” (*saṃvattayanti*).
Regarding the phrase "by this [it is shown] that they lead to concentration": here, he shows that the suffix *-anīya* frequently expresses the agent.

Regarding the phrase "having attained conformity in virtue" (*sīlasāmaññagata*): here, *sāmañña* is the state of being the same (*samāna*); one who has attained that is "one who has attained conformity. Thus, "having attained conformity in virtue" means "having attained conformity by means of virtue.
The construction is: "he dwells having become thus. Therefore it was said: "He dwells having entered into a state of shared being with respect to virtue."

Regarding the phrase "this view" (*yāyaṃ diṭṭhī*): although the word "view" (*diṭṭhī*) here is a general term, because it occurs in proximity to the other word "noble ones" (*ariyā*), its meaning is restricted to a specific domain;
thus he says "right view," namely "the right view associated with the Path. By the phrase "associated with the Path," he excludes mundane right view.
It is "faultless" (*niddosā*) because of its purity or because of its excellence.
By this, the word *ariya* is shown to signify "faultless" and to be an un-derived (*anipphanna*) primary derivative (*pāṭipadika*). "It leads out" (*niyyāti*) means it goes toward Nibbāna.
By this, it is shown that the suffix *-iya* frequently denotes the agent. The construction is: "for one who acts thus" (*takkarassa*), meaning for the one who acts accordingly.
"One who acts thus" (*tathākārī*) means one who acts by means of that right view associated with the Path. By this, [it is shown] through that right view...

"Karoti" (he does) shows the meaning of the word as "takkaroti" (one who does). Regarding "for the destruction of suffering" (*dukkhakkhayāya*): here, "destruction" (*khaya*) means the act of being destroyed;
the destruction of suffering is "dukkhakkhayo"; showing that it is for the sake of that, he says, "for the purpose of the destruction of all suffering.
"The rest" refers to the remaining words from what has been stated.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section of questions regarding the "Iti-kata.
Now begins the commentary on the section of questions and their answers concerning the Khandhakas.
320. The *Upasampadakkhandhaka* is part of the *Mahākhandhaka*. By the phrase “together with the introduction (*nidāna*) and the exposition (*niddesa*),” it shows the meaning of the words:

“with the introduction” means together with the introduction, which is defined as the place where the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) was promulgated; “with the exposition” means together with the exposition of individuals (*puggala*) and so forth.

Here, “by the introduction” refers to the introduction consisting of the location of the promulgation of the training rule. “By the exposition” refers to the exposition of individuals and other such categories.

"In that" means in the *Upasampadakkhandhaka*. Regarding the phrase "excellent words" (*samukkaṭṭhapadānaṃ*): here, the word *samukkaṭṭha* is a synonym for "supreme," which is why he says "the most excellent.
"Words" refers to the statements expressed in such a manner as, "Monks, a person less than twenty years of age is not to be ordained," and so forth.
By these words, [the compound] is analyzed as "the most excellent words are 'excellent words'."
This shows the meaning of the words. The word *iti* has this sense.
But why, in this context, is the designation made in the masculine form (*sāmivasena*) as "how many offenses for the most excellent terms," when it is offenses that belong only to persons?
To this he says: "by whichever [term]," and so forth. The word *hi* means "because. The connection is: "by whichever term they were formulated. *Sā sā* refers to the offense.
Regarding the phrase "two offenses," he says "an offense of expiation (pācittiya) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" while showing the specific nature of those two offenses.
"Nassantete" means "let these go"; "vinassantete" means "let these bhikkhus perish"—this is the meaning. "Tehi" means "by those bhikkhus. "Vadataṃ" means "of those speaking.
The connection is with "in the remaining cases of performing the Uposatha. "Dukkaṭāpatti yevā" means "it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing."
Regarding the phrase "by this, one offense": here, by way of the *Atthapakaraṇa* and so forth, it is shown that this is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In the expression "also in the *Pavāraṇakkhandhaka*," the word "also" (*pi*) refers back to the *Uposathakkhandhaka*.
In the expression "also in the *Cammasaṃyutta*," it means also in the chapter taught having been connected with hide; that is, also in the *Cammakkhandhaka*.
The word *attha* [is used]. The particle *pi* refers back to the *Pavāraṇakkhandhaka*. In the phrase "also in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka*," the particle *pi* refers back to the *Cammakkhandhaka*.
*Samanta* means all around the private parts (*aṅgajāta*).
*Tattha* means in the *Kathinakkhandhaka*. *Cīvarasaṃyutta* means in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka*.
"In the Campeyyaka" means in the Campeyya Khandhaka. In the phrase "also in the Samuccaya Khandhakas," the word "also" (pi) refers back to the Campeyya Khandhaka.

The construction is: "In the Samatha Khandhaka, these two offenses occur. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. "In the Khuddakavatthu" means in the Khuddakavatthu Khandhaka. "In the disposal of heavy goods" means in the relinquishing of heavy goods. "In the schism of the Saṅgha" means in the Saṅghabheda Khandhaka.
Regarding the statement, "When it is said, 'They will ask about proper conduct,' [it refers to] the Vatta Khandhaka."
By this term "proper conduct" (samācāra), it is shown that the *Vattakkhandhaka* is to be understood. "That" refers to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the phrase "only one offense of wrong-doing" is extended by way of reference.

By the phrase "in the suspension of the Pātimokkha," it shows the elision of the words "Pātimokkha" and so forth from the text where it says "they will ask for the suspension. In the *Pañcasatika* and *Sattasatika* [Vinaya commentaries]...
In the *Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka* and the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka*. Regarding the word "entrusted" (*āropito*):

here, because the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) takes two objects and because it belongs to the *ny-ādi* group [of verbal roots], only the primary object is stated as "the Dhamma," while the secondary object, "the collection" (*saṅgaha*), is not.
Therefore, it is said: "The Dhamma is the collection. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the *Pañcasatika* and *Sattasatika* [sections].
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the interrogation of the Khandhakas.
The Method of Single Increments (Ekuttarikanaya): the commentary on the section on single items.
321. Having thus provided the commentary on the interrogation of the *Khandhaka*, he now says, “An offense... [etc. ...in the method,” while providing that same commentary for the *Ekuttarikanaya*.
The construction here is: “In the *Ekuttarikanaya*, the analysis should be understood in this way.
By the phrase “six origins of offenses,” they are called “offense-makers” (*āpattikara*) in the sense that the origins produce the offense.
[The text] shows this. "Of these" refers to the six origins of offenses (*āpatti-samutthāna*). "For" (*hi*) means because; it is connected with the word "one incurs" (*āpajjati*).

"And in the training rule" (*sikkhāpade ca*) refers to the training rules of the *mātikā*. Regarding "a light offense" (*lahukā āpatti*): here, it is not called "light" because it is slightly blameworthy;
rather, it is so called because it is purified by a light disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*). Thus he says: "because of being purified by a light disciplinary act."
"Fivefold" means of five kinds, by way of *thullaccaya* (grave offenses) and so forth. "By anything" means by any mode whatsoever, whether light or heavy.
"With remainder" (*sāvasesā*) means that which has the state of a recluse remaining after the state of a householder; its opposite is "without remainder" (*anavasesā*).
"Two classes of offenses" means two classes of offenses by way of *pārājika* (defeats) and *saṅghādisesa* (formal meetings).
By the word “committing,” he shows the meaning of the suffix *ṇika* in the term *antarāyikā*.

He says, “even for one who has fallen into an obstructive offense,” and so forth, because obstructive offenses are obstructive in every respect. The connection is: “for one who has attained purity after having confessed.
“Worldly offenses” (*lokavajjā*) are those to be avoided by the world; “prescribed offenses” (*paṇṇattivajjā*) are those to be avoided according to the Blessed One’s prescription.
The connection is: "They go to whatever offense one commits. "Committing" (*karonto*) means from the act of performing; for here there is a substitution of *anta* for the word *māna*.
By this, he shows the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāvattha*), namely that "performing" (*karaṇa*) is "action" (*kiriyā*). "Commits" (*āpajjati*) means the person commits it.
The construction is: "That offense is said to have arisen from action. To the question "What kind of offense? he says: "An offense involving defeat (*pārājika*)."
"Thus it is said. This same method applies to the subsequent sentences as well.
Regarding the term "prior offense" (*pubbāpatti*), he says "an offense committed first," because here the word *pubba* has the sense of "first.

By the word "committed" (*āpannā*), he indicates the elision of the middle term. "An offense committed later" refers to the offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) arising from a breach of speech. "By means of purification at the root" (*mūlavisuddhiyā*)...
"Because of the purity resulting from the non-mixture with any offense at the root"—this is the connection with what is stated in the *Kurundi*.
"This too" refers to the statement also found in the *Kurundi*. By the word "too" (*pi*), one refers back to the previous statement in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*.
"By one way" means by one reason.
The connection is: "It becomes an offense that has been confessed. The construction is: "This [offense] that has been confessed is called 'countable' (*gaṇanūpikā*).
The construction is: "That which has been confessed is called 'uncountable' (*agaṇanūpikā*). "With enthusiasm" (*saussāhena*) means with the very same enthusiasm [thinking], "I shall commit it again.
"Indeed" (*hi*) means truth, or because. By the phrase "does not enter into counting," it does not reach counting; thus it is "uncountable" (*agaṇanūpikā*).
He shows the meaning of the word. In the eighth case, the connection is with "Pūraṇa.

This was stated with reference to the bhikkhunīs because it occurs in the Pāli in the context of the fulfillment of the eight cases for bhikkhunīs. It is indeed found in the same position as the second pārājika for bhikkhus as well.
Regarding the term *thullavajjā*, he says "thulladose" (in a grave fault), showing that it is called *thullavajjā* because its fault (*vajja*) is grave (*thulla*).
"…are prescribed. The construction is: "Whatever offense there is in the non-fulfillment of a legitimate promise, that is connected with householders.
Regarding "the commission of the five ānantariya karmas": this refers to an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) incurred through the five deeds of immediate retribution.
By the word "etcetera" in "Sudinna Thera, etc.," [the author] includes Dhaniya Thera and others. "An ādikammika" means one who commits the first act.
One who performs [the act], or one appointed to it. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "monks like the monkey-monks" (*makkaṭisamaṇādi*), the Vajjiputtakas and others are included.
The construction is: "He who occasionally commits an offense is called 'one who commits occasional offenses' (*adhiccāpattika*). This same method applies to what follows as well.

By the word "accuses" (*codeti*), he shows the etymological meaning of "accuser" (*codaka*) as "one who accuses. By the word "accused" (*codita*), he shows [the meaning of] "one who is to be accused" (*coditabba*).
The phrase "he who has been censured" (*cudito*) indicates that he himself is the one who has been censured; this shows the meaning of the words.

"In fifteen cases" refers to the fifteen matters set forth in the *Pātimokkha-ṭṭhapana-kkhandhaka*. "By him" refers to the one who censures unrighteously (*adhammacodakena*); the connection is with the word "censured" (*codito*).

Even if one does not abide by what is true and unshakable as stated in the *Pātimokkha-ṭṭhapana-kkhandhaka*, he is still called "one censured unrighteously. However, by one who censures righteously (*dhammacodakena*)...

One who becomes angry when being reproved is indeed called "one reproved unrighteously"; however, even if one becomes angry when reproved by someone who reproves unrighteously, one is not called "one reproved unrighteously.
Therefore, this is not mentioned here. By the word "endowed" (*samannāgato*), he shows the meaning of the term "certain" (*niyato*) as "one for whom these [qualities] are necessarily present."
"Bhabbāpattikā" means those capable of falling into an offense. One who has not been dealt with by any formal act (kamma) is indeed called "one who has not been suspended" (anukkhittaka);
however, because there is no suspicion that he is actually suspended, he is not mentioned here. "Ayaṃ" refers to the monk who has been subjected to a formal act such as censure (tajjanīya).
"Hi" means because; it is connected with "he does not disturb. By "liṅga-daṇḍakamma-saṃvāsa-nāsana," [it is meant] by the removal of the [monastic] mark (liṅga-nāsana).

"And by means of the act of penalization (daṇḍakamma), the suspension from sitting together (nāsanā), and the suspension from living together (saṃvāsanā). "By whom" means by a monk. "He" refers to one who belongs to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka).
The distinction between two persons belonging to different communions has already been stated below.
Regarding the phrase "the setting aside should be known," [the question] "What is meant here by 'setting aside'? is answered with: "The setting aside of the Pātimokkha."
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section on single items (*ekakavāra*).
The method of numerical progression (*ekuttarikanaya*): Commentary on the section on pairs (*dukavāra*). 322.

Regarding the pairs, the connection is with the phrase "an offense without consciousness" (*acittakā āpatti*). "An offense for announcing what is true" (*bhūtārocanāpatti*) refers to an offense of expiation (*pācittiyāpatti*). "An offense for announcing what is untrue" (*abhūtārocanāpatti*)... [text continues]
An offense of defeat (*pārājika*) or a grave offense (*thullaccaya*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "recitation of words and so forth," the subsequent six recitations are included.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "beds, chairs, and so forth," items such as cushions (*bhisi*) are included.

By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "going without asking permission and so forth," departing without having had [the bedding] removed is included. "One's own person" (*sapuggala*) means that person who is designated as "self" (*attasankhāta*) is one's own person. "Another person" (*parapuggala*)...

"Another person" means a person other than oneself. "Heavy" refers to an offense involving formal meeting (saṅghādisesa). "Light" refers to an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Again, "heavy" refers to an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Again, "light" refers to an offense of expiation itself.

In the phrase "even by as much as a finger's breadth," the word "even" (pi) includes the meaning "even by as much as a hair's breadth. "That" refers to the bed or chair. The grammatical connection is: "he incurs an offense called gamiya."

Regarding the phrase “One who takes up incurs [an offense],” etc., it demonstrates the method of construction (*yojanānaya*) as follows: “While taking up, one incurs” means that having become one who takes up, one incurs;

thus there exists an offense. For this being the case, the verbal form “incurs” (*āpajjati*) must be understood as the agent (*kattā*) in relation to the other action “exists” (*atthi*). Alternatively, it refers to the person who is taking up.
The construction is: "Whatever offense one commits, that offense exists. This same method applies to others as well.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the mute-vow and so forth," it includes the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and others. The connection is: "those such as those on probation (*pārivāsika*) commit [them].

Or, the construction is: "persons who have undergone formal acts (*kamma*) such as censure (*tajjanīya*). "Committing them while not undertaking [the training]" means: having become those who do not undertake [the training].
They incur [the offense]. "Those persons" refers to those individuals. "One who acts incurs [the offense]" means that having become one who acts, he incurs it; such is the construction.
The same applies to "one who gives incurs [the offense]," and so forth.
Regarding "in cases of exceeding one night, three nights, seven days, ten days, or a month," [it refers to the rule]: "He might be separated from his three robes even for a single night."
And [it concerns] the transgressions of the time limits stated as follows:

"that monk may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six nights," "it may be used after being stored for a maximum of seven days," "an extra robe may be kept for a maximum of ten days," and "it may be set aside for a maximum of one month."
"But he incurs this offense" is the connection.
"In whichever faction he sits" means in whichever faction he himself is seated. "Of them" refers to those seated in his own faction;
the connection is with the term "of different communion" (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*). "Of whom" refers to those seated in his own faction. "He subverts the transaction" because of being of different communion.
He invalidates the *kamma*. Regarding "those others": it refers to those sitting on the opposing side. The construction is: "Because he has not come within arm's reach, he invalidates the *kamma*.
Explaining the statement "The same method applies," he said: "Of whom... and so forth.

"Of whom" means of whichever monks, whether sitting on one’s own side or the opposing side. "He" refers to the monk. "From the state of being to be committed" means from the fact that [the offense] must be committed.
By the phrase "these offenses are to be committed by this person through six origins," he shows the meaning of the word *āpatti* (offense).
Regarding the expression "by means of a formal act (*kamma*) or by the drawing of lots (*salākaggāha*)," he says, "both the recitation (*uddesa*)... [and so on]...

one," showing that here the recitation is included under the formal act according to the method of applying characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*), while the proclamation of the motion (*vohārānussāvana*) constitutes the drawing of lots. "The preliminary stages" (*pubbabhāga*)... [and so on].
These occur prior to the schism of the Saṅgha. "Measure" refers to the cause for the schism of the Saṅgha.
Regarding the phrase "one deficient in time," the word *addhāna* here is a synonym for time; thus he says, "one who is less than twenty years of age.

By the phrase "those living in communion through theft," etc., the words "and so forth" (*ādi*) should include those who have gone over to other sects, those who have violated a bhikkhunī, and those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution. These are the eight persons incapable [of ordination].
The construction is: "they are called *karaṇadukkaṭaka*. Here, "that which is to be done" is *karaṇa*, meaning "action";
"badly done" is *dukkata*, meaning "action that is ill-performed. One for whom the action (*karaṇa*) is a transgression (*dukkata*) is a *karaṇadukkaṭaka*.

The modifier is placed after the word it qualifies, as in expressions such as "one who has set fire to" (*agyāhita*). To show this very meaning, he said: "the performance of a *dukkata*," and so forth. And "he does not ask."
In this context, he says “ordination” (*upasampadā*) while demonstrating the formal act of striving (*padhāna-kamma*); “the Saṅgha” should be understood as the non-striving act (*apadhāna-kamma*).

“One who knows the Three Piṭakas” (*Tepiṭaka*) means one who maintains the Three Piṭakas by way of having them committed to memory. In the phrase “even with the command” (*āṇāyapi*), the word “even” (*pi*) includes the meaning “even with [his] corpse.
“To him who is requesting” means to him who is requesting the teacher for dependence (*nissaya*). Regarding the matter which, while transgressing, [he commits]...
The construction is: "He commits an offense; that matter is called 'with transgression' (*sātisāra*).
Regarding the term *upaghātikā*: here, those who destroy are *upaghātā*; showing that these very ones are *upaghātikā*, he says "destructive" (*upaghātā*).

"Therein" refers to the two types of destructive [factors]. Regarding "two types of disciplinary" (*venayika*): here, showing that they are established by means of discipline (*vinaya*), he calls them "disciplinary."
He says, “established in the Vinaya. By the phrase “two meanings,” he shows the actual form of the word *ṇika*.
The connection is that it should be understood as “conformable to the formal rule” (*paññattānuloma*). “Destruction of the condition” (*paccayaghāta*) means the destruction of the condition.

By this, he shows that in the expression “destruction of the bridge” (*setughāta*), the word *setu* (bridge) denotes a condition. The particle *api* in “of the mind too” (*cittassāpi*) indicates that it goes without saying for body and speech.

In the phrase *itipi*, the word *pi* serves to include a second meaning. By the term *pamāṇena*, it is shown that in the expression *mattakāritā*, the word *matta* has the sense of "measure" (*pamāṇa*).
By the term *karaṇaṃ*, it shows that in the word *kāritā*, the suffix *-tā* (the state of being) functions as a primary derivative (*kitabhāva*), because of their common nature.
*Kāyadvārikaṃ* refers to an offense occurring at the door of the body. By this [term], it indicates the object of the verb "one incurs" (*āpajjati*).
He shows this. "He emerges by means of the body alone" means that because he gives with bodily harmony, he emerges by means of the body alone.
By the word "etc. in "anointing the head, etc.," one includes anointing the feet and so forth.
"That" refers to the burden. By the phrase "he exerts energy to cross over," he shows the manner of carrying [the burden]. "Being an elder... [is the meaning].
The construction [of the sentence]. In order to show the form of the nine [syllables], he says, “I allow,” and so forth.
By the phrase “he acts having become remorseful,” he shows that *kukkucca* is a verbal noun (*nāmadhātu*). By the phrase “by day and by night,” he shows the constant increase of the taints (*āsava*).
Therein, “in this and that” refers to those various sections of the Vibhaṅga and Khandhakas.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section on pairs (*dukkavāra*).
The commentary on the section on threes (*tikavāra*) according to the method of single-increment (*ekuttarikanaya*): 323.

Regarding the threes (*tikesu*), the application is as follows: while the Blessed One is still living, whatever offense one commits, that offense exists. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*)... [text continues]
"In all instances. Showing the detailed explanation, he says "therein," and so forth. The construction is: "Therein" means in the triads;
the detailed explanation should be understood in this way. "The offense of shedding blood" refers to the offense of a *pārājika* in the direct order (*anuloma*).
"By the address 'friend'" means by the conventional usage of the word "friend" (*āvuso*). "You" means by you.
"Kāle" means at the time before the meal; "vikāle" means at the time after the meal. The connection is: "the remaining offense. "I am ten years old" means "I am ten years [of standing].
"A novice" (nava) is one whose five years are not yet complete. "Intermediate" (majjhima) is one from five years up until ten years are not yet complete.
"One commits with a wholesome mind" means he commits it while being possessed of a wholesome mind. "With an indeterminate mind" (abyākata-citta) means...
This was said with reference to the *bhavaṅga*-consciousness of one who is sleeping. "That" refers to the offense (*āpatti*). "All" refers to the offense;
the connection is "one incurs [it]. The construction is: "having become possessed of painful feeling, one incurs [it]. "That" refers to the offense.
Regarding the phrase "three rejections," he says "of the Buddha, the Blessed One" in order to show the owner of that rejection.

Regarding "the practice for the wearing away of defilements" (*kilesasallekhanakapaṭipatti*): one who wears away (*sallikhati*), that is, makes thin, the defilements is a "wearer-away of defilements" (*kilesasallekhana*);
that very practice is the "practice for the wearing away of defilements," and [the phrase refers to] by means of that.

The connection is: "one who attends an assembly is a fool. The connection is: "one who attends an assembly is a wise man. The construction is: "the remaining offense. "In the dark" (*kāḷe*) means in the dark fortnight (*kāḷapakkha*). "In the bright" (*juṇhe*) means in the bright fortnight (*juṇhapakkha*).
“On the full moon day of Kattika” means on the final full moon day of Kattika. This is connected with the phrase “as stated in the Kurundi.
Showing the reason why it was well-stated, he said “for four months,” and so forth. The word “hi” (for) means because; the construction is: “the monks who were seeking and dwelling [there].
“Vatthuṃ” (the matter) refers to the matter of sexual intercourse and so forth.
“Paṭicchādī” (a covering) is so called because one covers with it; thus, the instrumental sense is also appropriate. Showing the detailed explanation, he says, “having closed the door,” and so forth.

“Etadeva” means precisely the preliminary work (*parikamma*). “Ubhayattha” means in both cases: the sauna-covering (*jantāghara-paṭicchādi*) and the water-covering (*udaka-paṭicchādi*). “Sabbam” means the entirety, including the preliminary work and so on. “Niyyanti” means they go away after having settled down.
Regarding the phrase “by this they carry”: * *Vahantīti*: They carry. * *Iminā*: By this [water]. * *Vahantīti*: They carry. [End of excerpt]

He shows that the verbal root *vah* has the sense of "going. "Free from clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu" means free from clouds (*abbha*), mist (*mahikā*), smoke (*dhūma*), dust (*raja*), and Rāhu (*rāhu*).
"In those"—that is, among the clouds and so forth—"likewise" means just as the lunar disk shines, so too does the solar disk.
The connection is: "having become one who has duties to perform.

"Making" means performing. The connection is: "the guest commits [an offense]. "Unrequested" means having been unasked; this is the connection. Regarding the settlement by covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*), he emerges by way of the body because of giving bodily harmony.
"He would intend for what is deep" (*āgāḷhāya ceteyya*): since the word *āgāḷha* is a synonym for "firm," he said "for the sake of firmness. It is grasped intensely (*ā bhuso gāhiyate*).
*Āgāḷho*, *gāḷho*, *bāḷho*, and *daḷho* are one in meaning. *Ceteyya* means he would intend. *Na pūrayato* means to one who does not fulfill [the requirements].

Regarding the phrase "he is shameless and foolish and not integrated into the Saṅgha," it is shown that the formal act (*kamma*) should not be performed merely on account of his being foolish or merely on account of his not being integrated;
rather, it should be performed by way of his actual offense. To this effect, he said "foolish" and so forth. Therein:
The connection is: "the fool does not know. "He goes" refers to the fool. "By this much" means by this mere lack of knowledge.
The connection is: "an offense rooted in the state of being a fool. "Two groups of offenses" means two bases of offenses, namely the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*.
"Of them" refers to the three types of persons; the connection is that [the offense] is to be committed.

“Bodily dalliance” means bodily joking. “Of the various kinds such as making gestures with the mouth” means the performance of acts such as making gestures with the mouth using scented powder (tūriya).
“By both doors” means by both doors, namely, by way of body and speech.

“Transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of the body” means the transgression of a training rule such as that concerning physical contact which is prescribed for the door of the body. “Transgression of a training rule prescribed for the door of speech” means...
It is the transgression of a training rule such as that concerning improper speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*) prescribed for the door of speech.
Regarding the phrase "by bodily harm," he says "by non-training" (*asikkhanena*), explaining that "harm" (*upaghātaka*) means non-training. To the question, "Why is non-training called harm?
he says, "For whoever... and so forth. In this context, "whoever" refers to a person; "that" refers to the training rule prescribed for the door of the body.
It is just so. For the connection is: "because it harms. The connection is: "endowed with the work of a physician.
The construction is: "by means of verbal wrong livelihood, such as receiving instruction, reporting [illness], and so forth.
By the phrase "do not cause quarreling," the sense that the prohibition "do not" (*mā*) must be connected with the remainder of the reading "cause" (*karī*) is established.
He shows this. Regarding the phrase "not to be spoken," he says "nothing at all should be said" because here the root *har* preceded by the prefixes *vi-* and *ava-* has the sense of "speaking.
The word "hi" means "truly. In the phrase "beginning with taking the seed," the word "beginning" (*ādi*) includes such things as seeking the Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase "of one who is having leave granted," he says "leave" because "leave" (*okāsa*) and "granting of leave" (*okāsakamma*) are synonymous.
"Should not be taken" means it should not be accepted. To demonstrate that very point, he said: "Where, having taken," and so forth. "Yaṃ" refers to the Vinaya.
"So" refers to the bhikkhu. "So" refers to the Vinaya. "Tassa" refers to the bhikkhu. "Idaṃ" refers to the formal act (kamma).
"Ask another" is to be construed as: "Ask me another bhikkhu. "Iti" means thus. "So" refers to one who is endowed with the three factors.
"Bhikkhu" means one who possesses these three factors. "Should not be conversed with" means he should not be spoken to together with.
By the word "adherence" (*laddhi*), [the author] shows the referent of the pronoun "this" in the phrase "without abandoning this.

By the word "not having abandoned" (*avijahitvā*), he shows that the verbal root *hā* takes the suffix *tvā*. "A pure practitioner of the holy life" (*suddhaṃ brahmacārin*): here, [he is] completely purified of defilements.
"One who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) alone should be accepted," thus he said, "a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed.

By the phrase "the state of being drinkable" (pātabyabhāva), he shows that here the suffix *tā* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvattha*). By the word "partaking" (paṭisevana), he shows that the word *pātabya* has the sense of enjoying according to one's desire.
"Purification of destiny" (gativisodhana) means purification from an unhappy rebirth into a happy rebirth. "And unwholesome roots... [The text continues: ...unwholesome roots.
By the word "ca" (and), he shows that the terms *akusala* and *mūla* share a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, the compound *akusalamūlāni* should be understood as a *tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa*, meaning "roots reckoned as unwholesome.
Regarding the term *duccaritāni*, showing that the prefix *du-* here carries the sense of "corrupt" (*duṭṭha*) or "deformed" (*virūpa*), he says: "badly practiced, or deformed..."
"Deeds" means actions. "Ugly" means having a distorted nature. By the phrase "by that which has become the instrument," he rejects the meaning of "by that which has become the agent.
"In this and that" means in each respective chapter (*khandhaka*).
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section of threefold groups.
The explanation of the section on the sets of four in the Ekuttarikanaya:
"The method of determination for the sets of four should be understood in this way" is the construction [of the sentence].

"The locus of the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass) means of settling" refers to the place where a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) has been settled by means of the *tiṇavatthāraka* means of settling. "By another’s formal proclamation" means by another’s...
"To the formal act (*kammavācā*) which serves as the instrument. "From that" means from the fourfold [set]. "In others" refers to other sets of four;

the construction is that the meaning should be understood in this same way. "That very thing" means that which pertains to the door of the body (*kāyadvārika*). "Again, that very thing" means that which pertains to the door of speech (*vacīdvārika*).
The construction is: "the offense to be incurred and the offense of sleeping in the same dwelling. "Attending" means being awake (*jāgaranta*).

“He incurs [an offense] while being without thought” means that the construction should be understood either as “the bhikkhu incurs [it] while being without thought,” or as “having become without thought, he incurs it.
“Of a similar nature” means having a similar objective basis (*vatthusabhāga*). “And that” refers to whichever particular offense it may be. “Thus” means in this way.
“By means of an act” means by means of the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*). “He emerges by means of an act” means he emerges by means of that very act.
"Heard" refers to household property; "has been brought" is the connection [to the verb]. "A lock" means a key. "Inside" means inside the storehouse.
"He emerges in her presence" means he emerges right in front of her.
The construction is: "of the nun who is lying down. "This" refers to the offense of sharing a sleeping place in the same room; "on account of" is the connection.
The connection is that the statement “by the manifestation of the gender-sign” has been spoken. “Of both” means of both monks and nuns.
“By the acquisition of the gender-sign” means by the acquisition of the female gender-sign. “First” refers to the time of the first eon (*ādikappa*).

By the phrase “by way of having arisen first,” he shows the meaning of the word *purima* (former) as that which arose previously. By the phrase “by way of being excellent,” he shows the sense of *pura* (foremost).
This indicates the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) as "that which has arisen in the state of being foremost" (*seṭṭhabhāvena uppannaṃ*).

By the phrase "male characteristic" (*purisaliṅga*), it shows the actual form of the suffix *-ima*. In the expression "manly behavior, manly appearance, etc. (*purisakuttapurisākārādi*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the male signs (*purisanimitta*) and so forth. The construction is:
"those which are the forty-six training rules" (*yāni chacattālīsa sikkhāpadāni*). Following this stated method, [the same applies] to the second tetrad as well.
The meaning should be understood. "By those" means by the one hundred and thirty training rules (*sikkhāpada*).

"Great authorities" (*mahāpadesa*) refers to the great authorities as they appear in the Vinaya. To the question, "Why are the great authorities called 'excellent' (*sāmukkaṃsa*)?", he says "For those...
and so forth. Therein, "those" refers to the four great authorities; the connection is with the word "are called. "By themselves" (*sayaṃ*)—

Regarding the phrase *iminā sāmukkaṃsā*: here, by the word *saṃ*, it shows the meaning of *sayam* (by oneself). By the word *ukkhipitvā* (having lifted up), it shows that the word *ukkaṃsa* has the sense of lifting up.
By the word *ṭhapitattā* (because of being placed), it shows the etymological meaning of *sāmukkaṃsā* as "those which, having been lifted up by oneself, have been placed [there].
By the phrase *ajjhoharaṇīyaparibhogā* (objects of enjoyment to be swallowed), it excludes external objects of enjoyment.
"But water" means clear water that has not been mixed with anything else. "At the time" means at the time of being bitten by a snake.
By the phrase "five or ten precepts," he shows that five or ten precepts constitute the *upāsaka*-precepts.
"Therein" means in the monastery. "Both" means both in terms of visitors and residents. "Not common" [means] to the two.
"Unshared" means an offense that is shared only with the bhikkhunīs. "In the group of four regarding going" (*gamiyacatukke*):

the word "also" (*pi*) refers to the group of four regarding arriving. "Due to the diversity of the basis" (*vatthunānattatāya*): this refers precisely to the diversity of the bases, such as sexual intercourse and so forth.
"Indeed" (*hi*): meaning truly, or because. "That" (*sā*): the offense. "In the same way" (*tathā*): just as it is in the case of bodily contact, so it is in the case of eating garlic.

The construction (*yojanā*). "In this" refers to the tetrad beginning with the diversity of the object (*vatthu-nānattatā*). "The four *pārājika* offenses" refers to those found in the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*.
The connection is that "this same method applies even when they are committed separately.

"In the first tetrad" refers to the tetrad beginning with the diversity of the object. "Which is the first question" is the construction. "Here" refers to the tetrad beginning with the similarity of the object (*vatthu-sabhāgatā*).
“Yo ca” means “which question. “Tattha” refers to the tetrad beginning with the diversity of the basis (*vatthu-nānattatā*). The connection is with the third and fourth questions.
The word “saddhivihārikassa” (of the co-resident) is the recipient (*sampadāna*) for the word “kattabba” (to be done).
“Garuka” means a *pārājika* offense; “lahuka” means a *thullaccaya* or a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Because eight bhikkhunīs must sit in succession, it is said, "starting from the ninth bhikkhunī.

"Worthy of rising to meet" means worthy of being attended to by approaching face-to-face. "And without distinction" means without making a distinction such as "bhikkhu" or "bhikkhunī," but by way of the general term (*sāmaññena*).
The phrase "of the tetrad of those worthy of a seat" has a part-whole relationship with the phrase "the first section."

"Uncommon" means not shared with the monks. "Permissible at the wrong time" means it is permissible on that very day during the period after noon. "Past the proper time" means past the seven-day limit for the time-period.
The construction is as follows: the triad beginning with "what is to be used during the day," unallowable meat, what has been stored up, and what has not been formally received.
"Multi-layered sandals, regular bathing, and leather rugs" refers to multi-layered sandals, regular bathing, and leather rugs.

"These four" refers to the granting of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth by a group consisting of five members. "Here" means in the border regions; "here" [again] means in the Middle Country.
"This" refers to the fourfold subject matter. "To illustrate" (*dīpetum*) means "also to illustrate. For the suffix *-tuṃ* indicates the sense of the gerundive (*katvā*-meaning).
This same method applies to the phrase "but to illustrate" (*dīpetuṃ pana*) as well. The connection is: "the rest is permitted" (*anuññātaṃ*).
“In both instances” means in both cases, according to the distinction between the border regions and the middle country.
Having grouped the explanations of desire (*chanda*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*) together as one, it is said “four. “Four preliminary duties” is a change of gender;
for the meaning is “four preliminary duties. The connection is: “these four have been thus stated. Thus they have come down [in the tradition].
"Designations" (*sammutiyo*) is the connection [to the following]. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in all the tetrads (*catukka*).
Thus, the application of the commentary on the section of tetrads is completed.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section of pentads (*pañcaka*) in the method of numerical progression (*ekuttarikanaya*).

325. Regarding the *pañcaka* (groups of five), the construction is as follows: the statement “five persons are fixed” refers specifically to those who have committed the *ānantariya* (immediate) offenses.
The connection is that these should be understood as the five offenses involving cutting off (*chedana*). The construction is: “that which was stated as ‘assignment’ (*vikappanā*) [is what is meant].

“Suspected” (*ussaṅkita*) means having become suspicious after rising [from a state of doubt]. “Apprehensive” (*parisaṅkita*) means being suspicious again and again. “Unshakable” (*akuppa*) refers to the fruit of *arahantship*.
"Dhamma of this one" means one whose nature is unshakable; that is, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). Although he is one whose taints are destroyed, the construction is:
"he is both suspicious and apprehensive. "To be avoided" means to be removed. "Hi" means truly, or because. "Among these" refers to improper resorts (agocara).
Regarding "a robe made like a stupa," he says this to show that a robe made by encircling a stupa is called a "stupa-robe" (thūpacīvara).
“Ant-hill,” and so forth. For an ant-hill (*vammika*) is called a “mound” (*thūpa*) because it piles up and rises upward.
“In the bathing place” means in the bathing place for all. For that which one sprinkles upon the body with water there is called an “ablution” (*abhiseka*).
That which is discarded at the ablution is “ablutional” (*ābhisekika*), namely, the robe. Therefore it is said, “discarded robe. “Brought as a gift for wages” (*bhatapaṭiyābhatam*):

Here, having rejected [the view] that it is for the purpose of nourishing the *bhara*-element (the body), he speaks in order to show that it is for the purpose of maintaining it, saying: "brought back again after being taken to the cemetery.
In this context, by the word "cemetery" (*susāna*), he indicates the action; by the word "again" (*puna*), he indicates the meaning of the prefix *paṭi*.

By these words, it is shown that because it was brought to the cemetery (*bhata*), it must be brought back home (*paṭiyābharitabba*); thus, it is "brought back from what was brought" (*bhatapaṭiyābhata*).

This shows the meaning of the word; the letter *ya* functions as a euphonic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). In the Pāḷi and in the manuscripts of the Aṭṭhakathā, there is a reading in the books as “*gatapaṭiyāgatan*” with the third palatal consonant (*kaṇṭhaja-tatiyakkhara*), but that is incorrect.

The body is first, speech is second, and body-and-speech together are third; it is with reference to this that it is said “by the third. “Right there” means within the intermediate section itself (*antarapeyyāle*).
Regarding the word *adinnam* (not given): here, showing that the letter *a* becomes *na* and that the suffix *-ta* expresses the object of the action, he says, "not given by another.
In this context, by the phrase "by another," he shows that the suffix *-ta* expresses the object;
by the letter *na*, he shows the grammatical modification (*kāriya*) of the letter *a*. For what reason is it "unknown"? He says: "I am receiving... [and so forth].
“By the absence of volition. “Unknown” means not manifest. “Giving of actors’ performances and so forth” means the giving of all such things as actors’ performances.
“The bestowing of a bull” means the giving away of a bull.
This is stated by way of illustration; however, there is also the giving of men to women—both human and non-human—for the purpose of sexual intercourse.
It should be understood. Regarding "the gift of women": here too, the gift of any woman whatsoever to any man whatsoever should be understood.
"The gift of artful paintings" means the gift of artful paintings for the purpose of engaging in sexual intercourse. "Of the world" means by the world.
"Desire to speak" means the wish to speak. By the phrase "it is not easily dispelled," it is indicated that [this] must be dispelled by means of suffering.
"Difficult to dispel" means it is not easy to dispel; this is what is shown. "By means of a method" means by way of reasoning (*yutti*).
The connection is: "The Elder Phussadeva stood, it is said. This accusative case ending in *ekaṃsaṃ* is used in the sense of the locative. For the meaning is "on one shoulder.
"Having the Buddha as its object" means having the qualities of the Buddha as its object. "Māra" refers to Devaputtamāra.

"Has gone" is the connection [to the previous context]. "Cow-dung" means that which is spat out by a cow. "Old bull" means an aged ox. "Just like that" means having the very same nature as the scattering of cow-dung.
"In a particular manner" means performing it in a specific way. "Crooked-footed" means having deformed feet. "Scratching all around" means making a boundary and then scraping.
"A man who has gone astray" (*vigacchapuriso*) means a man who has undergone a change, or a man who is ugly. It is also read as "a man who is disfigured" (*vibhacchapuriso*).
*Pāṭho*: specifically, it means "a person who eats beautifully. This very reading is found in the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* (verse 102).
*Samantā*: on all sides of the monastery enveloped in darkness. *Māro siyā nu kho*: "Could it be Māra?"—this is the construction.
*Na asakkhiṃ iti āha*: "I was not able"—this is the construction. *Diṭṭhapubbo*: seen before. *Mahānubhāvo*: of great power, by virtue of his divine majesty.
"Of great power. *Iṅgha* is a particle used in the sense of exhortation; the meaning is "I urge you. "Your own form" means your personal manifestation.
"A form such as that" means a form similar to the personal manifestation of the Blessed Buddha. "Resembling that" means similar to that form.
It is "suitable" (*patirūpa*) in the sense of being similar, not a form that is identical in every respect. Something that is merely similar is called "resembling" (*patirūpaka*).
“Of similar form” means having a likeness. “One’s own personal existence” (*sakattabhāva*): this belongs to him, thus it is his own (*saka*); that very same personal existence is *sakattabhāva*;
that [is what is meant]. “He” refers to Māra. “How? means for what reason does the Blessed One not shine?
The meaning is: he certainly does shine. To establish that very point, it is said: “Completely free from lust, hatred, and delusion. “I have been deceived” means: I [have been deceived].
"I have been deceived. "What is there? means: what indeed is there? The intention is that he has no mind to deceive.
This is to be connected with the words "the young bhikkhu receives," and so forth.
The connection is: "the young bhikkhu stood. The connection is: "behind the rubbish-heap. [The word] "rubbish" (saṅkāraṃ).
"Discards these" means a rubbish heap (*saṅkārachaḍḍanī*). "The Elder named Tissaḍatta asked" is the connection [to the context]. "From the ship" means from the boat.
"A thousand questions" refers to a thousand inquiries regarding the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"He asked" means he questioned the youth. "He finished" means he completed the duties (*vatta*) to be performed on that day. "From the realm of the Yonakas."

"From the Yona country. "He recollected eight eons" means that upon seeing the courtyard of the stupa, his mind became serene, and through the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*), he recollected eight eons.
"A certain monk went" is the connection [of the sentence]. "The deities with flower-offerings attained their goal" means that having assumed human form, they attained their purpose.
