They stood. Therefore it was said: “Inhabitants of which village are you? The construction is: “In which village do you habitually dwell?
You are [inhabitants] of such-and-such. “Right here” means in this very place. “We stand” means we are standing; this is the construction.
“This talk” refers to the talk about to be spoken. “Is the minister’s son indeed handsome?”—this is the construction. “No.”
The connection is: "The relatives of the Elder Abhayatthera, the son of the minister, arrived. The connection is: "The Elder’s mother also sent [a message].

By the word *pi* ("also"), he refers back to the relatives. Showing the manner in which she sent [the message], he said: "My son," and so forth. The connection is: "The son of the minister ascended [the chariot].
The connection is: "The Elder Abhaya said. *Tenā* means by the son of the minister. *Yugaggāhaṃ* means...
Regarding the phrase "the grasping of the age," he said, "In a past existence... and so forth, revealing the statement:
"Having discarded refuse in the place properly swept by the Elder Mahallaka. The connection is: "The minister’s son discarded it.
"That" refers to the duty of sweeping. "Therein" refers to the statement: "The Teacher’s instruction has been carried out. Venerable Sāriputta...
The connection is: "He sat down, it is said. The connection is: "The Blessed One returned. "Of the feet" (*pādāni*) means the places where the feet stepped;
the meaning is "foot-shrines" (*pādacetiya*). The connection is: "The Elder sat down.
Having supported himself on his knees, the remainder of the text, "having paid homage to the foot-shrine," must be supplied. The construction is: "The Teacher knew my state of being seated, indeed."
For the particle *mesaddo* (the word *me*) depends on what precedes and follows it. *Codanā* means the attribution of fault. *Kāressāmi* means "I shall have [an image of] the One of Ten Powers made.

The connection is with the words "The Blessed One said. *Gatosi* means "you have gone"; the construction is: "It is not fitting for you who are wandering [thus]. *Tato* means from the time of the censure.
The connection is: "so much analysis is found. "Limit of speech" means the delimitation of words.
"This" refers to the discourse. The connection is: "this much speech. "Worthy of being taken" means approaching the state of being graspable;
the meaning is that it is fit to be grasped. "Those two" refers to the two roots. "Again, those" refers to the six origins of offenses which constitute the collection.
“Basis” (vatthu) refers to the basis for sexual intercourse and so forth. In the phrase “it is also thus” (itipi), the word “also” (pi) refers back to the first method.
In this context, in the first method there is no distinction between the origin and the root, whereas in the latter method there is a distinction in every respect.
Therefore, it should be understood that the latter method alone is more appropriate. By the word “is stilled” (vūpasammati), the meaning of the term “ceases” (nirujjhati) is indicated.
It shows cessation by complete eradication. By "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna) is meant through formal acts of discipline (*vinayakamma*) such as probation (*parivāsa*).
Showing the actual forms of the thirty-three roots, he says: "There are twelve roots for a legal issue involving dispute," and so forth. The connection is with the phrase "one root.
"Those" refers to the thirty-three roots. "From another" means in another [text]. By the passage beginning "eighteen grounds for schism," etc.
This shows the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) of the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). The construction is: "It arises depending upon the four duties of the Saṅgha.
"This" refers to the subject matter (*vatthu*). "The source (*nidāna*) of the seven" means the source consisting of the basis for the formulation of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).

"In this place" (*ettha*) means in this context. Regarding the phrase "he does not know the formulation" (*paññattiṃ na jānāti*), since it will later be stated, "he does not know the subsequent formulation" (*anupaññattiṃ na jānāti*), [it implies he does not know either].
He said, "he does not know the first promulgation," meaning that the first promulgation must be grasped.
Regarding the term *anupaññatti*, the prefix *anu* here does not mean "subsequent" (in the sense of following immediately); thus he said, "he does not know the repeated promulgation.

Furthermore, the sense of "afterward" is also appropriate, because it was promulgated after the first promulgation. Regarding the phrase *anusandhivacanapatha*, here [the reference is] to the connections...

Showing that this refers to the "path of speech" (*vacanapatha*) by way of the determination of the connection between the discourse, he says: “The subject matter (*vatthu*) by way of the determination of the sequence of the discussion.
“*Ñattikiccaṃ*” means the function of a motion (*ñatti*). Here, in the phrase “by means of the motion” (*ñattiyā*), the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of identity (*sāmyatthe*).

Furthermore, in connection with the verbal root *kara*, the instrumental case is also appropriate. And here, in the word “instrument” (*karaṇaṃ*), he shows that the suffix *-ya* has the sense of the object (*kammatthabhāva*).

He says, "In the formal acts consisting of a motion, a motion followed by one proclamation, and a motion followed by three proclamations," etc., to show that it is not only in the formal act consisting of a single motion (*ñattikamma*) that he does not know the function of the motion, but that he likewise does not know it in the formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) or a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*).

"Should be placed first" means he does not know that what is called a motion must be placed before the formal utterance (*kammavācā*); by this, he shows his lack of proficiency in the preliminary stage.
By the word “afterwards” (pacchā), he shows that it is not subsequent to other wholesome states. By the particle “pi” (also/even), he refers back to the first method.
By the phrase “does not know the time,” he shows the analytical statement (viggahavākya) for the compound *akālaññū*. Showing what “time” means, he says “unasked,” and so forth.
By the phrase “not knowing the benefit of the ascetic practices” (*dhutaṅga*), he shows the result for those who are dull-witted and deluded. Regarding the term *pāpiccho*:
“Having evil desires” means a longing for the acquisition of requisites; thus he said, “longing for the acquisition of requisites.

“Seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions” is *kāyacittaupadhiviveka*; it is a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*) with elision of the latter member in the preceding terms.
“Of this” refers to the forest-dweller. “This is the purpose of this” is *idamattha*; he has that as his purpose, hence *etadattha*.

This shows the meaning of the expression "this exists. Regarding the phrase "only fewness of wishes" (*appicchaññeva*) and so forth, he says "no other worldly bait whatsoever" to show that the word *eva* (only/just) must be excluded from those instances.

"Ninefold" means the ninefold Uposatha, which is threefold according to the day, likewise threefold according to the manner in which it is to be performed, and likewise threefold according to the person who performs it.
Because bodily misconduct and so forth do not lead to confidence (*pasāda*), nor conduce to confidence, they are therefore called "uninspiring" (*apāsādika*).
Hence it was said: "The 'uninspiring' refers to unwholesome [states] such as bodily misconduct. "Having transgressed the time" means having passed beyond the proper time for eating and so forth.
By this, the sense of "transgression" (*atikkamana*) is shown for the prefix *ati-* in the word *ativela*.
The phrase “excessively” (*ativela*) shows that it functions as an adverbial modifier for the word “while dwelling” (*viharato*). The construction is: “for a short time.
Showing that “entry” (*avataraṇa*) means “descent” (*otāra*), he says “descent. “In all cases” (*sabbattha*) means in all the sets of five.
Thus ends the construction of the commentary on the section on the sets of five.

326. Regarding the commentary on the section on the sixfold sets (*chakkavāra*) in the *Ekuttarikanaya*, the construction is as follows: "In the case of the sixfold sets, the meaning should be understood in this way. *Iti* means "thus. The construction is: "These are the six modes of proper conduct (*sāmīci*). *Tattha* means "in those six aspects. *Satisammosenā* means "by the absence of mindfulness.
*Tattha* means "among the fourteen supreme qualities. *Tato* means "from the set of six. *Ekaṃ apanetvā* means "having removed any one [of them]."
*Śeṣeṣu* means "in the remaining eight *paramas* out of the six *paramas*. *Anyāny api ṣaṭkāni* means "other hexads as well" than the first hexad;
that is, there are eight other hexads.
*Ṣaḍ āpattayaḥ* refers to "three hexads"; the construction is that there are three hexads spoken of as "six offenses. This refers to the two [sections] already mentioned.

Having made one [category]. "In bathing" means in the training rule (sikkhāpada) on bathing. "The two sets of six" refers to the two sets of six by way of taking up (*ādāya*) and undertaking (*samādāya*).
"In all cases" means in all the sets of six.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section on the sets of six.
The Explanation of the Section on Sevens in the Ekuttarikanaya:
327. The connection is: "having included [them] among the six forms of respectful conduct within the sevens. "In that very [place]" means in the Samathakkhandhaka itself.
"In the Campeyyaka" means in the Campeyyakkhandhaka. Regarding the word "asaddhammā," there is a compound based on dependence on breaking and dependence on similarity.

Showing this, he said, “The qualities of the non-existent,” and so forth. Therein, by the phrase “the qualities of the non-existent” (*asataṃ dhammā*), he shows a genitive-dependent compound (*bhedanissita-samāsa*);
by the phrase “or qualities that are non-existent” (*asanto vā dhammā*), he shows a coordinate-dependent compound (*tulyanissita-samāsa*).
“In all cases” (*sabbattha*) means in all seven [grammatical] cases. The remainder is easy to understand.
Thus ends the exposition of the commentary on the section of seven.
Regarding the commentary on the section of eight in the method of numerical progression (ekuttarikanaya),
[the author] says "We do not," etc., showing the manner of teaching and the locations for teaching the eight benefits and so forth within the sets of eight.
In that context, by the phrase "We shall not... [etc.]... do," he shows the manner of the teaching;
by the phrase "in the Kosambaka-kkhandhaka," he shows the location of the teaching. "That too" refers to the second group of eight.
The connection is with the words "spoken in the Thirteen. Regarding the phrase "he corrupts families," here "corrupts" (*dūseti*) is the verb expressing the action.
Showing this, he said “by means of flowers,” and so forth. The construction is: “he corrupts by these eight.
By the phrase “by gain,” and so forth, he shows the actual nature of the “eight things contrary to the true Dhamma” (*asaddhamma*) mentioned here. *Sārāga* means passionate attachment;
the sense is “intense coloring. *Paṭivirodha* means hatred (*dosa*). For it is because it opposes [the mind] in the face of non-gain and so forth that it is so called.
It is called "contradiction. "In the Pāḷi" means in the Vinaya-pāḷi.
The two verses beginning with "pāṇaṃ" are composed of twelve syllables. Because the third quarter of the first verse is joined with the word *cariya*, it has one syllable in excess.
Here, however, is the construction: "One should not kill, nor should one cause to kill, living beings (*pāṇa*)," and so forth.
One should not take, nor should one seize; one should not speak falsehood, nor utter words that are untrue. One should not be a drinker of intoxicants, nor should one indulge in drinking intoxicants.
One should abstain from unchastity and sexual intercourse. One should not eat at night, nor should one consume food outside of the proper time.

One should not wear garlands, nor should one use perfumes. One should sleep on a mat upon the ground rather than on a high bed. For this is the eightfold Uposatha, which the Buddhas have proclaimed as the means for reaching the end of suffering—so say the wise.
“Saṅghabhedaka” refers to the Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka. “Of those very [women]” means of the bhikkhunīs alone.
Although the expression “the laywoman requests eight boons” is a general statement, it has a specific referent due to the context and other factors; thus he says, “Visākhā.
For she is called Visākhā because she possesses various (vi-) branches (sākhā) consisting of her sons and grandsons.
"In all cases" means in all the groups of eight. The remainder is easy to understand.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section on the groups of eight.
Now begins the commentary on the section on the groups of nine in the method of numerical progression (*ekuttarikanaya*).

329. Regarding the phrase "he has practiced among novices" and so forth: by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the author] includes such forms as "he practices" (*carati*) and "he will practice" (*carissati*).

"What can be obtained here?"—here, "this" (*taṃ*) refers to the practice of what is harmful or the provocation of anger. "What" (*ku*) means for what reason. "Here" (*ettha*) means in this person who practices what is harmful.
"Can be obtained" (*labbhā*) means found; it means it is possible to obtain, yet it is said "it cannot be obtained" (*na labbhā eva*).

This is the meaning. The construction is: "for the sake of nine monks. *Taṇhā* (craving) refers to craving for seeking (*esanataṇhā*) among the two types of craving, namely craving for seeking and craving for what is sought.
*Paṭicca* (dependent upon) means having taken as a basis. *Pariyesanā* (seeking) is repeated searching. *Lābha* (gain) is the acquisition of objects such as forms and so forth.
*Vinicchaya* (decision) is fourfold, consisting of knowledge, craving, views, and applied thought. For the Dhamma is fourfold.
It is called "determination" (*vinicchaya*) because one determines by means of such thoughts as, "This much shall be mine. "Lustful passion" (*chandārāga*) is intense greed.
"Clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) is a strong conviction that "this is I, this is mine. "Possession" (*pariggaha*) is grasping after having delimited [an object] by way of craving and views.
"Avarice" (*macchariya*) is the inability to endure others sharing in one's own state. "Guarding" (*ārakkha*)...
"Guarding" (*ārakkha*) means protecting thoroughly by means of locking doors, placing things in chests, and so forth. "On account of guarding" (*ārakkhādhikaraṇa*) means for the purpose of guarding;
here the nominative case is used in the sense of a causal factor (*hetvattha*). "Taking up the staff" (*daṇḍādāna*) refers to taking up a staff for the purpose of restraining others.
Likewise, "taking up the sword" (*satthādāna*) refers to taking up a sword with a single edge and so forth. "Quarrel" (*kalaha*) includes both physical quarrels and [verbal ones].
“Quarrel of speech” (*vācākalaḥo*) means the same. “Strife” (*viggaho*) is grasping by way of opposition.
“Dispute” (*vivādo*) is speaking by way of opposition. Speaking with a lack of respect, saying “you, you,” is *tuvaṃtuvaṃ-vādo*.
Speaking by way of slander is *pesuñña-vādo*. Speaking by way of falsehood is *musā-vādo*. Taking up sticks and taking up weapons, as well as quarreling and strife, constitute dispute.

“Tuvaṃ-tuvaṃ-vāda,” “pesuñña-vāda,” “musāvāda,” “daṇḍādāna”… [and so on] … up to “musāvāda. Regarding the term *musāvāda*, the word *vāda* (speech) should also be construed here with both “*tuvaṃ tuvaṃ*” and “*pesuñña*. The construction is: “those occurring as ‘I am superior,’ etc.
From the moment they have been determined, they must not be altered; this is called “determination and alteration” (*adhiṭṭhāna-vikappana*).
The intention is that it should not be made [into a formal assignment] on one side, nor should it be transferred once it has been determined.

"He diverts a diverted gain" is the connection. "Of these very gifts" means of these very unrighteous gifts. "Inclined toward the Saṅgha" means leaning toward the Saṅgha, or the gain has been directed toward the Saṅgha;
this is the connection. It is called "inclined" (*ninna*) because it leans toward or is directed toward the Saṅgha. "Of those very [people]"...
Of those very three types of righteous gifts (*dhammikadāna*). By combining each of the three recipients of the gift and the three modes of enjoyment, a group of nine (*navaka*) should be understood.
"In that very [place]" means in the *Samathakkhandhaka* itself. "Of the Chapter on Exhortation" means of the Chapter on the Exhortation of Bhikkhunīs.
"In that very [place]" means in the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*) of the Chapter on Exhortation. "In all cases" means in all the groups of nine.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the section of nines.
The Commentary on the Section of Tens in the Method of Single Increments (Ekuttarikanaya): 330.

Regarding the "tens," the phrase *aṭṭhāne vā pana* means "or even without cause. *Tattha* means "in the case of the nines. The phrase *natthi dinnam ity ādi-vasena* means "by way of [the thought] 'there is no gift,' and so forth."
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the nine types of nihilists (*natthika*)—beginning with "there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation"—are to be included.
By the phrase "by way of 'the world is eternal,' etc.," the word "etc. includes the nine types of extremist views (*antaggāhika*), beginning with "the world is not eternal.
The ten rightnesses (*sammatta*) are the opposites of the ten wrongnesses (*micchatta*); they are right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*), and so forth.
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation—thus ten dangers have been pointed out;
this is the connection [of the sentence]. "Rat-scratched" means gnawed by a mouse;
for here the verbal root *khad* has the sense of eating. "Fire-burnt" means burnt by fire. "Among these" means among these ten kinds of rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*).
"Either a bathing-cloth or a bodice" means either the bathing-cloth or the bodice of the bhikkhunīs.
Here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an indefinite option.
"A leaf-mat" is included within the category of grass-mats. "In all cases" means in all ten sections.
Thus ends the exposition of the section on tens.
The method of numerical progression (*ekuttarikanaya*): Exposition of the section on elevens (331).
Regarding the "elevens," "grass sandals" refers to sandals made of grass other than *muñja* and *pabbaja*. They are included within the category of wooden sandals.
"Wooden sandals" refers specifically to the inclusion [of the rule]. In the phrase "either made of copper or made of wood," the word *vā* (or) has the sense of an indefinite option.
"A noseless one," and so forth, are explained in the Bhikkhunī-kkhandhaka. "All those" means all those types of knots. "By a naked one" means by one who is unclothed (*acelaka*).
"All those" means all those persons not to be saluted. "In the former" means in the Dasaka. "In the Kamma-vagga" means at the end of the Kamma-vagga.
Thus, the construction is: "That which a bhikkhu would not encounter—that which he has not encountered—is an impossible situation, it is without occasion.
For this being so, the word *yaṃ* (that which) refers back to the action (*kiriyā*). Alternatively, the construction is:
"That reason by which he would not encounter [it]—that reason is an impossible situation. The construction is: "Samādhi not yet attained. *Saddhammāssa* means "of the true Dhamma."
*Assa*. For that monk who reviles and insults, the True Dhamma does not become purified nor is it cleansed;
such is the meaning. *Rogātaṅkam*: a disease characterized as an affliction (*ātaṅka*). *Nirayaṃ upapajjati*: he is reborn in hell.
Regarding the word *upapajjati*, because it is joined with the prefix *upa*, which is a term expressive of action, [it is used] here in the phrase "hell" (*nirayaṃ*).
The accusative case should be understood here as having the sense of the locative. Regarding the word *āsevitāya* (cultivated):
since the prefix *ā-* has the sense of "commencement" (*ādikamma*) here, he says, "cultivated from the very beginning.

By the word *nipphāditāya* (accomplished), he shows that in the phrase *bhāvitāya* (developed), the root *bhū-* has the sense of "existence" (*satta*); by the word *vaḍḍhitāya* (increased), he shows it has the sense of "growth" (*vaḍḍhana*).

[The text] shows this. Regarding the phrase "by being practiced frequently" (*bahulīkatāya*): here, "frequently" (*bahula*) means "repeatedly" in its sense; thus he says, "by having been done again and again.
Regarding the phrase "similar to a well-yoked vehicle": it is similar to a vehicle that is well-yoked.

By this, in the expression "made into a vehicle" (*yānīkatāya*), it is not made into just any kind of vehicle; rather, because it can be mounted at whatever moment one desires, it is like a well-yoked vehicle.
He shows that it is "as if made. The construction is: "just as there is a foundation when it is being performed.

Regarding the term *vatthukatāya*, he shows here that the word *vatthu* has the meaning of "foundation" (*patiṭṭha*). The etymological meaning of the word *vatthu* should be understood as: "that wherein one dwells or stands is a *vatthu*.
Regarding the term *anuṭṭhitāya*, here the prefix *anu-* has the sense of "not cut off," and the verbal root *ṭhā-* has the sense of "arising."
Showing this, he says: “because it has proceeded little by little. By the word “samantato” (all around), he shows that the prefix *pari-* here has the sense of “all around” (*samanta*).
By the word “abhivaḍḍhitāya” (fully increased), he shows that the verbal root *ci* has the sense of “increasing.
“Samāraddhāya” means “having been fully accomplished”; for the verbal root *rādh* has the sense of “accomplishing. By the phrase “vasībhāvaṃ upanītāya” (brought to mastery), [he shows...]

He shows that meaning by way of the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). In order to show the method of implication (*atthāpattinaya*) for the statement, “One does not see an evil dream,” he says, “But a auspicious one,” and so forth.
The connection is: “a dream that has become a cause for growth (*vuddhi*); it is a dream that serves as the cause for growth.
Regarding the phrase “deities protect [him],” although this is stated in general terms, it should be understood specifically as the deities who provide protection (*ārakkhadevatā*).
He said, "The guardian deities. The "guardian deities" (ārakkhadevatā) refer to the earth-deities and so forth. "Khippaṃ" is a neuter gerundive.
By this, he shows that in the phrase "the mind is quickly composed" (tuvaṭaṃ cittaṃ), the word *tuvaṭa* is a synonym for "quickly" (*khippa*).

Regarding the phrase "not penetrating further" (*uttarimappaṭivijjhanto*), because the term "further" (*uttari*) requires a limit, one must consider both its limit and the fact that the word *uttari* here denotes *arahatta* (Arhatship).
Showing the sense of realization for the verb root *vid*, he said, "From the jhāna of loving-kindness," and so forth.
Therein, by "from the jhāna of loving-kindness," he shows the limit; by "Arahatta," he shows the actual meaning of the word "further" (*uttari*);
and by "not realizing," he shows the sense of realization for the verb root *vid*. "In all cases" means in all the eleven sets.
Thus ends the summary of the commentary on the *Ekuttarika* [Nikāya],
concluding with the commentary on the section of eleven items.
332. Regarding the response to the questions on the Uposatha and so forth, the construction is:
"The meaning should be understood in this way in the response. The construction is: "The concord of body, etc. The act of reinstatement (*osāraṇakiriyā*) is the act of speaking.
"Having brought forward the consent and the invitation" means having brought forward both the consent (*chanda*) and the invitation (*pavāraṇa*). "The discourse on the invitation" (*pavāraṇākathā*).
The discourse on the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) begins with the words, “Venerable Sir, I invite the Saṅgha,” and so forth.

Regarding the formal acts such as the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*), what is meant by the “matter” (*vatthu*)? Who is meant by the “person” (*puggala*)? Someone said: “What is called the ‘matter’,” and so forth.

In that context, “by which matter” means by which matter—such as one who creates discord—that serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the cause (*hetu*). “By whom” means by the person acting as the agent (*kartṛ*). “Done” means...

Regarding the connection: the phrase “of each respective formal proclamation” (*tassā tassā kammavācāya*) has an *avayavi-sambandha* (part-whole relationship) with the phrase “the concluding statement” (*avasānavacana*).
“In all cases” (*sabbattha*) means in all the responses to the questions.
Thus concludes the explanation of the application of the questions and responses concerning the Uposatha and other ceremonies.
[The section on] "In its entirety. 334.

In the phrase "in the exposition of the purpose" (*atthavasapakaraṇe*), it is a container based on the whole (*avayavi-ādhāra*). In the phrase "the ten purposes," etc., it is a container based on the parts (*avayava-ādhāra*). "Which" (*yaṃ*)... [refers to the former].

“Vacanaṃ” means the statement. “Each successive phrase” (*uparimaṃ uparimaṃ padaṃ*) refers to each subsequent phrase stated in ascending order, such as “for the sake of the Saṅgha’s comfort” (*saṅghaphāsutāya*), and so forth.

“Of each preceding phrase” (*heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa padassa*) refers to each preceding phrase stated in descending order, such as “for the sake of the Saṅgha’s well-being” (*saṅghasuṭṭhutāya*), and so forth.
The construction is: “that which has been stated as this hundred phrases. “Therein” (*tattha*) means in that hundred phrases; this is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
“*Atthasataṃ*” means a hundred meanings (*abhidheyya*). “*Dhammasataṃ*” means a hundred designations (*abhidhāna*); this is the meaning of “*pāḷisataṃ*” (a hundred texts).
By saying “*atha vā*” and so forth, he shows an alternative interpretation of the terms “*atthasataṃ dhammasataṃ*. Therein, the construction is:
“of those ten purposes (*atthavasa*) on account of which [the teaching] was established. Regarding the ten purposes...
The construction is: "of those [qualities] previously described, for the sake of the ten and eight benefits. The connection is: "described in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
Regarding the phrase "in that [passage]," it refers to the reading beginning with "for the welfare of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasuṭṭhutāya*). "Suṭṭhu deva" means "well, O Great King.

He is called a "deva" because he shines (*dibbati*) by means of the power of his commands, the power of his wealth, and the power of his sovereignty. And as for "whoever"—this refers to a householder.

The connection is: "whether a householder or one gone forth, he accepts. "Therefore" means: because it leads to welfare and happiness, therefore. The connection is: "having shown the benefit, I shall prescribe [it].
The construction is: "I shall not prescribe it by way of overcoming [objections].

"Here" refers to this treatise on the purpose (*atthavasapakaraṇa*). "Of those that illuminate that meaning": that very meaning is "that meaning" (*tadattha*); those which illuminate it are "those that illuminate that meaning."
"Those which illuminate that meaning, of them. The connection is: "they are now to be understood. They are called *atthajotakā* (meaning-illuminators) because they illuminate the meaning;
these are words (*saddā*). They are called *niruttiyo* (linguistic expressions) because the meaning is expressed by means of these linguistic formulations, having been extracted or determined.
In the verse beginning with "The hundred meanings," the construction should be made as follows: "In this treatise, for the sake of the meaning, a hundred meanings are to be understood," and so forth.

*Iti hīti* means *iti eva*. The word *hi* has the sense of the word *eva*. *Idam* refers to the statement beginning with “one hundred and eight,” and it is connected with the word *vuttam* (was said).
*Etam* is connected with the phrase “depending on the meaning as it was stated.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Exposition of the Mahāvagga is concluded.
The First Collection of Verses.
Commentary on the Training Rules Enacted in the Seven Cities: 335.
Regarding the word *ekaṃsaṃ*, he says “on one shoulder” (*ekasmiṃ aṃse*), because here the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative.

“Radiant with the joining of ten fingernails” (*dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ*) means shining intensely due to the collection of the ten nails. Here, by the term “radiant” (*samujjalaṃ*), the meaning of the word *añjali* [is implied].
The meaning is shown as follows: it is called *añjali* because one pays respect and joins [the hands] facing forward, or because it shines (*dibbati*).
Regarding the phrase *āsīsamānarūpo va*, he says "as if desiring [something] in return" (*paccāsīsamānarūpo viya*) in order to reject the interpretation that it means "one who is merely desiring.
Here, by the word *viya*, he shows that after making the word-analysis *āsīsamāno iva*, the particle *iva* indicates the sense of a simile.

Regarding the word *kissā*, he says "for what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) to show that the sixth case ending (*chaṭṭhīvibhatti*) is used here in the sense of the instrument. The word *idha* refers to the place where I am sitting.
By the word *āgato* ("has come"), he shows that in the phrase "come here" (*idhamāgato*), the letter *m* is merely for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).
The connection is: "he answered this [question] to Upāli. The word *sabbattha* means "in all questions. The word *iti* means "thus."
*Tattha* means "in the response. Regarding the phrase *Bhaddako te ummaṅgo*, he says "your questions are excellent" because here the word *ummaṅga* is a synonym for "question.
In that context, *te* means "your. To the question "Why is a question called an *ummaṅga*? he replies with "For a question... and so forth. The construction is:
since it is called an *ummaṅga*, therefore a question is named an *ummaṅga*. "Because it stands having emerged" (*ummujjitvā ṭhitattā*).
"By this one emerges," thus he shows the etymological meaning of *ummaṅga*. In the verbal root *muj*, the letter *u* becomes *a*;

the meaning is that one emerges from the "water" known as the darkness of ignorance (*avijjā*). By stating "tagghā," he shows that the particle *taggha* has the sense of "good" (*sādhu*), saying "because" (*yasmā*) and so forth.
By the phrase "in the sense of receiving" (*sampaṭicchanatthe*), he shows that the word *taggha* has the sense of "excellent. *Taggha*...
The meaning is "it is good. "Only three" refers to these three alone: "having composed himself, he fans [the fire]" is one; "with material food" is one;
and "with rice-grains" is one. This is the commentary on the four failures (vipatti).
Regarding the phrase *yaṃ taṃ pucchimhā*: here, because of the elision of the vowel following a nasal consonant (*niggahita*), it says “*yaṃ taṃ apucchimhā*.
In that context, *yaṃ* refers to the question; *taṃ* refers to you. There is also a reading *tvaṃ*, which has the same meaning.
*Taṃ tadeva* means that very same question. *Aññathā* means in another manner.
Regarding the statement, "Those which are grave offenses (duṭṭhulla) are failures in virtue (sīlavipatti)": here, one might ask, is there not no question being asked about a failure in virtue?
Why, then, was the answer "those are failures in virtue" given? To this he says, "Even though," and so forth. "This" refers to the statement, "Those which are grave offenses are failures in virtue.
Expounding upon that very meaning, he says, "For in the four [cases]," and so forth. "Having stated" means having stated it in brief.
“Of the three failures” means of the three failures remaining after the failure of virtue (*sīlavipatti*). “Therein” refers to the statement beginning with “a grave offense” (*thullaccaya*).
To show the agent of the word “misrepresenting,” he says “speaking. By the phrase “thus indeed,” etc., he shows the manner of speaking.

With the words “this [is] by six,” he shows that here the particle *sā* (this) is a mere poetic ornament for the sentence. “By this much” means by this much—the mere statement beginning with “a grave offense. The connection is: “it is answered.”

337. Regarding the commentary on "How many are the cutting [factors]? and so forth: in order to show that these questions lack the nature of a sequential inquiry (*anusandhi*), he says, "But because...

and so on. For questions are of two kinds: those with a sequential connection and those without a sequential connection. Among these, by way of the answer, [the first kind is] through a sequential connection.

A question is called a "connected question" (*anusandhipucchā*) when it does not disregard the answer; a question asked according to one's own whim, without regard for the answer, is called a "disconnected question" (*an-anusandhipucchā*).
Their detailed exposition should be sought in the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* and other such works.

Here too, it is called a "connected question" because of the connection established by the answer, "There are eleven [cases] up to the third time. For it is connected [to the preceding] by the word "but" (*pana*), as in "but because it has been answered."
“By way of enumeration” means by way of the number eleven, or by way of what is dependent.

“Precisely by way of the connection of the enumeration” means precisely by way of the connection following the enumeration [of the question] “How many? “Of these” refers to the questions. “Therein” refers to the text beginning with “six things that cut off.
“This very” means this very statement. “Unprecedented” means not stated before; the sense is that it is ancient and new. That which...

Regarding the word *panetaṃ*: this refers to the statement [beginning with] “*soḷasā*. By means of this term, he shows that the reading *soḷasā* is also appropriate, having substituted the letter *ḷ* for the letter *d* in the word *sodasa*.
Regarding the phrase “*jānanti paññattā*,” he says “*jānaṃ evaṃ vatvā paññattā*” to show how it should be construed by supplying the ellipsis of the words “*evaṃ vatvā*” (having spoken thus).
The meaning is: "Training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed as 'one who knows'. "In this way" means according to the method that will be explained.
Regarding the phrase "should enter," the word *iti* here signifies completion. The construction is: "It should be understood thus.
This concludes the commentary on the non-common [offenses] and so forth.
338. “The former question” refers to the question previously stated, beginning with “How many are the cutting [fetters]?
and so forth. “Therein” refers to the reading beginning with “Two hundred and twenty. By saying “with two undetermined [fetters],” he shows that this is a coordinate dvanda compound;
thus he says, “by two undetermined [fetters]. By the word “together with,” he indicates that the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (sahādiyoga).
In this verse, the construction should be made as “the washing and the training rule,” and so forth. “Two hairs” refers to the two training rules concerning sheep’s wool (*eḷakaloma*).
The construction of the one and a half verses beginning with “entirely” is indeed easy to understand.
Regarding the phrase “he expels ten from the Saṅgha,” the method of construction here is to take it as “ten who are expelled from the Saṅgha,” as stated in that way.
Showing this, he said: “He is expelled from the Saṅgha,” and so forth. *Tattha* means in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga.
*Tathā* means just as [the minor rules] are; such is the meaning. *Iti* means thus.
*Tesam* refers to the Pārājika offenses. The construction is: they are difficult to approach, like venomous black snakes and the like. “*Durūpagamanā*... [is the phrase].
By this, he shows the meaning of "going" (*gati*) for the six elements. "Difficult to assail" (*durāsajjana*) means they are to be assailed with difficulty;
the sense is that they are not easy to assail. "Equal similes" (*samūpamā*) means identical similes. Showing the manner of the equal simile, he said "just as," and so forth.
"Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means common to the eight *pārājika* rules. The connection is "of each individual *pārājika*. "Non-increase" (*avirūḷhī*).
In the phrase "they become," he says "just as these" and so forth, showing the method of application by making clear the relationship between the simile and the subject of comparison.
"Of a nature not to grow" means having the inherent quality of not growing. "By way of their natural virtue" means by way of their being naturally virtuous;
there is also a reading "by way of the absence of natural virtue," meaning by way of the absence of natural virtue—that is, because of its absence.
The meaning is as follows. "By this much" means by the mere statement beginning with "There are eight pārājikas"; it is connected with the phrase "is shown.
"Classifications" (vibhattiyo) means they are to be classified according to the pārājikas and so forth. "In that context" refers to the textual passage beginning with "twenty-three saṅghādisesas.
"A comprehensive statement" means [a statement] regarding all three methods of settling disputes (samatha), and all...

This is a summary statement regarding the methods for settling offenses (*āpatti-samatha*). “By two methods of settlement” means by two methods: namely, by face-to-face resolution (*sammukhā-vinaya*) and by acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññāta-karaṇa*).
“This” refers to the statement: “There are two Uposathas and two Pavāraṇās. “Divisions” (*vibhajanāni*) refers to the act of dividing those things that are to be divided.

It is stated by way of existence because of its inseparable connection; therefore, the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*) of "case endings" (*vibhattiyo*) should be understood as "those which are to be analyzed.
The construction is: "These other case endings also exist. This provides another method of interpretation for the statement made previously:
"This was said merely to show the case endings, not by way of pacification through the means of tranquility (*samatha*). This is a different method of interpretation from the previous one.
Showing this, he says “Alternatively,” and so forth. The word “these case-endings” (*imāpi vibhattiyo*) is the unstated object (*avuttakamma*) for the word “depending on” (*nissāya*).
The connection is: “they incur [them] depending on. “Those” (*tā*) refers to the offenses. “By those very modes mentioned” means by those very modes mentioned as the three methods of settling.
“Rooted in those” (*taṃmūlikānaṃ*): those very [acts] such as the Uposatha are the root of these, thus they are “rooted in those”; [the word refers to] them.
By this metaphorical designation (*kāriyūpacāra*), he shows the method already stated. "Those classifications" refers to the classifications such as the Uposatha and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the offenses of *pārājika* and so on:
the connection is "having thus answered. The construction is "that which is called an offense of *pārājika*. "An offense of *pārājika*"—

The *pārājika* is defined as an offense (*āpatti*). By the phrase "one who has incurred defeat" (*parājayamāpanno*), the etymological meaning of *pārājika* is shown: it is so called because it defeats the person from the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
The suffix *ṇya* expresses the sense of being caused by; the letter *y* is replaced by *k*. *Cuto* means one who has fallen away.
*Paraddho* means one who has failed. *Bhaṭṭho* means one who has fallen. *Niraṅkato* means one who has been expelled from the Saṅgha.
“Not expelled from that person” means that he has not been removed from that person by being led out from the Saṅgha;
the meaning is “not having been expelled. By the phrase “divided into the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so forth,” he shows the nature of communal living (*saṃvāsa*).

Disregarding the literal phrasing, it is said: “this is an offense. “This indeed” means this which will be explained as follows. “In this” refers to the verse. “Therefore, for that reason” [is the meaning].
Here, by the word "therefore" (*tasmā*), the causal sense of the word "by that" (*tena*) is shown. "Here" refers to the second verse.
The connection is with the phrase "must be desired at the beginning. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly.

"Here" refers to the four formal acts, such as the granting of the *parivāsa* probation. The meaning of the expression beginning with "the Saṅgha" is a compound consisting of three words, where the case endings are split and the sense is external (*bahirattha*).
The word *ceva* (and) indicates that in the remaining words beginning with *sadda*, both members of the compound are equally predominant.
The word *icchitabbo* (to be desired) is inserted for the sake of the action, because grammatical agents require an action. *Assa* means "of the offense";

by this, he shows it to be a separate word. Some say that by adding the suffix *-tabb-*, which expresses the sense of being desired, it becomes a derivative (*taddhita*) form. However, this method is weak.

Now, the weighty method here is as follows: *ādi* (beginning) and *sesa* (remainder) constitute *ādisesa*; since the Saṅgha is desired among those things that are beginnings and remainders, it is called *saṅghādisesa*.
Regarding the phrase "the rule is made non-univocal": here, "rule" (*pada*) refers to the training precept (*sikkhāpada*).

Showing that it is "made non-univocal" (*anekaṃsikata*) because it is established by means of non-univocality, he said: "Because this training precept was made non-univocal. Because it was so made, it is therefore called "undetermined" (*aniyata*).

The construction is: "it is called" (*pavuccati*). "Therein" (*tattha*) refers to that which is unspecified. "Wherein" (*yattha*) refers to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "That too" (*so pi*) refers to the dhamma of the training rule as well. "In transgressions" (*accayeṣu*) means in faults (*dosesu*).
For they are called "transgressions" (*accaya*) because they go beyond, proceed toward, and occur outside of what is faultless.

"By that" (*tena*) means by the transgression. "Coarse" (*thūla*) means gross (*oḷārika*). By the word "because of its coarseness" (*thūlattā*), [the meaning of] "by this" (*ten' etaṃ*) in this context [is explained].
By this, he shows the sense of the word *tena* as "cause. The connection is with the phrase "the grossness of the transgression" (*accayassa thūlattā*). "This" refers to the nature of the offense.
With this verse, he shows the etymological meaning of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) as "a gross transgression" (*thūlo accayo*) among other light offenses.
It should be understood that when there is a doubling [of the vowel], it becomes short due to the subsequent conjunct consonant.

Since that [act] belongs to it, the analysis of the term shows it is called *nissaggiya*.

By the word *kusaladhamma*, only wholesome consciousness (*kusalacitta*) is to be understood; thus he says, “wholesome consciousness, which is reckoned as a wholesome state. By the phrase “it causes the mind to fall,” he shows the analysis of the term *pācittiya*: it is called *pācittiya* because it causes the mind to fall (*pātetī*). Here...
What should have been said as “*cittapātiyan*” (falling from the mind), by means of a transposition of words (*padavipariyāya*) and the elision of the letter *t*, it is stated as “*pācittiyan*.
For the method of the Pāḷi is indeed inconceivable. The suffix *ṇya* expresses the sense of being caused by something.

Now, is not the derivation of the word “*pācittiyan*” already established by the phrase “it causes one to fall away from wholesome states” (*pāteti kusalaṃ dhamman*)? Why, then, [is it said that] one “offends”?
Because it is stated [in the text] as "a place for deluding the mind," he said, "But as for that which... and so forth. The connection is with the word "because it occurs.
Why was it stated, "A bhikkhu who is a stranger... and so forth, without showing the etymology of the *pāṭidesanīya* rules? He said:

"Precisely for the purpose of showing the reason for the state of being censurable as mentioned. By the phrase "because they must be confessed," [it refers to] the method of confessing other offenses.
By stating "to be censured" (*gārayha*) and so forth separately, [the author] shows the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) as "those to be confessed" (*pāṭidesanīya*).
Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*), he says "badly done, or deformedly done," demonstrating that here the prefix *du-* has the sense of "badly" and the sense of "deformed.
"That" refers to the action. Furthermore, the connection is: "that very thing, namely the offense of wrong-doing, is a 'stumbling-block' (*khalita*)."

"Assā" means "of an offense of wrong-doing" (dukkaṭa). The construction is: "Its meaning should be understood in this way. "Hi" signifies "in detail" (vitthāra). "Yaṃ pāpaṃ" is the construction [meaning] "whatever evil.
"Yadi" means "then" (atha); for the word *yadi* is a synonym for *atha*. "Idampi" connects as follows: "this action too is evil.
By the word "lapita," he shows that the verbal root *bhās* has the sense of "speaking" in the phrase "durābhaṭṭhaṃ. "Yaṃ" refers to the speech.

It is the expression for speech (*vacanavācaka*). The construction is: "Because that speech is defiled. The construction [continues]: "How is it defiled?
By the word "because" (*yasmā*), he shows that the pronoun *yaṃ* has the sense of a reason. The word "that" (*taṃ*) is the subject.
"This is called thus" (*etaṃ iti vuccati*) is the term to be commented upon. "This is called 'ill-spoken'" (*dubbhāsitaṃ iti etaṃ vuccati*) is the commentarial phrase.
“*Etanti etan*” means “this is the word,” this is the meaning. “*Ettha*” refers to the *sekhiya* verses.

“*Idan*” is the statement that illustrates the derivation of the offenses; it is connected with the word “*vutta*” (spoken). To the question, “For the purpose of illustrating what was it spoken? he says: “For the purpose of illustrating the meaning that has been included.

“*Tattha*” refers to the statement beginning with “*Channam ativassatī*” (“The rain leaks through what is covered”). “*Gehan*” means a natural house. The construction is: “but this [is called] a *gehan*.”
Expanding upon this, he said, “Indeed, regarding a root offense,” and so forth. Having stated “uncovered,” he said “well-covered” to demonstrate its meaning.
“Covered” means not covered. Expanding upon the state of not being excessively rained upon, he said, “Indeed, regarding a root offense,” and so forth.
The connection is: “A monk who avoids [the rain] does not incur [the offense]. “In the pure portion” means in the part that is pure. And “therefore.”
“By that” (*tenā*) and “by that reason” (*tena kāraṇena*) are for the most part identical in meaning; therefore, it is said “by that reason. “And thus this is disclosed” (*evaṃ cetaṃ vivaṭaṃ*):
the construction is “if this [place] is covered, it is disclosed in this way.
“Of those being overwhelmed” (*paripātiyamānānaṃ*) means “of those being overcome. By the phrase “the forest is a thicket of trees, etc.,” the word *pavana* [is explained].

This shows that the word *pada* has the sense of "forest. Having rejected the meanings such as "state of existence" (*bhava*) for the word *gati*, he says "it is a refuge" (*paṭissaraṇaṃ hoti*) to show that it carries the meaning of "protection" (*paṭissaraṇa*). "That" refers to the forest. "They" refers to the deer.
By the word "breathing in," the meaning "seeing" should also be understood because they are inseparable; thus, they are performing *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).
Meaning: “Space” (ākāsa) refers to the cloudless sky. “Of birds” (pakkhīnaṃ) means of those that fly through the air.
By the phrase “of all conditioned phenomena” (sabbesaṃ saṅkhatadhammānaṃ), he shows that in this context [the word] “phenomena” (dhammānaṃ) must be understood specifically as conditioned phenomena.
By the phrase “or destruction” (vināso vā), he shows that the word *vibhava* denotes destruction (*vināsa*). “Of them” (tesaṃ) means of all conditioned phenomena. “Gati” means...
A foundation. Why is non-existence (*vibhava*) the destination of phenomena? To this he says, “For not...,” and so forth. “For” (*hi*) means because.

“They” (*te*) refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*). “Destruction” (*vināsam*) means non-existence. “Even for a very long time” (*suciram-pi*) means even for a period of eighty years or more.
“Nirvana is the destination of the Arahant” is the phrase to be praised. By the words “of one whose taints are exhausted” (*khīṇāsavassa*), the meaning of the term “Arahant” is [explained].
It shows this. By the phrase “the element of Nibbāna without residue,” it shows the specific Nibbāna intended here by the word “Nibbāna.
A *gāthāsaṅgaṇika* is that wherein various meanings are collected and enumerated within a verse.
Thus ends the exegesis of the first *gāthāsaṅgaṇika*.
The explanation of the division of legal issues (*adhikaraṇabheda*) beginning with reopening a settled case (*ukkoṭanabhedādi*): 340.
The construction is that the meaning should be understood thus regarding the division of legal issues. The connection is that [the author] spoke in order to demonstrate this. Two...
Regarding the term *samatha*, in order to show the nature of the two kinds of *samatha*, he says: "the *sammukhāvinaya* and the *yebhuyyasika*.
By the word "he rejects" (*paṭisedheti*), he shows that in the phrase "he reopens" (*ukkoṭeti*), the root *kuṭ* has the sense of cutting (*chedana*) in its underlying meaning.
The meaning is that "cutting" in this context refers, in substance, to the rejection of the *samatha*.

341. Regarding the phrase "among the twelve reopenings" (*dvādasasu ukkoṭesu*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*). In the expression "an act not performed, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) includes two reopenings: "an ill-performed act" and "an act to be done again.

In the expression "an act not struck down, etc.," the word "etc. includes two reopenings: "ill-struck down" and "to be struck down again. In the expression "not adjudicated, etc.," [the word "etc. includes...]
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the two reopenings (*ukkoṭa*)—"that which was wrongly decided should be decided again"—are to be included.
Regarding "not settled" (*avūpasanta*) and so forth: here, by the word "etc.," the two reopenings—"that which was not properly settled should be settled again"—are to be included.
Furthermore (*apica*), this refers to the general sense.
In that context, showing the scope of the word *tatra* (therein), he says: "in which monastery. The connection is:
"in which monastery it arose. Those who seek (*atthayanti*) their own selves or their opponents against one another are called "enemies" (*attapaccatthikā*).
"By means of a decision independent of the text" means by means of the methods of settling disputes (*samatha*) that have come down in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
"By means of a decision consisting merely of a teaching on the Dhamma apart from the Pāḷi. "This" refers to the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
"By whatever decision" means by whatever decision apart from the Pāḷi.
"Another" is connected to the phrase "another Vinaya-master asks, distinct from the resident monks (*nevāsika*). "And by them" means and by those resident monks.
"Of this" means of the one who upholds the Vinaya. "This one" refers to the one who upholds the Vinaya. "Therein" means in that village.
"Or they cause each other to persuade" means that those who are personal adversaries cause each other to persuade. "Those bhikkhus" refers to those bhikkhus who are personal adversaries.
"They incite" means they cause to persuade. "He who revokes" means whoever revokes. "These" refers to these bhikkhus who are personal adversaries.
"Having seen" is the connection [to the following]. "There" means in the village. "Right there" means on the very path.
"Right there" means in the village itself. "Right there" means in that very place. "Gone there" means gone to that village.
By the phrase "this same method applies," he extends [the rule] to the *pācittiya* offense as well.

The connection is: "even while speaking regarding a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) by the Saṅgha... and so forth. As for the construction: "that which is called the emergence from an offense (*āpattivuṭṭhāna*).

"That" refers to the emergence from an offense. Regarding the word "even" (*pi*) in "even while speaking": it shows that one is said to "reopen" not only when reopening the *tiṇavatthāraka* (covering over as with grass), but also when speaking [on the matter].

In the passage beginning with "one who goes to a wrong course" (*chandāgatiṃ gacchanto*), he says "having become a holder of the Vinaya" (*vinayadharaṃ hutvā*) and so forth, in order to show the manner of going to a wrong course.

The connection is: "he opens [the matter] for the sake of [his own] advantage. "Of him" refers to one who acts for what is disadvantageous. The connection is: "but the dull-witted one indeed opens it.
And "one is dependent on the powerful"—this is the connection. "The dense wrong view" (*gahanamicchādiṭṭhiṃ*) means a wrong view resembling a thicket.
"Wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is like a wind; this is the meaning of "wrong view. Regarding the phrase "and when it is powerful," the word "and" (*ca*) here should be applied to all [types of] kamma.

Regarding "because of being dependent on one," it is because of dependence on a single [factor]. Regarding the phrase "and when it is dependent on something powerful," the word "and" (*ca*) here too should be applied to all agents.
"Of that" refers to one who is dependent on the uneven, etc.
*Sota* means that novice (*sāmaṇera*). *Maṅkubhūtāttha* means having become abashed (*maṅkū hutvā bhūtā*), or the meaning is "you have reached a state of being abashed.
*Te* refers to those monks who were defeated. *Tassa* refers to that novice. *So* refers to that novice. *Te* refers to those monks who were defeated.
*Taṃ* refers to that novice. *So* refers to the youth. *Tato* means from the cause of the assembly. *Hiyyo* means on the day immediately preceding. *Iti* means thus.
"He says thus" means: "He" refers to the young man (*dahara*). The construction is: "This training rule has been laid down. "Go" means "go away.
"Thus" means "he should be addressed in this way"—this is the construction.
Having settled the legal dispute together with the Sangha, he approaches a certain nun who has gone to the courtyard—this is the construction.
"Kissāti kena kāraṇena" means "for what reason? The construction is: "Is it not thus to be determined in this manner?

"So" refers to the monk who makes the determination. The one who gives the consent is indeed easy to understand. [This concludes] the commentary on the source and other details of the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*).
342. Regarding the six phrases beginning with “What is its source” (*kiṃnidāna*), he says “What is its source for it? (*kiṃnidānam assā*) and so forth, demonstrating their status as compounds.

“For it” (*assā*) refers to the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). Although these phrases beginning with “What is its source” (*kiṃnidāna*) are indeed compounds, because they have the nature of ending in a consonant, the word “what” (*kiṃ*) must be pronounced with the nasalized *niggahīta* vowel.
“All these” (*sabbānetāni*) refers to all [the terms] beginning with “source” (*nidāna*).
These are the words. Regarding the term "synonyms" (*vevacanāni*): in the single sense of "cause," there are various expressions, which are *vivacanāni*;
these very ones are the synonyms (*vevacanāni*). Alternatively, that which has this teaching as its diverse expression is a "diverse expression" (*vivacana*), namely the meaning designated as "cause.
Because they are related to the diverse expression by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, these words are the synonyms (*vevacanāni*) of that diverse expression.
By the phrase “reckoned as the eighteen grounds for schism,” he shows the nature of the dispute (*vivāda*). “Dispute” refers to the dispute reckoned as the eighteen grounds for schism.
“This” refers to the statement “the source of dispute. “Of this” refers to the legal issue of censure (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*).
“This too” refers to the statement “the source of censure. “Of this” refers to the legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). “This” refers to the statement “the source of offenses.”
“Vacanaṃ”: it is stated that *kicca* itself is called *kiccaya* by way of the addition of the suffix *-ya*. “Assa” refers to the *kiccādhikaraṇa* (the legal issue concerning duties).
The connection is with the duties that arise from such things as formal admonition (*samanubhāsana*). “Etaṃ” refers to the statement “the source of duties” (*kiccayanidāna*).
“Ekapadayojanā” means the construction [of the compound] with the single word “source” (*nidāna*). “Sabbapadāni” refers to all the terms beginning with “origin” (*samudaya*).

"Ninefold" is stated here according to the triads, because the six roots are included within those nine by way of their birth. "Merely a verbal expression" means it is merely a verbal designation by way of root-conditions and supporting conditions.
"Hi" means truly, or because. "In this context" refers to the answer to the third question. 343.
Regarding "the twelve roots," showing the actual nature of these twelve roots, he says: "The dyad of anger and enmity, etc. and so forth.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), five pairs are included: the pair of hypocrisy and denigration; the pair of envy and avarice; the pair of deceit and fraud;
the pair of evil desire and wrong view; and the pair of dogmatic adherence and obstinate grasping.
"Occurring in one's own internal continuum" means occurring within the internal continuum of one's own individuality.
Explaining the origin of the eighteen grounds for schism through their etymological derivation, he says, “For that,” and so forth.

“That” refers to the legal issue of censure (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*); it is connected with the word “originates” (*samuṭṭhāti*). Here, by the phrase “among these,” he indicates the state of being the locus (*adhikaraṇabhāva*);
by the phrase “by these,” he indicates the state of being the instrument (*karaṇabhāva*). “Therefore” means for that reason. “Of this” refers to the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
"These" refers to the eighteen grounds for schism. "In all cases" means in all legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) and in all origins (*samuṭṭhāna*). 344. The connection is:

"By one legal issue, by a legal issue of business (*kicca-adhikaraṇa*)," as it has been stated. "These" refers to the legal issues. "Unilaterally" (*ekaṃsato*) means by one side, or by one portion; such is the meaning. "For" (*hi*) means truly, or because. The construction is:
"Just as a remaindered offense is settled, so too a non-remaindered offense is not settled. Why is it not settled?
He said, "Not indeed," and so forth. "Indeed" (hi) means because. "That" (sā) refers to the offense without remainder. "From that" (tato) means from the offense without remainder.
Here, by the phrase "it is not possible to confess," he indicates the absence of anything leading to confession. By the phrase "it is not possible...
to be established," he indicates the absence of anything leading to rehabilitation.

349. *Tato* means "from that. The connection is with the six pairs of questions beginning with "Wherein is there settlement through recollection" (*sativinaya*). *Tāsaṃ* refers to those questions. *Pakāsito* means "made manifest. 351.
*Dvinnampi samathānaṃ* means "of both methods of settling," namely by way of settlement in the presence (*sammukhāvinaya*) and settlement through recollection (*sativinaya*).

The connection is with "by which reason" (*yasmā*), which links to "it is not possible" (*na sakkā*). The connection is also with "the distinction between those who have reached the limit and those who have not" (*pattavaṭṭīnaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ*).
The connection is: "Of these" refers to the distinction between *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) and *sativinaya* (settlement by recollection). Here is the application of the meaning:

just as it is impossible to separate and show the difference between the leaf-sheaths of a plantain trunk, so too it is impossible to separate and show the difference between those two. "By that" means for that reason. "In all cases" means...
In all the explanations. 352.
The commentary on the seven origins of calm (*samatha-nidāna*):
"Assā" means of the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence). "Tattha" refers to the reading "the origin of the origin. "Idaṃ" refers to the tetrad of *sammukhā*.
"Laddhupavādo" means one by whom the reproach of others has been received; thus, "laddhupavādo" refers to one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
"Yassa ca" connects with "in whose presence. "Ubhinnaṃ" refers to the two: the teacher and the recipient. 353.

Is it not the case that in the question it was stated, "of the seven methods of settling [disputes]" (sattannaṃ samathānaṃ), yet why is it that in the answer only the *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) is mentioned?
He said, "Even though," and so forth, because the origin (*samuṭṭhāna*) had not been stated. Therein, the construction is: "even though it has been stated.
Here, the word *kiñcāpi* (even though) has the sense of acknowledgment, while the word *pana* (but/however) has the sense of censure. The construction is: "even though it was stated in that way.

"By the absence of inclusion in action" means by the absence of inclusion within the category of action. "Therein" refers to that reading beginning with "the performance of action. Action is performed.
“By this” refers to the act; it is the motion (*ñatti*). Therefore it is said: “The motion is to be understood as the performance of the formal act (*kamma*).
It is performed and established, thus it is the "performance" (*karaṇa*). One approaches it oneself, thus it is the "approach" (*upagamana*).

By means of a request, another is caused to approach, thus it is the "consent" (*ajjhupagamana*). It is endured, thus it is the "endurance" (*adhivāsanā*). It is not protested against, thus it is the "non-protest" (*apaṭikkosanā*). Such is the meaning of this.
Explaining this, he says: "The instrument is that very same [thing]," and so forth. *Etam* refers to the object (*kamma*). *Me* means "for me.

In the usage of the verbal root *kham*, the dative case is employed in the sense of the recipient (*sampadāna*). Alternatively, *me* means "by me"; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of the agent (*katva*), or it is a genitive.

*Khamati* is a form of the object (*kammarūpa*) that resembles a form of the agent (*katturūpa*). For indeed, a form of the object that resembles a form of the agent is said to be "it is acceptable" (*khamati*).
As in the cases of "of the Saṅgha" and so forth; and as for the form of the agent resembling the form of the object, as in "the lay follower undertakes the precept" and so forth.
Here, it should be understood that the suffix *ya* occurring in the sense of the object is elided.

354. The construction is: "This is a dispute between mother, son, and so forth.
By the phrase "because of being contradictory speech," he shows the etymological derivation: *vāda* is speech, and a contradictory *vāda* is a *vivāda*.

"By way of being subject to legal action" means by way of being settled. By this, he shows the meaning of the word *adhikaraṇa*: it is called an *adhikaraṇa* because it is brought before the court (*adhikariyati*) and settled by the methods of pacification (*samatha*). "In all cases" means...
In all the various classifications of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the classifications of legal issues.
The second collection of verses (*gāthā-saṅgaṇika*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Questions and Answers Regarding the *Codanā* (Accusation), etc., [Section] 359.
In the enumeration of the second verse, as for what is called "accusation" (*codanā*), it is said: "Having pointed out both the matter (*vatthu*) and the offense (*āpatti*), one accuses.
"Recalling the fault" (*dosasāraṇā*) means making one remember the fault. "An assembly of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghasannipāto*) means the gathering together of the Saṅgha.
In the phrase "by this [term] 'Saṅgha'," he shows that there is an elision of the latter member of the compound.
Regarding the term "matikamma" (consultation), he states that the word *mati* has the sense of "desire," saying, "it is called the taking of counsel. "That" refers to the consultation (*matikamma*).
The phrase "by that person who has been accused" functions as the agentive object (*kāritakamma*) for the phrase "for the purpose of reminding. "Of that person" [refers to the one being reminded].
This shows the function of the phrase "for the purpose of restraint" with respect to that person who has been reproved.

"Therein" means in that place for the adjudication of the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). "For the purpose of thorough examination" means for the purpose of grasping [the matter] after having investigated it thoroughly.
"Dhamma and adhamma" means what is real and what is unreal. By the phrase "for the purpose of establishing a decision," he indicates a textual ellipsis in the Canon.
Regarding the phrase "Do not harbor resentment," he says "do not give rise to anger" because here the word *paṭigha* is a synonym for anger (*kopa*).
By the words "toward either the accuser or the accused," he rejects the Sangha as the locus [of the resentment].

Regarding the phrase "if you are the investigator," he says "the master of discipline" because here the word *anuvijjaka* is a synonym for a master of discipline (*vinayadhara*); for it is the master of discipline who [investigates] for both the accuser and the accused.

Having inferred the statement, one discerns it by way of the subject matter, the offense, and so forth; therefore, one is called an *anuvijjaka* (an investigator). It is called *viggāhika* because it leads to a contradictory grasp.
With the words “not you,” etc., he shows the form of the suffix *-ṇika*. “By which” refers to the discourse. Showing the forms of the suttas and so forth, he says, “a sutta is named,” etc.
*Anuyuñjanavattaṃ* means the duty (*vatta*) of applying oneself, or the duty in the act of applying oneself. Regarding the phrase “by one who is skilled and wise”: here...
The word *kusala* is a synonym for "skillful," and the word *buddhimanta* is a synonym for "wise"; thus he said, "by one who is skillful and wise.

By the phrase "one who has attained the perfection of knowledge" (*ñāṇapāramippatta*), he shows that here it is not merely a general kind of knowledge, but rather omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"This" refers to the meaning already stated. "But this," however, refers to what is about to be explained.
"But. "In this" means in these verses. The construction is: "If you were an investigator (*anuvijjaka*). The construction is:
"That code of conduct for inquiry (*anuyogavatta*) which has been made well-laid down is in accordance with all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). "That" refers to the code of conduct for inquiry.
"Thus" refers to this brief commentary together with its underlying intention. "Of oneself" means of the investigator. "In the future life" means in the world beyond. "Who" refers to...
Anuvijjako means one who investigates. *Taṃ* refers to the duty of inquiry (*anuyogavatta*). *Gatiṃ* means a happy destination (*sugati*).
*Hitaṃ* means the welfare of both the accuser and the accused. *Gavesanto* means seeking with wisdom. By this, he shows the etymological meaning of the term *hitesī* as "one who seeks welfare.
*Mettañca* means loving-kindness that has reached absorption (*appanā*). *Mettāpubbabhāgañca* means the preparatory and access loving-kindness that occurs prior to the loving-kindness of absorption.
The construction is: "When the burden has been placed upon you by the Saṅgha.

"He" refers to the investigator (*anuvijjaka*). "Of these" refers to the accuser and the accused. By the word "spoken" (*bhāsita*), he shows that the term "discourse" (*vohāra*) is a synonym for "that which is spoken.

"That" refers to the discourse uttered impulsively. Regarding the phrase "connected with the sequence," he says, "it is called a connection of the discussion" (*kathānusandhi*), thereby rejecting a connection based on legal adjudication (*vinicchaya*).

*Kathānusandhi* (connection of discourse) is the linking [of topics] in accordance with the discourse. Regarding the phrase *paṭiññānusandhitena* (by means of a connection based on admission), he says "Alternatively," etc., to show that while the words *paṭiññā* (admission) and *anusandhi* (connection) share a common grammatical substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa*), there is another [usage] where they have different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*). The connection is with the phrase "a person who is conscientious" (*lajjiṃ puggalaṃ*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) refers to the verse. "By means of a connection based on conduct" (*vattānusandhinā*) means by means of the connection consisting of conduct, which is synonymous with *vatta*.
The construction is: “the promise of that shameless person coincides with his conduct.
“One who knows commits [an offense]” means that having become one who knows, he commits it. By this, he shows the meaning of the word *sañcicca* (intentionally) as “having intended.
The meaning is: “having intended together with the volition of transgression. “He does not confess, he does not emerge [from the offense].”
Regarding the phrase "he conceals by this," it shows that here "concealment" (parigūhana) means neither confession nor emergence from the offense.
"That" refers to the statement, "one intentionally commits an offense. "By you" refers to those who provide the defense.
"Truth" means what is real and not false. "I too" refers to the accuser; the word "too" (pi) includes the defender as well. "That" refers to the statement beginning with "intentionally."
*Tanti* means *tuvaṃ* (you), or *tvaṃ* (you).
Regarding the term *pubbāparaṃ*: here, that which is to be spoken first is "the prior" (*pubbaṃ*), and that which is to be spoken later is "the subsequent" (*aparaṃ*).
Demonstrating both the prior and the subsequent, he says "pure" and so forth. By the phrase "tasmiṃ pubbāpare," [he refers to] the Pāḷi text.
In the phrase *pubbaparassa*, it is shown that the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative.
"By two" means by way of the two categories of offenses: *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*. "By five" means by way of the five [offenses] beginning with *thullaccaya*.
"By wrong view" refers to the ten-based wrong view, such as "there is no giving," and so forth. "By extreme views" refers to...
“By ‘the world is eternal,’ etc., [it refers] to the ten bases of the view of extremes (*antaggāhikadiṭṭhi*). ‘In all cases’ means in all the collections of the second verse.
Thus ends the commentary on the collection of the second verse. The Section on Objections (*Codanākaṇḍa*).
Commentary on the Duties of the Investigator (Anuvijjakakiccavaṇṇanā):
360–1. Now, the connection is with the word "commenced" (*āraddha*). The construction is: "a certain bhikkhu [was seen] by a certain woman.

"He" refers to the bhikkhu who was observing. "Him" refers to the bhikkhu who was either going out or entering. "The other" refers to the one who was accused (*cuditaka*). "His" refers to the accuser (*codaka*).
"Does not approach" means he does not go near. "Does not acknowledge" means he does not make a formal admission.
"In this place" refers to the location where women enter and exit. "That" refers to the legal action (*kamma*). "By him" refers to the accuser.

"Of him" is connected with the words of the accuser. "The other" refers to the one being accused (*cuditaka*). "Suspected of impurity" means suspected of an impurity that has arisen in an improper place.
"Suspected" means "suspected of being groundless," which is shown by this [phrase]. "Of that person" is connected with "by the admission of the one who has been accused.
"In all cases" refers to all duties pertaining to the investigator.
Thus ends the exposition of the duties of the investigator.
The Explanation of the Questions and Answers (Codakapucchāvissajjanā) 362–3.
Showing that the exertion (*padhāna*) is the point of connection for both "truth" (*sacca*) and "the unshakable" (*akuppa*), he says: "it should be established.
By the words "that which," etc., he shows the state of being established in truth. "That which" refers to the action (*kamma*). By the words "nor," etc., [he shows] the unshakable.
It shows the state of being established. "And one who has entered" means one who has entered into the formal determination (*vinicchaya*).
By the word "speech," it shows the specific nature of those who have entered and those who have not. "Therein" refers back to the preceding statement; the meaning is:
"In the statement that 'one must know what has entered and what has not. "The authority of the accuser" refers to whether it is "Dhamma" or "non-Dhamma," or "foolish" or "wise."
Or it is the measure of the accuser. "The measure of the accused" means: whether he is one who has been legitimately accused or not—that is the measure of the accused.
"The measure of the investigator" means: whether it is possible to reach a decision or not—that is the measure of the investigator.
"The investigator should be questioned" is the connection [of the sentence]. In the passage beginning with "by which rule," etc., he shows the actual nature of the rule and so forth:
He said: "Dhamma means a real matter," and so forth. The construction is: "by this Dhamma, by this Vinaya, and by this teaching of the Teacher.
Therefore, the connection is: "it must be settled by the investigator. "In this" refers to the place where the investigator ought to proceed.
*Avaññā* means despising (*avajānana*). “These” refers to the elders. By the word “*khatattā*,” he shows the etymological meaning as follows: since one is wounded by oneself, one is called *khata*.
“*Upahaniyantī*” means they are impaired; thus, one by whom the faculties are impaired is *upahatindriyo*.
By the phrase “due to the absence of wisdom,” he shows that in the term *dummedho*, the prefix *du-* has the sense of absence, while the word *medhā* is a synonym for wisdom (*paññā*).
[The text] shows this. The derivation of *dummedha* should be made as: "one who has no wisdom (*medhā*) is *dummedha*.
The construction is: "that investigator, being corrupted... [and] foolish, approaches. The connection is: "therefore" means because he approaches, therefore it was said.
Regarding "of that": of the reading or of the verse. Showing the detailed explanation, he says: "In the case of the accused and the accuser," and so forth.
"Both" means both of these: support by material things and support by persons. "Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Dispensation.
"Iti" has this meaning. Regarding the phrase "whispers into the ear": here, *upakaṇṇa* means near the ear;

showing that this itself is *upakaṇṇaka*, he says, "speak thus," and so forth. By the expression "at the root of the ear," he shows that in the word *upakaṇṇaka*, the prefix *upa-* carries the sense of proximity.
He shows. "He speaks" means he talks. By this, he shows that the root *japp* has the sense of speaking. "He looks askance": here the word *jimha* denotes crookedness;
since "crookedness" in its actual meaning refers here to fault (*dosa*), he says, "only fault.

"The connection of the discourse" refers to the sequence of the conversation between the accuser and the investigator. "The connection of the decision" refers to the sequence of the determination of whether an offense was committed or not by the investigator. "In all instances" refers to the section on accusations (*codanākaṇḍa*).
Thus ends the commentary on the section on the Exhortation.
[Now begins] the commentary on the conduct of the investigator in the Lesser Battle.

365. Regarding the term *saṅgāma*: it is a *saṅgāma* because of the coming together (*samāgamana*) [of armies] in battle; or else, it is called *saṅgāma* because they come together (*samāgamenti*) or assemble (*sannipatanti*) therein.
Demonstrating this etymological meaning, he said: “*Saṅgāma* is said to be... [etc. ...the assembly of the Saṅgha (*saṅghasannipāto*). *Sannipāta* means an assembling (*sannipatana*);
or else, it is an *sannipāta* because they assemble there. The assembly of the Saṅgha is the *saṅghasannipāta*. *Saṅgāma*.
"Yuddha" is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*)—specifically as the root beginning with the letter *m* (number 18) in the *Saddanīti-dhātumālā*.
Therein, "battle" (*yuddha*) should be understood in its actual sense as the settlement of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa-vinicchaya*). Explaining its meaning in detail, he says:
"For therein," and so forth. Therein, "therein" refers to that battle; it is to be connected with the word "they assemble" (*samosaranti*). "Their own adversaries" (*attapaccatthikā*)...
They seek their own opposite. "Uddhamma" means separation from the Dhamma. The construction is: "being illuminators.
To the question "Who like? he says, "Like the Vajjiputtakas. "That bhikkhu practices" is the connection [of the sentence].
"Laddhi" means a doctrine such as *uddhamma* and so forth. "Tattha" means in battle. "Avacarati" means having entered, he moves about, he practices. That very meaning—
Showing this, he says: "Having plunged in, one carries out the investigation. Here, by the word "having plunged in" (*ajjhogāhetvā*), he shows the meaning of the prefix *ava* as "plunging.

By the phrase "carries out the investigation" (*vinicchayaṃ pavattetī*), since the root *car* is included within the category of agentive suffixes (*kāritanta*), he shows the meaning of "proceeding" through the action performed by the agent. By this [it is meant that] one proceeds in battle.

This indicates the etymological derivation of *saṅgāmāvacaro*. To the question "Who is like him?", he says, "Like the Elder Yasas. *Mānaddhajaṃ* refers to the banner known as conceit (*māna*), which manifests as the desire for renown.

Regarding the phrase *rajo-haraṇa-samena*, he explains it by saying "like a foot-wiper," showing that it is a "dust-remover" (*rajo-haraṇaṃ*) because one removes (*harati*) or wipes away (*apaneti*) dust (*rajaṃ*) with it; that is, a foot-wiper (*pādapuñjanaṃ*). Thus he says, "like a foot-wiper."
