“Foot-cleansing” (*pādapuñjana*) is that by which one cleanses and purifies the foot; one who is equal to that is “equal to a foot-cleanser” (*pādapuñjanasama*), and it is by means of that [term].
Showing the manner of equality, he said “just as,” and so forth. The connection is: “there is no passion for the dust-remover.
“In a fitting manner” (*yathāpatirūpaṃ*) means conformable to what is fitting, or not exceeding what is fitting. The connection is: “one should sit down without speaking.”
Regarding the phrase "the Dhamma itself," what is meant here by "Dhamma"? It is said: "That which pertains to the allowable and the unallowable," and so forth.

This includes the discernment of form and the formless, the conduct of serenity (*samatha*), the conduct of insight (*vipassanā*), the rules for standing, and the rules for sitting; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes the rules for walking meditation (*caṅkama*) and others.

Since the fourteen great rules (*mahāvatta*) and the rest are already included under the phrase "that which pertains to the allowable and the unallowable," they are not mentioned again by the term "rules" (*vatta*).
Only the rules regarding standing and so forth are to be understood; by the word "etcetera," the rules regarding walking meditation and so forth are to be included.
Regarding the phrase "another should be requested," he says "whoever" and so forth to indicate that anyone at all may be requested.

By this, he shows that it is not just anyone who may be requested, but rather one who is indeed capable. The manner in which one should speak, beginning with "Friend," is indicated [by the following].
It shows [this]. Regarding the phrase "the noble silence" (*ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo*): here, silence is not merely due to an inability to speak;
rather, it is due to attention to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, he says, "silence through attention to the meditation subject.
This belongs to the Noble Ones (*ariya*), thus it is "noble" (*ariyo*), [referring to] the silence. By the words "is not to be despised," [he implies] that it is not to be underestimated.
It shows that one should not think [of him] as having transcended [the status of teacher].
"Preceptor" (upajjhāya) refers to the preceptor of both the accuser and the accused. "In all cases" means in all such passages as "the teacher should not be questioned.
"Kulapadesa" is so called because it is designated as a "clan" (kula) by way of birth, name, and lineage. "Atrassa" means "in this regard."

Having made the word division as *assa* and *ati*, he says "with regard to this person" and so forth, because the word *atra* refers to a person (puggala-visaya) and the word *assi* is a verb (ākhyātika).
In that context, by the word "might be" (*bhaveyya*), he rejects both the pronominal nature of the word *assi* and its status as a present tense form [expressed by] "is" (*bhavati*).
"By one who conforms to the assembly" means by one who acts in accordance with the approval of the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "by this [means] of ours, which is a mental construction" (*parisakappika*), he shows that here the word *kappa* has the sense of "understanding" (*vijjā*). The word "this" (*yaṃ*) refers to speech.

It is called *muddā* because one "seals" (*mudati*) by means of it; a "hand-seal" (*hatthamuddā*) is so called because it is a seal on the hand's knuckles and fingers, being connected through the relationship of the whole and its parts.
One should understand that the modification of that [sealing] is "hand-seal," and thus he says "a movement of the hand" (*hatthavikāra*).

Regarding the phrase “by one conforming to the meaning,” here “meaning” (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the analytical determination (*vinicchaya*). “Conforming to” (*anuvidhiyantena*) means by one who observes (*sallakkhentena*).
Thus, showing this meaning, he said: “by one observing precisely the penetration of the analytical determination.

“In the assembly-circle” (*sannipātamaṇḍale*) means in the gathering or multitude of the assembly for the purpose of convening; the meaning is “in the midst of the assembly-circle. “It is not to be transgressed” (*na vītihātabbaṃ*).

Here, "shifting" (*vītiharaṇa*) means, in terms of its meaning, "diminishing"; thus he said, "the determination must not be diminished. "Ill-spoken words" refers to the ill-spoken words of both the accuser and the accused.
Regarding the phrase "by one who seeks the welfare": here, one who seeks (*parisesati*) welfare (*hita*) is a "seeker of welfare" (*hitaparisaka*);
compassion and the preliminary stage of compassion—such a person possesses this, and is therefore a "seeker of welfare" (*hitaparisakī*), that is, a person; [it is] by such a seeker of welfare.
To demonstrate this very meaning, he said: "by one seeking welfare, by one searching for welfare. "Compassion" (karuṇā) refers to compassion that has reached absorption (appanā).
"The preliminary stage of compassion" (karuṇāpubbabhāga) refers to the preparatory and access-stage compassion that occurs prior to the compassion that has reached absorption.
Regarding both phrases: "One should be compassionate, one should be sympathetic toward welfare; one who seeks the welfare [of others], one who refrains from frivolous speech."
The construction is: "This intention is to be understood" applies to both phrases [beginning with] "it must be so.
By the term "unpleasant speech" (*asundaravacana*), he shows the meaning of the word as follows: here, what is well-spoken (*sundaram uttam*) is *surutta*; that which is not *surutta* is *asurutta*.
"Should be grasped" means it should be taken after having investigated it thoroughly.

“Of him” means of the one who reproves unrighteously (*adhammacodaka*). Regarding the phrase “the matter has not been abandoned,” here the words “spoken by the reprover and the reproved” should be understood by way of context.
And here, “not abandoned” means that the formal decision (*vinicchaya*) has not been abandoned. To the question “What should be undertaken?
he says, “Is it not you? and so forth. The “duty of inquiry” (*anuyogavatta*) is that which was stated as “I shall speak at the proper time,” and so on.

“And in truth and in imperturbability”: this refers to the duty of inquiry (*anuyuñjana-vatta*). For it is because, by means of this duty, the accuser (*codaka*) inquires of the accused (*cuditaka*), or the accused inquires of the accuser;

and the accused is made to inquire by the accuser, or the accuser is made to inquire by the accused—that it is called the "duty of inquiry" (*anuyoga-vatta*). "Having had them speak" means having had the accuser and the accused speak.
“Of him” means of either the accuser or the accused; “they are afraid” means they feel fear. “Tet” means “of you. “Even having spoken” means even having spoken with the mouth.
By the word “even,” it includes [the case of] having shown it through a bodily gesture. “The procedure for formal questioning” refers to the *dhātukamma* (act of interrogation);
“that monk” refers to the *kāritakamma* (act of commissioning), which must be supplied; that action expresses the suffix *-tabba*. “Impurity.”
Regarding the term *vibhāvetabbo*: here, when it is said that one is "impure" (*asuci*) because "he has no pure virtue" (*suci-sīla*), it implies he is "shameless" (*alajjī*);
thus he says "shameless. The construction is: "He is upright and virtuous, free from crookedness of body and so forth.

And here, by the phrase "free from crookedness of body and so forth," he shows the cause of uprightness. The intention is that he is upright because he is free from crookedness of body and so forth. "He" refers to the bhikkhu. "By means of gentleness alone... [the text continues].

"By way of pliancy alone. "Should be addressed" means he should be spoken to. By this, he shows the place of connection for the phrase "by means of straightness and gentleness," as well as the elliptical portion of the text (*pāṭhasesa*).
"He" refers to the bhikkhu. "This very one" indicates by the word "only" (*eva*) that it should be understood:
he is not one who values the Dhamma, nor one who values the person; he is neither neutral toward the Dhammas nor toward persons.
366. And the construction is: "by that investigator. Regarding the phrase "in the suttas, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) should include the Vinaya-anuloma and the Paññatti-anulomika.
The construction is: "the sutta is for the purpose of reconciling. To the question "for the reconciliation of what? he says:
"for the reconciliation of offenses and non-offenses. The construction is: "the simile is for the purpose of showing the meaning. It is exactly the same.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Regarding the phrase "those who abide individually" (*paccekaṭṭhāyino*) and "those who abide in non-deception" (*avisaṃvādakaṭṭhāyino*):

he says, "They stand through their virtue in what is individual" (*paccekasmiṃ tiṭṭhanti sīlena*), thus they are "those who abide individually"; and "they stand through their virtue in non-deception," thus they are "those who abide in non-deception.
By the expression "in the positions of sovereignty, lordship, and leadership," he indicates the specific nature of the "individual" (*pacceka*).
[The text] shows this. "Tet" refers to those persons approved by the Saṅgha.

To the question, "For what purpose was it said, 'The Vinaya is for the sake of restraint' and so forth? he says, "Now," and so on. The connection is: "He says [this] in order to show now. The construction is:
"Those who, being dull-witted and of weak intelligence, might speak thus. Alternatively, "mandā" means those of weak intelligence.
The construction is: "those persons who might speak thus. The connection is: "the entire formulation of the Vinaya is a decisive support (upanissaya).

By this, he shows that in the thirteen statements beginning with "for the sake of restraint" and ending with "for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging," the phrase "is a decisive support" must be supplied as a textual ellipsis.
By the word "condition" (paccaya), [he indicates] "decisive support" (upanissaya).
This shows the meaning of the word *upanissayapaccayo* (decisive support condition). *Sabbattha* means in all twelve statements. Showing a distinction, he says, “Moreover, here,” and so forth.
Therein, the construction is: “Moreover, I shall state a distinction. *Ettha* refers to [the phrases] such as “for the sake of non-remorse,” and so on. *Taṃ* refers to happiness (*sukha*).
To the question, “Of what is ‘nascent insight’ (*taruṇavipassanā*) a designation? he replies: “It is a designation for the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*).”
One might object: "Since 'dispassion' (virāga) here includes the fourfold Noble Path, should not 'liberation' (vimutti) here also include the fourfold fruit?
Why then is it said that 'liberation is the fruit of Arahantship'? To this he says: "For even though it is fourfold," and so forth.
"Hi" means "truly" or "because. "For the sake of unconditioned parinibbāna" means for the sake of the unconditioned parinibbāna.
For in this final Nibbāna there is no condition whatsoever; therefore, it is called "conditionless final Nibbāna.
"That" refers to the knowledge and vision of liberation. "In its attainment" means when that knowledge and vision of liberation has been reached by degrees.
"Necessarily" means certainly or invariably. "For this purpose" means for the sake of this goal known as final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
"Payojanaṃ imissā kathāya" means "for the purpose of this discourse. "Kathā" is a discourse on the meaning (attha). "Mantanā" is a deliberation on the Dhamma.
Regarding "etadatthā upanisā," he says "also the conditionality of succession" because here the word *upanisā* denotes a condition (*paccaya*).
For it is called *upanisā* because, having approached the successive fruit (*paraṃparaphala*), it sits down (*nisīdati*) there; thus it is a condition of succession.
It is said: “The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint,” and so forth; this is the application [of the principle] of successive conditionality (*paraṃparapaccayatā*).
“Attentive listening” (*sotāvadhāna*): *avadhāna* is that which is held or established after having plunged [into it]; the holding of the ear is *sotāvadhāna*. “This discourse”:
this discourse beginning with “The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint. That knowledge which arises—this too has that as its purpose.

The construction (*yojanā*). Regarding the phrase "this, namely, the non-clinging of the mind" (*yadidaṃ anupādā cittassā*): here, the particle *yadidaṃ*, looking toward the word "liberation" (*vimokkho*), expresses the meaning "that which goes.
In the term *anupādā*, there is an elision of the letter *y*, as occurs in such expressions as "by one's own direct knowledge" (*sayam abhiññā*);
however, the instrumental function of that word should be understood as "by means of the four kinds of clinging" (*catūhi upādānehi*). Thus, showing this meaning:
He said: "That which, without clinging by means of the four kinds of clinging... Here, the construction is as follows:
that liberation—which is reckoned as the fruit of arhatship—exists for the mind when it does not cling by means of the four kinds of clinging;
and that [liberation] also serves this purpose. By the phrase "reckoned as the fruit of arhatship," he shows the meaning of the term "liberation. For the fruit of arhatship...
Because one was liberated from opposing states, or specifically from all defilements (*kilesa*), it is therefore called "liberation" (*vimokkha*).
By the phrase "for the sake of final *nibbāna* without remainder," he shows the meaning of the expression "for this purpose.
Regarding the passage "does not know the basis...," the construction should be applied as follows: "at this point. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of that connection; therefore.

“In these” means in these verses. Regarding the phrase “and by the even,” he says, “by that very even ignorance consisting in not knowing what precedes and what follows,” showing that the word “even” (*samena*) here is a conventional term (*rūḷhīpada*) expressing the meaning of “ignorance” (*aññāṇena*). He asks:

for what reason does the text say one does not know what has been done and what has not been done? He replies: “by the even [ignorance],” that is, by the even ignorance regarding what precedes and what follows.
The meaning is that he does not know what has been done and what has not been done. "Thus," and so forth, is the conclusion. The construction is: "this speech which was spoken.

Regarding the terms "therein" (*tattha*) and "unskilled in signs" (*ākāra-akovida*), there is no distinction between the locus (*ādhāra*) and the contained (*ādheyya*); therefore, it should be understood that the whole is the locus and the part is the contained.
Since the word *ākāra* means "intimation" (*iṅgita*), he says "reasons and non-reasons" (*kāraṇa-akāraṇe*). [This refers to] those designated as reasons and non-reasons.
The meaning is "by gestures. In the phrase *ākārassa*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative; for the meaning is "in the appearance" (*ākārasmiṃ*).
*Tatheva* means "just as," that is, just as he does not know the object and so forth. *Iti* means "thus. In the phrase *yvāyaṃ*, *yo ayaṃ* refers to this bhikkhu.
By the word *bhayena*, it is shown that in the expression *bhayā*, the ablative case is used in the sense of a cause; [it means] "from fear" or "by fear."

The construction is: "he goes. This same method applies here as well in the phrase "through delusion he goes from delusion. "Through desire" means by means of desire; "through hatred" means by means of hatred.
Because of his inability to know himself, he is not skilled in persuasion; thus he said, "because of his inability to persuade another.
Why is he unskilled in winning over? He said, "Because of the reason... [etc. ...of that. "Of the assembly..."
By the phrase "because it has been obtained," the meaning of the word *laddhapakkho* is shown as: "one by whom a faction (*pakkho*) consisting of an assembly has been obtained. The construction is:
"If a monk is of such a kind, that monk is called 'not to be opposed' (*apaṭikkho*).

This same method applies to what follows below as well. By the phrase "not to be opposed" (*na paṭikkhitabbo*), it is meant that he is not to be looked at face-to-face (*paṭimukhaṃ na ikkhitabbo*); thus he is "not to be opposed" (*apaṭikkho*).
This shows the meaning of the word. By the phrase "it must not be looked at," it shows that the verbal root *ikkh* has the sense of seeing.
Thus ends the commentary on the Cūḷasaṅgāma Sutta.
[Now follows] the Mahāsaṅgāma Sutta.
The commentary on what must be known by one who is conversing [is as follows]. 368–74. The connection is: "In the Great Battle, it should be understood by this very method.

Having shown the manner of shifting the basis (*vatthu*), he said "But whoever... and so forth, showing the manner of denying and then admitting. The connection is: "But whoever speaks... [and so on].
"Eseva" means "this very one"; the meaning is: "the monk who denies and then admits. 375.

"By way of blue and other colors, and by way of dispraise such as 'for the sake of health' and so forth": this refers both to the aspect of blue and other colors, and to the aspect of dispraise such as "for the sake of health" and so on.

It is called "the giving of wealth" because, through this training rule, wealth is handed over; therefore, it is termed "the handing over of wealth. "Prior application" (pubbapayoga) means that which was previously employed.
379. Regarding the commentary on "he practices for the harm of many people," he says, beginning with "by one who holds the Vinaya," while expanding upon the Pāḷi.
Therein, "by one who holds the Vinaya" refers to the investigator (*anuvijjaka*); it is connected with the word "judged. "Those who live by exhortation" refers to the monks.
Those who live depending upon the exhortation; "lay followers as well" means those for whom the Triple Gem is their refuge;

"givers as well" means those who provide the requisites for the monks; "of them" refers to the lay followers and the others; "in the same way" means that just as the lay followers and the rest are divided into two groups, so too [is this];
"from that" is connected with "by the protective deities"; "by that" means by reason of that twofold division.

382. Regarding the phrase "dependent on the thicket" (*gahaṇanissito*), the word "thicket" (*gahana*) here is a synonym for "view" (*diṭṭhi*); thus he said: "The 'thicket' is that which consists of wrong view and the view of grasping at extremes. 393.

Regarding the phrase "of him who despises," the word "of him" (*tassa*) must be connected with the word "speech" (*vacana*) by supplying it as a textual ellipsis; thus he said: "of his speech. "Of him" refers to the novice.

"Him" refers to the novice. 394. Regarding the expression "yaṃatthāya," this is a compound; thus he said: "yadatthāya" (for whatever purpose). Regarding the expression "taṃ atthaṃ" (that purpose), this is the word...
He says, "that is the meaning," because there is a reversal of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). For the word *attha* is masculine;
thus, even here in the phrase "it should not be omitted from the Pāḷi," a reversal of gender is to be understood. "In all cases" means in every great battle.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the Great Battle.
The Analysis of the Kathina;
the Commentary on the Nature of the Kathina, etc., 403.
"In the Kathina Khandhaka" means in the Kathina Section. "In the former" refers to the Kathina Section.
404. Regarding the phrase "of the preparation" (*payogassa*): here, "preparation" (*payoga*) refers to washing the robe and so forth; thus says the commentator.
Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the six preliminary acts—namely, examining [the cloth], cutting, stretching, sewing, dyeing, and applying the *kappa*-mark—are included.

The construction is: "that preparation which is performed, such as fetching water, and so on. "Immediate" (*anantara*) refers to the immediate [sequence] in terms of the past, the future, and the immediate [present].
Since there are two kinds [of proximity], and here only that which is immediate and future is intended, he says, "by way of the future.
For when the application such as fetching water has arisen, the subsequent arising of preliminary actions such as washing occurs;

thus, the condition for that application is by way of the future alone. Regarding the term *samanantara-paccaya*, the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "well" (*suṭṭhu*); therefore, he says, "by way of a well-immediate condition."
By the word “āsannataraṃ” (more proximate), he shows the sense of being well-established.

The word “payogassa” (of the application) is the genitive (*sāmī*) with respect to the word “ādhārabhāvaṃ” (the state of being a support), and it is the dative (*sampadāna*) with respect to the phrase “paccayā honti” (they become conditions). The word “nissayaṃ” (support) is glossed by the word “ādhārabhāvaṃ.
By the word “upetena,” he shows that the prefix *upa-* has the meaning of approaching (*upagamana*), as well as the meaning of strength (*balavattha*).
He rejects [the objection]. "First" means either in terms of the application (*payoga*) or prior to the application.

By this phrase, "by this condition of pre-existence" (*purejāta-paccaya*), he shows that the word "prior" (*pura*) has the sense of "first. "After" means either in terms of the application or subsequent to the application. "Neither before nor after" means simultaneously (*ekapahārena*).
By this, he shows the meaning of the term "co-nascent" (*sahajāta*).

"Having asked thus" is the connection. "Which" refers to the class of phenomena (*dhammajāta*). "Now he says" is the connection. "Of which" refers to the preliminary application (*payoga*) and so forth.

"That very same" refers to that very class of phenomena. The construction is as follows: "The meaning of the statement beginning with ‘the preliminary action is of the application’ should be understood in this way.
Regarding the statement that was spoken, beginning with “Which phenomena are of the application,” this is the response thereto.
The construction is: "It is said by me. By this, he shows that [the word] must be supplied from the text and joined [to the following].

While expanding upon the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*) by means of four conditions, he says, "Of the application," and so forth. The connection is: "The preliminary action of the application is the condition.
Regarding "among the states already mentioned": among those mentioned [in the text] such as, "It is a condition by way of the proximity-condition (*anantarapaccaya*)," and so on.
The connection is: "But this prior-arising condition (purejātapaccaya) [applies] among phenomena. Alternatively, the connection is:

"Among the phenomena mentioned"—that is, among the phenomena such as washing and so forth mentioned by way of preliminary action—"even a single phenomenon. "Does not obtain" means it does not obtain [the result] prior to the process of fetching water and so forth.

"This" refers to the process of fetching water and so forth. However, it "obtains the posterior-arising condition (pacchājātapaccaya)" means that the process of fetching water and so forth [obtains it].
It receives the postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*). To the question "Why does it receive it?", he says:
"Because of that which arises subsequently," and so forth. The construction is: "Since it is performed [subsequently], therefore it receives it.

However, the connection is that it does not receive the co-nascent condition (*sahajātapaccaya*). "Consisting of the eight matrices, the two obstacles, and the five benefits" means consisting of the eight matrices, the two obstacles, and the five benefits.

"Other" means different by way of fifteen factors. In the phrase "in the application and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the preliminary rites (*pubbakaraṇa*), the relinquishing (*paccuddhāra*), and the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"By this method" means by the aforementioned method.
This concludes the commentary on the classification of the preliminary rites, the causes, and so forth.
406–7. Because it was asked twice, it is called “the two questions. In order to show the actual nature of the root-cause (hetu) and the condition (paccaya), he said, “the six robes.
To the question “Why should they be known? he replied, “For [the sake of] prior effort, etc.
Here, *hi* means “because. *Tāniyeva* means “those very same [six robes]. The word *eva* should also be construed with what follows; thus the meaning is “those very ones. *Hi*... [end of fragment].
The construction is: “It is true that the preliminary acts (*pubbakaraṇa*) and so forth do not exist.
(408) By the words “With this outer robe,” etc., he shows the manner of verbal expression.

Because both relinquishment (*paccuddhāra*) and formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) are performed by the one who spreads the *kaṭhina*, it is therefore called an “action” (*kiriya*). Hence it is said: “Both relinquishment and formal determination.”

411. Showing the actual nature of those things such as "defective in material" (*vatthuvipanna*), he said: "It becomes unallowable cloth," and so forth. It is called *vipanna* because it reaches destruction or alteration; that which is defective in its very material is "defective in material" (*vatthuvipanna*). 412.

Regarding the phrase "of those very phenomena" (*tesaññeva dhammānaṃ*), showing the actual nature of these phenomena, he said: "In those phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), etc. *Kathinādijānitabbavibhāgavaṇṇanā* (Exposition of the Analysis of What Should Be Known Concerning the Kathina and Other Matters) [Ends].

In that context, "among phenomena such as form" (*rūpādi-dhammesu*) refers to the phenomena of the pure octad-form-aggregates (*suddhaṭṭhaka-rūpa-kalāpa*), such as color, odor, and so forth. "Existing" (*sati*) means while they are present.
"Of them" (*tesaṃ*) refers to those phenomena, beginning with form. By the word "conjunction" (*samodhānaṃ*), he shows the meaning of the term "assemblage" (*saṅgaho*).
By the word "intermingling" (*missībhāvo*), he shows the meaning of the term "combination" (*samavāyo*). [It is] the state of oneness (*ekabhāva*) of the constituent parts (*avayava-dhammānaṃ*).
*Gahaṇaṃ* means grasping. *Samavāyo* is the equal going (*samaṃ ayanaṃ*) or occurrence of the constituent factors (*avayava-dhammānaṃ*).

"In many phenomena" (*bahūsu dhammesu*) means in many phenomena consisting of ultimate realities (*paramattha*) and designations (*paññatti*). "A mere name" (*nāmamattaṃ*) means a mere designation by name (*nāma-paññatti-mattaṃ*). "Previously" (*pubbe*) refers to the Kathina-kkhandhaka.
By the word "by reasons" (*kāraṇehi*), he shows that the term *ākāra* has the sense of a reason. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to the statement.
416. "They arise" means that the grounds for the suspension of the *kaṭhina* robe arise. "What" refers to what kind of matter.

"All [grounds] for the suspension of the *kaṭhina*" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly, or because. "In this regard" (*ettha*) means among the grounds for the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. "The first two" refers to the first two by way of the internal suspension (*antarubbhāra*) and the simultaneous suspension (*sahubbhāra*).
"And of these" refers to the two preceding ones. "The others" refers to the remaining grounds for the suspension of the *kaṭhina*. "Among those too" refers to...
Regarding the other ways of suspending the *kathina* robe; "in all cases" means throughout the entire exposition on the *kathina*.
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning the rules (*paññattivagga*) within the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The Exposition is complete.
The Commentary on the Upāli-Pañcaka of the Anissita-Vagga.
417. To prevent anyone from thinking that there is no connection to the question, "But how many, venerable sir?
found in the *Upāli-pañhā*, he says, "This is the connection. "The Elder" refers to the Elder Upāli; "asked" is the connection.
"Of these" refers to the connection with the five groups. To the question, "For whose sake shall I establish the *tanti*? he says, "for those who dwell in dependence [on the Sangha]."
“For the sake of [the monks] who perform the act”—this is the connection with the monks who carry out the formal act (*vasanakārīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ*). “Of these” refers to the questions.

Regarding the phrase “one who has committed an offense is one against whom a formal act has been performed,” the word “committed” (*āpanno*) is shown to be the reason for the word “one against whom a formal act has been performed” (*kammakato*);

thus he says: “Having committed an offense, it is precisely on account of that that a formal act has been performed by the Saṅgha. “Precisely on account of that” (*tappaccayāva*) means: for the very reason consisting in having committed that offense.
Commentary on the Chapter on Non-Settling (Nappaṭippassambhanavagga) 420.

“This” refers to the monk who has had a formal act performed against him; “is not fit” is the connection [to the following]. “In accordance with the proper conduct” means in the conduct that conforms to the formal act that was carried out. “His” refers to the monk. “With a rope” means together with the rope known as the formal act;

thus, he is “with a rope” (*sarajjuka*). 421. “By monks who are in harmony” is the connection. “Indeed” (*hi*) means truly. “Having made him confess his transgression” means [having made him confess] one another’s [transgressions].
"Having caused the fault to be confessed. Regarding the phrase "the settlement by covering over as with grass," the word *vā* (or) indicates an alternative meaning.
Here, in the expression *tatra ce*, the word *ta-* refers to the object (*kamma*), while *ce* is a synonym for *sace* (if); thus he says, "if such an offense has occurred.

Regarding the phrase "even after making a disclosure of the view," the construction is "even after having made a disclosure of the view. By the word *pi* (even), he includes the sense of "even without having done so. As for the phrase *yatra pana*:
But regarding the object (*kamma*). "Therein" means in the object. "One should depart" means one who dwells in the sphere of battle (*saṅgāmāvacara*) should depart.
422. Regarding "one whose counsel is exalted" (*ussitamantī*): showing here that "one whose counsel is exalted" (*ussitamantī*) [means this], he says, "one who speaks... [greed]...".
Therein, by the phrase "speech saturated with greed, hatred, delusion, and conceit," he shows the meaning of the word *ussita*. "One who speaks" (*bhāsitā*)...
By this, he shows the meaning of the word “mantī” (counselor). Regarding the term “nissitajappī” (one who prattles depending [on others]):

showing that his prattle depends on another, he says “attano” (of himself), and so forth. Here, “jappa” means speech; for it is stated in the lists of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*) that “*jappa* means speech.
“Ussadayuttaṃ” means associated with greed and other such defilements; the connection is with the word “vacanaṃ” (speech).
*Evamaññanti*: they think thus, [meaning] they think otherwise by themselves. *Kathānusandhivacane*: in the speech that connects the conversation between the accuser and the accused.
Here, by the word "vacane" (speech), he shows that in the phrase "bhāsānusandhi" (connection of speech), the word *bhāsā* is a synonym for *vacana* (speech).
*Ussāreti*: he causes to go upward. By this, he explains the meaning of the word *ussādeti* as "he causes to go upward" (*upari gamāpeti*).
[The text] shows this. For here, the letters *da* and *ra* have similar meanings; indeed, these two syllables sometimes have similar meanings in certain contexts.
"Avasāreti" means he causes [someone] to go to a state of inferiority. By this, [the author] shows the meaning of the word "avasādeti" as "he causes to go to a lower state.
There is also the reading "apasādetā," where the difference is merely in the prefix (*upasagga*). And much frivolous talk...
Regarding the word *bhāsati*, it is said here that the term *sampha* refers to speech consisting of meaningless talk; thus he says, "meaningless talk" (*niratthakakatha*).
For since such meaningless talk brings about destruction and destroys well-being (*saṃhitasukha*), it is therefore called *sampha*.
Furthermore, both as the root *phā* and as the root *phala* are stated in the lists of roots (in the *Saddanīti* and *Dhātumāla*, under the section on roots ending in *l*).
"Without the burden being assigned" means when the burden has not been assigned to one by the Saṅgha with the words, "This is your burden. "Having overwhelmed" means having overcome.

By this, he shows that the word *pasayha* has the sense of overcoming in the phrase "it proceeds by force. "In a place where there is no authority" means in a position where one does not have mastery.
By the word "speaker," he shows that the verbal root *vad* has the sense of speaking. *Anokāsakamma* (the act of not granting an opportunity).

Regarding the word *kāretvā*, since the letter *n* here lacks the status of being joined with a consonant (*yutta*), he says, "without performing the formal act of granting space (*okāsakamma*)," in order to show the place where it ought to be joined.
Regarding *yassa*: this means *yā assa*. The construction is: "whatever view belongs to that bhikkhu himself. Alternatively, the construction is:
"whatever view might belong to himself. *Taṃ* refers to that view. By the word *kathetā*, [the meaning of] *byākatā* (declared) is indicated here.
This shows the purpose of the statement regarding the element of prior action.
Commentary on the Vohāravagga, §424:

“Neither by teaching nor by emerging”—this was said with reference to an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). “In accordance with the fault” means in accordance with the fault consisting of the objective basis (vatthu).

Regarding the phrase "he does not know the application" (*payoga*): if the application were different from and distinct from the root offense (*mūla*), then it could not be called the "application of the root.
Therefore, he says, "For of legal issues" (*adhikaraṇānaṃ hi*), and so forth. *Hi* means "truly" or "because.
The intention is that the root itself is what is called the "application," and nothing else.
"Does not know what should be done" means the construction is: "he does not know the performance of the legal act (*kamma*) that ought to be performed.

"The matter" refers to the basis for quarreling, strife, and so forth; it is connected with "the matters for censure and so on" (*niyassādīnaṃ vatthū*). "Of the four" refers to the four [legal acts] by way of censure (*tajjanīya*), demotion (*niyassa*), banishment (*pabbājanīya*), and reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*).
"He requests" means he requests the Saṅgha to settle the legal act.
Regarding the term "basis" (*vatthu*): here it is said that the "basis" refers specifically to the categories of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), hence the phrase "of the seven categories of offenses.

It is stated as "threefold presentation" (*paññatti*) because it is included within the presentation of the six types of presentation: presentation by partial rule, presentation by universal rule, common presentation, uncommon presentation, presentation on one side, and presentation on both sides. [The text continues: "In ascending and descending order..."
By the phrase "having made [the connection], he joins the words," it shows the meaning of *padapaccābhaṭṭha* as the slipping,
falling, or dropping away of words after they have been turned back through inversion (from bottom to top).
Regarding the word "Vinaya," he says, "both in the Vinaya Piṭaka and in its commentary," indicating that it is not only in the canonical text (*pāḷi*) but also in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Regarding the phrase "he does not know the *ñatti*," the author says "in brief" and so forth, in order to show the different types of *ñatti*. "Therein" refers to the two kinds of *ñatti*.
"The *ñatti* of the formal act" (*kamma-ñatti*) is the *ñatti* that stands in the place of the proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*).

The meaning is that there is no proclamation; it stands by itself in the place where a proclamation would normally stand. "The *ñatti* of the motion of the formal act" (*kammapāda-ñatti*) refers to the [initial] motion of the proclamation...
The motion (*ñatti*) is the foot and the root. "In nine instances" means in the nine instances beginning with reinstatement (*osāraṇā*).

"In two instances" refers to the two instances by way of the motion-second and the motion-fourth; the connection is that he does not know how to perform the motion which is the foot of the formal act (*kamma*).
The construction is: "this fourfold settlement" (*samatha*). "That" refers to the fourfold settlement. "By means of the motion" (*ñattiyā*)...
The term in the genitive case is used in the sense of identity (*sāmyatthe*). The connection is: "that legal issue which is being settled. "Of that" refers to the legal issue.
The connection is: "he does not know that settling.

Regarding the phrase "he does not know the *sutta*," here the word *sutta* sometimes, in certain contexts, refers to the *mātikā* (the summary table of contents) and sometimes to the *Suttanta-piṭaka*.
And because it proceeds in both ways, he says "both Vibhaṅgas" here: "the Ubhatovibhaṅga.

Regarding the phrase "he does not know the Vinaya," although the word *vinaya* here refers to the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, since the two Vibhaṅgas are taken as the meaning of "sutta" in this context, only the Khandhakas and Parivāra are to be understood here;
thus he says, "he does not know the Khandhakas and Parivāra."
Regarding the phrase "he does not know the Vinaya," it is stated here as "setting aside the Vinaya Piṭaka" because the Vinaya Piṭaka is what must be understood in this context.

Regarding the "four great authorities (mahāpadesa)" for a Suttantika: these four great authorities are established by way of the authority of the Buddha, the authority of the Saṅgha, the authority of many elders, and the authority of a single elder.
"Therein" refers to the group of five. "That" refers to the statement. "In all cases" means in all the groups of five.
Thus ends the exposition of the commentary on the Chapter on Non-Dependence, the Chapter on Non-Quiescence,
and the Chapter on Conventional Designation.

Commentary on the Chapter on the Manifestation of Views (Diṭṭhāvikammavagga) 425. Regarding the phrase "manifestation of views" (*diṭṭhāvikamma*) in the Chapter on the Manifestation of Views: here, *āvikamma* means that which is made manifest;
thus, showing that it is the manifestation of views, he says, "the manifestations of views. By the phrase "the disclosure of tenets" (*laddhipakāsanānaṃ*), [he indicates the same].
He shows that the word *diṭṭhi* (view) is a synonym for *laddhi* (adherence), and the word *āvikamma* (manifestation) is a synonym for *pakāsana* (explanation).

"This" refers to the name "manifestation of views. He says "of a grave offense" because, in meaning, that which does not lead to confession is grave. The word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even of a light [offense]" has the sense of censure;
the meaning is that the manifestation of views is illegitimate even when a light offense has been confessed, let alone when a grave one has been.
“As [he confesses]... so it becomes”: the construction is that when four or five have become one, the confession is made by those four or five.

“By four or five” indicates the final limit; it is not permitted to confess together with more than that number, and the offense confessed in such a manner is not cleared, and there is an *dukkaṭa* for the act of confessing. This is because “four or five” defines the ultimate limit.
Because it has been shown [in other contexts], it should be understood that it is permissible to teach two or three [terms] together.

Regarding the phrase "by the mind (mano-mānasa)," here the word *mano* indicates that the word *mānasa*—which can also apply to passion (*rāga*) and arahants—excludes those meanings and applies only to the mental faculty (*citta*).
Therefore, it is said: "by the mind designated as *mano*. By this, [it is shown that it is] that which has become the mind...
The phrase *mānasaṃ manomānasaṃ* shows the meaning of the word.

The word "also" (*pi*) in the expression "even for one of the same communion" (*samānasaṃvāsakassapi*) indicates that even for one of the same communion who is standing within a different boundary (*nānāsīmā*), the disclosure is invalid;
how much more so for one of a different communion (*nānāsaṃvāsaka*). "In the courtyard of the monastery boundary" (*māḷakasīmāya*) means in the open space of a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*).
"Within the non-separation boundary (avippavāsa-sīmā)" refers to the great boundary (mahāsīmā); it is connected with the phrase "in the presence of one who stands [there].

By the word "also" (pi), the meaning "even for one standing within a partial boundary (khaṇḍasīmā)" is included. 430. "Not sufficient" (na pariyattaṃ) means not capable. By this, in the expression "not enough" (nālaṃ), the word *alaṃ* has the sense of sufficiency (*pariyatta*) alone.

This shows that it is not for the purpose of ornamenting or warding off [danger]. "Here too" (*idhāpi*) refers even to the pentad; by the word *pi* (also/even), it refers back to the preceding pentad.
By the phrase "from the teaching" (*sāsanato*), it shows the ablative case of the root *cu*. By the word "desire" (*kāmo*), it shows that the term *adhippāya* is a synonym for *kāma*.

432. Regarding the expression "due to dullness and delusion" (*mandattā momūhattā*): here, the suffix *-tta* denotes the sense of abstract state (*bhāvatthe*), and the fifth case ending (*pañcamīvibhatti*) denotes the sense of cause (*kāraṇatthe*).
Showing the state of occurrence, he said: "by way of dullness and by way of delusion. Regarding "despising," showing that the meaning here is "those desiring to despise," he said:
"having become one desiring to impose contempt. "In other declarations" means even in the declarations of Arahatship.
"Everywhere" refers to the Diṭṭhāvikamma-vagga. "Yaṃ" is the word [referring to the person].
Thus ends the explanation of the commentary on the Chapter on the Manifestation of Views.
Regarding the commentary on the Chapter on False Speech (Musāvāda-vagga): 444.
With reference to the primacy of the Dhamma and the foundation of the Dhamma, it is said: "One who goes toward a defeat is 'one who goes to a defeat' (pārājikagāmī)."

This was stated by way of the simple agent (*suddhakattu*), with reference to the person as the primary factor and the person as the basis (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). It may also be stated by way of the instrumental cause-agent (*karaṇahetukattu*), as in: "one goes to a defeat (*pārājika*) by means of this, or causes another to go [to it], thus he is 'one who goes to a defeat' (*pārājikagāmī*).

Showing the detailed explanation, he said: "In that regard," and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) refers to the textual passage beginning with "false speech leads to a defeat," and so on. Thus...

The connection is that "the detailed exposition is to be understood. Among those [cases], in expressions such as "false speech leads to a *pārājika* offense," the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "by not seeing," he asks, "Not seeing what? and answers, "Of the one who holds the Vinaya. To show the detailed exposition, he says, "Regarding what is allowable and what is unallowable," and so forth.
"Him" refers to the one who holds the Vinaya. Regarding the phrase "by not hearing," he asks, "Whose word?"
Regarding the phrase "not hearing," he said, "even while dwelling alone," and so forth. "Even while dwelling alone" means even when dwelling alone with a holder of the Vinaya.
By the word "even" (pi), he indicates that it goes without saying in the case of dwelling with others. "Attendance" (upaṭṭhāna) means for the purpose of attending, or the place of attendance.
The construction is: "being one who does not hear the words of others being spoken. In the term *pasuttakato*, there is the elision of the letter *y*.
He said: "By way of being asleep. The word *pi* (also) in the phrase "by way of being asleep" includes other causes such as not seeing [the object] and so forth.

Regarding the term *tathasaññī* ("perceiving it as such"), he says "one who falls into [an offense] regarding what is unallowable... and so on, to show that the word *tathā* refers to the specific object.
By the phrase "by way of exceeding one night," etc., the word *ādi* (etc. includes exceeding six nights and so forth. "In all instances" refers to the Chapter on False Speech (*Musāvādavagga*).
Thus ends the commentary on the section concerning false speech (*musāvāda-vagga*).
Commentary on the section concerning instruction for bhikkhunīs (*bhikkhunovāda-vagga*): 450.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of non-gain" (*alābhāya*) in the *Bhikkhunī-vagga*, here the root *labh* (to obtain) functions as the object, and the word of dative case (*sampadāna*) has that same sense.

Showing this, he said: “for the sake of not obtaining the four conditions. By the word “exerts” (*vāyamati*), he demonstrates the meaning of striving (*vāyama*), rejecting here the meaning of capability for the root *sak* (as in “he endeavors”).
“The instruction of the Kali age” (*kalisāsana*) means a command for the defeat of evil.
“For the sake of extracting” (*nīharaṇatthāya*) means for the sake of removing by way of extraction.
451. Because it is stated generally as "kamma," [it means] "one of the seven types of kamma. 454. Regarding the phrase "not to be discussed":
what kind of course of discussion here is not to be discussed? Is it not the Vinaya itself? To this he says: "The course of discussion concerning what is allowable... [etc.
By the word "na kathetabbo" (is not to be told), the word *kaccha* is derived from the verbal root *kath*.

It illuminates the state of being accomplished (*nipphannabhāva*). But why, after rejecting [the possibility] with "not by one beyond training" (*na asekkhena*) in the first pentad, is it stated as "by one beyond training" (*asekkhena*) and so forth in the second pentad? To this he says: "Because... and so on. The construction is: "The other, the worldling (*puthujjana*), does not speak.

Regarding the phrase "one who has not attained the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*na atthapaṭisambhidāppatto*), "meaning" (*attha*) here is intended specifically as the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*); therefore, he says: "of the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathāya*).
Regarding the phrase “one who has attained analytical knowledge”: *paṭisambhidā* refers to wisdom (*paññā*) because it breaks through (*pati-sambhijjati*) each individual object such as meaning;

one who has attained that is “one who has attained analytical knowledge. By the phrase “attained analytical knowledge regarding meaning,” he shows that this is one who has attained analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

By the phrase “regarding the textual doctrine (*pāḷidhamma*),” he shows the specific nature of the doctrine (*dhamma*) in the expression “one who has attained analytical knowledge of doctrine (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).”
"In conventional terminology" (*vohāraniruttiyā*) means "in the terminology of designations" (*paññattiniruttiyā*).

By this, he shows the nature of the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) in the phrase "one who has attained the analytical knowledge of language. Regarding the phrase "one who has attained the analytical knowledge of perspicuity" (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāpatta*), he says "the knowledges beginning with the analytical knowledge of meaning" (*atthapaṭisambhidādīni ñāṇāni*), because "perspicuity" (*paṭibhāna*) refers precisely to those three preceding knowledges. "In them" (*tesu*) refers to those knowledges; whatever is liberated, and how it is liberated—this is what is meant.
"Citta" means mind. "Paccavekkhitā" means repeatedly observed. "Sabbattha" means throughout the section on nuns.
Thus ends the explanation of the commentary on the Section on Advice to Nuns (Bhikkhunovādavagga). [Now begins] the commentary on the Section on the Committee (Ubbāhikavagga).
455. In the section on the *ubbāhika* (committee of experts), while demonstrating the analysis of the compound in the phrase "skilled in the meaning" (*atthakusala*) and so forth, he says:

"skilled in the commentary" (*aṭṭhakathākusalo*), etc. "From the mouth of the teacher" (*ācariyamukhato*) means from the face of the teacher or in the presence of the teacher. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the lax, the emphatic, and so forth," he includes the long and short vowels and other such qualities.
Regarding "the delimitation of syllables" (*akkharaparicchede*), it refers to [knowing] that this much is lax and this much is emphatic, and so on.
"In the analysis of syllables" (*akkharaparicchede*). By this, he shows that in the phrase "skilled in phonemes" (*byañjanakusalo*), the word *byañjana* is a synonym for *akkhara* (syllable).

Regarding the phrase "not skilled in the sequence [of meaning]" (*na pubbāparakusalo*), he states that "sequence" (*pubbāpara*) refers both to the four preceding [sections] and to the sequence of the discourse;
thus he says, "in the sequence of the meaning" (*atthapubbāpare*), and so forth.

The connection is that the words beginning with "kodhana" have been stated. The construction is "because he is not able. Regarding the word *pasāretā*, since the verbal root *sar* here denotes a variety of meanings due to the influence of the prefix (*upasagga*), he says "a deluder.
Thus ends the commentary on the Ubbāhikavagga.
[Now begins] the commentary on the Adhikaraṇavūpasamavagga.

457. Regarding the section on the settlement of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇavūpasamavagga*), as for what is called "veneration of the Saṅgha" (*saṅghagaru*): it is said, "When [one honors] the Dhamma... [and so forth]... it is called veneration of the Saṅgha.

The word "those" (*tāni*) refers to robes and other such requisites. 458. Regarding the phrase "by five ways, Upāli": here, the word *ākāra* has the sense of "cause" (*kāraṇa*), thus he says, "by five causes.

In the passage beginning with "by an act" (*kammena*), showing the actual nature of the acts and so forth, he says, "in the case of the formal announcement (*apalokana*), etc. Regarding the word "grounds" (*upapattīhi*):
"By means of arguments. The construction is: "You know my status as one who has gone forth from a high-born family and my state of being well-versed in the scriptures.
The construction is: "Is it not fitting for you that there should be one such as I...? "At the ear" means near the ear.

"By means of proclamation" means by making a statement in their presence. "Of them" refers to the monks. "In the nature of not turning back" means having the character of not retreating. "By the drawing of lots" [is the phrase].
By means of causing one's own voting tally to be taken.

"In this context" refers to the formal acts (kamma) and so forth. "Measure" refers to the cause for the schism in the Saṅgha. "Preceding parts" refers to those occurring prior to the schism in the Saṅgha.
Revealing their status as preceding parts, he said: "By way of illustrating the eighteen grounds," and so forth. "Even while speaking" means...
The construction [of the sentence]. "Therein" means in common usage (*vohāra*). But when is the Saṅgha split? To this he says: "When, however," and so forth.
The connection is with the words "when... performs. "Kamma" (act) should be understood as an act other than the Uposatha-kamma.
"Uddesa" (recitation) refers to the Uposatha-kamma. "Iti" means thus. Regarding the statement in the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā*: "Thus... pe ... we shall explain."
The construction is: "We have spoken. Having supplied the reading "of that speech," it is to be connected with the phrase "this is its meaning.
Regarding the expression "paññattentaṃ," he says "this is what has been prescribed" because there is a sandhi involving the elision of the *niggahita* (anusvāra).

"Kva" means in which *khandhaka*. "Tatra" means in the *Vatta-khandhaka*. "Ettāvatā" means by this much, namely, merely by not performing the guest-observances (*āgantuka-vatta*) and so forth. "Anupubbenā" means...
In due order. Regarding the phrase *yathārattaṃ*: here the word *yathā* expresses the sense of "conformity" (*anurūpa*).

Showing that by the word *ratti* (night) the measure of the night is to be understood, he says, "in conformity with the measure of the night. By this, he demonstrates the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) as "that which is according to the night" (*yathārattaṃ*), meaning conformable to the night.
When it is said, "in conformity with the measure of the night," [it implies] because the measure of the night has been exceeded...
Regarding the phrase "atthato thero," he says: "The meaning is 'as an elder' (yathātheraṃ). "Vavatthāna" means delimitation.
For that which stands having been set apart individually is called "vavatthāna.
Regarding the expression "kammākammāni," having made the word-analysis as "kamma akammāni," he says "both small and great deeds," because the letter *a* has the sense of increase (*vuddhattha*).
And since the greatness of non-action is established, it follows by implication that action is indeed minor;
thus it is said, "and minor. By taking the negative prefix *a-* in the sense of "insignificant," the meaning "both great and minor actions" is also quite appropriate.
However, that [meaning] is not adopted here, though it is seen elsewhere. "High and low..."
For in the passage where it is stated by way of the words “kammāni,” the word *ucca* indicates the sense of greatness, while the word *avaca* indicates the sense of smallness.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as “great and small kamma.
Furthermore, since non-kamma possesses a small nature, it should be seen that the term “kamma” is established by implication as meaning “great.”
Commentary on the Two Chapters on Schism in the Sangha (Saṅghabhedavagga): 459.

In the two chapters on schism in the Sangha, *ete* means "these," referring to their intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*). *Te* refers to the unrighteous acts (*adhamma*) and so forth. *Iti* means "thus. *Yaṃ kammaṃ* is to be construed [with the preceding].
*Diṭṭhiṃ vinidhāya* is the connection [to be made]. In one of the fivefold sets, this application of the meaning (*atthayojanā*) should be made.
The connection [is as follows]. "In this too" means even in this pentad (*pañcaka*). By the word "too" (*pi*), it refers back to the pentad mentioned previously.

"In all cases" means in all the pentads. "Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. The construction is: that statement which exists according to the method not previously stated does not exist here in these pentads.
Commentary on the Chapter on Residents (Āvāsikavagga) 461.

In the Chapter on Residents, by the word “having carried away” (*haritvā*), [the commentator] shows that in the phrase “as it was brought” (*yathābhataṃ*), the verbal root *bhar-* has both the sense of carrying and the status of being an adverbial modifier of the action.
By the word “placed” (*ṭhapito*), [he shows that] in the phrase “deposited” (*nikkhittaṃ*), the verbal root *khip-*...
He shows it for the purpose of establishing. 462.
"Pariṇāmeti" means he causes it to reach its transformation. By the phrase "he determines and speaks," he shows the intended meaning; "here" refers to the section on resident monks (*āvāsika-vagga*).
This concludes the commentary on the section on the spreading of the kaṭhina cloth (*kaṭhina-atthāra-vagga*).

467. Regarding the phrase "one who has gone into darkness" (*otamasiko*) in the section on the *Kathina* ceremony: here, by saying "one who has gone into darkness," he shows that "gone into darkness" means having entered into obscurity.
By the word "darkness" (*andhakāra*), he indicates that the word "obscurity" (*tama*) is a synonym for darkness.
"That" refers to the state of being in darkness. "Not attending to it" means not attending to that; as to why he does not attend to it, he says: "because he is occupied with his duties."
"Vandanaṃ" means "with anger. "Ekato" refers to one who is hostile;
a person who is an enemy and of a different nature is called "ekāvatto" in the sense of being turned away from [virtue] due to anger. "Pahareyya" means he might strike him while he is paying homage.
By the phrase "aññaṃ cintayamāno," it is shown that one whose mind is directed elsewhere—that is, one who applies or places the mind upon another object—is called "aññavitho."

“Ukkhitto” (one who has been suspended) means one who, having been removed from the Saṅgha, has been cast out and excluded; he is thus called an *ukkhitaka* (one who is suspended). “By them” means by the four [categories of persons].
This connects with the phrase “among the fifteen persons not to be saluted. “And for the reason stated in between” refers to the reason stated in the interim:
“For if one were to salute him, his forehead might strike even the legs of the bed,” and so forth. “From this” means...
"From among the fifteen persons. "Iti" means "thus. If both the recitation teacher (*uddesācariya*) and the instruction teacher (*ovādācariya*) are junior (*navaka*), they are not to be saluted.
"In all cases" refers to the section on the spreading of the *kathina* cloth.
Thus ends the explanation of the word-by-word commentary (*yojanā*) for the section on the spreading of the *kathina*.
The commentary on the explanation of the five cases concerning Upāli is concluded.

Regarding the commentary on the origins of offenses (*āpatti-samutthāna*), in such passages as “one incurs [an offense] without intent,” the construction should be understood in this way: “one incurs [an offense] without intent.”
One commits [the offense] while being without consciousness (*acittaka*). The same method applies here regarding the phrase "one emerges from it while being without consciousness.
The connection is "any offense whatsoever" (*yaṃkiñci āpattiṃ*); the construction is "another offense" (*itaraṃ āpattiṃ*).

Regarding the thought "I am giving the gift of the Dharma," there is the word spoken by the Blessed One: "The gift of the Dharma conquers all gifts," and "He is a giver of the Deathless who instructs in the Dharma."

"Having heard [the teaching], I give the gift of Dhamma. "Domanassiko" means one who is possessed of mental distress (*domanassa*), or one who has mental distress. "Therein" refers to the roots of the indeterminate (*abyākata*). 473.
"Of whichever" refers to whichever training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "All that" refers to every respective training rule originating from those [roots].
This concludes the secondary collection of verses.
(1) Explanation of the Offenses of Body, etc. 474.
Regarding the phrase "six offenses are bodily," one asks: what are these six offenses? He says: "In the intermediate peyyāla," and so forth.
The connection is that they are stated in the intermediate peyyāla. By the phrase "because they originate at the door of the body," it is shown that they arise in the body.
This demonstrates the meaning of the term *kāyikā*. The connection is that [these offenses] were stated in that very same intermediate section (*antarapeyyāla*).

By the phrase “of one who conceals a fault” (*vajjapaṭicchādikāya*) and so forth, he shows the specific forms of the three [offenses] for one who conceals. By the phrase “of a nun” (*bhikkhuniyā*) and so forth, he shows the specific forms of the five conditions for physical contact (*saṃsagga*).
By the words beginning with “*ekaratta*,” he shows the nature of the three [offenses] mentioned in the phrase “at dawn, there are three.

Regarding the statement “two *yāvatatiyakā*,” he says “but by way of their formal establishment (*paññatti*), etc.,” in order to refute the contradiction with the commentary which states, “there are eleven called *yāvatatiyakā*” as things to be explained.
By the phrase “in this teaching (*imasmiṃ sāsane*),” he shows the scope of the word “here (*ettha*).”
Regarding the phrase "by one, there is the inclusion of all": as to what is meant by "one" and what is meant by "all," he says, "of whomsoever it may be," and so forth.

By the expression "by way of the introduction to the Nidāna," he shows the specific nature of the "one. By the words "of the training rules and of the recitations of the Pātimokkha," he shows the specific nature of the "all.
The term *saṅgaha* (inclusion) forms a compound with the genitive case of the action (*kamma-chaṭṭhī-samāsa*).
By the phrase “of one who conceals a *vajja*,” etc., [the text] shows the specific form of the two offenses of concealing a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*).
By the phrase “a monk [concealing] a nun’s,” etc., it shows the specific form of the four [offenses] regarding the interval between villages.
Again, by the phrase “a monk [concealing] a nun’s,” etc., it shows the specific form of those same four [offenses] regarding crossing a river.

It shows that they are of the same form. By the statement, “In the giving of a robe, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),” it is shown that because they are identical in their nature as offenses of expiation, no distinction in number should be made.
(2) Commentary on those [offenses] leading to confession, etc.
475. *Ekettha*: here the word *ettha* refers to the scope of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
The word *pi* (even) indicates the meaning: "there is not even a single training rule," implying "let alone many training rules," "let alone an offense," and "there is not even an offense.
By the phrase "in the entire Vinaya," he shows the scope of the word *ettha* in the reading *dvettha*. *Ubhinnam*...
[This applies] to both monks and nuns. However, to explain how many constitute a first offense otherwise, he says: "But otherwise," and so forth.
Therein, "otherwise" means in a manner different from the formal promulgation (*paññatti*). "And the motion" (*kammañca*) refers to the motion itself (*kammañatti*).

"And the proponent of the motion" (*kammapādikā ca*) refers to the motion that establishes the procedure (*kammapādañatti*). "In nine instances" refers to the nine instances beginning with reinstatement (*osāraṇa*). "In two" refers to [procedures] consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*).

Regarding the formal acts consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*): the arrangement is that these three—the *pārājika* for one who conceals a fault, the *pārājika* for one who follows a suspended monk, and the *pārājika* for one who possesses the eight grounds—are [to be understood].

"By way of being the cause" means by way of being the reason (*hetu*); there is also the reading "by way of being the instrument" (*karaṇabhūtena*), which means by way of being the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*).

"Of them" refers to those deficient in the requisites (*addhāna*) and so forth. "In this regard" refers to the textual passage, "Three persons are not to be ordained," or to these individuals who are deficient in limbs and so forth.

"He" refers to the person. The connection is: "one who is incomplete does not request [ordination]. The construction is: "Matricides and others are those who commit an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Therein" refers to those procedures such as the formal motion (*ñatti*). "The procedure of the motion" means the method of the motion. "An interrupted private interrogation" means...
"Unfinished" means "individual. "Past performance" means the performance of what is past. Expanding upon this, he said: "Endowed with the matter," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the three summaries of actions," here there is a loss of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) before the letter *n* for the purpose of protecting the integrity of the syllable *chanda*.

"Those to be expelled" (*nāsitaka*) refers to persons who ought to be expelled; they are called "expelled" (*nāsita*) because they are to be expelled, and those who are expelled are "the expelled ones" (*nāsitaka*). "Of the three persons":

The construction is: "having three persons seeking full ordination with a single preceptor (upajjhāya) and different teachers (ācariya). "A single proclamation" (ekānussāvanā) means a proclamation made together.
A "pāda" is one-fourth of a kahāpaṇa. A "māsaka" is one-fifth of a pāda. "Pārājika" refers to the second pārājika offense for one who cuts down a forest tree.
"Indiscriminately" (anodissa) means not specifying [a particular person], such as saying, "Let the man die," and so forth. "By that" means by the poison.
In the section on the exhorter of bhikkhunīs, there is a general rule (*sāmaññādhāra*). "Among the ten training rules" (*dasasu sikkhāpadesu*) is a specific rule (*visesādhāra*).
"In the very first training rule" means among the ten training rules, in the first training rule itself. The connection is with the phrase "for a fully ordained bhikkhunī.
By the words "there is an offense," he indicates the point of connection for the term "with a robe."

By the phrase “only four,” he shows the scope of the word *tā* in the term *tattikā*. They are called *tattikā* because those offenses have four as their measure (*parimāṇa*). The same principle applies here in the phrase “even for one lying down.
*Sā* refers to that nun. (3) Commentary on the *Pācittiya*: 476.
“Five kinds of medicinal tonics” refers to the five tonics beginning with flour-gruel (*sabbi*). The connection is: “this offense. “Subsequently incurred” is the construction.
"One mouthful" (*ekaṃ kabaḷaṃ*) means one morsel (*ālopaṃ*). "In your presence" (*tumhamūle*) means in your vicinity.
"According to the basis" (*yathāvatthukaṃ*) means in accordance with the specific offense; the construction is that the offenses have already been confessed.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Kokālika and the others," Kaṭamodaka-Tissa and others are included. Regarding the non-renunciation of a wicked view (*pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge*).
The construction is: "the *pācittiya* [offense] and the *pācittiya* [offense] of the nun Caṇḍakālikā.

"On account of speech that is instigated" means on account of speech joined with such modes as solicitation, signs, and so forth. "An offense of defeat" (*pārājika*) means the committing of a *pārājika*.
Alternatively, "of defeat" means that for this monk there is an offense of defeat, or it refers to the *pārājika* itself.
The construction should be made as: "there is an offense for him. The word "iti" (thus) is to be construed with: "he incurs these six offenses. The connection is:
"having taken food, while swallowing it. "In that very way" means: just as in the case of eating [solid food], so too is the construction:
"while swallowing meat or garlic. Furthermore, the words "delicate foods" (*paṇītabhojanāni*) and "unallowable meat" (*akappiyamaṃsaṃ*) [are to be understood accordingly].
These [terms] are to be connected with the word “while consuming.
“Five grounds” refers to five grounds consisting of offenses. “Therein” means among the five who share the same Dhamma.
“Of two” refers to monks and nuns. “Of them” refers to those such as female trainees (sikkhamānā) and so forth. “Only of five” means only of those who share the same Dhamma.
“Legal terminology” (*vinicchayavohāro*) means legal language. By this, he rejects the four types of legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*).
“A lawsuit” (*aḍḍakammaṃ*) means the legal action of those who bring an accusation.
By the phrase “of those who follow the true Dharma” (*sahadhammikānaṃ*), he shows the nature of the fivefold adjudication (*pañcavinicchayo*) here; it is the state of being excellent.
Explaining in detail, he said, “One who has committed an offense,” and so forth. “Of fresh virtue” means one whose virtue has newly arisen.
He said “ordinary” because, in its actual sense, “of fresh virtue” is synonymous with “ordinary virtue”; the meaning is that one who is endowed with ordinary virtue.

By the phrase “arising from the door of the body,” he shows that the word *kāyika* (bodily) is a derivative (*taddhita*) formation. The connection is: “It is stated here [in this context] that the face should be looked upon.”

Regarding the phrase "and by the teaching of the four," he says "by the teaching of transgression" (*accayadesanā*), taking the word "teaching" (*desanā*) as an elided initial term. "That" refers to the teaching of transgression. "They kill with a bow after lying in wait" refers to assassins (*abhimāra*).

Regarding the phrase "there is a cutting off" (*chejjaṃ hoti*), "cutting off" here means precisely the incurring of a *pārājika* offense; thus he says, "like Devadatta, one incurs a *pārājika*. "But these offenses" refers to the *pārājika* and *thullaccaya* offenses. (4) Commentary on Persons Not to Be Saluted, etc.
477. “Of them” means of the ten types of persons. By the word “together” (*saddhiṃ*), he shows that here the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahatthe*).
As for “by way of proper conduct” (*sāmīcena*): proper conduct (*sāmīci*) is the action (*kamma*) to be performed by way of proper conduct;
[it is] by that proper conduct. Rejecting the idea that the phrase “wearing the ten [days’] robes” is a compound, he says: “the wearing of extra robes for ten days.”

In the two verse-quarters beginning with *katisataṃ*, he says, "having concealed one hundred offenses for one hundred nights," demonstrating that among the four inflected words in those two quarters, the first should be construed with the first and the second with the second, respectively.
The same method applies to the first half of the subsequent verse as well. *Ayaṃ hi* means "this very [thing] which is about to be explained. *Ettha* means "in this verse."
The connection is: "Whatever monk conceals. "Thus" (iti) refers to this summary meaning.

It should be understood that among the four sets of four mentioned above, twelve faults of formal acts (*kammadosa*) have been stated, having excluded the legitimate united act (*dhammena samagga*). One should apply [the terms] as: "an illegitimate factional act" (*adhammena vaggakamma*) and "an illegitimate united act" (*adhammena samaggakamma*).
"In this regard" (*ettha*) means within the six types of formal acts. "This very thing" (*etadeva*) means precisely the legitimate united act.
Regarding the phrase "yaṃ desitā," it is said that here the word *yaṃ* is a grammatical inversion (vacanavipallāsa), hence [the commentary] says "yāni desitāni.

By the word "desitāni," it shows that in the phrase "desitā," the syllable *ni* has been replaced by the vowel *ā*. By the phrase "because it is devoid of the state of having a limit or boundary," it shows the etymological meaning of *ananta*:
that which has no end (*anta*) or limit (*pariyanta) is "endless" (*ananta*). *Taṃ* refers to Nibbāna.

The connection is "conquered. To the question "By whom? What? How? Having done what was it conquered?", he says: "By the Blessed One, having crushed the host of defilements. To the question "By whom? What? How?
Having done what was it conquered? What is it like?", he says: "As a king, having crushed the host of enemies, [conquers] his kingdom.
Therein, by the word "by the king," he answers the question "by whom? By the word "the host of enemies,"...
With the word “*ka*” (what), he answered the question “What?”; with the phrase “having crushed,” he answered the question “Having done what?”;
and with the word “kingdom,” he answered the question “What? “The host of enemies” means a host of adversaries. Here, however, is the construction:
just as a king, having crushed the host of his enemies, has conquered the kingdom—that is, the status of kingship—so too by the Blessed One...
"Having crushed the mass of defilements, Nibbāna is conquered. "Sveva" means the Blessed One himself.
By the phrase "nibbikāratāya," he shows that the word *tā* here expresses the sense of "state of being without agitation" (*nibbikāra*) and is an unformed (*anipphanna*) derivative suffix.
By the phrase "vivekapañcakaṃ," the threefold seclusion (of body, mind, and requisites) should also be understood, because they are identical in their nature as seclusion (*viveka*). Therefore...
The connection is with the word "by the Blessed One. By the phrase "the seven classes of offenses," he shows the scope of the word *eka* (one) in the expression *ekettha*.
"Therein" means among the seven classes of offenses. "But here," however, refers to the methods of settling disputes (*samatha*).

"Indeed" (*hi*) means truly. "Of that" refers to the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence). "In the commentaries" (*aṭṭhakathāsu*) means in all the commentaries. "We, however... [is as follows].
"But we, the compilers"—the meaning is "we who are named Buddhaghosa"; "we approve" is the syntactical connection.
To the question, "Whose [work] and for what purpose do you approve it?", he says: "'The mere sense of the negation of the particle *vinā*.
The phrase "of the particle *vinā*" has a denotative relationship with the phrase "the mere sense. This is his own statement establishing his position.
Establishing [the point] by means of the words of the Accomplisher—which are designated as the "Word of the Buddha"—he says: "And it is also said," and so forth.

"Eighteen eightfold [splits]" means that among the three types of splits—those based on wrong views regarding the Dhamma, those based on right views regarding the Dhamma, and those based on doubt—one takes each of these three as a root, resulting in nine; and within those [nine], taking the split based on right views regarding the Dhamma as a root...

It should be understood that by removing [the repetitions], there are eight [offenses]; when these eight are applied to the eighteen grounds for schism (*bhedakaravatthu*), they become eighteen sets of eight.
"One hundred and fifty minus six" means one hundred and forty-four. "In each individual ground" means in each of the eighteen grounds for schism.
Thus ends the commentary on the collection of verses.
Now begins the commentary on the *Avippavāsa-pañha* (The Question on Not Being Apart), the first of the *Sedamocika-gāthā*.

479. Regarding the *Sedamocikā-gāthā*: because the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*) is profound, it causes perspiration (*seda*) to break out on the bodies of the Vinaya-holders as they contemplate it;
thus it is called *Sedamocikā*. Those very verses are the *Sedamocikā-gāthā*, and [the commentary refers] to them.
By the phrase "unlawful enjoyment (*akappiyasambhoga*) is not permitted," it shows that lawful enjoyment (*kappiyasambhoga*) is permitted. In order to demonstrate lawful enjoyment:
“Bathing, feeding, and so forth” is what was stated. “There is no offense” means there is no offense for the mother nun.
Regarding the phrase “this is the question,” here the word *pañha* is said in the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*)—such as the *Saddanīti*, the *Dhātumāla* under the root beginning with *ha* (No.
16), and the *Abhidhānappadīpikā* verse 115—to be of both genders by its inherent nature; however, here it is used in the feminine gender. “By the wise” means...

By this, he shows the cause of skillfulness; the intention is that one is "skillful" because of wisdom (*paṇḍittatā*). "Assa" means "of the question. "Etaṃ" refers to the answer. "Assa" refers to the verse.

"Ekādasa vivajjiyā" is a construction without a case ending; the meaning is "one should avoid eleven. Therefore it was said, beginning with "ye. In the phrase "tepi," the particle *pi* indicates that which is understood even though not explicitly stated in the verse.
The monk who was formerly a barber approached. "A created Buddha" means a form of the Buddha created by the Buddha.
Regarding the word *vivajjiya*, the letter *y* is a grammatical modification (*kāriya*) of the suffix *-tvā*; thus he says, "having avoided. The construction is:
"that trunk which exists without a head. It is called a *kabandha* because, being headless, it binds life to a body [merely] by means of that [trunk].
“Yassa” means of Kabandha.
“Hi” means truly. “Te” refers to those persons incapable [of attaining the goal].
Regarding “vācā,” he says “vācāya” because of the elision of the letter *y*. “Iti me” means “thus for me”; that is, while I am speaking thus.
"Speech" (vacana) is the construction [of the compound]. Alternatively, "iti-me" means "thus these"; the construction is: "knowing that these people are speaking thus.
By the word "also" (api), he shows that the sound of the voice is a synonym for "sound" (sadda). "Hi" means "truly. The construction is: "of that bhikkhu who was sitting in silence.
If there is no such thing as an offense at the mind-door, then being the case, why would he incur one?
Regarding the phrase "it is said to be verbal," he says, "But because... and so forth. "By that" means for that reason. "His" refers to the bhikkhu. "She" refers to the bhikkhunī;
the connection is that she incurs [the offense]. "Of the kind described" means of the kind described as "included within the village boundary.
"In those two" refers to the two bhikkhunīs.
Regarding the phrase "four persons," he says "the teacher and three pupils" in order to show the specific nature of these four individuals.
"By one's own hand" means stolen by one's own hand. "Also by command" means even that which has been stolen by one acting under an order. "Of the others" refers to the pupils;
the connection is that each [of them] received a *māsaka*. "Here" refers to the *Parivāra*, specifically in the verse on the "sweat-wiping" (*sedamocika*).
(2) Commentary on the Questions concerning the Pārājikas, etc.
480. “And the section on the spread” refers to the section on the spread as stated in the analysis of the first Pārājika.
“With reference to the change of sex” means that it is stated with reference to the relinquishing of what has been accepted when there is a change of sex.
The connection is "that monk transforms. The construction is "for his own sake. "Of this" refers to the verse.
"Crow-droppings" means the excrement discharged by crows. "Smeared with mud" means covered with mud. The connection is "having become directed toward the body itself.
"Hi" indicates an expansion [of the meaning]. The construction is "he would kill that ignoble woman or that man," [the latter] being due to a change in gender.

The connection is with the phrase "by means of that which has become a cause, [namely] that which has become female and that which has become male. "That which has become female" (*itthibhūta*) means having become a woman (*itthī hutvā bhūta*), or having attained the state of a woman (*itthibhāvaṃ vā pattaṃ*).

The construction is: "like the mother and father of animals, such as the ascetic Migasiṅga, Prince Sīha, and others. "The ascetic Migasiṅga" refers to the ascetic named Migasiṅga. "Prince Sīha" refers to Prince Sīhabāhu. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Bhūridatta and others are included.
The connection is that [this] has come down in the *Kurundi*.
