Regarding the phrase "of the verse ‘Speaking the truth’," the word "iti" should be connected with the statement "for one speaking the truth, there is a light offense. The construction is: "the meaning of the verse ‘Speaking the truth’ is thus.
(3) Explanation of the Questions on the *Pācittiya* and Other Offenses.

481. The construction is: "For that bhikkhu who gives the voting-ticket (salāka), there is cutting off (chejja). By the phrase "there is a pārājika," he shows the meaning of the word-pair *hoti* and *chejja*.
Regarding "a tree-root like a well-established banyan," either that [specific type] or any such tree-root should be taken.
Regarding "three women," he says "tāsupi" (among them too), indicating that here the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative, or alternatively, it is the nominative case.
By the phrase “that which is called sexual intercourse,” he shows the state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) between the two words “sexual intercourse” and “that.
By the phrase “does not indulge in,” he shows that in the expression “does not indulge in” (*na sevati*), there is a substitution of the letter *e* for the letter *i*.
Regarding the phrase “three men,” he says “three,” demonstrating that the word “having approached” (*upagantvā*) must be supplied and connected [to it].
“Having approached even men”: by this, he shows that in the phrase *tayo purise*, the accusative case is used in the sense of the accusative (*upayogatthe*).
Alternatively, following the previous method, it is also appropriate to interpret it here as the accusative in the sense of the locative, as in “among three men” (*tīsu purisesu*).
Following this latter method, one may also interpret the first phrase as “having approached three women” (*tisso itthiyo upagantvā*), where the accusative is used in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning is indeed appropriate. Therefore, it should be understood that those two methods are called "methods that provide instruction to one another.
By the ignoble term "ubhatobyañjanasaṅkhāte," he shows that only a person with both sexual characteristics (ubhatobyañjana) is to be understood here.
By the word "nācarati," he shows that even in the phrase "na cācareti," there is likewise the substitution of the vowel *e* for the syllable *ti*.
The construction is: “of that bhikkhunī who makes an effort to engage in bodily contact, which is the preliminary stage to sexual intercourse.

The construction is: “of him [‘assā’]—he becomes a successful heretic (ārādhaka) in the verse. “Right there” means in the very practice of a heretic. “Of him” means of the heretic. “That very” means that very practice of a heretic.
The connection is that the verse beginning with “a saṅghādisesa offense” has been spoken. “That” refers to the swallowing.

The connection is with the phrase "the novice who has gone into the air. The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "by the Sangha also" indicates that it is not only one who is subject to formal legal action (*kammāraha*). By the words "it should not be done," it is shown that both the Sangha and the one subject to formal action must be on the ground.
The connection is with the phrase "the exposition of the verse.
In order to show the agent of the verbal actions "does not give" and "does not accept," he says "nor is she an instigator," and so forth.
“Tassa” means “of that lustful man. By the word “kāraṇena” (by reason), the meaning of the term “tena” (by that) is shown.

The word “eva” (only/just) is applied in the sense of possibility; the meaning is “not by any other reason. The grammatical connection is “of the lustful man. “Gahaṇe” means “at the time of taking up” [the gift] by the one who was incited.
And regarding the phrase “tañca paribhogapaccayā” (and that for the purpose of use), here [is the function] of the pronoun “ta-” (that).

Showing the object (*visaya*) and the connection (*sambandha*) with the enjoyment, he says, “And furthermore,” and so forth. Therein, by the word “offense” (*āpatti*), he shows the object of the pronoun *taṃ*.
By the phrase “of that [nun] who has been sent away,” he shows the connection with the enjoyment. “Of that” means “of her who has been sent away.”
The connection is: "among the seventeen *saṅghādisesa* offenses. To show the meaning of the phrase "it does not touch upon a fault," he said: "another new offense.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the *Sedamocika-gāthā*.
[End of] the Pentad.
Commentary on the Chapter on Formal Acts (Kammavagga) 482.
By the phrase "a statement delimiting the number," it is shown that this is not a statement of measure.

By this, he precludes the state of the formal acts being either less than or more than that [number]. It is "counted" (*gaṇiyate*), thus it is "counting" (*gaṇana*); it is "delimited" (*paricchijjati*) by means of this, thus it is a "delimitation" (*pariccheda*).

The delimitation of counting is the "delimitation of counting" (*gaṇanapariccheda*). Alternatively, that by which one counts is "counting" (*gaṇana*); the delimitation of that very thing is the "delimitation of counting," and that itself is the "statement of the delimitation of counting" (*gaṇanaparicchedavacana*).
Regarding the phrase "called a *ñattikamma* (act of notification)," the connection is "the act that is to be performed.
"In the manner already stated" refers to [the procedure] beginning with: "Having cleared the Saṅgha within the boundary, for those entitled to give their consent..."
It is according to the same method as that stated [in the rule]:

“having brought forward the formal motion (*chanda*)”. “Therein” refers to the four types of legal acts (*kamma*); the connection is that “there is, however, a *ñattidutiyakamma* (an act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation) therein.
“Therein” refers to the two types of legal acts. “The remainder” means those remaining after the six types of legal acts. If it has been performed by reversing [the order].
If there is no strengthening [of the recitation], then what should be done for the sake of strengthening it? To this he says, "But if... and so forth.
Therein, "whether a syllable is omitted or a word is omitted" is said with reference to the dropping of syllables or words.
"Or a word is mispronounced" is said with reference to an incomplete utterance, such as through laxity or excessive emphasis. Herein—

The phrase “or harsh words” (*duruttakkharaṃ vā*) is to be supplied. “This” (*idaṃ*) refers to the repeated speaking. “Having become an action” (*kammaṃ hutvā*) means having become a wholesome action (*sukkammaṃ*).

483. Regarding those matters to be dealt with in the presence (*sammukhākaraṇīya*) and those not to be dealt with in the presence (*asammukhākaraṇīya*), he says “therein” (*tattha*) and so forth, showing that among these two, the matters not to be dealt with in the presence are shown first because they are few, and then demonstrating that the remainder are matters to be dealt with in the presence. Therein, “therein” (*tattha*) means in those two.
The connection is that there are eight kinds of what is called "not to be done in the presence. In this context, "in those respective [sections]" means in those various Khandhakas.
From the force of the expression "it is well-done," the meaning should also be understood as: "even that which has been done in the presence is well-done.

"The others" refers to those remaining from among the eight formal acts (*kamma*). "These" refers to the formal acts. "Deficient in their basis" means deficient in regard to the subject matter (*vatthu*).
“Of these too” refers to those matters that are to be dealt with by way of counter-question (*paṭipucchākaraṇīya*).
“In this” refers to the word “to be dealt with by way of counter-question. By the word “having asked,” he shows that the term *paṭipucchā* has the suffix *-tvā*.

By the word “to be done” (*kātabba*), he shows that in the word *karaṇīya*, the suffix *-anīya* has the sense of the object (*kammattha*). “By the one who has been accused according to what was given” means by the one who has been accused in accordance with what was stated.
“Vippalapantassa” means of one who prattles on with various distorted words; it is connected with the phrase “of the one being accused.
“Sabbattha” means in all [the cases], such as “one deserving of a *tajjanīya-kamma*,” and so forth.
“Anuposathadivase” means on a day other than the Uposatha day. To demonstrate that very meaning, he said: “The Uposatha day...”
“Nāmā” and so forth. “The month of Kattika” refers to the latter month of Kattika; because it is the month of Pavāraṇā, the word “excepting” is stated.
The connection is that the day of concord (*sāmaggidivasa*) and the days of the Uposatha as previously mentioned—the fourteenth and fifteenth—are what are meant.
“In which” (*yatrahīti*) means in whichever monastery; the connection is with the word “they set aside. “Between” (*antarā*) means in the interval between the fourteenth and the fifteenth.
"Having postponed and set [the date]" refers to the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kattika that was later drawn forward and established;
this is said with reference to that. "Even here" means even at the place where the invitation (pavāraṇā) is held.

Saying "Moreover," etc., he speaks while showing another method than the one appearing in the canonical text (Pāḷi). "The final matter" refers to a matter involving defeat (pārājika). "Of whom" refers to...
[This refers to] the person (*puggala*). By this, he shows that the person who is subject to the formal act (*kamma*) is called the "basis" (*vatthu*).

484. Taking hold of the substance (*dabba*) is not what is meant by "not touching the basis"; rather, it is precisely taking hold of the name (*nāma*). Thus he says, "he does not take his name. Showing the manner of not touching, he says, "Let my words be heard," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "he does not touch the person," here "person" means the preceptor (*upajjhāya*); thus he says, "the one who is the preceptor of the candidate for full ordination. "Him" refers to the preceptor.
“*Sabbena sabbaṃ*” means “in every way, all”; this is a collective compound of particles. Alternatively, the construction is: “all the motion (*ñatti*) in every aspect.

Having first performed the formal act (*kamma*) and subsequently establishing the motion is indeed called “establishing the motion later. Thus, the passage beginning with “By these [means]” and so forth is the conclusion. 485.
Although it was referred to by the phrase “in the very manner stated,” because the formulas for the motion (*ñattikammavācā*) are dissimilar, the mode of non-referring [to them] is [now explained].
Pointing this out, he said, “But in this way,” and so forth. Therein, “of them” refers to the objects, the Saṅgha, and the individuals;
the connection is that he speaks while the first, second, or third proclamation (*anusāvane*) ought to be recited.

Regarding the phrase “he omits the proclamation,” he says, “he does not perform the *anussāvana* (re-proclamation),” because here the prefix *anu-* signifies omission. Thus, “he omits the proclamation.”

Here, he says "And whoever... and so forth, showing that it is not only one who fails to perform the proclamation in its entirety who is said to omit the proclamation, but also one who discards what has been poorly uttered during the proclamation is likewise said to omit it.
By the phrase "either once or twice," he shows that one omits the proclamation even while failing to complete it three times.

From the force of this statement, it is understood that one does not fail [the procedure] by reciting the *kammavācā* more than once in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*),
or more than three times in a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*).
Regarding the word "discards" (*chaḍḍeti*) here, since the discarding is evident through the omission of words and syllables, that [omission] is not explicitly shown.
Regarding the phrase “he commits a durutta,” in order to demonstrate what a *durutta* actually is, he says: “In this context, ‘he commits a *durutta*’... and so forth.
The connection is that it is to be characterized by the monk who is performing [the act].
As for the phrase “the distinction of lax... [etc.]... the distinction,” the construction is: “this which has been stated as the distinction of phonemes (*byañjana*) is the distinction of phonemes.”
In this verse, *dasadhā* means "in ten ways. Regarding *byañjanabuddhi*: *buddhi* is that which increases (*vaddheti*);
thus, the understanding of the phonemes (*byañjana*) themselves—that is, the syllables (*akkhara*)—according to their tenfold qualities such as being soft (*sithila*), etc., is *byañjanabuddhi*.
By this [term], the word *dasadhā* within the compound *byañjanabuddhi* is shown to be elided; as in the example: *kammajaṃ*.

As in the phrase “evā” and so forth, here the word *eva* forms the compound *kammaja* (born of karma) with the word *kamma*, and it shows the elision of the word *eva* within the middle of the compound.
*Pabheda* means distinction. Here, however, the construction is as follows:
loose and tense, long and short, heavy and light, nasalized (*niggahita*) and connected, and fixed.
And as for the phrase "and liberated," the distinction consisting of its tenfold classification should be understood through the intellect regarding the phonemes (*byañjana*) alone.

It should be seen that the ten terms beginning with "loose" (*sithila*) are stated based on the textual reading expressed in the neuter gender as "syllable, word, and phoneme" (*akkharaṃ padaṃ byañjanaṃ*).
Showing the detailed explanation of the verse, he said, “In this case, however,” and so forth. A syllable to be uttered with a non-restrained vocal effort is *sithila* (soft).
A syllable to be uttered with a restrained vocal effort is *dhanita* (hard). “In those very [groups]” means in the five groups (*vagga*) themselves.
Not only is a long vowel called heavy (*garuka*), but also that which is followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*); thus he said, “Or whatever,” and so forth.
The construction is as follows: that syllable which is spoken by making a conjunct (saṃyoga) follow it is also called "heavy" (garuka).
That of which a conjunct is subsequent is "saṃyogaparaṃ. There is also a reading: "saṃyogapadaṃ. The construction is as follows:
that which is spoken by not making a conjunct follow it is also called "light" (lahuka). That which is to be uttered with a nasalization (sānunāsika) is the *niggahīta*.

The construction is: “nāma-iti. Regarding “niggahetvā,” he says “without releasing” because *niggahīta* means, in terms of its meaning, the non-release or non-abandonment of the place of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the mode of formation (*karaṇa*).
The construction is: that which is spoken by connecting [words] together is called a “connection” (*sambandha*).
The construction is: that which is spoken by making [words] unconnected is called “determined” (*vavatthita*). That which is spoken without having been nasalized (*aniggahetvā*)...
The construction is: “that which is called ‘liberated’. Regarding the term “without refuting,” he says “having answered,” because an answer is, in its meaning, what is called non-refutation.

Having thus shown the distinction in the intellect regarding the phrasing (*byañjana*), he now says “therein,” etc., in order to show in detail the distinction in the recitation of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
Therein, “therein” means among those ten types of intellectual phrasing. By the word “thus” (*tathā*):
The substitution of *th* for *t*, as well as the substitution of a hard consonant (*dhanita*) for a soft one (*sithila*), is extended [by analogy];
likewise, the statement “this motion (*ñatti*) is appropriate and timely” (*pattakallaṃ*) and so forth is the substitution of a hard consonant for a soft one—this is the construction.
“Thus” (*iti*) means in this way. The connection is: “he makes a hard sound where a soft one should be made. “Four consonants” (*cattāri byañjanāni*) means four.
"Letters. For here, the word *byañjana* (consonant/syllable) signifies a letter (*akkhara*).
Having shown the defilement of the ritual action (*kamma*) through the four types of cognition regarding consonants, he says "But in the others," etc., showing that the others are not so defiled.

"Arrived in due order" means having descended from the Noble Ones and arrived gradually. "Tradition" (*paveṇi*) means continuity. If [the tradition] were destroyed, what would be the violation of the ritual procedure (*kammavācā*)?
He says, "If, however," and so forth, to explain why it does not fail. "It does not fail" means it is not lost. But why does the *kammavācā* (formal ritual proclamation) not fail?
Is it not the case that the *kammavācā* fails when it causes the *kamma* (the formal act) to fail? To this he says, "For these," and so forth. The construction is as follows:
because they do not cause it to fail, therefore the *kammavācā* does not fail.
The connection is: "but that which the Suttantika Theras say. They are called *suttantika* because they compose the *Suttantas* such as the *Kaccāyana* and others;
thus, the *suttantika* Theras are those who are both *suttantika* and *theras*.

"It is not permissible" means that a modification of the letters is not permissible. The connection is: "the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) must be performed by one who is an expert in the Vinaya. "According to the text" means...
“By the Blessed One according to the text as it has been stated. Regarding “by means of the phrasing and terminology”: this refers to the phrasing and terminology.
“Otherwise” means in a manner different from avoiding the faults already mentioned.

“Or he announces at an improper time”: here, “improper time” means “without an opportunity,” which is why he says “in the absence of an opportunity. “Absence of an opportunity” refers to [the lack of] the motion (*ñatti*) and the announcements (*anussāvana*).
He said, "The sequence is erroneous," in the passage beginning with "having set aside the motion" (*ñattiṃ aṭṭhapetvā*).

The construction is: "Having first set aside the motion, having first performed the act of proclamation. Indeed, the word "first" (*paṭhamam eva*) refers to the preceding and following context. The phrase beginning with "thus" (*iti*) is the conclusion. 486. The construction is:
"That which does not include twenty-one bhikkhus is called an excessively small boundary (*atikhuddakasīmā*). Twenty-one...
"Bhikkhus" refers to twenty-one bhikkhus together with the one who is subject to the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*).
The construction is as follows: "where they are unable to sit within the boundary" refers to what is called a "very small boundary" (*atikhuddaka-sīmā*).
"To sit" means to sit in a circular formation without relinquishing hand-contact with one another. "Therein" means in the very small boundary; "herein" means in the remaining boundaries.

The construction is: "That which is agreed upon is called 'excessively large'. In the phrase "even by the measure of a hair-tip," the word *api* (even) indicates that it is even more so with anything exceeding that.

"Aghaṭitanimittā" means that for this [person], the sign (*nimitta*) is unjoined and disconnected. Saying "of the eastern [direction]," etc., he makes manifest the state of being a broken sign (*khaṇḍanimitta*) by means of seeing a sign that is not broken (*akhaṇḍanimitta*). "Previously described" (*pubbakittitaṃ*)...
This was stated first. "In that very place" means in the northern direction itself. "Another also"—here the word *api* (also) serves to include a second point. The construction is:
"That which is agreed upon is named 'the mark of the broken' (*khaṇḍanimitta*). "Approached by the unmarked" (*animittupaga*) is merely a qualification of speaking according to reality;

it is not an exclusionary qualification, because the state of being approached by the unmarked is already evident through the inclusion of [trees] such as those with bark-cores (*tacasāra*). "In between" (*antara*)...
"In the middle. The construction is: "That which is authorized is called 'having a shadow-sign' (chāyānimittā) and 'signless' (animittā).
"Standing outside, he authorizes" is the construction. However, it is permissible to designate the signs even while standing outside.

The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even when thus authorized" indicates that it goes without saying that [it is permissible] when not authorized. Because of the requirement for syntactic connection between the words "of the boundary" (*sīmāya*) and "the boundary" (*sīmaṃ*).
And because that [boundary] is not common to them, he says, "the boundary of others within his own boundary," showing their respective connections.

"Sambhindati" means he makes a connection. For here, it should be understood that while the verbal root *bhid* expresses the sense of "making twofold," it becomes expressive of "connection" through the prefix *sam*, which subverts the original meaning of the root. "Tattha" means "in those."
"In two boundaries. "Iti" means "thus. "Tāsu" means "in those [boundaries]. 487–8. The construction is:
"that which has the characteristic of being subject to the failure of the motion and the consent. "Therein" (tattha) means "in that assembly, regarding the failure of the formal act" (kamma-vipatti).

"That too" (tampi) refers to "the characteristic of being subject to the failure of the motion and the consent"; the connection is that it has already been stated. "Therein" (tattha) refers to the four...
In the text: "The monks are regular (pakatatta) and eligible for formal acts (kammappatta). "Not suspended" (anukkhitto) means they have not been subjected to an act of suspension by the Saṅgha.
"Of pure virtue" (parisuddhasīlo) means they have not committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika).

By these words, he shows the meaning as: "those whose nature (pakati), self (attā), and individual essence (sabhāvo) are [normal] are 'regular' (pakatatto). "[Eligible] for the formal act" (kammassa araho) means...
By this, he shows that the phrase "kammappattā" is a genitive compound (*chaṭṭhīsamāsa*) and that the word *patta* has the sense of being worthy or suitable for the action.
"By them" means by those four who are *pakatatta*. "He goes" means he comes. "The rest" means those remaining apart from the four *pakatatta*.
"But of whom" means but of which person. "Worthy of the action" means worthy of the ritual act.
489. *Ettha* means in the place where it is shown that eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others do not constitute a formal assembly (*avatthu*). Discussion on the Act of Seeking Permission (Apalokanakamma):

495–6. *Tattha* means among the four types of legal acts (*kamma*). *Ettha* refers to the textual passage concerning reinstatement (*osāraṇa*) and so forth. *Padasiliṭṭhatāya* means because of the smoothness of the words in common usage.
Because of its smooth nature. "Therein" refers to the five [procedures], beginning with reinstatement (*osāraṇā*).
The construction is: that which is the suspension by means of a disciplinary act (*daṇḍakamma*) for the novice Kaṇṭaka, that is "expulsion" (*nissāraṇā*).

Having stated, "He holds wrong view," in order to demonstrate that very point, it is said, "endowed with an extremist view. For wrong view is the cause for the removal of the religious emblem (*liṅganāsanā*).
"He is. "That novice" refers to the act of having [the robe] forfeited (*nissajjāpetabbo*), which is either an act already stated or an act to be performed.
"That opinion" refers to the act of determining the elements (*dhātukamma*), which is an unstated act. To the question "How should it be done?", he says: "And thus the act should be performed.
Showing the manner in which it should be performed, he says: "Venerable sirs, to the Saṅgha," and so forth. The construction is: "that they obtain a shared sleeping place."

“Of him” means of that one who shares a sleeping place. “For the sake of non-gain” means for the purpose of not obtaining [robes, etc.]. By the words “Go away! Perish! Be destroyed! he shows the manner of expulsion.
However, its meaning has already been stated below. “He” refers to the novice;
the connection is that he is to be reintegrated [into the community].
The connection is: "This novice monk, being humble, confesses his transgression.
"Soratā" means delighting in excellent acquisitions, or being well-restrained from bad acquisitions. "Yathā pure" means as it was pleasing before; "tathā" (so) is the construction.
"Kāyasambhogasāmaggidānaṃ" means the giving of harmony through both the person and the enjoyment.
The passage beginning with "Thus," etc., is the conclusion. However, since the Brahma-punishment was prescribed specifically for Channa in the Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka, it must be given to him alone;
thus he says, "Not only... and so forth. "This" refers to the Brahma-punishment;
the connection is that it should be given even to any other monk who lives [in such a manner]. To the question "How is it to be given?", he says, "And furthermore, it should be given in this way."
Showing the manner in which it should be given, he said, "In the midst of the Saṅgha," and so forth.
The construction is: "Whatever speech one should desire, that speech [one should speak]. "Of him who is asking for forgiveness" means: "of that bhikkhu who is asking the Saṅgha for forgiveness.
"Having reflected" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means having reflected by means of knowledge; the sense is "having examined with wisdom."
The connection is that they go to an act of non-worship, which has been permitted. By whom was it permitted? He says: "By the Blessed One.
In which section (khandhaka) was it permitted? He says: "In the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka. Regarding what matters (vatthu) was it permitted?
He says: "Then indeed... [etc. ...in these matters. Having done what was it permitted? He says: "Having prescribed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
“How was it authorized? He said: “I authorize... [etc] ...it should be performed. “Of that” means of one who is not to be saluted (*avandiya*).

By the phrase “not the reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) and so forth,” he shows the meaning of the word *eva* as the exclusion of other possibilities. “Of that” means of the one characterized by the formal act (*kamma*), who is not to be saluted.
“In that very place” means in the Bhikkhunī-khandhaka itself. “That” refers to the characteristic of the formal act. “Even here” means even in the Kammavagga of the Parivāra.
"Uninspiring" (*apāsādika*) means that which brings about lack of confidence, or that which generates lack of confidence.
"Than that" means than the act of making [the person] unworthy of veneration. "This" refers to the monk. "Veneration" (*vandiya*) means that which is to be venerated, or the act of veneration itself.

"In this" refers to the formal act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*); the construction is: "it was laid down having made the community of nuns the basis. "Of the community of monks as well" means...
The word *pi* indicates that it is not only for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. The word *pana* has the sense of esteem; thus the meaning is:
"even that which is prescribed based on the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs. Showing in detail the state of being obtainable, he said, "For that which... and so forth. The construction is:
"that which one performs as an act of seeking permission (*apalokanakamma*). The connection is: "but they are to be given by the distributor of trifles (*appamattakavissajjaka*)."
"Those" refers to needles and so forth. "That very person" means the one who distributes trifles. "From that" means from what is trifling.
"Therein" refers to the commentary on the Senāsanakkhandhaka. The connection is: "even medicine for the sick of the kind already mentioned.
The connection is: "and whoever [is a bhikkhu] also... and "to him it should be given. "From the local source" means from that great monastery.

The connection is with the phrase "having taken from the perspective of the condition for arising. By the words "of one who is virtuous" (*pesala*), etc., he shows that it is not permissible to give [the robe] to those who are immoral and so forth.

Regarding the statement "it is permissible to have [him] look after it," he says "this monk," etc., to indicate that it is permissible to have him look after it without having asked permission first. "Specifically" (*odissa*) means having designated [a particular person].

"Either a sitting hall" (*āsana-gharaṃ vā*) or "a shrine room" (*paṭimā-gharaṃ vā*); the connection is with the phrase "a person who is the maker. "Having taken from a deposit" (*upanikkhepato gahetvā*).

“Connected with. Regarding the phrase “even with what belongs to the Saṅgha,” the word *api* (even/also) indicates that it is not only by means of an offering placed at a cetiya, but also by means of what belongs to the Saṅgha.
The construction is: “by those who act while obtaining no more than what is necessary for their livelihood”; the connection is: “having become those who consume [it]. “The duty...”
By the words beginning with “I shall do,” he shows the meaning of the phrase “just enough for maintenance. The construction is: “those fruit trees planted in the monastery.
“Of which” means of the trees. “In them” means among those trees. “But those which” refers to the trees, and the connection is that they are unenclosed (apariggahita).
“But that” refers to the formal act of seeking permission (apalokanakamma). It is called a “voting-assembly” (salākagga) because they take voting sticks there.
The place. Regarding the phrase “the row for the sacrificial meal,” the same principle applies here as well. “In the Uposatha row” means in the place where the Uposatha is held;
the meaning is “in the Uposatha hall. “Therein” means in the Uposatha row. “That” refers to the formal act of obtaining permission (*apalokanakamma*). The construction is:
“whatever root, bark, leaf, sprout, flower, fruit, edible food, and so forth. “Within the boundary” means within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"Whatever has been done by the Saṅgha" means exactly what was performed by the Saṅgha. "On the uposatha day" is merely an illustration, because it may be performed on any day whatsoever.
"By the fruit-gathering turn" means by the turn for gathering the fruits of trees. "The trees endure" means the trees stand, or they exist.
"By whom" refers to the monks who planted them; this is to be connected with "they are. "That very agreement" refers to that very same agreement previously made.
The intention is that no other agreement (*katikā*) should be made.
"In another monastery" means in a monastery other than the one where the trees are situated. "Of them" refers to the trees; this is the connection with the word "owner" (*sāmī*).
"Even those which" refers to the trees; this is the connection with the word "planted. The construction is "from another place. "Among them" refers to the trees.
“Here” means in the monastery. “But by them,” however, refers to the monks who are the owners of the surrounding cloister (pariveṇa).
“A tenth part” means one-tenth. By the phrase “the same method applies,” he extends the meaning to include the giving of a tenth part.
“A venerable monk” refers to a monk who is worthy of respect due to his virtue, learning, and so forth. “There” refers to the ancient monastery.
“Mūle” means at the beginning, that is, at the initial time. “Nikkukkuccena” means by being free from remorse, thinking, “This has not been divided.
“Khiyyanamattameva taṃ tan” means that very act of criticizing is merely an act of criticizing; the criticism of novices does not take root. “Panasarukkhan” means a thorny fruit tree.
“Ayaṃ sāmīcī” means this is the proper conduct, the accordance with the Dhamma, of eating [the fruit] after it has been divided.
"Khāyitaṃ" means "eaten. Since it would be possible to understand the resolution of the agreement for two or three [monks] by way of the method already explained, he did not show that;
rather, showing the resolution of the agreement for only one, he said: "But when there is only one monk," and so forth.
"The previous agreement" refers to the agreement previously made, thinking, "It is pleasing to enjoy [the food] as one likes. "Of them" refers to the novices.
"Phātikamma" (the act of giving) is the connection [with the preceding]. "Having distributed" means having distributed among the novices (*sāmaṇera*).
By this, he shows that even a portion which is not to be given as a *phātikamma* to the novices must be distributed.
"From the neighboring villages" means from the nearby villages; "having come" is the connection. The construction is: "one mango, one breadfruit."
Showing that when a fault is pointed out if [the gift] is not given, and when it is given the benefit is also to be understood by way of its meaning, he said:

"If it is not given," and so forth. This is to be connected with the phrase "of the people who take [it]. "From that" means from the establishing of the formal agreement (*katikavatta*). "Should not be spoken of" means they should not be spoken of because they corrupt families by giving fruitless results.
To explain what should be pointed out, he said: "Coconuts, etc.," and so forth. "Having investigated" means by following the sequence of the words.
"Having deliberated. "A half-portion" means a portion equal to half of what is obtained by the monks. "Having informed" means having requested permission from the Saṅgha.
"A caravan leader traveling on the road" means a caravan leader who is going along a path. "He" refers to the one who seizes [the goods] by force and eats them.
Regarding the phrase "shadows and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should include monasteries and groves. "If there is" means if there is need.
“*Phalabharitā*” means filled with fruit. There is also a reading, “*phalabhāritā*,” which means endowed with a burden consisting of fruit.
“*Apaccāsīsantena*” means without expecting a return gift from them.

“*Pubbe vuttamevā*” means exactly as was stated previously in the section concerning the Saṅgha, beginning with “For he is angry,” and so forth. “*Ettha*” refers to the section concerning individuals.
“*Tanti phalārāman*” means that fruit-grove. “*So*” refers to a capable bhikkhu. “*Bhāriyaṃ kamman*” means that the work of looking after it is heavy.
“*Ettakenā*” means by even as much as a third or a half portion. “*Sabbaṃ phalārāman*” is the connection [to the previous]. “*Mūlabhāgan*” means the first portion.
By the phrase “*dasabhāgamattan*,” he shows the purpose for that. “*Datvā*” means having given it to the Saṅgha.
"Sota" means that monk. "Akatāvāsaṃ" means a new dwelling-place not previously built. "Ārāmaṃ" means the monastery of the Saṅgha.
"Tehipi" means even by those who are dependent [on him]. The word "pi" (even/also) refers back to the teacher. "Tesaṃ" means of those who are dependent.
"Jaggita-kāle" means at the time when the trees have been tended and are laden with flowers and fruit. "Jaggana-kāle" means at the time of mere tending; that is, at the very time of tending alone.

There is no flower or fruit that exists for the purpose of being tended; this refers to the time [when they are available]. By the words "much," etc., he shows the manner in which [the offense] is to be avoided.

The construction is: "one who tends [them] by means of *phātikamma* does not exist. "Without having asked permission" (*anāpucchitvāva*) means without having sought leave from the Saṅgha. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way.

Regarding the classification of the *ñattikamma* (formal act consisting of a motion), the construction [of the sentence] should be understood as: "the exposition should be known thus. *Osāraṇā* (reinstatement) means that one is brought back (*osāreti*) into the midst of the Saṅgha by means of this motion (*ñatti*).
*Nissāraṇā* (expulsion) means that one is expelled (*nissāriyati*) from the Saṅgha, cast out, by means of this [motion].

The statement "the motion is called the Uposatha" is said by way of metaphorical designation based on the cause; therefore he said, "established by way of the Uposatha formal act. This same method applies here as well regarding the phrase "the motion is called the Pavāraṇā."
A motion (ñatti) established by means of the first person plural ending (*anusāseyya*, etc.
is called a motion established by oneself to appoint another. A motion established by means of the third person plural ending (*anusāseyyuṃ*, etc.
is called a motion established by oneself to appoint oneself. In this way, either oneself or another is appointed.
"By this motion" (*ñatti*) means formal authorization (*sammuti*). "Gift" (*dāna*) refers to the motion (*ñatti*) by which bowls, robes, and so forth that have been relinquished are given;

it is called "gift" because it is the instrument through which they are bestowed. It is expressed in the neuter gender because the word *ñatti* is fixed in the neuter regardless of the gender of the referent.
"Receptacle" (*paṭiggaha*) is that by which an offense (*āpatti*) is received.
*Paccukkaḍḍhanā* (reversal) means that by which one is drawn back toward oneself.
*Kammalakkhaṇaṃ* (the characteristic of the formal act) means that by which the formal act itself is characterized.

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), the phrase "called the characteristic of the formal act" is extended [to the subsequent cases]. "From that" (*tato*) refers to the motion that encompasses all [three types]. The construction is: "The other two motions are called the characteristic of the formal act. "Thus," etc., is the conclusion.

In order to show the specific distinctions regarding restoration (*osāraṇa*) and so forth within the classification of formal acts consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), he said, "Of Vaḍḍha the Licchavi," and so on. The construction should be made with the words "and the authorization of the boundary" (*sīmāsammuti*) and so forth.
As for the phrase "the two proclamations following the motion have been stated," this is the construction. The section beginning with "Thus" (*iti*) is the conclusion.
The method of construction regarding the classification of formal acts consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakamma*) is indeed evident.
497. Demonstrating the connection with the teaching beginning with “In a formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a quorum of four,” he says, “Thus, the formal acts (*kammāni*), etc.

Therein, “thus” (*iti*) is connected as “having thus shown. Its meaning is connected as “the meaning of that statement, ‘In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four,’ etc., is to be understood.”
Thus ends the exposition of the commentary on the Kammavagga.
Regarding the commentary on the Atthavasavagga and following: 498.
Having thus shown the commentary on the Kammavagga, [the text proceeds] with the section beginning "In dependence upon two purposes," which was stated immediately after it.
Showing the connection (*anusandhi*) for the teaching, he said "Now," and so forth; the connection is with the words "now commenced. The construction is: "those training rules which...

Regarding "of enmities pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammikaverānaṃ*): they are "pertaining to the present life" because they occur in the present life and because one must abstain from them.
Regarding "for the sake of restraint" (*saṃvarāya*): here, the verbal root *vṛ*, preceded by the prefix *sam*, has the sense of covering or closing.

And since the word *āya* has that meaning, he says, “for the purpose of closing. “Of those reckoned as suffering in the form of karmic result” means of those reckoned as suffering which constitute the results of killing living beings and so forth.
“Of those pertaining to the future life” means of those occurring in the next world. “Here” means in this place where the benefits of the formulation of the training rule reside.
By the phrase “because of their state of being things to be avoided,” it is shown that they are called *vajjāni* because they are to be avoided (*vajjetabbāni*).
This shows the meaning of the word. They are called "fears" (*bhayāni*) because one fears them. "In the sense of being unbearable" means in the sense of being unendurable.
By the phrase "they are called unwholesome," he shows that they are named "unwholesome" by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*), since their results are painful.
The reading is thus: "The training rule was laid down for the purpose of breaking up groups. However, in some manuscripts it reads: "The training rule on group-meals was laid down."
The reading has been written down. "In all cases" means in the entire Atthavasavagga. "This" refers to the word. "Here" means in this chapter.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the Atthavasavagga. 499.
That by which a person who is undergoing a formal act (*vatta*) is reinstated is called *osāraṇīya*, the formal act. Therefore it is said:
“The action by which one is reintegrated is the action that has been prescribed. By the phrase “by which action,” etc., he shows the etymological meaning of *nissāraṇīya* (to be sent away):
those who cause quarrels and so forth are sent away (*nissāriyanti*) by this action; thus it is called *nissāraṇīya*. 500. The connection is:
“The seven classes of offenses are what is called ‘prescribed’ (*paññatta*). Regarding the word *antara*: [it refers to] the three [Buddhas], Kakusandha and the others.
"Between the Buddhas and our Blessed One. By the word "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*), he shows the meaning of the phrase "when not yet laid down.
The connection is that stories concerning those disciplined [by the Buddha], such as the story of the female monkey, are called "subsequent laying down" (*anupaññatta*).
By the word "training rule," he shows the meaning of the phrase "when already laid down. "In all cases" means in the entire *Ānisaṃsa-vagga*.
Thus ends the commentary on the section on benefits (*ānisamsavagga*).

501. The connection is: "They comprise all the training rules (*sabbasikkhāpada*). Regarding that, the construction is: "In the text beginning with 'nine compilations' (*nava saṅgahā*), the meaning should be understood as follows.
By the phrase "compilation by way of subject matter" (*vatthunā saṅgaho*), [it is implied] "in a subject matter, or the compilation of subject matters."
It excludes the meaning. "In this" refers to the text beginning with "the inclusion of the bases" (*vatthusaṅgaha*). "Hi" indicates the detailed explanation. The connection is "because there is not.

"All" refers to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*). By the word "included" (*saṅgahitāni*), he shows the etymological derivation: it is called an "inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) because that which is to be included is so named.
"Thus, first... and so forth is the conclusion.

But because it is connected with the words "since they are included," the conclusion is shown by summarizing the origin of the aggregates and the settlement of legal disputes through the passage beginning with "Thus herein" and so forth. "Herein" refers to the Saṅgaha-vagga (the Chapter on Inclusion).
Thus ends [the section] from the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya.
The application of the commentary on the *Navasaṅgahita* is completed.

"Completed" (*niṭṭhita*) means they have gone to (*itā*) completion (*niṭṭha*), that is, to fulfillment; or alternatively, they have gone to (*itā*) and remained in (*ṭhitā*) completion (*niṭṭhe*), which is fulfillment.
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of emphasis, for the meaning is "indeed completed. This concludes the commentary on the words whose meanings were not previously explained.
This is the commentary on the meanings and words that were not previously explained.
Thus ends the application of the commentary on the Parivāra.
And the application of the commentary on the Pācittiya and so forth is also completed.
By me, under the name marked with the *jāḍila* [seal], the method of interpretation for numerous sections of the *Parivāra-vinaya* has been recited; it is now complete.
Commentary on the Concluding Statement.
Having thus provided this commentary on the Vinaya, he now concludes it by saying, "To this extent," and so forth. Therein,
"to this extent" means by this sequence of speech consisting of the collection of syllables, words, and phonemes, beginning from the statement,
"He who is immeasurable even in ten million eons," and ending with the statement, "The commentary on the Navasaṅgahita-vagga is finished."
"Samatta" means "connection.

"The teaching analyzed into the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka as the teaching that is to be analyzed by means of the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhakas, and the Parivāra;
this is the connection. "Nātha" (Protector) refers to [the Buddha] of the monks and nuns.

He is the *Nātha* (Protector) in the sense of requesting the practice of what is beneficial, in the sense of scorching the defilements, in the sense of wishing for the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*), and in the sense of sovereignty over the mind. "Those to be trained" (*veneyya*) means one who is to be guided (*vinetabba*).
"The Victor" (*Jina*) means one who has conquered the five Māras. Herein, the construction is as follows: the Protector, while guiding those to be trained...
The Jina taught the Vinaya Piṭaka, which consists of the exposition divided into the two Vibhaṅgas, the Khandhaka, and the Parivāra.
"By a measure of more than twenty-seven thousand" is connected to the phrase "by a text measuring seven thousand plus twenty thousand.
"Of that" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka. "Samantapāsādikā" means bringing about confidence on all sides.
[It may be] a small volume (*vahikā*) or a manuscript (*janikā*). Herein, this is the construction:
"The commentary named *Samantapāsādikā* is completed by means of a text measuring more than twenty-seven thousand [units].
Regarding the phrase "tatridaṃ" (herein this): "tatra" (therein) is a word that refers back to the preceding statement. Therein, [is] the *Samantapāsādikā*.

The meaning is: "in the statement 'named Samantapāsādikā'. In the phrase "because of being Samantapāsādikā," this locative case ending is used in the sense of the direct object (paccattatthe), as in "this too is in the virtue" (*idaṃ pi sīlasmiṃ*) and so forth; thus, the meaning is "because of being Samantapāsādikā. This, however, is the construction here:
in that statement "named Samantapāsādikā," this state of being Samantapāsādikā (*samantapāsādikattaṃ*) belongs to the Samantapāsādikā.
This means "the state of being entirely admirable" (*samantapāsādikabhāva*).
In the verses beginning with "From the lineage of teachers" (*ācariyaparaṃparato*), the nine qualifying words mentioned should be connected with the word "is not seen" (*na dissati*).
"Sampassataṃ" is to be connected with "of the wise who see correctly" (*sammā passantānaṃ viññūnaṃ*). "Yato" [means]...
The connection is "because it is not seen. "In this" means in the commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*). "Indeed, the *Samantapāsādikā*" means that its name is precisely "Samantapāsādikā.
"Of the Vinaya" means of the Vinaya Piṭaka. "By one skilled in the taming of those to be tamed" means by one expert in the subduing of those who need to be disciplined.
"By the Lord of the World" means by the protector of the worlds. "Compassionate toward the world" means feeling compassion for the world.
This is the construction here: from the lineage of teachers...

[as before] ...because nothing unpleasing is seen here by wise people who perceive it through the demonstration of the divisions of the method of analysis, therefore this commentary, titled the *Samantapāsādikā* (The All-Surpassing), proceeds as the exposition of the Vinaya spoken by the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, who was skilled in training those to be disciplined and who felt compassion for the world.
The connection is: "Tissa also, having heard these Sinhalese commentaries... To the question "In whose presence did he hear them?", he says:
"...in the presence of Buddhamitta... The construction is: "Having heard [them] in the presence of the renowned, illustrious, wise Elder who was learned in the Vinaya, named Buddhamitta.
The word "having heard" (*sutvā*) is a qualifier of the temporal action preceding the word "undertaken" (*āraddhā*).

The construction is as follows: "There is a Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra) situated on a plot of ground in the Mahāmeghavana garden, adorned by the Teacher’s Great Bodhi tree. Regarding that Great Monastery, the construction is:

"In the southern direction of that Great Monastery, he had built there a meditation hall—known by the name *padhānaghara*—an excellent cloister (*pariveṇa*) frequented by the Saṅgha of monks who possess pure conduct and virtue.
As to the question "Who built it?", he says: "Born of a noble family... renowned. Therein, "born of a noble family" refers to the attendant of the Saṅgha.
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "A lay follower (upāsaka) renowned as ‘Mahānigamasāmī,’ who was always undisturbed and possessed clear confidence in the Three Jewels, had it built.
To the question "What did he have built?", it says: "Charming... [etc. ...a reservoir of excellent water.
Therein, "accumulated with a charming rampart" means well-constructed and built with a beautiful wall; "delightful, endowed with cool-shaded trees" means [endowed] with trees providing cool shade.
The construction is: "He caused that palace to be built, which was endowed with, possessed of a reservoir of water, and a storehouse of sweet water.
The connection is: "For those dwelling in that palace, [the protection] of the Lord of the Great City [was provided].
To the question, "With reference to whom was it begun, and what kind of commentary on the Vinaya was it? he says: "Sucisīlasamācāraṃ... pe... Vinayavaṇṇanā. Therein:

The construction is as follows: having designated the Elder named Buddhasiri, who was of pure conduct and virtuous behavior, the commentary on the Vinaya—which is prosperous and complete through its analysis of the meaning and so forth—was begun.
To answer the questions, "In whose reign was it begun? and "At what time was it completed?", he says: "While [the King] was protecting... [etc.]".
"...is completed. Therein, the connection is: "having made the entire island of Laṅkā free from the *abbuda* hell.
The connection is: "in the victory-year (*jayasaṃvacchara*) of King Siripālaya, who is renowned for his prosperity and whose dwelling is glory (*sirinivāsa*).
This commentary on the Vinaya was begun in the twentieth peaceful victory-year (*khema-jayasaṃvacchara*), and in the twenty-first [year], the twenty-first year of the king.
The construction is: "When [the work] has been reached, it is completed.

He said, "In that which is crowded with calamities," and so forth, showing his aspiration: "Just as my own commentary has reached its conclusion quickly and without hindrance, may [this work], endowed with the Dhamma, likewise proceed swiftly for the world. In that context, "crowded with calamities" means [afflicted] by calamities.

The construction is as follows: just as this commentary on the Vinaya has reached its conclusion in a single year— remaining free from obstacles and devoid of calamities in this troubled world of beings—
so may all matters connected with the Dhamma, once undertaken by the whole world,
also swiftly reach their conclusion, being free from obstacles.
Showing the dedication of the merit he has accumulated himself toward a desired purpose, he said:

“For the long endurance of the Dhamma,” and so forth. Therein, by the power of all that merit which was accumulated by me through great reverence for the True Dhamma while composing this commentary on the Vinaya for the sake of the long endurance of the Dhamma—
May all living beings become partakers of the essence of the True Dhamma of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma.
May the True Dhamma endure for a long time. May the deity, raining at the proper season, long satisfy the people, the multitude of beings.
May the king protect the earth with righteousness—this is the construction of the sentence. The word *iti* signifies completion; thus it is concluded.
The meaning is: "they must be seen as having reached [perfection] well.
Faith, wisdom, and energy are "faith, wisdom, and energy"; these are "purified faith, wisdom, and energy" because they are both purified and constitute faith, wisdom, and energy;
and these are "supreme purified faith, wisdom, and energy."
"And" (*ceti*) refers to supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; "adorned by those" means adorned by supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy.
This is to be connected with the word "by that elder. "Virtue, conduct, uprightness, and gentleness" (*sīlācārajjavamaddavāni*);
those for whom these are primary are "those characterized by virtue, conduct, uprightness, and gentleness, etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), patience, fortitude, and so forth are included.

"Those very qualities" refers to the qualities of virtue, conduct, gentleness, humility, and so forth; "the collection of those" is the collection of the qualities of virtue, conduct, gentleness, humility, and so forth.
"Well-endowed with that collection" means well-manifested by that collection; this is the connection with the word "by that elder.
"One's own system and other systems" (sakasamaya-samayantara) refers to one's own school and other schools; however, because they are like a thicket, they are called a "thicket" (gahana).

The "dense thicket of one's own and other systems" (*sakasamayasamayantaragahana*) refers to that; "plunging into" (*ajjhogāhaṇa*) it is the plunging into the dense thicket of one's own and other systems.
One who is capable of that is "capable of plunging into the dense thicket of one's own and other systems. This is to be connected with the phrase "by that elder.
One who makes something known or clear through distinction is *viyatta*; [such] a person is *viyatta*, and this state of being *viyatta* is *veyyattiya*, which is mindfulness (*sati*).

“Wisdom and proficiency” (*paññā-veyyattiya*) means wisdom together with proficiency; the connection is “endowed with that. The construction is “by the Elder who was so endowed. “The three baskets” (*tipiṭaka*) refers to the Tripiṭaka;
because it is to be mastered, it is the “learning” (*pariyatti*), thus “the learning of the Tripiṭaka” (*tipiṭaka-pariyatti*). Its various divisions constitute the Teacher’s Dispensation here;
[the phrase] is “in that [Dispensation], which consists of the divisions of the learning of the Tripiṭaka. “Together with the commentaries” (*saha-aṭṭhakathāya*)—means:
The Teacher’s Dispensation together with its commentary (*sāṭṭhakathaṃ satthu sāsanaṃ*); the connection is "in that Teacher’s Dispensation" (*tasmiṃ satthusāsane*).

The Teacher’s Dispensation is threefold, by way of the Teacher’s mastery (*pariyatti*), practice (*paṭipatti*), and realization (*paṭivedha*); this analysis is indeed appropriate. In that Teacher’s Dispensation, it should be connected with the word "unobstructed" (*appaṭihata*).
Unobstructed knowledge is "unobstructed-knowledge" (*appaṭihatañāṇaṃ*); this [is used] at the time of commenting upon the Vinaya.

It should be understood that this was said with reference to the knowledge consisting of hearing (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) and reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*), because the Elder lacked the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).
"One whose power of unimpeded knowledge is such" means one who possesses the majesty of unimpeded knowledge; by this, the connection is made with the Elder.
"One for whom there is great exposition" means a Great Expositor (*mahāveyyākaraṇa*); by this, [he is distinguished] through the six factors, such as training (*sikkhā*) and grammar (*nirutti*).

This demonstrates the Elder’s unimpeded power of knowledge regarding great exposition (*mahantaveyyākaraṇa*); thus, the connection is "by that Elder, the great expositor" (*mahāveyyākaraṇena therenā*).
*Karaṇa* is said to mean "place," in the sense that it is performed (*kariyati*) or uttered therein; or else, by the meaning of the word, it refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*).
*Karaṇasampatti* means perfection of expression; that which is produced by it is *karaṇasampattijanita*. *Sukhaviniggataṃ* means issued forth from the mouth of the Elder with ease (*sukha*);
*karaṇasampattijanitasukhaviniggataṃ* means issued forth with ease, having as its cause that which was produced by the perfection of expression.
*Madhurodāravacanaṃ* means sweet speech and noble speech; this is a compound where the latter member of the first term has been elided. By this—

It demonstrates the state of being endowed with both the quality of sweetness (*madhuratā*) and the quality of loftiness (*udāratā*) among the ten qualities of speech mentioned in the *Keṭubhapakaraṇa* (in verses 127–142 of the *Subodhālaṅkāra*).
And that sweet and lofty speech, which has emerged from the pleasure produced by the perfection of the [vocal] instruments,
is called "speech that has emerged from the pleasure produced by the perfection of the instruments, being sweet and lofty."

Alternatively, it is speech that is both produced by the perfection of the vocal organs and sweet and noble, having issued forth from happiness; thus it is "speech produced by the perfection of the vocal organs, sweet and noble, having issued forth from happiness.
*Ela* is said to mean the fault of ill-spoken words; that which has no *ela* is *nela*. That very quality is *nela-vaṇṇa* (faultless color/quality).

That which is endowed with this is *nelavaṇṇayutta*. Thus, it is one whose speech—produced by the perfection of the vocal organs, sweet and noble, and having issued forth from happiness—is endowed with faultless quality.
The Elder was endowed with a sweet and noble voice that issued forth from the pleasure produced by the perfection of his vocal organs, which was possessed of *nelavaṇṇa*.
This is a compound where the qualifying word comes last; for the meaning is:

"one whose sweet and noble voice issues forth from the pleasure produced by the perfection of vocal organs possessed of *nelavaṇṇa*. The connection is with "by that Elder. And it was appropriate because it was suited to the ears of the assembly, and it was liberated because of the assembly's confidence.
One who speaks what is fitting and excellent by way of their character is a "speaker of the fitting and excellent" (*yuttamuttavādī*); the connection is with that Elder.

Those who possess various doctrines (*vāda*)—such as the doctrines of eternalism, nihilism, and non-causality—are "holders of various doctrines" (*nānāvādino*); these are "people of various doctrines.
One who is the best among such holders of doctrines, or because he is a proponent of the doctrine of karmic action, is a "supreme proponent" (*vādivaro*); the connection is with that Elder.
Because he is capable of explaining the meaning of the Pāḷi, he is a great poet, a *mahākavi*; this is how it connects with the word "by that elder.

One who is surrounded by the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) that have become fully developed through mastery of meaning, doctrine, language, and ingenuity is called "one whose analytical knowledges are fully developed" (*pabhinnapaṭisambhidāparivāra*);

this connects with the phrase "in that superhuman state" (*uttarimanussadhamme*). The six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) together with the analytical knowledges are the "six direct knowledges and analytical knowledges" (*chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidā*).

Those things which have "those" as their beginning are the sixfold direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), he includes the three types of higher knowledge (tevijjā) and others.

That which has the sixfold direct knowledges, the analytical knowledges, and so forth as its divisions is "that which is divided into the sixfold direct knowledges, the analytical knowledges, and so forth" (chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādippabheda).

That very quality is the "quality divided into the sixfold direct knowledges, the analytical knowledges, and so forth" (chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādippabhedaguṇa). Adorned by that is "adorned with the quality divided into the sixfold direct knowledges, the analytical knowledges, and so forth" (chaḷabhiññāpaṭisambhidādippabhedaguṇapaṭimaṇḍita).

The connection is with the phrase "in that state surpassing human phenomena" (*uttarimanussadhamme*). A "state surpassing human phenomena" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) refers to the qualities (*dhamma*) of those who have surpassed ordinary humans, such as those who have attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), and so forth;

or alternatively, it is a state surpassing the human phenomena consisting of the paths of wholesome action (*kusalakammapatha*), namely the qualities of the meditative absorptions and so on. This is to be connected with the word "well-established" (*suppatiṭṭhita*).
"Suppatiṭṭhitabuddhino" means those whose intellect (*buddhi*) is well-established; this is the connection with "those elders" (*therānaṃ*).
They shine forth in a distinctive manner within the lineage of the elders, like a lamp; thus they are "lamps of the elder-lineage" (*theravaṃsappadīpā*), and [the text refers] to them.
Those who possess the stable quality (*guṇa*) consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom are "elders" (*therā*); [the text refers] to them, in the sense of being the ornament of their lineage.
"Mahāvihāravāsino" means those whose habit is to dwell in the Mahāvihāra, whose nature it is to dwell there, or who perform well in dwelling;
"of them, of the elders" (*tesaṃ therānaṃ*) is the connection. "Vaṃsālaṅkāro" means an ornament for the lineage, or belonging to the lineage;
having become such, or having attained the state of being an ornament for the lineage, he is "vaṃsālaṅkārabhūto"; "by that elder" (*tena therena*) is the connection.
"Vipulavisuddhā" means both "vast" and "pure"; it is a compound of two qualifying adjectives (*visesanobhayapada*). One whose intellect (*buddhi*) is vast and pure is called "Vipulavisuddhabuddhi.
The connection [in the original text] is with that Elder. "Nāmadheyya" is simply another term for "name" (*nāma*);
one whose name has been taken is "Gahitanāmadheyyo," meaning one who has assumed a name. This work, titled *Samantapāsādikā*, was composed by that Elder.
The connection is: "let the commentary on the Vinaya remain.

The construction is as follows: "As long as even the mere name 'Buddha' circulates in the world for the Pure-minded One, the Neutral One, the World-leader, the Great Seer, so long may this [commentary] remain in the world, showing the method for the purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) to those sons of noble family who seek to cross over the world."
Thus ends the explanation of the meaning of the conclusion.
And up to this point— the discourse on the conclusion— [is finished].
In the royal capital of the city named Ratanapuṇṇa,
to the south-southeast of the Sage’s image,
there is a monastery with a palace that was built by the queen of the king.

The application of the *pācittiya* rules and so forth which was undertaken by me while residing there was successfully completed when the seventeenth year of King Māpitaratnapuṇṇa reached its eighteenth year of victory.
To the south of the royal capital city called Ratanapuṇṇā, at a distance of five yojanas, lies the city named Mithilā,
which is beautifully adorned by two great lakes. To the east of that city, at a distance of one and a half gāvutas,
there is a place beautifully graced by many rows of palm trees, a delightful site belonging to the four clans.
The great village established and designated as "Kaphrū" is where I was born by way of rebirth; there,
praised for my virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and given the name "Jāgaro" by my teachers, I composed this commentary on the *Pācittiya* and other rules—
stamped with the royal seal of three kings— at the arrival of the Victor’s Wheel of Dharma, [in the year] one thousand three hundred and thirteen.
In the Sakkarāj year two thousand three hundred and thirty-one, on the fifth day of the waxing moon in the month of Jeṭṭha during the summer season,
it was completed without effort. By the power of this composition, may this [work]— its arrangement being complete— [attain its goal].
May I, throughout many births, be a bearer of the Three Piṭakas,
skilled in both meanings, and confident among assemblies;
may the noble intentions of myself and all living beings be fulfilled.
"May the rain-god pour forth properly, not transgressing the bounds of Vappa and the other [seasons];
and may kings protect the earth as they would their own offspring.
Thus was it composed by the venerable elder Jāgara.
The application of the commentary on the *pācittiya* and following rules is completed.
